====================================================================================================

ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, and Gemini overrate facial attractiveness compared to human judges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
10:00:50 UTC
19:00:50 KST

Artificial intelligence models are remarkably good at reproducing the rank order of how humans rate facial attractiveness, but they tend to score faces much higher on an absolute scale than human judges do. This suggests that while artificial intelligence can grasp relative beauty, it systematically overrates attractiveness compared to average human standards. The findings were published as a preprint on arXiv.
Facial attractiveness is a psychological phenomenon that exists in the mind of the observer rather than as a strict physical property. Human judgments of beauty are shaped by shared preferences for traits like facial symmetry and youth, as well as individual tastes. Different demographic groups also display distinct patterns. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2026 found that both male and female human raters consistently score female faces as more attractive than male faces.
The research was led by Santiago Grandas, head of psychological research at QOVES, a personal beauty consultancy with a lab that researches perceptions of physical attractiveness. The study aimed to test whether modern artificial intelligence evaluates faces in the same way human observers do.
Multimodal large language models, or MLLMs, are artificial intelligence systems trained on vast amounts of internet data. They do not perceive a face purely as pixels. Instead, they interpret visual features through the captions and text that typically accompany similar images online.
“We noticed that more and more people were using MLLMs like ChatGPT and Claude to evaluate their looks,” Grandas told PsyPost. “So we got curious about whether these models actually reflect the average person’s opinion, especially since these tools can have an air of objectivity.”
Because these models learn from internet text and are fine-tuned to interact safely with users, their outputs are heavily influenced by a desire to be agreeable. A study covered by PsyPost in 2025 indicated that large language models consistently exhibit a social desirability bias, opting for answers that seem polite or positive. As people increasingly ask AI apps to evaluate their looks, the researchers wanted to explore whether these systems offer objective aesthetic assessments or simply reflect polite language patterns.
The researchers used the Face Research Lab London Set, a standardized collection of 102 front-facing human photographs. The dataset was almost evenly split between male and female faces and included several different ethnic backgrounds. The team obtained existing attractiveness ratings for these faces from 2,513 human participants. These individuals had rated each face on a scale from 1 to 7, with 1 being “much less attractive than average” and 7 being “much more attractive than average.”
The team then prompted four popular AI models to rate the same images on the identical scale. They tested GPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok. To mimic how a typical user interacts with these systems, the researchers used the models in their default settings with external web search and advanced reasoning disabled. To account for the random variation common in AI responses, the scientists ran the test multiple times and calculated a stable average rating for each face from each model.
The models proved highly capable of replicating the relative rank of the faces. If the human participants agreed that one face was more attractive than another, the AI models almost always agreed with that specific order. In fact, the models reproduced the average human ranking of faces more closely than a typical individual human rater did.
“It’s worth noting that although AI models do not rate faces like humans, their scores do track the rank order of faces we see in the human data,” Grandas explained. “So, ask an AI model to order 10 faces from least to most attractive, and I would expect the result will look quite similar to the arrangement of any given human. Ask it to evaluate a face in isolation, and that’s where human-AI agreement disappears.”
Despite this alignment in ranking, the AI models and humans showed poor absolute agreement. The average human rating across all faces was 3.02, while the combined average AI rating was noticeably higher at 4.71. The AI models also used a narrower portion of the 1 to 7 scale. They never gave out the lowest possible score to any face, suggesting an ingrained reluctance to rate human appearance as highly unattractive.
“I did not expect AI to compress their ratings so much,” Grandas said. “Not a single model gave any of the 102 faces the lowest rating, and only Grok ever gave the highest rating to a face. This was in stark contrast to humans, who used the full range of the scale to judge facial attractiveness.”
When comparing the models to one another, GPT, Claude, and Gemini showed strong agreement. They produced similar absolute scores and ranked the faces in nearly identical ways. Grok was a notable outlier in the group. It gave the highest average ratings of all the models, scoring faces at an average of 5.21. Grok also showed the weakest alignment with the other AI models and the poorest agreement with human judges.
Macken Murphy, chief scientist at QOVES and a co-author of the study, noted that evaluating this behavior is a new and challenging frontier. “Traditionally, in psychology, facial attractiveness has been measured by human perception. Machine psychology, as a field, is new and hard to think about clearly, but it seems these tools perceive beauty in faces more readily than people do–if ‘perceive’ is even the right word,” Murphy said. “Or, perhaps they may perceive attractiveness similarly, internally, but then report more favorable numbers as part of the broader phenomenon of MLLM sycophancy.”
The study also examined how facial characteristics influenced the scores. For both humans and AI models, older faces consistently received lower attractiveness ratings. However, other human biases did not translate as strongly to the AI models. Human raters scored male faces roughly 0.65 points lower than female faces, but the AI models only penalized male faces by 0.1 to 0.2 points. The AI models also provided more equal ratings across different ethnic backgrounds than the human sample did.
While the models do factor in traits like age and gender, the real-world consequences of their aesthetic judgments are still unfolding. “What the implications are in the broader context remains an open question, but some preliminary research already suggests AI also exhibits an attractiveness Halo effect, where it judges more beautiful faces positively across unrelated traits,” Grandas said. “I’m personally curious as to whether this has an effect on AI hiring tools or social media algorithms, for example.”
“Building on that: Companies could use these tools with good intentions to remove human bias from things like assessing candidates, but then cement pretty privilege even further,” Murphy added.
When looking at specific human subgroups, the researchers noted minor differences in alignment. The models’ ratings tracked slightly more closely with the preferences of female human raters than male raters. All the models except Grok also showed marginally stronger alignment with human raters who reported being attracted to either gender, compared to those strictly attracted to men.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2025, which found that ChatGPT’s judgments of facial social traits agreed heavily with human impressions. Both studies indicate that multimodal AI models can approximate human consensus on relative facial qualities, even if their absolute rating scales operate differently.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study was published as a preprint, meaning it has not yet been peer-reviewed. Peer review is a process where independent, outside experts evaluate a study’s methods and conclusions before it is officially published in a scientific journal. Because this step has not happened yet, the findings should be treated as preliminary.
Additionally, the human ratings were based on single responses from each participant, while the AI scores were averaged across multiple test runs. This difference in measurement makes the AI scores more stable by design. That stability might slightly inflate how consistent the models appear when compared to the noisier judgments of individual humans.
The human raters in the dataset were predominantly young, female, and attracted to men. A sample drawn from a different cultural or age demographic might produce a different consensus for the AI to be measured against. The researchers also noted that the exact phrasing of the survey used to collect the original human ratings is no longer available. As a result, the prompt given to the AI might have been slightly different from the instructions the human participants received years ago.
The face photographs themselves were heavily skewed toward White individuals. This means the data on how AI handles different ethnic backgrounds rests on a small number of images and should be interpreted cautiously. The researchers also did not have access to the ethnic backgrounds of the human raters, making it impossible to check if people preferred faces from their own demographic group.
Ultimately, Grandas cautioned against viewing these models as impartial arbiters of appearance. “These popular AI models overrate facial attractiveness compared to humans; they tend to say faces are above average regardless of how they actually look,” he said. “Users should be aware of this when treating AI tools as an objective judge of beauty.”
Going forward, the team hopes to map out exactly what drives human aesthetic consensus and disagreement. “We want to better understand what people perceive as attractive, across a wide and diverse range of both perceivers and faces,” Grandas said. “Our aim is also to get a more accurate picture of the shared and individual preference components in face perception, that is, understanding the things people generally agree and disagree on. We took the time to build a website page with a summary of our findings and data, including some interactive graphs, so we encourage readers to check it out if they’re curious to know more about our results.”
The study, “Beauty is in the AI of the beholder: MLLMs systematically overrate facial attractiveness,” was authored by Santiago Grandas, Juan Sebastian Cely-Acosta, Mohit Mendiratta, Shafee Hassan, and Macken Murphy.

Israeli election: Why the decision on Abu Shehadeh’s disqualification matters - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
10:00:24 UTC
19:00:24 KST

- i24NEWS
- Analysis & Opinion
- Israeli election: Why the decision on Abu Shehadeh’s disqualification matters - analysis
Israeli election: Why the decision on Abu Shehadeh’s disqualification matters - analysis
The Central Elections Committee's disqualification of Abu Shehadeh, if upheld by the Supreme Court, would make him the first Arab candidate barred from running since 1965
In what may be the ultimate irony, the 138,617 people who cast ballots for the ultra-nationalist Palestinian Balad party in the 2022 Israeli election may have enabled the formation of the most right-wing government in Israel's history.
Balad received 2.91% of the vote, which was just short of Israel's 3.25% electoral threshold. Those votes were discarded, increasing the pool of right-wing votes among the ballots that were counted.
Had those votes been cast instead for another Arab party, it is unlikely that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would have received the blocking majority he needed to form a government.
Now, it is possible that Balad will decide its second election in a row.
The Central Elections Committee voted as expected to disqualify Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh o. Wednesday. What was more of a surprise was that both Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara and Supreme Court deputy president Noam Solberg supported the disqualification.
They cited what Abu Shehadeh wrote on October 8, 2023, praising the perpetrators of the massacre. Endorsing terrorism is grounds for disqualification by Israeli law.
If the Supreme Court rules in favor of the disqualification, Abu Shehadeh would be the first candidate prevented from running since Michael Ben-Ari in 2019 and the first Arab since 1965.
The disqualification could either ignite Arab voters to cast ballots in the October 27 election, or it could make them feel disempowered and persuade them to stay home on Election Day.
Their decision could be critical because of the volatility of Arab electoral turnout.
The last Knesset elections, going backward, have seen Arab turnout of 53.2%, 44.6%, 64.8%, 59.2%, 49.2%, and 63.5%. The two peaks came in 2015, when the Joint List of Arab parties was founded, and in 2020, when the Joint List won 15 seats and became Israel’s third-largest party. The nadirs came after the Joint List split up.
That large difference between those highs and lows could be decisive enough to determine whether a candidate for prime minister obtains enough support to form a government or whether we will be going back to the polls at the beginning of 2027.
Either way, Balad voters will continue to play a key role in deciding Israel's future.

In its push to subordinate women, the American right is embracing raunch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
10:00:14 UTC
19:00:14 KST

Under Kash Patel, the FBI will now hire you even if you have a history of hiring prostitutes, or of having sex with animals. The rightwing Maha influencer Alex Clark had a guest on to her talk show to discuss the idea that wives should provide sex for their husbands on demand. A new ad for a sports gambling website is being hailed as a victory for the political right, because it features a nude Sydney Sweeney clutching footballs to her breasts. The Tate brothers, who encourage their male followers to pursue compulsive sexual conquest and who have been accused of sex trafficking and violence in the operation of their online cam porn business, have reportedly been friendly with members of Trump’s circle. A dizzying array of elites on both sides of the aisle – conservatives very much included – seem to have been socializing with a pedophile financier, and were so unfazed by his constant coterie of underaged girl companions that one begins to wonder whether they were habituated to such scenes. A prominent conservative writer, best known for her opposition to gender transition care for children, has announced a new book claiming to tackle the problem of young women who are supposedly unwilling to have enough sex. And the women of the president’s members club, Mar-A-Lago, are so well known for their dramatic facelifts, and their lips so stuffed with filler that they cannot quite close their mouths, that their faces are now a shorthand in the world of plastic surgery.
Raunch, vulgarity, a boorish entitlement to women’s sexual service, and the aesthetics – and, indeed, the business – of pornography are being embraced by the right.
For those old enough to remember the rise of Pat Buchanan and Phyllis Schlafly in the Reagan era, or even the earnest displays of Christian faith that characterized the George W Bush administration, this can all be a bit dizzying. For decades, it was the left that embraced public sexuality, taking the lead on comprehensive sex education, gay rights, and abortion access, and celebrating the sexual revolution that was ushered in by the advent of the birth control pill in the 1960s. It was liberals who embraced feminism, and worked to make women’s new freedom to delay marriage and childbearing enforcible in civil rights law. It was the left that retheorized family and marriage, reshaping the age-old institutions into ones that could better accommodate gay relationships and women’s equality. It was the progressives who embraced abortion as a means of sexual freedom and women’s self-determination, and who fought for birth control and sexually transmitted disease testing to be funded by the federal government. And it was the left that championed pornography as a free speech issue – shouting down the feminists in their own camp who critiqued the misogyny of its content, and making porn production and distribution into cornerstones of the liberal vision of the first amendment.
The right, meanwhile, was long married – pun intended – to a politics of sexual prohibition. When the Christian right was at the peak of its power, the Republican party had many of the same policies it does now: demanding bans on abortion, opposing gay rights, looking askance at birth control, pushing cuts to sexual health programs, rolling their eyes at civil rights protections meant to protect women workers from sexual harassment, and opposing comprehensive sex education, favoring instead abstinence-only models. But back then, when Evangelicism and the prim repression of the Protestant right were the dominant cultural force within the Republican party, these policies came packaged in a distinct style: one of sexual prohibition and shaming, that emphasized a kind of sexual self-discipline in the guise of decency. Back then, it really was a scandal when a pastor was caught cheating on his wife, even when his partner in infidelity was an adult woman. Sexual morality was a virtue that the right trumpeted in a very particular style: no sex until marriage, and even then, only the baby-making, heterosexual kind.
Was this all a ruse? The sexual morals of the Christian right seem to have evaporated as soon as the nation heard Donald Trump utter the words “grab ‘em by the pussy.” Now, an ostentatious lasciviousness reigns. In today’s Republican party, raunch is the coin of the realm, a “locker room talk” style of sexual vulgarity is de rigeur, and positions of power in the Trump world sometimes seem to go hand in hand with sexual assault allegations for men, and very specific kinds of surgical enhancements for women. The preachers have retreated, and the perverts have taken over. In the Maga era, sexual domination is synonymous with manliness, and porn is the lingua franca.
But is this really such a great change? After all, the transformation of the Republican party from a Christian culture that prioritized sexual prohibition to a pornified culture that celebrates sexual force has been a stylistic change, not a policy change: Republican politicians are still voting to make casual, premarital, non-procreative sex as dangerous, expensive, and risky as they can possibly make it – at least for women. If the left’s celebration of porn as a free speech issue always somewhat undermined their supposed commitment to women’s equality, the right’s onetime finger-wagging at pornography’s glorification of women’s sexual humiliation always clashed with the reality that the Christian right shared the same message and goal. Sexual prohibition and sexual force, after all, are just two different styles of what is ultimately a single project: the use of sex to subordinate women. At least now we can stop pretending that they’re not the same thing.
- 
  Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

America, China and the Evolving New World Order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

On Thursday, President Xi Jinping of China is meeting President Donald Trump at the White House. The United States and China are in significantly different places and the world increasingly fragmented and multi-polar since he last visited the White House to meet President Barack Obama in 2015. As the American and Chinese leaders meet, the most consequential question is: who is shaping the international order, and according to whose principles and rules?
The answer may be more nuanced than many expected: while the U.S. remains the world’s most powerful country, China is emerging as an architect of that order.
Beijing is creating institutions, proposing diplomatic initiatives, establishing technological standards and offering infrastructure to countries across the world. But its influence extends beyond diplomacy. China offers developing countries alternative paths to prosperity, mobilizing its technological champions as sources of power. Rather than replicating the American system of military alliance and security guarantees, Beijing is building networks of trade and alternative financial institutions. China is also promoting a new vocabulary of international affairs—one that is deliberately distinct from the American language of power.
China does not have a miraculous, surefire plan to succeed the U.S. as the world’s new hegemon. Nor is there evidence that other countries are prepared to embrace a Chinese-led system entirely. China’s ambition appears more complicated: it seeks greater influence over the ideas and institutions that determine how the international system works. Beijing wants not merely a decisive vote in the game, but a hand in writing its rules.
Beijing is pursuing this ambition at a moment when Washington, despite its power, appears less willing to shoulder the traditional burdens of global leadership. Its domestic political divisions, the Trump Administration’s apparent disregard for international law, and its erratic approach to foreign policy and global conflicts have raised questions about the future of American stewardship.
Yet China is not inheriting a vacuum. Thanks to its power, Washington remains deeply entrenched in the institutions, alliances, and technologies that underpin its supremacy. China is gaining room to shape the international order, but it is not yet replacing the power that built much of it. Instead, Beijing is creating alternatives that allow other countries to become less dependent on the existing American-led system.
China’s new new world vision
Perhaps the most powerful element of China’s vision for a different international order is not its defense of national sovereignty or multipolarity, but its proposition about development. Beijing is asking a pointed question: what if countries need not follow the Western path to modernity?
For much of the past eight decades, the prevailing vision of development was associated with a broadly Western model: foreign aid, privatization, and political liberalization. China offers something different, defying the hopes of Western intellectuals and policymakers who believed that Beijing’s entry into the World Trade Organization in 2001 would eventually lead to its political liberalization.
China’s own experience suggests that economic success can be built, at least partly, through investments in infrastructure, financed by public finance and state loans. The old Chinese expression about “getting richer by building roads” has also shaped its approach abroad: Beijing has committed itself to financing and promoting across the Global South the type of infrastructure that helped power its own economic miracle.
The developing world has been receptive. China’s Global Development Initiative places development at the center of its international engagement. Although the Belt and Road Initiative has been heavily criticized since its inception, it has provided Beijing with a practical platform for financing and building infrastructure overseas. Beijing is making its case not through elegantly written standards of governance but through tangible things: roads, railways, and ports.
Over the past decade, the Chinese government and its state-owned enterprises invested approximately $634 billion into building physical infrastructure around the world, along with $419 billion in direct investments outside the financial sector in the developing world. For many governments in Latin America—a region Washington has long regarded as its strategic backyard—access to Chinese development finance and Chinese markets has led to significant economic gains.
China’s development strategy creates economic relationships that should endure for decades, especially when its financing carries conditions that serve Beijing’s interests, including privileged access to critical minerals and resources. But the era of immense Chinese overseas spending is becoming harder to sustain as Beijing grapples with its own economic woes.
The ultimate test of Beijing’s economic statecraft, then, is whether it can build lasting relationships across the globe that rest on more than financial largesse and accumulated diplomatic capital. China must demonstrate that it understands what developing countries actually need and that those needs will evolve over time.
A new age of Chinese tech
Influence is no longer exerted through explicit military might but built quietly into the infrastructure of everyday economic life. As development becomes increasingly intertwined with technology, a country that adopts Chinese cloud computing may also embed itself in a Chinese-led ecosystem that endures for decades.
Artificial intelligence offers the clearest example of technology as a source of geopolitical power. China is rapidly promoting its AI capabilities globally, including open-weight models that can be deployed at a fraction of the cost of their Western competitors. For much of the developing world, the appeal is obvious: those countries can gain access to cutting-edge technology without having to rely exclusively on American tech giants.
The technological race is also becoming a competition over the development choices countries make. If most economies build their digital infrastructure and AI systems primarily around American technologies, Washington will retain an enormous structural advantage. As countries invest in those systems, they will become increasingly dependent on them, while American tech giants gain access to vast stores of user data. If more countries come to rely on Chinese technologies and the standards and supply chains associated with them, China will acquire greater influence: less visible than military power, but potentially just as consequential and enduring.
This is why China’s enormous industrial capacity has become a central instrument of its effort to shape the global order. Beijing is not merely exporting products: it is helping determine which technologies countries use to modernize themselves, and by extension, the systems their economies will rely on.
A central ambiguity lies at the heart of China’s development strategy. Chinese technology can expand a country’s economic opportunities but is bound to increase its dependence on China. That tension is likely to persist longer than many anticipated. Many governments are choosing Chinese technology for its affordability and not because they have been persuaded by Beijing’s governing philosophy. A country may adopt Chinese systems while remaining aligned with the U.S. on security.
China therefore does not depend on others becoming “pro-China”. It may be enough for them to become less dependent on the West. This is a vital distinction. Beijing need not convince the world that its model is superior. It only needs to show that alternatives to Western technologies exist. The cumulative effect of those alternatives could gradually alter the balance of the global order.
China’s statecraft is a way of redistributing economic and technological power. Unlike the U.S., China’s most significant export may not be a political model but the infrastructure and technology through which other countries seek to build prosperity. In adopting those systems, they become part of a world less dominated by the U.S. and its European allies.
Networks, not alliances
Before arriving in Washington, President Xi undertook a flurry of overseas travel, visiting places that American presidents have largely neglected: Bishkek, Cairo, New Delhi. His itinerary illuminated an interesting pattern. Each of his September stops connected China to the expanding international networks Beijing has championed and some Western governments regard with suspicion, notably the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) and BRICS.
Consider BRICS. What began as an informal gathering of emerging economies has become a much larger political forum, with countries from the Middle East, Africa, and elsewhere seeking membership or closer connections. It would be a mistake to consider BRICS as a Beijing-led anti-American bloc. Its members have sharply different interests, and countries such as India have no intention of joining an anti-Western alliance. But the group’s expansion reflects a critical shift: a growing number of countries want access to institutions in which the Group of 7 does not set the terms.
The Group of 7 is an exclusive club whose members broadly share political values and standards of governance. China does not demand that other countries abandon institutions led by Washington; instead, it builds alternatives that exist alongside them. That distinction matters.
This is why I expect that the emerging world order will not be divided neatly between a Chinese camp and an American one. Most countries will continue to use the dollar, trade with the U.S., and participate in Western institutions while simultaneously joining BRICS, borrowing from Chinese-backed institutions, and engaging with the SCO. For many governments, the fundamental attraction is the freedom to choose among competing sources of finance, technology, and diplomatic support.
Beijing’s advocacy of multipolarity is neither merely about building a fairer world, nor is it about replacing one hegemon with another. It is an attempt to widen the range of choices available to other states. By establishing new institutions and initiatives, Beijing is accelerating the movement of power away from the traditional centers of the West. For China, being an architect of the international order does not necessarily mean replacing America, but building a world where the U.S. can no longer design all the rules or define legitimate international behavior by itself.
Yet the China dilemma remains. Beijing opposes an international order dominated by a single power, but fragmenting that system would inevitably increase China’s global influence. And the more influence China acquires, the more other countries may begin to question whether Beijing’s vision is truly intended to produce greater equality, or merely a new distribution of power that benefits China most.
An order shaper in the making
President Xi’s meeting with President Trump will be scrutinized for the usual signs of rivalry: tariffs, technology restrictions, and strategic tensions. But beneath those headlines lies the great contest over how the international order itself should work.
China is not seeking to inherit the world America built. It is trying to change how that world works by giving other countries choices beyond the American-led system. For decades, the U.S. was identified with policing the rules-based international order, while China was portrayed primarily as its challenger. But during President Trump's second term, questions of sovereignty and international law have themselves become more contested, blurring what once seemed a clear distinction between the American and Chinese approaches.
Whether China’s ascent produces a fairer international order, a more genuinely multipolar one, or simply a new system in which Chinese power carries greater weight remains uncertain. The answer will depend not only on what Beijing wants, but also on what other countries are willing to accept. For now, China’s ambition may not be to write all the rules, but to ensure that Washington is no longer the only power capable of writing them.

Philanthropy Must Build the Architecture of Hope
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

I grew up in a middle class family in Mumbai, where my parents taught us the importance of giving back. Our success, they insisted, was meaningful only if it helped others rise. As a girl, I spent most Sundays accompanying my father as he distributed food to those in need. As a young teacher at an elementary school, I learned that the greatest gift a teacher offers is not knowledge itself but the confidence and capabilities it awakens in a child. And, as a mother, I experienced most profoundly that there is no greater joy than nurturing another life.
Mahatma Gandhi taught us that service to others is among life’s highest forms of fulfilment. His ideas have shaped me and my ideas of philanthropy profoundly: sarvodaya, his vision of the welfare of all, and, antyodaya, his insistence on the uplift of society’s most marginalized.
But the highest purpose of philanthropy is to make itself obsolete. To do that, we must turn acts of care and generosity into lasting change by building institutions. Societies shape the future through the institutions they build: universities, hospitals, museums, scientific laboratories, and schools. Every generation has a responsibility to pass on stronger institutions to the next.
Our world is awash in plenty. Yet roughly between two to three billion people, especially in the Global South, remain deprived of nutritious food, adequate housing, clean water and sanitation, quality education and healthcare, secure livelihoods, and protection from environmental hazards. The primary responsibility for meeting these needs rests with governments, multilateral institutions, and businesses. But social transformation also requires philanthropic institutions capable of combining excellence with compassion, innovation with integrity, and purpose with performance.
Across India, I have encountered incredibly talented and dedicated doctors and nurses; teachers and artists; farmers, athletes, and volunteers. Extraordinary things happen when these talented and dedicated people find opportunity and support.
This belief guides my work as chair of India’s Reliance Foundation, on every institution we have built—from excellent schools to a global university still taking shape; from high quality, affordable and accessible healthcare to a cultural center that showcases arts and artists from the world’s great cities and India’s remotest towns and villages; from an initiative that offers dignity and opportunity to millions of India’s skilled craftspeople to an organization dedicated to protecting and caring for animals.
The most remarkable people I have met rarely ask for aid. What they seek is a chance: a chance to learn, to create, and to contribute. When society provides such opportunities reliably and at scale, lives are transformed. Institutions make this possible. They do more than solving the problems of our today; they prepare humanity for the possibilities of our tomorrow.
But building institutions demands patience. Institutions are gifts to those who inherit them; in time, they might create things their founders never imagined. I often think about the world our children, and their children, will inherit. I hope it will be healthier, kinder, more harmonious, more creative, and more com- passionate. I hope it will be a world where every child has the freedom to dream without limits and the means to pursue those dreams with confidence.
The Sanskrit phrase Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam teaches us that the world is one family. I believe that institution-building is one of the purest expressions of this philosophy: it enlarges the circle of care to embrace humanity as a whole. And since all nations, communities, and cultures are branches of a single tree, we share a responsibility to tend it together.
Philanthropic institutions should forge bonds of mutual learning, exchange, and collaboration; partnerships help multiply the impact of philanthropy. Ultimately, philanthropy is not measured by the wealth we give away but by the futures we make possible, by the dreams that become reality because someone built something lasting. Time may dim the memory of who builds institutions, but the institutions themselves must shine on.

Press review: US, NATO hamper nuclear dialogue as US gains partial control of Greenland
Unknown

2026-09-24

MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. The United States and the North Atlantic Alliance hinder efforts toward restoring the nuclear dialogue, while the US-Iran dialogue appears stalled, despite a recent meeting between the two countries. Meanwhile, US leader Donald Trump secures partial control over Greenland. These stories topped Thursday's newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: US, NATO hamper efforts to restore nuclear dialogue
Seven months into the expiration of the New START Treaty in February, the global security system is facing new threats. Russian Permanent Representative to the United Nations Office and other international organizations in Geneva Gennady Gatilov told Izvestia that France and Britain have begun an opaque buildup of their strategic arsenals, disregarding their own principles of transparency in the nuclear sphere. The destabilizing practice of holding joint NATO-led nuclear missions is being expanded further, and "some new schemes of deterrence" that heighten nuclear non-proliferation risks are being introduced, he said.
Earlier, US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said that the United States possesses orbital weapons for space control. The Western media said his remark could imply electronic warfare systems rather than kinetic weapons. Outer space is a sphere covered by the Golden Dome, a proposed US multilayered anti-missile defense initiative, Dmitry Stefanovich, research fellow at the Center for International Security at the Primakov Institute of World Economy and International Relations of the Russian Academy of Sciences (IMEMO), emphasized.
He views the likelihood of talks about a new agreement in the nuclear sphere as low, even as the number of challenging issues that require compromises has increased, the expert stressed.
Pavel Anisimov, deputy director of the International Relations and Political Science Institute at Russian State University for the Humanities, said the parties could soon attempt to agree on at least temporary limitations or channels to prevent a crisis. Now that the US has obtained orbital weapons, nuclear arms control can no longer be discussed separately from anti-missile issues, space and high-precision non-nuclear weapons, he argued.
Meanwhile, contacts at various levels between Russia and the United States are ongoing, and the two leaders regularly exchange phone calls. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio held a meeting in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly High-level Week in New York. However, no dialogue on strategic stability is currently underway, and whether it will be resumed depends on whether Washington acknowledges the need to improve relations with Russia, Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov said.
Izvestia: US-Iran dialogue stalled, despite contacts at UNGA
The meeting between Iranian and US officials at the UN General Assembly is unlikely to end the confrontation between the two countries, experts interviewed by Izvestia said as they warned about escalation risks instead, even as US President Donald Trump described the three-hour talks as "very good." The US leader himself was absent from the meeting as he refused to tone down harsh rhetoric toward Tehran, saying that a deal could be made and threatening to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic. However, Tehran is standing its ground: the Iranian side said it could reopen the Strait of Hormuz as soon as the US lifts its naval blockade, unblocks frozen assets, pays compensation, and ends the war "on all fronts."
The US-Iran meeting on the sidelines of the UNGA was the first after the June ceasefire completely collapsed. The US team of negotiators included special presidential envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, while Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi represented Iran. At that, the two countries’ diplomats did not communicate directly, and Qatari officials acted as mediators as they moved between the two delegations during the day.
Experts interviewed by Izvestia do not expect any breakthrough from the New York meetings. The contacts themselves were positive, as they could help ease tensions for a while, Yelena Suponina, an expert in Oriental studies, said. However, she continued, one should not expect any lasting settlement amid the deep mutual mistrust and fundamental differences between the two countries.
Each side pursues its own pragmatic goals in this round of talks, with Tehran, for one, seeking to demonstrate readiness for dialogue, Igor Pshenichnikov, a political analyst, said. The talks could also help Trump to demonstrate to the US electorate at least minimal progress on the foreign policy track before the congressional midterms.
There is no chance of an actual settlement right now, another political analyst, Alexander Kargin, said. According to him, the points of the Islamabad memorandum, signed last summer, were basically never implemented, except for the brief reopening of the Hormuz Strait for purely pragmatic purposes: Tehran needed to resume oil exports and Washington sought to bring fuel prices down. Transit is blocked again, and the two sides are waiting to see who will be first to make concessions.
According to Pshenichnikov, Trump cannot get out of the conflict, as this would mean capitulation for the White House. However, he cannot continue the protracted campaign either. Since Tehran's conditions remain unacceptable to the United States, the confrontation may flare up with renewed vigor and escalate to a large-scale regional crisis after the November election, the analyst warned.
Kommersant: US gets partial control of Greenland
At a ceremony on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly session in New York on September 22, the United States, Denmark and Greenland signed an agreement on defense cooperation that will allow the Americans to expand their military presence on this strategically important Danish island and make it almost inaccessible to non-Western countries. Even as Greenland remains an autonomous Danish territory, the document gives such broad powers to the US that a case could easily be made for its partial control of the island.
Among other things, the US will get the right to modernize and expand the Pituffik space base, formerly known as Thule, and build two new facilities in Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig. Besides, the agreement provides a legal opportunity to accelerate the deployment of additional military bases there.
Alexander Yermakov, researcher with the Center for International Security at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of World Economy and International Relations, explained in a column for Kommersant that the US decided to resume expanding its military activities on the island after their gradual reduction there peaked in the 1950s-early 1960s.
Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig will likely host patrol aircraft and drones for monitoring the northern Atlantic Ocean and the Arctic, even as other activities, including the deployment of offensive arms or anti-missile systems, cannot be ruled out either, the expert argued. It’s hard to predict for now but it is a matter of modernizing space surveillance systems as the US base there has primarily served this purpose over the past few decades.
As regards the Pittufik space base, a line in the new agreement reads that the sides agree to deploy elements of the new generation Golden Dome missile defense system currently being built on Trump’s orders there. "This could perhaps imply anti-missile deployments as a radar modernization would hardly require a separate article in the agreement," Yermakov argued.
"It would be useful for the US to set up a permanent base for patrol flights and long-range UAVS there to monitor the Northern Sea Route and the broader Arctic and deploy infrastructure for more frequent and longer deployment of fighter jets in order to provide air defense purposes on the island and approaches to the United States," the expert concluded.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: Trump seeks to pave way for new meeting with North Korea’s Kim
US President Donald Trump held a meeting with his South Korean counterpart, Lee Jae-myung, on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York. As the US leader wished, he and Lee mostly discussed $350 billion in proposed South Korean investment in the US economy in exchange for lower tariffs on South Korean exports. Among other issues, the two leaders discussed the potential resumption of Trump’s contacts with North Korea’s Kim Jong Un.
Besides, the Trump-Lee meeting discussed fuel supplies to nuclear-powered submarines and South Korea’s push to secure US agreement to transfer wartime operational control to Seoul. Even as no combat has been conducted on the Korean Peninsula since 1953, the US maintains an 18,000-strong military contingent in South Korea that would form the backbone of an allied group of forces should war break out again. This does not sit well with the government led by the Democratic party which came to power in 2025 as it seeks to appeal to nationalist sentiments in society.
Alexander Vorontsov, head of the Korea and Mongolia Department at the Oriental Studies Institute under the Russian Academy of Sciences, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta in an interview that this was a long-standing issue. "Under the US-South Korea agreement signed in the 1950s, the US should hold the core war-fighting command of a combined US-South Korean force. Under a South Korean government led by Democrats, as is the case now, they say that this infringes upon the country’s sovereignty. <…> Therefore, they seek the transfer of operational command over their forces to South Korea. The Americans were previously skeptical of this idea. On the contrary, Trump takes a different view as he believes that allies should pay the US more for their defense and, whenever possible, defend themselves independently. Given this stance, he is more constructive toward South Korea’s ambitions."
Lee also hinted that Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping scheduled for September 24 could contribute to improving South Korea’s relations with China.
Also, Lee told Trump that he expected the US leader to help him restore ties with North Korea. Trump agreed to help as he also said he had established a good relationship with North Korea’s Kim. There has been no confirmation that Trump-Kim relations have been established indeed. There was only a statement from the US president that he would agree to meet with the North Korean leader and that he looked forward to such a meeting. If work toward this goal is underway indeed, a partial transfer of control over the joint US-South Korean battlegroup to Seoul could be part of the effort to create positive conditions for a meeting with Kim.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Moscow might need new mega-tall skyscraper
There are 2,594 buildings over 200 meters tall globally, including 256 supertalls of 300 meters or more, Oleg Bogdan, the creative director of Genpro architects, said at a discussion hosted by the Moscow State University of Civil Engineering. As many as 222 cities across 52 countries have at least one skyscraper of more than 200 meters. Burj Khalifa in Dubai is the world’s tallest at 828 meters, but it will soon lose that status as Saudi Arabia should build Jeddah Tower at 1,008 meters in 2028.
Russia appears to be an outsider against this background. The 462-m tall Lakhta Center in St. Petersburg is Europe’s tallest, and the Federation East tower in Moscow City, which is 373.7 meters tall, is second-tallest. Moscow is among the top ten global cities for buildings over 300 meters.
Moscow is currently building more skyscrapers than all European capitals combined, Vasily Solomin, the creator of the Neboskryoby (Skyscrapers) channel on Telegram, said. Almost as many towers as there already are is currently being built in Moscow City, meaning the number of skyscrapers in the business center will double in the next two to three years. And even more skyscrapers are being erected outside that area in the Russian capital.
The growing number of skyscrapers in and around Moscow City even distorts the silhouette of the business quarter and may deprive it of its postcard appearance, Filipp Nikandrov, chief architect at Gorproekt, argued. To prevent this, the capital needs a new mega-tall building, or a taller flagship building rising to 800-900 meters.
Projects are no longer being developed solely for PR, the expert said, as economic viability is increasingly being considered. In 2025, 114 skyscraper projects, or a record high, were put on hold worldwide. Only projects with genuine demand for commercial space survive, Bogdan explained.

Why No One Wants to Date Tech Bros
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Engaged in a flirtatious conversation at a bar in Manhattan, 23-year-old Gary stood with a Guinness in hand as he explained to a woman why he took an engineering job at Palantir, the data analytics company cofounded by Alex Karp and Peter Thiel. Raking in a $250,000 salary would allow him to help pay off his parents’ mounting medical bills, he explained.
Gary wasn’t met with sympathy. Medical debt, the woman told him, was “not an excuse to work somewhere like that.” She was referring, of course, to Palantir’s controversial work with governments, including the US and Israel, which use the company’s surveillance tools for law enforcement and military operations.
Since joining the tech company in 2025, Gary has noticed that naming his employer prompts brutal reactions from prospective paramours. One woman, he says, called him the devil; another asked how he lives with himself. “Sometimes people would just straight up stop talking to me,” he says.
Recently, Gary’s buddies requested he not mention Palantir on their nights out together so as to not tank the whole group’s chances of getting laid. “I get nervous now. I don’t bring it up,” he says. (Gary, along with the other daters in this piece, have been given pseudonyms to protect against professional, if not romantic, repercussions.)
Gary has resorted to saying he works in AI. “Even that gets some pretty bad responses sometimes,” he says. His Hinge profile doesn’t mention his employer. And sometimes he makes up stories out of thin air to justify working for Palantir—like that line about the medical debt. His parents don’t have any, nor are they ill.
The bachelors of Palantir aren’t the only tech bros dealing with the industry’s fall from grace. Take 29-year-old James, who lives in San Francisco and works at Tesla. Earlier this year, on his third date with a woman he met on Raya, she asked whether he’d voted for Donald Trump in the 2024 election. A self-described “moderate liberal or moderate progressive” who “always votes blue and always will, probably,” James was offended. “I was like, ‘Are you kidding me? Did I really give that off?’” She replied, “You work for Tesla, so I just need to check.”
James says skepticism of his politics has “come up repeatedly” in his dating life. “If I don’t immediately say that I don’t like Elon Musk, people think that I’m conservative, which is generally not something that people like in San Francisco,” he says.
Once seen as a groundbreaking leader in sustainability and a quirky futurist, Musk—recently crowned the world’s first trillionaire—is better known these days for his record-breaking donation to Trump’s 2024 campaign, being the brain behind DOGE, the dismantling of Twitter, an apparent Nazi salute, frequent ketamine use, racist tweets, and something of a breeding kink.
Long gone is the cliché of the optimistic tech guy in flip-flops and a ratty old hoodie. The tech industry is now seen as the locus of unchecked power. Meta created an environment where Russian bots could influence elections and designed features that foster social media addiction among teens. Amazon, which has been widely accused of unfair labor practices and of generating a staggering amount of waste, has aided in the collapse of small, independent businesses, while a glowed-up Jeff Bezos has become a poster child for extreme wealth inequality. More recently, the AI industry is being widely maligned over claims that it’s exacerbating job loss, pollution, and a critical-thinking crisis.
Amy Laurent, the founder of a high-end matchmaking company, has a front-row seat to the way Big Tech’s moral failings are causing problems for single, rank-and-file tech bros. Turns out their cushy paychecks often aren’t enough of an upside anymore.
“I think 10 years ago, saying you worked in tech was more about innovation, ambition, intelligence,” says Laurent. Now, many people charge Big Tech with “causing the breakdown of society,” whether they’re worried about “AI, job displacement, wealth inequality, privacy and surveillance, content moderation, or political influence.”
Laurent says that when she pitches her tech-employed male clients to women, she acknowledges their hesitation right off the bat: “Listen, I have a great guy to tell you about. He’s such a good match for you. Now hear me out: He’s in tech.” The justifications are a new feature of her work.
Jessica Engle, a family and marriage therapist, has noticed that men in tech worry about being perceived as red pilled. Recently, one of her clients expressed concern about having his Apple Watch visible in his dating profile photos. He wondered whether the gadget “would make him look like a tech bro” and whether it might signal a “very particular kind of toxic masculinity that we’re seeing more and more in the news.”
Engle’s client wasn’t wrong to worry. Mira, a 29-year-old Bay Area resident, says she perceives a career in tech as a possible “right-wing flag” or a sign that someone might be “manosphere-coded” or libertarian.
When 28-year-old Helen was an undergraduate at Stanford from 2016 to 2020, she viewed men in tech as guys who “stay up late and maybe have bad hygiene.” But her feelings toward them have gotten even worse over time as she’s questioned the industry’s overall impact.
Helen’s family is from the Tigray region of Ethiopia, whose population, beginning in 2020, was subjected to a prolonged period of human rights abuses. “When I started thinking about questions around genocide and the technology that kills or tracks or excludes,” Helen says, “I realized that the things these people are building are secretly, or under the surface, really nefarious, and I could not personally be with someone who is a puzzle piece in that tapestry.”
Helen herself has worked in tech. Soon after graduating from college, she accepted a job at Grammarly. But after about a year, she went to work for a mutual-aid platform and now is employed at an impact investing firm funding technology for underserved communities. Similarly, Sasha, a 31-year-old Oakland resident, had a brief stint working in AI before heading to a sustainability-focused tech company, where she is now chief of staff. In dating, when she meets someone who works or wants to work in AI, she wonders, “Does that mean that we have the same values in terms of climate and sustainability and thinking about human rights?”
Even if they do, she adds, “then the issue I have is there’s clearly this cognitive dissonance happening between what you’re working on and what you care about, which I have a really hard time accepting.”
James, the Tesla employee, confesses that he embodies plenty of tech bro stereotypes that might work against him, including “paying too much in rent” (or “just generally gentrifying”), ordering most of his meals on DoorDash (“I suck at cooking”), and not “really contributing to the culture of the city that much.”
“I really fit the mold so much that it’s sort of like, I have to at least be self-aware of it,” James says.
The pushback James gets IRL makes him wonder how much more happens behind screens. “There’s less visible rejection because you kind of get prefiltered out,” he says. “If I were to write on the dating app that I work at Tesla, I think it would just cut a lot of people right away.” His experience seems to bear this out. On his Hinge profile, he disclosed his place of work; on Raya he decided against it. He says he’s had more success on Raya.
In fact, about four months after joining Raya, he met someone. His new girlfriend had recently moved to the Bay Area for medical school and, before dating James, had managed to stay insulated from tech culture. “I was talking to my now girlfriend, and she was like, ‘Yeah, I feel like I’ve gotten lucky. I didn’t really know what the tech bro stereotype is.’”
“I was like, ‘Thank God. I don’t think I would have made it if you did.’”
