Where a land ethic blooms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
29 minute listen
Forty iron rectangles, each one blunt as a piano key, rotate into a blurring fury that hides the eight-foot-long shaft at the heart of the flail chopper. I am perched atop several tons of iron, with 80 horsepower at my command. This part of farming is straightforward – even a mechanically challenged tree-hugger like me can manage to depress the clutch, shift into second, and ease the throttle forward. The tractor’s tall, deeply treaded tires churn, revolving into a smooth spin. Everything is spinning: fans, belts, alternator, the driveshaft, axles. I don’t understand the mechanism fully, yet the tractor and chopper and I are propelled forward across the knee-high whiskers of a coarsely bearded cornfield.
It is Indian summer in southern Wisconsin. My wife and I and our young son live here on her family’s farm. Both of us are employed off the farm, but on weekends and many evenings I am an apprentice to my father-in-law, David. Today, we are taking advantage of a brief period of warm, dry weather. Winter is approaching, and I could be spending the day beside our woodsplitter – the gasoline-sipping, hydraulically heroic mechanism that makes it possible to put up several cords of firewood quickly each year – but that work can wait until the cool, sunny days of fall are shoved aside by the relentless spin of the earth into darkness, sleet, snow and frozen ground.
The wall of tall green corn that stood here this summer has been transformed by fall and harvest. Little is standing after the field was stripped by a seed-combing combine. The mechanical tornado flails so loudly behind me: wailing against the air, grinding off the root-buttressed corn-stalk stumps, sucking up spent leaves and stripped cobs. In my wake, dry corn litter passes through the chopper like water compelled into frothy turbulence, falling again into an even, silent surface that hides so much activity below.
No time to waste – the weather is expected to hold for another day, and I need to cover the field before the light fails this afternoon. Tomorrow, David will rake this chewed-up detritus into windrows and then come back for another round to bale them up. While it is good to leave some of this thatch on the field – to keep a roof over the soil and guard against erosion by wind and rain – we can afford to borrow some of this, which also makes good straw. Wherever livestock are gathered in close quarters, their waste can produce concentrations of ammonia and other gases that can be harmful to animals and people alike. Adding straw slows the breakdown of manure and urine, reducing the production of noxious gases and suspending valuable nutrients in a semi-solid mixture. The straw and excrement will come back to this field loaded with nitrogen, phosphorous and other nutrients.
The ‘barn-pack’ is also heavy with organic matter that keeps a significant portion of the nutrients locked up for longer periods of time until it is broken down by the creatures who are at work beneath the calm surface of the field: literally tons of worms and beetles and other invertebrates; many miles of fungal hyphae; and countless diversity of bacteria. The denizens of this foodshed work to decompose the thick cell walls of the straw, as well as the partially digested grass stems and leaves that passed through the cattle and into their manure while the livestock fed on hay.
The creatures of the soil also feed on the bodies of the gut microbes that helped ruminants digest their hay. The gut-borne microbes are the true herbivores in this system: the power of the sun is harnessed by plants and turned into grain or hay, which is gathered by the farmers and transported to the barn, then delivered to the habitat of the gut by a large mammal whose brain, mouth and muscles spend their days gathering food for its microbial tenants. However, the microbes are short-lived and quickly finish their shift at the top of the system. As they die, they pass through the threshold of hind gut and, finally, the anus. Shit.
Is it fair to call any of this waste? The spark of life in the stinking barn pack is not yet exhausted, not yet lost to entropy. Roots burrow deep in search of more phosphorous, nitrogen and water to carry on the busy work of building ion transporters, enzymes, lignin and proteins – from root to stem to leaf to seed. Through spring, summer and fall, the straw, plant fibres and dead microbes that re-enter the field will take shifts in resurrection. Such is the life of the soil.
The end of the row breaks my reverie. I turn the tractor in a half-circle and feather the lever again until the tornado touches down just as I straighten out and catch the next row. Ready for another trip across the field, aimed down the rows, now due west. My route takes me just a few degrees north of where the late afternoon sun hangs in the soft yellow light of mid-latitude autumn.
I crest and ease on over oak-dappled ridges – glacial moraines – that attest to the furthest advance of the recent Ice Age glaciers and the fire-centric economy of the people who covered this land with effigy mounds and who later began to grow corn and other crops in fields they weeded using the shoulder blades of bison. Further west, a narrow, rusty-girdered bridge threads over the Mississippi River, carrying water that fell as rain and snow on north country forests, coulee pastures in the tri-state Driftless Area, and the broad, flat corn-and-soybean lands of central and western Minnesota. Each fall, the skies above fill with white pelicans, bald eagles and a paradise of waterfowl. Against this pattern of gathering and flow, I’d continue west, west: chopping through the dried stalks of compass plant and tall tassels of big bluestem at Hayden Prairie State Preserve in Iowa and fording the Big Sioux beneath the watch of yucca and side oats grama.
End of the row – decision time again.
Last September, I accompanied David to check out a field that lies due west of the stubble-chopping field, on the north bank of Prentice Creek. We were there to measure and mark a grass buffer that will separate row crops from the creek – a practice encoded in the conservation easement that is now a part of the deed to the property. Given the flash floods that have repeatedly swept across this low ground over the past few years, leaving this land in grass makes good economic and ecological sense. During the last major flood in 2008, David baled dusty hay from this field, while a substantial portion of his corn crop would have been completely lost. As we moved upstream to place more flags, I repeatedly plunged through the field-edge tangle of burdock, mulberry, eastern blackberry, woodland sunflowers and pointed-leaf tick-trefoil to find the eroded edge of the creek bank. It is not a pilgrim’s creek, but a real one, cut deep into topsoil that has eroded off the long-planted fields and into its dynamic basin. David planned to follow this line of flags a few days later, while spraying the rest of the old hayfield with glyphosate to kill the grass and alfalfa, and prepare for next spring’s planting of herbicide-resistant corn.
We spent an hour flagging the buffer, and the heat of the day was lapsing as we reached the property line. To get back to the truck, we followed a strip of weedy foxtail grasses that waved yellow seed heads in a rolling sea of hay. We were moving due west, as the foxtail marked precisely where the soil had been disturbed when David’s brother bulldozed the old fenceline a few years earlier. Halfway back to the truck, I was surprised when David stopped at a short, west-facing slope, where the field dropped about 10 feet over the course of 30-40 feet.
‘Let’s flag this, too,’ he said. Though I couldn’t see much of the soil beneath the late summer growth of alfalfa and grass, David said he knew the soil on this slope was light – a band of sand and gravel. Probably where an outwash stream trickled from the collapsing glacier. David pried up a few stones with his jackknife, and I turned over a few rounded and smooth stones in my hands. He quickly pointed out a pattern in the vegetation: ‘You can sort of see the change in soil in how the brome and alfalfa grows differently here. It’s thinner. This won’t be any good for corn, and it will erode away if the crop doesn’t take hold, so I’m going to leave it in hay. I’ll leave a broad-enough strip so I can come in from the buffer to bale it. The neighbours might laugh at me, but it’s the right thing to do.’
A land ethic cannot spring from the mind but must live, renew and evolve among families and communities
In that moment, I was an elated farm ecologist – I sensed that we shared a respect for the soil and a sense of responsibility to hold this ground. His decision could limit if not reverse soil erosion and perhaps build thicker topsoil, higher fertility and greater yields in the long run. In the short run, too, holding this ground with hay will be more profitable than buying seed, fertiliser and herbicide to plant hybrid corn. David uses all of those tools on his farm, yet they don’t drive all his farming decisions. He farms with a forethought that gives a fuller accounting of costs that come both out-of-pocket and at the expense of the health of the land.
Out in the field, he expressed his knowledge of the system and loyalty to the land through the language of conversation rather than the rhetoric of seminar or sermon. His knowledge was hard-won. He was now able to translate what he had observed in many a plough furrow to a subtle but discernible pattern in the field, which would otherwise appear as a uniform sea of green to the inattentive mind. He could make predictions, weigh costs and benefits, and chart a sustainable strategy without hardly pausing in his walk across the field. That kind of knowledge is not simply to be stored up, harboured and lost; it can be relayed along in the evolution of a locally adapted culture as he conveys, in situ, the knowledge to following generations.
With another year to add to my perspective, I have finally acknowledged what I could barely sense on that afternoon. My father-in-law was not talking to me as farmer to ecologist but as elder to apprentice. We agreed as professionals, but what was far more important than the congruence of our disciplined perspectives was the relationship we were building. When we choose to stay in place, we begin to feel the rub of constraints, responsibilities and uncertainties now placed on us by the past and future, while simultaneously the process provides opportunities for stronger human connections. There is within this a deep joy, satisfaction and hopefulness that is not readily available – perhaps not comprehensible – when we are in the process of pulling up stakes and heading out on the open road. The time I’ve spent learning to work on this farm has reinforced the idea that a land ethic cannot spring from the mind but must live, renew and evolve in the work and conversation that unfolds among families and communities.
Our antecedents derived the word ‘conversation’ from the Latin conversari. The root is also related to convertere, ‘to turn around’. On this level, conversation reflects the simple act of taking turns listening and speaking. Yet conversari itself meant ‘to live with or associate with’. Conversation, in this older sense, was more than just an exchange of words – it was an expression of shared life, of dwelling alongside one another in relationships of mutual dependence.
This ancient truth remains valid, even as the scale of our mutual turnings stretches far beyond family and village and watershed to encompass national and global communities through economic and cultural exchanges and the shared cycles of carbon and nitrogen, dust and pollution. No matter the distance that separates us, the lives of urban and rural people still turn around one another. An ethic grounded in this truth must be expressed in mutual interest in and concern for one another.
The goal of public policy for agriculture continues to be guided by the desire for cheap food
In the summer of 1947, the conservationist Aldo Leopold worked to integrate his thoughts on land use, weaving lands, wildness and ethics into a single essay, ‘The Land Ethic’, which became the capstone to his collection A Sand County Almanac (1949):
A land ethic, then, reflects the existence of an ecological conscience, and this in turn reflects a conviction of individual responsibility for the health of the land. Health is the capacity of the land for self-renewal. Conservation is our effort to understand and preserve this capacity.
The land ethic remains relevant in part because Leopold recognised his effort as a synthesis, as an articulation of the best of current understanding of people, land and the connections between them, rather than as the final word.
We still have far to go in the attempt to encode a land ethic sufficiently strong to temper our appetite for Earth’s resources and focus our work towards restoring land health. A land ethic, good land use, and an equitable and civil society arise from countless actions and conversations, constantly unfolding, as the nation’s citizens go about their daily lives.
Agriculture is an ecologically embedded enterprise, and we should not tolerate actions that degrade our natural capital, the diversity and function of our ecosystems, or the health of the atmosphere, soils and waters that surround and support us. At the same time, we must recognise that agriculture is embedded in society – a farm practice that runs counter to society’s goals is hard to maintain. I agree that a farm can and should be valued by its owners as a place to live, and as a source of pleasure in good farming, good eating and engagement with both domestic and wild neighbours. Society continues to measure farms, and judge farmers, on their production of grain, meat, biomass and other commodities. Farmers are caught up in a highly competitive market system that typically allows only a slim margin between money coming in and money going out. Meanwhile, the goal of public policy for agriculture continues to be guided by the desire for cheap food.
While the predicament of modern agriculture may appear so dire that we will inevitably adapt and organise a more sustainable system, ecologists at Murdoch University in Australia came to a different conclusion after analysing the problems facing farmers in the semi-arid southwestern part of that continent. Farmers and policy-makers continue to invest in production systems that don’t fit the land because they are now tightly bound up in patterns of modern agribusiness and food production. Financial capital goes to conventional farmers more easily than to alternative farmers, and social capital – in the forms of agronomic research, technical assistance (for addressing issues with animal health, soil fertility, soil erosion and water pollution), and especially processing, distribution and retail – supports the energy- and natural-capital intensive system. The authors describe this as a ‘lock-in trap’, ‘an industry that has so much “sunk-costs” that it may continue to degrade the resource it relies upon until the capital is totally removed.’ Shifting the system to a more desirable state – one that is ecologically as well as socially resilient – requires us to forge new social connections in the quest to establish more sustainable patterns of land use.
Can a community of well-connected but individually small actors hope to break agriculture out of its lock-in trap? There is little room for optimism, but our prospects are not hopeless. As David Orr reminds us: ‘Hope is a verb with its sleeves rolled up.’ When Orr encouraged us to be hopeful in times like these, perhaps he was continuing a literary conversation with Wendell Berry, a Kentucky hill country farmer and writer. Berry stated that he had no reason to be optimistic about the prospects of people becoming reconnected with the ‘wealth, health, knowledge, and pleasure of their country’, but still he concluded that ‘hope is one of our duties … The health of nature is the primary ground of hope – if we can find the humility and wisdom to accept nature as our teacher.’
We may have much to learn from how nature’s economy operates in the prairie. In the Flint Hills of Kansas, the prairies are truly dominated by tall grasses – big and small bluestem, switchgrass and Indiangrass account for around 80 per cent of the prairie’s windswept greenery. These grasses are so dominant because they are remarkably efficient. Unlike many other grasses, these species build channels in their leaves to make the process of photosynthesis more efficient than it is for their competitors. The grasses need comparatively fewer enzymes to carry out photosynthesis and thus require less nitrogen – a building block of enzymes. This is a major advantage, as the amount of nitrogen in the soil is often the limiting factor for plant growth – hence the artificial nitrogen we’re counselled to add to our gardens and crops as fertiliser. The tall grasses also lose less water thanks to their innovation, which helps put them ahead in dry climates with high evaporation rates.
In the language of microeconomics, the tall grasses have the lowest costs for construction and operations. As a result, these ships in the prairie sea can cast vast nets of roots below the surface to capture water and nitrogen, and set huge sails of green leaves to catch the sun to propel photosynthesis. These photons and molecules are finite resources that plants cannot share and for which they must compete. The highly efficient tallgrass fleets should rule the prairies. Paradoxically, the tallgrass prairies are blessed with an abundance of smaller, less efficient wildflowers and legumes, prospering from sub-boreal Manitoba in Canada to the subtropical coastal plains of Louisiana and Texas. As with the mystery of decay and renewal that abounds in the soil, microbes dwell at the heart of this paradox.
In the cycles of evolution, the efficiency and dominance of the tall grasses built a palace of greenery
All of us mammals have microbes in our guts, facilitating and regulating digestion. Large-bodied herbivores take this to an extreme – huge body cavities accommodate an intricate digestive system that shelters, feeds and harvests a community of microbes. Mouth, teeth, tongue, digestive tract and brain are all organised to harvest and process grass, leveraging the ability of microbes to consume the fibrous grasses and excrete easily digestible sugars.
In the tallgrass prairie, American bison select where to graze based, to some extent, on where they can maximise their intake of the plant resource to which they are best adapted. The ecological niche of an organism is perhaps most aptly translated as its palace, as the poet, translator and ecological activist Gary Snyder has re-discovered, and interpreted for us, in the work of the philosopher Dōgen. In the cycles of evolution, the efficiency and dominance of the tall grasses built a palace of greenery. The bison evolved to dwell in this palace. Among the tall grasses, they are fully at home.
As the ecologist Alan Knapp and his colleagues at Kansas State University digested from their research in the Flint Hills, the microbially facilitated bison play a key role in making their home a palace for others too. As they fulfil their needs by feasting on leaves, the bison demolish the tall grasses’ leafy superstructures. The rest of the prairie blushes and blooms in gratitude.
The leaves of big bluestem might otherwise have overshadowed a short-statured wild petunia seedling. Because the microbe/bison superorganism is adapted to make use of the abundant grass, the young wildflower now spends much of the summer bathed in light, taking in carbon dioxide, releasing oxygen, and building leaves and roots through photosynthesis. Furthermore, nitrogen in the big bluestem leaves would have been locked up through the rest of the growing season, unless a passing band of grasshoppers landed for a meal and carried it off, driven by the instinct to mate and lay eggs before the days become any shorter. As the bison eat and excrete, the nitrogen and other nutrients once held in the leaves overhead are returned in forms accessible to other community members. After pausing to scratch her belly on a compass plant, a bison cow returns a cascade of nitrogen-rich urine that the wildflower may absorb just as it begins to send its flowering stalk skyward.
The compass plant, in turn, could produce one more flower than it might have, had the nitrogen remained locked up in big bluestem. Its saucer-sized flowers attract and nourish many native pollinators, while its nutritious seeds are a staple for seed-eating birds. Both flowers and seeds are costly to produce because they concentrate large amounts of nitrogen. The compass plant and wild petunia are only two of hundreds of wildflower and grass species that can be outcompeted by the dominant tall grasses. When the bison home in on a patch of tall grasses, the dominance of the highly efficient big and small bluestem, Indiangrass and switchgrass may be depressed such that the prairie’s balance sheet might take a hit on the single measure of tons of biomass per acre – but, as Robinson Jeffers puts it in his poem ‘Bixby’s Landing’ (1928):
… what a good multitude
Is here in return …
In the process of reorganisation, exchange in other ecological currencies multiplies, for countless organisms dwell in the palace of wildflowers. Most herbivores and omnivores are smaller than a bison and lack the microbial symbiosis that provides access to grass. Instead, they depend upon the more digestible leaves, pollen, nectar, sugary fruit, starchy tubers and seeds, and protein-rich leaf buds that wildflowers and flowering shrubs produce. Badgers, rabbits, mice and voles, prairie chickens, grouse, turtles and waterfowl can all benefit. The less efficient plants host many species of insect larvae, which in turn feed predatory insects, songbird hatchlings and others on the food web. And so the web of connections rolls out and across the prairies in this fashion.
If we are to transform agriculture for better outcomes, we need a similar roll-out of networked and diverse people and organisations who collectively act as a keystone species. But we cannot simply wait for the bison of federal policy reform to come trampling through the industrial agriculture complex. We must act lest the bison of more sustainable agriculture stumble, allowing the most ruthless forces in industrial agriculture to continue unchecked – to the degradation of soil, extinction of wild plants and animals, and hollowing-out of communities. To restore agriculture to a more diverse and resilient community, each of us must express our individual land ethic through the food markets and by giving voice to our values in the public sphere. There are deep congruencies between sustainable agriculture and conservation, and we cannot afford to lose the incremental but crucial gains that pioneers have made over the past few decades.
Investing in local food and energy production creates demand for more types of agriculture, renewing ecological and social diversity across landscapes long simplified in the name of industrial efficiency. Such landscapes might include small, intensively cultivated vegetable fields and orchards supplying fresh produce and local processors; trellised hops adapted to local conditions and supporting regional breweries; perennial grasslands producing healthy animal products from cattle, sheep, swine and poultry; small fields of corn, wheat and other grains integrated with livestock or supplying locally owned mills; and oak woodlots thinned to provide firewood and lumber. Wetlands now choked with reed canarygrass and shrubs could once again support wildlife while providing hay, bedding and renewable biomass capable of heating homes, businesses and schools during winter’s deep freeze. By turning more of our dollars away from large agribusiness and toward these small-scale, locally integrated systems, we will be rewarded with healthier soil, cleaner and more abundant groundwater, fewer and less severe floods following intense rains, stronger communities with the skills to manage biologically complex farming systems, and a richer, more secure tapestry of semi-natural-to-wild habitats. Many semi-domestic parts of the rural landscape are important for the wild creatures that enrich our lives and testify to the care we take of the land. The touchstones of these partly wild/partly human landscapes are small pastures and sweeping grasslands, scattered woodlots and deep forests, shady valleys and sandstone-capped bluffs, clean headwater springs, and wetlands alive with waterfowl.
A diverse rural landscape, shaped by goals of complexity and resilience, rather than maximum production and minimal accounting, will be invaluable to our communities in the coming years. The landscape of diverse farming systems that rely much less on fossil fuels for energy and fertility is much more likely to remain productive despite shocks such as intense rains, flooding, drought, rising fuel and fertiliser costs, declining soil structure and fertility, and limited access to credit and financial capital. Such shocks are predicted to become more frequent and more severe because of climate change, continued population growth, increasing demand for resources, and economic and social inequality.
What could a large agribusiness, food-processing or cut-throat retail corporation fear more than for us to begin acting like we don’t believe there is much congruence between their sales and quarterly earnings, and our security and happiness? Berry has described such a social shift as nothing less than secession.
Love is at the heart of conservation, good farming and strong communities
Among the trade-offs that come with taking personal responsibility for investment in infrastructure and community is that much of the pay-off will come in the long term rather than in the next quarter or next few years. Building a long-term outlook and sustaining collective commitment will require cultivating the skills needed to navigate disagreements between individuals and factions, to face the uncertainty of alternative models of community development, to weather economic hard times, and to engage in both practical and joyful scepticism of the intense propaganda that flows from the anonymous economy to its victims. This demands vision, sincerity and the arts of neighbourliness and community engagement.
Nowhere in the frameworks of sustainability have I come across love for our neighbours and the land as a guiding principle, yet love is at the heart of conservation, good farming and strong communities. We do not know what the future will bring, but resilience to coming shocks cannot be secured through better technology, greater efficiency or improved communications infrastructure alone. We need all of these advances, but conservation asks even more of us. Leopold’s words resonated with this call when he summarised his goals for an ecological education:
If the individual has a warm personal understanding of land, he will perceive of his own accord that it is something more than a breadbasket. He will see land as a community of which he is only a member, albeit now the dominant one. He will see the beauty, as well as the utility, of the whole, and know the two cannot be separated. We love (and make intelligent use of) what we have learned to understand.
Each of us is an individual, but ecology and ecological economics remind us that we exist only in relation to the land and our neighbours. By enacting our love for the land and our neighbours, we assume great risk. We will likely face changes in consumption patterns and the nature of work and exchange that will feel like severe sacrifices. However, many rich harvests are indeed possible when we choose to act as members of our community, to transcend efficiency and strive toward harmony among people and between people and land. Much that might otherwise go to waste is brought back into cycles of renewal. As we nurture the life of community, we tend a field in which many of our hopes and pleasures can bloom.
End of row. Decision time again.
Craig Maier died in 2024. This essay has been lightly edited from his original manuscript for publication, with the guidance of Craig’s graduate advisor, Randy Jackson. With thanks to Randy for his valuable input in the editing process, and for helping to honour Craig’s memory.

Australia calls for 'absolute consensus' on Pacific military group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:59:47 UTC
18:59:47 KST

Pacific defence ministers call for consensus on military response group
In short:
Pacific defence ministers are taking a cautious approach to expanding the Pacific Response Group, a military force.
Although ministers previously agreed to consider giving it a broader role in responding to civil unrest, they have put the brakes on, not wanting to be rushed.
What's next?
Australia's defence chief says any change must have "absolute consensus" among Pacific countries.
Pacific defence ministers have signalled they will not rush to expand the remit of a new military response group, with Australia's defence chief saying there must be "absolute consensus" about how it evolves.
The South Pacific Defence Ministers' Meeting (SPDMM) — which draws in Australia, Chile, Fiji, France, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea and Tonga — has wrapped up in Fiji.
On top of the agenda was the Pacific Response Group (PRG), which was formed in 2024 as part of a push from Australia and several other governments to develop a more coordinated response to natural disasters in the region.
Last year, the ministers endorsed a move to broaden the mandate of the PRG so it can also conduct "stabilisation operations" for Pacific nations that request military help to deal with civil unrest.
And in May this year, senior Pacific military officers endorsed a push for a new regional treaty that would govern how deployments take place, recommending Pacific leaders kickstart negotiations on a framework that would make it easier to rapidly send personnel to countries grappling with crises.
But while there is enthusiasm for the idea, it is also politically sensitive.
That is partly because the PRG can easily be seen as part of a broader push by Australia and its allies to block China from the security space, and partly because it will have to grapple with fraught questions around what legal immunity is offered to personnel deployed to other countries.
Some Pacific nations are also dealing with internal political issues — for example, Fiji is embroiled in an intense domestic debate on constitutional reform, and is likely to go to the polls before February next year.
On top of that, Pacific bureaucracies have also struggled to keep pace with the push for rapid change within the PRG just a couple of years after it was established.
When Pacific leaders met in Palau, they did not agree to kickstart negotiations on the treaty, signalling that they wanted to move more slowly on the issue.
And this afternoon, SPDMM defence ministers released a communique saying they had told senior military officers that the framework had to "consider the privileges and immunities relevant to HADR [humanitarian and disaster relief] and any future PRG stabilisation function".
The ministers also said they had agreed to take a "phased approach" to expanding the PRG's mandate, "recognising the importance of first consolidating and enhancing the PRG's humanitarian assistance and disaster relief [HADR] capabilities" before working to "include stabilisation operations".
Australian Defence Force chief Admiral Mark Hammond, who represented Australia at the meeting along with Assistant Defence Minister Peter Khalil, told the ABC that the group "must pay due respect to sovereign constitutional processes" and there had to be an "absolute consensus of an overlap with respect to national interest".
"We still need some time to work things through their constitutional processes and some of the nations at the table are on the cusp of national elections, some have only recently elected them or had a cabinet reshuffle, so these take time to bed down," Mr Hammond said.
But Admiral Hammond told the ABC there was still rock-solid support for the PRG at a "macro level" because it embodied the idea of Pacific-led security.
"When you look at the Pacific Response Group and the number of nations that are present in that, and you see that arriving as an initial response force to one of our Pacific Island nations, there will be representatives from that nation, in the PRG, that will be able to speak to the local issues, to help us cut through bureaucracy and to interpret their national interest into individual language that enables us to get on, deliver and support," he said.
One Pacific government representative, who requested anonymity to speak frankly, said there was not any "opposition" to the PRG, which they said was largely seen as a "great idea."
But they said some of the questions around immunity and sovereignty, as well as the geopolitical backdrop, could be "a little bit sensitive".
"Everyone wants to take this slowly and carefully and get this right,"
Pacific security expert Anna Powles from Massey University said it was "not surprising that securing regional consensus is proving challenging".
"Some countries are suggesting the process has been rushed and have questions about where the agreement will sit within the regional security architecture," she said.
"It could be useful to locate the framework under the Biketawa Declaration, which has the credibility and the tested mechanisms to support regionally led responses."
The seven countries represented at SPDMM also expressed "grave concern" over China's ballistic missile test earlier this year, using much stronger language than was adopted at the Pacific Island Forum (PIF) leaders' meeting in Palau earlier this month.
"Ministers highlighted that the manner in which this activity was conducted risked undermining PIF leaders' declaration of the Blue Pacific Continent as an Ocean of Peace," they said.
"It also undermined leaders' call to engage with the Blue Pacific Continent in a manner that honours the Pacific Way, respects national sovereignty and supports national and Pacific-led approaches."

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

09:58:52 UTC
18:58:52 KST

MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. Russian Federal Security Service (FSB) officers detained an organizer of a drug shipment from Latin America to EU countries red-handed, seizing 311 kilograms of cocaine, the FSB press office reported.
"The FSB has thwarted the illegal activities of a Russian citizen born in 2001 who was involved in organizing an international smuggling channel for the shipment of particularly large quantities of cocaine from Latin America to EU countries for subsequent illegal distribution," the statement said.
According to the press office, "the FSB officers caught the drug trafficker red-handed in the Moscow Region, while transporting an exceptionally large shipment of drugs. A total of 311.6 kilograms of cocaine was seized from illicit circulation."
The statement noted that security agencies received information on an unemployed Russian citizen who was an active member of an organized criminal group that specialized in large-scale, contact-free drug distribution via underground online resources.
Interestingly, a photograph of smiling Vladimir Zelensky was found on the cocaine bricks, the FSB noted, releasing a video depicting the drug trafficker’s detention. He had 12 bags on him, each containing 25 bricks of the drug.
Zelensky’s public behavior has led some to suspect he is addicted to drugs. His former spokeswoman Yulia Mendel previously confirmed that he uses drugs, specifically cocaine.
The FSB has opened a criminal case against the detainee under Articles 30 and 228.1 of the Russian Criminal Code (Attempted Distribution of Drugs on an Especially Large Scale). By court order, he has been remanded in custody. Investigative actions are ongoing.

Ukraine's disgraced ex-prosecutor general moves to Austria, media report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:57:22 UTC
18:57:22 KST

Ukraine’s disgraced former Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko has moved to Austria, the media outlet Ukrainska Pravda reported late on Sept. 23.
The Kyiv Independent has requested comment from Kravchenko and will publish his response once it is received.
Kravchenko was fired by parliament on Sept. 15 amid a major corruption investigation.
He left Ukraine on Sept. 14, under the pretext of an official trip to a conference in Paris. But the organizers told the Kyiv Independent that they had not expected him to attend, strengthening the suspicions that the trip was a fig leaf for fleeing Ukraine to avoid potential charges.
Ukrainska Pravda cited records from Austria’s Central Register of Residents.
According to the register, Kravchenko and his wife are registered on 7 Jordangasse, apartment No. 12, in downtown Vienna.
Apartment No. 12 at 7 Jordangasse is the office of CS Corporate Services GmbH, a company that provides registered addresses to Austrian limited liability companies, secretarial services, management services, and the sale of shelf companies that are already incorporated and ready to be transferred to a new owner, according to Ukrainska Pravda.
There is speculation in the media that Kravchenko may apply for political asylum in Austria.
Austria does not generally extradite Ukrainian citizens, and several former Ukrainian officials live there.
Kravchenko's personal office was searched by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau in early September as part of a large-scale corruption investigation into an alleged scam call center protection racket run from the Prosecutor General's Office.
Within the investigation, a top prosecutor described as a “confidant” of Kravchenko was charged. Publicly revealed evidence hints at Kravchenko being implicated, and he submitted his resignation on Sept. 7.
Kravchenko left Ukraine on Sept. 14 and simultaneously approved charges against the head of the anti-corruption agency investigating him.
The charges against Semen Kryvonos, head of the National Anti-Corruption Bureau, and an unnamed “close associate” of Oleksandr Klymenko, chief of the Special Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO), were seen by many as a petty vendetta rather than pursuit of justice.
The charges were canceled by the Prosecutor General's Office late on Sept. 14, and Kravchenko was dismissed by parliament the next day.
On Sept. 17, President Volodymyr Zelensky appointed Anton Kovalsky, chief prosecutor of Khmelnytsky Oblast, as acting prosecutor general.
Media reports suggest Kovalsky could ultimately be appointed prosecutor general, rather than merely serving in an acting capacity.

Ukrainian Defense Forces strike two Russian radars, drone launch site
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:57:00 UTC
18:57:00 KST

Ukrainian Defense Forces strike two Russian radars, drone launch site
According to Ukrinform, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this on Facebook.
In temporarily occupied Donetsk, a site used to store, prepare and launch attack drones was struck. Hitting such facilities is one of the priority areas of combat operations by the Defense Forces.
In temporarily occupied settlements of Chekhohrad (formerly Novohrodivka) and Yakymivka in the Zaporizhzhia region, 35N6 Kasta and P-18 radar stations were struck.
The 35N6 Kasta is a Russian mobile all-round surveillance radar designed to detect aerial targets, including those flying at extremely low altitudes, and transmit data to air defense systems.
The P-18 is a mobile long-range early-warning radar operating in the meter wavelength range that was developed during the Soviet era. It is designed to detect aerial targets, determine their coordinates (azimuth and range), and transmit data to users. It is operated by the Russian military as an early-warning asset for air defense.
In temporarily occupied Velyka Bilozerka in the Zaporizhzhia region, a fuel and lubricants depot of Russian forces was struck.
As reported by Ukrinform, Ukrainian Defense Forces units also struck Russian UAV command posts, a drone depot of the Rubicon unit, and other facilities of the Russian invading forces.

Zelenskyy called the G20 summit in the United States &quot;one of the best&quot; opportunities to meet with Putin

12:56:43 EEST

Zelenskyy called the G20 summit in the United States "one of the best" opportunities to meet with Putin
Kyiv • UNN
Zelenskyy considers the G20 summit in Miami an opportunity for a productive meeting between Ukraine, the United States and Russia. The Kremlin is working on an invitation for Putin.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy believes that the G20 summit in Miami, United States, could provide "one of the best" opportunities for a trilateral meeting between Ukraine, the United States and Russia "with a real result." He said this to journalists during a briefing in New York in the early hours of September 24, UNN reports.
We discussed with the American side whether such a G20 format could take place and whether Ukraine was ready to meet. I believe this is one of the best opportunities proposed by the American side, by President Trump, regarding the G20; it seems to me that it is December 12. I believe this is a potential opportunity for a trilateral meeting with a real result
"Let me explain why. First, there is Trump — he is the president, influential, number one. The second point is the G20, meaning that this is not just Europe, which Putin either likes or is irritated by; it is up to him. But what is important here is that these are our partners, the Europeans, and it is important that representatives of the Middle East and other countries are also here, as well as China and India. (…) In other words, in my view, this could be an atmosphere in which a result could be achieved. Of course, Ukraine will support it if such a format and an appropriate agreement are reached," the President emphasized.
Supplement
This statement came after U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that Washington had invited Kremlin head Vladimir Putin to the G20 summit.
The Kremlin approved the invitation for Putin to attend the G20 summit. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov initially said that Moscow would work through diplomatic channels on the proposal for Vladimir Putin to attend the G20 summit in Miami. He later clarified that it was premature to talk about Putin’s trip to the G20 and a meeting with Donald Trump.
The Kremlin representative noted that the decision on the response to the invitation for Putin to attend the G20 summit "will be worked out, and an appropriate decision will then be made."
"In any case, Russia intends to continue its participation in the work of the G20 and all the forums held within this framework," Peskov added.
Zelenskyy and Putin last met in person in Paris in December 2019 during talks in the Normandy format, mediated by France and Germany.

Danish intelligence service warns Russia may intensify hybrid attacks against West and NATO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:56:41 UTC
18:56:41 KST

Russia is expected to intensify its hybrid war against the West and NATO in the coming months, with attacks becoming more frequent and potentially having greater consequences for affected countries, according to a new assessment from the Danish Defence Intelligence Service, FE.
The assessment is being presented Thursday at a press conference at Kastellet in Copenhagen.
FE says the increased threat could include destructive cyberattacks with serious consequences for critical societal functions, as well as sabotage attacks with a high risk of casualties.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus, a member of the Social Democrats, said the situation was serious.
“The situation is serious, and we take it seriously,” Bruus said.
“That is why we are standing here today. We are presenting the assessment because having as much openness as possible is important,” he said.
FE also assesses that there is a “low, but increasing risk” that Russia could launch a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia.
“It is unlikely that Russia will initiate an actual invasion of a NATO country, but we cannot rule it out,” FE chief Thomas Ahrenkiel said.
Ahrenkiel said it was new that FE could no longer rule out such an invasion.
According to the assessment, Russia would need at least six months to prepare for an actual invasion of a NATO country.
Bruus stressed that the assessment does not concern a possible military attack on Denmark.
“One is not talking about military attacks on the Kingdom of Denmark” in the assessment, he said.
Chief of Defence Michael Hyldgaard, who also attended the press conference, said the Danish military is adapting to the assessment.
“We will fight and win with what we have, and those we fight alongside. That is our task. That is what we are preparing for. We are ready for that – regardless of the threat,” Hyldgaard said.
The assessment does not concern Greenland or the Faroe Islands, according to the information presented at the press conference.
The new assessment comes just over a week after a Russian frigate fired flares at a Danish helicopter in international waters off Gedser.
Ahrenkiel described the incident as “unprofessional behavior” by Russian soldiers aboard the frigate.
“It is also our impression that such risky behavior was not sanctioned by the Russian military leadership,” he said.

People in Italy can expect around 11 more years without health-related limitations than people in Denmark, according to figures from the EU’s statistical office, Eurostat.
The figures cover healthy life years across the 27 EU countries. Danes have 62.4 healthy life years, while Italy ranks highest at 73.4.
Healthy life years measure the number of years a person can expect to live without limitations in daily life because of health. Eurostat’s indicator is based on people’s own assessment of their health.
Denmark ranks below 18 other countries in the figures.
Neighboring Sweden and Norway also rank above Denmark, with 67.5 and 64.8 healthy life years respectively.
Diabetes Association calls for greater focus on prevention
The Diabetes Association has described the Danish figures as a “health alarm.”
“Because the figures show that we in Denmark have dragged our feet for too long when it comes to health promotion and preventing chronic illnesses such as type 2 diabetes, which is growing explosively,” the association’s CEO, Claus Richter, said in a press release.
The Eurostat figures cover 2024. It is the first year in which Denmark’s figures have been calculated using the same method as the rest of the EU.
Life expectancy in Denmark has increased year by year. But Richter said the figures show that Danes are living longer “but not better.”
He attributed this in part to a health care system that prioritizes treatment over health promotion and prevention.
He also pointed to what he described as an outdated financial silo mentality, in which an expense in one area “can rarely be justified” by gains in another.
“It is a tragedy for each individual, but also for our society. Illness pulls many thousands of full-time equivalent jobs out of the workforce. Therefore, there is a need for a paradigm shift where we view prevention and health promotion as an investment – not an expense,” he said.
The Diabetes Association is proposing that Denmark set a national target for healthy life years in legislation.
Its vision for 2045 is for Denmark to be among the European countries with the highest number of healthy life years.
Among its proposals is the creation of a Health Economics Council that would assess and prioritize preventive measures based on their long-term value.
The Diabetes Association is due to present the proposal Thursday morning at a health policy debate at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, the Folketinget.
Denmark’s wolf population has grown to 77, an increase of 28 from the previous monitoring year, according to a new count by Aarhus University and the Natural History Museum Aarhus.
The figures are included in a memo from the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment.
The population is approaching a size at which it may become possible to regulate the predator, Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said in comments to DR and TV 2.
The ministry will now count the wolves individually. It expects that the results will allow Denmark to “demonstrate to the EU that the wolf has a favorable conservation status.”
“Then we can begin hunting, and we should,” Rabjerg Madsen told DR.
According to the Danish Nature Agency, a species has a favorable conservation status when its population development shows that it can maintain itself in the long term.
Wolves have been protected under the EU Habitats Directive since 1992. The directive “prohibits deliberate killing.”
In Denmark, the protection is implemented through the Hunting and Game Management Act, which prohibits hunting or capturing wolves. Shooting a wolf can result in a fine or imprisonment for up to two years.
However, the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment can grant permission to regulate, meaning shoot, an individual wolf in special circumstances.
The authorities can grant permission if there is no other solution and the action does not threaten the wolf’s natural range.
This can include cases involving “public health, safety, and security, or to prevent serious damage to livestock and other forms of property.”
An exemption can also be granted if a wolf “lacks an instinctive shyness towards humans.”
The 77 wolves are spread across 11 packs, which have produced a total of 61 pups this year. There are also two pairs of wolves and two lone male wolves in Denmark.
They have been identified in at least 15 locations, all in Jutland, from Løgumkloster in Southern Jutland to the northernmost part of Northern Jutland.
Wolves may also be present in three additional locations, but further investigations are needed to confirm this.
Without “human persecution,” the Danish wolf population is expected to continue growing.
The wolf returned to Denmark from Germany in 2012 after being absent from the country for almost 200 years.
A new resident has arrived among the leopards at Copenhagen Zoo after an Amur leopard gave birth to a cub last week.
The zoo announced the birth in a press release.
The Amur leopard is “the rarest subspecies of leopard,” according to zoological director Mads Berthelsen.
“Even though the species is experiencing slight growth, there are still only around 110 individuals in the wild,” he said in the press release.
Amur leopards generally live alone in the wild. The newborn cub is still small and blind, however, and is completely dependent on its mother.
The mother spends most of her time with the cub and only leaves for short periods, including to find food.
Because of this, zookeepers are keeping their distance for now. They are monitoring the cub’s development by listening for sounds from the stable.
Zoo visitors will also have to wait before they can see the cub.
“The first weeks are about giving the mother and the cub as much peace as possible. We expect it will take about two months – maybe a little longer – before the cub begins to come out enough that guests can have the opportunity to experience it,” Berthelsen said.
In addition to the approximately 110 Amur leopards known to live in the wild, 93 males and 97 females are kept in zoos around the world, according to the international zoological database Zims.
Only one Amur leopard cub has been registered in the database over the past 12 months, Copenhagen Zoo said.
This does not necessarily mean the animals are having difficulty breeding, Berthelsen said.
“We are increasingly seeing that zoos choose not to let their animals breed because they are concerned about what to do with any surplus offspring,” he said.
The Amur leopard lives mainly in the Primorye region of southeastern Russia. In summer, temperatures in the large forest area can reach 40 degrees Celsius, while winter temperatures can fall below minus 30 degrees.
Cold cuts, filter coffee, chocolate and olive oil were among the products that became cheaper in Denmark in September, according to a monthly analysis by food price monitoring service Madprisluppen.
Overall shelf prices were slightly lower than in August, with the decline most noticeable at discount chains Lidl, 365discount, Rema 1000 and Netto.
Online supermarket Nemlig.com has also lowered prices because it matches the prices of nearly 400 products sold by Rema 1000.
“The cheapest baskets have become cheaper, and the distance from the cheapest to the most expensive basket has grown larger,” Madprisluppen commercial manager Lars Smidt said.
Consumers now pay 27 percent more for the most expensive shopping basket than for the cheapest, with Lidl and Rema 1000 offering the lowest-priced baskets, according to Smidt.
Lidl began cutting prices on a range of products in May as part of its permanent low-price program. Rema 1000, Netto and 365discount soon followed.
A survey conducted by analysis institute Norstat for Lidl found that seven in 10 Danes know about the permanent low-price concept and have bought products at permanent low prices. More than half said they prefer stores with permanent low prices to stores offering frequent special deals.
Lidl Denmark purchasing director Peer Sandtner said the chain now has permanent low prices on more than 300 products.
Smidt said it remains uncertain whether grocery prices will continue falling across supermarket chains. Higher oil and gasoline prices could eventually affect food prices, he said.

Denmark could become one of the four largest contributors to the Global Partnership for Education under a new funding plan running through 2030.
The government plans to provide up to 1 billion DKK to the global education fund, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a press release Wednesday.
The funding would begin with 250 million DKK in 2027 and reach a total of up to 1 billion DKK by 2030.
The money is intended to support education in developing countries.
“Education is one of the best investments we can make, both for the children who directly benefit from Denmark’s support, but also for Denmark itself,” Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said during the UN General Assembly in New York.
The funding is included in the government’s proposed 2027 finance bill. It is conditional on the proposal being passed and the funding being approved annually by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The announcement comes as the global education fund faces financial pressure, with several donors expected to reduce their contributions.
Rasmussen said better access to education could also support economic development.
“When more children in the world’s poorest countries go to school and learn to read and do math, it creates fertile ground for economic growth and new markets for Danish business,” he said.
The updated defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the U.S. does not introduce new restrictions on how the American military can use its bases in Greenland, according to Danish government officials.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats and Greenland’s head of government signed the agreement with the U.S. in New York on Tuesday.
The agreement largely confirms rights granted under a 1951 defense deal, Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates said.
“But subtracting that, the agreement is an opportunity for the US to establish itself with a military footprint in Greenland, as they already can,” Rasmussen said.
One restriction remains unchanged: nuclear weapons are prohibited in Greenland.
The issue has historical significance. In 1957, Danish Prime Minister H.C. Hansen secretly allowed the U.S. to keep nuclear weapons in Greenland. In 1968, a U.S. B-52 bomber carrying hydrogen bombs crashed near Thule, causing radioactive contamination.
Denmark and the U.S. subsequently agreed that nuclear weapons could not be kept in Greenland.
Rasmussen said the new agreement does not give the U.S. greater military access than it already had.
“The important thing for us is that our nuclear policy is intact, and that in this context we do not give the US any greater access than they actually had beforehand,” he said.
The agreement also introduces stricter requirements for the U.S. to protect Greenland’s environment. American military bases have previously caused pollution affecting local communities.
Before the updated agreement can take effect, it must be approved by Inatsisartut, Greenland’s parliament, and Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.

The security and defense agreement between the United States, Greenland and Denmark is based on all three parties being members of NATO, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said Tuesday evening.
“If the USA withdraws from the agreement, it thus no longer applies,” Frederiksen said after the agreement was signed.
“It is a very clear premise for this agreement that the countries that have signed the agreement are in NATO. All three countries are now,” she said.
Frederiksen pointed to a change from the original agreement signed in 1951: Greenland is now fully included in the agreement.
“In connection with an independence process, if that situation should arise, this agreement conditions a membership of NATO for an independent Greenland. That is the change,” she said.
“But the entire foundation of the agreement is that we are members of NATO. And I have no expectations that the USA will withdraw from NATO,” Frederiksen said.
The agreement was signed Tuesday by Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, and U.S. President Donald Trump.
The signing took place in New York during the United Nations General Assembly.
After the agreement was signed, Nielsen said that Greenland’s population must now rebuild trust in the United States.

Some 363,600 people who receive prescription allergy medication in Denmark will need to renew their prescriptions if they want to continue receiving a subsidy.
The Danish Medicines Agency announced the changes following a new decision on subsidies for prescription allergy medicines.
Under the new rules, subsidies for some medicines will only be available to specific patient groups, while other patients will no longer be eligible for a subsidy.
If a patient is no longer eligible for a subsidy for their current medicine, they can ask their doctor for a prescription for another medicine with the same effect that is eligible for a subsidy.
Patients who experience side effects or cannot use an alternative for other reasons can have their doctor apply for an individual subsidy.
The changes affect various nasal sprays, eye drops, tablets and capsules, according to the Danish Medicines Agency.
Patients who can use an alternative will no longer be able to receive a subsidy for medicines including Allergone, Altifex, Benadryl, Beconase and Benarhin once the changes take effect on February 1, 2027.
Around 750,000 people in Denmark receive prescription allergy medication. The Danish Medicines Agency encourages patients to check its website to see whether they are affected.
The decision follows a recommendation from the Reimbursement Committee, which advises the Danish Medicines Agency on medicine subsidies.
Deciding which medicines should receive subsidies is part of the Danish Medicines Agency’s routine work.

There appears to be broad political support in Denmark for a new security and defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the United States.
The agreement, signed Tuesday in New York by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen and U.S. President Donald Trump, must now go through approval procedures in Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut, and the Folketing, Denmark’s national parliament.
The agreement is intended to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic. The signing took place at the United Nations headquarters during the U.N. General Assembly.
Trump has repeatedly expressed a desire for the United States to own Greenland, citing national and international security concerns. His statements led to a prolonged diplomatic crisis between the United States, Denmark and Greenland.
Several Danish political parties have welcomed the agreement, including Venstre, the Conservative Party, the Red-Green Alliance and the Denmark Democrats.
Venstre’s chairman, Troels Lund Poulsen, described the agreement as “an extraordinarily good agreement.”
Poulsen was defense minister in the former SVM government, a coalition between the Social Democrats, Venstre and the Moderates, and played a significant role in the negotiations with the Trump administration.
“It is a joyful day for Greenland, Denmark, the Realm, and for the cooperation with the USA in the future,” he told TV 2 on Tuesday.
When Frederiksen held a press conference for Danish media in New York, she gave particular thanks to Poulsen for his efforts. Poulsen described it as “beautiful” that the agreement had become a reality.
The Conservative Party’s chairman, Mona Juul, also praised the agreement on Facebook.
“An agreement has been reached. And that is unequivocally good. Therefore, I would also like to praise the enormous political and diplomatic work that preceded the agreement,” she wrote.
The Denmark Democrats’ chairman, Inger Støjberg, also expressed support.
“It is an agreement we can be proud of, because it both emphasizes our sovereignty and cements NATO’s presence,” she told TV 2 on Tuesday, referring to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
The Red-Green Alliance, a party that supports the government in parliament, also backed the agreement.
“It is an agreement that does not in any way alter Danish sovereignty. An agreement that Greenland signs with Denmark and the USA. They have stayed within the red lines,” the party’s Greenland spokesperson, Trine Pertou Mach, told Jyllands-Posten on Tuesday.
The agreement will enter into force only after the necessary parliamentary procedures have been completed.

Small public schools in rural areas are set to receive more state support as falling numbers of children put some schools at risk of closing.
The government is allocating 500 million DKK through 2030 to support small schools and slow further closures.
Minister for Economic and Interior Affairs Pia Olsen Dyhr from the Socialist People’s Party, is presenting the plan today at a visit to a school in Toksværd in Næstved Municipality, according to TV2 ØST.
“A school is a gathering point for parents, teachers, and students, and they help create local life and connection in our rural districts,” Dyhr said.
The initiative follows a commitment in the government’s platform from June to prevent a new wave of school closures. Small public schools in rural areas are also expected to receive greater financial support and more freedom.
One school facing possible closure is Vesterlandsskolen’s branch in Hyllinge. Only fifty-four students attend this school, and Næstved Municipality’s administration has proposed ending teaching and after-school care there from August 1, 2027.
Closing the branch would save 7.53 million DKK annually from 2028. The proposal has not been approved, and the city council is expected to adopt its budget on October 6.
School board chair Karina Wolan said additional state funding could help keep the Hyllinge branch open.
“If it means that the school can be allowed to exist, that would be wonderful,” she said.
It remains unclear how the 500 million DKK will be distributed, which municipalities will qualify and whether the funding is included in the government’s previously announced five billion DKK annual investment in children, daycare, schools and leisure.
Social Affairs Minister Monika Rubin of the Moderates says the government wants more freedom to change Denmark’s disability system after withdrawing from a political agreement reached two years ago.
The framework agreement was signed in May 2024 by the government and Liberal Alliance, the Conservative People’s Party and the Social Liberal Party. It was not a formal political settlement with special rules governing withdrawal.
“With the framework agreement, one had bound oneself in a way that made it more difficult than it needs to be to cooperate broadly across the Folketing,” Rubin said, referring to Denmark’s parliament.
“The original agreement has outlived its potential,” she added.
When the deal was reached, then-Social Affairs Minister Pernille Rosenkrantz-Theil of the Social Democrats described it as a “completely new chapter in Danish disability policy” and the “first major agreement in the disability area ever.”
Rubin’s Moderates also supported the agreement at the time.
Rubin now says she will work on initiatives involving “fundamental changes to the disability area,” with more trust, structure and coordination of professional expertise around people with disabilities.
The decision drew different responses from other parties.
Katrine Daugaard, social affairs spokesperson for Liberal Alliance, a Danish liberal party, accused Rubin of “running away from an agreement.” She said ending it risks “more uniform, mediocre public services, less specialization, and less freedom of choice.”
Torsten Gejl, political spokesperson for the Alternative, a Danish green party that was not part of the agreement, welcomed the decision.
“The framework agreement for disability, which has tightened the finances in the disability area and made people with disabilities feel like a cost-cutting exercise, was suddenly dropped this evening. That is fantastic,” Gejl wrote on X.
Queen Mary and Minister for Research, Education and Digitalization Christina Egelund will present the Teaching Prize 2026 to teachers from seven higher education institutions.
The award recognizes educators for inspiring and engaging students, the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization said in a press release.
Each recipient receives 500,000 DKK. Of that amount, 200,000 DKK is a personal award, while 300,000 DKK must be used to develop new teaching activities.
The awards will be presented at the Opera in Copenhagen.
“For this year’s seven prize recipients, good teaching is about awakening the students’ curiosity and creating engagement,” Egelund, from the Moderates, said.
She added that the recipients had also created learning environments where students felt comfortable asking questions and making mistakes.
The seven recipients come from different areas of higher education.
Assistant Professor Amalie Trangbæk teaches political science at Aarhus University. Assistant Lecturer Brian Jørgensen teaches communication design at Design School Kolding, while Associate Professor Bjarne Schmidt teaches mathematics, physics and engineering didactics at the University of Southern Denmark.
The other recipients are Associate Professor Lars Plauborg Pedersen from Syddansk Erhvervsakademi, Associate Professor René Kirk Johansen from the maritime and polytechnic education center Martec, Associate Professor Gry Segoli from Københavns Professionshøjskole and Associate Professor Lene Krogstrup Jakobsen from UC SYD in Esbjerg.
Educational institutions nominate candidates for the prize each year. Relevant groups of rectors then assess the nominations and decide which candidates are put forward to the Minister for Research, Education and Digitalization.
Several Danish newspapers said Wednesday that Denmark and Greenland welcomed the new security and defense agreement, even as they raised questions about its consequences.
Berlingske called the deal a “triumph for wise and persistent diplomacy” in an editorial.
“If the agreement turns out to be worth the paper it is written on, foreign policy history was written in New York on Tuesday,” the newspaper wrote.
Politiken described the agreement signed by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen and U.S. President Donald Trump as a “diplomatic masterpiece.”
Politiken said the deal protects Greenland’s territorial integrity, but also described it as a high-risk agreement whose details remain open to interpretation.
Kristeligt Dagblad called it a “historic agreement on the security of the Kingdom of Denmark’s Arctic area” and said the Danish government could be satisfied with the result.
Other newspapers focused more strongly on the risks.
Ekstra Bladet described the agreement as a costly victory. It raised concerns that the U.S. could use Greenland for activities unrelated to NATO, including establishing its “Golden Dome” missile defense system there.
“We are paying a high, but unavoidable price,” Ekstra Bladet wrote. “We can well call it a victory, as long as we remember how dearly it was bought.”
Information described the agreement as a victory for the Kingdom of Denmark but also as a “submission to a tyrannical superior power.”
Despite its positive assessment of the agreement, Berlingske also warned that uncertainty remains because Trump is president.

The leaders of Denmark, Greenland and the United States are expected to sign a security and defense agreement concerning Greenland on Tuesday.
The ceremony is scheduled for 10:30 a.m. local time, or 4:30 p.m. Danish time, at the United Nations headquarters in New York.
The Danish Prime Minister’s Office described it as “a joint agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic region.”
The agreement will be signed by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, US President Donald Trump and Jens-Frederik Nielsen, head of Naalakkersuisut, Greenland’s government.
Few details about the agreement have been released since it was announced Friday.
Trump said on Truth Social that the agreement gives the United States “permanent control over security and all other necessities in Greenland.”
Frederiksen has said the agreement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, as well as Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
“We are not ceding sovereignty, and I can give a guarantee that I never will as Danish prime minister,” Frederiksen told Danish broadcasters DR and TV 2 on Monday.
She said sovereignty could be maintained alongside closer defense cooperation with other countries.
The USA plans to reopen a former military base in Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland and establish a military presence on Greenland’s east coast, Reuters reported Monday.
The eastern site is currently used by the Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, a Danish military unit operating in Greenland.
Reuters attributed the information to three unnamed sources familiar with a defense agreement involving Greenland, Denmark and the USA. Danish public broadcaster DR also reported that the USA plans two new bases.
The agreement’s text has not been published, and its details may change before it is signed, Reuters reported.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, US President Donald Trump and Greenlandic head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen are expected to sign the agreement Tuesday at the United Nations headquarters in New York.
The Danish Prime Minister’s Office said the agreement would strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.
Trump has said it gives the USA “permanent control over security and all other necessities in Greenland.”
Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said the agreement recognizes the Kingdom of Denmark’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
“We do not surrender sovereignty, and I can give a guarantee that I will never do that as Danish prime minister,” Frederiksen told DR and Danish broadcaster TV 2.
More than 20 percent of Nordic teenagers drink energy drinks at least once a day, according to a survey of 4,916 people ages 15 to 19.
The study covered Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden. Six in 10 respondents drank energy drinks at least weekly.
Almost half said they could not get through the day without an energy drink or sometimes felt that way.
The report found that 46 percent began drinking energy drinks at age 14 or younger. One in 10 started before age 12.
Among those who consumed the drinks, 30 percent reported feeling unwell or experiencing other negative health effects. Heart palpitations and sleep problems were among the most common complaints.
“When a habit begins to affect sleep, well-being, or everyday life, there is reason to act,” said Sabina Litens Karlsson, a toxicologist at Livsmedelsverket, Sweden’s national food authority, which conducted the study.
Taste was cited by 73 percent of consumers, while 51 percent wanted more energy and 34 percent wanted to stay awake.
Weekly consumption was highest in Sweden at 75 percent and lowest in Denmark at 43 percent.
Norway has banned sales to people under 16. Denmark has no legal age limit, but its food authority advises children under 15 not to consume energy drinks.
Denmark now expects to complete the final compensation cases for the mink industry in the third quarter of 2028, at least six months later than previously planned.
The Danish Civil Aviation and Railway Authority disclosed the delay in a briefing shared with the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“The decisions on compensation have unfortunately proven to be more time-consuming than assumed,” said Transport and Rural Affairs Minister Signe Munk of the Socialist People’s Party.
The authority previously expected the final cases to be completed during 2027.
The delay is linked to European Commission approval for state aid, which expires on April 1 and cannot be extended.
Officials must prioritize partial decisions determining whether applicants qualify for compensation before that deadline. Two teams have been reassigned to the Mink Secretariat unit preparing those decisions, leaving fewer employees to complete final compensation awards.
The delay could add about 40 million DKK in costs, the authority estimated.
At the beginning of 2026, the total expected cost of compensation, farm demolitions and administration was 29.1 billion DKK.
Denmark ordered all 15 million farmed mink killed in November 2020 over concerns about a mutated coronavirus.
When lawmakers agreed on compensation in 2021, the total bill was expected to be between 15.6 billion DKK and 18.8 billion DKK.

They are expected to take part in the signing of an agreement involving Denmark, Greenland and the United States during the week.

Seven emergency medical vehicles in Denmark’s Central Denmark Region will begin using direct blood pressure monitoring during cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or CPR.
The regional prehospital emergency service said the method could help staff adjust chest compressions and improve survival after cardiac arrests outside hospitals.
“With blood pressure measurements, we get a better idea of whether the cardiopulmonary resuscitation sufficiently drives the blood around the body, or whether we need to adjust and adapt the chest compressions,” emergency doctor Jesper Fjølner said.
Fjølner, who developed the project, said the method had already contributed to successful resuscitation in several cases.
The procedure, called invasive blood pressure measurement, involves placing a catheter with a monitor into an artery. Hospitals already use it to monitor patients in operating rooms and intensive care units.
Using the method outside a hospital is more complex and requires training, equipment and experience.
Chief physician Allan Bach said the service expects the procedure to help resuscitate more people without reducing patient safety or the quality of CPR.
The European Resuscitation Council, which prepares European guidelines for cardiac arrest treatment, recently recommended the method. The Central Denmark service said it is among the first in the world to introduce it.
About 5,000 people experience cardiac arrest outside hospitals in Denmark each year. Around 15 percent survive.
Diabetes patients taking a low dose of Novo’s experimental drug Cagrisema lost more weight than those taking a low dose of Eli Lilly’s tirzepatide in a new study.
Patients receiving 1 milligram of Cagrisema lost an average of 12.4 percent of their weight over 60 weeks, Danish pharmaceutical company Novo said.
Those receiving 5 milligrams of tirzepatide lost 9.1 percent during the same period. Tirzepatide is the active ingredient in Eli Lilly’s approved weight-loss drug Zepbound.
Cagrisema has not been approved. Novo expects the US Food and Drug Administration to decide on its application near the end of 2026.
The treatment combines semaglutide, the active ingredient in Novo’s Wegovy, with a newer substance called cagrilintide. Novo hopes the combination can produce greater weight loss than semaglutide alone.
Results from another study released in February favored tirzepatide. Participants taking tirzepatide lost 25.5 percent of their weight over 84 weeks, compared with 23 percent for those receiving Cagrisema.
Novo shares fell more than 16 percent after those earlier results.
The company released the new findings during its capital markets day. Novo shares were down more than five percent around 1:15 p.m. Monday, and the announcement did not significantly change the share price.
Drivers using Denmark’s Vejlefjord Bridge should expect daily queues and longer travel times while two expansion joints are replaced, the Danish Road Directorate said.
Preparation work will take place during the final two weeks of September. The main repairs will run from early October until early November, with work continuing seven days a week.
Two of the bridge’s five expansion joints in the southbound lanes will be replaced.
Expansion joints are movable sections that allow a bridge to expand and contract as temperatures change. The joints have repeatedly caused problems in recent years, leading to emergency repairs, delays and traffic queues.
The Road Directorate, the Danish government agency responsible for national roads, expects the work to reduce the need for emergency repairs in the near future.
Almost 100,000 vehicles cross the nearly 50-year-old bridge each day.
“When we take lanes for a work area, and road users only have one lane in each direction, queues will occur,” project manager Allan Højgaard Madsen said.
Queues are expected in both directions from about 7 p.m. and for several hours afterward throughout the repair period.
Morning and afternoon rush-hour traffic is expected to face delays only in the southbound direction.
