Three-year-old girl sold into marriage for $9000 under 'walwar' custom sparks international outrage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
07:37:59 UTC
16:37:59 KST

The alleged marriage of a three-year-old girl to a 60-year-old man for 2.5 million Pakistani rupees, around $9,000, has drawn attention to child marriage and the traditional practice of walwar in Pakistan’s southwestern province of Balochistan.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Police in the border city of Chaman arrested the girl’s father, Abdul Baqi, after the case surfaced on social media. The 60-year-old man, identified as Salah Uddin, remains at large.
Walwar is a Pashto term for money paid by a groom or his family to the family of a bride.
At the time police intervened, the alleged marriage existed only on paper because the full walwar payment had not been made. According to The Media Line’s reporting, once the agreed amount was paid, the arrangement would have taken effect, and the 3-year-old would have been regarded as Salah Uddin’s wife.
That did not necessarily mean she would immediately have begun living with him. But she could have remained bound to the arrangement for years if payment was delayed. If her family later attempted to arrange a different marriage after she reached adulthood, the unresolved agreement could have triggered a serious dispute between the families, potentially including violence.
Balochistan case draws widespread outrage
The case drew widespread attention online, prompting Balochistan Chief Minister Mir Sarfraz Bugti to direct authorities to investigate. Police acted after the allegations became public rather than waiting for a formal complaint from a relative.
Israr Ahmed Umrani, assistant inspector general of Balochistan Police for gender issues, told The Media Line that police arrested the girl’s father after receiving information about the case and were pursuing the man identified as her alleged husband.
Umrani said the investigation was continuing and that authorities firmly opposed child marriage.
Chaman Police Subdivisional Police Officer Abdul Jabbar Khan told The Media Line that “a case had been registered on behalf of the State in connection with the incident. Police are looking for the 60-year-old suspect who absconded.”
Khan said the 3-year-old girl, Babbo, and her mother had been placed under police protection.
Asked how many walwar-related cases were currently registered with his police unit, Khan said this was the only one.
The investigation has also become linked to the killing of the girl’s older sister, Shukria Bibi, about two weeks earlier in Kuchlak, on the outskirts of Quetta.
Dispute may have led to murder of child
According to Khan, police allege that Baqi had previously arranged Shukria’s marriage, when she was 13, to Kamran, Salah Uddin’s son, in exchange for a walwar payment of 1.5 million rupees.
Months later, Khan said, Baqi allegedly arranged for his 3-year-old daughter to marry Salah Uddin for 2.5 million rupees. Police say Salah Uddin subsequently demanded that Baqi send his 8-year-old daughter instead.
Khan said a dispute between the families followed, and police were investigating whether it was connected to Shukria’s killing.
Quetta police arrested Shukria’s husband, Kamran, on suspicion of killing her. Police say Kamran told investigators that he became enraged after his wife looked outside through a doorway, then struck her with an iron rod, killing her.
In a Pashto-language interview with a local vlogger before his arrest, Baqi said he had arranged Shukria’s marriage for 1.5 million Pakistani rupees in walwar.
He alleged that she was subjected to violence after the marriage and that her father-in-law, Salah Uddin, repeatedly pressured him to arrange the marriage of another minor daughter.
Baqi said he eventually agreed to marry his 3-year-old daughter to Salah Uddin for 2.5 million rupees, saying poverty and his desire to obtain a home had influenced his decision.
Balochistan law prohibits child marriage. The Balochistan Child Marriages Restraint Act, 2025, sets the minimum marriage age at 18 and makes it a criminal offense for an adult man to enter into a child marriage.
An adult man convicted under the law can face two to three years of rigorous imprisonment and a fine of 100,000 to 200,000 Pakistani rupees. Similar penalties can apply to those who perform, conduct, direct, promote or assist such a marriage.
Police can investigate cases and make arrests without a warrant, and such cases cannot be ended through a private settlement between the parties.
Child marriage remains a substantial problem across Pakistan despite a long-term decline. The Pakistan Demographic and Health Survey for 2017-18, the most recent national survey used for the country’s child-marriage prevalence estimate, found that 18.3% of women ages 20 to 24 had been married by age 18 and 3.6% by age 15. UNICEF’s Child Marriage Data Portal estimates that about 20.5 million girls and women living in Pakistan were married before age 18, including about 5 million who were married before 15.
The figures also show wide differences by geography, wealth and education. UNICEF’s latest available subnational data, from 2018, put the prevalence of marriage before 18 among young women in Balochistan at 21.6%, compared with 18.3% nationally. Across Pakistan, the rate was 21.6% in rural areas and 12.5% in urban areas. It reached 34.1% among the poorest households, compared with 7.3% among the richest, and 33.7% among women with no schooling, compared with 7.5% among those with secondary education or higher.
Yet the existence of laws against child marriage does not mean authorities learn about every case.
There are no reliable province-wide figures showing how widespread walwar remains across Balochistan or how often it involves minors. Interviews conducted for this report indicate that the practice persists mainly in remote, predominantly tribal communities, particularly along or near the Pakistan-Afghanistan border, while becoming less common in cities.
Families may never report such arrangements to police or other state institutions, making the practice difficult to measure.
Enforcement can also run up against a social order in which tribal norms and customary authority strongly influence family decisions. In some remote communities, those traditions can carry greater practical weight in daily life than formal law or religious principles, allowing illegal marriages to be arranged beyond the immediate reach of the state.
Authorities have not publicly specified which provisions of the 2025 law, or any other statutes, have been invoked against Baqi or Salah Uddin.
Critics say walwar becomes especially problematic when the payment is treated primarily as income for the bride’s family, leaving girls with little or no say in marriages arranged on their behalf. They say it can contribute to forced marriages and large age disparities between brides and grooms.
Allauddin Khilji, resident director of the Aurat Foundation in Balochistan, a civil society organization focused on women’s rights and violence against women and girls, said the case appeared to be closely connected to walwar.
Khilji described the practice as a serious problem in tribal society and said disputes surrounding it could contribute to domestic violence and, in some cases, killings.
Balochistan has not enacted legislation specifically prohibiting walwar itself, Khilji said, though child marriages resulting from such arrangements can be prosecuted under the province’s 2025 child marriage law.
He said one obstacle to legislation targeting walwar was the difficulty of challenging deeply rooted tribal traditions and winning support in the provincial assembly, where many members come from influential tribal families.
Khilji cautioned against treating walwar as representative of Pashtun or Baloch culture as a whole, saying the focus should instead be on practices that contribute to coercion, exploitation and child marriage.
Imran Takkar, a child rights activist based in Peshawar, told The Media Line that “such insane marriages” deprive children of fundamental rights to education, protection, recreation and a safe childhood.
Takkar said such cases were not simply social issues but serious child-rights concerns that could violate child-protection laws and Pakistan’s obligations under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, which Pakistan ratified in 1990.
He called for nationwide awareness campaigns drawing on religious teachings, Pakistan’s Constitution, existing laws and the country’s international human-rights commitments, as well as better training and coordination among officials and organizations responsible for child protection, justice and accountability.
Hazar Khan Baluch, a Quetta-based political observer, told The Media Line that “the practice persists because of widespread poverty, limited income opportunities and unemployment, which can leave families financially dependent on receiving walwar.”
But Baluch said money was not the only factor.
Social pressure can encourage families to seek such payments, he said, with some fearing criticism or loss of status if they marry their daughters without receiving walwar. In some communities, large payments can also become a source of prestige.
Family authority and customary expectations can reinforce the practice even when financial need is not the sole consideration.
Opposition to walwar exists, Baluch said, and some families that have moved to urban areas have abandoned it. He called for greater access to education and sustained public awareness campaigns to reduce practices that can leave girls vulnerable to coercion and abuse.
The Media Line also spoke with Islamic cleric Hafiz Iqbal Muhammed about whether walwar and the marriage of young girls have a religious basis.
He said that “Islamic teachings do not prescribe walwar or any similar bride-price customs, as these practices hold no basis in the core principles governing Islamic marriage.”
Muhammed said marriage in Islam is based on mutual consent and that cultural customs cannot override rights granted under Islamic teachings.
“Islamic law fundamentally recognizes a woman’s right to consent to marriage and strictly forbids forcing her into a union against her will,” he said.
Muhammed said customs followed in the name of tradition should not be confused with religious requirements.

The Australian national health care database was hacked by an OpenAI agent, marking the first identified case of AI hacking a government network, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Wednesday.

Australian government orders urgent review of AI rules and governance
The Australian government has initiated an urgent review of its approach to artificial intelligence.
According to a government statement, the review will assess whether current laws and governance frameworks are “fit for purpose” when it comes to preparing for and responding to cyber incidents involving AI.
The Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet will lead the review, which will also examine how Australia shares information with AI companies and other Commonwealth nations.
The government said the findings will contribute to its wider efforts to develop an effective framework for AI governance.
The move comes just a week after OpenAI released reports outlining six incidents involving unexpected or potentially concerning behavior by its AI models. The company also announced plans to monitor and publicly disclose similar incidents in the future.
The reports covered incidents identified between April and August. However, they do not appear to include the latest incident, which OpenAI said it became aware of in June.

Moon once had own magnetic field: Swiss research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
07:34:27 UTC
16:34:27 KST

Moon once had own magnetic field: Swiss research
The Moon once had its own magnetic field, according to Swiss researchers who analysed data collected by probes flying over the far side of the Moon.
The analysis, published on Wednesday in the specialist journal Science Advances, lends support to the theory of a phenomenon known as a ‘geodynamo’ in the Moon’s core.
On Earth, the magnetic field is generated deep within the planet. In the outer core, liquid iron is in constant motion. This movement generates electric currents which, in turn, create the Earth’s magnetic field.
This process is known as a ‘geodynamo’, much like a bicycle dynamo, which converts movement into electrical energy. This magnetic field surrounds the Earth and protects it, in particular, from the charged particles of the solar wind.
Unlike the Earth, the Moon currently has no magnetic field. The question of whether this was different in the past has, until now, been the subject of scientific controversy, writes the Swiss federal technology institute ETH Zurich.
More
Switzerland eyes mediation role amid rising risk of conflict in outer space
Rock samples collected during the Apollo space missions had provided conflicting evidence.
Conflicting data
For their new study, Swiss researchers did not use rock samples, but rather measurements of gravity and the magnetic field taken by probes orbiting the Moon. The analysis focused on the Dewar region, located on the far side of the Moon.
Using this data, they developed a model of the subsurface structure. According to this model, there is a rocky strata approximately 60km wide and up to 9km deep.
This area is thought to be denser than the surrounding lunar crust and strongly magnetised. Taken together with the geochemical data and topography, this evidence suggests the presence of solidified magma originating from an underground volcanic complex.
Based on the iron content, the researchers estimated that the Moon’s magnetic field was at least 10 microteslas 4.2 billion years ago. This represents between one-fifth and one-third of the current strength of the Earth’s magnetic field, which is approximately 50 microteslas.
The researchers have ruled out the possibility that a massive meteorite impact could have caused this magnetisation.
As the Dewar region is located outside the exposed zones, it is still unclear how the Moon’s relatively small core could have generated such a powerful magnetic field.

Video: Finnish workers report high levels of work-related stress
Finland

10:27:27 EEST
16:27:27 KST

Forty-five percent of Finnish workers say their work has caused or worsened stress, depression or anxiety, according to a recent OSH Pulse survey by the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work's recent
The figure was among the highest figures in the EU, second only to Greece.
The answers given by Finnish respondents suggest excessive job demands are one factor, with 51 percent reporting severe time pressure or work overload, compared with 44 percent across the EU.
Meanwhile, 46 percent reported fatigue caused or worsened by work, compared with 37 percent across the EU.
Another factor may be problems within organisations themselves. Some 42 percent of Finnish respondents experienced poor communication or cooperation at work, compared with 29 percent across the EU.
Economic uncertainty may also play a role. Finland has experienced prolonged weak economic growth, while 40 percent of working-age Finns said in a separate Finnish Institute of Occupational Health survey that they were worried about what their jobs would look like in the future.
However, cross-country comparisons should be treated with caution, as differences may partly reflect how people recognise and report these experiences.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union, following the setup of Russian control over Crimea, more than 4,000 Ukrainian children without parental care were declared Russian citizens. Despite formal requests from the Ukrainian government, Russian authorities refused to hand them over and instead initiated illegal adoption procedures.
The European Court of Human Rights granted the application priority and departed from standard practice by holding oral hearings on both admissibility and merits due to the significance of the case.
The legal application was originally submitted in January 2023 by the Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union acting on behalf of the ten children. The claim states that these children were subjected to forced citizenship changes, listed on Russian adoption platforms, and placed into Russian foster or adoptive families.
The applicant argues that these cumulative actions constitute an enforced disappearance. The case relies on Article 5 regarding the right to liberty and security, alleging unlawful detention and location concealment. It also cites Article 8 on respect for private life, arguing that imposing Russian citizenship erased their social identity as Ukrainians.
The International Bar Association’s Human Rights Institute entered the proceedings as an independent third party to assist the court. The organization urged the court to account for the vulnerability of conflict-affected children, address procedural rules when explicit consent cannot be obtained from minor victims, and evaluate the broader systemic policy of identity removal.
The Ukrainian government also participated as a third party, represented by the Ministry of Justice, which linked the case to larger inter-state legal claims against Russia regarding Crimean occupations.
Russian authorities failed to submit rebuttal arguments and did not attend the hearing despite receiving all case documentation. The court will deliver its ruling at a later date following deliberation on oral and written statements.
The identities of the ten children remain confidential under court anonymity orders.
“When Russia occupied Crimea, these children were between one and five years old. Their guardian was the Ukrainian state, and since then it has been unable to receive an answer to a simple question: where are they. Today, these are already teenagers who may be living with foreign citizenship and in foreign families. Justice for them is not just about punishing the guilty. It is the right of every child and their loved ones to know the truth: where they are, who they are with, and who decided they are no longer Ukrainian. This is the fundamental importance of this case,” said Maksym Maksymov, head of Bring Kids Back UA.
“This case is about much more than ten children. It represents thousands of Ukrainian children whose whereabouts remain unknown and whose identity, family ties, and future have been systematically destroyed. The Court has an opportunity to clearly state that these children are not collateral damage of war, but victims of a systematic policy that requires accountability,” said Lady Helena Kennedy, director of IBAHRI.
The events in Crimea from 2014 build upon previous legal findings by the European Court of Human Rights in inter-state decisions against Russia. Additionally, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants on March 17, 2023, for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children.
The legal effort aligns with Bring Kids Back UA, an initiative established by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy alongside international partners to secure the return of all deported Ukrainian children and develop protection mechanisms. These efforts build on foundational work, including two White Papers published in 2024 regarding child protection and reintegration.
Previously, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that over 2,100 Ukrainian children forcibly taken by Russia had been successfully returned as part of the "Bring Kids Back UA" initiative.
According to his statement, this figure included 150 children who had been repatriated since the beginning of 2026.
The update followed a report presented by initiative representatives Oleksandr Bevz and Maksym Maksymov, after which Zelenskyy expressed gratitude to international partners for their support, noted the recent UN classification of the forced deportations as a crime against humanity, and highlighted upcoming coalition meetings aimed at securing further returns.

In the United States, a court overturned Trump&apos;s ban on media outlets in the White House and ordered access to be restored

In the United States, a court overturned Trump's ban on media outlets in the White House and ordered access to be restored
Kyiv • UNN
A federal court ruled Trump's ban on CNN, MS NOW, and Politico unconstitutional. The administration must immediately restore the journalists' press passes.
A federal judge on Thursday ordered U.S. President Donald Trump to restore White House access for journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico, ruling that his ban on the three media outlets was unconstitutional. Reuters reports, UNN writes.
Details
U.S. District Judge Tim Kelly issued the ruling in a case brought by the news organizations challenging the ban announced by the Republican president on September 18.
Kelly ordered the Trump administration to immediately return the press passes to the media outlets and barred officials from enforcing the ban for 14 days. The judge rejected the government’s claim that the ban was motivated by national security concerns.
"The record contains no factual support for defendants’ contention that revoking plaintiffs’ permanent passes would in fact protect national security or that national security would be threatened if the Court ordered their passes reinstated while this case is litigated," he said, adding that Trump himself had stated that the ban was related to the media outlets’ materials’ "likely lack of truthfulness and negative character."
The White House and media representatives did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Trump previously said on social media that these media outlets "should not be allowed to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES." The U.S. Department of Justice, meanwhile, sought to justify the ban on national security grounds.
Addendum
CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed a lawsuit in federal court in Washington on Monday. They argue that the ban violates the freedoms of speech and of the press guaranteed by the First Amendment, as well as the right to due process. The media outlets asked the court to temporarily lift the restrictions and restore their access to the White House.
At a hearing on Wednesday, Kelly said that two decisions by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit affirm journalists’ right to due process before their press passes are revoked. According to him, the White House appears not to have given the three media outlets a meaningful opportunity to challenge the decision.
A Justice Department attorney said that the administration had provided sufficient justification in letters sent to the media outlets on Tuesday. However, Kelly noted that they were sent only after the passes had been revoked and the lawsuit filed. In court filings, the Justice Department also argued that access to the White House is a privilege, not a right, and that the president has the authority to restrict it for media outlets.

US judge orders Trump administration to restore banned mainstream media access to White House

A US federal judge on Thursday ordered the Trump administration to immediately restore White House access for reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico after they were banned from the premises.
US President Donald Trump barred the outlets from the White House on Friday as punishment for distributing what he branded as "fake news" and "fiction and lies."
CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed a joint lawsuit seeking a temporary restraining order against the ban, arguing it violates the First Amendment of the US Constitution, which upholds the right to a free press.
Judge Timothy Kelly found that revoking press passes "likely violated their constitutional due process rights," according to the ruling.
"The 'general rule' is that 'individuals must receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before the Government deprives them' of a constitutionally protected interest," Kelly wrote.
The billionaire former reality TV star has long attacked media outlets that have aired critical coverage of his campaigns and administrations, repeatedly blasting the press as the "enemy of the people."
The ban comes at a time when his approval ratings are at record lows, his Republican Party risks losing control of Congress in November's midterm elections, and the US-Iran war drags on with no end in sight.

CIA reportedly warns of Russian plans to attack Spain, France or Italy with sea-launched drones
Spanish newspaper El Mundo has learned from its sources that the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) has warned of Russian plans to attack Spain, France or Italy using drones launched from ships at sea.
Source: European Pravda, citing an El Mundo report
Details: The newspaper reports that European foreign ministries have received a detailed report prepared following CIA Director John Ratcliffe's visit to Moscow.
According to information from the Lithuanian government, Russia plans to launch Gerbera drones with a range of 600 km from ships. Russia is thus reportedly preparing new drone attacks in Europe, this time targeting Mediterranean countries.
"They will use drones launched from the sea, concealed in a container on a ship. It is not difficult at all," a source told the newspaper.
El Mundo's sources say the governments of Spain, France and Italy have also been informed that Russia was preparing a possible drone operation against one of these countries. The warning coincides with an unusual move by Emmanuel Macron: after convening a meeting of the Defence Council on 16 September, two days later he invited the leaders of all parties and candidates in the 2027 presidential election to the Élysée Palace.
Several defence analysts interviewed by the newspaper confirmed that they were aware of the existence of a CIA report that had been circulated among European foreign ministries.
The attacks are reportedly being prepared specifically against France, Italy and Spain because elections will be held there in 2027 and right-wing political forces are already gaining support.
El Mundo says the main purpose of the Russian operation would not be to cause significant destruction. With an explosive payload of around four to five kilograms, a Gerbera drone would more likely be used to shut down an airport, start a fire, fly over a military facility or demonstrate that Russia is capable of reaching Europe's rear areas.
Background:
- Moscow has repeatedly stated that supplying Ukraine with weapons, intelligence and military advisers makes Western countries participants in the war and legitimate targets.
- However, Russia has so far sought to avoid crossing the "threshold of war" by refraining from actions that could provoke a coordinated NATO response, while testing the Alliance's reaction through individual incidents in Poland and the Baltic states. In particular, on 15 September, Italian fighter jets on a NATO patrol mission shot down a drone that had entered Lithuanian airspace. On 23 September, a Russian Mi-8 helicopter violated Polish airspace.
- An Italian media outlet published an investigation by Rome prosecutors that uncovered a network of Russian spies at the Russian embassies in Italy and the Vatican.

Switzerland maintains efforts to find global peace: foreign minister

Switzerland maintains efforts to find global peace: foreign minister
Switzerland intends to continue offering its diplomatic channels to help unblock peace processes that have stalled in the conflicts in Iran and Ukraine, Swiss foreign minister, Ignazio Cassis, said at the UN in New York.
Bern could facilitate talks and launch the first initiatives, but it does not have the political and military power of the United States to compel the parties to the conflict to reach a compromise, he added.
“Without the United States, not much happens in this world,” Cassis told media representatives in New York. “Despite all their weaknesses, despite a style that we may not like, and despite [President Donald Trump’s] choice of words, which are not always appropriate.”
More
Explainer: Why does Switzerland host peace talks?
Since 1980, Switzerland has represented the interests of the US in Iran. This role has helped to keep a channel of communication open between Washington and Tehran, even during the most difficult times.
In New York, Cassis also met with Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi. Thanks to its access to Iran, Switzerland can facilitate talks at a discreet level. The main objective is not so much to reach spectacular agreements as to make the dialogue itself possible.
According to Cassis, dialogue with the Gulf Cooperation Council – comprising Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman – should be strengthened in light of the growing regional interconnection of the Middle East conflict.
In February, at the World Economic Forum in Davos, a consultation mechanism was agreed upon. The participating states are to hold regular discussions on political issues and assess possible joint initiatives.
More
Need a diplomatic messenger? Switzerland is eager to help
Lavorov meeting
As stated on the social media platform X, Cassis also met his Russian counterpart, Sergei Lavrov, during the UN General Assembly. They took stock of Switzerland’s chairmanship of the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) since Cassis’s visit to Moscow in February and are said to have discussed the next steps regarding the OSCE’s agenda.
As for the conflict in Ukraine, Cassis believes that Switzerland’s role lies primarily in diplomatic efforts. As the current chair of the OSCE, Switzerland could draw on the organisation’s tools and experience to support a negotiated solution. Actual mediation between Moscow and Kyiv must now come from the US.
Cassis identified the lack of willingness on the part of both states to take a decisive step as the main obstacle to peace. Both sides continue to believe they can win the war militarily.
Cassis and Guy Parmelin, who was in New York in his capacity as President of the Swiss Confederation, have now returned to Switzerland.

In Tunisia, a tribute to Claudia Cardinale: movies under the stars in La Goulette
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:20:37 CEST
16:20:37 KST

One year after the actress’s passing—who was also known as “the most beautiful Italian woman in Tunis”—the Italian Embassy and the Italian Cultural Institute in Tunis, in collaboration with Cinématdour, a Tunisian traveling cinema project, are organizing on September 27, in the presence of her granddaughter Lucille Cristaldi, a free outdoor screening of the film “L’Île du pardon” by Tunisian director Ridha Béhi. The choice of La Goulette gives this tribute a significance that goes beyond the purely cinematic. Cardinale, born in Tunis in 1938 to an Italian family of Sicilian origin, grew up in the port town and its “Little Sicily,” a place where Tunisians, Italians, Maltese, and French people, as well as communities of different faiths, lived side by side for decades. In May 2022, during one of her final visits to Tunisia, a street and the large mural in La Goulette—in front of which Sunday’s screening will take place—were dedicated to her. “I still feel a little Tunisian,” Cardinale had said during that visit, recalling her family’s Tunisia as a land of “sharing, joy, and exchange.” The actress had also emphasized the importance of preserving the shared past between the two shores of the Mediterranean, recalling how Tunisia had been a welcoming land for generations of Italians. This connection makes the choice of *L’Île du pardon* particularly meaningful. Ridha Béhi’s film, released in 2022 and among the last in which Cardinale starred, is set in 1950s Tunisia and tells, through the story of an Italian Christian family, of the coexistence of different communities, cultures, and religions. Filmed in Djerba, the feature film—in which Cardinale masterfully portrays Agostina—was presented in the international competition at the Cairo International Film Festival. The screening in La Goulette thus takes the form of a return to her roots: an actress who became one of the icons of Italian and international cinema is honored in the Tunisian neighborhood where her Mediterranean identity took shape, through a Tunisian film that addresses precisely the themes of memory, coexistence, and the encounter between cultures. And the collaboration with Cinémadtour reinforces this dimension. Cinema leaves the theater and returns to the urban space, in front of Cardinale’s portrait painted on a building in the old Piccola Sicilia neighborhood—a place that continues to represent one of the most visible symbols of the historical and cultural intertwining between Italy and Tunisia. In addition to Cinémadtour, the initiative also includes Bif&st, the Bari International Film & TV Festival, and the Tunisian association Ciné-Sud Patrimoine as partners.

China’s secretive spaceplane recaptures its own satellite
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
07:19:27 UTC
16:19:27 KST

- China's Shenlong spaceplane released a subsatellite in June, retrieved it in July, then redeployed and recaptured it again by Sept. 13, according to tracking data.
- Shenlong has repeated similar release-and-recapture sequences on its previous two missions, and China has disclosed few details about the vehicle's purpose.
China’s spaceplane has spent the past three months releasing, retrieving, and then recapturing the same small satellite in orbit, according to a timeline astrophysicist Jonathan McDowell posted Sept. 23 based on U.S. Space Force tracking data. It’s the clearest look yet at what the vehicle, known unofficially as Shenlong, has been doing during its fourth trip to orbit.
According to McDowell, Shenlong released the satellite, cataloged as object 2026-024H, on June 21 and brought it back aboard around July 12, likely using a robotic arm. In late August, the spaceplane released the same satellite a second time and moved several thousand kilometers away. It then closed back in for a new rendezvous on Sept. 10 and recaptured the satellite again on Sept. 13. U.S. tracking systems briefly logged what looked like a second object during this period, but McDowell said he believes that was a duplicate catalog entry for the same satellite rather than a new one.
China has never officially named the vehicle or released its technical specifications. “Shenlong,” meaning “Divine Dragon,” is the label trackers and space enthusiasts have settled on based on years of outside observation, since Beijing has said almost nothing about the program directly. The vehicle launches on a rocket and lands on a runway, a configuration that draws frequent comparisons to the U.S. Space Force’s X-37B, another spaceplane whose missions are also largely classified.
This is not the first time Shenlong has repeated this pattern. On its second mission, which ran from August 2022 to May 2023, observers tracked the spaceplane deploying an object and recovering it more than once. Its third mission, spanning December 2023 to September 2024, included a similar sequence. The current flight launched Feb. 6 from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, and the tracking firm LeoLabs first detected the newly released satellite in June, noting the behavior matched what Shenlong had done on earlier missions.
The maneuvers Shenlong keeps practicing, closing in on an object, grabbing it, and letting it go again, fall under a category analysts call rendezvous and proximity operations. Those skills could support satellite servicing, but the same techniques could also be used to inspect, disable, or capture another country’s satellite without permission, which is why Western analysts track each instance closely.
The Secure World Foundation, a space policy nonprofit, has noted that the U.S. X-37B has never approached or rendezvoused with another object in orbit during its public missions and generally operates below the altitudes where most working satellites sit, a contrast that has fueled continued attention on Shenlong’s behavior.

Indifference, the view from Gaza on UNGA amid Israel's genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
07:17:46 UTC
16:17:46 KST

Breadcrumb
Indifference, the view from Gaza on the UN General Assembly amid Israel's genocidal war
For many Palestinians in Gaza, the annual gathering of world leaders in New York at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) has become increasingly disconnected from the reality they face in their war-torn territory.
As the 81st session of the UNGA enters its third day, world leaders and senior officials are discussing wars, global crises and the future of the Palestinian issue, with Gaza once again taking centre stage in speeches and diplomatic meetings.
Today, Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu set scheduled to speak, despite being wanted by the International Criminal Court for crimes against humanity and other war crimes. Meanwhile, Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas was denied a visa to the United States, and will speak via video.
After nearly three years of the Israeli genocidal war, displacement and destruction, many Palestinians in Gaza, speaking separately to The New Arab, said they were focused on immediate concerns such as finding food and clean water, securing shelter, earning a living and protecting their children from the consequences of a war that continues to shape every aspect of their lives.
Three UN sessions, the same questions
The current General Assembly meeting is the third to take place since the Israeli genocidal war began in October 2023.
The proceedings are difficult to separate from the previous two sessions and what followed them for many Palestinians.
Mohammed Abu Jarad, a displaced man living with his family in a tent in central Gaza, told TNA that he finds it difficult to attach much significance to another round of international meetings.
"This is the third time the UNGA convened during the war. What was the outcome of the previous two times?" he asked. "Did the war stop? Did the UN, or the countries that gathered, manage to stop Israel from continuing the killing and bombing?"
"Each time, we heard about meetings and calls to end the war, protect civilians and allow aid to enter, only to return to the same reality. Israel persists, appearing stronger on the ground each time, while receiving American support, and we see the international community remaining silent in the face of what is happening to us," he added.
The question reflects a broader frustration among Gaza's residents who have watched successive diplomatic initiatives unfold while their own circumstances have continued to deteriorate.
Hadi Kamal, another Gaza-based man, told TNA that the repeated meetings have made many Palestinians focus less on the speeches themselves and more on their consequences.
"We have watched the General Assembly convene time and again since the war began. What has changed for us?" he said. "Gaza is still being killed and destroyed, people remain displaced, and Israel continues to control parts of the Strip and impose a new reality, while there is now talk of displacing the population."
"We aren't saying that General Assembly meetings are worthless, but we do question the results. If nations gather and issue statements, only for Israel to go right back to what it was doing, what are we supposed to expect from a third meeting?" he added.
World leaders talk peace, but do nothing
Gaza remains central to international discussions in New York.
French President Emmanuel Macron criticised what he described as the international community's failure to act over Gaza, while advocating recognition of a Palestinian state and warning about Israeli actions in the occupied West Bank.
At a high-level meeting on Palestine and the two-state solution, UN Secretary-General António Guterres also warned against measures that undermine the possibility of an independent and geographically contiguous Palestinian state, citing settlement activity, settler violence and other developments.
US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, met Arab and Muslim leaders in New York, with Gaza and Iran among the issues discussed. Trump spoke of a "historic peace agreement" for Gaza.
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas participated in the high-level meeting by video link after the US refused to grant him a visa to attend the UN General Assembly in person.
According to the Palestinian news agency Wafa, Abbas said 160 countries had recognised the State of Palestine and called for an end to the war, an Israeli withdrawal, reconstruction and a political process leading to Palestinian statehood.
Yet these diplomatic developments have failed to generate the same level of attention among many Palestinians as they might have before the war.
Jamila Abu Sweireb, from al-Nuseirat refugee camp, recalled how closely she followed international meetings at the beginning of Israel's genocidal war.
"At the start of the genocide, we followed every word from the United Nations and every international meeting. We thought the world would stop the war," she said.
"Over time, people lost interest because they saw no tangible outcome. Today, when we hear about a new meeting, we immediately ask: Will anything actually change in Gaza this time?" she added.
A widening gap between words and reality
Gaza-based political analyst Ahed Ferwana told TNA that the indifference among some residents in Gaza reflects their experience of the war and what they perceive as a gap between international positions and their ability to influence events.
"The average citizen in Gaza has come to view the international position through the lens of its results," he said. "They might welcome any stance calling for an end to the war or supporting Palestinian rights, but ultimately, they ask: What has actually changed on the ground?"
He added that residents were no longer asking simply what governments could say, but what they could do.
"Can they stop the war? Can they protect civilians? Can they ensure delivery of aid? And can they prevent Israel from continuing its operations?" he said.
He explained that, from the perspective of Gaza's population, Israel had continued its operations despite international criticism, while US support remained an important factor in the course of the war.
"That is why citizens feel that Israel returns stronger each time, whereas international statements remain powerless to bring about the change they are waiting for," he continued.
Akram Atallah, another political analyst, similarly argued that Gazans have little opportunity to engage in international diplomacy as a separate issue from their daily survival.
"For the citizens in Gaza, the crisis is not a distant political issue but a matter of daily life," he told TNA. "They are living in a tent, have lost their home or a family member, or are searching for food, water and medicine. Naturally, their concern for what is happening on the ground far outweighs their interest in a meeting in New York."
"There is a gap between international rhetoric and the ability to implement it," Atallah added. "The Palestinian citizen clearly sees this gap because they live with its consequences every day."

Asian Games | Feature: From Olympic rings to Asian Games gold, China's Alex Hua Tian finds joy in every stride
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:12:24 CST
16:12:24 KST

by sportswriter Zhang Can
TOKYO, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- Alex Hua Tian was relaxed when he sat down for an interview ahead of the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games.
The 36-year-old Chinese rider spoke enthusiastically about the competition, his horse and a career that has taken him to four Olympic Games and, now, another Asian Games title.
Hua chose a spot outside the Tokyo Olympic Museum, beneath the Olympic rings. It was a fitting setting for a rider whose career has been closely associated with the Olympic and Asian Games, and with the horses that have accompanied him along the way.
Hua arrived in Tokyo with a clear objective: to defend the individual eventing title he won at the Hangzhou Asian Games in 2023. On Wednesday, he achieved that goal.
Riding nine-year-old Manjushri, also known as Bodhi or Miaojixiang, Hua finished on his dressage score of 26.90 penalty points to retain the title. He produced a clear show jumping round on Tuesday before completing the cross-country phase in 6 minutes 49 seconds on Wednesday, 11 seconds inside the seven-minute optimum time and without adding any penalties.
For a rider defending an Asian Games title, however, the pressure was never far away.
"I'm just very relieved, mainly," Hua said afterward. "Obviously, there's some pressure coming into a championship when you're defending a gold medal, but also bringing such a good horse like Miaojixiang."
The final phase was made more demanding by rain and a technical course featuring numerous turns. Hua later said he had been concerned about the slippery ground and the challenge of managing Miaojixiang's big stride on a twisting track. After the first few obstacles, however, he was able to find his rhythm, trust the horse and relax.
That trust has been years in the making. Hua has trained Miaojixiang since the horse was five. He describes him as "very greedy" and says food is "number one for him." The horse also has "quite a cuddly personality," affectionate while sometimes preferring his own personal space.
But once he enters the competition arena, the personality changes. "He really wants to work with you in training and in competition," Hua said before the Games. That was one of the reasons he believed the horse could be reliable and competitive in Tokyo.
For Hua, that relationship is at the heart of eventing. Horses, he explained, are prey animals that have evolved over millions of years to flee from perceived threats, including humans. Building enough trust to work together as one is what makes the sport so special to him.
"It's a very addictive feeling," he said, comparing it to a musician searching for the perfect pitch.
That sense of connection was also visible after the finish. In the mixed zone, Hua exchanged high-fives with journalists and stayed for some time, smiling, greeting people and sharing the moment after his victory.
Beneath the easy smile, however, is a rider who has spent years learning how little can be left to chance in eventing. Dressage demands precision and harmony. Show jumping requires accuracy and control. Cross-country demands speed, courage and trust. A championship result requires all three to come together at the right time.
Hua arrived in Tokyo after another landmark result in his career. He finished 12th with Chicko at the 2026 FEI Eventing World Championships in Aachen, the best-ever result by a Chinese rider at the eventing world championships. But he deliberately chose a different horse for the Asian Games, believing Miaojixiang's strength in dressage made him better suited to the competition.
For Hua, though, the gold was not only personal. "The most important thing is that I didn't let the team down," Hua said. "So I'm very, very, very happy about that."
As China's national equestrian team goes through a generational transition, Hua has become its most experienced member. Looking at the younger riders, he said, "They are the next generation of Chinese equestrian sport. They are the future of the sport."
Beyond competition, Hua has also devoted himself to making equestrian sport more accessible in China. Since 2017, he has been involved in the "Horsemanship Movement", which introduces children to horses and teaches them about horse care and safety.
For Hua, the future of the sport is not only about producing more competitive riders, but also about helping more people understand and experience the connection between humans and horses.
"I hope to make equestrian more widespread and more accessible," he said.
His latest Asian Games victory adds another chapter to a long continental career. He won individual silver at the 2014 Incheon Games and bronze at Jakarta in 2018 before taking individual and team gold at Hangzhou in 2023. His latest title gives him a second consecutive individual Asian Games gold.
Yet Hua's reflections on the sport rarely center solely on medals. For him, the defining element remains the partnership between horse and rider.
The horse changes, as do the course, weather and circumstances. The challenge is to build enough trust and understanding that, when everything comes together, horse and rider can perform as one.
"When it comes together, and you feel like one," he said. "And it's very, very special." ■

Coral reproduction study sheds light on reef recovery
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:12:23 CST
16:12:23 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have identified the reproductive timing of two key coral species at the state of Western Australia's Ningaloo Reef, providing a baseline that could help monitor reef recovery and guide restoration efforts.
Researchers visited Ningaloo Reef off the Western Australian coast to investigate Porites corals, a group of reef-building corals that play a major role in creating and maintaining reef habitats throughout the Indo-Pacific, according to a statement released Thursday by Australia's Curtin University.
For the first time, the team determined when some of Ningaloo Reef's key corals reproduce, providing a baseline to track marine heatwave impacts, reef recovery and restoration opportunities, the statement said.
Understanding coral reproduction was essential because reefs could not recover unless corals successfully produced the next generation, said PhD candidate David Juszkiewicz from Curtin's Coral Conservation and Research Group.
A damaged reef recovers because surviving corals produce offspring that go on to "replenish and rebuild the reef," said Juszkiewicz, lead author of the study published in Marine Biology.
The researchers examined 20 coral colonies from Ningaloo Reef and found evidence that two important reef-building species, Porites lutea and Porites lobata, were preparing to spawn during the reef's annual early autumn mass spawning period, providing the first reproductive baseline for these species at Ningaloo.
No signs of reproduction were found in a third species, Porites australiensis, suggesting it may spawn at a different time of year and highlighting the need for year-round monitoring, according to the study.
The researchers said the regional differences in reproductive timing could mean the populations are reproductively isolated, potentially limiting their ability to replenish each other after marine heatwaves or cyclones. ■

UN calls for renewed efforts to realize right to development
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:12:19 CST
16:12:19 KST

This photo taken on Sept. 23, 2026 shows a scene of a high-level meeting to commemorate the 40th anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development held on the sidelines of the 81st Session of the UN General Assembly at the UN headquarters in New York. (Xinhua/Zhang Fengguo)
by Ada Zhang
UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- UN officials and representatives of member states on Wednesday called for renewed efforts to realize the right to development at a high-level meeting to commemorate the 40th anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development.
UN General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman said that progress remains uneven while the past four decades have seen major gains in global human development.
"Development is not merely about economic growth. It is a comprehensive economic, social, cultural and political process," Rahman said at the meeting held on the sidelines of the 81st Session of the UN General Assembly in New York.
Adopted by the General Assembly on Dec 4, 1986, the declaration recognizes development as an inalienable human right and affirms that every person and all peoples are entitled to participate in, contribute to, and enjoy economic, social, cultural and political development.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said the declaration recognizes that "development, human rights and international cooperation must advance together."
Despite progress over the decades, "the promise of development faces new tests," Guterres said.
"Inequalities are widening, leaving countries and communities behind," he said, adding that rising debt, conflicts and economic instability are impeding development and economic growth.
Guterres also pointed to climate change and new technologies as growing challenges. While artificial intelligence and the digital revolution hold "enormous potential to improve lives," they can also become "drivers of exclusion and division," he said.
"This anniversary reminds us that development, human rights and peace are not separate ambitions," Guterres said. "They advance together."
Sun Lei, charge d'affaires of China's Permanent Mission to the United Nations, called for joint efforts to advance common development and create a fair environment for development. All countries have an equal right to pursue economic and social development and improve the living standards of their people, Sun said.
He called for upholding multilateralism, building balanced and inclusive development partnerships, and opposing unilateral sanctions and additional tariffs.
Sun also called for joint efforts to address emerging challenges related to artificial intelligence, climate change and public health, and to advance the formulation of a Convention on the Right to Development. Realizing the right to development is an ongoing endeavor, he said.
Representatives of developing countries also called for stronger international cooperation and changes to the global financial system to address obstacles to development.
Speaking on behalf of the African Group, a Burundian representative said the declaration remains "a blueprint and a reference in addressing inequalities within and between developed and developing countries."
The group called for the "meaningful operationalization of the right to development," stressing that development should not be limited to economic growth but should also include "the enhancement of human well-being and the realization of individuals' full potential."
The group stressed that countries, particularly those historically marginalized or exploited, should have the right to pursue their own development paths without external interference.
European Council President Antonio Costa said development "is not just about economic growth" but also concerns "the rights, dignity and freedom of all persons and their ability to shape their own future."
Sustainable development, democracy, good governance, the rule of law and respect for human rights "reinforce each other and demand the same emphasis," Costa said.
"If we are serious about the right to development, we must also be serious about building a more just, more inclusive and more effective multilateral system," he said. ■

(Xinhua/Zhang Fengguo)

Asian Games | China finishes 1-2 in women's mountain bike cross-country at Asian Games
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24

16:12:14 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- China's Wu Zhifan and Liang Zhenglan claimed gold and silver respectively in the women's mountain bike cross-country event at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Thursday.
Wu pulled away from her teammate on the final lap to cross the line first in one hour, 26 minutes and 14 seconds, while Liang finished 51 seconds behind. Indonesia's Dewi Sayu Bella Sukma took bronze in one hour and 28 minutes.
The race, held at Obata Ryokuchi Park, featured 16 riders competing over seven laps and a total distance of 25.9 kilometers.
Unlike road cycling, mountain bike cross-country courses feature natural and artificial obstacles including rocks, tree roots and steep drops. Riders must constantly adjust their pace and racing lines on climbs and descents, testing both endurance and bike-handling skills.
Dewi led after the opening lap, with Wu and Liang in second and third. The two Chinese riders moved into the top two positions on the second lap, but Dewi remained close behind. By the end of the fourth lap, she had cut the gap to the leader to just 11 seconds.
"The rider behind us was pushing quite hard in the first few laps, so we took turns at the front. Whoever felt better would set the pace," Wu said after the race.
"Our first priority was to open up a gap over the others, because we both felt that the most important thing was to make sure the gold medal belonged to China," she added.
The Chinese pair gradually extended their advantage over the rest of the field, while the battle between them remained close. On the final lap, Wu broke clear and built a 51-second advantage before crossing the finish line.
Speaking about their exchanges at the front, Liang said that once they had established a sufficient gap over their rivals, "whoever had the ability could go ahead."
Although she missed out on gold, Liang said she was equally pleased to see her teammate win.
"It doesn't matter whether she wins or I win. We're both representing China," Liang said. "As long as the gold medal goes to China, that's what matters."
China coach Tong Weisong said the team had conducted heat-acclimatization training in Yunnan Province ahead of the Games and carried out race simulations focusing on training volume, intensity and technical weaknesses.
Mountain biking became an official Asian Games sport at Bangkok 1998. China has won the women's cross-country gold medal at every edition of the Asian Games in which the event has been contested.
Tong said the race had provided valuable major-event experience for the Chinese riders, while noting that they still trail leading European and American competitors in technical ability.
He added that the team would continue to work on technical skills over obstacles, high-speed riding and endurance. ■

Around 70 people in Netherlands branded “security threat”
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Dutch immigration ministry has labelled around 70 people a threat to national security in the past 10 years, revoking residency permits and, in the case of dual nationals, their passports.
The figures from IND were uncovered in an investigation by Nieuwsuur.
Most of those have been convicted of terrorism-related offences, the news programme found. Three of the men involved in planning an attack in Arnhem were among those given the designation.
Not everybody on the list is a terrorist. A Russian national who is suspected of stealing secrets from Dutch chip machinery makers ASML was also labelled a threat.
The justice ministry would not confirm how many people on the list were still in custody.
Dual nationals or foreigners who are classed as a threat to national security are deported and banned from re-entering the Netherlands. However, not everyone has actually left the country.
In May, the justice ministry acknowledge that it has not been possible to remove everyone. Many countries will not take their nationals back or revoke their travel documents.

====================================================================================================

Nuclear physicists: Plant would be Estonia's security guarantee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
07:05:00 UTC
16:05:00 KST

Nuclear physicists: Plant would be Estonia's security guarantee
Estonia has no future alternative comparable to nuclear power, which would also provide a security guarantee, two nuclear physicists told ERR.
The world's first nuclear power plants were built in the 1950s. As in other areas of life, this one also witnessed a Cold War-era race between the U.S. and the Soviet Union. Both considered themselves the winner; in the U.S. state of Idaho, EBR-1 became the first nuclear power plant to produce electricity in 1951, going on to power the nearby town of Arco.
Three years later in 1954, the Soviet Union, however, achieved the first in opening a plant which could generate energy at a steady rate. This was at the Obninsk nuclear reactor in Kaluga Oblast. Both EBR-1 and Obninsk have ceased operations since then, Obninsk in 2002 and EBR-1 much earlier, in 1964.
Subsequent talk in the Soviet corridors of power in the 1960s concerned building a nuclear power plant near Lake Võrtsjärv, in Estonia. While nothing came of the idea, early on that decade, at the peak of the Cold War, the Soviet state started work on a land-based training center for the Soviet navy's first nuclear submarines, based in Paldiski. This went on to become a reality.
No real practical work took place at the training center in the wake of the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster, and after the restoration of Estonian independence, Russian authorities removed the nuclear fuel from the reactors and dismantled the training rigs. However, both submarine sections containing nuclear reactors remained. To deal with this issue, reinforced-concrete sarcophagi were built around them.
The question of constructing a nuclear power plant came up again in the mid-2000s, when then Environment Minister Villu Reiljan proposed a feasibility study. Fermi Energia was founded, aiming to build the first nuclear power plant in Estonia, was set up in 2019. Although no concrete plan is yet in place, the Riigikogu this year adopted the Nuclear Energy and Safety Act, and the government has initiated a national designated spatial plan for a potential nuclear power plant.
While it has said and said again in the past that Estonia lacks experts in the field, that is changing, as this fall ,two nuclear physics PhDs were added to the ranks: Andrei Goronovski and Hando Tohver. Goronovski works as a nuclear engineer at the aforementioned Fermi Energia, while Tohver works as an adviser on radiation and nuclear safety at the Climate Ministry.
A nuclear power plant as a security guarantee
If a seven-year-old child is asked what they want to be when they grow up, the answers are often police officer, say, or doctor. Seldom is the answer a physicist; much less a nuclear physicist. Goronovski said his path to the field was complicated and thorny, as physics was not presented in an interesting way at school. "It was one of those subjects that was all very theoretical," he recalled.
An interest in machines and how they work nevertheless remained undimmed, and so Goronovski ended up studying electrical power engineering at Tallinn University of Technology (TalTech). Subsequent studies took him to Sweden, where he earned his master's, and then back to Estonia, where he recently defended his doctorate.
Tohver's path was in comparison more straightforward. "By the end of high school I was quite interested in physics; I had a very good physics teacher, Neeme Lumi," he explained. After completing military service, he went to Tartu to study physics, where in his third year, while searching for a topic for his bachelor's thesis, he came across nuclear physics.
Both newly minted PhDs agree the question is not so much whether Estonia will get a nuclear power plant, but when. "If Estonia wants to remain a successful and developing country, then nuclear energy aside, we have no other sustainable and economically suitable alternatives for electricity generation," Goronovski stated.
Tohver agreed, invoking the EU's carbon-neutrality principle, which according to current plans should be achieved by 2040. He added the precise role nuclear energy will play in Estonia is a matter for public debate.
"Looking at the next couple of decades, however, I believe nuclear energy is technologically the most mature and probably the only solution capable of offering reasonable prices in our market," he said. At the same time, nuclear power plants have their own risks, and Estonia's geopolitical situation adds another layer to this.
One can look to Ukraine for a precedent here. The country has four nuclear power plants, and while the worst case scenario since the Russian invasion started four-and-a-half years ago has so far been avoided, the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant has featured in the media a lot, including when it has gone offline: The facility lies in occupied territory.
"First, I'll use the Zaporizhzhia plant as an example: Rven though this plant is in occupied territory and bombs and missiles have fallen on it, no radiation has leaked from it. This shows that modern plants are protected. The plant has been placed in cold shutdown, it is sitting safely and nothing is leaking from it," Goronovski said.
"The plants themselves are designed so that even an aircraft can crash into them without causing a critical failure," Tohver noted.
Furthermore, nuclear plants have their own in-fixed implied security guarantee – an aggressor state hitting a nuclear facility would in effect be escalating the situation and face far wider consequences than solely those from the country it is aggressing against.
"Personally, I think that if we are talking purely about a conflict situation, I don't see nuclear energy as a greater problem. I even see it as a certain security guarantee," Tohver said on this.
Public opposition stems from lack of knowledge
Estonian society has split into two camps over the question of building a nuclear power plant here. For example, the Estonian Fund for Nature (Eestimaa Looduse Fond) is vigorously fighting it, arguing that building a nuclear power plant in Estonia is both unnecessary and harmful to the environment.
Goronovski said opposition often stems from ignorance of what nuclear power actually is. "People don't know what nuclear energy is or what the risks and dangers are with a nuclear power plant. Much of the information is based on ageing technologies. For instance, many people still associate nuclear power stations with the Chernobyl plant, and hold to a belief that modern facilties can explode in the same way and carry similar risks, which is not the case," Goronovski said.
Tohver meanwhile pointed out opinion polls which show public support for nuclear power plants in Estonian running quite high. Over the past couple of years, reported support has fluctuated 60-70 percent, which he said is higher than for any other energy source.
According to both nuclear physicists, there does not appear to be any problem with the next generation of specialists, even as there is a shortage of teaching staff. "This is inevitable with every new field – when we start doing something new, initially there are no people. It is largely a matter of inertia: once you get the process going, competent people start emerging in the country who can in turn train new people, and that is how the system gains momentum," Tohver said.
Although highly educated specialists are needed to plan and construct the plants, those responsible for a facility's day-to-day operations do not need that level of qualification. "A nuclear power plant is similar to conventional power plants – there are lots of pumps and pipes. They need maintenance and operation, and doing that does not necessarily require higher education," Goronovski explained.
According to Goronovski, Fermi Energia's plan is precisely that, to retrain specialists who already work at Estonia's conventional power plants today, giving them the additional knowledge required for the nuclear field.
Tohver and Goronovski's doctoral theses
In his doctoral thesis, Tohver proposed an innovative solution for managing radioactive waste in countries which are only beginning to adopt nuclear technologies. According to the dissertation, open-source programs can be used successfully in assessing safety, rather than using restricted commercial software.
Using the Wastimate software he developed, Tohver found a shortcut for managing nuclear waste. It emerged that by as it were deliberately mixing fresh and old waste together in a single package, the hazardous load can be placed in a safe location decades earlier than planned.
In addition, Tohver studied how Estonian oil shale ash and basalt-boron fibers (BBF) could be used in a new type of radiation-shielding concrete. The results demonstrated that BBF reduces hazardous secondary radiation by more than half. The finding is also important for Estonia because more than a thousand cubic meters of shielding concrete will be needed to package waste generated during the decommissioning of the Paldiski nuclear site.
In his doctoral thesis, Goronovski studied naturally occurring radioactive materials (NORM) found in red mud, an industrial waste product of the aluminium industry. He developed a new NORM impact category and integrated it into life cycle assessment (LCA) methodology.
He found in the course of his work that natural radiation in the built environment has previously been underestimated and that its impact on people is significant. Through practical measurements, Goronovski showed that using red mud in construction materials entails an extremely low radiological risk, lower even than the impact of traditional materials.

During the search, officers seized an M16 rifle, a sniper rifle, ammunition, and magazines. Police arrested four suspects found at the site and took them for further questioning.
Police said operations against such infrastructure would continue.
“Israel Police will continue to act proactively to uncover excavation infrastructure and weapons in the Samaria area, locate those involved and bring them to justice,” police said.
Serious security incident endangering Israeli citizens
The discovery of the tunnel raised concern among heads of local authorities near the seam line. Kfar Saba Mayor Rafi Saar described the incident as “serious” and said it demonstrated what he viewed as the danger facing residents of the area.
“This is not a theoretical warning, this is a security reality that requires determined action,” Saar said.
Drom Hasharon Regional Council head Oshrat Gani Gonen also warned about the significance of the findings.
“A tunnel near Qalqilya is an incident that cannot simply be ignored,” she said. “This is further evidence that the threat to seam-line communities is becoming increasingly established just across the fence.”
Gani Gonen also referred to the weapons and other threats in the area.
'Meters from our homes': Tunnel, drones, weapons
“We are looking at what is happening meters from our homes: a tunnel, drones, weapons, and terrorist infrastructure. As far as we are concerned, every one of these things is the crossing of a red line.”
She said the events of October 7 required a change in the way such threats are addressed.
“No one can afford anymore to close their eyes to incidents like these, minimize them or settle for saying that the area is under control. The responsibility is to identify the threat before it becomes a disaster.”
The council head added that local authorities in the area had, in her words, been forced for years to fight for funding for security systems in seam-line communities.
“This danger is not theoretical. It is right before our eyes. The seam line is a front, and it must be treated as a front, with forces, equipment, technology, and budgets. This has to happen now, not after the next incident.”

OECD cuts Turkish economic growth forecast to lowest rate since 2020 amid Iran war, rising prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
07:03:45 UTC
16:03:45 KST

The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) cut its forecast for Turkey’s economic growth in 2026 to just 2.7% on Thursday, below the 3% threshold and the country’s lowest growth rate since 2020, as the economic fallout from the war in Iran and rising energy and fertilizer prices weigh on the outlook.
The organization, which published its latest economic outlook under the title “Navigating Successive Shocks,” also lowered Turkey’s 2027 growth forecast to 3.6%. In its previous forecast, the OECD had projected growth of 3.1% in 2026 and 3.8% in 2027.
Despite pressure from energy and fertilizer prices, the OECD expects Turkey’s disinflation process to continue, with inflation projected at 31.5% in 2026 and 24.7% in 2027. At the same time, monetary policy easing in emerging economies such as Turkey and Brazil is expected to support economic growth.
Globally, the organization slightly raised its 2026 economic growth forecast to 2.9%, up 0.1 percentage points from its June projection, after the global economy expanded by 3.4% in 2025.
Global economies remain strong despite Middle East conflicts
Although growth slowed in the first half of the year, many economies remained resilient despite geopolitical risks in the Middle East, while the growing strength of artificial intelligence continued to support investment, manufacturing, and trade.
The US economy is projected to grow by 2.2% in 2026 and 2.1% in 2027. The eurozone is expected to grow by just 1% in each of those years, while China’s economy is forecast to expand by 4.5% in 2026 and 4.2% in 2027.
India is expected to post the highest growth rate this year, at 7.8%, followed by Indonesia at 5.2%. Saudi Arabia, by contrast, is projected to record the sharpest contraction, shrinking by 1.8% following a decline in oil production and exports against the backdrop of the war in the Middle East.
The OECD warned that the global economic outlook depends largely on reaching a sustainable resolution to the war in the Middle East. Production bottlenecks have increased refinery margins and put pressure on consumer prices.
At the same time, energy and agricultural commodity prices have remained high, partly because of supply disruptions linked to extreme weather.
The organization said significant uncertainty continues to hang over its forecasts, particularly in energy markets. Global inflation is expected to accelerate in the short term before moderating in 2027. While a rapid normalization could ease pressure on the economy, further prolonged disruptions could push prices higher and constrain economic growth.

Pakistan conducted airstrikes on 10 locations in Afghanistan that it said were being used to launch and store drones, some of which had been used against Pakistan a day earlier, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said on Thursday.
The strikes come as tensions escalate between the allies-turned-foes, who have long been at odds over attacks by Islamist militants, which also triggered their worst fighting in years in February.
Islamabad accuses Kabul of harboring militants who stage cross-border attacks, but Afghanistan's Taliban government denies harboring anti-Pakistani insurgents and says militancy is Pakistan's internal problem.
Pakistan's air defense systems detected drones launched from Afghan territory on Wednesday, which were tracked and neutralized before they could reach any of their intended targets, Tarar said in a post on X/Twitter.
Pakistan then conducted the "precision aerial and drone strikes" on 10 locations, which were "limited to identified military objectives" linked to the attempted attacks, he said.
Afghan Taliban will be met with 'firm and resolute response'
"Any further provocative act by Afghan Taliban will be responded with firm and resolute response," the minister said.
The Pakistani airstrikes were conducted in several areas of the southeastern Khost province, Mustaghfir Gurbaz, spokesperson for the Khost governor, said.
There were no casualties, he said. However, a Taliban spokesperson said that four were killed in the strikes.
An attack on a police facility in northwestern Pakistan last week, which killed at least 24 people, has reignited fighting between the countries after nearly three months of relative calm.
Pakistan's government earlier this week also said it had launched airstrikes in the Afghanistan-Pakistan border region, killing 28 militants, while Afghan Taliban officials accused Islamabad of killing three civilians in overnight strikes on Afghan territory.
The worst single incident, however, occurred in March, when more than 400 people were killed in a Pakistani airstrike on Kabul, which the Afghan Taliban said hit a drug rehabilitation center.
Islamabad denied the charge, saying it "precisely targeted military installations and terrorist support infrastructure."

Two US Army battalions will arrive in Lithuania in late October as part of a regular troop rotation, Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said Wednesday.
“The preparation process and logistical arrangements are currently underway, and two battalions will arrive in Lithuania at the end of October,” Kaunas said.
The number of US troops will remain similar to previous rotations, at around 1,000 personnel, he said. One unit will be a heavy battalion equipped with heavy weaponry, including Abrams tanks. The other will be an engineering battalion tasked with supporting the development of Lithuania’s division, border protection and defence-related projects.
The US troops will remain in Lithuania for nine months.
Kaunas discussed the deployment with US Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defence Elbridge Colby during a visit to the Pentagon on Wednesday. The Lithuanian minister also proposed considering the possibility of establishing a permanent US military base in Lithuania, although he said no decisions had been made.
More than 1,000 US troops completed their previous rotation in Lithuania this summer.
The United States has regularly deployed battalions to Lithuania since 2019. Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Washington changed the status of its forces in Lithuania to a continuous rotational deployment.
Lithuania has previously said it is prepared to host up to 1,500 US troops.
