President Erdogan’s UN address published as book in three languages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
05:20:04 UTC
14:20:04 KST

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s address to the 81st United Nations General Assembly has been published as a book in Turkish, English and Arabic, turning his speech on global crises and international reform into a permanent publication.
The book, released by Türkiye’s Presidency on Wednesday, brings together Erdogan’s messages on Gaza, regional conflicts, the Russia-Ukraine war and what he describes as shortcomings in the current international system.
The publication is presented under the motto “A Fairer World Is Possible.”
The address, delivered in New York on Tuesday, focused heavily on Gaza and called for broader international action while arguing that the existing global order needs reform.
Erdogan also renewed his long-standing call for changes to the UN Security Council structure, summarized by his “The World Is Bigger Than Five” principle.
From Gaza to global governance
The book also covers the conflict involving Iran, developments in Lebanon and the Russia-Ukraine war, according to the Presidency.
Beyond immediate geopolitical crises, it addresses terrorism, climate crisis and artificial intelligence, presenting Erdogan’s views on how the international system could become more effective in responding to global challenges.
The Presidency described the publication as a resource for international audiences and future generations, with its three-language format designed to broaden access to the speech’s messages on peace, stability and prosperity.
Publication closes with Sezai Karakoc poem
The book concludes with lines from famous Turkish poet Sezai Karakoc, whose work is used to underline themes of truth, history and accountability.
The publication comes as world leaders gather in New York for the 81st General Assembly, with conflicts in Gaza, Ukraine and the wider Middle East, alongside questions over the future of global governance, dominating the international agenda.
The book concludes with a poem from Karakoc:
“They think that if we remain silent, the issue will disappear.
Yet, if we remain silent, history will not.
If history falls silent, the truth will not.
They think that if they get rid of us, the issue will disappear.
Yet, even if they get rid of us, they will not escape their remorse.
Even if they escape their remorse, they will not escape the punishment of history.
Even if they escape the punishment of history, they will not escape the wrath of God.”

Australian gas giant and Traditional Owners locked in $300 million compensation battle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
05:17:37 UTC
14:17:37 KST

in brief
- The NYFL argues the resources industry generates billions in a region where many Aboriginal people are disadvantaged.
- Woodside says the partnership has delivered "significant benefits" and is seeking to build on them.
Woodside is at a stalemate with a Traditional Owners organisation that is seeking hundreds of millions of dollars more in compensation from the Australian energy giant.
It's understood negotiations between the nation's largest gas producer and the Ngarluma Yinjibrandi Foundation Limited (NYFL) over an agreement that compensates the Indigenous organisation for use of its land in Western Australia's resource-rich Pilbara region have stalled.
Sources close to the negotiations have told SBS News that Woodside offered the NYFL $87 million over 12 years in May, $303 million short of the $390 million package the organisation sought last November. Neither party commented on the figures when approached by SBS News.
The negotiations aim to update an agreement drawn up in 1998 between the two parties, in which the NYFL receives funding for community programs, but no royalties from resources.
The NYFL wants the agreement to be "fit for purpose", arguing the resources industry has made billions of dollars from the region while many Aboriginal people who live there are "worse off than before the expansion of the mining, oil and gas industries".
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Woodside says it is "proud of the positive relationship" it has built with the NYFL and has delivered "significant benefits" to it.
Neither Woodside nor the NYFL commented on the status of the negotiations. The energy giant said it is "looking forward to continuing" its "positive relationship" with the Traditional Owners organisation, which said it remained "committed to engaging in good faith".
Woodside administers the North West Shelf gas facility on behalf of a joint venture of energy companies. The project encompasses the onshore Karratha Gas Plant, which was built on the Burrup Peninsula in the late 1970s and early 1980s.
It is now one of Australia's major energy projects.
The peninsula is culturally and spiritually significant to First Nations peoples and is part of Murujuga, which holds the densest known concentration of petroglyphs, or rock carvings, in the world. The Murujuga Cultural Landscape was World Heritage-listed in 2025.
The NYFL represents the Ngarluma and Yindjibarndi peoples, who are among the recognised Traditional Owners of the area where the expansive onshore gas plant operates.
Native title, which recognises Indigenous connections to land, does not exist over the Burrup Peninsula. In 2003, the WA Government reached the Burrup Agreement with three Aboriginal claimant groups, including the Ngarluma and Yindjibarndi, providing for land, conservation, cultural, employment and other benefits.
The 1998 agreement
Ngarluma and Yindjibarndi representatives and elders signed a Land Access Agreement in 1998 with the North West Shelf joint venture, operated by Woodside, covering the project's use of their traditional lands, including the site of the Karratha Gas Plant.
The agreement, seen by SBS News, was signed 14 years after the project began operating, by which time sacred sites had been cleared to build its onshore gas plant. It provides for "payments relating to native title and grants of interests in land" and "donations relating to goodwill".
The Ngarluma and Yindjibarndi groups received one-off establishment payments of $500,000, in part used to set up the NYFL and $2.5 million for the Roebourne Cultural Centre.
The deal also included annual goodwill payments of $1.25 million partially indexed to inflation, and other economic and cultural commitments.
It's understood the payments have increased, but the extent remains unclear. Both the NYFL and Woodside did not comment on this, with the NYFL citing contractual confidentiality.
Woodside reported operating revenue of about $10.4 billion for the first half of 2026. The Pilbara more widely generates more than $125 billion in economic output a year, according to economic analysis platform REMPLAN, and supports close to 60,000 jobs.
The exchange between the NYFL and Woodside, along with estimates of revenue and expenditures seen by SBS News, may not be a full account of interactions between the parties nor indicative of the final offer.
Negotiations to update the agreement
In November 2025, the NYFL sought to modernise its 1998 agreement with Woodside.
The NYFL requested a one-off payment of $30 million and annual compensation of $30 million.
Over 12 years, this request to Woodside would amount to $390 million.
In May this year, Woodside responded. The gas giant offered the NYFL an additional $39 million to the original agreement (including $15 million in housing assets), totalling $87 million to the NYFL over 12 years.
That leaves a $300 million gap between the NYFL's initial request in November and Woodside's counteroffer six months later.
A NYFL spokesperson did not comment on the figures, saying the negotiations were confidential. But, they said, "agreements must be fair, equitable and outcomes focussed".
"Ngurrara-ngarli (Traditional Owners) across the Pilbara are increasingly seeking to modernise longstanding Land Access and compensation agreements to ensure that they are fit for purpose, are built around self-determination and reflect contemporary First Nations principles," the spokesperson said in a statement.
Unlike some other Traditional Owner groups in the Pilbara, the NYFL does not receive royalties from the project it deals with — the 1998 agreement contained no provision for them.
In addition to one-off payments for housing and infrastructure refurbishments, the NYFL sought $30 million annually to support its membership and the remote town of Roebourne, including operating its not-for-profit community supermarket, job creation and self-sufficiency.
Roebourne, 39km east of Karratha, is one of Australia's most disadvantaged areas, according to cumulative data from the Ieramugadu Data Unit, government statistics and the Census.
An estimated 87 per cent of Indigenous people in the town reported a weekly income below the national median of $805.
According to the 2021 Census, almost one in five Aboriginal households in Roebourne were living in overcrowded homes (those needing at least one more bedroom), nearly double the rate across Western Australia.
"For decades, the resources industry has generated billions of dollars from the Pilbara," the NYFL spokesperson said. "At the same time, independent research shows persistent economic disadvantage across the region, including findings that around two-thirds of Aboriginal people in the Pilbara are economically worse off than before the expansion of the mining, oil and gas industries."
A Woodside spokesperson said a modernised agreement between the two parties would "build on the significant benefits already delivered".
"It intends to further promote sustainable outcomes for the Roebourne community in areas such as economic participation, capacity building, safer and healthier communities and cultural heritage," the spokesperson said,
"We look forward to continuing our positive relationship with NYFL to support the continued delivery of positive outcomes for NYFL members and the Roebourne community."
Compensation claims on the rise
Native title is not applicable in the case of Woodside and the NYFL, but their negotiations come against the backdrop of court rulings in favour of Traditional Owners organisations over loss of native title cultural heritage.
The Federal Court ordered the NT Government to pay over $54.7 million to the Gudanji, Yanyuwa, and Yanyuwa-Marra peoples in February for cultural and spiritual loss regarding the McArthur River Mine.
Separately, the Federal Court awarded Yindjibarndi people $150.3 million against Fortescue in July for unauthorised mining at its Solomon Hub operation, about 240km south-east of Karratha.
While Fortescue paid the funds, the decision is being appealed by Yindjibarndi Traditional Owners, who had initially sought $1.8 billion from the court.
"There are several active compensation claims still waiting in the system that'll take a while to come through, but I would suspect there'd be a great deal more after that," said Ed Wensing, a lecturer at the University of NSW and an expert in native title rights and Indigenous human rights.
He said the recent decisions could influence how future native title compensation claims are negotiated and litigated.
"The compensation era arising from the Native Title system, it's only just begun."

Taiwan-Japan drone trade remains marginal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
05:05:29 UTC
14:05:29 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Taiwan-Japan drone cooperation needs to translate into steady orders, a DSET report published on Wednesday said.
National security analyst Teng Hung-yuan (鄧閎元) said that despite Taiwan and Japan beginning drone cooperation in 2017 and accelerating in 2025, the relationship has not led to steady trade, with Taiwan exporting only 45 drones to Japan and receiving 3 in turn. Both sides have signed at least 20 agreements, and only half have been fulfilled by 2025, indicating stagnant progress.
Teng said that the war in Ukraine compelled both countries to escalate domestic drone production, defense purchases, and a China-free supply chain. Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae proposed increasing the defense budget and unmanned systems production in March.
In terms of scale, Japan's drone production remains limited, as only 940 commercial drones were made in 2024, and 2025 exports totaled 1,132, while 90% of drones used in Japan were from China. Taiwan's production and export volume exceed Japan's, with 3,473 units exported in 2024 and 122,706 in 2025.
On policy, both countries increased investments. The Legislative Yuan rolled out a drone industry development plan to spend NT$44.2 billion (US$1.38 billion) on purchases and R&D. In August, the legislature passed a NT$240 billion drone development bill, to be financed over six years at NT$60 billion per year.
Japan amended its Three Strategic Documents to invest NT$204 billion from 2023–2027. It further passed the Japan Economic Security Promotion Act to spend NT$280 million subsidizing carriers and key parts.
On diplomacy, Taiwanese and Japanese enterprises have established partnerships with firms in the US, the EU, and elsewhere. However, bilateral trade in 2025 was negligible, as exchanges are limited to MOUs.
On barriers, Teng believes there are three main obstacles:
- No government-to-government framework due to geopolitical tensions
- Japan's production scale and logistics network
- No mutual certification, which raises the barrier to entry
Teng suggested that Taiwan position Japan as a strategic market and promote itself as a trustworthy supplier of drones and key components. He said drone companies should increase investments, co-research and produce with Japan, and explore opportunities with allies.
Teng said Japan should view Taiwan as a valued partner. He said that as China disrupts supply chains, Japan should strengthen ties with Taiwanese suppliers and provide more trade incentives.
On validation, Teng recommended that both countries establish a Taiwan-Japan drone task force to identify weaknesses and reference Green UAS certification between Taiwan and the US. He added that both nations develop an approval mechanism for drones and key parts.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Paraguayan President Santiago Pena called Taiwan’s exclusion from the UN system "a stain" on the organization Wednesday while warning that a potential conflict in the Taiwan Strait could have global economic consequences.
Speaking at the 81st UN General Assembly in New York, Pena said, "Paraguay is not neutral on this issue. Paraguay stands, and I say this loud and clear, with Taiwan." He said the position was not based on expediency, but on shared values of "democracy, the rule of law, human rights, and peace."
Pena said 70 years of uninterrupted diplomatic relations between Paraguay and Taiwan are "a testament to the real friendship between our peoples." He then reaffirmed Paraguay's support for Taiwan's full and meaningful participation in the UN and its specialized agencies.
"Taiwan has concrete contributions to make to peace, development and human rights," Pena said. Excluding Taiwan, he argued, deprives the international system of capabilities that could benefit its members, "and it is a stain on the United Nations."
Pena warned that "ominous clouds" were gathering over the Indo-Pacific, particularly over the Taiwan Strait. He said a conflict would affect Japan, East and Southeast Asia, and the global economy, including the microchips that power industry, defense, and AI.
"Anyone pretending that this is far off or too distant to matter simply has not understood the 21st century," Pena said, comparing the importance of microchips in the 21st century to that of oil in the 20th century. "The stakes of this potential conflict could scarcely be higher. The very future of humanity is at stake."
The issue should not be viewed as concerning Taiwan alone, Pena said, because developments in the region are "simply too dangerous for us all." He urged the international community to move from words to “concrete action” and said Paraguay would be “on the front row ready to help” at a negotiating table for peace and concord.

The Finnish men's volleyball team progressed to the semi-finals of the European Championships after a stunning 3-2 win over reigning world champions Italy on Wednesday evening.
The Italians, playing in front of a home crowd in the city of Torino, were hot favourites to reach the tournament's last four.
Finland had also not beaten Italy in a competitive volleyball game for 48 years.
But despite losing the first set, the Finnish team powered back to take the second and third sets on a scoreline of 28–26 and 25–16. Italy won the fourth 25–20, meaning the tie went into a dramatic fifth and final set.
Inspired by Joonas Jokela and Luka Marttila, Finland came from behind in the tiebreaker to win 15–13 and set up a semi-final with France on Friday.
The game will begin at 10pm Finnish time and it will be broadcast on Yle TV2 as well as on Yle Areena.
"This is an absolute bombshell for Finnish volleyball," Yle pundit Timo Tolvanen said. "And also in Finland's sports history, to beat the world champion on their home court. I can't remember anything like this for quite a while. It rises to a pretty high position in my ranking at least."
The victory means Finland will now at least match their best ever performance at a European Championships, a 4th place finish in 2007.
The other semi-final is between Slovenia and Poland.

Live: Lachie Neale appeal to be heard ahead of GF team announcement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
05:01:47 UTC
14:01:47 KST

Thu, 3 Sept, 8:10 pm, Final score, Dockers 40, Hawks 72
Brisbane's Lachie Neale free to play in AFL grand final after Appeal Board overturns his striking ban
Lachie Neale has succeeded in his bid to overturn a one-game striking suspension at the AFL Appeals Board and is free to play in the grand final.
Neale lost on Tuesday with the AFL Tribunal upholding his ban for striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan.
In a hearing that took nearly two hours, the panel of chair Richard Loveridge, Steven Jurica and Wayne Henwood took less than half an hour to return with their verdict.
Neale's defence team chose not to challenge the decision of the Tribunal to uphold the grading of intentional conduct, medium impact and body contact, which resulted in the one-match ban.
The case turned on the question of the "exceptional and compelling circumstances" clause in the rules, which allows the Tribunal discretion to not apply a ban, and whether the Tribunal considered Neale's record of 320 games without suspension and two Brownlow Medal best-and-fairests in reaching their decision.
Neale's counsel Adrian Anderson said the exceptional circumstances should have been reached because of Neale's amazing record, the fact that Ginnivan had not been injured in what he said was a "pretty minor" incident, and the fact that the consequences of the decision were that Neale would miss a grand final.
"We find that the Tribunal did err in having regard to whether the conduct was intentional," Loveridge said in the Appeal Board reasons.
"We accept the position of Neale in his written submissions that the intentional aspect was an element of the charge which had already been established.
"The relevant inquiry was whether, despite the charge having been established, there was exceptional and compelling circumstances.
"In this case, that was Neale's record.
"We find that Neale's record is exemplary, and that he should be afforded the benefit of the provision.
"In conclusion, we allow the appeal."
Neale was fined $10,000 and he will be able to play in Saturday's grand final.
Both teams released their line-ups for the decider, with no changes for either Brisbane or Fremantle.

Seven savvy pieces from London Design Festival made of material offcuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
05:00:01 UTC
14:00:01 KST

Seven savvy pieces from London Design Festival made of material offcuts
On the heels of London Design Festival, we have rounded up a selection of furniture and products presented during the city-wide event made of scraps that would otherwise have gone to waste.
London Design Festival (LDF) concluded on Sunday, after a week of product launches, exhibitions and installations that showed the best of the capital's design scene.
Throughout the event, a trend that stood out was the presence of designers using materials leftover from manufacturing, whether as an attempt to slash costs, preserve resources or simply experiment visually.
Here are seven examples of the technique spotted during London's main design week:
Dagwood Bench by Lewis Duckworth
Lewis Duckworth is one of London's many emerging talents. As the co-founder of guerrilla collective Design Everything, he is always looking for ways to create furniture with the inevitable limitations that come with being a young, independent designer.
Dagwood Bench is one such project, made from timber end pieces leftover from furniture production, which are often too narrow or short to be reused and would normally go to waste.
Duckworth created the bench from a single laminated plank, sandwiched between two timber faces. The designer explained that offcuts were arranged within these pieces of wood to create a form that "appears visually thick while remaining lightweight and structurally capable".
"This project explores ways to re-evaluate these 'un-usable' elements by incorporating them into a larger, cohesive material system," he said. "Given that they started as an industrial byproduct, it felt most appropriate to reprocess them in a standardised format".
Duckworth's Dagwood Bench is among the 34-strong shortlist of buildings, furniture and objects nominated for a 2026 Wood Award. A selection of these designs were on display at the Material Matters exhibition during LDF.
Second Song by Spared
Second Song is a selection of bird-shaped collectible objects by Brighton-based design studio Spared.
The studio is known for transforming waste generated from its own varied practice into furniture and products, such as tables made from old coffee grounds developed for the Corner cafe at London's Tate Modern museum.
Cast using a resin-free mineral binder, the collectible birds were made of offcuts ranging from shell and stone to workshop sawdust and thin scrapings from the surfaces of plastic chopping boards used in industrial kitchens.
Second Song was another project presented at Material Matters.
Tissue box by Tom Golland
This statement tissue box was part of Out of Worky, an exhibition of bespoke pieces made using scrap materials that the participants had collected over years of taking on myriad jobs as emerging designers.
Tom Golland combined offcuts of walnut and white oak to form the unusually tall tissue dispenser, which is held together with two zinc-plated steel bolts.
The show was presented by The Worky, a collective founded by Marley Wellings, Jake Robertson, Kieran Slater and Milo Tonry-Brown.
Chair by Oscar Warman
Dubbed "everything I could find in my shed", this timber chair by emerging designer Oscar Warman is a Frankenstein-like hodgepodge of old pieces of furniture that were partially damaged.
The chair features a duo of rotten and frayed front legs, which had to be cut and altered.
This meant that Warman needed to source a strong piece of timber for the back legs, which he found in the form of part of a shelf that he "cannibalised" by taking it off the wall and using it alongside its brackets.
"By designing in this way I spent time mocking up and offering each part to one another to try and resemble a chair shape," said Warman.
"I like how few processes were used in the making of this piece and the time was spent problem solving how to make them function as a chair."
The chair was on display as part of Design Everything's With Limitations show at Aram Gallery.
Fused by Audra Grays and Maxim Lester
Fused is one of a handful of lamps made by emerging designers Audra Grays and Maxim Lester, who, quite literally, fused together different material offcuts from their respective practices to create lighting.
After Lester came across Grays's decorative glass experiments on Instagram, the designers combined the glass offcuts with scrap metal and electrical back boxes found in Lester's workshop. LED strips were pulled from old lamps to illuminate the pieces.
Also displayed at Aram Gallery, the rectilinear sconce lights are not the only pieces the duo made from offcuts that were on show during LDF. The pair also presented a chunky desk lamp as part of the Kiln Shift exhibition by Clink Street Ceramics.
Graywacke OffCut Chair by Carsten in der Elst
Based in Cologne, designer Carsten in der Elst has spent the last six years utilising "the full potential of industrial by-product material" when crafting pieces of furniture.
Central to In der Elst's portfolio is his Graywacke Offcut series – monolithic tables and chairs made from rough-hewn lumps of stone salvaged from a quarry in Lindlar, western Germany.
One of these ancient-looking chairs was presented as part of the Progressive Permanence exhibition by Max Radford Gallery at the Christopher Farr showroom in Shoreditch.
Coat rack by Duy Huynh
Emerging designer Duy Huynh was another exhibitor in With Limitations, who presented a timber coat rack made from offcuts salvaged from a stand he crafted to show work at his recent degree show.
The size of each piece of wood, reassembled by the designer, was determined by where the previous joints had been cut to create the stand.
"This piece is a bit smaller than a conventional coat rack, but I wanted to keep that acknowledgement of where it came from to show the idea that if we treat our materials right, they can serve us for a long time," said Huynh.
London Design Festival 2026 took place at various locations around the city from 12 to 20 September. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

Kaunas tram line: big ambitions, as yet few details
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Kaunas plans to begin designing its first modern tram line, which would also be the first one in the country. Before the ambition could be implemented, the city will need to iron out funding – and overcome scepticism from even some Kaunas residents.
The city council last week approved an updated sustainable mobility plan, clearing the way for the tram project. City officials say they will seek European Union funding, while the estimated cost remains uncertain.
Kaunas Deputy Mayor Andrius Palionis said the main goal was to develop environmentally friendly public transportation that would be less vulnerable to traffic congestion.
“We will begin the procurement of design work for this particular route,” Palionis said. “A project and an idea of this scale are never realised overnight. Cities can implement such projects based on the experience of other European Union cities, but only with European funding.”
The proposed first route would run along Savanorių and Šiaurės avenues. Palionis said the streets were selected in part because their existing infrastructure is sufficiently wide to accommodate tram tracks.
“Naturally, trams need tracks, but the route was chosen as the first one that could be implemented because the existing street infrastructure is sufficiently wide,” he said.
The city has not yet determined the final cost of the project. Palionis said an initial estimate of 150 million euros had been included in the sustainable mobility plan based on an analysis, but stressed that the figure was only theoretical and could change substantially.
Kaunas residents have expressed mixed views about the proposal.
Some said a tram could improve public transportation and help reduce congestion. One resident told LRT RADIOo that she had spent one and a half hours traveling from the Saulėtekis area to Giraitė because of traffic congestion.
“Traveling by tram would be faster,” she said.
Another resident welcomed the proposal, saying improved public transportation could benefit the city.
A representative of the blind community also said the project could be worthwhile if accessibility needs were considered.
“I think it could be a good thing,” she said. “We haven’t had anything like this here before. [...] If the needs of blind people are also taken into account, so that people from our community could use the tram to travel from one place to another, then why not?”
Others questioned the need for a new form of public transportation and said the money could be better spent elsewhere.
“We should refrain from such extravagance,” one resident said.
Another said existing buses were no longer as crowded as they once were and that spending money on a tram would be wasteful.
A third resident said the city should instead invest in more trolleybuses and buses, particularly because of congestion during rush hour on Savanorių Avenue.
The proposal has also drawn criticism from the opposition in the city council. Vaida Pranarauskaitė, head of the Lithuanian Farmers and Greens Union faction, said the project raised questions about both financial responsibility and long-term strategy.
“Expensive design work has no firm guarantees regarding a source of funding,” Pranarauskaitė said. “If European Union or government funding is not secured, this project will simply end up in a drawer.”
She also said the proposal disregarded findings from feasibility studies commissioned by the municipality and questioned the need to replace or supplement the existing trolleybus and bus network on Savanorių Avenue.
Transport Minister Juras Taminskas, however, welcomed Kaunas’ plans and said he hoped the city would become the first in Lithuania to introduce a modern tram system.
“Excellent plans, and I believe Kaunas will overtake Vilnius,” Taminskas said. “If we have opportunities in the next EU funding period, starting in 2028, we will certainly support this and look for every possible way to include the project in potential funding lines.”
He cautioned that it was too early to say whether Lithuania’s state budget could contribute because public finances were under pressure.
Taminskas said legislation adopted in 2018 on the development of metropolitan transportation systems provides a legal basis for municipalities, including Kaunas, to develop tram projects. He said some legislation might need to be amended before construction could begin.
Potential changes could involve traffic rules and legislation governing construction and environmental impact assessments, as well as possibly the Roads Law, he said.
Kaunas would be the first Lithuanian city to introduce a modern tram system if the project proceeds. The city currently relies primarily on buses and trolleybuses for public transportation.

Anthropic touts AI-led biology discovery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Anthropic touts AI-led biology discovery
- Anthropic's AI model Claude discovered a new enzyme system called ART by analysing DNA sequences, potentially revealing a new gene-editing mechanism similar to CRISPR.
- The AI autonomously analysed over 200,000 genes in 21 hours, accelerating research that usually takes weeks or months.
- The discovery, still preliminary and unreviewed, could lead to advances in gene therapy and disease treatment, with experts calling for further investigation.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – US artificial intelligence start-up Anthropic on Sept 23 unveiled the first discovery from its molecular biology laboratory, a previously unknown enzyme system spotted by its Claude model and touted by the company as proof that AI can speed up basic research.
Enzyme systems found in nature have led to some of biology’s biggest breakthroughs, from the tools that launched the biotech industry to the DNA-copying method behind many medical tests.
According to the company, some 950 Claude-powered software agents combed through a database of DNA sequences for 21 hours.
The agents found more than 200,000 genes for one type of enzyme and picked out 20 worth a closer look – work that would take an expert scientist weeks or even months.
Anthropic said its researchers’ involvement was limited to the initial instructions and the lab experiments, with the AI agents working autonomously to decide which leads to pursue.
One of the agents spotted something in viruses that infect bacteria that scientists appear to have missed: a string of short, repeating pieces of DNA sitting next to two genes, one for a known enzyme and one for a mystery protein.
The set-up looks like CRISPR, a natural defence system in bacteria that scientists turned into a gene-editing tool now used in medicine.
Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, who recently called for slowing AI development because of its risks, cited the discovery on Sept 23 in remarks to the UN Security Council, which he addressed by video link.
The finding is “preliminary”, he said, but “may constitute a new gene-editing mechanism that could have applications in gene therapy”.
He predicted “profound progress in the near future on diseases that have plagued humanity for millennia”.
The function of the newly identified system, dubbed ART, remains unknown, Anthropic said.
The company added that its initial experiments suggest the system could, like CRISPR, be programmable.
The results, published as a preprint, have not yet been reviewed by other scientists.
Feng Zhang, one of the pioneers of CRISPR and a professor at Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the Broad Institute, called the identification of the repeated DNA fragments “genuinely intriguing” and said it “merits further investigation”, in remarks released by Anthropic.
Amodei also said on X that a team at Stanford University had independently described a comparable but distinct system.
Formed in the spring, Anthropic’s lab team works in the San Francisco Bay Area and does not handle pathogens capable of infecting humans.
All experiments are carried out by human scientists, Anthropic said. Amodei did not rule out Claude eventually operating lab equipment itself, with appropriate safeguards. AFP

“In terms of Operation Economic Outcast, we are squeezing the Iranians like they've never seen today,” he said.

Bessent also warned financial institutions, companies and other businesses supporting Iran that Washington would target their operations and bank accounts.

Bessent also said the US had attempted to reach an agreement with Iran earlier in the year but accused Tehran of subsequently escalating attacks in the Strait of Hormuz.
"If there is a deal, I guarantee you they're going to stick with it," he said.
The US launched Operation Economic Outcast in August as a broad campaign to isolate Iran economically and target companies, financial institutions and other entities helping Tehran circumvent US sanctions.
The Treasury Department has since expanded the campaign to target Iranian aviation networks, financial institutions and cryptocurrency-related infrastructure.

Stubb Slams Russia’s ‘Waste of Life’ at UN as Finland, Ukraine Seal Major Drone Deal

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
04:53:15 UTC
13:53:15 KST

Finland and Ukraine forged a major new defense partnership in New York, hours after Finnish President Alexander Stubb used a Sept. 23 UN Security Council address to demand that Russia end what he called a catastrophic “waste of life” on a largely stalled frontline.
Speaking on behalf of the five Nordic countries, Stubb delivered a stark assessment of Russia’s Donbas campaign.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to the Finnish president, Russian forces have captured roughly 900 square kilometers (347 square miles) of Ukrainian territory this year, while Ukraine has retaken around 800 square kilometers (309 square miles).
“So the line of contact is basically not moving,” Stubb said.
If Moscow intends to seize the rest of the Donbas at that pace, he warned, “it will take years.”
Stubb said roughly 25,000 soldiers are being killed every month as the two sides fight over a frontline that has barely shifted.
He contrasted that toll with the Soviet war in Afghanistan, which lasted a decade and, according to the figure he cited, resulted in roughly 18,000 deaths.
“This, in my mind, is a waste of life,” Stubb said.
“So the continuation of this war is a lose-lose.”
“There’s not a military solution to this,” he added. “Someone needs to tell, obviously the aggressor, that this is not going to have a military solution.”
Drone “death zones” freeze the front
Stubb said the brutal arithmetic of the battlefield is being driven by a new form of warfare dominated by drones, unmanned systems, and near-constant surveillance.
Ukraine Pushes Forward in 4 Frontline Sectors as Russia Struggles for Gains
“We haven’t seen anything like this previously,” he said.
The Finnish president described stretches of the battlefield as roughly 20-kilometer-wide (12-mile-wide) “death zones” where troops can barely move without being detected and targeted.
“We’re seeing unmanned vehicles, we’re seeing death zones of roughly 20 kilometers [12 miles] to which you cannot enter, because with a 95 percent certainty, you’re going to be wiped out,” Stubb said.
His description underscored how drone warfare has transformed the front into a vast surveillance and strike belt, where exposed troops and vehicles can be detected and attacked within minutes.
For Stubb, those “death zones” help explain why neither side can simply exhaust the other and why Russia’s offensive has produced only marginal territorial movement despite staggering casualties.
The result, he argued, is a battlefield where Moscow is sacrificing enormous numbers of troops for gains measured in only hundreds of square kilometers.
Speaking with what he called “three hats” – representing the Nordics, serving as president of a country sharing a 1,340-kilometer (833 mile) border with Russia, and as a supporter of the UN system – Stubb condemned Russia’s invasion as a direct violation of the UN Charter.
“We see Russia violating these rules every day,” he said.
Stubb, who said he has visited Ukraine six times over the past three years, said Russia is systematically targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure while also attacking humanitarian operations.
“The aim is to instill fear and wear down Ukraine,” he said.
Stubb called for an unconditional ceasefire – or at minimum a limited ceasefire covering areas such as energy infrastructure and grain – before longer negotiations over security, territory, justice, and a permanent settlement.
“There has to become a time when the killing stops,” Stubb said.
Concluding with the words of former Finnish President and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Martti Ahtisaari – “what humans began, they can also end” – Stubb turned directly to Moscow.
“Please, Russia, end this war.”
Finland and Ukraine deepen defense partnership with Drone Deal
Hours after confronting Russia at the Security Council, Stubb and Zelensky signed a new Drone Deal – the 11th agreement Kyiv has concluded under the special format.
The pact goes far beyond a conventional purchase agreement.
According to Finland’s presidency, it provides for transfers of technology, knowledge, and expertise, as well as joint industrial projects including drone development.
“This is not simply a contract or an agreement on the sale and purchase of drones,” Zelensky said. “This is about security – our shared security and joint production.”
Finland has already delivered 34 support packages to Ukraine, while Helsinki is increasingly looking to Ukraine not only as a recipient of military assistance but as a source of battlefield knowledge and defense innovation.
“That is exactly why we began saying that this is not a one-way street where we simply provide something to you,” Stubb said.
“On the contrary, it is a two-way process in which we learn from you.”
“By learning from Ukraine’s experience, we are strengthening our own capabilities,” Stubb added.
The New York meeting, which also included Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, focused heavily on protecting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and strengthening air defenses before winter.
“We are working to strengthen air defense as much as possible before winter sets in and to deprive Russia of its bet on ballistic terror,” Zelensky wrote on X.

Rare Moomin mug sells for record-breaking €46k
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
07:50:11 EEST
13:50:11 KST

An online store specialising in discontinued Moomin products has reported selling a rare mug for a record-breaking price.
The site, called Muumimukit rahaksi (which roughly translates as Moomin Mugs for Money) and operated by Mukilaakso Oy, said it sold the extremely rare 'Diving with Shells' Moomin mug at auction for the eye-watering price of 46,023 euros.
CEO Rasmus Rantanen confirmed to Yle that the price is the highest sum ever paid for a single Moomin mug, according to the company's information.
"We have been buying and selling mugs for 14 years now. Based on that, we can say quite confidently that none have ever been sold for more. Or at least there has never been [information] in the public domain, and I would be surprised if mugs more expensive than this had been sold somewhere else," Rantanen said.
He added that the site held a closed auction for the Moomin mug in December 2025, and the actual sale was completed in April of this year.
The buyer is understood to be a Nordic "long-time Moomin collector" who does not want their name or more specific nationality made public.
The sale was also not announced until September at the buyer's request, but Rantanen did not wish to comment any further.
"They [the buyer] had their own reasons for wanting to keep it quiet," he explained.
"Pent-up fervour"
The 'Diving with Shells' mug resembles the more widely produced 'Diving' version, which was released in 2006, but the former has additional shell and coral motifs.
According to Moomin Arabia, which manufactures Moomin mugs, a small test batch of the mugs was made at the time, but the mug never made it into actual production.
By sliding the image below, you can compare the difference between the two versions:
Mukilaakso Oy sold a similar mug in 2019 for about 9,000 euros, while another of the batch was sold at auction in Sweden in 2021 for over 23,000 euros.
According to Rantanen, Mukilaakso Oy bought the 'Diving with Shells' mug for 27,000 euros from the same Swedish auction site that set the previous sales record for the mug in 2021.
He noted that the price jumped dramatically because of the increasing popularity of Moomin mugs as collector's items, adding that the company received offers of over 40,000 euros from as many as five different bidders in the closed auction.
"It is believed that only ten pieces of the Diving with Shells mugs were made. There has been a five-year break between the previous Swedish record and a new mug coming up for public sale again. During that time, the Moomin mug collecting scene had grown in popularity, and a certain kind of pent-up fervour was evident among collectors to get the mug into their collections."
Moomins are the creation of Finnish author and illustrator Tove Jansson. Residing in the peaceful Moominvalley, they are gentle trolls who somewhat resemble hippos in appearance. Jansson focused her stories about the Moomins on themes including community, nature and inclusion.

NATO member Turkey, which has maintained cordial ties with both Moscow and Kyiv since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, has repeatedly urged the warring sides to stop attacks in the Black Sea.
"During the meeting, President Erdogan stated that Turkey was ready to do all it can for the Ukraine-Russia war to end with lasting peace, that we will continue our efforts to revive direct negotiations," the Turkish presidency said in a statement.

Earlier, Zelenskiy told leaders at a "Crimean Platform" summit on the sidelines of the General Assembly that Kyiv was ready for a maritime truce in the Black Sea based on proposals such as those put forward by Egypt, India and Turkey.
Top wheat importers in Asia, the Middle East and Africa which count on the Black Sea region for wheat have been finding it hard to secure supplies. Global wheat prices have soared.
Turkey and the United Nations helped to mediate the so-called Black Sea Grain Initiative in July 2022 to allow for the safe export of Ukrainian grain amid the war, but Russia withdrew from the agreement the following year, complaining that its own food and fertiliser exports faced serious obstacles.
Ankara has provided Kyiv with military backing and voiced support for its territorial integrity, but refused to join Western sanctions on Moscow and maintained commercial ties with Russia. It has hosted previous rounds of direct talks between the sides and offered to mediate. REUTERS

Italy greenlights return of nuclear power after decades-long ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Italy greenlights return of nuclear power after decades-long ban
Parliament clears legal framework for next-generation reactors nearly 40 years after the Chernobyl disaster
Italy’s Senate on Wednesday gave final approval to legislation paving the way for a return to nuclear power nearly four decades after the Chernobyl disaster prompted the country to abandon atomic energy.
The measure cleared the upper house 81-51 with seven abstentions. It marks a major step in Premier Giorgia Meloni’s drive to bolster energy security and meet climate goals, even though the construction of possible new reactors is still years away.
The bill, which earlier passed the lower Chamber of Deputies, establishes a legal framework for next-generation nuclear technologies. It authorises the government to draft implementing decrees over the next 12 months covering reactor licensing, safety standards, waste management and criteria for future sites.
The vote puts Italy on a path towards reintroducing nuclear power after voters twice rejected it in national referendums, first in the aftermath of the 1986 Chernobyl disaster and again following Japan’s Fukushima accident in 2011.

The Trump administration is preparing to impose a 90-day ban on diesel exports in a bid to bring down soaring energy prices, the Politico news outlet reported Wednesday.

If the ban is enacted, it would be the first restriction on US energy exports since the Obama administration lifted a decades-old ban on oil exports in 2015, according to the report.

An industry executive told Politico that Trump is inclined to announce a ban by the end of the week and said the president considers any blowback "a December problem."
“What has overpowered cooler heads (in the White House) is the absolutely, sky-is-falling, we-have-to-do-something concern about prices at the pump” faction, said the oil executive. "That camp has been swept aside by the political camp, which says, 'dammit, something has to happen,'" they added.
The White House and the Department of Energy did not acknowledge the report.
"This is another fake news story from Politico," said a White House official.
Industry experts said a diesel ban would have a domino effect on the rest of the world, noting that "countries around the world have grown more dependent on US diesel."
"A ban on diesel exports by the US would exacerbate the existing severe strains in the global diesel market and drive prices outside of the US even higher in the short term," said David Oxley, chief climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, in a statement to Politico.
“Nonetheless, given that a surplus of diesel in the US could paradoxically force American refiners to cut supplies of oil products – potentially within a few weeks – a ban would ultimately be self-defeating,” added Oxley.

Asian Games | Feature: Age no barrier to Asian Games glory
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:41:23 CST
13:41:23 KST

by sportswriter Cao Yibo, Sun Zhe and Lin Deren
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- Nasser Al-Attiyah does not look, or shoot, like a man of 55.
The Qatari, who claimed his sixth Dakar Rally title barely eight months ago, teamed up with two compatriots on Wednesday to win gold in the men's skeet team event at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, his third gold and sixth medal across nine Asian Games spanning 32 years.
"To start from the Hiroshima Asian Games and to come back here again, and today for our team to win two gold medals, is really amazing," he said. Al-Attiyah described his performance as "one of the highest scores in the field," despite having only about two months to prepare between rally races.
Al-Attiyah is far from alone among the older competitors at these Games. At Nagoya City General Gymnasium this week, 51-year-old Uzbek vaulter Oksana Chusovitina, known to fans simply as "Chuso," was competing at her seventh Asian Games, a run stretching back to Hiroshima 1994, the same edition where Al-Attiyah made his debut.
At Aichi-Nagoya 2026, Chusovitina qualified fourth for the vault final with a score of 13.266, adding another chapter to a career that has already brought her two golds, four silvers and two bronzes since 1994.
Chusovitina's longevity, however, has never been only about medals. In 2002, her three-year-old son Alisher was diagnosed with leukemia, and she turned gymnastics into a lifeline, competing wherever prize money and support were available.
Her son had recovered by the time she won vault silver at Beijing 2008. Rather than step away, she chose to keep competing, through Tokyo 2020 at 46 and an injury-forced absence from Paris 2024, before returning at 50 to win World Cup gold in Baku.
Asked in Nagoya, inevitably, when she might retire, she shot back with a grin: "What, don't you want to see me anymore?" With Los Angeles 2028 in her sights, she is not ruling out a ninth Olympics.
The same refusal to be counted out defines Nosheen Aslam's Asian Games debut. At 55, the Pakistani table tennis player was the oldest competitor in the women's team event in Nagoya, sharing a roster with a 15-year-old teammate and facing opponents decades younger.
She took up the sport 12 years ago, already a mother of three, and often trains at night after cooking, working and caring for her children. "Every time I play, I feel happy and forget the worries of my life," she said. "Age is just a number."
Her results in Nagoya did not go her way, but she left already looking ahead to next April's South Asian Games. "Maybe I can play for another two or three years," she said, before adding with a smile: "Maybe next time my performance will be better."
China also has its own example of longevity. Wan Antao, a 41-year-old shooter, is making his Asian Games debut as the oldest member of an 815-strong Chinese delegation whose average age is 24.
At the opposite end of that same delegation is its youngest athlete, nearly three decades his junior: 12-year-old skateboarder Cao Shiqi.
The Beijing native discovered the sport by chance at a shopping mall at age four, balancing on a demonstration board before she could properly ride a bike. She has spent this year making progress in her specialty, park, an event in which competitors perform tricks in pool-like courses up to 4.5 meters deep.
The seventh-grader won the junior title at the Asian Skateboarding Championships in April and the national title in July, bouncing back after a fall at China's National Games last November left her in tears.
Her coaches have been careful not to make results the sole focus. For a 12-year-old, her family says, simply experiencing the atmosphere of a major Games matters more than a place on the podium, with the Olympics a longer-term target.
Youth is making itself felt well beyond the Chinese team.
Should eleven-year-old Kurihara Yuki, a fifth-grader from Tokyo, medal in Nagoya in Esports, he would break the record for the youngest medalist in Asian Games history, currently held by a 12-year-old Indonesian skateboarder who took bronze at Jakarta 2018.
No teenager at the Games has made a bigger impact than 13-year-old Chinese swimmer Yu Zidi. Making her Asian Games debut, she broke the Games record to win the women's 200m butterfly, then broke the Asian record in the 200m individual medley two days later, edging compatriot and defending champion Yu Yiting in one of the closest races of the meet.
On Wednesday, she added a third gold in the 400m individual medley, finishing nearly four seconds clear of the field. "It's the final 50 meters, so I just told myself not to hold anything back," she said of her closing kick.
Out of the pool, she is unmistakably 13, calling her parents from training camps and insisting people remember she is "just a kid" her age. In the water, she sounds like anything but a novice: "Even when I'm very tired, I have to keep training. When I feel I can't hold on, I still have to keep going."
From Yu at 13 to Chusovitina at 51, from Al-Attiyah's three decades of elite competition to a fifth-grader's rise through the ranks of a video game, the Asian Games have shown that high-level sport does not belong to any single age group.
What connects them is not the number of years behind them, but a determination not to let age decide when their time in competition is over. ■

PAM party leads Morocco’s legislative elections with 97 seats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
04:29:47 UTC
13:29:47 KST

Diyar Guldogan and Ikram Kouachi
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
Morocco’s Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) emerged as the leading party in the country’s legislative elections, securing 97 seats, according to results announced by the Interior Ministry.
 
Interior Minister Abdelouafi Laftit announced the preliminary official results at a news conference in the capital Rabat early Thursday.
 
Laftit said voting across the country took place under “normal conditions, except for isolated cases,” which he did not specify, that “did not affect the electoral process.”
 
The National Rally of Independents (RNI) followed PAM with 66 seats, while the Istiqlal Party won 65 seats.
 
The Justice and Development Party (PJD) placed fourth with 54 seats.
 
The Popular Movement won 29 seats, followed by the Socialist Union of Popular Forces with 26, the Party of Progress and Socialism with 19 and the Constitutional Union with 17.
 
The Left Alliance and Social Democratic Movement each won eight seats, while the Democratic Forces Front and Insaf Party each secured two seats. The New Democrats and Unity and Democracy parties each won one seat.
 
The results determine the composition of Morocco’s 395-member House of Representatives.
 
Under the country’s constitutional system, the king appoints the head of government from the party that wins the largest number of seats.
 
The ministry said voter turnout stood at 38.02% nationwide, down from 50.18% in the 2021 legislative elections.
 
According to official data, the number of voters registered on the electoral rolls stood at 15,801,162.
 
A party needs at least 198 seats for a majority in the House, opening the way for consultations to form a governing majority following the announcement of the results.
 
In the 2021 elections, RNI topped the results with 102 seats, followed by PAM with 86 and Istiqlal with 81.
 
RNI leader Aziz Akhannouch currently heads a coalition government that also includes PAM and Istiqlal.
 
The next government will face political, economic, and social issues, as well as projects related to Morocco’s preparations to co-host the 2030 FIFA World Cup.

AI model Claude discovers CRISPR-like enzyme system, Anthropic says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
04:26:34 UTC
13:26:34 KST

AI model Claude discovers CRISPR-like enzyme system, Anthropic says
AI giant announces discovery amid global debate about how to safeguard against catastrophic risks.
AI giant Anthropic has announced the discovery of a new enzyme system in bacterial DNA that it said could “represent a new gene editing mechanism” similar to the groundbreaking CRISPR tool.
Anthropic said on Wednesday that its signature AI model, Claude, had “autonomously” discovered the system at the prompting of researchers working at the company’s recently established biology research lab in San Francisco.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4OpenAI, Anthropic CEOs call for global AI regulation at UN
- list 2 of 4China’s Xi visits US as Trump bets on stabilising global relations
- list 3 of 4Turkiye agrees to gradual handover of Bashiqa base to Iraq
- list 4 of 4Venezuela’s Delcy Rodriguez promises elections at UN, gives no date
The tech giant said the system showed characteristics found in only a handful of other “programmable” structures and displayed a “pattern reminiscent of CRISPR”, a genome-editing mechanism found in bacteria.
CRISPR technology has been credited with advancing the treatment of a range of diseases, including sickle cell disease and cancer.
Anthropic, which is at the centre of a vigorous global debate about how to maximise the benefits of AI while mitigating catastrophic risks, said it had not determined the function of the system. It said Claude discovered the system after spending 21 hours searching a large database of DNA sequences.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who has claimed that AI could cure most diseases within five to 10 years, said in a post on X that his company suspects the “molecular machine” could “represent a new gene editing mechanism”. He said AI was only at the “very beginning” of making discoveries that could lead to medical breakthroughs.
“I’m genuinely rooting for all of the frontier labs to seriously get into biological discovery, and I’m excited about what comes out of it,” Amodei added.
Stanley Qi, an associate professor of bioengineering at Stanford University, described the reported discovery as “incredibly exciting.”
“What stands out is its ability to recognize an unusual biological pattern that was difficult to detect before, and to pursue it comprehensively as a research question,” Qi told Al Jazeera.
“Nature contains an enormous diversity of molecular systems we barely understand, and some patterns are very complicated but highly meaningful; AI could greatly expand our ability to explore them more effectively and rapidly, in this case, in just 21 hours,” he said.
However, Kevin Blake, a microbiologist at Washington University School of Medicine, expressed scepticism about the scientific significance of the announcement.
“Because the identified array is ‘CRISPR-like’, some have leaped to conclude Anthropic discovered the ‘next CRISPR’ – ie, a Nobel Prize-winning gene editing technology,” Blake told Al Jazeera.
“CRISPR-the-technology is very different from CRISPR in nature, which is basically a bacterium’s immune system. It has long been known that there are countless CRISPR-like sequences we have yet to identify and catalogue because there are millions of bacterial species we have yet to study,” Blake said.
“There’s nothing to indicate this is a rival to CRISPR-the-technology, or could be developed into any kind of therapeutic or practical application,” he added.
Emmanuelle Charpentier, a microbiologist at the Max Planck Unit for the Science of Pathogens, and Jennifer Doudna, a biochemist at the University of California, Berkeley, pioneered the use of the naturally occurring CRISPR system to edit DNA in living organisms, earning the pair the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Last year, the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia in the US announced that doctors had treated a patient with a customised CRISPR gene-editing therapy for the first time.
In what the hospital called a “historic” medical breakthrough, researchers developed a bespoke therapy to successfully treat an infant born with carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 deficiency, a rare metabolic disease.

Nova massacre survivor gets light sentence for drug dealing, judge cites his severe PTSD
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
04:22:22 UTC
13:22:22 KST

The trauma of the Nova massacre tipped the scales. Despite the enormous quantities of cocaine, MDMA, ketamine, LSD and other drugs found in the home and car of 32-year-old Shahar Luca, a survivor of the Nova music festival massacre who had previously been convicted of drug offenses, he was sentenced to just nine months of community service.
Prosecutors sought a five-year prison term over what they described as a “drug supermarket,” and the court found that the appropriate sentencing range was four to seven years behind bars. But Luca’s severe post-traumatic stress disorder and the rehabilitation process he had undergone led to the unusual outcome.
Luca admitted the facts in the indictment and was convicted of possession of drugs not for personal use. According to the indictment, a little over a year ago he kept a wide variety of drugs at his home in central Tel Aviv and in his car.
Police found 835.37 grams of cannabis in dozens of containers in the bedroom and kitchen, 4.68 grams of ketamine in a living room cabinet and 50 milliliters of GBL in the refrigerator door.
In his car, authorities found, among other things, 198 grams of P-METHYLMETHCATHINONE, nearly a kilogram of MDMA, about 773 grams of psilocin in 14 colorful chocolate packages labeled “Magic Mushroom,” around 627 grams of cocaine, hundreds of MDMA and methamphetamine tablets and 1,114 paper squares containing LSD.
Authorities also seized 126 vials containing 4.375 liters of ketamine, as well as amphetamine, GBL and other synthetic drugs. Prosecutors said the haul included more than 4.5 kilograms of solid drugs and tablets, along with more than three liters of liquid drugs.
The prosecutor argued that the case involved the large-scale possession of an extremely varied “drug supermarket.” She said the range of substances, the large quantities and the fact that some had already been divided into packages pointed to an intent to sell and broad distribution potential.
The prosecution asked the court to set a sentencing range of six to eight years in prison and argued there was no justification for departing from it on rehabilitation grounds.
Prosecutors stressed that Luca had two prior convictions. One was a 2020 conviction for possession of drugs not for personal use and drug trafficking in 2017, for which he served 10 months in prison.
They argued that Luca had struggled to take full responsibility for his actions and that the treatment process he had entered still did not justify avoiding imprisonment. Still, given his exceptional circumstances as a Nova survivor, prosecutors asked that he be sentenced to five years in prison.
His defense attorney, Yuval Zemer, described the severe trauma Luca experienced on October 7. According to the sentencing decision, his best friend, Mor, was shot in the head and killed while they were fleeing, and Luca lay for about five hours beneath his body inside an overturned vehicle while terrorists carried out executions nearby to ensure victims were dead.
After he was rescued and hospitalized, Luca left the hospital covered in blood and later shut himself away for months at his parents’ home in northern Israel.
The defense submitted documents showing that Luca had been recognized as a victim of hostile acts and was initially assessed as having a temporary disability of 50%, followed later by a permanent psychiatric disability of 40%.
His attorney argued that sending him to prison would “sentence him to psychological ruin,” destroy his prospects for rehabilitation and worsen the PTSD from which he suffers. He asked the court to adopt the Probation Service’s recommendation and impose community service, along with a one-year probation order.
Luca himself expressed remorse and told the court that he committed the offense during a period when he was not functioning and could see no future ahead of him.
He described the treatment process he had undergone and said he wanted to continue on the path of rehabilitation and return to a normative life. The Probation Service said he had completed a day-treatment program at the Ma’ayan Hanefesh center, cooperated fully and provided clean drug tests, apart from medical cannabis, which he uses under license.
Judge Shmuel Melamed spoke at length about the seriousness of Luca’s actions and found that he “did not possess a single drug in a minimal quantity, but operated a real ‘drug supermarket,’ containing an extremely wide range of some of the hardest and most dangerous drugs listed under the law.”
According to the judge, the enormous quantity “demonstrates the depth of his involvement in the world of drugs and drastically increases the severity of the harm to the public interest.”
The judge also ruled that the possession was not spontaneous or accidental, but involved an inventory that required planning, financial means and connections with various parties.
He said distribution of the drugs could have created “enormous destructive potential for public health and safety,” although the drugs were seized before reaching users.
At the same time, the judge said the trauma Luca experienced at Nova had drastically impaired his ability to exercise balanced judgment.
“Although this condition does not exempt him from full criminal responsibility, it significantly diminishes the gravity of his moral culpability,” the judge wrote.
He set the appropriate sentencing range at four to seven years in prison, but decided to depart from it because of Luca’s rehabilitation prospects.
“I am convinced that in this special and exceptional case, the clear prospects for rehabilitation and the profound change Luca has undergone outweigh the principle of retribution,” the judge ruled.
He said Luca’s treatment relationship, persistence in therapy and proven abstinence from drugs showed that Luca “has returned to the right path and should be allowed to continue on it.”
Ultimately, Luca was sentenced to nine months of community service, fined 5,000 shekels, given a suspended driving disqualification and placed under a one-year probation order.
The judge warned him that drug use, refusal to undergo urine tests or violation of the terms of his community service could result in its termination and require him to serve the remainder of the sentence behind bars.
The court also declared him a “drug dealer.” The question of whether a seized Rolex Oyster watch will be forfeited will be decided separately.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Beijing seeks to control the first island chain and push US military presence back to the second island chain, a Taiwan national security official has said.
Beijing’s campaign consists of three phases, they said. First, it has covertly supported Iran, Russia, and North Korea to raise the cost for the US in managing global affairs, per Liberty Times. This creates conditions for US concessions in the first island chain.
Second, Beijing has used think tanks and academics to shape US public discourse by labeling Taiwan, Japan, and the Philippines as “troublemakers” and amplifying the narrative that the first island chain burdens the US, the official said.

The official said China is aware that once Taiwan gains full asymmetric defense capabilities, it will have to reassess its military posture in the region and in the Taiwan Strait. A shift in strategy would potentially require even greater military investment and undermine its strategic objectives, they said.
On US arms sales to Taiwan, the official said China is attempting to create the impression that tensions would ease if the US steps back, Liberty Times reported. However, in reality, Beijing is expanding its influence and pushing to change the regional status quo.
The official said that given close Taiwan–US security cooperation, arms sales will continue as long as they align with mutual regional security needs.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Demand for AI servers and semiconductor equipment is driving a surge in high-tech air cargo between Asia and North America.

Starlux Airlines, which currently relies mainly on passenger aircraft for cargo, is also benefiting from rising high-tech shipments.

China Airlines Americas cargo head Lo Pao-jen (羅保仁) said the surge became noticeable after AI infrastructure investment expanded in 2024, per CNA. AI servers and other IT products have become major cargo sources, while semiconductor demand has also increased shipments of related manufacturing equipment from the US, he explained.
Lo said higher fuel costs following the outbreak of fighting in the Middle East in February have been offset by strong AI-related demand, keeping freight rates at reasonable levels. He said China Airlines operates more than 40 freighter flights a week in North America, with the region accounting for more than 60% of its cargo revenue.
EVA Air President Sun Chia-ming (孫嘉明) said in June that AI-related cargo accounted for about 40% to 50% of the airline’s cargo business, while North America generated about 70% of cargo revenue. He added that the company plans to expand its freighter fleet from nine aircraft to 12 by 2028.
Starlux, which has no dedicated freighters yet, has seen cargo revenue rise 41% year on year to NT$713 million (US$22.39 million) in May and NT$672 million in August and has ordered 10 Airbus A350F freighters, with deliveries potentially delayed until 2028.
The surge in air cargo comes as AI demand continues to drive exports. August exports hit a record NT$2.62 trillion, up 41% year on year, with electronic components and information, communications, and audiovisual products among the strongest performers, according to the Ministry of Finance.

Taiwan environment ministry to expand list of hazardous air pollutants

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
04:13:30 UTC
13:13:30 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Ministry of Environment announced plans Wednesday to add 31 hazardous air pollutants to its regulated list, expanding the number of substances subject to controls to 104.
The amended list includes specialized solvents and chemicals used in precision manufacturing that have mutagenic, reproductively toxic, or highly bioaccumulative properties, according to a press release. On the list is benzo[a]pyrene (BaP), a common carcinogen at the center of a food safety scandal in July.
The ministry said it will establish emission standards for the newly listed pollutants and consider imposing air pollution fees based on their environmental impact.
Existing regulations cover heavy metals such as lead and mercury, as well as certain volatile organic compounds including benzene and trichloroethylene.
To amend the list, the ministry reviewed regulatory lists in the US, Germany, Japan and South Korea, as well as hazard assessments by the WHO, the International Agency for Research on Cancer, and the EU.
The government is seeking to tighten overall air quality rules, with the ministry announcing Monday amendments to the Indoor Air Quality Management Act targeting indoor facilities used by young children and older adults.
Huang Wei-ming (黃偉鳴), director-general of the ministry’s Department of Atmospheric Environment, said the ministry hopes to establish standards for indoor air quality monitoring by the end of the year.
Chou Nan-chun (周南君), chair of the Taiwan Indoor Environment Quality Management Association, said people in Taiwan spend more than 80% of their time indoors and that a science-based management system is critical to addressing risks such as extreme heat and emerging infectious diseases.
Deputy Environment Minister Hsieh Yen-ru (謝燕儒) said Taiwan has a high rate of air-conditioner use, but keeping windows closed while running air conditioning for long periods of time means indoor air quality needs greater attention.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan wrapped up his four-day visit to the US on Wednesday.

On Monday, Erdogan met with his Vietnamese counterpart To Lam at the Turkish House, or Turkevi Center, where they addressed bilateral relations as well as regional and global issues.
Welcoming Vietnam’s positive response to Türkiye’s proposal to elevate bilateral relations to the level of a strategic partnership, Erdogan said Ankara is working to further expand cooperation with Vietnam in many fields, particularly in investment, trade and the defense industry.
Erdogan met separately with Mohamed al-Menfi, chairman of the Libyan Presidential Council, at the Turkish House.

(UNIFIL).

"The conflicts, wars and crises we face in our region and around the world require Türkiye and the United States to maintain close dialogue," he said, adding the two countries are achieving "favorable outcomes" on a number of issues with global implications, particularly in the Middle East as well as in Africa and Asia.
Ankara is determined to sustain and intensify its efforts in the coming period, he added.
"At this point, I would like to emphasize: We can never consider our strategic relationship with the United States separately from our economic and trade ties, nor do we."
Despite global economic and political fluctuations, Erdogan said the bilateral trade volume has doubled over the past 10 years.
"Our bilateral trade, which exceeded $38 billion in 2025, reached $28 billion in the first eight months of this year. It appears that by the end of the year, we will surpass the 2025 figure, reaching $40 billion. WATCH Catholic priests and nuns make Gaza ‘genocide’ march to Vatican
Unknown

WATCH Catholic priests and nuns make Gaza ‘genocide’ march to Vatican
Around 150 Catholic priests, bishops, friars, and nuns have marched to the Vatican as part of a procession through Rome demanding an end to what they describe as Israel’s “genocide” in Gaza.
The group stopped near St. Peter’s Square before continuing to the Palestinian and Lebanese embassies and ending outside the headquarters of Italian arms manufacturer Leonardo.
Participants carried olive branches and posters depicting the Madonna holding an emaciated child with the words “Christ Died in Gaza.” They also carried a large white banner bearing the names of hundreds of Palestinian and Lebanese children killed in Israeli airstrikes.
Outside Leonardo, which has supplied weapons and military equipment to Israel, Italian Archbishop Franco Moscone called for international arrest warrants targeting arms-industry executives. Moscone has previously compared Israel’s conduct in Gaza to Nazi methods and urged European countries to consider withdrawing recognition of Israel.
Tuesday’s event was organized by Priests Against Genocide, an international Catholic network established last year. The group said clergy from eight countries took part, including South Africa, England, Ireland, Germany, the US, and Spain.
The network has taken a more categorical position than the Holy See. The late Pope Francis called for an investigation into whether Israel’s actions in Gaza met the legal definition of genocide, while his successor, Leo XIV, has said the Vatican is not prepared to make such a determination.
A UN commission of inquiry concluded in September 2025 that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, citing killings, serious bodily and mental harm, deliberately destructive living conditions, and measures intended to prevent births. A separate case brought by South Africa remains before the International Court of Justice, which has yet to issue a final judgment.
Israel strongly rejects the genocide allegation, saying it targets militants and seeks to minimize civilian casualties while accusing Hamas of operating in densely populated areas.
Israel launched its offensive in Gaza following the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, which killed around 1,200 Israelis, mostly civilians. Gaza health authorities say more than 73,000 Palestinians have since been killed, nearly half of them women and children.
