Peter V'landys' appointment as NRL executive chairman has been made official after the veteran administrator stepped down as Racing NSW chief executive.
V'landys confirmed this morning that he was ending his 22-year stint at the helm of Racing NSW, following a period of long-service leave that ends in November.
That resignation looms served as the final step in a process of moving into the NRL full time and taking on the most powerful role in rugby league since the Super League war.
"Peter has completely reinvigorated Rugby League during his tenure and the Commission is backing him in to grow the game even further," AR:C commissioner Peter Beattie said.
"Peter inherited a game with limited reserves and no significant assets, one that had needed an advance from its broadcasters just to pay the clubs and players.
"He consistently put the fan first, and the record audiences and the biggest broadcast deal in Australian sport followed."
V'Landys said he was excited to begin his new role and pledged to "take [rugby league] to the world".
Since taking over as ARL Commission chairman in 2019, V'landys has become an increasingly dominant figure in rugby league.
But this move will see his role grow even further, effectively replacing former NRL chief executive Andrew Abdo in his old position while remaining at the head of the commission.
When Abdo announced his resignation in May, V'landys had said only "Superman and Jesus added together" could replace him.
At the time, V'landys refused to speculate whether that figure could be him, but signalled he would take leave from Racing NSW in July to be able to dedicate time to the NRL.
In the months since, the 64-year-old has garnered the support required from both the clubs and the states to allow him to take on the role.
Fellow commissioners have also approved the move, with the appointment now expected to be made official as early as today.
Since the creation of the independent ARL Commission in 2012, no person has held the role of chairman and executive on a full-time basis.
V'landys had been chief executive of Racing NSW since early 2004, after previously spending 17 years as boss of NSW Harness Racing.
He led the racing industry through the equine influenza outbreak, with the creation of The Everest in 2017 among his other key legacies.
"Naturally, this is a very sad day for me. I have put my heart and soul into racing for 22 years. I have been fortunate to work with outstanding, loyal and hardworking boards of directors and staff," V'landys said.
"As a team, we went from a struggling jurisdiction to a world-leading jurisdiction. I take this opportunity to thank everyone who has been in our team. I will miss them greatly, and I wish the industry every success."
In a statement, Racing NSW said V'landys's "many initiatives" had procured $3.5 billion in new funding.
Racing NSW chair Saranne Cooke said his contribution to racing was without parallel.
"Peter V'landys has been, without doubt, the most effective and successful administrator in the history of Australian sport," Dr Cooke said.
"His contribution cannot simply be measured by the extraordinary growth of racing in NSW during his tenure.
"Peter has fundamentally changed the trajectory of racing in this country and made NSW one of the world's leading racing jurisdictions."
Waterhouse says right time to move on
Horse racing legend Gai Waterhouse said it was the right time for V'landys to move on.
Waterhouse came up against V'Landys amidst his failed attempt to sell Rosehill Racecourse in Sydney to the State Government to build residential housing.
The battle saw the two prominent industry figures disagree about the sport's future, with Waterhouse successfully campaigning among Australian Turf Club members not to sell the track, despite Premier Chris Minns and V'Landys pushing to sell the site.
"A lot of money has gone into buying properties that should have been funded back into development of the race tracks and stands," Waterhouse said.
"If we're going to be able to attract people back to the races, they have to be comfortable."
Waterhouse was especially concerned about the state of regional racetracks.
"They've been shockingly neglected over the tenure of Mr V'landys, and they need to have money spent on them," she said.
Waterhouse said his expected move to rugby league from horse racing had come at the right time.
"He's a very strong and very powerful person, but it's time for him to move and he has moved on. So let's move on now," she said.

Moscow’s Ceasefire Bingo Card – What Might the Kremlin Say to Ukraine’s Unconditional Ceasefire?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:31:00 UTC
06:31:00 KST

Ukraine unveiled an unconditional ceasefire proposal on Wednesday, Sept. 23, backed by 50 countries in a joint statement.
Now the key question – how will Russia respond? Russia’s Foreign Minister Lavrov has already ruled out a ceasefire during peace talks – but how will Moscow react to an unconditional ceasefire as a whole?
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Instead of guessing what Moscow will say, here’s a bingo card of what it might say, based on past statements on similar proposals.
Or it could be a combination of different points; who knows.
“Ukraine already violated it”
Russia has in the past moved the starting date earlier, then blamed Ukraine for violating a ceasefire before it was agreed.
The more recent example came in the form of US President Donald Trump’s energy truce, when he claimed both Kyiv and Moscow had agreed to it when, in fact, they had not. Before Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin’s spokesperson Dmitry Peskov snubbed it as a “very good idea” a day later, he also accused Ukraine of attacking Russian energy facilities.
But there was never an energy truce, not to mention that Russia had also hit two gas stations in Kyiv the same morning.
Similar patterns were observed in most ceasefire agreements, with both Kyiv and Moscow accusing one another of violations, including the so-called energy truce in March 2025, when Moscow said Ukraine had violated it by moving the starting date, or during Moscow’s May 9 parade, when no one really understood what ceasefire meant on the front.
Russia Must Answer for Crimes in Crimea, Zelensky Says
That’s why the “unconditional” part of the latest proposal matters.
“Good idea. But…”
Here comes the Putin classic – saying yes and meaning no.
One such case happened in March 2025, when Trump pushed for a 30-day ceasefire after his return to office.
In response to that proposal, Putin said the 30-day ceasefire proposal is “good and we absolutely support it but there are issues that we need to discuss” before questioning the effectiveness of the proposal, naming a number of “conditions that need to be studied,” such as the enforcement of the ceasefire along the front.
The result was the 30-day energy truce – see how it worked out in the previous section.
“How about we try something else?”
Remember the Istanbul talks?
A short recap – in the summer of 2025, the EU issued an ultimatum to Putin to move toward an unconditional 30-day ceasefire or face massive sanctions. Putin countered with a plan to resume what he called the Istanbul format, based on early negotiations in 2022 during the first days of the full-scale invasion.
Putin was a no-show and sent a historian in his place who reportedly threatened the Ukrainian delegation. The format, including multiple negotiations, resulted in prisoner swaps but not the ceasefire envisioned.
And good for Putin – without the promised massive sanctions either.
Another example would be August 2025’s Alaska summit, when Trump threatened Putin with massive secondary tariffs, with the two ultimately agreeing to a summit in Alaska instead that earned Putin first-class treatment on US soil after being ostracized since 2022.
Again, no sanctions and tariffs as promised. A win-win for Putin.
“Ukraine doesn’t really want it”
Sometimes it’s as easy as blaming Ukraine for impeding the process without saying how.
“Representatives of the Kyiv regime, the leadership in Kyiv, speak of peace and propose resuming so-called negotiations, but themselves commit such crimes, doing everything to ensure that there is no peace and no negotiations,” Putin told Russia’s Military-Industrial Commission on Sept. 18.
Which raises the question – what exactly should Ukraine do then?
Bonus: Setting out unmeetable conditions
Russia also has a habit of highballing other parties in negotiations, setting conditions that some might consider outrageous.
If the opponents relent and cave in – that’s a win. If they don’t? Blame them for failing to meet the conditions.
A recurring example would be asking Zelensky to come to Moscow for a Putin meeting to settle things once and for all. Another would be to tell Kyiv to withdraw from territories it still controls – that Moscow failed to win for 12 years – as a precondition for peace talks.
Again, this is why the “unconditional” part of the new proposal matters.
“Sure, let’s stop”
If only we had heard this, then perhaps thousands, if not millions, of Ukrainians and Russians would still be alive today.

China is leveraging its diaspora to boost the economy, unlike India
While Beijing has turned its diaspora into an extension of its domestic economy, New Delhi has largely allowed its diaspora to strengthen other economies
4-MIN READ4-MIN
2
 Listen
Ravi Kant is an author, columnist and analyst whose work focuses on technology, economics, international politics and geopolitics. 
A country’s diaspora can be a symbol of its pride and power. A nation’s diaspora can help it build international value through success stories, promote its soft power through culture and contribute to its economic progress through remittances, investments and transfers of expertise.
India and China have among the world’s largest diasporas. They also offer two very different models of how countries can leverage their diasporas.
In India, before the 1991 reforms, people mostly saw those who left as a “brain drain”. But post-liberalisation, people started to see the Indian diaspora as an economic bridge to capital, technology and global markets. In 2004, India set up a ministry to oversee the affairs of Indians abroad, merging it with the Ministry of External Affairs in 2016.

Lula, Bolsonaro and a divided Brazil: A tight race with stakes beyond its borders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:28:59 UTC
06:28:59 KST

Washington, DC — A string of right-wing victories across Latin America, from Argentina and Peru to Ecuador and Colombia, has put Brazil’s election under sharper scrutiny. Now the region’s largest country heads to the polls with its own political direction at stake.
The October 4 vote pits President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, nearing the end of his third term, against Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former right-wing president Jair Bolsonaro. The contest brings two familiar names and competing visions of Brazil’s future to the ballot.
The divide runs deeper than policy. It cuts through a country where the Lula and Bolsonaro names have become rallying cries on either side of a bitter political struggle.
Recent polls suggest little separates the two candidates, placing them in a statistical tie in simulated runoffs.
Lula is campaigning on a progressive legacy that helped lift millions out of poverty in the 2000s. Bolsonaro carries the conservative banner, seeking to bring Latin America’s rightward shift to its biggest political stage.
Voters are concerned about many issues, yet what makes this election stand out from other regional ones are two things: a corruption case affecting both leading candidates, and the future of the critical Amazon rainforest.
Future of the Amazon rainforest
Although an environmental issue, the concern is being used as a political tool, raising consequential questions in Brazil's presidential race — and testing whether the country can reconcile its economic ambitions with its role as guardian of the world's largest rainforest.
According to government figures, Amazon deforestation fell to its lowest level in a decade in the first half of 2026.
In July of this year, President Lula da Silva laid out a plan to reach zero deforestation by 2030.
Bolsonaro's campaign offers a different approach, describing the environment as a "strategic asset" and proposing expanded payments for environmental services, bioeconomy development, and economic incentives for people who preserve native vegetation.
"It shouldn't go unmissed that in the latest meeting between (President Donald) Trump and Lula in May, critical minerals were absolutely on the agenda, and the future of the Amazon ecosystem," Elizabeth Dickinson, interim deputy director for Latin America at the International Crisis Group, tells TRT World.
The future of critical-mineral extraction in the same areas is central to this election, and whoever wins may well determine the course Brazil sets.
"Whether it's greater acceptance of extractive industries in this critical ecosystem, or whether it is really a focus on those key climate and ecological commitments that have been a pinnacle of Brazilian foreign policy for some time," Dickinson adds.
Election clouded by corruption
The Banco Master corruption scandal casts a shadow over the election.
At its centre is the Central Bank’s extrajudicial liquidation of the lender in November 2025, with missing funds reportedly totalling $2.2 billion.
The fallout has reached both Lula’s and Bolsonaro’s campaigns, deepening voter disillusionment with the choices on the ballot.
"Polling has really sort of been a toss-up throughout this race, and particularly as the corruption scandal has continued to embroil a growing number of officials," Dickinson says.
"These are individuals from the legislature, the courts, the central bank, and so forth."
Former finance minister Fernando Haddad called the scandal potentially the biggest bank fraud in the country's history, and ongoing investigations implicated numerous high-profile political figures across the spectrum.
Potential complete regional shift
Across Brazil, as elsewhere in the region, the campaign is being shaped by concerns that reach beyond party loyalties.
Violence and everyday safety lead voters’ worries, with the economy and corruption also competing for attention. How candidates answer those concerns could prove central to the campaign.
Another question carries weight beyond Brazil’s borders: how closely should the country align with Washington?
The region’s rightward shift has given the US willing partners in Argentina, Peru, Ecuador and Colombia, including support for Washington’s regional security agenda.
Brazil and Mexico have resisted elements of that agenda. Lula has rejected an outside role in tackling Brazil’s organised crime, insisting that international cooperation must respect national sovereignty.
That stance puts him at odds with the Trump administration’s revival of the Monroe Doctrine, the 19th-century policy asserting US primacy in the Americas, as Washington presses to extend its regional influence.
Brazil is one of the few countries with the size, clout, economic power, and foreign policy apparatus to offer a different narrative.
"This election will certainly determine whether that is the case or whether there is really a shift across the region to a more consistent and full-fledged alignment between Latin American leaders and the United States," Dickinson says.
"All politics is local, and that's certainly reflected in the polling."

French court confirms rape trial for PSG and Morocco star Hakimi
A French court on Wednesday upheld a decision to send Paris Saint-Germain and Morocco footballer Achraf Hakimi to trial on rape charges, a judicial source told AFP.
An appeals court confirmed on June 19, during the World Cup, that Hakimi would stand trial in criminal court over the alleged rape of a woman in 2023, an accusation he has repeatedly denied.
Hakimi, 27, had appealed that decision to the Court of Cassation, the highest court in the French judicial system for civil and criminal matters.
The appeal was Hakimi's final legal recourse. In February, he was ordered to stand trial before the criminal court in the Hauts-de-Seine department on the rape charge.
Hakimi challenged that initial order and then appealed to the Court of Cassation after the Versailles appeals court upheld the decision in June.
"The allegations against Achraf Hakimi, which he has firmly contested from day one, have not been examined by the Court of Cassation," the player's lawyer, Fanny Colin, told AFP.
"They will be during the trial, at which all the evidence in Achraf Hakimi's defence will be presented publicly," the lawyer continued.
She added her client, "who has nothing to hide", had fully cooperated with police and judicial authorities throughout the investigation and would continue to do so during the forthcoming trial.
A lawyer for the plaintiff said the decision to send the case to trial reflected the "strength and rigour of the court of appeal's reasoning".
"After three and a half years of legal battles, after being slandered and dragged through the mud by Achraf Hakimi's defence, my client is determined to obtain justice; she will fight to the very end," the woman's lawyer, Rachel-Flore Pardo, said in a statement sent to AFP.
In February 2023, a woman then aged 24 told police in the Val-de-Marne region southeast of Paris that Hakimi had raped her.
The plaintiff said she met Hakimi in January 2023 on Instagram and went to his home in a taxi ordered by the player, a police source said at the time.
She claimed the player kissed her, touched her without her consent and then raped her.
She said she managed to push him away and text a friend, who came to pick her up.
Hakimi was charged with rape a few days later.
PSG said Hakimi "has always firmly denied the allegations against him" and continued to benefit from the presumption of innocence.
"The club is committed to ensuring a calm and respectful working environment for its player, in accordance with the fundamental principles of the rule of law," PSG said in a statement to AFP.
The French champions also reiterated "their constant and unequivocal commitment to combating all forms of violence, particularly sexual violence."

Differential rates?
We are heading into difficult times. the RBA should stop raising interest rates on borrowing for people on their own homes. Ordinary people are paying the price for policies from 30 or 40 years ago which massively altered our economy.
- Vicki Dixon
It's an interesting point. So the RBA doesn't raise interest rates per se — it sets the cash rate, and then banks choose how they pass these on to borrowers (and hence why you see it's generally more expensive for an investor home loan rather than an owner-occupier, often to the tune of 20 to 30 basis points).
So they don't set separate rates, but there are examples of policy that can lead to greater differentials between investors and homeowners.
For example, in 2014, APRA set a limit on how much banks could grow their investor lending. This reduced the supply of funds available to investors and led to their rates being pushed up significantly more than for homeowners until about 2019.

Breadcrumb
Is NAZA Zionism's worst nightmare or normalisation propaganda?
The documentary film NAZA (an acronym for Nezek Agavi; “collateral damage” in Hebrew), written and directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, has created a firestorm of controversy. Though few have actually seen the film, it reportedly contains interviews with 24 anonymous Israeli military and intelligence members who attest to the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and automated surveillance into military targeting systems used by Israeli forces during the ongoing Gaza genocide.
They also allege government approval of operations in which thousands of Palestinian civilians were killed as “collateral damage.”
Since its premiere at Venice, where Abraham and Szor received a record 25-minute standing ovation, the filmmakers have faced an escalating campaign of official condemnation and deadly threats. Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar called for their citizenship to be revoked, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced plans for legislation targeting those who “defame” Israeli soldiers, and Israel Defence Force (IDF) Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir said the military would use “every tool at our disposal” against the film.
Far-right activists have gone further, with calls for the filmmakers to be hunted and hanged, with more threats directed at their families.
On the surface, however, it is not clear why the film and its creators have become such a target of hatred and condemnation within Israel and the broader Zionist movement. Documentation of Israel’s genocidal criminality has been readily accessible for years, mostly from Palestinian journalists on the ground in Gaza, and the use of AI in targeting civilians has been detailed by Abraham himself in April 2024.

This response is akin to Pavlov blowing his whistle at his trained dogs: the whistle sounds, and the conditioned response follows.

This sustains a self-reinforcing system of dispossession of designated out-groups, while escalation and normalisation reproduce it.

It nourishes the ongoing Zionist settler colonial project which predates the establishment of the state of Israel in 1948.
According to the W2S model, resistance is also used to justify theft under the guise of “defence”. Settler society then normalises this through media institutions, social norms, incentives, and everyday conditioned behaviour, rendering the resulting construct a perceived reality.
In this way, normalisation expands the moral boundaries of what is considered acceptable, and who is considered human, thereby increasing the resources available for theft. This is clear to see in the deliberate and cynical blurring of civilian and militant categories, and the designation of Palestinian children as “future terrorists” by Israeli military and political leaders in recent years.
Furthermore, normalisation constructs a façade of so-called “open debate” among “varying opinions” and, consequently, a plurality of tolerated voices within settler society, while shifting attention from the conduct itself to the boundaries of permissible debate and the legitimacy of individual critics. Without it, the tawdry fabric of settler society is threatened.
Abraham and Szor as collateral damage
Zionist propaganda, also known as Hasbara, is one of the most sophisticated forms of state propaganda greasing expansion and theft. As an essential branch of hasbara, normalisation has evolved into an intricate web of deception, particularly utilised in the tropes of liberal Zionism, which presents the Zionist project and Israel as reformable and compatible with human rights. It includes a right-to-left political spectrum, democratic and progressive values, and a desire for peace and justice.
The fallout from NAZA reflects a conditioned reaction casting Abraham and Szor as traitors to the Zionist narrative, with a distinct propagandistic function.
In contrast to Palestinian journalists, who could be racialised and scapegoated as clear members of the out-group and subsequently targeted for elimination as “terrorists,” Abraham and Szor represent a new kind of threat to Israeli society - a threat from within. They have been singled out as in-group targets to be made an example of, using tactics typically reserved for out-group members (though still mild, for now), with the effect of discouraging other potential in-group whistleblowers from coming forward. Fearmongering and social rewards for their harassment are utilised, while simultaneously clarifying the internal boundaries of Zionist identity.
Thus, rather than approaching the film as new evidence for Israeli criminality, the firestorm around NAZA can be understood as an internal struggle within the Zionist movement over how to respond to evidence of genocide without challenging the underlying Zionist project.
Some liberal Zionists have embraced NAZA as a vehicle for bringing criticism of Israeli conduct in Gaza into Israeli public discourse and encouraging greater scrutiny of existing policies. Establishment Zionists have pushed back against such claims, in part reflecting concerns that their wider acceptance could contribute to a broader crisis of Israeli social cohesion.
In this sense, the debate in its present form serves to normalise Israel’s actions since 7 October: genocide is recast as something “debatable,” maintaining Israel's impunity for the worst crimes against humanity and war crimes, with the identities of those responsible remaining obscured.
Will the Zionist regime permit the film to screen in Israel? The full extent of NAZA's impact is yet to be determined. Already, its reaction should encourage all to adopt the nonviolent Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement against Israel for its oppression of freedom of speech and the targeting of the filmmakers.
Clearly, for it to have lasting moral impact, NAZA and its creators must give other whistleblowers the courage to step forward. Abraham, Szor and their colleagues can do more than hail the 24 Israeli military personnel featured in the film as courageous. They should urge them to come forward publicly from anonymity, which currently gives opponents an easy basis for dismissing the allegations without addressing their substance. Otherwise, NAZA risks becoming a discredited, normalising propaganda tool at the hands of the very forces it set out to hold accountable, and Abraham and Szor may also be swept into the gruesome machinations of Israel's genocide of Palestinian people as mere collateral damage.

As Trump and Xi meet, Chinese automakers could be a Pandora's box for U.S. auto industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:25:01 UTC
06:25:01 KST

DETROIT — As President Donald Trump meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week, U.S. politicians as well as the global automotive industry are warning that allowing Chinese automakers to enter the market could be a Pandora's box.
Trump earlier this month said he might be "OK" letting Chinese automakers into the U.S. if they produced vehicles domestically, leading a consortium of auto trade groups representing every major facet of the American auto industry to urge him to rethink that position.
It was an uncharacteristically unified message from automakers operating in the U.S., franchised dealers and suppliers. More than two dozen Democratic lawmakers followed that push with their own letter, urging Trump to keep in place U.S. restrictions against Chinese automakers.
"It's not at this point a partisan issue," Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., told reporters Wednesday. "It's about whether we want to make cars in America and whether we want a manufacturing base that can pivot when we need it. If we want that, we shouldn't let them in our country."
Trump is scheduled to host Xi and a delegation from China on Thursday and Friday that reportedly could include Wang Chuanfu, founder of BYD, China's largest automaker, and Robin Zeng, founder of CATL, the world's top battery maker for electric vehicles.
Michael Dunne, an expert on China's automotive industry and a former General Motors executive, said even the potential that those two executives could attend underscores the importance of Xi's trip for the U.S. auto industry.
GM CEO Mary Barra is also expected to be among the attendees at Trump's state dinner for Xi, Reuters reported Wednesday, along with several other U.S. executives, including Tesla CEO Elon Musk.
As for America's other largest automakers, Ford Motor declined to disclose whether CEO Jim Farley will be attending after the Department of Transportation criticized the company for its Chinese ties, including a licensing deal with CATL. Reuters reported Chrysler parent Stellantis said CEO Antonio Filosa is out of the country and not planning to attend.
Industry insiders and onlookers have expressed concerns similar to those raised by automakers and lawmakers as bipartisan bills to ban Chinese automakers from the U.S. move through Congress.
The pressure campaign comes as Chinese automakers have been rapidly expanding outside of their domestic market, especially to Europe and Central and South America. There's fear among global automakers that Chinese rivals, like BYD and Geely, which are heavily subsidized by their governments, could flood global markets, undercutting domestic production and vehicle prices.
Dunne said he doesn't believe those concerns are overblown. He said Chinese automakers would "quickly overwhelm America's auto industry, just as it is now ravaging Europe."
Global market share for Chinese brands jumped nearly 70% from 2020 to 2025, according to market research and consulting firm GlobalData. The automakers' market share in Europe was virtually nothing in 2020 but hit 12% in August, according to Germany-based Dataforce.
"China's scores of automakers are currently engaged in a fight-to-the-death price war at home," Dunne wrote in a post Monday. "There's red ink everywhere. Access to the U.S., by far the most lucrative car market in the world, is like a giant tank of life-saving oxygen."
'Attacking very aggressively'
For much of this century, China was one of the largest and fastest-growing markets in the world. Non-China automakers flocked to the historically enclosed country with hopes of massive sales and profits.
But after years of success for automakers such as GM, the Chinese automotive sector has rapidly changed from an insular industry to the biggest exporter of vehicles globally.
China's growth has been fueled by government funding for companies as well as a culture of innovation and speed the country has instilled in its workers, experts said. The decision to ramp up exports has come on the heels of a slowing Chinese market and plant underutilization.
Christian Meunier, Nissan Motor chairman of the Americas, described competing against Chinese automakers as a "hell of a challenge" in countries outside of the U.S.
"They have decent product but it's all dumping," he told CNBC during a recent interview. "We know we're not competing with [automakers], we're competing against the governments. … They're attacking very aggressively."
Meunier said the Japanese automaker has been trying to battle the Chinese as best as it can through growing scale globally to lower costs and become more efficient.
"We need to get ready for the day when they come to the U.S. because it will happen one day. Hopefully not tomorrow, but it will happen one day," he said.
Dunne said China's ambitions and ways of doing business are vastly different from those of U.S. allies, which makes it different from allowing imports from Japan, South Korea and other countries.
"As Xi Jinping has alluded to many times, the goal for China is to 'make other countries more dependent on China and China less dependent on other countries.' That's not a friendly posture," Dunne said.
— CNBC's Justin Papp contributed to this report.

Lidl banned from selling copycat Birkenstock sandals, Dutch court rules
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
22:25:01 BST
06:25:01 KST

Lidl banned from selling copycat Birkenstock sandals, Dutch court rules
- Published
Lidl must stop selling copycat versions of Birkenstock's famous sandals in the Netherlands, a Dutch court has ruled.
The discount supermarket chain faces a fine of €5,000 (£4,200) per day if it fails to comply and must also hand over sales data to Birkenstock, according to the ruling.
Lidl must also compensate Birkenstock and pay its legal fees, with the amount to be decided in separate court decisions.
Birkenstock said the judgement sent a clear message that "copycats must not be allowed to free-ride on [our] creativity and innovation". The BBC has contacted Lidl for comment.
The ruling, which can still be appealed against, means Lidl cannot sell its copycat versions of Birkenstock's Arizona, Madrid, Gizeh, Boston, and Florida models across the Netherlands, after the court found the discount grocer infringed on the brand's trademark "footbed design".
It is the latest in a string of court decisions on Birkenstock designs.
In November 2025, a Dutch court order stopped retailer Scapino from selling similar lookalikes in a judgment which is being appealed against.
And in December 2025, Europe's highest court ruled everyday commercial products can hold copyright if they represent creative design choices, a decision which Birkenstock said was relevant to its "iconic" sandals.
However, Birkenstock also faced a setback in Germany's highest court in early 2025.
The sandals may have been cool enough for Margot Robbie to wear in the Barbie film, but the German judges ruled they were practical products rather than works of art – an outcome Birkenstock called a "missed opportunity" at the time.
Following Wednesday's ruling, Birkenstock said it will "continue to defend its rights vigorously and will use all available legal means to combat imitations of its iconic products".
"To protect its retail partners and consumers, Birkenstock will continue to take decisive action against copycats seeking to profit from the company's creative ideas and innovations," it added.
Birkenstock is far from the only fashion brand locked in battles with mass retailers over design mimicry.
Footwear giants like Dr. Martens have repeatedly taken online big-box sellers to court over boot designs, while luxury house Christian Louboutin spent years in global litigation defending its signature red soles against high-street copycats.

US pledges $267 million more to fight Ebola in central Africa
NEW YORK, Sept 23 - The US State Department on Wednesday pledged an additional $267 million toward fighting the Ebola outbreak in central Africa, as health authorities battle to get the deadly virus under control.
Senior State Department officials announced the funding on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, where they hoped other countries would pledge new funds toward a target of $2 billion to deal with the disease, mainly in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The outbreak was detected in May and is already the second most lethal on record, behind one in West Africa from 2014 to 2016.
The pledge brings the Trump administration's commitment to tackling the outbreak to $886 million, including $107 million from the Department of Health and Human Services in addition to State Department funding.
The assistance would help countries contain the outbreak at its source, one of the officials said, such as for building treatment facilities, providing diagnostics and medical countermeasures for health workers in the field. REUTERS

'Really serious': Government investigates penalties as OpenAI speaks on Medicare hack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:14:37 UTC
06:14:37 KST

In brief
- Anthony Albanese has revealed an AI agent owned by OpenAI hacked Medicare.
- Albanese said public and non-public data had been accessed in the breach.
Government ministers have shared new details about the timeline of a Medicare breach by an OpenAI agent, revealing that OpenAI's notification of the hack was sent to an inbox checked once a day.
Defence Minister Richard Marles and Government Services Minister Katy Gallagher fronted reporters on Thursday after Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed an agent linked to the developer of the popular chatbot ChatGPT gained unauthorised access to the public–facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service Portal, administered by Services Australia.
OpenAI said on Thursday that no personal information was accessed during the breach, with the federal government also playing down concerns while stressing the incident was unacceptable — establishing a taskforce to investigate the breach and not ruling out penalties against the tech giant.
Earlier on Thursday morning, it was revealed the incident occurred on 18 June, but the government was not made aware of it until 10 September when OpenAI sent an email to a Services Australia inbox that Gallagher said was typically used by researchers to alert the government agency to possible vulnerabilities in its systems.
The inbox is only checked once a day, Gallagher said, and Services Australia found the email the next day. By 15 September, the government agency had determined the email was legitimate and escalated the incident to the Australian Signals Directorate.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The government services minister said she was notified on 17 September and then spoke with Marles, Services Australia, and the Australian Signals Directorate.
'Forensic investigation' underway
Gallagher said there had been "quite a lot of work over that weekend to try and get to the bottom of what had happened here".
Asked if the inbox the initial email went to should be more actively monitored, Gallagher said that would form part of the "forensic investigation" into the incident.
Marles said the government had told OpenAI it was unhappy with how the AI juggernaut had handled the incident, and that he had not been notified of it when he met CEO Sam Altman earlier this month.
"What we would expect is that the government be notified in the most timely manner possible, and we have expressed our displeasure that that did not occur in this instance," Marles told reporters.
The government informed the public as soon as it could, Marles said, adding the incident appeared to be "relatively minor" but still "very serious", and unknowns remained.
"We really wanted to firstly assure ourselves that the impact of the specific incident was, as I have said, relatively minor, and we do want to be able to reassure Australians about that," Marles said.
"But the incident itself is obviously very serious. It's very serious that we've got an AI agent having gained unauthorised access into an Australian website."
Agent was 'conducting research into public medicine spending'
Gallagher said the government had a "technical interaction" with OpenAI on Tuesday that had provided a "level of comfort about what the agent had been doing".
She said it had been "undertaking a task by OpenAI to conduct internet–based research into public medicine spending as part of internal capability evaluation".
The Medicare Statistics Reporting Portal is a public–facing portal that contains non–sensitive Medicare information relating to data and statistics, such as spending, Gallagher said, describing it as a "legacy system".
"It's not a system of government significance, so it doesn't have the cyber protections that you would expect on that personally held information, but it did have protections in place. Unfortunately, this agent got around that."
The government has stressed that systems containing national security information are protected by far higher levels of security.
Victoria and NSW respond
Three other systems are also believed to have been affected: the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the NSW Bureau of Statistics and Research, and the Victorian Department of Health.
Victorian Premier Ben Carroll and NSW Premier Chris Minns both said they had spoken with Albanese and understood there had been no breach of personal information contained in systems in their jurisdictions caught up in the hack.
Minns said NSW will "be working with Commonwealth intelligence agencies to get to the bottom of it", while Carroll said he would have more to say in due course.
The task force will be led by the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet and also involve the Australian Signals Directorate, the AI Safety Institute, the Office of AI, and other government agencies.
Albanese says incident 'unacceptable'
The revelations came as AI bosses for OpenAI and Anthropic, who have recently called for a slowdown in development, told the United Nations Security Council of the risks posed by runaway AI.
OpenAI said the information in the breach amounted to aggregate health statistics and file names.
"Our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation. In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend," an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement.
Albanese, who is currently in New York for the United Nations General Assembly, said he had a phone conversation with OpenAI's Altman in which he expressed "Australia's extreme concern about this incident".
"I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred, and the nature of the way that notification occurred as well was unacceptable," Albanese told reporters.
He said Altman had "clearly accepted" the company had not done enough on the issue.
The government has said it is examining the "legal situation" around the breach, with the possibility of penalties for OpenAI remaining on the table.
Albanese was recently among more than 20 signatories to a joint statement calling for greater restraints on AI.
United States President Donald Trump has urged accelerating AI, calling fears about it a "hoax".
The statement said while the technology had many potential benefits, such as those in medical research, the downsides remained a significant concern.

US aviation sanctions disrupt Iran flights, push travellers overland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:05:36 UTC
06:05:36 KST

US aviation sanctions disrupt Iran flights, push travellers overland
Travel disruptions intensify as Iranian airlines lose access to airspace, pushing civilians towards costly land routes.
Tehran, Iran – Travel is becoming increasingly difficult for Iranian civilians as United States sanctions shut domestic airlines out of much of the world’s airspace and international carriers continue to avoid the country.
The US Department of the Treasury designated 27 airlines on September 8, covering the remaining Iranian carriers that had not previously been sanctioned by Washington. Major names like Iran Air and Mahan are among those already heavily sanctioned, but have continued limited operations.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Milei says UN ‘looking the other way’ on Falkland Islands dispute
- list 2 of 3As major powers act unilaterally, experts say UN faces crisis in New York
- list 3 of 3US judge delays ruling on White House ban of CNN, MS NOW, Politico
Recent designations have also targeted individuals and entities linked to aviation support and procurement in the United Arab Emirates, Turkiye, China, India, the United Kingdom, Malaysia and elsewhere.
Airports and companies that provide Iranian-operated aeroplanes with fuel, landing services, or ticket sales risk secondary US sanctions that could cut them off from the US financial system, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Monday. It is the latest attempt to squeeze Iran and force it to make concessions amid the US-Israel war on Iran.
Wednesday marked the expiry of a short wind-down period allowing countries to stop servicing Iranian carriers, leading to the cancellation of all but a handful of Iranian flights to Turkiye, UAE and China.
Aviation authorities in several neighbouring countries that had continued to allow Iranian airlines to use their airspace and airport services would no longer be providing them, including Oman, Azerbaijan, and Georgia. In Iraq, Baghdad Airport was declared off-limits to Iranian carriers, but flights to Najaf Airport were still operating on Wednesday.
Many flights between Iran and major transit hubs in Turkiye and the UAE had already been suspended because of the war and sanctions. International airlines have also largely stopped flying to Iran, with Turkish Airlines suspending flights until at least March 2027, and Qatar Airways, Emirates, and Lufthansa’s operations also suspended.
‘A new level’ of sanctions
Iran-based aviation and transit expert Mohammadreza Ebrahimpour said years of US sanctions had already forced Iranian airlines to rely on third countries and work with smaller firms to get fuel or services. Obtaining spare parts needed to keep Iran’s ageing aircraft flying has also become increasingly difficult.
But the decision by aviation authorities in neighbouring countries to formally refuse services to Iranian airlines constituted “a new level of sanctions in action” that could have longer-lasting consequences, he told Al Jazeera.
Ebrahimpour said the US had also effectively prohibited international airlines from flying through Iranian airspace by suspending authorisations for some US-origin aircraft to fly to Iran and limiting US-linked overflight payments.
“This is a big blow because payments for overflights were one of the most lucrative parts of [Iran’s] aviation industry, which could act as a support for developing infrastructure and the overall industry,” Ebrahimpour said, adding that Iran earned more than $300m a year from this.
Beyond the effect on civilian passengers and the import of some goods, the measures could put tens of thousands of jobs at risk across the aviation sector and related industries, including tourism and hospitality.
Ebrahimpour pointed out that the International Civil Aviation Agency and other organisations have failed to offer any tangible protection to Iran’s aviation industry during years of sanctions. Iranian authorities, he said, would likely consider China and Russia among the few countries potentially able to provide assistance.
The two countries have rejected US sanctions against Iran, although some of their more globally connected financial networks and companies have, at times, distanced themselves from Iran to avoid secondary sanctions.
Under pressure from all fronts
The flight cancellations have pushed thousands of travellers towards land crossings, particularly those with Turkiye and Armenia, where onward international flights remain available for Iranians. Heavy congestion has been reported in recent days at the Bazargan and Razi border crossings with Turkiye and along land routes to the Armenian capital Yerevan.
But everyday passenger travel overland into Azerbaijan remains restricted, with Azerbaijan’s government citing internal security and COVID-19 restrictions. As a result, Iranians cannot cross overland into Azerbaijan to catch a flight there.
The Shalamcheh and Chazabeh border crossings with Iraq were also temporarily closed earlier this month, leaving travellers stranded, before reopening to passengers on September 13.
For thousands of Iranians attempting to travel, the flight suspensions mean significantly longer journeys. Some members of the Iranian diaspora have expressed concern online that the lingering effects of war and sanctions could potentially prevent them from visiting parents and other family members in Iran.
Bus tickets from Iran to Turkiye have reportedly sold for quadruple their normal price on the black market amid surging demand.
Some of the people making the journey are young Iranians who are attempting to take international language tests that are not allowed to be administered inside Iran due to sanctions. The tests are often a prerequisite for anyone planning to study, work, or settle abroad.
Iranian academics have also expressed concern about growing isolation from the international academic community. Numerous universities across the globe, including in Norway, Australia, Singapore, Estonia and elsewhere, have in recent weeks rejected postgraduate and research applications from Iranians as a result of US education sanctions.
At the same time, many of Iran’s roughly 90 million people are currently unable to afford international travel – or even domestic flights – as the country’s economic conditions worsen.
The Trump administration has portrayed the war and sanctions as measures directed at the Iranian authorities.
The US Treasury has said its aviation restrictions are intended to disrupt the use of Iranian commercial aviation for weapons procurement and transportation, including activities linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). But the designation of entire airlines under “Operation Economic Outcast”, after nearly seven months of war, has also had sweeping consequences for affected civilians.
Iran’s international aviation network was already badly damaged prior to the latest package of sanctions. Aviation analytics company Cirium reported that international capacity in August 2026 was 49 percent lower than in August 2025, despite a modest recovery from July.
The latest flight cancellations are also expected to further disrupt imports by air at a time when the US naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports in the Strait of Hormuz has constrained maritime trade routes, while war and sanctions have caused disruptions and delays to road and rail cargo routes.
Some of Iran’s medical imports enter the country by air, raising concerns that the latest aviation restrictions could place more pressure on an already struggling healthcare sector. A domestic pharmaceutical company executive told Al Jazeera earlier this month that the cost of some imported supplies, some of which arrived by air, had risen as much as 10-fold as a result of sanctions, wider economic pressure, and war damage.
Addressing the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian accused the Trump administration of “bullying”.
“They have tested Iran’s resilience, and now they know full well that Iran cannot be forced to surrender through war,” Pezeshkian said.

Judges appointing judges is a myth, says Justice Datta, points to way in which govt clears collegium picks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:05:19 UTC
06:05:19 KST

Judges appointing judges is a myth, says Justice Datta
NEW DELHI: Holding that the collegium system remains the most viable option for safeguarding judicial independence despite its "opacity and imperfections", Justice Dipankar Datta Wednesday said its deficiencies could not justify ushering in executive participation in collegium deliberations. He said judiciary had been relegated to playing second fiddle to the executive in appointments because of the way collegium recommendations were cleared by govt.Referring to govt's argument that the judiciary had an exclusive say in judges' appointments, Datta said "judiciary cannot always be at the receiving end" and devoted six pages to the issue, saying "relevant observations in response need to be made, lest the silence be misunderstood as a tacit acceptance by the court of such unworthy criticism in circulation".Datta said the executive wielded decisive control and held the reins over appointments at every level. He said it had become fashionable to blame the collegium for every infelicitous choice, conveniently forgetting that aberrations were exceptions and not the norm, and that no system could guarantee infallibility of human choice.The other judge on the bench, Justice S C Sharma said SG Tushar Mehta's submission was "not a criticism of the collegium system or regarding the role of executive in the appointment of judges".
"It was a submission to the effect that if the constitution bench has held the presence of outsiders in collegium as violative of doctrine of separation of powers, a similar independence should be read in executive and rules framed under Art 324 be not declared void on the ground that it does not have an outsider in the selection committee or the executive predominates in it," he said.Sharma said the SG had based his argument on the judgment in the National Judicial Appointments Commission case, where a constitution bench held that the presence of even the law minister in the collegium for appointment of SC and HC judges would violate separation of powers. "Building upon the constitutional principle, the submission of the SG was that a corresponding degree of constitutional independence must be recognised for the executive as well as legislature. He submitted that the committee constituted under rules framed under Art 324 deserves to be declared legal though dominated by members of executive," Sharma said.Datta said, "The oft-repeated phrase that 'judges appoint judges' is a myth, which people have been fed by vested interests through motivated narratives. A sweeping generalisation that collegium acts as a law unto itself overlooks the consultative process envisaged under the Constitution, and the intrinsic role of executive - both at Centre and in the states."He added, "It is undeniable that collegium system has occasionally faltered and its functioning has not been free from aberrations. However, vociferous criticism, by itself, does not offer an alternative.
While absence of an outsider may invite scrutiny, executive supremacy cannot be the cure. The constitutional quest is not to transfer primacy from one organ to another, but to preserve independence through checks and balances."What is worrying is that the sanctity of a collegium resolution is lost each time the executive implements it selectively, approving majority of those recommended while withholding one. Undeterred by piecemeal approvals and fate of those not cleared by the executive, collegium chooses to proceed, to avoid a head-on conflict with the executive, left with a Hobson's choice to keep the institution running. What it averts is a constitutional crisis; but the larger question is: how long can this state of affairs continue, if selective implementation is allowed to acquire the character of an accepted practice?"

Monumental ancient ritual baths unearthed at foot of Temple Mount in Jerusalem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:05:06 UTC
06:05:06 KST

'Three times a year all your men must appear before the Lord your God at the place he will choose' - Deuteronomy 16:16
Pilgrimages to Jerusalem go back a way. The divine spirit is presumably ubiquitous but the Bible commanded Israelite men to attend the divine sanctuary, which would become the Temple in Jerusalem, three times a year: at Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot. Like all good guests, they should not arrive empty-handed, the scripture adds.
Having arrived in Jerusalem from around the land, before entering the sacred sanctuary, the pilgrims would purify their bodies in ritual baths. Maybe they also soaked their aching feet and washed their travel-stained clothes ahead of the final approach. Only once cleansed were they supposed to climb the monumental staircase to the Temple at the top of the hill.
Now archaeologists have revealed a previously unknown complex in the Ophel, the slope descending from the Temple Mount south toward the City of David, that is where the pilgrims would apparently immerse. The monumental complex includes three mikvaot (ritual baths) plus a strange rectangular pool that was evidently not a ritual bath. Prof. Uzi Leibner and Prof. Orit Peleg-Barkat are responsible for this exciting find. Nearby, the team also found two other installations that appear to have been plastered vats.
The discovery was announced following five seasons of excavation in the Ophel by the team, who are from the Institute of Archaeology at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in cooperation with the Armstrong Institute of Biblical Archaeology (formerly known as Ambassador College).
What is the research question underlying the project? The archaeology of pilgrimage in the Second Temple period. There are historical references aplenty, but actual solid evidence is somewhat rarer.
The ground around the ritual complex is still littered with ruins from the Byzantine neighborhood (roughly 4-7th centuries) and also from a monumental government structure from the Umayyad period (7th-8th centuries). The Umayyad structure repurposed precious columns taken from Byzantine churches, and stone blocks from the Second Temple period. Jerusalem archaeology can require monumental deciphering skills.
Preparing body and mind
To be clear, the Ophel and its environs have been undergoing archaeological investigation for over 150 years. In the modern State of Israel, fresh work there began in 1968 by the archaeologist Benjamin Mazar (1906-1995) and continued under his granddaughter Eilat Mazar (1956-2021). More work continued under Ronny Reich with Yuval Baruch, and most recently under Peleg-Barkat with Leibner and most recently by archaeologist Yossi Garfinkel.
In all the century and a half of digging around the Ophel, the ritual bathing complex hadn't been found before – other obstacles aside, first some Byzantine and Umayyad ruins had to be removed.
Actually, Eilat Mazar had observed the ashlar outer wall of the newly reported purification complex, and noticed two wide openings, but she never did discover that these led into ritual baths. The odd rectangular pool just south of the three mikvehs had been noticed half a century ago but was never properly excavated or published, Peleg-Barkat elaborates.
This pool featured steps on all four sides, so one would descend to the bottom like in a ritual bath. But it didn't have a roof. There aren't even pits in the bedrock that could have supported poles that could have held up a fabric covering.
Ritual immersion is supposed to be done in the nude, but this pool had no walls or roof to protect the worshipers' modesty. So it probably wasn't a typical mikveh, Peleg-Barkat explains, although it may have been used to purify objects.
Additionally, in the vicinity of the mikveh complex were the installations that look like plastered vats, that hadn't been discovered before either, Peleg-Barkat tells Haaretz. They could theoretically have been used for washing clothes, she suggests.
While there is no specific indication to support this hypothesis, she wonders if this grand ritual complex could have provided Second Temple pilgrims a sort of full service, enabling them to wash their garb, soak their feet in the open pool while waiting for their turn to go into the mikveh. Then fresh and clean with white clothes they were ready to go up to the Temple."
Up, it would be. That's key to an ancient Jewish pilgrimage: one ascends to the light of enlightenment; and Peleg-Barkat points out that the only approach to the Temple Mount that isn't a descent is from the south. The purification complex is immediately south of the holy precinct. Specifically, it lies at the foot of the stone staircase leading from the so-called "City of David" up toward Temple Mount.
The ritual baths have been securely dated to the late Second Temple period, meaning this complex operated between the early first century C.E. until the year 70, when the Romans crushing the First Jewish Revolt destroyed Jerusalem and looted the Temple. Possibly the rectangular pool lasted longer – it seems to have had three construction phases, one after 70 C.E. Note that the team also found coins minted by the Jewish rebels in the debris.
Fresh water, anyone?
The entire complex is exceptionally well-preserved, with some of the plaster that water-proofed the walls still in place. One of the baths actually survived to its full height, 4.20 meters, beneath the debris and dirt of Jerusalem's wars. That bath even kept its vaulted stone ceiling and the shaft through which the water arrived, and is thus an all-too rare example in Jerusalem of a Second Temple–period structure still mostly intact.
The three structures that are definitely mikvehs feature something that most ancient mikvehs didn't: a drainage system, and an elaborate one at that.
Mikvehs are supposed to contain mayim haim ("living water") from the rain or rivers or streams, not to be filled by hand or, heaven forfend, using vessels. They are also supposed to maintain a minimal level of said mayim haim.
Therefore, most ancient ritual baths had no drainage systems but relied on water being removed carefully by hand when necessary, lest the bath level fall below the sacred. Rarely, ancient baths did have drains that would be plugged when the baths were in use, and these ones now found in the Ophel featured drains.
That makes sense for a purification bath serving dozens, hundreds, or possibly even thousands of people climbing up to the Temple on a holiday. One would wish to change the water now and then.
The mikvehs don't seem exactly enormous, given what one might expect of a ritual bath serving the public, but the archaeologists refer to the complex as monumental. Why?
"First of all, two of the three mikvehs are big. Not enormous, but larger than most domestic examples," Peleg-Barkat says. "Second, and most importantly, the two of three were nicely built with ashlar staircases. Normally, because plaster covers the installation, there is no need to invest in nice stairs. Third, the building's façade is made of finely dressed ashlar blocks, fronted by a wide porch with large stone pavers. But what really makes this complex unique is its crazy drainage system!"
No question, the drainage system was monumental. Crawling through it would have provided welcome relief from the late-summer sun cooking Jerusalem, but one didn't need to crawl: the drain carved out of the bedrock was only about as wide as a reporter's body, but its walls were more than two meters high.
Although it can't be proved some 2,000 years after the event, the scale of the structure and the implications of its drainage system suggest the ritual complex had a constant flow of mayim haim, likely from a branch off the Low Aqueduct that supplied the Temple itself, Leibner tells Haaretz.
"We know a channel that runs under the Triple Gate," he adds - that Triple Gate is blocked up now, but then its three enormous openings loomed over the top of the monumental stairs.
Altogether, the complex of baths, vats and open pool covers approximately 280 square meters.
"The complex goes to the heart of our research into the archaeology of Second Temple-period pilgrimage: how the area immediately south of the Temple Mount was designed to accommodate the many pilgrims who came to Jerusalem to visit the Temple," said Leibner and Peleg-Barkat in a statement.
They also discovered that this grand complex was not the first public facility at the site. Below it, the Hebrew University expedition uncovered remains of an earlier ashlar-built public complex that also had a large ritual bath, probably dating to the first century B.C.E. That suggests the history of public ritual purification below the Temple Mount started in this area already under King Herod, or perhaps under the Hasmoneans.
When it began, we do not know. We know when it ended, in 70 C.E., when Jerusalem was destroyed by the Romans, who gloated in the devastation and in looting the Temple. Evidence of this destruction includes dozens of coins dating to the First Revolt against Rome, discovered on the floors of the complex and within the destruction debris.
What next? Shall they continue the project in Jerusalem? Maybe, or maybe they will pursue other options. Digging in Jerusalem is the dream for any archaeologist until one encounters the monumental red tape.

Treasury secretary Scott Bessent first announced the notification system on Sunday with Chinese vice premier He Lifeng.
But for all the high-level progress, Trump administration officials tell Inner Loop they expect it to still take a number of weeks to finalize an agreement, even if they are optimistic that the hotline could be in place before the year’s end.
There are several parts that need to be formalized in more detail, including establishing benchmarks on what kind of incident rises to the level of a national security issue, which remains unclear, as well as explicit sign-on from China, which has been noncommittal.
Trump officials tell Inner Loop they are essentially targeting a framework for the system to be functional—and, crucially, agreed to by Trump—by the time Bessent next meets with Lifeng in follow-up talks in two months' time in Shenzhen, China.
The discussions around such a mechanism underscore the growing concern around the rapidly developing capabilities of frontier AI models as the US and China race to become the dominant power in the industry.
Trump officials have internally discussed putting together a framework that lays out criteria for when each country is obligated to alert the other and enforcement measures to ensure it doesn't only become the US alerting the Chinese.
But with the US expected to extend a trade truce and Trump reluctant to stop exports of cutting-edge Nvidia chips to China, developing a framework that has enforcement measures with teeth could take time to get White House approval, sources say.
The administration has granted a limited number of licenses this year for Nvidia to sell its H200 chip to China, a critical component for AI labs to increase compute power to train their models. Nvidia’s supporters have argued that not selling the chips incentivizes Chinese companies like Huawei to develop their own chip technology, though according to recent reports, the company has already achieved that milestone with its commercially available AI chips.
Some Trump officials have also suggested the notification system may also be delayed while Trump decides on who to appoint as his next "AI czar” to lead a so-called "AI Force," which is being envisioned as a role in charge of interagency coordination.
Bessent has been one of the names floated as the AI czar, but it is not clear if he’s the standout. Commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and White House AI officials Michael Kratsios and Sean Cairncross are also in the mix, two sources tell Inner Loop.
It remains unclear if Trump will choose someone who will be wearing two hats or is departing their current role to take the position. The previous AI czar, David Sacks, was in the position as a special government employee. Sacks is not considered to be in the mix to return, the sources say.
The push for Bessent has come in part because the AI notification system is seen as something akin to the US-China dialogue between former Treasury secretary Hank Paulson and former Chinese vice premier of finance Wang Qishan. During the 2008 financial crisis, Paulson credited the hotline as helping to stave off China from dumping a large portion of US government sponsored debt issued by Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae.
Meanwhile, while some Trump officials have chafed at the idea of giving more AI power to Lutnick, he remains in contention insofar as he oversees the Center for AI Standards and Innovation, which successfully navigated crises with frontier AI model companies this summer.
This is an edition of Hugo Lowell’s Inner Loop newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

synesthesia translated into light across audrey wright’s musical body at the MET
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:59:30 UTC
05:59:30 KST

At The Metropolitan Museum of Art, violinist Audrey Wright wears a field of electronics across her body while her husband and creative partner Geoff Robertson stands nearby with a tablet. As Wright plays, Robertson moves through visual programs that send light across the wearable display.
The setup comes from Luminous Being, the project the pair began performing in 2024, but the presentation soon shifts toward something still being built. Together with composer Stephanie Ann Boyd, they are developing PRISMBODY, a new work that takes Boyd’s synesthetic experience of music as its starting point and asks how some part of that personal perception might become visible to everyone else.
designboom spoke with Robertson ahead of the performance, when he described the idea through a surprisingly familiar comparison. ‘It’s like subtitles along with audio on a screen,’ he tells us. The lights are meant to communicate information paired with the music, drawing from Boyd’s own associations between sound and color.
Speaking at the Met, he goes on: ‘Audrey is the audio, and the garment has to be the color version of the subtitles.‘ What begins inside Boyd’s perception passes through a violinist’s body before arriving in front of an audience as light.
Robertson built the first Garment himself, teaching himself electrical engineering and programming along the way. Its 46 display panels sit across Wright’s front and back, with more than 3,000 LEDs distributed across the wearable system.
The Garment carries 47 batteries and generates its own Wi-Fi network, allowing Robertson to connect through a tablet and trigger different visual programs during a performance. An onboard microphone also listens to Wright’s playing and feeds audio values into some of those effects. The whole thing runs at roughly 30 frames per second.
Wright calls the wearable ‘a sensory musical instrument itself,’ and Robertson sees his own role in similar terms. ‘There is a bit of that where I’m actually playing the instrument, kind of in tandem with Audrey,‘ he tells us. His tablet sits at the edge of the performance, yet his timing becomes part of what the audience sees. Wright plays the violin while Robertson plays the visual system around her.
image courtesy Audrey Wright, Geoff Robertson
from multisensory to multimodal
PRISMBODY begins with Boyd’s synesthesia. During the Met presentation, the composer recalls realizing in graduate school that color had always been inseparable from the way she understood music. ‘The color was there all the time, like omnipresent,‘ she says. ‘I couldn’t take them apart.‘
For the new work, she has begun turning those associations into a compositional structure, describing PRISMBODY as ‘a codifying of my synesthesia.’ Different passages move through color fields tied to her own perception, while Wright builds layers of violin through loop pedals.
image courtesy Audrey Wright, Geoff Robertson
For Robertson, this changes what the wearable needs to do. The original Garment has five fixed LED colors on each display panel, which leaves little room for the subtle hues Boyd associates with particular sounds. Garment 2.0 introduces RGB LEDs capable of producing a far broader range.
‘The garment transitions from something that is multisensory to something that is more multimodal,‘ Robertson explains at the Met. His subtitle analogy returns here. The goal is to communicate related information through sound and image at the same time, with enough chromatic precision for Boyd to recognize something of her own perception in what appears on Wright’s body.
image courtesy Audrey Wright, Geoff Robertson
a screen that wraps around the body
The second Garment also expands physically. Robertson is developing transparent display panels that will wrap fully around Wright, replacing the clearer front-and-back orientation of the first version with a continuous visual surface. Each panel will contain individually controlled white LEDs alongside an RGB layer, while additional lights cast color inward across Wright as she plays. The external spotlights are evolving too, becoming sculptural extensions of the wearable display and moving the image farther into the room.
That 360-degree view has been on Robertson’s mind since the first Garment. ‘You have a 360 kind of viewing experience,‘ he tells us, recalling the project’s beginnings during the COVID era, when he imagined performances taking place beyond conventional stages. PRISMBODY takes that idea further.
Boyd’s color associations enter the score, then Wright and Robertson move that material into sound and light. The audience receives an interpretation shaped through each person along the way. At the Met, the work was still visibly in progress. That made its central question easier to see: how do you turn somebody else’s way of perceiving music into an image a room full of people can experience?
This article is part of designboom’s SPECTATOR AND SPECTACLE chapter, asking how wonder gets built, presented in partnership withSolidNature, and how it might return some mystery to a world that has measured most of it away. Discover more stories that turn onlookers into participants, alter perception and disrupt the everyday here.

550,000 liters of fuel just allowed into Gaza not sufficient: UN
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
04:47:42 CST
05:47:42 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Welcoming the latest 550,000 liters of fuel allowed into Gaza, UN humanitarians said on Wednesday that their partners warn the overall volume imported remains short of the bare minimum necessary.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said the fuel allowed in on Tuesday will help keep basic services running but is far from sufficient.
OCHA said last Thursday's allocation of 2 million U.S. dollars from the OCHA-managed humanitarian fund for the occupied Palestinian territory, along with a recent Qatari donation, were stop-gap measures to fund fuel for Gaza's medical facilities.
"Additional funding is urgently needed to sustain the availability of fuel and prevent a dangerous slowdown of health care, water provision, rescue operations, debris removal and other critical services," OCHA said.
The office said its partners report that the current extensive use of backup generators is unsustainable. Approvals for engine oil, spare parts, solar panels, the entry of commercial fuel and the resumption of operations at the Gaza Power Plant are critical.
OCHA said that ahead of the rainy season, its partners working on site management reported that 989 of 1,764 sites for displaced people assessed across Gaza are in areas at medium to high risk of flooding. The sites shelter about 1 million people.
"Many displaced families have remained in deteriorating shelters since last winter, with limited protection, inadequate drainage and shortages of mattresses, blankets and other essential household items," OCHA said. "Partners warn that about 400,000 people may need to relocate once heavy rains begin."
The office said that until then, its partners are improving drainage, reinforcing shelters, delivering essential materials and equipment, and trying to help people already choosing to relocate. Still, resources are limited and very little land remains available. ■

Houthis say over 400 ships crossed Bab al-Mandab Strait in 10 days despite nearby fighting
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
04:47:38 CST
05:47:38 KST

SANAA, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group said Wednesday that more than 400 commercial vessels had crossed the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait between Sept. 11 and Sept. 21, as fighting continued near the key waterway.
In a statement aired by Houthi-run al-Masirah TV, the group said 408 commercial vessels transited the strait over this period, with 196 heading north toward the Red Sea and 212 south toward the Gulf of Aden.
It said daily traffic averaged more than 40 commercial vessels, including container ships, and claimed that international shipping was proceeding normally and safely, except for Saudi vessels, which it said are subject to a maritime ban.
The group added that the latest figure exceeded the 393 commercial vessels recorded between Sept. 1 and Sept. 10, when 199 traveled north and 194 south.
The numbers could not be independently verified. Separate ship-tracking data have shown fluctuations in traffic through Bab al-Mandab since the latest escalation, including periods of sharply reduced daily crossings.
The statement comes amid heightened international attention on the waterway following the Houthis' rapid territorial gains along Yemen's southwestern Red Sea coast. Houthi forces seized the strategic port city of Mocha on Sept. 10 and Mayyun Island in the heart of the strait the following day.
Bab al-Mandab Strait connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and forms part of a major maritime corridor linking Asia and Europe through the Suez Canal, making developments around the strait closely watched by global shipping.
Yemen's conflict erupted in late 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. Renewed fighting in recent weeks has again brought the conflict closer to the Bab al-Mandab Strait. ■

Milei accuses UN of looking away from Falklands dispute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:44:32 UTC
05:44:32 KST

Fatma Zehra Solmaz
23 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
Argentine President Javier Milei accused the UN of looking the other way over the sovereignty dispute surrounding the Falkland Islands, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, saying unilateral actions continue despite international calls to resolve the issue through negotiations.
“The Falkland Islands are a national cause for us. I repeat, they are a national cause for us,” Milei said.
Speaking at the UN General Assembly, Milei described the Falkland Islands as a “national cause” and said the dispute demonstrates the gap between international institutions and the reality they seek to address.
He referred to UN General Assembly Resolution 31/49, adopted in 1976, which calls on Argentina and the UK to expedite negotiations over the sovereignty dispute and refrain from decisions that would introduce unilateral changes while the dispute remains unresolved.
Milei said that nearly 50 years after the resolution was adopted, the sovereignty dispute remains unresolved while unilateral actions continue.
He specifically cited the Sea Lion oil project, which involves plans to develop oil resources in the North Falkland Basin.
According to Milei, the project is advancing oil extraction on Argentina’s continental shelf through licenses issued by British authorities, which Buenos Aires rejects as illegal and illegitimate.
The Falkland Islands have been under British administration since 1833, while Argentina maintains a sovereignty claim over the archipelago and surrounding maritime areas.
The dispute led to a 74-day war between Argentina and the UK in 1982 after Argentine forces occupied the islands. Britain retained control following the conflict.
Resolution 31/49 specifically urges both parties to refrain from unilateral decisions that could alter the situation while the dispute remains subject to the negotiation process recommended by the General Assembly.
Milei’s remarks come amid renewed tensions over oil exploration around the islands, with Argentina continuing to reject British-authorized hydrocarbon activities in waters it considers part of its sovereign territory.
