The Kremlin has responded to the invitiation the US has extended to Russian President Vladimir Putin to attend the upcoming G20 summit in Miami, Florida in December.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed earlier today that Washington had invited Putin to attend the gathering.
Russia is “grateful and appreciative,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told RIA Novosti on Wednesday night.
Peskov added that a decision on Putin’s possible attendance will be made and relayed through diplomatic channels.
The summit is scheduled for December 14-15 in Miami, with US President Donald Trump set to host it at his Doral golf resort. Putin has not attended a G20 summit in person since 2019, initially because of the pandemic and later amid the fallout from the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022.
Moscow said earlier that Russia will be represented at the summit at a high level but it remains unclear whether Putin plans to attend personally.
Speaking to journalists earlier on Wednesday, Rubio expressed his hope that the Russian president would arrive for the summit. “We hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept. There’s an opportunity in December if that happens.”
Trump himself had stated earlier that he would like to see his Russian counterpart at the summit. “If he came, it would be probably very helpful,” the US president said in April. He also welcomed the presence of a senior Russian delegation at the G20 in early September despite protests from EU officials who refused to appear alongside Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov in the gathering’s traditional “family photo.”

OpenAI, Anthropic chiefs tell UN Security Council no single nation, company should control AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:41:50 UTC
05:41:50 KST

Merve Aydogan
23 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
The heads of OpenAI and Anthropic on Wednesday told the UN Security Council that no single actor should dominate artificial intelligence, calling for international cooperation to manage the technology’s risks as it advances.
Addressing a Security Council session on AI and international security, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said: “We have a choice in front of us. AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray.”
He said AI “should be built for people, not simply to turn the crank of the machines faster for their own sake,” adding that some statements from people working on the technology “are so dystopian that they sound like the plot of bad science fiction movies.”
Altman warned that “no one person or company or country should be able to use the most powerful AI models to impose their worldview on everyone else,” arguing that decisions about AI “cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone” and must instead be “shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve.”
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei identified two central risks: misuse of AI models, including by “bioterrorists to create biological weapons,” and the danger of “model capabilities accelerating beyond developers’ ability to control them.”
He stressed that “if managed poorly,” artificial intelligence “could be a risk to humanity as a whole.”
Amodei said his company would “slow down as much as necessary” to ensure each new AI system it releases is safe, but stressed that managing the risks is “bigger than any one company” and has “an industry-wide and global scale.”
He called for “common global standards for testing AI models for loss of control risks and misuse risks,” describing the issue as “the most important global security issue facing the world today.”
Yoshua Bengio, co-chair of the UN International Independent Panel on AI, pushed back against industry framing of AI development as an unavoidable competition.
“Citizens and governments should not accept the companies’ claim that they are trapped in a race,” he said, adding that “the race is not a law of nature; it is the product of choices, choices made by the companies themselves.”
Bengio told Security Council members that despite fragile trust among nations, “the race threatens every nation.”

Breaking: OpenAI agent hacked Medicare portal, PM says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:31:06 UTC
05:31:06 KST

OpenAI hacked Medicare portal, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says
In short:
The prime minister has had a "frank" discussion with OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman after an AI agent breached an Australian government website.
The company did not notify Services Australia of the incident until three months after the fact, via email.
What's next?
The prime minister has announced a taskforce to investigate further.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has revealed an AI agent hacked into an Australian Medicare data portal earlier this year.
Speaking in New York, Mr Albanese said the OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to the Medicare statistics reporting service portal administered by Services Australia on June 18.
The AI agent accessed both public and non-public files, but Mr Albanese said it did not appear anyone's personal Medicare details were accessed.
Mr Albanese said he had a "frank" discussion with OpenAI's chief executive Sam Altman, saying the company took three months to notify the government of the breach and, when it did, the notification was in an email sent to the Services Australia public inbox.
"Today I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, to express Australia's extreme concern about this incident," he said.
"And I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred."
He said the "nature" of the notification was also "unacceptable".
"The notification was an email sent just to the public mailbox," Mr Albanese said.
What do we know so far?
OpenAI accessed non-public aggregate health statistics and internal files from an old Australian government website that carried Medicare statistics.
It is understood an AI crawler, which is an automated program that scans websites and collects information from them, was able to find a security workaround to access the data.
Often deployed as a tool by AI agents, crawlers collect data that usually trains AI models, builds datasets or retrieves information for AI systems.
Who knew what, when?
Read more
June 18: A Medicare statistics reporting service portal, administered by Services Australia, is breached by an OpenAI agent
August 11: OpenAI becomes aware of the breach during a review of OpenAI misaligned model activity during training
September 1: OpenAI chief executive officer Sam Altman meets Defence Minister Richard Marles in San Francisco, but Mr Marles says the breach wasn't disclosed
September 10: OpenAI sends an email to publicdisclosures@ servicesaustralia.gov.au — an address used by academics and researchers to notify weaknesses in Services Australia's systems
September 11: Services Australia sees the email
September 15: Services Australia notifies the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD)
September 17: Minister for the Public Service Katy Gallagher is told and seeks further information
September 19-20: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and his office are informed of the incident, while Minister Gallagher holds several discussions with Mr Marles, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke, Services Australia and the ASD
September 22: First "technical exchange" between OpenAI and Services Australia
September 24: Mr Albanese calls Mr Altman and informs the public of the breach
The prime minister said OpenAI was conducting research into public medical spending when it found a way to break through privacy protections.
"The AI agent found a way around those blocks, didn't accept 'no' for an answer, if you like," Mr Albanese said.
The prime minister said Services Australia was not notified until September 10.
On September 15, Services Australia reported it to the Australian Signals Directorate's cybersecurity centre.
Last week, Services Australia got in touch with Katy Gallagher, the minister for the public service. Mr Albanese's office was notified over the weekend.
He said there was no evidence any individual personal information had been accessed, but an investigation aided by the Australian Signals Directorate was now underway.
"[The] evidence currently available is there is no broader compromise to the Services Australia network. Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable," Mr Albanese said.
The prime minister said three other websites may have been affected: the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Victorian Department of Health.
But Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles later clarified that the interactions on those three websites were "entirely normal" and public information was accessed.
Mr Albanese announced a taskforce would be set up to provide an "urgent and immediate review" of the incident.
The investigation will be led by the prime minister's department and will work with the Australian Signals Directorate and the AI Safety Institute.
OpenAI says 'several' Australian government websites involved
The prime minister was asked if Mr Altman apologised.
"Yes, he clearly … we can get into word games, but he clearly accepted that the company had not done good enough," Mr Albanese said.
In a statement, an OpenAI spokesperson said the company was "conducting an extensive review of misaligned model activity" during training, and notifying third parties when there was a potential impact on their systems.
"During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation," they said.
"In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend.
"Our review found no evidence of patient records being accessed. The information accessed included aggregate health statistics and internal file names."
The company said the information accessed included aggregate health statistics and internal file names.
"We notified the organisations and are providing technical information to support their investigations and help address potential security vulnerabilities," the statement said.
They said OpenAI's overall review was ongoing and it remained "committed to transparency".
Back in Australia, Mr Marles said the fact a non-human AI agent gained unauthorised access represented "a very serious incident", but the impact on the system was minor.
"For what that's worth, that's relatively minor, and so it's important to assure people of that. No personal information has been accessed here. There's no impact on the system."
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said the hack was a "serious warning". He accused the prime minister of "failing to pre-empt" the incident and called on him to focus more on cyber defence.
"I would have thought that cyber defence is the number one issue when it comes to AI," Mr Taylor said.
"It's not the only issue, but it's got to be top of the list, and it hasn't been the focus of the government … It should be, it must be."
Acting Greens leader Mehreen Faruqi said the incident was "disturbing" and called for a moratorium on AI data centres in Australia until further regulations were in place.
"This breach by a foreign AI company on an Australian government database is deeply alarming and brings home the risks that these out-of-control tech corporations pose," she said.
Mr Albanese said the incident was complex and unprecedented.
"It was a shock that it occurred because it was real and serious," he said.
"But it also, I think, was something that had been predicted, including by the AI companies themselves."

Kyiv Faces Internet Disruptions as Russian Strikes Hit Data Centers and Communications Infrastructure

Ukraine’s Ministry of Digital Transformation confirmed this on September 23.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Emergency response teams and specialists are currently assessing the extent of the damage across the local network.
Crews are actively working on repairs to restore regular service and bring stable connectivity back to the impacted areas as quickly as possible.
The Ministry of Digital Transformation has not provided a specific timeline for when full service will be restored to the capital and the neighboring region amid ongoing recovery efforts following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
At least three internet service providers in Kyiv—Pavutyna, UTELS, and Crazy Network—reported service disruptions following a attack by Russian forces. Data centers belonging to Pavutyna and UTELS sustained damage, causing network interruptions.
The attack on a traffic exchange point in Kyiv also led to internet connectivity issues for Crazy Network users in Vinnytsia and the Khmelnytskyi region.
The Russian Ministry of Defense has officially claimed to be deliberately targeting internet communication infrastructure in Ukraine, stating that recent strikes against Kyiv-based internet service providers were aimed at "striking facilities supporting the Armed Forces of Ukraine," according to Ukrainian political analyst, Andrii Smolii.
Russian forces are actively targeting Ukrainian data centers in an effort to disrupt early warning systems and leave civilians without critical safety information, according to Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha.
By striking data infrastructure, Moscow aims to cut off access to life-saving air raid notifications, compromising the nation's civil defense network and putting more civilian lives at risk during ongoing aerial attacks.
The latest strikes followed another daytime Russian attack on Kyiv on September 22, when Russian forces deployed jet-powered Shahed drones.
One of the drones directly struck fuel storage tanks in the capital’s northern Obolonskyi district, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko.
That attack injured eight people across the city. Three were hospitalized, while five others received medical assistance at the scene or were treated on an outpatient basis.

Vote counting begins in Morocco's parliamentary elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:22:09 UTC
05:22:09 KST

Khalid Mejdoub, Mohammad Sio
23 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
Vote counting began across Morocco on Wednesday after polls closed in parliamentary elections that will determine the composition of the country's 395-seat House of Representatives.
Polling stations opened at 8 am GMT and closed at 7 pm, according to an Anadolu correspondent.
Morocco's Interior Ministry said voter turnout had reached 28.05% nationwide by 5 pm GMT, adding that voting took place under "normal conditions."
Final turnout in the previous parliamentary election, held on Sept. 8, 2021, was 50.18%.
A total of 3,206 observers, including 200 foreign monitors, oversaw Wednesday's vote.
Official figures show that 15,801,162 people were registered to vote. Twenty-eight political parties competed through 1,850 candidate lists comprising 7,288 candidates, including 2,658 women, for the 395 seats in the House of Representatives.
The Interior Ministry is expected to announce preliminary results in the early hours of Thursday.  
Under Article 47 of Morocco's Constitution, the king appoints the head of government from the political party that finishes first in the House of Representatives election. Cabinet members are appointed by the king on the recommendation of the head of government.
A parliamentary majority requires at least 198 seats, making coalition talks likely if no party secures an outright majority.
The next government will face political, economic and social challenges, as well as major projects linked to Morocco's preparations to co-host the 2030 FIFA World Cup.
In the 2021 election, the National Rally of Independents (RNI) finished first with 102 seats, followed by the Authenticity and Modernity Party with 86 and the Istiqlal Party with 81.
The current government is headed by RNI leader Aziz Akhannouch in coalition with the Authenticity and Modernity Party and Istiqlal.

Why McDonald's is following Walmart and Amazon into the advertising business
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:21:17 UTC
05:21:17 KST

McDonald's on Wednesday announced plans to create its own media network, following in the footsteps of retail giants like Amazon and Walmart.
In August, 450 of its company-owned U.S. restaurants began displaying advertising for other companies on its digital drive-thru order boards as part of a pilot. It is early days for the program, which has not yet rolled out to the franchisees who operate the rest of its roughly 14,000 U.S. locations.
Still, McDonald's hopes that it could eventually grow to be a $1 billion business for the company.
"Commerce media is one of the fastest-growing areas in advertising, and it's expected to reach more than $100 billion in the U.S. alone by 2028," Morgan Flatley, McDonald's global chief marketing officer and executive vice president of new business ventures, said during an investor presentation.
"It's an opportunity to generate revenue for the system with little in the way of additional cost, no operational complexity and no disruption to our customer experience," Flatley added.
The move could eventually bring McDonald's a steady stream of high-margin revenue as costs for key inputs like beef climb and as the chain plans to invest billions of dollars in restaurant upgrades over the next decade.
In the restaurant industry, McDonald's would be a pioneer for creating its own media network. CFO Ian Borden said that the company is uniquely positioned to make it a success.
"We have one of the most valuable brands of any company of our size and scale in any industry," Borden told CNBC. "We serve about 85% of the U.S. population at least once a year, so we have reach that's quite unique, and we have 14,000 locations across the U.S., which means we're in every community, and we're connecting with every consumer."
Retailers like Amazon and Walmart have found success running their own media networks, which tend to be high-margin businesses. Amazon reported $68.6 billion in advertising service sales in 2025, accounting for just under 10% of the company's overall revenue. Amazon's ads appear across its portfolio, from its shopping pages to Prime Video to lockers and live streaming platform Twitch, as well as third-party apps and websites.
Walmart does not share specific sales results for its advertising unit, but the company said that Connect, its U.S. ad business, grew sales 43% in its fiscal second quarter. The retailer's media network shows ads on its app, website and inside its more than 4,600 U.S. stores, plus outside apps like Instagram. It also bought TV maker Vizio in late 2024 with an eye toward its ad business.
McDonald's newest venture was announced as part of the company's investor day, which was hosted at its Chicago headquarters. In addition to the media network, executives shared more details about plans to grow sales through pricey restaurant upgrades and better food quality.

Netanyahu heads to UN for brief visit with few high-level meetings, protests expected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:19:52 UTC
05:19:52 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is set to arrive in the New York area Thursday for an unusually brief visit to address the United Nations General Assembly, with few meetings with foreign leaders and no scheduled meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump as Israel faces intense international criticism.
Netanyahu is expected to spend only several hours in the United States, delivering his speech, holding a small number of diplomatic meetings and returning to Israel without staying overnight. The abbreviated schedule marks a departure from previous General Assembly visits, when Netanyahu used the annual gathering to meet numerous world leaders on the sidelines.
Israeli officials have made efforts to arrange meetings with leaders of countries considered friendly toward Israel, particularly in South America. Netanyahu is expected to meet Argentine President Javier Milei and Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Janša during the visit.
A meeting with Trump, however, is not scheduled. A senior U.S. official said the two leaders' schedules do not overlap, with Netanyahu expected to arrive after Trump has already left New York.
Netanyahu is traveling primarily to deliver his General Assembly address before quickly returning to Israel.
A hostile reception at the UN
The United Nations has long been a venue for sharp criticism of Israeli policy, but Israeli officials are preparing for a particularly contentious reception this year.
Officials expect some diplomats could walk out during Netanyahu's address, while others may stage protests inside the chamber, including by displaying signs accusing Israel of genocide. Israel rejects accusations that its actions in Gaza constitute genocide.
An Israeli official said images involving National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and incidents of Jewish extremist violence in the West Bank have further damaged Israel's standing internationally. The official said there was a perception abroad that Netanyahu had failed to restrain far-right members of his government.
Outside the UN, several demonstrations are planned around Netanyahu's appearance, involving Israeli anti-government activists, left-wing Jewish organizations and pro-Palestinian and anti-Zionist groups. Major Jewish organizations, meanwhile, organized a rally against antisemitism near the UN on Wednesday, a day before Netanyahu's address.
The demonstrations come amid Netanyahu's escalating public confrontation with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has accused the Israeli prime minister of war crimes and genocide, allegations Netanyahu rejects. Mamdani previously said he would seek Netanyahu's arrest based on an International Criminal Court warrant but later acknowledged that he lacks the authority to do so.
Netanyahu said this week that he intends to use his UN address to “tell the truth” about Israel and its military and respond to Mamdani's accusations.
Netanyahu expected to focus on Iran
Iran is expected to feature prominently in Netanyahu's speech.
In recent days, Israeli officials have held intensive discussions over whether classified intelligence related to Iran could be cleared for public release for use in the address. Netanyahu is expected to present aerial imagery concerning Iranian reconstruction efforts and Tehran's nuclear and missile programs.
He is also expected to refer to a series of recent attacks against Israelis, including the latest attack in which IDF reservist Neriya Leiter, the son of Israeli Ambassador to the United States Yechiel Leiter, was seriously wounded.
The speech comes just over a month before Israel's Oct. 27 election, giving Netanyahu one of the world's most prominent diplomatic stages at a critical point in the campaign.
Netanyahu has portrayed the appearance as an opportunity to defend Israel before an international audience that he says has accepted false claims about the country and its conduct. His critics, however, argue that the speech is aimed at least as much at Israeli voters as at the diplomats in the General Assembly hall.
No Trump meeting, no overnight stay
Netanyahu's official aircraft is expected to land Thursday morning at a military airfield in New Jersey rather than John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York.
Reports about the change have cited a combination of security, logistical and protest concerns. Netanyahu is then expected to travel in a secured motorcade directly to the United Nations.
His wife, Sara, and son Yair are expected to accompany him.
Israel's ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, has worked to arrange diplomatic meetings around the compressed visit.
Netanyahu had sought a meeting with Trump, according to Israeli sources, but none was arranged. U.S. officials have publicly attributed the absence of a meeting to scheduling, saying Netanyahu will arrive after Trump leaves New York.
Israeli officials also believe there is frustration within the Trump administration over Netanyahu's handling of Gaza, though U.S. officials have not publicly cited that as the reason the two leaders will not meet.
Netanyahu had also sought a meeting with Elon Musk in Texas, but the stop was canceled after security and logistical difficulties arose. The planned Texas visit would also have required an additional U.S. landing for refueling. Reports this week confirmed that the Texas stop was dropped from Netanyahu's itinerary.
The prime minister ultimately decided on a lightning visit that will not include an overnight stay at his usual Manhattan hotel, the Loews Regency.
Israel had already reserved three floors at the hotel, however, potentially leaving the government with a substantial bill despite Netanyahu not staying there. Finance Ministry officials are expected to negotiate with the hotel in an effort to secure credit toward a future stay.
The visit comes as Netanyahu faces protests not only from pro-Palestinian and anti-Zionist activists but also from Israelis opposed to his government. The Israeli expat group UnXeptable, which emerged as a prominent organizer during the 2023 protests against Netanyahu's judicial overhaul, is among those planning demonstrations Thursday.
For Netanyahu, the visit will therefore be markedly different from many of his previous appearances at the annual gathering: hours rather than days in New York, a limited diplomatic schedule, no meeting with the U.S. president and an address delivered amid demonstrations both inside and outside the United Nations.

Wired for War: The empire’s propaganda wing honors Palantir
Germany’s Axel Springer media monolith is about to award its highest honor to Palantir founder Peter Thiel, in a ceremony illustrating the incestuous relationship between the mainstream media, the defense tech industry, and the US-Israeli order.
Thiel will receive the ‘2026 Axel Springer Award’ at a ceremony in Berlin on Thursday. According to Axel Springer CEO Mathias Dopfner, Thiel “is one of the rare entrepreneurs who does not merely found or finance companies but helps determine the direction of technological development.”
“He reminds us that progress requires courage and nonconformism,” Dopfner added.
Previous recipients of the Axel Springer Award include Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, and Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky. None of these laureates have proven as controversial as Thiel, however.
According to Status News, employees at Politico and Business Insider – both of which are owned by Axel Springer – have pushed back against the decision. In a letter to management on Tuesday, 120 staffers argued that Thiel, who funded the lawsuit that destroyed Gawker, should not be honored by a company which, in the words of Dopfner, “stands for freedom of speech and a culture of open discussions.”
They’re missing the point. Palantir and Axel Springer are cogs in the same machine. They share an almost identical world view, marked by a devotion to US-Israeli hegemony, a belief that private companies must serve the interests of this hegemony, and a common parent: the CIA.
The CIA connection
During the Cold War, the US saw strategic control of media outlets as key to preventing the rise of socialism and communism in Western Europe. Axel Springer, the anti-communist press baron who gave his name to the company, was a natural ally in this fight. Springer received $7 million in funding from the CIA in 1957, two former agents told The Nation in 1982. Adjusted for inflation, the donation would be equivalent to more than $80 million today.
Although the agents claimed that Springer ended his relationship with the agency in the mid-1970s, declassified documents show that he was still in contact with the United States Information Agency (USIA) – which funded pro-American news outlets – in the early 1980s. In 1982, Springer was introduced to CIA Director William Casey as “a strong supporter of the United States” who “is doing all he can to strengthen the ties between the United States and Europe.”
Thiel, who co-founded PayPal, launched Palantir in 2003 with the stated goal of taking “the approaches that PayPal had used to fight fraud…into other contexts, like fighting terrorism.” The CIA took notice, and invested $2 million in the company in 2005 via its in-house venture capital firm, In-Q-Tel.
“I wish I had Palantir when I was director,” former CIA chief George Tenet – who set up In-Q-Tel – told Forbes magazine in 2013. “I wish we had the tool of its power.”
The Axel Springer investment pays off
In both cases, the CIA’s investments paid off. Axel Springer is now Europe’s largest publisher, and owns Politico, Business Insider, Bild, Die Welt, The Telegraph, and nearly a dozen other outlets. The American deep state continues to finance its operations, with the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) and the State Department’s National Endowment for Democracy (NED) pumping just under $34 million into Politico between 2016 and 2025.
In return, Axel Springer has openly pledged fealty to American neoliberalism. Whereas Springer himself described his first newspaper, the Hamburger Abendblatt, as “geared to the underdog and the little man,” staff at Axel Springer publications are today required to adhere to the following code of conduct:
- “We stand up for freedom, free speech, the rule of law, and democracy”
- “We support the right of existence of the State of Israel and oppose all forms of anti-Semitism”
- “We advocate the alliance between the United States of America and Europe”
- “We uphold the principles of a free market economy”
- “We reject political and religious extremism and all forms of discrimination”
In practice, this means that Axel Springer publications will feature lively debate over ‘red versus blue’ politics in the US and Europe, but will never question key tenets of US foreign policy, including America’s alliance with Israel, its dominance over Europe through NATO, and the legitimacy of its proxy war with Russia in Ukraine.
The world according to Palantir
More than two decades after taking CIA money, Palantir is now the largest of the Silicon Valley defense kingpins, and a synonym for the burgeoning surveillance- and military-tech sector as a whole. Palantir is valued at around $427 billion, a figure bolstered by lucrative contracts with the US’ defense and intelligence agencies, including all six branches of the US military, the CIA, FBI, NSA, and DIA.
Palantir’s flagship product is an operating system called ‘Gotham’, which is essentially a data analytics platform for military, intelligence, and law enforcement agencies. Gotham pulls together and analyses existing data that may otherwise take days to sift through. For example, if US Central Command is planning a missile strike in a foreign country, Gotham can combine maps and satellite footage from that country, data from other agencies, including human intelligence from the CIA and signals intelligence from the NSA, and local surveillance data to present CENTCOM with potential targets for military strikes.
Palantir’s international customers include the British, Israeli and Ukrainian militaries, NATO, domestic intelligence agencies in France and Germany, and police departments in Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, and the UK, among others.
However, Palantir is not a mercenary company selling its products to anyone with money. According to CEO Alex Karp, Palantir is inseparable from the US deep state, and “was founded to strengthen US national security, to protect Americans and their freedom.”
Because we get asked a lot.
The Technological Republic, in brief.
1. Silicon Valley owes a moral debt to the country that made its rise possible. The engineering elite of Silicon Valley has an affirmative obligation to participate in the defense of the nation.
2. We must rebel…
Earlier this year, Karp set out Palantir’s world view in a manifesto, which RT already covered in depth in our ‘Wired for War’ series. In the 22-point bulletin, Karp argued that “the engineering elite of Silicon Valley has an affirmative obligation to participate in the defense of the nation,” that “free and democratic societies” must pursue AI superweapons to preserve the hegemony of the US, which “has advanced progressive values” more than “any other nation on the planet.”
In separate comments, Karp has described pro-Palestinian protesters as a “cancerous” influence on American politics, while Palantir describes its work with the Israeli state as “in line with our global support of US allies and liberal democracies.”
Critics called Karp’s manifesto “technofascist,” but it differs little in substance from Axel Springer’s code of conduct. Karp’s remaining points wade into US-centric culture war territory, but the core argument of both documents is the same: the US and Israel are a benevolent force and the private sector has a duty to aid their foreign policy goals; by argument, in the case of Axel Springer, and by force, in the case of Palantir.
The incestuous security state
Back in Berlin, the guest speakers at Thursday’s ceremony further illustrate the incestuous relationship between Axel Springer, Palantir, and the US-Israeli order. Before Dopfner hands him his award, Thiel will be lauded by CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss, a self-described “Zionist fanatic” who was appointed head of the network following its acquisition last year by billionaire and pro-Israel megadonor David Ellison, whose family has donated more than $26 million to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) since 2014.
Before the acquisition, Weiss repeatedly complained about CBS’ supposedly “anti-Israel bias.” Once in control of the network, she set about hiring pro-Israel editors and reportedly intervening personally in stories concerning the Jewish state.

Russian invasion of NATO country ‘highly unlikely’ but cannot be ruled out: Danish spy agency

Russian invasion of NATO country ‘highly unlikely’ but cannot be ruled out: Danish spy agency
COPENHAGEN - The Danish Defence Intelligence Service (DDIS) said on Sept 24 that the risk of Russian military action against NATO countries was growing and an outright invasion was “highly unlikely” but possible.
European countries have been on high alert for any Russian interference, with fears that Moscow could target Kyiv’s Western backers as the Kremlin’s invasion of Ukraine drags on into its fifth year.
“There is a low but growing risk that Russia will launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries bordering Russia,” Thomas Ahrenkiel, the head of the DDIS, told a press conference at which he presented an updated assessment of the threat from Russia.
He said that the agency still considered it “highly unlikely that Russia would see any interest in invading a NATO country, but we cannot rule it out”.
In the assessment, the agency said that Russia would likely carry out more so-called “hybrid attacks” against targets in the West.
It noted that in the past such attacks had “mainly been aimed at creating fear and weakening public support for aid to Ukraine”.
But they had now started to include actions meant to stop support from reaching Ukraine, such as sabotage against defence companies or railway transports carrying military equipment, the agency said.
The DDIS said it thought Russia would intensify such attacks, which could also include “destructive cyber attacks that cripple critical societal functions”.
The agency also said there was a low risk of a limited military attack even if the war in Ukraine continued, as an attempt to redirect European resources away from Ukraine.
“A limited military attack would be a desperate move on Russia’s part and, like the intensified hybrid attacks, could potentially take place in the coming months,” the agency said.
However, the DDIS also noted that “a build-up of forces would require several months of preparation and will be difficult to conceal.”
Ahrenkiel also stressed that although “Russia’s increased willingness to take risks has consequences for the security situation in Denmark”, notably through hybrid attacks, this does not mean that Russia is going to attack the Scandinavian country.
“We do not expect a conventional Russian military attack against Denmark,” he stressed. AFP

UN rights chief ‘appalled’ by Yemen conflict’s swelling civilian toll
GENEVA - The UN rights chief voiced outrage on Sept 24 at the growing civilian toll in Yemen, as the conflict between the Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces and their allies intensifies.
The recent Houthi takeover of Yemen’s Red Sea coast has left hundreds dead and heightened fears over global trade and shipping through the vital Bab al-Mandab strait.
It has also forced thousands to flee, with the United Nations on Sept 22 forecasting the number of displaced could swell from over 130,000 today to more than 230,000 in the coming months.
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk said he was “appalled” at the situation.
“As if the people of Yemen haven’t already endured enough misery, civilians are now bearing the brunt of this latest upsurge in fighting,” he said in a statement, insisting that “civilians must never be targeted, and their protection must be the overriding priority”.
Turk’s office said at least 125 civilians had been killed or injured in Houthi attacks since the start of August, adding that it had documented the killings of 32 of those civilians, including 15 children and three women.
It also said it had documented three Houthi attacks on sites hosting internally displaced people in Marib province on Aug 7 and Sept 9.
The Houthis meanwhile say Saudi Arabia has conducted hundreds of strikes in Yemen since the collapse of a four-year truce in July.
“Warring parties must distinguish at all times between civilians and combatants and between civilian objects and military objectives,” Turk said.
The UN rights chief also stressed that warnings or designations of so-called “kill-zones”, which he said had recently been declared by the Yemeni government, do not “remove the protection afforded to civilians and civilian objects”.
Turk called on all sides in the conflict to allow and facilitate humanitarian aid to reach civilians in need.
“People fleeing the fighting, as well as those already displaced, must be protected and have safe access to food, water, shelter, healthcare and other essential services,” he said, urging all sides to “step back from further escalation”.
“The people of Yemen cannot withstand another full-scale conflict.” AFP

Inside NATO’s online propaganda machine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:11:23 UTC
05:11:23 KST

Inside NATO’s online propaganda machine
NATO has spent years researching online influence techniques involving fake profiles, targeted advertising and purchased social media engagement. RT’s America Now has examined the bloc’s experiments and what they could reveal about efforts to shape online narratives.
Host Ben Swann and investigative journalist Elizabeth Lane reviewed NATO promotional material, published research and reports on experiments involving social media manipulation.
One example is a 2024 NATO promotional video featuring predominantly white European women as the alliance’s “future” in a potential conflict, apparently with Russia. Swann and Lane argue that the unusually non-diverse casting could be intended to prepare European audiences for women taking a greater role in a possible confrontation as Ukraine struggles with manpower shortages.
They also examined two 2019 experiments by NATO strategic communications researchers. In one, researchers created fake Facebook pages and profiles, collected publicly available information on military personnel and used targeted advertising to reach them. They reportedly identified around 150 soldiers, tracked troop movements and even induced some personnel to act against orders. The experiment cost roughly $60.
In another test, researchers spent €300 on artificial engagement, buying more than 3,500 comments, 25,000 likes, 20,000 views and 5,000 followers. They identified over 18,000 accounts involved in providing fake engagement. Four weeks later, roughly 80% of the purchased activity remained online, highlighting weaknesses in platforms’ ability to detect manipulation.
NATO described the experiments as defensive research aimed at identifying online threats. Swann and Lane, however, questioned why a military alliance was developing practical expertise in techniques that could also be used to influence public opinion. They also pointed to NATO researchers’ cooperation with Ukrainian social media analytics company Singularex.
The episode also revisited false stories that had circulated during the early stages of the Ukraine conflict, including the “Ghost of Kiev” fighter pilot and initial claims about the “defenders of Snake Island.” Lane argued that journalists who repeat compelling wartime stories without verifying them can amplify false narratives.
Lane also said independent journalists covering Russia and Ukraine regularly face bot attacks, abuse and threats. She said she had received such messages herself, including one stating, “Zelensky sends his love,” which she suggested could point to coordinated activity.

“Last year, you will remember, I stated here that Türkiye was bidding to host COP31. This year, we will hold COP31 in Antalya from Nov. 9-20, 2026,” he said.
He said Türkiye is working to ensure that the gathering focuses on implementing decisions taken on climate change.
Erdogan also pointed to planned meetings in the Pacific, saying the Pre-COP meeting in Fiji and the leaders’ gathering in Tuvalu would help ensure that the voices of Pacific island countries are heard.
“The last 11 years have been the hottest period on record,” Erdogan said, adding that floods in Nepal had demonstrated “in the most painful way” that there is no time to lose.
Erdogan said the first 10 years of the Paris Agreement were focused on establishing common targets, while important decisions were taken in the Brazilian city of Belem last year for the success of the agreement’s second decade.
“We must achieve much more in Antalya,” he said. “We must bring ambition and capability, and targets and implementation, closer together.”
Erdogan stressed that climate policies must take into account countries' social and economic circumstances.
“Any proposal that we cannot reconcile with our climate targets and social and economic realities will be doomed to failure,” he said.
He also said it was unrealistic to expect all countries to move at the same pace while inequalities persist in access to financing and technology.
“As inequalities in access to financing and technology persist, it is not realistic to expect all countries to progress at the same speed,” he said.
The president emphasized the relationship between climate action, development and prosperity.
“To the extent that we can establish a strong link between climate targets and development and prosperity, we can also make a just transition permanent,” he said.
Guterres convened the high-level meeting to focus on accelerating a just and orderly transition to renewable energy, mobilizing affordable financing and investment for developing countries, and strengthening adaptation and resilience amid rising climate risks.

Details
In June 2025, 74-year-old Weinstein was found guilty of committing a first-degree criminal sexual act against Miriam Haley at his apartment in Manhattan. This marked the culmination of a six-year legal saga during which his 2020 conviction was overturned by New York State’s highest court. Weinstein denies assaulting anyone or engaging in nonconsensual sexual acts.
On Wednesday, Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg praised Haley’s testimony and said he was moved by her courage.
A representative for Weinstein said that he continues to maintain his innocence and categorically disagrees with the verdict handed down by Judge Curtis Farber.
Weinstein was first found guilty in New York in 2020—for assaulting Haley and raping actress Jessica Mann—and was sentenced to 23 years in prison. During the retrial in 2025, jurors found him guilty on the count involving Haley, acquitted him of charges that he assaulted former model Kaja Sokola, and were unable to reach a verdict on the rape charge involving Mann.

 Karl Leonhard Reinhold (1757 – 1823), Austrian philosopher and first occupant of the chair on Critical Philosophy established at the University of Jena in 1787, first achieved fame as a proponent of popular Enlightenment and as an early and effective popularizer of the Kantian philosophy. During his period at the University of Jena (1787 – 94), Reinhold proclaimed the need for a more “scientific” and systematic presentation of the Critical philosophy, one based upon a single, self-evident first principle. Ontario Jewish community saddened, but not shocked, by synagogue shooting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:08:40 UTC
05:08:40 KST

Doug Warren, 56, was attending Kol Nidre services at the Sons of Jacob synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, on the eve of Yom Kippur on Sunday. Prayers were just about to begin when he heard the gunshots.
“The rabbi had just started to call us into the sanctuary. We were stepping inside, and we heard this loud bang, and we all stopped,” Warren, a member of the congregation, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency. “It sounded like someone was banging the window or the door.”
It was a 29-year-old former Canadian soldier exchanging gunfire with a police officer stationed outside the synagogue. The shooter, Sean Ward, 29, of Quinte West, Ontario, died from his wounds on Tuesday. The officer, Const. Jeff Smith, a 13-year veteran of the force, remains in the hospital in critical condition.
Little is known of Ward, who served in the Canadian military from 2017 to 2022, and was never deployed.
“We knew this was going to happen,” Warren, a member of Sons of Jacob and a resident of Belleville. told JTA. “We’ve been saying as Jews that we’re very concerned with the rise of antisemitism. What did you think was going to happen? People weren’t taking it seriously.”
Congregation extremely grateful to 'hero,' police officer Smith
As the gunfire continued, congregants scrambled to find safety. “Some people suggested we should go to the basement, others said we should go out the back door,” he recalls. “At the same time, you’re just frozen because you don’t know what’s going on or what to do. Eventually the shots stopped.”
Warren said the congregation is extremely grateful to Smith, who was stationed outside the synagogue in an unmarked vehicle. “This guy’s a hero. I can tell you the gunman was coming for us inside, and he was trying to take out our armed protection first,” he said. “We’re praying for [Smith’s] recovery.”
Once police arrived at Sons of Jacob, they instructed everyone to wait inside until the area was clear. Congregants were then taken to the Belleville police station, where they were offered donuts and coffee, which Warren said they politely declined on account of fasting for Yom Kippur.
Richard Marceau, General Counsel and Senior Vice President of The Center for Israel and Jewish Affairs, echoed Warren’s concerns. “I wish I could say that I was surprised or shocked, but I was not,” says Marceau. “Unfortunately, in 2026 in Canada, we’ve come to expect this type of thing. It just tells us that the promise of Canada has been broken.”
The Belleville shooting came two days after the arrest of 19-year-old Alexander Parfitt after posting online threats to shoot up a synagogue in Southern Ontario.
Marceau said that Canadian politicians have not sufficiently addressed the threat of antisemitism. “There has been an all-level failure in the political sector and in law enforcement,” he said. “It is a failure to understand the threats that Jews are facing.”
Rising antisemitic discourse endangers Canadian Jews
According to Marceau, anti-Israel and anti-Zionist discourse have also contributed to rising antisemitism and endangered Canadian Jews. “Anti-Zionism is driving violence against Canadians, and the double standard against Israel is playing a role,” Marceau said. “Politicians need a clear plan, not just to talk about extremist ideologies, organizations and foreign state actors. There needs to be a meeting of all levels of government to ensure that the extremist networks are disrupted.”
Anti-Israel sentiment was a point of contention Sunday evening. Canadian Jewish politician and leader of the New Democratic Party (NDP) Avi Lewis posted on X shortly after 8 p.m. that on Yom Kippur he was “reflecting on the fact that we have not done our part to stop an ongoing genocide being committed in our name.”
About an hour earlier, Ward opened fire outside Sons of Jacob. It was not clear whether Lewis knew the shooting had occurred when he had posted. He did not respond to a request for comment.
Canadian Member of Parliament Anthony Housefather responded to Lewis’ post, stating that “holding Canadian Jews and Jews across the world collectively responsible for events over which they have no control is despicable.”
Lewis said in a post the following day that the attack “is yet another reminder of the work that remains to create a Canada that is truly safe for people of all faiths, including Jewish people – to worship, to come together, to live without fear.” In a press conference, he rejected claims that he was collectively blaming Jews for Israel’s actions.
Despite the events Warren witnessed on Sunday evening, he remains assured in the resilience of his local Jewish community. Unable to access their synagogue, Warren says the Sons of Jacob congregation gathered at a Best Western hotel on Monday evening for services.
“We want to keep going, but we know it’s not going to be easy. We might get emotional when we first get back inside the synagogue, and we’ll just have to work through that,” he says. “This will not stop us.”

PM set to warn China and US the Indo-Pacific not their 'chessboard'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:00:10 UTC
05:00:10 KST

Albanese tells China and US the Indo-Pacific not a 'chessboard' for superpowers
In short:
In a major foreign policy speech, Anthony Albanese has declared the post-1945 world order "is no longer fit for purpose", and issued a warning to China and the US.
The prime minister has signed a decade-long security agreement with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, committing $60 million to help the country defend itself against Russia.
The new agreement provides a "framework" for defence and security cooperation, including military training, rebuilding Ukrainian military facilities and exploring joint manufacturing of missiles and drones.
Anthony Albanese has declared the post-1945 world order "is no longer fit for purpose" and warn China and the United States that the Indo-Pacific is not a "chessboard" for global superpowers.
In a major foreign policy speech delivered in New York, the prime minister said Australia needed to help shape the new global order by building new relationships, standing up for the rules governing how countries interact with each other and rejecting the notion that might is right.
Underscoring the stark warning, Mr Albanese signed a decade-long security agreement with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Wednesday, local time, and announced another $60 million in funding to help the country defend itself against Russia.
The two leaders shared a hug, and Mr Albanese was on the verge of tears when describing his admiration for the "extraordinary" leadership of his "friend" Mr Zelenskyy.
"I think Russia thought it could just steamroll through in a matter of weeks, and what we have found is the people of Ukraine were underestimated," Mr Albanese said during the meeting.
Indo-Pacific not a 'chessboard'
Mr Albanese's comments about the rules-based order echo similar warnings from like-minded leaders, including Canada's Mark Carney, who has said middle powers must unite because "if we're not at the table, we're on the menu".
Mr Albanese identified the strategic competition between China and the US as the most consequential factor shaping the region.
"The Indo-Pacific is not a chessboard on which superpowers move the pieces,"
"How Washington and Beijing manage their relationship matters profoundly. But it cannot be the only lens through which we see the region.
"Its countries are not spectators. They are shaping its future and writing their own script."
PM named 'global citizen'
Mr Albanese gave the speech at a ceremony where he was awarded the Atlantic Council Global Citizen Award, alongside Finland's President Alexander Stubb, Broadway star and actor Cynthia Erivo and Formula 1 boss Stefano Domenicalli.
It comes a day after US President Donald Trump stood on the floor of the United Nations and threatened to "annihilate" Iran, if the country failed to agree to a deal to end the war, and warned Cuba, a "failed state", would fall.
In a wideranging speech, Mr Trump very publicly slapped down a push from a coalition of middle powers, including Australia, for global regulations to ensure humans remained in control of AI, declaring the US had no plans to rein in the powerful technology.
As Australia launched its bid for a two-year term on the UN Security Council, Mr Albanese argued global institutions needed to be modernised and strengthened.
"The post-1945 world order is no longer fit for purpose," Mr Albanese said.
"Universal institutions that remain necessary are now not always sufficient for the challenges we face.
"Australia's response to this is to actively seek to shape and build the order that replaces the old."
Rules essential to Australia
Australia has long been caught between two competing forces — relying on China as its biggest trading partner and on the US as its most important security ally.
But with Mr Trump up-ending the global order, and a more assertive Chinese president in power, Mr Albanese said the imperative for countries to agree and abide by rules remains.
"Australia depends on a region where ships and aircraft move freely, where trade reaches markets unimpeded, and where the sovereignty of small states is respected as fully as that of large ones," he said.
"The rules that connect our nations remain essential — and they matter to Australia, to the Indo-Pacific and globally."
Australia's bilateral relationship with Ukraine has deepened substantially since Russia's invasion in 2022. Canberra has committed more than $1.9 billion in assistance to the country, including Bushmasters, armoured tanks and other military equipment.
The new agreement provides a "framework" for defence and security cooperation, including stepping up military training, rebuilding Ukrainian military facilities and exploring the joint manufacturing of missiles and drones.

China-US dialogue takes centre stage in Washington
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
22:58:38 EEST
04:58:38 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping begins a state visit to the United States on 23 September, returning to Washington for the first time in a decade as Beijing and Washington seek firmer channels for managing trade, technology and security disputes. President Donald Trump will receive Xi at the White House on 24 September for talks on trade and technology.
The visit runs from 23 to 25 September at Trump’s invitation.
The programme includes an arrival ceremony, formal meetings and a state dinner, giving the two presidents another opportunity to build on months of direct contact between Beijing and Washington.
The meeting gives both governments another chance to put their framework for constructive strategic stability into practice. The approach centres on cooperation where interests overlap, and controlled competition.
That effort carries weight outside the two countries because the scale of their economic relationship reaches through global supply chains, commodity markets and manufacturing networks. US goods exports to China reached $65.2 billion from January through July 2026, while imports from China reached $156.4 billion. Two-way goods trade over those seven months stood at about $221.6 billion.
The direction of US-China policy affects sourcing, investment decisions and prices for companies trading across Asia, North America and Europe. A steadier relationship gives companies more information when planning production, contracts and long-term investment.
Trade is expected to take a large share of the Washington talks. Negotiators have discussed a Board of Trade and reciprocal tariff reductions covering up to $30 billion of goods in each direction.
The product list under discussion includes consumer goods, farm products, energy products and medical devices. Chinese officials want the reductions implemented at an early date, while the final scope will depend on the outcome of negotiations.
Previous talks produced commitments across agriculture, aviation and market access. China agreed to purchase at least $17 billion a year in US agricultural products in addition to an earlier soybean commitment.
Agriculture remains one of the most direct links between political decisions and businesses in both countries. China is an important market for US soybeans and other farm products, while American farmers depend on access to large export markets.
Questions remain over beef, poultry, dairy and seafood access, while technical issues continue to affect some shipments. Further movement in Washington would give both sides a way to show that earlier commitments are turning into commercial activity.
Boeing sales form another part of the unfinished agenda. China agreed earlier this year to purchase 200 aircraft, though the orders had not been completed by September.
Boeing chief executive Kelly Ortberg said this month that the process was progressing and that Chinese airlines would announce orders on their own schedules. The issue links diplomacy with jobs, manufacturing and airline demand in both countries.
Artificial intelligence has also moved higher on the agenda. Washington and Beijing compete over chips, models and global standards, but officials in both capitals face similar questions about safety, cyber risks and crisis management.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said Washington proposed a notification mechanism for AI incidents with national security implications.
Such a mechanism would create a direct point of contact if an AI-related incident threatened national security or produced wider risks. It would not settle disputes over chips or export controls, but it would give both governments another channel for managing unexpected events.
An AI channel represents one area where rivalry and risk management meet. American technology executives and policy specialists have supported some form of US-China contact on AI safety even while Washington keeps export controls on advanced chips and Beijing objects to US technology restrictions.
Chinese officials have also called for dialogue on AI governance. A regular communication mechanism would offer both sides a practical starting point without requiring agreement on every part of technology policy.
The immediate purpose of the summit is to keep high-level contact in place and reduce the risk that disputes spill into a wider breakdown in relations.
Republican Senator Steve Daines, who has worked with the Trump administration on China policy, has stressed the importance of meetings between the two leaders alongside any agreements reached.
The White House visit follows months of contact between the two administrations. Xi and Trump have spoken by phone, exchanged letters and met face to face since late 2025.
During Trump’s earlier trip to Beijing, the two presidents discussed trade, investment, technology and security. Their governments also restored communication channels intended to support negotiations between senior officials.
Business groups in both countries have placed predictability near the top of their expectations for Washington.
Sean Stein, president of the US-China Business Council, has said leader-level meetings help build trust and make work on other issues easier.
Chinese and US business representatives have also called for clearer policy signals on tariffs, investment rules and market access.
Bilateral goods trade grew 13.7 per cent year on year in the second quarter of 2026, while US companies had established more than 84,000 enterprises in China by July.
Those figures show the depth of commercial ties after a period marked by tariffs, export restrictions and political disputes.
The international impact of steadier interaction extends beyond bilateral trade.
The relationship between China and the United States reaches far beyond government meetings.
People-to-people ties form another part of the visit. More than 50,000 young Americans from all 50 states have travelled to China in just over two and a half years under an exchange initiative announced by Xi in San Francisco in 2023.
The programme has taken students to factories, rural communities, schools and cultural sites.
Such exchanges give students and communities direct contact at a time when political disputes often dominate public discussion.
Universities, tourism groups, business organisations and cultural bodies continue to operate alongside the government relationship. Direct contact between citizens offers another layer of communication when official relations face pressure.
The Washington programme also includes cultural events.
First Lady Melania Trump and Peng Liyuan are due to visit the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art.
The two presidential couples are also scheduled to visit the National Archives to view records linked to the history of US-China relations before the state visit ends.
Expectations for the summit remain focused on incremental progress rather than a single agreement that settles the larger disputes.
Work on a trade board, tariff reductions, agricultural purchases, aircraft sales and an AI incident channel gives officials several areas where movement is possible.
Investment talks face greater obstacles because both governments continue to apply national security tests to Chinese investment in the United States and US technology exposure to China.
The trade proposals give officials one of the clearest routes towards an agreement during the visit.
Reciprocal tariff reductions would follow months of negotiations and provide a visible sign that the two sides remain willing to turn summit commitments into policy.
Agriculture gives negotiators another area with defined targets.
China remains an important market for US farm products, while producers in the United States want stable access to Chinese buyers. Progress on technical barriers and purchase commitments would support trade in both directions.
Tariffs influence trade flows and consumer prices. Export controls influence technology supply chains. US-China demand affects agriculture, aircraft manufacturing, energy and shipping. AI policy increasingly reaches firms and regulators across several regions.
The talks therefore carry consequences well beyond Washington and Beijing.
A period of steadier communication between the two largest economies gives businesses more certainty, creates space for diplomatic negotiation and gives officials more routes for dealing with crises.
The formal programme will continue through Friday. Trump and Xi are due to hold meetings during the state visit, while the two first couples will attend a state dinner and later travel to the National Archives.
The visit gives both governments an opportunity to move practical negotiations forward while keeping channels open on the disputes that continue to divide them.

Owing to a cycle of retrials, appeals and judicial proceedings, Weinstein has remained incarcerated since his 2018 arrest and is now serving time in a prison medical ward.
Weinstein, first publicly accused of wrongdoing in 2017, was detained a year later. In 2024, New York’s highest court overturned the original 2020 conviction that had sentenced the former Hollywood producer to 23 years in prison, ruling that the inclusion of extraneous, non-indicted testimony had compromised the equity of the trial.

As major powers act unilaterally, experts say UN faces crisis in New York
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23

As major powers act unilaterally, experts say UN faces crisis in New York
Experts warn the UN faces crises of funding, relevance, and Security Council gridlock.
As world leaders gather in New York for the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), experts say the institution is battling an existential crisis of funding, relevance and Security Council gridlock.
Major conflicts appear intractable, and powers like the United States and Russia can bend the UN’s Security Council to their will; member states are looking for new mechanisms to bring accountability to the venue and for a new secretary-general to voice their concerns. The body has been accused of failing to stop what its own experts have said is a genocide in Gaza.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Geopolitical divides fueling Security Council inaction, UN chief warns
- list 2 of 3State of world getting worse as UN Security Council paralysed: Guterres
- list 3 of 3UN launches hunt for next chief amid rising challenges
World leaders are not under any illusion that the UNGA is in good health, said Daniel Forti, head of UN Affairs at the International Crisis Group. Yet many still understand the venue’s power.
“The vast majority of leaders, from small states, from middle powers, and even a few from major powers, recognise the importance of a UN that is a global conversation platform,” Forti said.
Trying to weigh in where the Security Council fails
The UN is juggling multiple conflicts – from high-profile wars involving Iran to the often overlooked catastrophes in Sudan and Myanmar.
In the Ukraine war, the UN says more civilians were killed in the first eight months of 2026 than in the whole of 2025, and even NATO powers now say they worry about spillover into their countries.
Russia has repeatedly vetoed Security Council resolutions, but Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has continued to appear before the UNGA to urge member states to help stop Moscow.
On Wednesday, Zelenskyy spoke for the fifth time before the assembly since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, urging leaders to further tighten economic measures meant to punish Moscow despite its vetoes of Security Council resolutions.
“Many of you here have seen more than once how the abuse of the veto at the UN weakens the world and pushes peace further away,” Zelenskyy said.
In the Israeli war on Gaza, the UN has labelled Israel’s conduct there a genocide, but it has struggled to exercise real agency. Security Council resolutions have been repeatedly vetoed, and UN relief agencies have been targeted by Israel without any accountability.
The ongoing war between the US, Israel and Iran is having economic impacts across the globe and threatens to plunge Yemen back into a civil war.
“From Ukraine, to Gaza, and Sudan, and also with what’s happening now in Iran, the veto problem leaves the UN hamstrung,” said Alanna O’Malley, professor and chair of Global Governance and Wealth and head of the Department of History at Erasmus University.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told Al Jazeera’s James Bays this week that these conflicts were having real humanitarian impacts worldwide, including reduced food access, rising fuel prices, and global inflation.
The UNGA will allow the opportunity for some discussions for parties involved in these kinds of conflicts, but it is unlikely they can reach major agreements, said Forti.
But the assembly is still the only forum where all 193 member states are equal, and nations have tried to invoke new procedures and reach back into historical mechanisms to try and mitigate the veto deadlocks, O’Malley said.
A 1950 resolution, dating from a deadlock over the Korean War, has allowed the UNGA to debate issues vetoed in the Security Council. And in 2022, an impasse over Ukraine generated a new mechanism forcing any permanent council representative – China, France, Russia, the UK, and the US, often called the P5 – to come before the UNGA and explain when it uses the veto.
“The idea is to build more accountability into the system for the P5, to make the veto not just harder to use, but also ensure it uses a lot of political capital,” O’Malley said.
Calls for reforms have only increased since 2023 and Israel’s war on Gaza, O’Malley said, with “unprecedented” majority votes in the UNGA challenging the Security Council.
Getting major powers to buy in
Perhaps the greatest challenge facing the UNGA, though, is remaining relevant as major global powers go their own way.
The administration of US President Trump has pushed through its own Board of Peace, a body that has accomplished few of its goals but has secured Security Council approval and claims to take on responsibilities previously handled by UN agencies, like distributing aid or managing refugees.
Unhappy with the UN, Trump has also imposed sanctions on the body’s special rapporteurs, as well as organisations like the International Criminal Court.
Washington, though, may not be the only government looking to strike out on its own.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is in the US this week, but he will not be attending the UNGA. He last addressed the body in 2021 via video, but this year he will skip it altogether, opting instead for one-on-one talks with US President Trump. China has positive views of the UN, often using the Security Council to weigh in on global issues, Forti said, but it is also looking for alternatives, through venues like BRICS and the SCO, to strengthen multilateralism.
The impetus to look for alternatives to the UN, even Secretary Guterres admits, is driven by the fact that the Security Council is unable to pass binding resolutions in the most controversial situations, because permanent members can simply veto them based on their own interests.
Guterres told Al Jazeera this week that kind of inaction was creating an “environment of impunity”, where the behaviour of major global powers was inspiring middle powers and others to “believe that they can do whatever they want because nothing will happen to them”.
The search for the next secretary-general
Guterres’s term ends on December 31, and the Security Council is expected to announce its recommendation for who will replace him.
“We had a secretary-general who didn’t have a lot of political capital to expend to solve these conflicts, and he hasn’t taken great initiative on a lot of them,” said O’Malley.
Guterres did, for example, draw on rarely used Article 99 powers in 2023 to bring the Gaza issue before the Security Council. But the UN also faces major funding problems, with major donors like the US cutting back, making it difficult to deliver aid in places like the West Bank and Gaza. “So he [Guterres] also has no actual financial capital,” O’Malley said.
Candidates to replace Guterres must win at least nine of the 15 votes from the council, and avoid a veto by any of the P5, to be put before the UNGA for a vote.
Forti said member states are looking for someone to refocus on preventing wars, and also deal with criticism that the UN has become unwieldy and costly.
“They will have to balance the UN’s diplomatic work, its impact, with financial cuts and racing to the bottom,” Forti said.

====================================================================================================

New study links evolution to weaker human joints
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
03:52:06 CST
04:52:06 KST

JERUSALEM, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- An international team of researchers has found that human evolution may have left people more vulnerable to joint disease, Israel's Weizmann Institute of Science said in a statement on Wednesday.
In their new study, published in the journal Nature, the researchers examined genetic differences between humans and other great apes, including chimpanzees and gorillas.
The researchers found that humans produce significantly lower levels of glycosaminoglycans, or GAGs, in their cartilage. GAGs are sugar molecules that attract water and help cartilage absorb shocks and cushion joints.
The team found that human cartilage contains about one-third as much GAG material as the cartilage of chimpanzees, gorillas, orangutans and bonobos.
The finding may help explain why osteoarthritis and other joint disorders are common in humans but rare in other great apes, even those that reach old age. Osteoarthritis affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide and can cause pain, stiffness, and disability.
The researchers suggested that the evolutionary change may have contributed to other human traits, including lighter bones and a more flexible brain.
They concluded that the findings could help scientists better understand joint diseases and potentially identify new approaches to their prevention and treatment. ■

====================================================================================================

Study led by researchers at University of Sheffield reveals cancer survival mechanism
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
03:51:58 CST
04:51:58 KST

LONDON, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Researchers have identified a mechanism that allows some aggressive cancers to survive when deprived of their normal energy supply, a finding that could offer a new way to slow tumor growth and improve the effectiveness of existing treatments, the University of Sheffield said on Wednesday.
The study, led by researchers at the university and published in the journal PLOS Biology, focused on aggressive breast and pancreatic cancers surrounded by dense, scar-like tissue known as the extracellular matrix.
According to the university, the extracellular matrix can account for up to 90 percent of the mass of some breast and pancreatic tumors. While the dense tissue restricts blood supply and the delivery of nutrients, cancer cells can adapt by using type I collagen, a major component of the matrix, to help them survive.
The researchers found that when levels of glucose, normally a major energy source for cells, fall, collagen activates signals that enable cancer cells to switch their source of fuel and take up essential amino acids needed for growth and survival.
The process depends on a transporter protein known as LAT1, which helps move amino acids into cancer cells. Laboratory experiments using cellular models showed that blocking LAT1 while disrupting the interaction between cancer cells and collagen deprived the cells of vital nutrients, according to the university.
Dr. Elena Rainero, senior lecturer at the University of Sheffield and lead author of the study, said cancer cells can adapt rapidly, which means a single treatment often fails to eliminate a tumor completely.
"If we can block this collagen-driven survival mechanism, we could slow the growth and spread of cancer cells while making them more sensitive to existing treatments like chemotherapy," Rainero said.
She said such an approach could potentially allow clinicians to use lower treatment doses, reducing severe side effects while improving treatment effectiveness.
The researchers said the findings could offer a promising target for future cancer therapies. ■

Instead, speaking to reporters on September 8 in Florida before traveling to Latin America, Rubio refrained from outright criticism of the decision or any particular country.
"Obviously, we’re not going to do what the UK did. We saw their announcement today, but I don’t have any comment on it right now," Rubio said.
A widening divide between the White House and Trump's senior diplomats in Israel
The episode illustrates a widening divide between the White House and Trump's senior diplomats in Israel about how best to respond to the expansion of Israeli settlements under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing government.
It also highlights a growing ideological split within the American right over support for Israel, with polling showing younger Republicans holding an increasingly unfavorable opinion of Washington's closest Middle East ally.
US President Donald Trump earlier this year expressed his opposition to settlement expansion, a growing source of friction with Israel's Arab neighbors, but his administration has put little pressure on Israel to change its policy.

The US embassy referred questions, including requests for comment from Huckabee and Milstein, to the State Department.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
US public support for Israel questioned
US public backing for Israel has fallen since the Israel-Hamas War began in 2023, particularly among Democrats. A June Quinnipiac University poll found 48% of voters and 66% of Democrats believe the United States is too supportive of Israel, up from 16% and 20% when the question was first asked in 2017.
While large majorities of Republicans aged 50 and older view Israel positively, younger conservative Americans have grown more critical, a Pew Research Center poll from late March showed. Some 57% of Republicans aged 18-49 have an unfavorable opinion of Israel, up from 50% a year previously.
In December last year, Trump said that he and Netanyahu, whose government has overseen a rapid expansion of settlements, did not fully agree on the West Bank following a meeting with the Israeli leader. That September, Trump said he would not allow Israel to annex the territory.
Violence by Jewish settlers against Palestinians in the territory has risen sharply this year, some of them emboldened by support from Netanyahu's right-wing government, which includes ministers who are themselves settlers.
Huckabee has publicly condemned the violence and called for perpetrators to be prosecuted. He has also said violent settlers were a minority and do not represent the wider settler community.

Sa’ar rejects claim of global consensus against Israel, says UN majority cannot dictate policy
