Araghchi holds extensive diplomatic talks on UNGA sidelines
TEHRAN- Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called on the international community to hold the United States accountable for its violations of international law and war crimes against Iran, warning that indifference to genocide will have far-reaching consequences for all countries.
Speaking during a meeting with Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis in New York, Araghchi outlined Iran's positions on regional developments following US-Israeli aggression against Iran, as well as the continuation of interventionist measures, a naval blockade, and economic warfare against the Iranian people.
He stressed the responsibility of all countries to safeguard the UN Charter and international law, particularly the prohibition on the use of force, and referred to war crimes committed by the US and the Israeli regime against Iran during their military aggression over the past year and a half.
Referring to Washington's repeated breaches of commitments, including its violation of the Islamabad memorandum of understanding, Araghchi said the international community has a responsibility to hold the United States accountable for the consequences of its unlawful actions.
He further pointed to grave violations of international humanitarian law and multiple war crimes, including the tragedies in Minab and Lamerd, stressing the duty of all states party to the 1949 Geneva Conventions to investigate and punish perpetrators.
Araghchi warned that indifference toward genocide and war crimes, along with continued impunity for perpetrators, would have extremely far-reaching consequences for the entire world.
Restoring Hormuz strait security requires end to US' destabilizing actions
Insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz is solely the result of US and Israeli aggression, Araghchi said, stressing that restoring security to the strategic waterway hinges on an end to US actions that create insecurity.
During a meeting with Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein, the two diplomats reviewed the progress of Iran-Iraq cooperation in economic, trade, consular, and security affairs, and stressed the need to expand relations in all areas of mutual interest.
They described safeguarding the security of their shared border as highly important, emphasizing the implementation of agreements reached in this regard and the need for effective measures to counter terrorist activities.
Araghchi outlined the latest developments concerning shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, including the understanding reached between Iran and Oman on establishing safe routes for commercial shipping.
He stressed the need for all regional countries to adhere to the principle of good neighborliness, particularly by preventing aggressor parties from using their territories and facilities to prepare for and carry out illegal and aggressive actions against Iran.
Europeans criticized for double standards over Iran, regional developments
Araghchi criticized European double standards toward regional developments, particularly their response to US and Israeli acts of aggression against Iran.
During a meeting with Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen, Araghchi strongly criticized European countries' "double standards" toward regional developments, particularly their silence and leniency regarding the "aggressive actions and crimes" committed by the US and the Zionist regime against Iran.
He said European countries cannot claim to support the rule of law and human rights while remaining indifferent to, or even supporting, overt US and Israeli military aggression against Iran.
The Iranian foreign minister also recalled Iran's responsible approach to diplomacy aimed at removing US pretexts over the nuclear issue, saying Washington's repeated breaches of commitments and its "warmongering" were the main causes of the current insecurity in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz.
He stressed that the only way to restore peace and stability in the region is to halt the US' illegal and aggressive actions and respect Iran's rights and national interests.
Iran warns Italy over US bases, complicity in aggression
Araghchi warned Italy that hosting US military bases and assisting in preparations for or implementation of acts of aggression against Iran would be considered complicity in aggression and could entail international responsibility for the host states.
During a meeting with Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, Araghchi described the decision by some European countries, including Italy, to host US military bases and any cooperation in preparing for or carrying out acts of aggression against Iran as "very dangerous" and tantamount to complicity in aggression.
Pointing to the continued aggressive and destabilizing actions by the US and the Israeli regime in West Asia, Araghchi said rising fuel and commodity prices in global markets were a direct consequence of the US-Israeli military aggression against Iran.
He stressed that any responsible country should hold the US accountable for continuing its adventurist actions and threatening commercial shipping in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz.
On human rights, particularly women's rights, Araghchi criticized the double standards of some European countries, saying those who remained silent over the most blatant human rights violations by the Israeli occupying regime in the occupied Palestinian territories have no standing to lecture others on human rights.
Belarus resolved to strengthen strategic ties with Iran
Belarusian Foreign Minister Maxim Ryzhenkov reaffirmed his country's determination to strengthen brotherly and strategic relations with Iran during a meeting with Araghchi.
Ryzhenkov expressed satisfaction with the meeting and described safeguarding the UN Charter and the national sovereignty of countries as a fundamental principle governing international relations.
For his part, Araghchi pointed to the excellent and growing relations between the two countries and stressed Iran's determination to fully implement previous agreements and deepen bilateral and multilateral cooperation.
Strongly criticizing the unilateral and illegal Western sanctions imposed on independent countries, Araghchi underscored the need for Iran and Belarus to enhance coordination and jointly resist political and economic pressure stemming from unilateralism.
Iran, Azerbaijan discuss South Caucasus security
Araghchi and his Azerbaijani counterpart Jeyhun Bayramov discussed security and cooperation in the South Caucasus, as well as bilateral ties and regional and international developments.
The two sides reviewed agreements and understandings reached between the two countries in various economic and trade fields, as well as issues related to security and cooperation in the South Caucasus.
They also stressed the two countries' determination to implement the agreements reached and strengthen cooperation and coordination in line with the interests of the two nations.
Araghchi also explained the latest developments in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, stressing Iran's determination to defend its sovereignty and national interests against illegal US and Israeli aggression and pressure.
Iran urges EU to avoid appeasement of US bullying
Araghchi urged the European Union to play a constructive role in international developments and avoid double standards and appeasement in the face of US bullying, warning that such approaches undermine international peace and security.
During a meeting with EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, Araghchi highlighted Iran's practical commitment to diplomacy as a means of achieving peace and security in the region, saying repeated US breaches of commitments have been the sole factor disrupting diplomatic processes.
He said the European Union had unfortunately, on numerous occasions, chosen appeasement in the face of US bullying instead of adhering to principles it claims to uphold, including the rule of law and respect for human rights.
Iran calls French positions on regional developments unacceptable
Araghchi slammed France's "unacceptable" positions on regional developments, particularly the US and Israeli military aggression against Iran.
During a meeting with French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot, Araghchi criticized France's "interventionist" positions toward Iran and stressed the need for the French Embassy in Tehran to respect Iran's domestic laws and regulations.
He decried France's double standards on human rights, saying France cannot claim to be concerned about human rights while remaining silent over "crimes against humanity" committed by the US and the Zionist regime against the Iranian people, including the killing of Iranian women and
children, while also cooperating in the implementation of illegal US sanctions against the Iranian people.
Araghchi stressed that Iran seeks relations based on mutual respect and interests with all countries, including France, but will act firmly and decisively in defending its interests and national objectives.
Iran blames Hormuz insecurity on US-Israeli aggression
Araghchi described insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz and disruption to maritime shipping as the direct result of US and Israeli aggression.
During a meeting with Austrian Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger, Araghchi stressed that restoring security for maritime navigation in the region requires an end to destabilizing actions and US "economic terrorism."
He also pointed to the continued genocide of Palestinians and the Israeli regime's flagrant violations of international law, as well as the regime's continued aggression against Lebanon and other countries in the region.
Araghchi stressed the responsibility of all countries, particularly the European states, to halt any support for the occupying Zionist regime and bring an end to its impunity.

Turkey Develops Dron Kalkanı Turret Armed with 12-Gauge Shotguns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:24:02 UTC
02:24:02 KST

The Turkish company Turaç has developed the Dron Kalkanı (Drone Shield) turret, designed to protect military equipment and facilities from FPV drones.
Fatih Altunbaş, CEO of Turaç, spoke about this to the Anadolu news agency. According to the developers, the system scans the area using various sensors and detects and tracks targets at a distance of 600–800 meters.
The turret is based on a twin mount of two Derya 12-gauge semi-automatic shotguns, which, at a distance of 150 meters, fire simultaneously to create a dense cloud of projectiles to neutralize UAVs.
The system can be integrated onto wheeled and tracked armored vehicles, ships, ground-based robotic systems, and fixed installations. Thanks to its low power consumption, the module operates from a standard onboard power supply and does not require the installation of additional generators.
The Derya MAX (or MK-12) is a semi-automatic 12-gauge smoothbore shotgun based on the AR-15 platform with a gas-operated action. The weapon is equipped with detachable box magazines holding 2 to 10 rounds (higher-capacity drum magazines are also available) and features barrels that are primarily 50 cm long with muzzle attachments.
As a reminder, in May, Italy’s Beretta Defense Technologies unveiled a similar remotely controlled anti-drone turret, the LIVET.
In addition, Ukrainian Armor has developed an unmanned module that automatically detects, tracks, and destroys drones using shotguns.

France, UK, Denmark urge Russia at UN Security Council to end war on Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:21:27 UTC
02:21:27 KST

Merve Gül Aydoğan Ağlarcı
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
The foreign ministers of France, the UK and Denmark on Wednesday urged Russia to end its war on Ukraine, warning that Russian sabotage, cyberattacks and airspace violations are creating wider security risks across Europe.
Speaking at a high-level UN Security Council session on Ukraine, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot, who is chairing the council this month, said Russia is “using winter, the cold, and denial of the most basic needs as weapons of mass destruction, targeting civilian population.”
He said Russia is “lashing out at Europe in its entirety” through alleged targeted killings, sabotage, cyberattacks and disinformation, adding that repeated airspace violations involving Romania, Poland, Moldova, Lithuania, Estonia, Latvia and Finland mean “there is not one state who is not now ill at ease” because of Russian aggression. He also pointed to a recent incident in Leipzig, Germany.
Barrot warned that Russia, “trampled upon by a permanent member of the Security Council,” is weakening the UN’s authority, and said Ukraine “is ready for peace” but has met only “Moscow’s stubbornness.”
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said sham elections in occupied Ukrainian territory are “a blatant violation of Ukraine’s sovereignty,” warning that “we cannot accept the changing of borders by force.”
He said NATO “is and always will be a defensive alliance” and pledged to “continue to call out and act against Russia’s hostile activity.” Miliband, whose parents fled Poland and Belgium as refugees during World War II, said “it is time ministers told President Putin the truth,” adding that “the Russian people can feel” Russia is “failing” in the war.
Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said “if Russia stops fighting, the war ends. If Ukraine stops fighting, it will be the very end of Ukraine.”
He said Denmark “strongly condemns all attacks in violation of international humanitarian law,” warning of a “dangerous spiral of escalation” as civilian infrastructure and energy facilities come under attack ahead of winter.
Rasmussen said attacks on Ukrainian ports and grain infrastructure “threatened trade, livelihoods, and global food supplies,” and cited Germany’s attribution of a “failed hybrid attack” at Leipzig-Halle airport to Russia as one of several “reckless and dangerous acts” affecting Europe.
He said Denmark “will continue to provide financial and security assistance” to Ukraine, pledging support for reconstruction, humanitarian aid and increased pressure on Russia “through tough EU sanctions.”
All three foreign ministers linked the war in Ukraine to broader security risks across Europe and called for sustained diplomatic and economic pressure on Moscow to bring it to the negotiating table.

Russian Insurgents Blow Up Tank Cars Carrying Over 10,000 Metric Tons of Oil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:19:12 UTC
02:19:12 KST

An insurgent movement in Russia carried out attacks on railroad tank cars, destroying over 10,000 metric tons of oil.
The rebels carried out Operation Barrel with the support of the Freedom of Russia Legion.
Following precision strikes on oil refineries and ports, the Kremlin attempted to hide the crude oil by shifting the responsibility for its storage and logistics to the Russian railway network.
The aim of the strategy was simple: by distributing reserves across the country in tank cars, ensure the oil’s preservation until it could be exported at the highest possible price per barrel.
The insurgents infiltrated the relevant agencies to obtain the necessary information.
They then conducted on-site reconnaissance, intercepted train schedules, and analyzed vulnerabilities and escape routes.
As a result of explosions and arson, over 10,000 metric tons of crude oil were destroyed.
Operations at a number of key rail junctions were also halted—a multi-day “traffic jam” on the tracks blocked supplies and paralyzed key logistics corridors.
Within the oil supply chain, rail logistics has traditionally been one of the most efficient and practical modes of transportation.
Railways crisscross the entire country for thousands of kilometers—this is one of the key advantages of this mode of transport.
“Over the past six months, we have destroyed dozens of locomotives and hundreds of other railway infrastructure facilities,” noted a member of the insurgent movement.
Without these locomotives and rail junctions, the regime has faced difficulties delivering fuel across the country.
“Destroying locomotives is just part of our systematic work,” added a member of the insurgent movement.
The enemy is forced to keep large quantities of petroleum products on the railroad tracks because it cannot ship them to refineries. This, in turn, creates an even greater logistical bottleneck along this route.
Faced with a shortage of locomotives and threats on the roads, the regime began using tank cars en masse as mobile storage units, periodically moving them between stations within the region.
“Operation Barrel has dealt a blow to Putin and the oligarchs that will have catastrophic consequences over time. As a result of the tanker explosions, the regime has lost over 10,000 metric tons of oil. Together with the cost of the tankers, that amounts to over $10 million,” said a member of the insurgent movement.
In addition to the direct damage to the war economy, the attack forced the Kremlin to spend additional resources on guarding such facilities.
In June, the insurgent movement in Russia helped Ukraine strike factories near Orenburg.

Netherlands to return to Eurovision after 2026 boycott
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:17:47 BST
02:17:47 KST

Netherlands to return to Eurovision after 2026 boycott
- Published
The Netherlands will return to the Eurovision Song Contest next year despite a boycott by the broadcaster that was previously in charge of the country's participation.
Dutch network Avrotros withdrew in 2026 and said it would also not take part in 2027 because the competition could "no longer be considered neutral" given divisions over Israel's involvement and the Gaza war.
The NPO, which oversees public broadcasting in the country, has now stepped in, saying coverage of the contest will be provided by broadcasting organisation NOS, while an independent panel will select the Dutch participant.
Jurre Bosman, NPO's director of media, said: "It is important that, as a public broadcaster, we remain part of this unifying European event at this moment in particular."
Israel's participation in the contest has become highly controversial, and five countries, including the Netherlands, boycotted this year's event.
Eurovision organiser the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) has subsequently announced a number of changes, including to exclude any country involved in an armed conflict from hosting the competition.
That means that, although Israel can still compete, the EBU would ask another country to host if it won.
The EBU has also proposed changes to to the voting, saying politically motivated voting has become "persistent" and is widely seen as "deeply worrying".
However, Avrotros said those changes did "not provide sufficient confidence that the independent and neutral character of the Eurovision Song Contest has been restored".
In a statement on Wednesday, the NPO said the EBU has "taken significant steps regarding the rules" of the contest, and that the Netherlands will return.
Acknowledging that the contest provokes "mixed feelings" in the Netherlands, the NPO said it had "explicitly asked the EBU to once again make the unifying character of the festival an important part of the event".
The NPO also said the Dutch entrant would be chosen by "an independent team of experts" who would "carefully guide the process surrounding the act".
Eurovision director Martin Green said in a statement: "We are delighted to welcome the Netherlands back to the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027.
"We value the constructive conversations we have had with NPO and look forward to working together to reinforce the Contest as a place that truly reflects the spirit of 'United By Music'."
Iceland, Spain, Ireland and Slovenia all pulled out of the 2026 contest in addition to the Netherlands.
The 2027 contest will take place on 14 May in Burgas, after Bulgarian singer Dara won this year's contest with Bangaranga.
Last month, it was announced that Canada will enter the contest for the first time.

Emine Erdogan calls for new systems to address environmental crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:17:21 UTC
02:17:21 KST

Türkiye's First Lady and chair of the UN Advisory Board of Eminent Persons on Zero Waste, Emine Erdogan, has highlighted the global environmental crisis in a video message at the opening of the Sustainable Development Impact Meetings, organised by the World Economic Forum in New York.
“Our planet resembles a ravaged mine, the oceans cannot breathe, and cities are struggling to cope with their waste. Therefore, a circular economy is not one of the options before us; it is a necessity for our future,” she said in the video on Wednesday.
The first lady expressed her regret at being unable to attend the gathering and said that current production and consumption systems are not capable of carrying humanity into the future.
'We see zero waste as a key'
Emine Erdogan noted that achieving a transition to a circular economy means strengthening sustainable development, expanding recycling, improving waste management and turning towards renewable energy sources.
“We see zero waste as a key to achieving all of this. Because zero waste is not merely a waste-management approach that individuals incorporate into their daily lives. Zero waste means redesigning our production and consumption models and redefining our relationship with nature,” she said, stressing the need for new economic models to transform the entire system from production to consumption.
“We must establish an order in which people who adopt zero waste in their lives are supported by the right systems, and in which the production of durable, repairable products whose materials can be reused is encouraged,” she added.
“Indeed, we still have a window of opportunity to combat the climate crisis and build a sustainable future. I believe that Zero Waste, which we launched in Türkiye in 2017 and which has now become a global movement, is a transformative force in making the most of this opportunity,” she said.
“With the right steps we take together, I hope we can make a new beginning — one in which we protect our resources rather than consume them, and create value instead of waste,” she added.
Thanking the World Economic Forum for organising the meeting, Emine Erdogan expressed her hope of meeting the participants at COP31, which will be held in Antalya.

Israel blocks 900 wheelchairs for Gaza's child amputees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:16:44 UTC
02:16:44 KST

Breadcrumb
'Calculated effort to destroy Palestinian life': Israel blocks 900 wheelchairs for amputee children in Gaza
More than 900 wheelchairs donated by two Australian charities for wounded and amputee children in Gaza have been blocked by Israel from entering the enclave, with the shipments stuck in storage in Jordan since 2025 and staff from the charities calling on Australian members of parliament to intervene in the matter.
The charity Kids on Wheels Alliance sent two shipments that arrived in Jordan in February 2025, while another shipment from Wheelchairs for Kids arrived in October that year.
The wheelchairs remain at a storage facility managed by the Jordan Hashemite Charity Organisation (JHCO), which said COGAT, the Israeli defence ministry body that oversees the entry of humanitarian aid into Gaza, had blocked their delivery.
Shaoquett Moselmane, the chair of the Kids on Wheels Alliance, told The New Arab that they have been raising funds for wheelchairs for over 15 years, with enormous efforts from local communities in covering the cost of the wheelchairs intended for Gaza. He added that the Palestine Australia New Zealand Medical Association (PANZMA) assisted with the shipping costs and delivery; however, Israel gave no reason, and "no security issues were raised," despite reports.
"In any event, there could be no legitimate reason to hold up wheelchairs for children with special needs. No reason of any nature given as they are just wheelchairs for the thousands of amputee children and the thousands more in need of support," he said.
"We have sought representations from Australian members of parliament at both house of reps and senate seeking their help to make high-level representations and doing what we can to alert people of this inhumane behaviour in the hope that Israeli authorities grant consent to deliver the wheelchairs," he continued.
Moselmane said a community meeting was held on Wednesday to discuss further follow-up action, with many suggesting to take the issue up with local federal members, the Australian government, and the Jordanian government, as well as other authorities in the hope that enough pressure is exerted to move those containers to Gaza.
According to Moselmane, Israel blocking the shipment will affect over 11,000 children in Gaza.
"The pain and suffering of the Palestinian people can not be ignored. Our humanity is at stake if people around the world don’t stand up and rally against the injustices perpetrated on the people of Palestine. They’ve suffered for over seven decades; this indignity of occupation and oppression must cease. For a peaceful future for all, humanity in Palestine must prevail".
Mohammad Helmy, a Melbourne-based pro-Palestine activist, told The New Arab that Israel's refusal to allow the wheelchairs into Gaza was intentional, accusing authorities of seeking to make life in the devastated enclave "impossible".
“Israel’s blockade of over 900 custom, all-terrain wheelchairs—hand-built by Australian volunteers to help amputee children navigate destroyed streets—exposes a calculated effort to destroy Palestinian life and render life in Gaza impossible,” Helmy said.
“By undertaking non-stop bombardment and then systematically denying the basic medical aid needed to survive it, Israel is actively executing an ongoing genocide. Trapping mobility gear in warehouses while children crawl through rubble is not a security measure—it is a deliberate policy of collective punishment and total destruction directed against the Palestinian people,” he continued.
The restrictions come as the UN has said Gaza has the largest group of child amputees in modern history as a result of Israel's attacks on the territory.
Greg Hebble, the CEO of Wheelchairs for Kids Australia, said their team is currently trying to figure out next steps, with the hopes that the wheelchairs reach people with difficult mobility challenges.
"We are currently working with our logistics, humanitarian and distribution partners to better understand the situation and explore all available avenues to facilitate the delivery of the wheelchairs. This includes seeking clarification regarding the reasons for the blockage and whether alternative pathways or approvals may be available," he said.
"Should the shipment ultimately be denied entry, it would be deeply disappointing, particularly for the individuals who have been identified as recipients. We will continue to explore any lawful and practical options available to ensure this assistance reaches those most in need," he continued.
Hebble said that aside from the shipment leaving thousands without independence, social participation and access to essential services, a great deal of financial and logistical resources were put into making the delivery.
"Significant financial resources have been invested, along with countless hours of planning, coordination, sourcing, transportation and compliance work to ensure the Wheelchairs could reach those in need. The cost to our organisation to supply this shipment of Wheelchairs is more than $100k AUS," he said.
"Our message is a simple humanitarian one, people living with disability should never be forgotten. Regardless of geography, politics, or conflict, vulnerable children and civilians deserve access to equipment that supports their mobility, wellbeing and dignity," he continued.
Status 'pending'
The JHCO said it filed an application in late February 2025 for the Kids on Wheels Alliance shipments to enter Gaza as part of an aid convoy, but COGAT rejected the request. According to reports, Israeli authorities said medical equipment and medicines had not been approved for inclusion in that convoy.
JHCO said its application has since remained "pending", with no further updates, leaving the organisation unable to submit a new application for the other shipments.
COGAT has not responded to media requests concerning the Australian donations. However, the Israeli agency has previously said that thousands of wheelchairs have been allowed into Gaza.
The wheelchairs donated by Wheelchairs for Kids are designed to withstand difficult terrain, including the rubble that now covers large parts of Gaza, and can be adjusted as children grow older and taller.
"The sooner they come out of there and get to the kids, the better, and the little kids can get a much better life," Brother Olly Pickett, co-founder of the charity, said in a statement.
"I think there's a lot of children waiting for them who have had amputations, and so they won't be able to walk around or get around. Once they get a wheelchair, they can get out and about, which would be wonderful,” he added.
Australian media reports, citing an informed source outside the region, said Israeli authorities had denied the wheelchairs entry because they considered them potentially "dual use", a classification applied to goods that authorities say could also have military applications.
Israeli rights group Gisha earlier this year published a report saying Israel had arbitrarily classified essential items, household goods and medical supplies as "dual use" since the start of the war on Gaza.
Items subjected to such restrictions have included flashlights, sleeping bags and portable toilets.
Rights groups have warned that restrictions on such goods have serious consequences for civilians, including tens of thousands of Palestinians attempting to recover from injuries and rebuild their lives amid the widespread destruction in Gaza.

Fifty-one countries backed Ukraine in a joint statement on Wednesday, urging the Kremlin to agree to a full ceasefire and enter meaningful negotiations as large-scale Russian attacks on Ukraine continue in the fifth year of war.
The statement was delivered during the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York by Kaja Kallas, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, alongside Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, according to Democrata.

Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed the decision in a statement on Telegram.

Call for civilian returns
Russia was also urged to ensure the immediate, safe and unconditional return of Ukrainian civilians who have been illegally detained, forcibly transferred or deported.
Children have been particularly singled out.
Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale war in February 2022, Russian forces have killed at least 707 Ukrainian children and injured 2,548 others, while more than 2,318 minors remain officially classified as missing, according to official statistics released by Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets.
Russian Drone Attacks Kill 2, Injure 62 as Explosions Rock Ukraine Nationwide
The number of casualties and unlawful adoptions is believed to be much higher than the released information shows. However, verifying the true extent remains impossible due to lack of access to Russian-occupied territories.

Black Sea crisis continues
The 51 states accused Russia of trying to impede Ukrainian grain exports, warning again that continued disruption in the Black Sea threatens global food security.
They endorsed efforts to safeguard freedom of navigation and protect commercial maritime traffic and infrastructure tied to shipping routes.
The concern follows months of intense reciprocal strikes between the two countries at war.
Civilian vessels, export terminals and other shipping infrastructure have been targeted, constraining shipments of grain, oil, fertilizers and other crucial commodities, creating a large disruption to the Black Sea trade.
Speaking during the sixth International Crimea Platform Summit earlier on Wednesday, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine was ready to support a safe-passage regime for vessels in the Black Sea, provided Russia took genuine and reciprocal steps toward de-escalation.
On Tuesday, during a meeting with US President Donald Trump, Zelensky offered Russia a truce on energy strikes.

Badrinath Dham sees record 17.79 lakh pilgrims so far this year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:09:14 UTC
02:09:14 KST

People visit the Badrinath Temple amid the ongoing 'Char Dham Yatra', in Chamoli district, Uttarakhand. (PTI Photo)
More than 17.79 lakh pilgrims have visited Badrinath Dham so far this year, surpassing the shrine's previous annual footfall record.A total of 1,779,805 devotees had visited the shrine as of September 22, 153 days after the Badrinath Yatra began on April 23. The shrine's portals are expected to remain open for another one-and-a-half to nearly two months before closing for the winter.The latest footfall has exceeded the previous record of 1,780,429 visitors recorded in 2023 when comparing the current figure with the year-to-date data provided by the government. The 2025 figure stood at 1,778,298.
According to the Tourism Department data, 695,332 pilgrims visited Badrinath in 2000, the year Uttarakhand was established.The number rose to 768,107 in 2007 and crossed the one-million mark in 2008 and 2010.The 2014 disaster led to a sharp decline in pilgrimage numbers, with footfall falling to 159,575.Visitor numbers subsequently recovered, with 1,048,051 pilgrims visiting Badrinath in 2018 and 1,244,993 in 2019. The Covid-19 pandemic again resulted in a steep decline, with 155,055 visitors recorded in 2020 and 199,409 in 2021.Footfall increased significantly from 2022 onwards. The shrine recorded 1,763,578 visitors in 2022, followed by 1,780,429 in 2023, 1,774,264 in 2024 and 1,778,298 in 2025.
On September 22, 6,685 devotees visited Badrinath, according to the data released by the state government.
Government focuses on pilgrim facilities
The government said arrangements for pilgrims had been strengthened in view of the increased footfall during the second phase of the Char Dham Yatra, including health and safety measures and facilities at the shrines and along the pilgrimage route.
“Keeping in view the increasing number of pilgrims during the second phase of the Char Dham Yatra, special focus has been placed on strengthening pilgrim facilities at the dhams and en-route halts. Health and safety arrangements have also been strengthened. Under the guidance of Hon’ble Prime Minister Narendra Modi ji, work is being carried out at a rapid pace to give Shri Badrinath Dham a grand, divine and well-organised form in keeping with its religious and mythological significance. This will provide better facilities and a more comfortable experience to devotees”, said Uttarakhand chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami.

The Alliance aims to transform global solidarity into coordinated, concrete, and long-term support for Ukraine’s recovery.
The inaugural meeting of the Diaspora Alliance for Ukraine’s Recovery took place on March 2, 2026. Drone and suspected explosives found near Bundeswehr base are  possibly linked to Leipzig airport incident
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:08:08 UTC
02:08:08 KST

A suspicious substance that investigators believe is likely explosive material was found just a few meters from the wreckage of a drone that was discovered near the Bundeswehr’s Wunstorf air base in Lower Saxony late last week. As Süddeutsche Zeitung, NDR, and WDR report, Germany’s Federal Prosecutor General’s Office and the Federal Criminal Police Office are examining a possible link between the find and the early August attempted act of sabotage at Leipzig/Halle Airport, which the German government has blamed on Russia.
In the latest incident, a farmer discovered a drone broken into several pieces near the Wunstorf military airfield. A few days later, police discovered a suspicious substance just a few meters away. According to German journalists, investigators are operating on the assumption that they are dealing with explosive material; however, forensic analysis of the substance has not yet been completed.
The drone found at Wunstorf is similar in design to those used in the attempted attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport. At least one of its components was made on a 3D printer. Investigators also suspect that the drone may have been lying near the base for an extended period of time — potentially as long as two years.
Wunstorf is a key base for Germany’s military transport aviation, hosting the 62nd Air Transport Wing and all 53 of the German Air Force’s Airbus A400M aircraft, according to Bundeswehr data. Germany received its 53rd and final A400M in April 2026. The Bundeswehr itself describes the A400M as the backbone of Germany’s military transport aviation.
It remains to be determined whether the two drone incidents are connected. Overnight into Aug. 5, a drone carrying explosives and a detonator was discovered in Leipzig. Investigators believe the target may have been Ukrainian cargo planes. In early September, the German government officially blamed Russia for the attempted attack, citing the results of a police investigation and intelligence data. Moscow denied any involvement.
Investigators have identified two suspects in the Leipzig case. One of them, Oleg L., a Latvian citizen with a Russian passport, had maintained contact with Russian military intelligence for years, including with Colonel Denis Smolyaninov of the Main Intelligence Directorate (GRU), according to reporting by Süddeutsche Zeitung, NDR, and WDR.
A spokesperson for the Federal Prosecutor General’s Office declined to comment on details of the investigation into the more recent Wunstorf incident. Nevertheless, the drone discovered there was discussed on Tuesday at the weekly meeting of the heads of Germany’s security services at the Federal Chancellery.

Ukraine Turns to Formula 1 Engineers for Its Next Generation of MAGURA Naval Drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:07:15 UTC
02:07:15 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Turns to Formula 1 Engineers for Its Next Generation of MAGURA Naval Drones
Ukraine’s defense technology company UFORCE, whose portfolio includes the MAGURA naval drone, is recruiting engineers with Formula 1 experience to apply technologies developed for high-performance motorsport to Ukrainian unmanned systems.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to an interview with UFORCE CEO Oleg Rogynskyy published by DOU on September 23, specialists from Formula 1 have increasingly joined the company, bringing expertise in composites, carbon fiber, sensors, engine optimization, and reducing weight without sacrificing reliability.
“Formula 1 specialists have started coming to us en masse,” Rogynskyy said.
He said their experience is particularly relevant because Formula 1 engineers routinely work to remove unnecessary weight while maintaining reliability and rapidly redesigning systems—a combination that translates directly into requirements for unmanned platforms.
UFORCE pairs the Formula 1 specialists with Ukrainian engineers to work jointly on development projects. According to Rogynskyy, the company is particularly interested in their ability to optimize electric and conventional engines, work with advanced composite materials, and balance weight against energy consumption, computing power, and operational range.
The recruitment effort comes as UFORCE expands its engineering operations both inside and outside Ukraine. The company employs more than 1,000 people and operates R&D capabilities in several countries, while most of its workforce remains in Ukraine, Rogynskyy told DOU.
UFORCE has R&D operations in the UK and the US, where it has announced cooperation with ReconCraft on development and manufacturing. Rogynskyy said overseas engineering teams allow the company to develop systems for operating conditions that differ significantly from those in Ukraine, including larger waves in the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.
Such requirements involve larger vessels, Kevlar reinforcement, and different approaches to autonomy, with some of the resulting engineering methods later applicable to systems developed for Ukraine.
The company is also looking beyond motorsport for specialists. Rogynskyy said UFORCE recently searched for Ukrainian engineers working at major Western technology and defense companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Anduril, and Palantir.
The company says its overseas structure allows Ukrainian specialists abroad to contribute to defense projects without relocating their families to Ukraine.
Software is a central part of UFORCE’s development strategy. According to Rogynskyy, the company’s different unmanned platforms operate on a common software layer, requiring engineers to integrate hardware, autonomy, sensors, and computing systems across multiple types of equipment.
UFORCE’s portfolio includes the MAGURA naval drone family, Nemesis and R18 aerial systems, and ground robotic platforms. DOU reported that the company’s systems have collectively conducted more than 150,000 combat missions, while MAGURA naval drones have damaged or destroyed more than a dozen Russian vessels.
Rogynskyy said the company ultimately intends to integrate unmanned platforms operating on land, at sea, in the air, and in counter-drone roles through a common software architecture.
MAGURA naval drones have also been adapted for air-defense missions. In May 2025, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence said MAGURA V7 drones armed with US-made AIM-9 Sidewinder missiles shot down two Russian Su-30SM fighter jets over the Black Sea—the first documented case of a sea drone downing manned combat aircraft with such weapons.

Russia’s industrial output flat in January-August 2026 — statistics service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:07:11 UTC
02:07:11 KST

MOSCOW, September 23. /TASS/. Russia's industrial output remained unchanged year-on-year in the first eight months of 2026, while declining by 0.6% in August compared to the same month last year, according to the federal statistics service (Rosstat).
Month-on-month, industrial production also fell by 0.6% in August.
In the reporting period, mining output fell by 1% year-on-year, while manufacturing grew by 0.4%. Utilities (electricity, gas, and steam supply) rose by 0.5%, whereas the water supply, sewerage, and waste management sector saw a 2% decline.
In January-August 2026, the highest year-on-year growth rates were recorded in the manufacture of other transport equipment, including aircraft and shipbuilding (+18.6%); pharmaceuticals and medical/veterinary supplies (+11.5%); fabricated metal products, except machinery and equipment (+11%); computer, electronic, and optical products (+4.8%); motor vehicles, trailers, and semi-trailers (+4.7%); metal ore mining (+4.1%); other finished products (+2.6%); coal mining (+1.6%); furniture (+1.3%); food products (+0.7%); leather and leather products (+0.4%); and rubber and plastic products (+0.3%).
At the same time, output contracted in the following sectors: coke and refined petroleum products (-10.3%); paper (-8.2%); basic metals (-5.2%); other non-metallic mineral products (construction materials) (-4.7%); beverages (-4.4%); wearing apparel (-4.2%); other mining and quarrying (-3.8%); wood processing and wood/cork products (-3.8%); machinery and equipment not elsewhere classified (-3.4%); chemicals and chemical products (-3%); machinery and equipment repair (-2.7%); textiles (-2.2%); tobacco products (-1.8%); and electrical equipment (-1.5%).

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:06:36 UTC
02:06:36 KST

The man seriously wounded Wednesday in a terrorist ramming attack near the Maccabim checkpoint in the West Bank was identified as Neriya Leiter, the son of Israel’s ambassador to the United States, Yechiel Leiter.
Neriya is also the brother of Major (res.) Moshe Yedidyah Leiter, who was killed fighting in Gaza during the war.
Leiter, a member of a police patrol crew, was seriously wounded when a 29-year-old terrorist drove toward a police vehicle at the Bell checkpoint on Route 443 and struck him, police said.
He was evacuated unconscious to Shaare Zedek Medical Center in Jerusalem, where he underwent lifesaving treatment before being transferred for further examinations while sedated and ventilated.
The terrorist was killed by forces at the scene.
Terrorist accelerated toward police crew
An initial investigation found that the terrorist had been driving from west to east on a road used by Palestinian traffic when he suddenly veered left, accelerated and attempted to hit a police officer and another patrol crew member standing outside their vehicle.
A soldier stationed at the checkpoint moved toward the terrorist and attempted to neutralize him. According to the initial investigation, the terrorist then tried to strike the soldier as well, after which other troops opened fire and killed him.
The vehicle used in the attack had previously been ordered off the road.
Police said: “A short time ago, a terrorist drove his vehicle toward a police patrol car from the Judea and Samaria District and ran over one of the crew members, who was seriously wounded. Forces at the scene killed the terrorist. Additional police forces are on their way to the scene and an investigation has begun.”
Official Palestinian sources identified the terrorist as Mahmoud Sliman, 29, from the village of Beit Ur al-Tahta, west of Ramallah.
Shaare Zedek Medical Center said Leiter arrived at its trauma unit unconscious after suffering severe injuries in the ramming.
“He underwent lifesaving treatment in the trauma room and was transferred in serious condition for further examinations while sedated and ventilated,” the hospital said.
Magen David Adom said it received the first report of the attack at 4:54 p.m. after a man was struck by a vehicle on Route 443, west of Beit Horon.
MDA paramedic Yishai Mor and medics Yechiel Frankenhaus and Avraham Lavi said: “We saw a great deal of commotion and a man in his 40s who was unconscious and suffering from severe injuries after being run over. Together with IDF medical forces, we provided lifesaving treatment and evacuated him by MDA ambulance to the hospital in serious condition.”
IDF deploys 98th Division headquarters
Against the backdrop of the latest attacks, the IDF announced an unusual reinforcement of its forces in the West Bank.
The headquarters of the 98th Division will be deployed in the southern West Bank and take command of the Etzion Brigade, a significant move that military officials said has not been carried out in the area in recent years.
The deployment is intended to strengthen command and control in the sector following the recent attacks.
Wednesday’s ramming came three days after Netanel Shukrun, 48, of Alei Zahav, was killed in a shooting attack at the Ein Raya spring in the Binyamin area.
Shukrun had arrived at the spring with his 16-year-old eldest son. When the terrorist opened fire, Shukrun spotted him and shouted a warning to his son, allowing the teenager to escape unharmed.
Shukrun was shot and later pronounced dead at Beilinson Hospital.
The terrorist in that attack was wounded by an IDF tracker at the scene and captured several hours later at a hospital in Ramallah.

 Johann Georg Hamann (1730 – 1788) lived and worked in Prussia, in the context of the late German Enlightenment. Although he remained outside ‘professional’ philosophical circles, in that he never held a University post, he was respected in his time for his scholarship and breadth of learning. His writings were notorious even in his own time for the challenges they threw down to the reader. These challenges to interpretation and understanding are only heightened today….

Kwaśniewski: Problem of “murdered brothers and sisters” in Ukraine-Russia relations will last for generations
The former Polish leader expressed this view in an interview with Ukrinform.
The war may end, but the level of hatred, pain, tragedy and suffering it has caused will not disappear quickly, he said.
“Even if some wonderful leaders come to power in Russia, the reconciliation process will still take many, many years, because something like this is not easily forgiven,” the Polish politician emphasized.
Kwaśniewski believes that Putin is making a fundamental mistake by calling Ukrainians “brothers and sisters,” as these words contradict Russia’s actions.
“And from the Ukrainian side comes the question: if we are your brothers and sisters, why are you killing us? Why are you taking our children and Russifying them? Why are you setting fire to and attacking our cities and villages? Why are you forcing us to freeze to death by shelling power plants?” Kwaśniewski said.
According to him, such rhetoric is unacceptable to Ukrainians because it does not correspond to the reality of the war.
“If we are brothers and sisters, you have no right to treat us this way. You may love us more or less, but you cannot treat us this way. And this problem of ‘murdered brothers and sisters’ will last for generations. You cannot resolve it with one, two or three gestures. This will remain a difficult issue in Ukrainian-Russian relations for a long time,” the former Polish leader said.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, Russian presidential press secretary Dmitry Peskov said that Moscow sees no conditions for resuming dialogue on ending the war with Ukraine.
U.S. President Donald Trump said in his address to the UN General Assembly that the United States hopes to achieve peace between Ukraine and Russia. “This will happen sooner than expected,” he said.

Nicholas Galanin "interrupts sightline" of Gateway Arch with animal-hide sculpture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Nicholas Galanin "interrupts sightline" of Gateway Arch with animal-hide sculpture
Alaska-based artist Nicholas Galanin has created a metal sculpture resembling a stretched animal hide in front of the St Louis Gateway Arch to challenge "narratives of westward expansion" for art festival Counterpublic.
Land is Never a Gateway (Sightline/Lifeline) is located in front of the Eero Saarinen-designed monument, on a small sidewalk plot. From there, visitors can crouch down and look up at the piece, which is meant to create an optical illusion with the gateway.
When viewed from below, the sculpture resembles animal hide stretched across the arch, transforming it visually from a monument into a hide-processing frame.
Galanin created the piece to challenge the narratives surrounding the ideologies of Westward expansion and Manifest Destiny, movements under which colonial settlers, ranchers and the US government began to migrate past the Mississippi River and into the western United States beginning in the early 1800s.
Eero Saarinen's Gateway Arch, a grand, 630-foot-tall ( 94-metre-tall) swooping structure located on the banks of the Mississippi River, was designed as a monument to Westward expansion and is referred to as "The Gateway to the West" in popular culture.
"The work developed through thinking about the Gateway Arch and the narratives of westward expansion it monumentalizes," Galanin told Dezeen. "I wanted to interrupt that sightline."
"That alignment is both a sightline and a lifeline: a reminder that perspective determines which histories are visible and which have been obscured."
Galanin, who is based in Sitka, Alaska and is of local Lingit and Unangax̂ descent, was informed by visits to St Louis for the piece, where he researched local history as part of the commission for Counterpublic.
Specifically, he examined "the histories held in the land itself" and "Indigenous dispossession, racial capitalism, segregation, and extraction," he told Dezeen.
Processing a hide, or animal skin, is a traditional art practised by many Native American and First Nations people. One step in the lengthy process involves tying the hide to a frame to stretch and cure it, which is pictured in Galanin's sculpture.
Galanin often explores "adaptation, resilience, survival, active cultural amnesia, dream, memory, cultural resurgence, connection to and disconnection from the land" through his work, according to his artist statement.
The third edition of the Counterpublic brings together local and global artists to create commissioned pieces and works around the city.
This year's festival, Coyote Time, invited artists to explore the history, present and future of St Louis, and included installations by artists such as Oglála Lakȟóta artist Kite and Los Angeles-based artist Alice Bucknell among fifty others.
It is led by executive director James McAnally and assistant curator Charlie Farrell, with guest curation by Jordan Carterm, Rapheal Fonesca, Stefanie Hessler, Nora N Khan and Wanda Nandibush.
In 2023, New York artist Torkwase Dyson designed a monolithic black structure that highlighted the ragtime music of American composer Scott Joplin for the event.
The photography is by Jon Gitchoff, courtesy of Counterpublic
Counterpublic runs from 10 September to 12 December. For more architecture, design and art events across the world, visit Dezeen Events Guide.

23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
 Senior officials from the Board of Peace on Wednesday briefed members on progress in the reconstruction and security transition of the Gaza Strip, describing a year of political milestones alongside the scale of work still ahead.
Nickolay Mladenov, the Board's lead envoy for Gaza, said the process had achieved what once seemed unlikely.
"Over the last year, we've had politically significant milestones. The 20-point plan, endorsed by the Security Council Resolution 2803, gave us the framework. Later, the roadmap we negotiated with Hamas, and I want to personally thank our mediating team from Türkiye, Egypt, and Qatar -- achieved what many, if not all, thought was impossible: a commitment to give up weapons," he said.
UN Resolution 2803 stipulated the establishment of a Board of Peace, an International Stabilization Force (ISF), and an administrative committee in the enclave.
"NCAG's (National Committee for the Administration of Gaza) authority in Gaza will grow, with step by step, and it will increase with every weapon that is accounted for, and every Israeli force that moves back to the perimeter. Our aim is to have Gaza under a unified transitional administration of the National Committee. And I want to be very clear that we're not bound by a calendar or dates; we're bound by verification," he said.
Noting that the NCAG is not meant to be permanent, Mladenov said, "It is a bridge. It is a bridge to a reformed Palestinian Authority and to a genuine political horizon for the Palestinians and Israelis to peace."
US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff said the situation had shifted markedly compared with a year earlier.

There is a ceasefire, imperfect as it may be, but it still exists. Humanitarian efforts have achieved historic results with billions of dollars shared, donated, and pledged to meet urgent needs and support the long work of recovery," he said.

Board member and former British Prime Minister Tony Blair called Resolution 2803 a "remarkable achievement," noting it was the fourth Gaza conflict in less than two decades.
"What was remarkable, however, about 2803 was not only that it ended the formal conflict, but that there was unanimity around a coherent architecture for Gaza's future, one which would end the cycle of conflict and not perpetuate it," he said.
Blair said the coming year would mark a shift from planning to execution. "So, for the next year, we move from preparation to implementation," he said, adding that Gaza "must live in peace with its neighbors and with itself."
Ali Shaath, chief commissioner of the NCAG, said his body was working to bring order to a chaotic environment on the ground.
"We have started our planning process because the current situation on the ground is chaotic," he said. "We are building a lean, slim governance body, not over 120,000."
He said recovery plans span dozens of sectors. "The projects we have developed by the early recovery plan has really about 71 programs starting from humanitarian development to infrastructure, economic revivification, and security, as we are following one principle: one authority, one law, and one weapon will not allow things to go back," said Shaath.

A new EU status for Canada? Israel has lived the model for decades - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

Ursula von der Leyen made a striking proposal in Strasbourg on September 16. With Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in attendance, the European Commission president opened the door to Canada becoming what she called the European Union’s first “associate member.”
There is only one problem. The European Union has no such status.
Associate membership does not appear in the EU treaties. There is no established package of rights and obligations attached to it, no predetermined place for an associate member in the Union’s institutions, and no agreement about how much access to the Single Market it would entail. Von der Leyen supplied a name before Europe had designed the institution.
But Brussels does not need to start with a blank sheet of paper.
It should look at Israel.
Canada may indeed become the first country formally granted whatever new status the EU eventually calls “associate membership.” But it would hardly be the first country to inhabit the space between membership and an ordinary third-country relationship. Israel has spent nearly seven decades constructing one version of such a relationship: integration without membership.
The story began almost as soon as the European project itself. In April 1958, only months after the Treaty of Rome entered into force, Israel became the third country, after Greece and the United States, to request the establishment of a diplomatic mission to the European Economic Community in Brussels. Full diplomatic relations followed in February 1959.
And Israel wanted more than trade.
From the beginning, Israeli policymakers sought association with the emerging Community. The Israeli ambition was substantially political as well as economic. Israel eventually accepted agreements that fell short of association, but the larger objective was to secure a recognized place alongside the developing European project.
What Israel was asking Europe in the late 1950s sounds surprisingly familiar in 2026: how close can a non-member country come to the European project without actually joining it?
The answer emerged gradually rather than through grand constitutional design.
Over the decades, Israel and Europe built their ties layer by layer. The 1995 EU-Israel Association Agreement, which entered into force in 2000, established the central institutional framework. The European Neighbourhood Policy later added an Action Plan intended to bring Israel closer to European policies and programs. Cooperation expanded into research and innovation, aviation, pharmaceuticals, education and regulatory cooperation.
Israel's largest trading partner
Today those ties reach remarkably far. The EU is Israel’s largest trading partner, accounting for 31.7% of Israel’s trade in goods in 2025, worth €43.3 billion. Israel participates in Horizon Europe. The EU-Israel aviation agreement connects the Israeli and European aviation markets, while another agreement facilitates trade in pharmaceuticals. Israel also participates in the Pan-Euro-Mediterranean system of rules of origin.
This is not EU membership. But neither is it a conventional relationship between two separate markets.
Nearly two decades ago, Joel Peters and I described the logic behind this arrangement as “integration without membership.” We proposed a Euro-Israeli Partnership that would sit deliberately below full membership while moving beyond the existing Association Agreement. It envisaged deeper political cooperation, Israeli participation in European agencies and programs, gradual convergence with relevant parts of the European acquis, and greater access to the Single Market.
The objective was not to prepare Israel for eventual accession. It was to recognize that European integration need not end at the Union’s formal borders.
Israel is not the only precedent. Switzerland offers the EU’s most developed example of sector-by-sector integration outside membership, with extensive agreements connecting it to large parts of the Single Market and numerous European programs. But Switzerland is geographically and economically embedded in Europe. Israel offers a different lesson: a country outside geographical Europe, with no realistic membership perspective, can nevertheless become deeply connected to selected parts of the European system.
That distinction suddenly matters far beyond Israel.
Carney has ruled out Canadian EU membership. What Ottawa is seeking instead is what he has called a “unique alliance,” extending across trade, defense, technology, energy, and critical minerals. Canada has already moved closer to European defense structures through its participation in the EU’s SAFE defense program.
Here the analogy with Israel has limits. Israel’s integration has developed overwhelmingly through economic, regulatory, scientific, and sectoral cooperation. It does not provide a blueprint for the defense and security dimension that Canada and the EU are now considering. If associate membership eventually encompasses defense procurement and strategic coordination, Brussels will be constructing something new.
But the Israeli experience does offer a model for how such a relationship can be constructed.
Closer ties do not have to be all or nothing. They can proceed sector by sector. Research systems can connect without political membership. Aviation markets can open. Regulations can converge in selected areas. European programs can admit non-member states. New areas of cooperation can be added as political circumstances and mutual interests change. None of that necessarily requires the full institutional rights of an EU member state.
The Israeli case also cautions against romanticizing such arrangements. EU-Israel relations are currently experiencing a period of severe political strain. EU institutions have debated Israel’s compliance with the human-rights provisions of the Association Agreement and possible restrictions on parts of the relationship over the war in Gaza.
That does not invalidate the model. It demonstrates something important about it. Deep institutional ties do not eliminate political disagreement. They create structures within which cooperation, conditionality, and conflict can coexist.
Canada has, therefore, exposed a gap in the EU’s institutional architecture. There are countries that may want much more than a trade agreement without seeking membership. Switzerland demonstrates how far that principle can extend within Europe. Israel demonstrates that it can extend beyond it. Canada may now add a strategic and defense dimension neither model fully provides.
Canada could still become the first country formally designated an EU associate member. But it would enter territory Europe has been exploring for decades.
The Canadian question is how a country can move much closer to the EU without becoming a member of it.
The name may be new. Much of the model is not.
The writer is a senior fellow at the Jewish People Policy Institute (JPPI) and a professor of European studies and international relations in the Department of Politics and Government at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev.

Participants in 6th Intl Crimea Platform summit call for tougher sanctions on Russia, condemn 'elections' in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories, back ICC
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:59:14 EEST
01:59:14 KST

Participants in the sixth summit of the International Crimea Platform, held in New York City on Wednesday, September 23, adopted a joint statement in which, among other things, stated that ending Russia's armed aggression against Ukraine is absolutely essential for restoring Ukraine's territorial integrity and sovereignty and is a decisive step toward restoring international peace and security; they also reaffirmed their support for international judicial and other mechanisms, including the International Criminal Court; called for unity and the strengthening of sanctions against Russia; and condemned any illegal elections in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine.
As stated in the text of the declaration published on the website of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine (MFA), the summit participants reaffirmed once again that the Autonomous Republic of Crimea, the city of Sevastopol, and other parts of Ukraine's territory temporarily occupied by the Russian Federation, were and remain integral parts of Ukraine's sovereign territory, and that their temporary occupation does not create any legal grounds for changing their status.
"We are convinced that the liberation of all temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, including the Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the city of Sevastopol, as well as the restoration of Ukraine's territorial integrity and sovereignty within its internationally recognized borders, including its territorial sea, are crucial steps toward restoring international peace and security, strengthening the international legal order, and ensuring respect for the fundamental norms of international law," the summit participants said.
The statement also states that any illegal "elections" held by the aggressor state in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine cannot alter their status under international law, and that the liberation of Crimea is an integral part of restoring Ukraine's territorial integrity and a necessary prerequisite for restoring a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace and strengthening international security.
According to statement, restrictions on and infringements of freedom of navigation in the Black and Azov Seas, along with Russia's militarization of the Crimean Peninsula and its use as a military base for a full-scale military invasion of Ukraine, pose a threat to regional and global security and undermine international trade, energy, and food security.
Separately, the platform's participants emphasized the need to ensure full accountability for any war crimes and other serious international crimes committed in connection with Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine. "To this end, we support the work of international judicial and other relevant mechanisms, in particular the International Criminal Court, the European Court of Human Rights, and other institutions, to ensure accountability for international crimes and violations of international law, and we also encourage further sustained efforts within the Council of Europe aimed at facilitating the operational activities of the Special Tribunal on the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine and the International Commission for the Settlement of Claims for Ukraine," the document reads.
The summit participants called on the international community to take "decisive, coordinated, and consistent action," in particular, strengthening international sanctions against Russia and enhancing international coordination to prevent the circumvention of sanctions, intensifying efforts to secure the release of all civilians and political prisoners illegally detained and held by the Russian Federation, the return to Ukraine of Ukrainian children deported to Russia, countering Russia's policy of assimilating children in the temporarily occupied territories, and supporting the Global Coalition for Ukrainian Studies, an integral part of which is Crimean Tatar studies.
"We demand that the Russian Federation immediately cease its armed aggression against Ukraine and withdraw all its troops and occupation administrations from all temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine in accordance with international law," the statement reads.
Participants in the sixth summit of the International Crimea Platform called on states and international organizations to join the Platform and participate in its activities, and on partners to expand their participation, contribute to the achievement of its goals and objectives, and jointly intensify international pressure on Russia.
Approximately 50 states and international organizations are participating in the sixth summit of the International Crimea Platform in New York on September 23, 2026. It is taking place at the UN Headquarters in New York (during the high-level segment of the UN General Assembly). The core topics of the summit are the situation in the temporarily occupied Crimea, human rights violations, the militarization of the peninsula, and next steps toward de-occupation.
The previous fifth summit in New York in 2025 was attended by representatives from 54 countries and 7 international organizations (more than 60 participants in total).

Eviction of 87-year-old woman sparks protests in Madrid
September 23, 2026
The dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman sparked protests in the Spanish capital Madrid on Wednesday.
Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her residence on Alcalde Sainz de Baranda Street, where she had lived for at least 70 years of her life.
"I have lived here for 71 years and I don't want to leave," Maricarmen told reporters as the eviction was being carried out.
Dozens of people protested behind the police cordon, chanting, "Maricarmen, you are not alone" and "Murderers!"
The case highlights the growing pressure on long-term tenants in Spain's major cities, where rental prices have surged in recent years. Gentrification and the shortage of affordable housing have fueled public discontent.
With only 30 minutes to gather her belongings, Maricarmen was escorted by riot police officers. She was removed from her home on a stretcher and taken to an ambulance.
An 8-year-long battle
Spanish newspaper El Pais reported that Maricarmen had rented the apartment from a private landlord until 2018, when a real estate company acquired the property and took over its management.
According to the newspaper, the legal dispute between Maricarmen and the real estate company has lasted eight years, and this was the fourth attempt to evict her from the home.
The elderly woman's lawyer, Beatriz Duro, said that the real estate company had rejected proposals from the legal team as well as requests to postpone her removal from the property.
The company has not made any public statements on the matter.
Alicia del Rio, spokesperson for Inquilinas de Madrid, a tenants' association that seeks to combat what it describes as the "rental bubble" in the Madrid region, said that Maricarmen was taken by ambulance to a local hospital.
She also announced that a writer, who wishes to remain anonymous, had offered to pay the elderly woman's rent, but the real estate company rejected the proposal.
Spain's housing crisis
Spain remains divided over how to address the worsening housing crisis.
The country's left-wing coalition government has pushed for stronger tenant protections and broader rent controls. However, it argues that as long as Parliament remains divided, it will be difficult to pass such measures.
Meanwhile, Madrid's regional government, led by the conservative People's Party, has favored a more market-oriented approach.
The president of the Community of Madrid, Isabel Diaz Ayuso, is currently embroiled in a controversy related to the purchase of luxury properties valued at €6.3 million ($7.2 million).

Israel’s election panel bars Ra’am and Joint List; Supreme Court fight looms
The Arab-led alliance can appeal to the Supreme Court, which will have the final say on whether it appears on the ballot
Israel’s Central Elections Committee voted Wednesday to bar both Ra’am and the Joint List from the October 27 parliamentary election, setting up a Supreme Court fight over whether the two Arab-led slates can appear on the ballot.
The challenge to Ra’am came from three petitioners: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit party, and the Choosing Life forum of bereaved families and victims of terrorism.
They alleged that Ra’am supported armed struggle by a terrorist organization and rejected Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state. The committee voted 18–5 to disqualify the party.
The petitioners pointed to alleged connections between Ra’am, the Southern Branch of the Islamic Movement and charities they claimed had assisted bodies linked to Hamas. Ra’am denies that the evidence connects the party to support for terrorism. Its leader, Mansour Abbas, called the committee’s decision political and said the party would challenge it in court. Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara also opposed barring Ra’am, finding that the evidence did not establish grounds for disqualification.
The committee separately voted to disqualify the Joint List, an alliance of Hadash, Ta’al and Balad. Likud’s challenge to the alliance cited party positions and statements that it argued justified excluding the list. The panel also voted to bar two Joint List candidates individually: Hadash lawmaker Ofer Cassif and Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh. Those are separate decisions from the vote against the alliance as a whole.
The bans are not the final word. Ra’am and the Joint List can appeal the decisions against their full slates to the Supreme Court. The decisions against Cassif and Abu Shehadeh must receive Supreme Court approval before those candidates can be excluded. The court is expected to hear election disqualification cases next week.
The legal test is demanding. Israeli law permits disqualification for rejecting the state’s existence as Jewish and democratic, inciting racism, or supporting armed struggle against Israel by a terrorist organization or enemy state.
The Supreme Court has required clear evidence that a prohibited position is central to a list’s or candidate’s activity, and it has overturned earlier committee bans on Arab parties. Its rulings will determine whether Wednesday’s votes change the October ballot.

Massive Israeli blast in Lebanon's Khiam damages school miles away, cuts power
A massive Israeli explosion in the southern Lebanese town of Khiam late on Tuesday damaged a school, homes and other buildings in surrounding towns, forcing at least one school to close and cutting power to nearby areas.
The blast occurred at around midnight, when Israeli forces reportedly demolished several chalets in the hilltop town.
The force of the explosion was reportedly felt miles away, shattering windows and damaging doors in neighbouring Marjaayoun and Qlayaa.
Images shared online showed the scale of the explosion, which lit up the night sky over the area.
Among the buildings damaged was Marjaayoun National College, where several classroom windows were shattered, forcing the school to temporarily suspend classes while repairs were carried out.
💥تفجير إسرائيلي عنيف في مدينة الخيام في القطاع الشرقي جنوب لبنان#لبنان #اسرائیل pic.twitter.com/Xn4mN6QgX4
— ديوان (@DiwanDaily) September 22, 2026
Most students across Lebanon have begun returning to school, but thousands remain unable to do so because their families are still displaced from the south or because some schools elsewhere in the country continue to shelter displaced people.
Electricity infrastructure was also damaged by the explosion, cutting power to the Nabeh al-Hamam area and parts of the Arqoub subregion.
The blast comes as Israeli property destruction in southern Lebanon continues at a high rate following the June ceasefire, with Khiam the most affected village, according to exclusive figures shared with The New Arab.
Nasser Khdour, Middle East Assistant Research Manager at the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), said more than 320 property destruction events were recorded in August, the highest monthly figure so far, followed by another 210 between 1 and 21 September.
"The number of property destruction events has been rising since June’s ceasefire, reaching more than 320 in August, the highest monthly figure so far. There were another 210 events from 1 to 21 September. Al Khiam has been the most affected village," Khdour told The New Arab.
"Israel’s destruction of villages puts pressure on displaced residents, including Shia communities in southern Lebanon. Many of these villages were also centres of Hezbollah activity and held symbolic importance for the group," he added.
Khiam has been largely devastated by Israeli attacks, with extensive destruction reported in the town.
The strategically located hilltop town is among a number of areas in southern Lebanon where Israeli forces have maintained a presence following Israel's invasion, which began in October 2024.
Later on Wednesday, videos shared online appeared to show Israeli troops raising the Israeli flag at the northern entrance to Khiam.
Khdour said September had also seen an increase in Israeli air and drone strikes across a wider stretch of southern Lebanon.
"In September, we have also seen more Israeli air and drone strikes around Nabatiyeh al-Fawqa, Kfar Tebnit, Zawtar al-Sharqiya and Qantara, down to Wadi Slouki. Some of these places are already within the Yellow Line," he said.
"This seems to be part of Israel’s efforts to clear the area after the fall of Ali al-Taher Ridge. Strikes on Nabatiyeh al-Fawqa have also become more frequent since then."
Further Israeli attacks were reported elsewhere in southern Lebanon on Wednesday, with airstrikes, shelling and home demolitions continuing despite the US-sponsored framework agreement signed between Lebanon and Israel in June.
Tensions have fuelled fears of renewed large-scale fighting between Israel and Hezbollah.
Israel has said it will not fully withdraw from southern Lebanon until Hezbollah is disarmed, while the group has rejected demands to surrender its weapons as long as Israeli forces continue to occupy Lebanese territory.
