Malaysia furor after ex-PM wins house arrest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:40:35 UTC
01:40:35 KST

A conditional royal pardon letting former Malaysian prime minister Najib Razak serve the rest of his jail sentence under house arrest has ignited a new row surrounding the US$4.5 billion 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB) scandal.
Critics say Najib should remain behind bars, while supporters have rallied around the former leader and launched a campaign to help him pay a fine tied to his transfer to house arrest.
Najib, 73, was jailed in 2022 for his role in one of the largest-ever global plunders of a sovereign wealth fund, the now-defunct 1MDB.
Photo: AP
King Sultan Ibrahim on Friday granted Najib’s request to complete the remainder of his six-year sentence under house arrest — provided he pays a 50 million ringgit (US$12.26 million) fine.
Najib is also appealing a separate 15-year prison term in another 1MDB-related case.
Prosecutors say about $4.5 billion was siphoned from the state fund in the 2010s, triggering investigations from Malaysia to the US.
The scandal helped bring down the United Malays National Organization (UMNO), ending the party’s six-decade grip on power in 2018.
Yet Najib remains a popular figure among his base and UMNO’s grassroots supporters.
“How can a convicted felon with more cases awaiting trial be allowed house arrest?” said James Chow, a 49-year-old entrepreneur.
“It’s a waste of time and money and a mockery of the law,” he said.
Shyam Priah, 52, chief executive of a nonprofit organization, said she respected the king’s “constitutional prerogative to grant a pardon,” but questioned efforts to raise money for Najib’s fine.
“Seeing ordinary Malaysians being mobilized to contribute 10 ringgit towards a 50 million ringgit fine for a former prime minister raises a bigger question for me about our priorities as a society,” she said.
“Ten ringgit can mean a meal for someone who is struggling,” she said.
Najib’s supporters welcomed the king’s decision.
“The supporters who love Najib have been looking forward to the moment he would be granted house arrest,” Radiaa Rashid, 68, said.
“We miss Najib Razak. Even though he can’t be released, at least he’ll be at home with his family, with his grandchildren and children,” supporter Suzzalina Anura, 43, said.
Local media reported that donations topped 1 million ringgit by Monday after the campaign was launched, although some critics responded by contributing as little as 0.01 ringgit in protest.
The episode has also highlighted UMNO’s ongoing struggle to balance loyalty to its former leader with efforts to move beyond the scandal before the next general elections due by February 2028.
Bridget Welsh, an expert on Malaysian politics at the University of Nottingham Malaysia, said UMNO’s fundraising initiative has put the party in a “difficult position.”
On one hand, the party must show support for Najib and reassure traditional supporters. On the other, it must appeal to younger voters who tend to have a far harsher view of corruption.
“The house arrest serves to build party unity, but it comes at the cost of outreach for the party, as it speaks to the legacy baggage the party still carries,” she said.
Fundraising “within some traditional supporters ... is seen as important given that Najib’s accounts are believed to be frozen,” she said.
Yet the campaign risked pushing away younger voters and those in the political center.
“With younger voters and those in the middle ground, this is alienating, seen as a party not willing to admit mistakes,” Welsh said.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:40:34 UTC
01:40:34 KST

The UEFA Nations League kicks off today, but all eyes would be on the touchlines as a starry cast of new coaches, including Zinedine Zidane and Juergen Klopp, prepare to make their debuts in international soccer.
The end of FIFA World Cup cycles usually herald in a host of new faces; however, this year’s vintage is particularly bountiful, with no fewer than 10 European nations having appointed a new coach since this summer’s tournament in North America.
Most notable are 1998 World Cup winner and France legend Zidane, who succeeds Didier Deschamps as Les Bleus boss, and former Liverpool manager Klopp, who takes over his native Germany.
Photo: Reuters
When Deschamps announced this year’s World Cup would signal the end of his 14-year reign as France boss, only one name was on the lips of soccer fans in the country: “Zizou.”
They got their wish when it was announced in July that the three-time Champions League-winning coach was replacing his old teammate and captain at the helm of Les Bleus.
“It’s like a film, but it’s amazing. It’s real,” France skipper Kylian Mbappe told Spanish daily AS on Monday.
Finally, the 54-year-old will oversee his first matches as coach away to Turkey tomorrow and in Belgium three days later, before making his touchline bow at the Stade de France on Friday next week against Italy. A second meeting against the Belgians in Paris the following Monday would bring the curtain down on Zidane’s opening salvo in international management.
“The France job was the only one I wanted,” former Real Madrid coach Zidane said in July.
“I’ve had offers over these four or five years to take charge of a club, and I turned them all down for the French national team,” he said. “I’m ready for the challenge, that’s what drives me.”
If Zidane’s appointment marks the long-awaited return of an iconic figure to the national team in France, Klopp’s has been greeted with no less excitement in Germany, even if it is the former Mainz defender’s first taste of the Nationalmannschaft.
Uncapped as a player, Klopp made his name in soccer as a coach. After legendary spells at Borussia Dortmund and Liverpool, and a period away from the touchline as Red Bull’s global sports director, Klopp will begin an adventure many in Germany thought would never happen.
“This is ideally the high point of my career, of my life, my professional life. I will give it everything I have,” Klopp said at his unveiling after Julian Nagelsmann departed following Germany’s disastrous World Cup.
The charismatic 59-year-old Klopp has already shown he would do things his way by calling up 44 players, divided into two squads, for his first matches in charge.
Those games are against the Netherlands in Amsterdam today and at home to Greece three days later, before a meeting with Serbia in Munich on Thursday next week and a trip to Greece on Oct. 4.
Other arrivals for this opening round of Nations League matches include Jorge Jesus, who will make his Portugal debut when the competition’s reigning champions welcome Wales today.
Former Barcelona metronome and 2010 World Cup winner Xavi Hernandez replaces Ronald Koeman as Netherlands coach.
Roberto Mancini, who masterminded Italy’s UEFA Euro 2020 victory, returns to try and right the course of the floundering Azzurri.
Former Bayern Munich and Netherlands midfielder Mark van Bommel is to oversee his first Belgium match against Italy and Slaven Bilic takes over the Croatia reins for a second time, following a successful six-year spell in charge of the Vatreni between 2006 and 2012.
Spain’s World Cup and European Championship-winning coach Luis de la Fuente is staying put. He was on Monday rewarded with a contract extension until 2032.
His world champions are to begin their tilt at a second Nations League title with an eye-catching clash against Thomas Tuchel’s England at Wembley on Saturday.

Production indices hit new high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:40:34 UTC
01:40:34 KST

Taiwan’s industrial production last month set a new record, with the index soaring more than 23 percent from a year earlier due to robust global demand for artificial intelligence (AI) applications, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said yesterday.
Ministry data showed the local industrial production index rose 23.47 percent from a year earlier to 145.97, beating the previous high of 143.32 in July, while the subindex of the manufacturing sector, which accounts for more than 90 percent of the country’s production, rose 24.61 percent to 148.42.
Last month was the 30th consecutive month that both indices moved higher on a year-on-year basis, the data showed.
Photo: Ritchie B. Tongo, EPA
In the first eight months of this year, the industrial production index rose 20.80 percent from a year earlier to 132.24, with the subindex of the manufacturing sector rising 22.14 percent to 134.60, the ministry said.
Last month, the electronic components industry saw its production rise 21.68 percent from a year earlier as demand for high-performance computing devices and other AI-related applications pushed up production by Taiwanese 12-inch pure play foundry operators, DRAM suppliers, IC assembly and testing firms, and IC designers, the ministry said.
Inside the electronic components industry, production by integrated circuit firms rose 24.24 percent from a year earlier last month, it said.
Riding the waves of AI applications and cloud services, which boosted demand for AI servers, switches, semiconductor inspection and automation equipment, the local computer and optoelectronics industry posted a 95.72 percent year-on-year increase in production last month.
The traditional sector appeared mixed due to uneven strength in recovery, ministry data showed.
Last month, production in the machinery industry rose 18.65 percent from a year earlier largely because semiconductor suppliers were keen to expand capacity through equipment purchases to meet global AI demand, the data showed.
The base metal industry’s output slid 0.36 percent year-on-year last month as demand for select products such as hot rolled steel sheets stayed slow, while the chemicals and fertilizer industry fell 5.81 percent on weak demand, with some firms cutting production in response to the market, the ministry said.
Chen Yu-fang (陳玉芳), deputy head of the ministry’s Department of Statistics, said the old economy sector has shown signs of improving since March, as AI development created spillover, allowing some industries to move more raw materials used in tech gadgets.
The ministry said that while the global economy remains impacted by various trade policies and geopolitical unease, Taiwan’s exports are expected to continue to benefit from the AI boom, which would boost production in the manufacturing sector.
The subindex of the manufacturing sector is expected to range between 146.03 and 150.03 this month, or 22.5 to 25.8 percent from a year earlier, the ministry said.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

01:40:32 KST

The first shuttle talks between the US and Iran for months raised hopes yesterday that the adversaries could make some progress toward ending the Middle East war, although neither side spelled out any change in their positions.
Iranian Minister of Foreign Affairs Abbas Araqchi and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner communicated through mediators on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, the first such contacts since an interim ceasefire agreement collapsed in July.
“Steve and Jared had a very productive meeting today with mediators of Iran, merely mediators. Let’s see what happens with that,” US President Donald Trump said. “They’ve been mediated for a while, but I think there’s a lot of momentum for them to make a deal. It’s what we’re hearing from everybody.”
Photo: AFP
Earlier, Trump had told the UN General Assembly in a speech that he had to decide whether to make a deal with Iran or “annihilate” the country.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that Trump is open to meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who was yesterday to address the General Assembly.
“This is a president that will meet with anybody for the most part, because he believes that engaging with people is important if you’re going to solve problems,” Rubio said on NBC’s Today show. “It doesn’t mean you’re going to end up agreeing with them, but it’s important.”
Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Tehran had engaged with the US through a Qatari mediator in New York and conveyed conditions, including an end to the war on all fronts and a halt to US “acts of aggression.”
Some Iranian state media had earlier reported that Araqchi and Witkoff had met, but Iranian officials clarified that this was not face-to-face. Araqchi met the Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, who has been one of the main mediators at previous talks.
The diplomatic opening helped keep oil prices near two-week lows, with Brent crude holding just below the US$100-a-barrel threshold it had shot through this month, after Houthi fighters in Yemen launched a major offensive and fired into Saudi Arabia.
The war, launched by Trump in February alongside Israel as “Operation Epic Fury,” has lasted nearly seven months, killing thousands of people, disrupting global energy supplies and spreading to other countries in the region — first to Lebanon and more recently to Yemen.
Trump repeated previous assertions that the war could end around the time of November’s US midterm elections, although he has not explained why.
Since diplomacy broke off in July, the sides have repeatedly exchanged fire, although Trump has held back from a full-blown resumption of strikes after receiving advice from his military commanders that munitions were running low.
In his address to the General Assembly, Trump made the case that he has shown fortitude while other leaders have equivocated as he defended his decision to start a war with Iran.
Trump also suggested that he could be at a crossroads in the conflict even as he called on the Islamic republic to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz and return to the negotiating table to find a settlement to end the conflict.
“I have a big decision to make,” Trump said. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world, or do I annihilate the Islamic republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”
The president’s comments came in his wide-ranging address to the international body in which he also celebrated this year’s US military operation to oust Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro from power, hailed a new agreement to expand the US military presence in Greenland and pushed back against calls for greater regulation of the artificial intelligence industry.
At the heart of the address was a fulsome defense of the war and pushback on the notion that Iran has shown a measure of resilience.
“The terrorist regime is behaving badly, not because they are strong and confident, but because they are weak and desperate,” Trump said.
Most of Iran’s delegation walked out of the chamber as Trump railed against the Islamic republic.

National Palace Museum takes flight with Tigerair
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:40:32 UTC
01:40:32 KST

Taiwanese airlines are turning to culture and cuisine to enhance their flying experience, with Tigerair Taiwan unveiling a National Palace Museum-themed aircraft ahead of its 12th anniversary this weekend.
Tigerair yesterday announced a three-year collaboration with the museum to decorate the fuselage of one of its aircraft with renowned Chinese artworks and artifacts.
The design incorporates the mountain contours of the museum’s Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains painting, and well-known artifacts such as the Jadeite Cabbage, the Meat-shaped Stone and the Mao Gong Ding bronze vessel. Other objects featured were a carved olive-pit boat, the Jade Dragon, the Jade Cat and the Doucai Chicken Cup. It also includes six headrest covers featuring museum artifacts.
Photo courtesy of Tigerair Taiwan
Tigerair plans to reimagine the iconic Along the River During the Qingming Festival as “Taiwan Along the River During the Qingming Festival,” incorporating landmarks from cities served by the airline.
The redesigned artwork would appear on boarding passes and service items, while characters including Tigerair’s mascot, Hu Jiang, and the museum’s mascot, Little Jade, would be incorporated into the cabin decor.
The aircraft’s exterior is expected to be completed by mid-November and begin service by the end of the year. Cabin upgrades are expected to be completed by the first quarter of next year.
National Palace Museum Director Hsiao Tsung-huang (蕭宗煌) said the partnership is part of the museum’s effort to bring its collections to international audiences.
The museum holds about 700,000 artifacts and has been involved in commercial collaborations.
The airline is offering passengers a 10 percent discount on admission to the museum’s Taipei and southern branches, as well as select museum store products, through the end of next year.

It is projected to continue moving west-northwest to reach waters south of Taiwan before pivoting north on Saturday, the agency said.
Photo: Screen grab from the Web site of the Central Weather Administration
It would then move northeast passing over waters east of Taiwan and toward Japan’s Ryukyu Islands, it said.
The storm is expected to come closest to Taiwan on Sunday and Monday while remaining at moderate strength, and then gradually weaken as it moves north.
It would bring scattered showers from Taoyuan northward and Yilan County on Monday and Tuesday.
Through Sunday, most parts of Taiwan would generally see partly cloudy to sunny weather, CWA forecaster Lai Hsin-kuo (賴欣國).
Tomorrow, windward areas including the north coast of Keelung, greater Taipei, eastern Taiwan and the Hengchun Peninsula could see isolated brief showers.
By today, Keelung’s northern coastline, the eastern half of Taiwan proper and mountainous areas around Taipei should experience sporadic showers, with afternoon rains expected throughout Taiwan proper, the CWA said.
On Mid-Autumn Festival, the weather is likely to be sunny or cloudy, with the evening moon visible except in the mountains north of Chiayi County, it said.
Sporadic rains in the Hualien-Taitung region and afternoon showers in the mountains throughout Taiwan proper are expected, although forecasts could change with the typhoon’s course, it said.
Starting on Saturday, Keelung’s northern coastline, Taiwan proper’s eastern region, Green Island (綠島) and Orchid Island (Lanyu, 蘭嶼) would likely experience sea swells, the agency said.
At the same time, the highest tide in Penghu County is expected to coincide with the typhoon’s rains and winds, resulting in flooding risks, it said.
The week’s midday temperature could exceed 30°C, and parts of Taiwan could experience temperatures of about 33.5°C, the CWA said.
For Hsinchu and Miaoli counties, a lack of clouds could lead to cool weather, with morning temperatures of less than 20°C, resulting in large temperature swings during the same period, it said.

EDITORIAL: Chinese spouses in Taiwan’s politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:40:31 UTC
01:40:31 KST

The growing number of Chinese spouses participating in Taiwanese politics should not, in itself, be cause for alarm, but does warrant scrutiny of candidates, their political networks and their sources of support. Taiwan is a democracy, and voters should ultimately decide who is suitable to represent them — provided that candidates and voters are participating free from coercion, concealed foreign funding and other forms of interference.
The issue has become more prominent ahead of the Nov. 28 local elections.
The Central Election Commission said 26 candidates are naturalized Chinese spouses.
Taiwan places substantial restrictions on the political participation of people from China. Under the Act Governing Relations Between the People of the Taiwan Area and the Mainland Area (臺灣地區與大陸地區人民關係條例), people from China must have established a household registration in Taiwan for at least 10 years before they can register as candidates for public office.
That requirement provides considerable time for them to establish their lives here and become part of Taiwanese society. It also gives them a lengthy period of exposure to Taiwan’s democratic institutions. Residency and integration do not by themselves establish where a person’s loyalties lie, but scrutiny of Chinese-born candidates does not mean demanding that they support de jure Taiwanese independence.
A significant portion of the electorate supports closer relations with China, while some favor eventual unification. A Chinese-born candidate is entitled to appeal to those views, provided they meet all legal requirements. The question is not where a candidate was born, but whether the Chinese government or organizations are using that person to attempt to influence Taiwan’s electoral process.
Last month, the New Taipei District Court convicted Chinese-born spouse Xu Chunying (徐春鶯) of, among other offenses, campaigning for the Taiwan People’s Party’s 2024 presidential ticket under instructions from people linked to Chinese political organizations.
That case does not establish that Chinese spouses as a group are acting on behalf of Beijing, but it does illustrate why political relationships, sources of funding and contacts with Chinese government or organizations deserve scrutiny when there is evidence of possible interference.
This is also worth considering in a broader historical context. Following the administration of former US president Richard Nixon’s opening to China, other Western countries increasingly embraced economic engagement with Beijing under the expectation that greater prosperity, international integration and the growth of a middle class would eventually encourage political liberalization in the country. That expectation has not materialized.
The lesson for Taiwan should not be that Chinese immigrants cannot participate in democratic politics, but that assumptions about political integration should not substitute for evidence about a person’s political activities and relationships.
Taiwan should apply rigorous transparency and enforcement rules to campaign financing and political relationships. Candidates who previously held Chinese nationality or household registration should be subject to the same legal standards as everyone else, and their ties to China should be transparent enough for voters and election authorities to assess.
One question for any candidate is where their political loyalties lie. If a candidate supports closer relations or unification with China, that is a political position voters can accept or reject at the ballot box. However, if there is evidence that a candidate is taking direction from the Chinese government or organizations acting on its behalf, that becomes a matter of election integrity and compliance with laws.
The number of Chinese spouses seeking political office also raises questions worth investigating. That 26 such people have registered as candidates does not demonstrate coordination or outside influence, nor would it be reasonable to assume that Chinese spouses are uniquely susceptible to political influence because of their origins. Nevertheless, authorities and journalists should ask how these candidates became involved in politics, whether they share common organizations or political networks, or have received support from people or groups connected to China; and if there is evidence that they are taking direction from the Chinese government.
The same standards of transparency and scrutiny should apply to other naturalized citizens who seek public office. The goal is to identify foreign interference, not to single out a particular nationality.
Voters decide who represents them. Protecting that principle does not mean treating Chinese spouses as a threat, nor ignoring security concerns, but ensuring that the democratic freedoms that allow new citizens to participate in politics are protected from coercion, foreign funding and attempts by foreign actors to manipulate Taiwan’s electoral process.
Taiwan’s democracy and high-tech economy play a crucial role in global affairs and are central to the world’s embrace of a raft of next-generation technologies, including AI. It is underpinned by a security relationship with the United States that’s existed in several iterations since 1949 and the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) retreat from China. A central pillar of that security relationship is the American willingness to sell arms to Taiwan. Indeed, since 1979 it has been embedded in US law, with the Taiwan Relations Act (TRA) charging the US with helping to improve the island’s ability to deter an attack from

TCC Group Holdings Co’s (台泥企業) board of directors has approved a plan for the company’s Dutch subsidiary to acquire Ukrainian cement company Ivano-Frankivskcement (IFCEM) and three other companies for about 750 million euros (US$857 million).
The transaction includes roofing materials company Ivano-Frankivsk-Dakh, gypsum products maker KRU Gips and dry-mix mortar producer KRU Mix, TCC Group Holdings vice president Shelly Yeh (葉毓君) said at a news conference yesterday.
The final acquisition price would be adjusted when the deal is finalized based on factors such as net debt and net working capital, Yeh said.
Photo courtesy of TCC Group Holdings Co
The plan is still subject to regulatory approval in Taiwan, Ukraine and other jurisdictions before the transaction can be finalized, Yeh cautioned.
The company is hoping to expand its European cement operations from southern and western Europe into eastern Europe and position itself to participate in Ukraine’s long-term reconstruction once the war ends.
IFCEM represents a strong vehicle through which to expand its European presence, with a roughly 36 percent market share in Ukraine and a sales network that extends mainly to Poland and Romania as well as Moldova, Slovakia and Hungary, TCC said.
Another major consideration was the growing importance of low-carbon practices in the cement industry, especially given the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, the company said.
TCC expects to introduce its low-carbon cement technologies to the acquired businesses and advance its sustainability vision in leading post-war reconstruction, it said.
IFCEM’s production base is in Ivano-Frankivsk in western Ukraine, about 760km from the front lines in the southeastern part of the country.
The company’s plant has maintained production without interruption since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, TCC said.
According to IFCEM’s 2025 financial report, revenue rose 20.3 percent year-on-year to UAH16.25 billion (US$362.41 million), while gross profit climbed 40.3 percent to UAH6.44 billion.
Gross margin surged to 39.6 percent, up from 34 percent in 2024, while net income increased 44.5 percent. Net margin was about 26.4 percent.
TCC said it has appointed Morgan Stanley as financial adviser for the transaction, while international legal, accounting, tax and environmental consultants have conducted due diligence covering sanctions, labor, operations and foreign exchange controls.
The company said it retains the flexibility to bring in international financial institutions as co-investors, with interest already expressed by supranational investment funds.
The plant has installed 50MW of solar power capacity and 19MW of gas-fired power generation capacity to reduce its reliance on the external grid, the company said.
Ukraine’s reconstruction needs over the next decade could reach US$588 billion. Severely damaged housing, transportation and energy infrastructure are the most urgent needs, according to an assessment by the World Bank and the UN earlier this year.

Trump, Xi expected to discuss trade, AI, Taiwan: academics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:40:24 UTC
01:40:24 KST

US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) are expected to discuss trade, artificial intelligence (AI) and Taiwan at a summit beginning in Washington today, with academics saying the talks would also aim to manage competition between the two countries.
The summit, the leaders’ second face-to-face meeting this year following talks in Beijing in May, is expected to build on their agreement to establish a “constructive relationship of strategic stability,” said Bao Chengke (包承柯), a researcher at the Shanghai Institute for East Asian Studies.
The two sides have made progress in implementing agreements reached in May, including China’s purchases of US agricultural products, Bao said.
Photo: Reuters
Negotiators are also working on a reciprocal framework to reduce tariffs on about US$30 billion of non-sensitive goods from each country, with an announcement on the framework expected after the summit, he said.
Ensuring a stable supply of Chinese rare earths to the US could also be discussed, Bao added.
On broader strategic issues, Beijing and Washington have common interests regarding Iran and Russia, Bao said.
Both support freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and favor a peaceful resolution to the Russia-Ukraine war, leaving room for greater cooperation to help preserve global stability, he said.
Taiwan is also expected to feature in the talks, with Beijing hoping Washington would provide greater clarity on US arms sales to Taiwan to reduce unnecessary risks, Bao said.
On AI, the two countries should establish mechanisms to manage risks and prevent competition from escalating uncontrollably in a field critical to national security, economic competitiveness and military capabilities, he said.
Separately, Wu Xinbo (吳心伯), dean of Fudan University’s Institute of International Studies, said at the Xiangshan Forum in Beijing that the US and China need to begin discussing AI risks and safeguards, adding that the two countries account for about 90 percent of global AI capabilities.
Although no government-to-government AI dialogue has begun, Beijing should remain cautious because Washington could use such talks to slow China’s AI development, Wu said.
Taiwanese academics offered a different assessment, saying trade, procurement commitments and AI are likely to dominate the agenda, while Taiwan is expected to play a secondary role.
Trump is seeking tangible outcomes to boost Republican prospects ahead of the US midterm elections in November, said Wang Hsin-hsien (王信賢), a professor at National Chengchi University’s Graduate Institute of East Asian Studies.
Meanwhile, Xi aims to show that China’s foreign policy and domestic governance remain stable ahead of the Chinese Communist Party’s 21st National Congress next year, Wang said.
Beijing is expected to press Washington to slow the pace of arms sales to Taiwan and limit high-level US-Taiwan exchanges, said Wang Hung-jen (王宏仁), a professor of political science at National Cheng Kung University.
However, China recognizes that it is unlikely to persuade the US to halt arms sales to Taiwan altogether, Wang Hung-jen said.
While Taiwan would be discussed, it is unlikely to feature more prominently than it did during the leaders’ meeting in May, he said.
Meanwhile, Jakob Lengacher, the US Department of State’s Chinese-language spokesman, told Voice of America in New York that US policy toward Taiwan remains unchanged.
Washington continues to support Taiwan’s meaningful participation in international organizations, including the APEC forum, Lengacher said.
He reiterated that the US opposes unilateral changes to the “status quo” by either side of the Taiwan Strait and remains committed to maintaining peace and stability in the region.

The number of diarrhea cases was relatively high, with 70 outbreaks reported nationwide over the past four weeks, concentrated in the food and hospitality industries, he said.
Pathogens were detected in 28 of the 70 outbreaks. Of those, 25, or 89.3 percent, were viral, all involving norovirus, while three, or 10.7 percent, were bacterial, with two involving Staphylococcus aureus and one involving Salmonella, Kuo said.
August norovirus testing showed that GII.17 was the predominant circulating genotype, accounting for about 34.2 percent of cases, he said.
CDC Deputy Director-General Lin Ming-cheng (林明誠) said that one of the most common mistakes in food preparation is cross-contamination of raw and cooked food.
For example, using the same tongs or plates that have come into contact with raw meat to handle cooked food can increase the risk of cross-contamination, as can allowing raw food to come into contact with cooked food, Lin said.
People should use separate cutting boards, knives and utensils when handling raw meat, seafood and vegetables, and keep raw and cooked food separate, he said.
Food should be thoroughly cooked before being eaten, not served partially raw or undercooked, he said.
Norovirus is highly contagious and can be transmitted by consuming contaminated food or water, or through contact with infected people or contaminated surfaces, Lin said.
People should wash their hands thoroughly with soap and running water, particularly after using the toilet, before eating and before preparing food, he said, adding that alcohol-based hand sanitizers should not be considered a substitute for handwashing.
People with symptoms of gastroenteritis, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea or abdominal pain, should avoid preparing food for others or attending gatherings, seek medical attention as soon as possible and stay home to rest, the CDC said.
They should also drink plenty of fluids, and replenish electrolytes and nutrients to prevent dehydration. Those who must go out should wear a mask and maintain good hand hygiene to reduce the risk of transmitting the virus to family members and others, it said.

New fundraiser raises money for warm clothes for political prisoners in Russia’s frigid Far North
Anyone sent to a Russian prison or penal colony faces harsh conditions, especially in the Far North.
Prisoners are issued uniforms, but the clothing is often poor quality and fits badly. Russia’s prison system does not provide thermal underwear at all.
Having their own good-quality warm clothing is an important part of daily life for prisoners, including political prisoners, who often cannot receive such items from relatives. That is why the “You Are Not Alone” campaign to support political prisoners has launched a fundraiser to buy warm clothing.
For political prisoners in penal colonies, donations will pay for:
- Mittens
- Gloves
- Socks
- Thermal underwear
- Warm insoles
- Tights for women
- Shawls and headscarves for women in colonies where prison authorities allow them
The list is slightly different for people in pretrial detention centers. These prisoners are not made to work outdoors, but the facilities themselves can be very cold. The following items can be sent to people in pretrial detention:
- Warm shoes without laces
- Socks
- Tights for women
- Thermal underwear
- Sweaters without drawstrings
- Warm pants without drawstrings
- Hats
- Jackets and down coats
- Mittens
- Gloves
- Warm insoles
A donation of just €3 can buy warm insoles for a political prisoner. A €10 donation can buy warm mittens or gloves, and €50 can buy a pair of warm shoes.
Although the fundraiser has a specific purpose, its organizers, including Meduza, are encouraging people to sign up for recurring donations. These donations enable the campaign to provide ongoing support to political prisoners.
The campaign does not accept donations made with ruble-denominated cards and urges people who travel to Russia not to donate.

Metallurgy situation catastrophic: 5 furnaces destroyed at Metinvest, 2 at AMKR, steel plants shut down – top manager
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:37:34 EEST

The situation in Ukraine's metallurgy sector is currently catastrophic, in particular due to shelling: five furnaces at Metinvest Group's enterprises have been destroyed, two furnaces at ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih (AMKR, Dnipropetrovsk region) have been destroyed, and the steel plants are not operating, Oleksandr Vodoviz, head of the office of the CEO of Metinvest Group, said at the Economic Resilience Forum organized by Forbes Ukraine in Kyiv on Wednesday.
"All the plants have been destroyed. This is Arcelor, Metinvest, Petrovsky Plant (DMZ of Yaroslavsky – IF-U) and Interpipe. They have been hit several times. Many people have been killed. We are not operating. I know that Arcelor is not operating. As far as I know, Petrovsky Plant has also been shut down. And Interpipe, as far as I know, has not repaired its transformer either," Vodoviz said.
According to him, there was a week in September when Ukraine did not produce a single tonne of steel for the first time in 100 years, while Metinvest's enterprises remain shut down.
"We are standing idle and assessing the possibility of resuming operations. We tried to restart at Zaporizhstal: we started up a furnace, it operated for 10 hours and then there was another strike. To give you an idea, starting up a furnace costs from $50 million, while the furnace itself costs $500 million. Repairing it somehow requires enormous funds," the top manager said.
He added that the company had sought assistance from various ministries, but the aid offered was at the level of UAH 2-5 million.
While agreeing on the need to support small businesses, Vodoviz stressed that big business is the foundation around which small businesses operate.
"They supply us with water and cables and carry out work. We have 50,000 contractors. Unfortunately, there is no solution for big business today. Here, a respected person asked the Economy Ministry what the plan was. Did you all hear the plan? I did not. There is no plan right now. So we would like to hear what the plan is. What next? Should we lay people off or not? We are all living in anticipation," the head of Metinvest's CEO office said.
According to him, the group is currently planning its actions for no more than a month ahead.
"Nobody is looking beyond six months. Everyone is sitting and watching what happens next. My view is that the situation in the economy is extraordinary. Extraordinary decisions are needed. You cannot live in an extraordinary situation and make decisions that are always made," the expert said.
Asked about the amount of investment needed for recovery, Vodoviz said the group had not yet calculated it.
"We have not calculated it yet, but, for example, I told you that one furnace costs $500 million if it is built virtually from scratch, and all our furnaces are destroyed – five. Two have been destroyed at Arcelor. That's billions of dollars. But we are studying the situation. We definitely will not invest money in recovery now because we do not understand how the situation will develop," the top manager explained.
He noted that if the situation changes somehow over the next month or two, relevant decisions will be made, but there are none at present. He clarified that Metinvest's decision-making depends on three factors, not all of them military. The first and main one is shelling and strikes on enterprises.
"The second is ports. We are currently not shipping or exporting, although until 2026 we were the country's largest exporter. And the third, strange as it may seem, is our European friends and partners, who have completely closed their markets to our exports of metal products. They introduced CBAM, they introduced quotas. At the same time, they promised us that this would not happen. We took part in negotiations with the Ministry of European Integration and the Economy Ministry. But the EU introduced them anyway," Vodoviz said.
According to him, these are the three major problems that need to be resolved.
Regarding government assistance, the manager said: "We are not getting involved in the government, we are not asking for any grants, we do not want the government to finance us. We simply want to be on equal terms. There is, for example, the Ukraine Facility program. I know that some funds are allocated from the Ukraine Facility. Unfortunately, we do not have access to this program, although we would like to have it," the top manager said.
As for proposals to raise taxes, he said he believed they "would lead to nothing good."
"Here, probably every business would say: do not get in our way," Vodoviz concluded.
Metinvest is a vertically integrated group of mining and steelmaking enterprises. The group's enterprises are located mainly in Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions. The group's main shareholders are SCM Group (71.24%) and Smart Holding (23.76%), which jointly manage it. Metinvest Holding LLC is the group's management company.

How and why the UN General Assembly is gaining prominence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:36:09 UTC
01:36:09 KST

How and why the UN General Assembly is gaining prominence
The gridlock in the UNSC and emerging multipolarity are shifting political weight to the UNGA.
As world leaders attend the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York this week, there is a chorus of criticisms about the organisation’s failures and limitations. From the inability to sanction Israel amid its genocidal campaign against the Palestinian people, to the failure to condemn the United States’ illegal bombing of Iran or to respond effectively to Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, the UN has appeared increasingly constrained in recent years.
The veto system of the UN Security Council, by which the five permanent members (China, France, the Russian Federation, the United Kingdom, and the United States) can effectively bypass any oversight of their activities, has meant that the Security Council has not intervened in world crises in any meaningful way since the end of the Cold War.
And yet, despite these limitations and external attacks, there are bodies of the UN that still play a significant role in world politics.
Given the paralysis of the Security Council and the shifting dynamics across the Global North and South, as small and middle powers gain more ground, the General Assembly is steadily rising in prominence as a place where politics doesn’t always trump policy.
The UNGA is comprised of 193 member states, each with an equal vote. This nominally even playing field means that lobbying for votes is intense and the horse-trading between states has shifted the dynamics on crucial questions at key moments.
Given its representative nature, the UNGA has traditionally played a very important, if overlooked, role in defining the UN’s work. Since 1960, Global South states have held a numerical majority in the assembly, which has allowed this group of states to set the agenda for issues that are discussed and to play a pivotal role in the political dynamics of the forum.
The collective agency of this disparate group of states – from small island members such as Jamaica to large states such as Brazil and India – has ebbed and flowed through various formations, from the Afro-Asian bloc to the Group of Seventy-Seven (G77). Their collective power has been considerable in moulding the economic and social development system and pushing forward a human rights agenda.
For example, the proposal to create the post of UN High Commissioner for Human Rights was led by Costa Rica in the General Assembly in 1965. Although the role was not officially created until 1993, the resolution provided the pathway towards institutional change, and importantly, put human rights at the centre of the agenda.
In this way, much of the General Assembly’s work has been gradually generated towards specific gains in the area of decolonisation, self-determination and inequality, reflective of the bonds of solidarity that hold different Global South states together, but also of the longer and wider arc of commitment to addressing global inequality and injustice.
It is in this light that the real potential of the General Assembly as a barometer that offers a reading of the position of the international community on various issues becomes clear. This is a dual-sided function, reflecting the general views of the majority of member states on a range of issues, as well as the global public opinion.
This was most evident recently in the resolutions passed condemning Israel’s military campaign in Gaza and its obstruction of aid delivery. The unprecedented number of votes in favour reflected not just the political will of the states involved to sanction the Israeli government, but the wider outrage among the general public at the appalling slaughter taking place.
And it is not just Gaza where the UNGA has taken initiative from the UNSC.
In the first weeks of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the General Assembly met under the “Uniting for Peace” mechanism outlined in Resolution 377. This was an initiative originally taken in November 1950 when the UN was embroiled in the Korean War, and the Security Council was paralysed.
The resolution put forward the most important constitutional changes to the UN. It outlined a route to bypass the Security Council when it is deadlocked and allowed a debate to be held in the UNGA. Under this resolution, the UNGA can make recommendations for action, including the imposition of sanctions and even the use of force to restore peace and security.
Between 2022 and 2023, the United for Peace resolution was invoked three times, moving the debate out of the Security Council, where Russia has a permanent veto, to the General Assembly, where three separate resolutions demonstrated support for Ukraine and criticism of the violation of sovereignty and territorial integrity by Russia.
Considering that the current dysfunction of the Security Council does not look set to change any time soon, the role of the General Assembly is becoming increasingly important to hold large states accountable and maximise the agency of smaller and middle powers.
The Liechtenstein Initiative is one such example. Introduced by the small, landlocked state in 2022, the initiative requires the General Assembly to meet automatically when one of the five permanent UNSC members uses their veto. Within 10 days, the assembly should convene and debate the issue that was vetoed. Crucially, the veto-wielding power must explain its position and justify its use of the veto to all UN members.
It is another way to create accountability for state behaviour, and allows the Security Council to be circumvented, especially when humanitarian catastrophes, atrocities and major conflicts occur that require an emergency response. Taken together, what these resolutions reflect is a growing trend towards moving debates about peace and security out of the Security Council and into the General Assembly.
This trend fits into the long history of initiatives by smaller states, often from the Global South, to defy the influence of great powers in the UN. Indeed, the General Assembly has been the place where the Global South has successfully shifted the needle on the world’s most pressing issues by flexing its collective agency over the last 80 years in ways that are not fully appreciated.
While the UNGA is not devoid of pressures from the great powers, it provides a space and a place for collective responses to the world’s biggest crises. Far more than being merely the bully pulpit for leaders like US President Donald Trump today, the UNGA chamber is the world’s leading forum for quiet diplomacy.
In the past, this forum has served as the measure of humanity’s greatest achievements in the areas of development and human rights. Looking ahead, the broken pathway towards a fairer world is most likely to be carved out of this space, as it is the General Assembly that has historically been the strongest reflection of this ambition.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Is Burnham right to blame Russia for spreading online disinformation?
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:35:11 BST
01:35:11 KST

Is Burnham right to blame Russia for spreading online disinformation?
- Published
After Prime Minister Andy Burnham put Russia-linked disinformation campaigns under the spotlight, BBC Verify has been examining how these attempts to influence people's opinions work.
We have tracked – and debunked – numerous online disinformation campaigns produced by Russia-linked groups that have attempted to shift public opinion on issues like the war with Ukraine, influence elections in the US and Germany, damage social cohesion and undermine trust in authorities or institutions.
What kind of disinformation is being spread?
In his UN speech, Burnham said there was an "insidious campaign" being carried out by the Russian government to target people in the UK.
Last year, a series of fake videos featuring British public sector workers appeared online.
Among them was a 999 call operator in Preston named Aaron, who told BBC Verify he was shocked to find out his voice had been cloned with AI to create a fake video of him talking about the 2025 Polish presidential election.
Those videos are part of a major Russian-linked disinformation campaign known as Matryoshka, which BBC Verify and other research groups have been tracking.
AI is used to create fake videos - sometimes dozens a day - which impersonate journalists and major news organisations like the BBC to push disinformation about Ukraine and Western countries onto people's social media feeds. But Aaron's case indicates ordinary British citizens could also be a target.
In the run-up to the 2024 US presidential election, BBC Verify reported how there was a shift in focus from Ukraine to post fabricated videos about the US election. We are once again seeing early evidence of similar misleading videos ahead of November's US midterm elections.
BBC Verify has previously exposed a large-scale disinformation campaign run by a former US police officer now based in Russia. With the help of AI, the operation created hundreds of fake local news websites in the UK, US, France and other Western countries with the aim of spreading completely made-up stories.
One of these was a fake news website called the London Crier which falsely claimed that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had bought a mansion owned by King Charles at a bargain price.
It was seen by hundreds of thousands of users on X and shared by an official Russian embassy account.
We also found that a fake AI-narrated video on YouTube was the source of the bogus story. The platform removed it after we reported it.
And in 2023, BBC Verify found a major propaganda operation involving bogus accounts on TikTok, which posted misleading videos in multiple languages - including English - generating millions of views, with the aim of influencing the views of users in several European countries about the war in Ukraine.
TikTok removed more than 12,000 fake accounts involved in the operation, saying its investigation indicated that the accounts originated from Russia.
Another campaign was discovered during the 2019 UK general election campaign when a trove of confidential documents about a possible trade deal between the UK and US was posted by an anonymous user on the platform Reddit and later used by the Labour Party in its campaign.
While the documents appeared to be genuine, Reddit later confirmed in a statement the leak "was part of a campaign that has been reported as originating from Russia".
But there are questions about how widespread or effective some of these disinformation campaigns are in reality.
While many of them appear to be extensive and organised, it is hard to determine how widely they have spread or how significant a role they have played in actually influencing people.
Do other countries sponsor disinformation campaigns?
Russia is also not alone in using industrial-scale disinformation campaigns which spread false information to further its own geopolitical aims, as other authoritarian governments like China, North Korea and Iran are also major players in online disinformation.
BBC Verify has previously reported on a number of X accounts posting in support of Scottish independence, but whose location information indicated they originated from Iran.
And, at the height of the Coronavirus pandemic, the BBC discovered a network of more than 1,200 faked or hijacked accounts on Facebook, Twitter and YouTube that posted pro-Chinese government and anti-US messages.
There is evidence to suggest Western governments also engage in disinformation campaigns, although the scale of their operations are not always clear.
An investigation by Reuters in 2024, external revealed that during the Covid pandemic, the US military ran a covert anti-vaccine influence operation to discredit China's Sinovac jab.
AI has also exacerbated the spread of disinformation, as images can now be more easily faked and videos misleadingly edited using text prompts.
Text generation has also improved and can create plausible, authoritative and coherent sounding fake news reports.
BBC Verify saw evidence of this during US-Israel war with Iran. While in the early weeks of the Russia-Ukraine conflict most of the disinformation published online consisted of old or misleading videos and inaccurate claims, we have seen a deluge of AI-generated images and videos since the Iran war began back in February of this year.
Carl Miller, an author and founder of the Centre for the Analysis of Social Media at Demos, told BBC Verify that state-run influence operations "amplify and exploit existing grievances and fissures - making it really hard to work out exactly what sort of effect they might have".
"Influence operations are quite fragile things, usually, and we need to find ways of making them much more likely to fail if they target us," he added.

Zelenskyy also said he was ready for a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, said there is currently no agreement on an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine. He said the war would end not through a military victory but through a negotiated agreement.

Syria's economic reckoning: The greatest test yet for al-Sharaa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:34:37 UTC
01:34:37 KST

Breadcrumb
Syria's economic reckoning: The greatest test yet for al-Sharaa
Damascus, Syria - Syria witnessed its largest protests last week since the fall of Assad’s regime in 2024. Across northern Syria in the government’s heartland of Idlib, and in Aleppo and Hama, large crowds protested against a recent decision by the government to lift subsidies on fuel.
This comes amid lingering economic collapse and, according to analysts, growing anger from much of the population at the government’s failure to address their economic grievances.
On 13 September, the Syrian government lifted Assad-era fuel subsidies, citing “higher global procurement costs,” due to the Iran war. The changes were set to see diesel prices rise by 40%, and petrol to increase by 25%.
In a country in which, according to UN estimates, 90% of the population remain under the poverty line, such increases, and their inevitable knock-on effect in the wider economy, were clearly deemed unacceptable by large parts of the population.
Over four days, large crowds took to the streets, where they blocked traffic and set fire to tyres in anger. The protesters were calling for the reversal of the decision to lift subsidies and the resignation of Mohammed Al-Bashir, the Minister of Energy.
Economic headwinds and liberalisation
According to analysts, Syria is facing twin pressures contributing to rising fuel costs - a global rise in energy prices, compounded by the government’s liberalisation strategy.
The government has argued that rising global energy prices have burdened the import-dependent country with steeper energy bills, necessitating the lifting of subsidies.
It is true that energy prices are climbing, driven primarily by the Iran war, but also by Ukrainian strikes on energy infrastructure in Russia - which is Syria’s largest energy provider.
However, the government’s explanation is not the full story. Price increases are also resulting from the government’s post-Assad economic vision.
The Syrian government has committed itself to unwinding Assad’s ‘Baathist’ economic model. In a meeting of the Arab Media Summit in Dubai last week, President Ahmed al-Sharaa said that Syria is undergoing “a shift from a system resembling socialism, dominated by corruption and bureaucracy, to a more liberalised system based on a free market economy”.
Under Assad, the economy was defined by “corruption, bureaucratic bloat and inefficiency,” Benjamin Fève, a Senior Consultant at Karam Shaar Advisory, tells The New Arab.
The government has sought to liberalise the economy by slimming down overstaffed state institutions, cutting subsidies, and opening the Syrian market to foreign investment.
These reforms have created a positive impact in some sense, with the IMF forecasting more than 10% growth in 2026. However, “this growth has not translated into a lower cost of living or reduced poverty rates,” Caroline Rose, a senior director at the Soufan Centre, explains to The New Arab.
Rose explains that much of the significance of lifting fuel subsidies comes from the major knock-on effects it has in almost every aspect of the economy, causing a cascade of price increases - perhaps most impactfully in the price of food.
Food insecurity remains widespread, with 7.2 million Syrians acutely food insecure according to the World Food Programme - an issue compounded by rising prices for foodstuffs and a cut in humanitarian aid budgets globally.
The rising fuel costs are also “a byproduct of Syria’s broken energy system,” says Rose. Although Syria has natural reserves of fossil fuels, “its energy infrastructure is damaged by years of war and sanctions, exacerbated by reductions in local refining capacity with Baniyas [Syria’s sole refinery] currently under repair”.
Fève, whilst recognising the importance of correcting the Assad-era economic model, acknowledges that “every lever to fix the economy has a first-order regressive impact”.
Prices in Syria have increased dramatically over the last two years, but “wages have not kept pace with rising cost of living,” he explains to The New Arab. In November 2025, previous protests broke out following the government’s decision to lift subsidies on electricity, which sent electricity prices skyrocketing by 6,000%.
Such decisions have meant that “the economic reality remains brutal for most Syrians, and there is an increasing sense that people's economic situation has worsened since the fall of Assad”.
An empty narrative
The Syrian government has also struggled to match its narrative of progress with the reality experienced by most.
“Whilst the removal of sanctions, the injection of foreign capital and the stabilisation of the exchange rate have projected a positive narrative,” explains Fève. “It hasn't translated into more disposable income.”
“There is a widening gap between the story the government tells about the recovery and what ordinary Syrians feel,” adds Fève.
The Syrian government frequently touts large instances of foreign investment into Syria, but many of the Memorandums of Understanding are not actually materialising as real investments.
There has also been a spate of investment in high-profile projects that will do little to benefit ordinary citizens. For example, in August, the Syrian Sovereign Wealth Fund and a number of investors from Saudi Arabia announced a joint investment project to construct the five-star ‘Narcissus Hotel’ in an upmarket neighbourhood of Damascus.
Furthermore, some proposed reconstruction projects appear to favour investors over displaced residents.
A planned redevelopment of the destroyed neighbourhood of Jobar in Damascus’ suburbs sparked protests after it emerged that under the deal, valued at $21bn, residents would only be provided 50% ownership shares in their former homes - and 30% for those whose homes were classed as ‘informal’.
Equally, there is a “legitimacy gap” regarding the optics surrounding the new government. Syrian government officials can be frequently seen travelling around with large entourages in large convoys of imported SUVs.
Many government ministries have been extensively refurbished to match Syria’s new ‘visual identity' - a coherent design launched by the Syrian government last year.
“Such optics convert an economic grievance into a moral one about who this post-Assad transition is actually for,” argues Fève.
It is this sense of moral grievance that has contributed to the intensity of the anger around these protests, which represent the first real test of the government’s legitimacy on bread-and-butter issues.
Government revises its position
These protests are the largest since the fall of Assad’s regime, and a major test for the government’s governance strategy.
“The government decided not to react aggressively,” Issam Al-Reis, a researcher with ETANA, a Syrian research organisation, tells The New Arab. “They understand that this is a red line for the Syrian people, and so they allowed the protests to take place without a strong response.”
“However, the protests represent an early alarm for the government about the problems in their governance and economic management of the state,” explains Al-Reis.
He notes that much of the protest movement has been centred on Idlib - the government’s former heartland - which feels increasingly marginalised as the government “moved all its officials and institutions to the capital to run the country, leaving Idlib behind,” he says.
“Whilst much of the progress is commendable, for example, managing to increase the availability of electricity to 20 hours a day, which was only a dream under Assad,” Al-Reis adds. “If no one can afford to pay for it, then what is the overall benefit?”
The government has also shifted its policy as a result. Last Thursday, Syria’s Minister for Energy, Mohammed Al-Bashir, said that “exceptional and complicated circumstances” had forced the government to remove subsidies.
He announced the decision would be revised and instead diesel would see a partial subsidisation of certain types of diesel used in agriculture and heating - as well as for consumers eligible for government support. However, the standard grade would remain the same and prices at the pump would not be affected by the revision.
“This is certainly not a U-turn,” says Fève, “as fuel prices will still increase on average.”
Although it seems that the government is receptive to the public mood, it remains equally committed to its broader economic strategy and so unwilling to entirely walk back its reforms.
However, according to analysts, without targeted social support, the burden for these reforms will continue to be borne by the poorest for whom essential costs like food and transport make up the largest share of their expenditure.
Rose believes that “the government has sought to address this” through its revisions, creating exceptional subsidies for agriculture and heating, but that ultimately “this will not address the broader feedback loop of nationwide cost of living increases”.
As a result, this is likely not the last protest movement that Syria will witness as the government seeks to navigate the country through the perilous post-conflict phase.
How the government responds and how successful its economic vision is will ultimately determine the fate of millions of Syrians.
Cian Ward is a journalist based in Damascus, covering conflict, migration, and humanitarian issues

French far-left presidential candidate Melenchon blames Ukraine's deep strikes for war escalation
France's far-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon sought to reaffirm his opposition to Russia's invasion — even as he blamed Kyiv for escalating the war by drone strikes.
French voters are set to elect a new president in April 2027, with incumbent President Emmanuel Macron nearing the end of his two terms in office and, therefore, ineligible to run again.
Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally (RN), consistently polls first, while Melenchon, presidential candidate for the far-left France Unbowed, is also gaining ground.
Both candidates have come under fire over supposedly favorable views toward Russia and have attempted to challenge that image.
Melenchon on Sept. 23 posted a video of himself speaking about Russia's war on Ukraine, with the accompanying message: "From the very first day we have condemned Russia's invasion of Ukraine."
"We demand the withdrawal of Russia from Ukraine," the message continues.
However, Melenchon makes comments in the video suggesting that Kyiv shares the blame for the escalation of the war.
"We hear a lot about the threat posed by Russia... but what worries us is that no one seems concerned about why the threat from Russia appears greater today than it did some time ago. Why?" Melenchon asked.
He then went on to speculate whether "this is related to the deep strikes carried out by Ukraine."
"Who can imagine that a country would allow its own capital to be attacked and provide no response to such a situation?" Melenchon asked rhetorically, in what appeared to be a reference to Ukrainian drone strikes on Moscow.
In the video, Melenchon made no reference to Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities, including Kyiv, which has been subject to an unprecedentedly high number of strikes from ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones.
read also
"Even if Russia is the invader of Ukraine, the fact remains that in this circumstance, the escalation continues," Melenchon said.
The hard-left politician instead called for diplomacy and peace talks to bring the war to an end.
However, ongoing peace efforts have so far failed to achieve a breakthrough, as Moscow continues to push its territorial demands and reject a ceasefire. Melenchon did not explain how to resolve that situation in his video speech.
The far-right struggles with Ukraine too
France's far-right is also grappling with an internal shift away from Russia, which has been underway since 2022.
Within the last week alone, Le Pen has criticized Russia for seizing the assets of European companies operating in the country, but also said Paris should give less financial aid to Ukraine.
Le Pen's remarks on Ukraine have been denounced as "unbearable and irresponsible" double-talk by centrist candidate Gabriel Attal, who thinks "turning off the tap to Ukraine... would only worsen Russia's domination, and therefore its threat."
Attal's positions on Ukraine are clearer-cut: he considers supporting Ukraine to be France's "duty and interest," and he even supports using Russian financial assets frozen in Europe to help Kyiv.
However, he is but one of several candidates splitting the center of French politics, which, under France's electoral system, would mean a run-off between Le Pen and Melenchon if the situation remains as polls currently indicate.
Other candidates hoping to mop up the political center include Edouard Philippe — who visited Kyiv in May — as well as Raphael Glucksmann and Bruno Retailleau.

Scientists warn super El Nino could cause 450,000 deaths: Should we worry?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:29:55 UTC
01:29:55 KST

Scientists warn super El Nino could cause 450,000 deaths: Should we worry?
Global South countries will be worst affected by the phenomenon sweeping the planet from June to February.
The record global heat caused by this year’s powerful “super El Nino” could cause nearly half a million excess deaths worldwide by early next year, according to a report (PDF) published by the global research collaboration, Climate Impact Lab, on Wednesday.
So what does the report reveal, how has climate change supercharged the effects of El Nino and should we all be really worried?
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3UN warns El Nino could be ‘off the charts’, strongest in decades
- list 2 of 3Global ocean temperatures hit record high as El Nino intensifies
- list 3 of 3El Nino set to be most intense ‘for over a century’: UK forecasters
What does the report say?
Climate Impact Lab (CIL)’s report has found that as many as 451,000 more heat-related deaths between June this year and the end of February 2027 could be caused by the effects of El Nino, than the number expected in an average year.
The study’s authors came to their projections after researching the relationship between temperature and excess mortality in 24,378 regions, taking local climate and vulnerability into account.
They combined those findings with temperature forecasts to estimate excess deaths which could arise from heat caused by El Nino compared with the 1996-2025 average.
Their methodology will be published in a peer-reviewed journal.
The number of extremely hot days is likely to rise by 44 percent compared with normal years, according to the report, titled, “451,000 at Risk: Where Action Can Save Lives During the Super El Nino”.
The researchers described this year’s El Nino as a “postcard from the future”, ushering in temperatures that will become the new normal in just a few decades.
It recommended that emergency response efforts should be directed to high-priority regions to tackle heat-related mortality in the coming months.
CIL’s Adaptation Inventory recommends implementing a number of measures to help vulnerable populations cope with extreme heat, including issuing heat warnings, increasing the number of staff at medical facilities during the hottest periods, establishing cooling centres where people can shelter and implementing protections for outdoor workers.
“This report allows decision-makers to see exactly where emergency actions can be taken now to save tens of thousands of lives in the coming months,” said Michael Greenstone, economist at the University of Chicago and cofounder of CIL.
What is super El Nino?
El Nino is the period of time during which the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean heats up to at least 0.5 degrees Celsius (0.9 degrees Fahrenheit) above average temperatures. It takes place every few years and is part of a natural climate cycle that alternates between a warm phase – El Nino – and a cool phase, known as La Nina.
During El Nino, the warmer ocean water can drive major changes in global weather patterns.
Scientists and meteorologists classify El Nino as “super” when ocean surface temperatures reach or exceed 2C (3.6F) for a few months. The current El Nino reached 2.7C last month, and some forecasts say it could rise to 4C when it peaks somewhere between November and December.
Why is it so bad this year?
The way El Nino develops depends a lot on “how the atmosphere and the ocean are behaving”, Akshay Deoras, senior research scientist at the University of Reading’s National Centre for Atmospheric Science & Department of Meteorology, told Al Jazeera.
Early in the year generally, “you get winds blowing towards Indonesia and these winds pile up warm water over there. But sometimes, if the winds weaken or the wind pattern is reversed, then that’s when you get strong winds from the Indonesia side, and that leads to a lot of transport of warm water”, Deoras explained.
This warm water then heads towards the eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, resulting in El Nino.
“This year, we have really seen these strong winds from Indonesia blowing in the spring season, and they help to transport a large amount of hot water or let’s say warm water, and that’s why we have a super El Nino.”
What effects will it have?
Despite its unprecedented strength, it remains unclear what effects this year’s super El Nino will have on weather around the world.
“Scientists are still assessing whether the impacts will be in proportion to its magnitude, but we are already seeing expected effects worldwide,” said Adam Scaife, head of long-range forecasting at the United Kingdom’s Met Office.
“Historical evidence shows that El Nino can significantly alter global rainfall patterns,” the Met Office said in a statement.
Regions that often experience reduced rainfall during this period include parts of Central and northern South America, the western Pacific and areas affected by the Indian summer monsoon.
Other areas, including Southern Africa, may face an increased risk of drought.
El Nino also reduces tropical cyclone activity in the Atlantic, with the Met Office adding that no hurricanes have been observed yet this year.
The disruption to rainfall can have severe consequences on global food supplies as agriculture suffers and natural food-growing and harvesting seasons are altered.
Why could El Nino cause so many excess deaths?
The main thing that El Nino does “is it just dumps a lot of heat into the atmosphere and we know that this heat and high temperatures basically supercharges extreme rainfall and weather events”, said Deoras.
A super El Nino not only increases the frequency of these events, but also amplifies their intensity and severity, meaning that there is a “general expectation that we would get more of these extreme weather events across the globe over the next couple of months, and unfortunately, that could translate into a lot of deaths,” said Deoras.
How is climate change involved in this?
Friederike Otto, professor of climate science at Imperial College London, said that climate change has worsened the impact of El Nino around the world.
“El Nino is likely to bring higher global temperatures and extreme weather impacts in the months ahead, and climate change will further exacerbate these impacts, as the underlying heat driven by fossil fuel emissions continues to push global temperatures higher,” said Otto.
“However, while El Nino patterns are a natural phenomenon that come and go, climate change does not and will only continue to worsen unless we take much faster action globally to move away from fossil fuels.”
Which countries will be worst affected and why?
The Climate Impact Lab report warns that countries in the Global South will bear the heaviest burden of the excessive heat.
The country likely to suffer the most excess heat-related deaths is Nigeria with 31,400, followed by Indonesia with 19,300 and Sudan with 17,600.
Heat in Africa’s Sahel region, including Niger and Chad as well as Nigeria and Sudan, is likely to cause an additional 66,800 deaths.
The researchers also predict that the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand and Cambodia will suffer an additional 19,400 deaths combined.
The number of excess deaths could climb higher if El Nino extends further into next year, with key areas of the Northern Hemisphere, including India and Pakistan, especially vulnerable during their summer months.
Tom Burke, cofounder and director of the climate change think tank E3G, agreed that the Global South would be disproportionately affected.
“Coping with the additional stresses caused by El Nino is harder on countries that have weaker institutions. So the poorer a country it is, the weaker institutions it has,” he told Al Jazeera.
Countries of the Global North, by contrast, have “a whole variety of institutions to respond to these kinds of stresses: fire departments, health systems, etc. They have a quite complex set of institutions to respond to events like this”.
Deoras said added that “it’s quite difficult to” assume that El Nino will impact the Southern Hemisphere more, as “we haven’t really seen an El Nino of this nature in the past, so there could be surprises and extreme weather events can happen even in the Northern Hemisphere”, adding that he expects “to see these impacts happening across the globe”.
Are nearly half a million people really going to die?
Burke told Al Jazeera that he believes this figure is actually a conservative estimate, since it only refers to heat-related deaths.
El Nino also has “an effect because of fires and floods, which will lead to increased deaths” and is compounded by conflicts like the US-Israel war on Iran, which will “likely lead to a big impact in food price inflation and in turn to a harder-to-record increase in deaths”, said Burke.
Deoras said the report’s figures are “subjective” and that he’s “sceptical about regional distributions”, all of which makes it difficult to calculate such an exact toll.
“For example, over 15,000 excess deaths are projected for India until February 2027, which is not so convincing, since it’s not going to be summer for India when deadly dry heatwaves strike.”
However, he does maintain that there’s a “good chance that we would expect a lot [in the coming 12 months] of these impacts in terms of deaths and also damage to property, infrastructure and the economy”.
