How Experts Are Reimagining Early Childhood for a Changing World
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:29:30 UTC
01:29:30 KST

Most experts working in early childhood development agree: the first years of a child’s life shape not just their academic readiness, but also a child’s lifelong health, resilience, emotional well-being and brain development.
But Jack Shonkoff, a professor of child health and development at Harvard University, believes that researchers and policymakers need to expand those conversations in order to address disparities in early childhood.
“My plea is: Let's move beyond quickly on the fact that children are our future, and say what we are going to do about that,” said Shonkoff, who is also the director of Harvard’s FirstPlace Partners, an initiative that works with neighborhood leaders and other organizations to apply developmental science and improve outcomes for children, families, and communities. “We need new ideas, we need to be bold.”
Shonkoff spoke at a TIME100 Talks panel moderated by TIME executive editor Nikhil Kumar in New York City on Wednesday. The panel, which centered on reimagining early childhood in a changing world, also included Pia Rebello Britto, global director of education at UNICEF, and Rosemarie Truglio, senior vice president of global education at Sesame Workshop.
Britto said that UNICEF is trying to create “practical steps” to better the lives of children around the world and prevent perpetuating unequal circumstances. These steps include investing in children’s abilities to “eat, play, and love.”
“Eat: We are working to ensure adequate, right, appropriate nutrition. Play: Because it's all about that interaction with children, the stimulation that sparks the brain connections,” Britto said. And love, she continued, is “the foundation of it all.”
“That human trust, the protection,” she said. “We talk about children in humanitarian contexts. We talk about children being affected by war and by climate change. How do you nurture that love?”
Sesame Workshop, the global nonprofit educational organization behind the beloved childhood show Sesame Street, works especially in that “play” step, Truglio said, emphasizing the importance of opportunities for children to learn cognitive processing skills, self-regulation, and social empathy.
“Our mission is to help kids grow smarter, stronger, and kinder,” she said. She highlighted how important the last goal on that list is for building a better future full of kinder adults, adding: “Boy, do we need more perspective-taking and collaboration and truly listening and seeing the people in our lives and treating them with compassion and respect.”
Sesame Workshop attempts to teach children those lessons through media and with “joy and fun and happiness,” she said.
The panelists discussed the challenges in implementing more equitable programs for children at the local and government levels. One of these challenges is the “our children versus other people’s children” mentality, according to Shonkoff.
“I think that the problem is that there's too much focus on what's good for my children and who cares about other people’s children, whether it's in a country or around the world,” he said. “We all pay a price for that lack of finding common cause—that we all benefit from everyone in the world being healthier.”
Britto said that another challenge was trying to convince governments to invest in caring for children, and convincing them that both maternal and child health is a public sector issue, rather than just a nonprofit or private sector issue.
“The universal aspiration of every adult, which is wanting the best for their child … has not converted to a vote-getting issue,” Britto said. “It hasn't converted into a commercial incentive, and it hasn't converted into a way that a country can stand tall, or a nation or a district can stand tall and say, ‘We're doing this well.’”
One way to address this is to bring the community into conversations with policymakers, she said, while explaining that UNICEF is trying to bring teachers, parents, and caregivers to the forefront to understand what they need to care for children and give them what they need.
Sesame Workshop, Truglio said, is trying to do the same in order to create “blueprints” for caregivers of all kinds.
“Let's just not create content in a vacuum,” she said. “Go talk to the parents, talk to the teachers, talk to the administrators, and talk at the systems level because you could create all the content and it’s going to sit in a drawer. We want this to be practical and useful.”
These voices are going to be even more important, the experts said, as artificial intelligence and rapidly developing technologies change the way that children learn and that adults care for and educate children.
Shonkoff said that while AI will certainly change how childhood education occurs, certain needs like a child’s “social connection” will never change.
“Social connection, which is like hunger and thirst for humans, it's survival. That's not going to change no matter what happens with the digital world,” he said.
Early childhood educators may be able to apply AI—but with caution and specific purposes, Truglio said, adding that Sesame Workshop is exploring the “developmentally appropriate” uses for it.
“We have to increase the level of awareness and embrace it as a tool, but still hold sacred those fundamental cognitive early processing skills that children need, and that we just can't give onto a machine,” she said, adding: “That would be a huge mistake.”
TIME100 Talks: Starting Strong: Reimagining Early Childhood for a Changing World was presented by Reliance.

Russia seeks new ways to terrorize civilians -- Sybiha on strikes on data centers

Red Cross says no access to prisoners of war in Russia since 2024
- The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has not had access to prisoners of war held in Russia since 2024, despite previously visiting thousands on both sides of the Ukraine conflict.
- ICRC emphasises that visiting prisoners is essential under the Geneva Conventions to check conditions, provide support, and communicate with families.
- The organisation is seeking to regain access to Russian detention facilities to ensure prisoners' welfare and provide families with information about their loved ones' fate.
AI generated
GENEVA - The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has been denied access to visit prisoners of war held in Russian detention since 2024, the organisation confirmed on Sept 23.
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of neighbouring Ukraine in February 2022, the two countries have swopped thousands of prisoners of war and are both believed to be holding thousands more in captivity.
ICRC said on Sept 23 that it from the start and through August had visited more than 9,800 PoWs on both sides in the conflict, but “mainly in Ukraine”.
While it did conduct visits of prisoners held by Russia early on, an ICRC spokeswoman told AFP in an email that it currently “does not have full access to all PoWs”.
“We visit PoWs and detained civilians in Ukraine, (but) in Russia our last visit was in 2024,” she said, confirming a report by the BBC.
“We seek to regain access to facilities to visit those deprived of liberty (including PoWs) consistent with our mandate.”
Visiting prisoners of war is core to the ICRC’s mission enshrined in the Geneva Conventions, which define the laws of war.
Countries, it pointed out, were responsible for ensuring it had access to “see all prisoners of war and other persons deprived of their liberty... (and) to all places where they are held and be allowed to repeat visits as often as needed”.
The organisation insists that such visits are vital for checking detention conditions, offering support and sometimes books, hygiene items and other personal necessities, and also to relay information between the prisoners and their loved ones.
“Families have the right to know about the fate of their loved ones, whether they are alive, wounded or dead,” it said.
“Many have waited anxiously for many long months, and they need answers today,” it added.
“They are impatient, as are we.” AFP

Israel’s climate crimes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:22:21 UTC
01:22:21 KST

Israel’s climate crimes
TEHRAN - Israel’s environmental damage in Palestine has accompanied the destruction of Palestinian lives, homes and livelihoods. Farmlands and olive groves have been burned or destroyed, while homes, vehicles, cities and refugee camps have been repeatedly bombarded.
The thick clouds of soot produced by the bombardment of Gaza have also raised alarm among environmentalists over the war’s devastating impact on the environment.
In September 2025, the Palestinian Institute for Climate Strategy, together with Tipping Point North South, estimated that Israel and its allies owed Palestinians $148 billion in military- and conflict-related climate reparations dating back to the Nakba. The estimate is based on the calculated climate costs of traceable military-related emissions and assigns $103 billion to Israel and $40.8 billion to the United States, with smaller amounts attributed to several European allies. The researchers stressed that the figure represents only a measurable portion of the broader environmental and social damage.
Israel’s burning of agricultural land and forests in southern Lebanon and the destruction of homes in villages and cities, including Beirut, have further compounded the environmental damage caused by the conflict.
The war on Gaza has also generated enormous greenhouse-gas emissions. A study published in One Earth in March 2026 estimated that direct emissions from the conflict exceeded 1.3 million tons of CO? equivalent by January 2025. When emissions associated with pre-war military infrastructure and post-war reconstruction are included, the estimate rises to 33.2 million tons of CO? equivalent. Reconstruction alone accounts for an estimated 31.4 million tons.
The environmental consequences, however, extend far beyond carbon emissions. The war has created serious risks for both the Mediterranean marine environment and Gaza’s groundwater system. The two problems are closely linked: the destruction of water and sanitation infrastructure has allowed pollutants from the land and underground water system to reach the Mediterranean.
The most immediate impact has been the enormous discharge of untreated sewage into the sea. Gaza’s wastewater-treatment system has largely collapsed. UNEP estimated that in March 2024, around 60,000 cubic meters of wastewater and sewage were being discharged into the environment every day, primarily into the Mediterranean.
This wastewater can carry pathogens and disease-causing microorganisms, nitrogen and phosphorus that contribute to eutrophication and oxygen depletion, microplastics, organic pollutants, industrial chemicals and other hazardous substances. Damaged infrastructure and military activity may also introduce heavy metals and other contaminants.
UNEP’s September 2025 assessment found that Gaza’s marine and coastal ecosystems had been contaminated by sewage, solid waste and munitions. However, it said the precise scale and chemical composition of the contamination could not yet be determined because adequate environmental sampling has been severely constrained.
The war has also devastated marine life and fisheries. Pollution threatens Gaza’s coastal ecosystems, fish stocks and other marine organisms. UNEP has said the conflict has virtually eliminated Gaza’s fishing livelihoods, while the destruction of environmental-management systems has made contamination of the seafood chain more difficult to control.
There is also a longer-term concern. If enormous quantities of war debris are dumped into the sea or used for land reclamation without proper sorting and treatment, asbestos, heavy metals, hydrocarbons and other contaminants could enter marine ecosystems and potentially the food chain.
The war has also placed Gaza’s Coastal Aquifer, the enclave’s principal natural freshwater resource, under severe additional pressure. This could prove to be one of the conflict’s most serious long-term environmental consequences.
The destruction of sewage networks and wastewater-treatment plants, combined with widespread reliance on cesspits, allows contaminated water to infiltrate the porous ground and reach the aquifer. UNEP’s 2025 assessment says groundwater contamination is likely and warns that the destruction of piped systems and increased reliance on cesspits have increased the risk of aquifer contamination.
Potential contaminants include sewage and pathogens, nitrates and other nutrients, chemicals, heavy metals, hydrocarbons, and pollutants associated with munitions and destroyed infrastructure.
Soil contamination has further aggravated the groundwater problem. The crisis is not simply a matter of sewage. The destruction of buildings has generated tens of millions of tons of rubble, while military activity has contaminated soil with munitions, solid waste and untreated sewage.
UNEP’s September 2025 assessment estimated that the destruction of some 78 percent of Gaza’s buildings had generated approximately 61 million tons of debris. It warned that around 15 percent of the debris could pose relatively high contamination risks because of asbestos, industrial waste and heavy metals if waste streams are not properly segregated.
Rainwater moving through contaminated soil and rubble can carry pollutants downward toward groundwater. At the same time, the destruction and compaction of soil have reduced its capacity to absorb water, increasing runoff and reducing groundwater recharge.
Seawater intrusion could become an even greater problem. Gaza’s aquifer was already being over-pumped before the war. Excessive groundwater extraction lowers freshwater levels and can allow Mediterranean seawater to penetrate the aquifer.
The war has severely damaged pumping, storage, desalination and wastewater systems, making it much more difficult to manage both groundwater depletion and contamination. UNEP’s assessment found extensive damage to Gaza’s water infrastructure and warned that the environmental consequences could persist for decades.
The environmental damage is therefore not necessarily confined to Gaza’s shoreline.
The Mediterranean is a semi-enclosed sea, and pollutants discharged from Gaza can be transported by currents and coastal circulation. The precise regional extent of contamination remains uncertain because environmental monitoring has been severely restricted. Scientific modeling has nevertheless examined how wastewater pollutants can disperse from Gaza’s coastal waters into the Mediterranean.
UNEP’s latest assessment warns that repairing the damage to Gaza’s water resources, soils, freshwater ecosystems and marine environment could take decades.
Israel’s environmental impact on Palestinian land also predates the current war. Palestinian environmental advocates have for years documented the destruction of agricultural land and restrictions affecting water and other natural resources. Among the practices cited by Palestinian environmental groups is the spraying of herbicides on agricultural areas in Gaza and the destruction of farmland.
Palestinian environmental advocates have also accused Israel of policies that systematically restrict Palestinian access to water resources. Najla Abdellatif, founder of Zero Waste Palestine, told Middle East Eye that she had met Palestinian farmers whose groundwater sources were affected by measures involving Israel’s state-run water company.
Taken together, the destruction of agricultural land, water and sanitation infrastructure, soil, coastal ecosystems and natural resources has created an environmental crisis whose consequences are likely to extend well beyond the end of the fighting.

Explainer-Why new war in Ethiopia’s Tigray threatens to trigger wider conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:21:36 UTC
01:21:36 KST

Explainer-Why new war in Ethiopia’s Tigray threatens to trigger wider conflict
LONDON, Sept 23 - Regional forces in northern Ethiopia's Tigray on Wednesday seized control of three airports and clashed in multiple locations with federal troops, signalling the start of a major offensive after months of growing tensions.
The move shatters a peace deal that ended the 2020-2022 conflict between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and federal forces, and comes amid a backdrop of deteriorating ties between Ethiopia and Eritrea, Sudan's civil war, tensions over Red Sea access, and the Horn of Africa being dragged into Middle East conflicts.
WHY DOES NEW FIGHTING IN TIGRAY THREATEN A WIDER WAR IN ETHIOPIA?
The Pretoria Agreement, which formally ended a conflict that killed hundreds of thousands of people, has been under strain for months, each side accusing the other of violating the deal.
The peace process began to unravel after splits emerged within the TPLF, and a hardline faction of the party reasserted control over the region, kicking out an interim administration.
Most recently, the TPLF formed an alliance with six other armed groups from across Ethiopia, including former enemies from the war, aimed at overthrowing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government.
It is not clear how many members of the alliance were involved in clashes on Wednesday but Ethiopia is home to many heavily armed regional groups.
Abiy's government has accused Eritrea of financially backing members of the alliance, allegations Asmara has denied.
WHAT ROLE WILL ERITREA PLAY?
As the situation unfolds, all eyes will be on Asmara, which has endured a turbulent relationship with Addis Ababa since independence in 1993.
Soon after coming to power, Abiy won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2019 for ending two decades of hostility between Ethiopia and Eritrea.
When the civil war erupted the following year, Eritrean forces then supported Ethiopia's federal army. Relations have deteriorated since the Pretoria peace agreement, which Eritrea was not party to despite having fought in the war.
Access to the Red Sea is another flash point.
Landlocked Ethiopia had a coastline for decades until Eritrea broke away. Since then, Addis Ababa has repeatedly argued that restoring access to the sea - specifically the port of Assab - is vital for its long term security and economic development. Asmara has said it fears Addis Ababa will try to take Assab by force.
Earlier this month, the US government lifted sanctions on Eritrean Defense Forces and other entities.
It is not clear what impact removing sanctions would have on any conflict in Ethiopia, but the move is seen as a nod by the Trump administration to Eritrea’s strategic coastline opposite Saudi Arabia, and warning Ethiopia not to go to war with Asmara.
WHICH REGIONAL RISKS RAISE THE STAKES THIS TIME AROUND?
Diplomats warn that a renewed Tigray war would no longer be a largely isolated Ethiopian conflict.
Instead, it would unfold as the Horn of Africa faces its most volatile security environment in years, with war raging in Sudan, persistent instability in Somalia, tensions over the Nile and expanding war and geopolitics from the Middle East spilling into the region.
Ethiopia has been accused of backing the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary group, which is fighting Sudan’s army in one of the world’s deadliest conflicts.
This support, which Ethiopia denies, is in line with its close relationship with the United Arab Emirates, the most active Gulf power in the region which UN experts say is also supporting the RSF. The UAE has denied the accusations.
For its part, Eritrea is closer to Sudan and has cultivated relatively close ties with Egypt, which is a long-time rival of Ethiopia. Egypt and Sudan both see Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, built on a tributary of the Nile, as a serious threat to their vital water supplies. REUTERS

Yemeni government in military and diplomatic push to reverse Houthi gains

2026-09-23

Yemeni government in military and diplomatic push to reverse Houthi gains
Government claims battlefield advances as diplomats attempt to put anti-Houthi fight at UN centre stage.
The Yemeni government suffered a significant blow earlier this month when it lost the country’s Red Sea coast to the Houthi rebels. It is now working on a two-pronged strategy, militarily and diplomatically, to restore the initiative and prevent the Houthis from consolidating their gains and pushing further into government-held territory.
Saudi-backed government forces claimed on Tuesday to have seized the strategic Mount Qarafan in southern Taiz’s al-Shamayatayn district. The military reported killing five Iranian-allied Houthi fighters and injuring 20 others during the operation.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3How much is UK supporting Saudi Arabia in its war with Iran-backed Houthis?
- list 2 of 3Despite flurry of New York diplomacy, US-Iran deal remains elusive
- list 3 of 3Yemen government forces claim control of Mount Qarfan in Taiz
Pro-government Homeland Shield Forces, also known as the Quwat Dira’ al-Watan in Arabic, also thwarted a Houthi infiltration attempt on the Kahboub front, which overlooks the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait. Government forces also reported the capture of Mount Zalat, near Kahboub, on Tuesday.
The battles in the mountainous regions of southwestern Yemen are critical because of the commanding positions the peaks being fought over provide. Qarafan overlooks valleys linking southern Taiz with western coastal areas, as the Houthis attempt to encircle government-held areas in the governorate. Kahboub, meanwhile, is significant because Houthi forces have been attempting to secure the high ground overlooking Bab al-Mandab to prevent a government counterattack and expand the territory under their control.
The Houthis, meanwhile, have claimed Saudi Arabia has conducted air strikes in Taiz, al-Jawf, and Marib. Riyadh has not confirmed the strikes.
The humanitarian toll is mounting, with recent hostilities displacing approximately 132,000 people, including 75,000 in Taiz alone, according to the International Organization for Migration.
UNGA diplomatic push
Meanwhile, at the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Yemeni government officials are attempting to rally support for their push against the Houthis.
Presidential Leadership Council member Abdullah al-Alimi is leading Yemen’s delegation and will address the General Assembly later this week, but has already met US politicians.
Foreign Minister Afrah al-Zouba is also attending the world gathering, and called for the disarmament of non-state armed groups at a meeting on the General Assembly’s sidelines.
Other world leaders have included references to events in Yemen in their own addresses to the General Assembly.
Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani addressed the assembly, reaffirming support for UN efforts to reach a comprehensive political resolution. He emphasised that any settlement must be based on the outcomes of Yemen’s 2013-14 UN-facilitated national dialogue, in a manner that preserves Yemen’s unity, sovereignty, security, and stability.
Ireland also highlighted the crisis, expressing deep concern about the humanitarian situation and stressing that freedom of navigation must be protected in the Bab al-Mandab strait.
Tactical coastal battles
The Yemeni government is focusing its diplomatic efforts on impressing on other countries the dangers of Houthi control of the Bab al-Mandab strait, and the threat of more attacks against shipping in the region.
While the government has the support of Saudi Arabia, many other world powers are avoiding any involvement in the conflict, including the US. Washington is already entangled in a war with the Houthis’ primary ally, Iran.
The Yemeni government’s current military counterattacks against the Houthis therefore remain localised, rather than a larger campaign, analysts say.
Ibrahim Jalal, a Yemen-focused analyst, told Al Jazeera that the government’s recent attacks are an attempt to shift the momentum.
“Partially and tactically, the Yemeni Armed Forces stopped part of the Houthi rush seeking to secure and stabilise expansion on the coast, and moved to limited counter-attacks in the Taiz-Lahj [region] … while regaining dominant heights and positions,” Jalal told Al Jazeera. “The government is gradually regaining the initiative, but it has not yet launched a broad military campaign to reclaim the coast and other areas.”
Jalal noted the significance of the geography being fought over.
“Taiz is considered a key to protecting Bab al-Mandab from the east and communication routes with Lahj and Aden; therefore, regaining its dominant southern and western heights prevents the Houthis from stabilising and securing coastal gains and expanding south,” Jalal added.
Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa Programme, told Al Jazeera that reasserting control remains a severe challenge for government forces.
“It is impossible for the government to regain momentum unless it manages to reclaim Bab al-Mandab,” Al-Muslimi said, adding that he believes it is unlikely, despite the flat and open nature of the geography of the region, which would make it easier for air power to target the Houthis.
Al-Muslimi said that, for the Houthis, the battles in Taiz may not be about seeking full control of the governorate, but instead be a way of keeping the main battle away from their newly gained territories.
“In Taiz, in my opinion, the Houthis do not need to control it as long as they besiege it, and in reality, they will not try to control it because it is a burden more than an opportunity,” Al-Muslimi noted.

EU court overturns 2024 and 2025 sanctions decisions against former Russian senator Oleg Tkach (but he remains on the sanctions list)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:20:28 UTC
01:20:28 KST

EU court overturns 2024 and 2025 sanctions decisions against former Russian senator Oleg Tkach (but he remains on the sanctions list)
The General Court of the European Union annulled the Council of the EU’s September 2024 and September 2025 decisions to keep former Federation Council member Oleg Tkach on the sanctions list. An entry for the ruling is posted on the court’s website.
The EU initially imposed sanctions on Tkach in March 2022 because, as a Federation Council member, he had voted to ratify the treaty “on friendship, cooperation, and mutual assistance between the Russian Federation and the Donetsk and Luhansk People’s Republics.”
The court ruled that Tkach’s vote had provided sufficient grounds to impose sanctions on him but was not enough to keep him on the list in subsequent years.
The court concluded that Tkach had “withdrawn from Russian political life”: He did not seek reelection in September 2022 and had also acquired “citizenship in two other countries,” which disqualified him from holding political office in Russia.
The court also rejected the Council’s argument that the former senator had not publicly condemned the invasion of Ukraine. The ruling said his failure to do so could not automatically be taken as a sign of support, particularly given the harsh repression of anti-war views.
The Council also cited Tkach’s ties to the publishing company Olma Media Group, which he founded in 1991, as grounds for extending the sanctions. The group included the publisher Prosveshcheniye, which helped promote anti-Ukrainian narratives through school textbooks.
The Council maintained that although Tkach had formally stepped away from managing the company long ago, he continued to exert influence over it through a trust fund and entities linked to his family. The court rejected this argument because the Council had failed to explain Tkach’s specific role in the company. The court also said VEB.RF, the Russian Direct Investment Fund, and Sberbank had controlled a 75% stake in Prosveshcheniye since 2021.
The court therefore found that the grounds cited in the Council’s September 2024 and September 2025 decisions did not justify keeping Tkach on the sanctions list.
Tkach remains on the EU sanctions list under a March 14, 2026, Council decision. He has already filed a lawsuit seeking to overturn that extension, but the court has not yet ruled on the case. The Council’s September 22, 2026, decision lifting sanctions on billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman does not mention Tkach.

Governments Must Prohibit Superintelligent AI While We Still Can
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:19:48 UTC
01:19:48 KST

This month, Jacob Coxon, a researcher at Anthropic, resigned, warning that AI companies are racing towards “self-improving superintelligence” and that he and those building it believe it “could kill us all by the end of the decade.” And in July, a rogue swarm of AI agents escaped containment at OpenAI and hacked their way into another AI company just to cheat on a test. Over 1,000 employees at the top AI companies then implored the US government to ‘pace’ AI development.
Instances like these have shown that AI companies cannot reliably control their most advanced AIs. It is therefore clear to me that “pacing” while continuing on the same track is not the solution to the enormous risks at hand—and that the only way to keep humanity in control of AI is to prohibit the development of superintelligent AI altogether.
AI companies are not just building chatbots. Their stated goal is to build superintelligent AI: AI systems that can fully replace and outcompete humans at any task. Because there is no way to keep superintelligence under control, Nobel Prize winners, AI engineers like Coxon, and even the CEOs of AI companies have repeatedly warned that it poses an extinction risk to humanity.
Let me be clear: AI is the crucial technology of the 21st century, vital for ensuring national defense and economic competitiveness. But unlike controllable AI systems that should be integrated to strengthen our security, superintelligent AI would pose unprecedented national and global security threats. It would not be a tool humans can leverage: it would be an adversary, able to autonomously pursue its own objectives and permanently evade human control.
We have only to look at the Hugging Face hack this summer to understand how close we are to losing control. A rogue swarm of hundreds of AI agents broke out of OpenAI’s systems, reached the internet, and then hacked into the multi-billion-dollar company Hugging Face, all to cheat on an “internal” evaluation. For almost two weeks, OpenAI had no idea that this was happening. In the company’s own words, this incident was a “‘warning shot’ for us and for the world” that demonstrated how advanced AIs can now “take dangerous actions that no human directed.”
Instead of waiting for another warning shot, governments need to act now to prohibit superintelligence. Luckily, we do not need to search far for a framework on how to tackle this threat. On Sept. 8, Alex Sobel MP introduced my organization ControlAI’s Artificial Superintelligence Security Bill into the UK Parliament, making it the first legislature in the world to introduce a bill prohibiting superintelligence. Rather than a verdict on all AI, this bill targets superintelligence development specifically: prohibiting it domestically and requiring the UK to pursue an international agreement prohibiting it around the world.
This legislative framework allows the government to monitor and restrict precursors to superintelligence, such as AI capabilities like hacking. Crucially, it enables the detection and shutdown of superintelligence development well before any project gets dangerously close, enabling the country to make use of such precursors for legitimate AI purposes. It is an actionable framework that governments should evaluate and adopt, particularly by accelerating international efforts toward a ban on superintelligence.
But what about China? If superintelligence is developed anywhere, every nation and every citizen is under threat. This means that any American ban on superintelligence needs to be paired with America and its allies brokering international agreements that prevent and deter the development of superintelligence anywhere in the world.
This does not require creating an international regulator. All we need is a strong coalition of countries that bans superintelligence at home, and ensures that no one builds it abroad.
While announcing his resignation on Sept 8., the now-former Anthropic engineer Jacob Coxon wrote, “I don’t feel like we’re on track to prevent a global race” toward superintelligence. We might not be today, but we can change course quickly.
The momentum behind an international ban on developing superintelligence is picking up speed. Over 200 cross-party lawmakers across the UK and Canada have been ahead of the curve on superintelligence risks by recognizing it as a global and national security threat as part of ControlAI’s campaign. In addition to the newly introduced UK bill, Vice President J.D. Vance told AI companies this week, "If you're building Frankenstein, stop." Further, U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Greg Casar announced in early September that they will introduce a bill prohibiting superintelligence development and calling for international agreements to prohibit it.
And in October 2025, a broad coalition called to prohibit superintelligence internationally. This was signed by the scientific “godfathers” of AI Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, and bipartisan political figures like former President Trump advisor Steve Bannon, Ambassador Susan Rice, and former Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Admiral Mike Mullen, former President Trump advisor Steve Bannon.
Right now, many government officials and members of the public are hearing about the extinction risk from superintelligence for the first time. The warnings have reached millions. The next step is concrete action to address this national and global security threat.
This is a watershed moment, and we can’t afford to waste it. Governments have a clear choice: champion an international ban, or let the race to superintelligence reach its catastrophic end

Rare Earths at the Trump-Xi Summit: Relief Without a Resolution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:18:00 UTC
01:18:00 KST

Rare earths entered the Trump-Xi summit before the two leaders even sat down. On September 21, two days before President Xi Jinping’s arrival in the United States, China’s Foreign Ministry faced a series of questions on whether Beijing had “fully resumed rare earth deliveries,” whether a “November 10 deadline or expanded restrictions on rare earth exports” could be extended, and whether rare earths controls involving Japan would feature in the Washington talks. The responses were deliberately cautious: Beijing reiterated its commitment to “keeping the global industrial and supply chains of critical minerals safe and stable,” but emphasized that dual-use exports would remain subject to legal and security considerations.
The Foreign Ministry’s responses captured the central paradox of the summit: it may temporarily ease anxiety over rare earth supplies, but it is unlikely to lower the political and regulatory threshold for access.
In April 2025, China’s Ministry of Commerce and General Administration of Customs placed several medium and heavy rare earth elements – including samarium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium, lutetium, scandium, and yttrium – under export controls. Exporters of these items are required to apply for licenses, with the stated legal basis including China’s Export Control Law and regulations on dual-use items. This does not amount to a blanket ban on exports, but it does shift rare earth access from a purely commercial transaction to a regulated process shaped by licensing, end-use review, and national security considerations. Once such controls are embedded in a legal and bureaucratic system, they are not easily removed. A summit can improve predictability, but it will not result in the dismantling of China’s carefully built legal framework for export controls.
The same logic applies on the U.S. side. Even if the summit reduces short-term pressure, Washington is unlikely to abandon its effort to diversify away from China-centered critical mineral supply chains. In January 2026, the White House framed U.S. dependence on imports of processed critical minerals and their derivative products as a national security concern, noting that even where the United States has domestic mining capacity, it often lacks sufficient downstream processing capacity. The policy response has therefore gone beyond asking China for more predictable deliveries. The United States is investing in domestic processing, recycling and alternative supply chains, while also working with allies and partners to reduce exposure to single-source dependence. In this sense, any relief produced by the summit may buy some time, but it will not weaken Washington’s broader push for supply-chain diversification.
Rare earths occupy this strategic space because they are not simply another category of traded minerals. Their importance lies less in the raw materials themselves than in the capabilities of the downstream industries they support: high-performance magnets, electric vehicles, wind turbines, advanced electronics and defense systems. This gives rare earths a dual character. They are commercial inputs for global industries, but they are also strategic enablers for military and technological power.
Once a commodity acquires this dual-use profile, access to it is unlikely to be governed by market logic alone. For China, this strengthens the case for licensing and end-use scrutiny. For the United States, it reinforces the argument that dependence on China-centered supply chains is not merely an economic risk, but a strategic vulnerability. Rare earths can be discussed at the summit but the underlying strategic issues are not easily resolved.
This creates an asymmetric form of interdependence. China does not control every part of the global rare earth supply chain, but its position in processing and export licensing gives it a more immediate ability to shape access. The United States is not without options, but its alternatives require time: new processing capacity must be built, recycling systems expanded, and supply arrangements with allies and partners made commercially viable. This mismatch between China’s immediate leverage and the United States’ long-term adjustment capacity creates bargaining space, but not enough for a full reset. The result is a prolonged period of managed vulnerability on rare earths.
Where the summit could still matter lies in the management of risk. Neither side benefits from an uncontrolled shock to the rare earths market. China wants to preserve its right to screen sensitive exports, but it also has an interest in presenting itself as a stable supplier of critical minerals. The United States, meanwhile, wants to reduce dependence on China-centered supply chains, but it also needs time to build alternatives. This creates room for limited accommodation: clearer licensing procedures, smoother civilian trade, and more regular communication over end-use concerns. Yet these would be instruments of crisis management rather than signs of strategic convergence. The summit may reduce uncertainty over how the rules are applied, but it is unlikely to change the rules themselves.
The Trump-Xi summit, therefore, should not be read as a turning point in rare earth politics. Its significance lies less in changing the direction of policy than in clarifying the limits of what diplomacy can achieve. For Beijing, rare earths will remain a strategic resource subject to state control. For Washington, any temporary easing will not remove the underlying concern that dependence on China-centered supply chains creates long-term strategic exposure.
This is the meaning of relief without a resolution. In the emerging logic of China-U.S. geoeconomic competition, critical minerals are instruments of leverage, symbols of vulnerability, and test of strategic resilience.

Bangladesh premier says ‘humanitarian generosity’ cannot excuse political inaction on Rohingya crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Faisal Mahmud
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
The prime minister of Bangladesh said Wednesday that humanitarian assistance for Rohingya refugees cannot be substituted for political action, as he urged a clear international roadmap for their return to Myanmar.
“Humanitarian generosity cannot become an excuse for political inaction. Nor can Bangladesh be expected to shoulder this responsibility indefinitely,” Tarique Rahman told a high-level side event of the UN General Assembly on the Rohingya crisis in New York, co-convened by Bangladesh and The Gambia.
A media statement was issued by the Prime Minister’s office in Bangladesh.
Bangladesh hosts more than 1.2 million Rohingya, while thousands of babies are born in refugee camps every year, he said.
“The crisis originated in Myanmar. Its solution lies in Myanmar,” said Rahman, citing forced recruitment, arbitrary detention, movement restrictions and forced labor in Rakhine State.
He proposed action in five areas: a roadmap for safe and voluntary repatriation; an end to violence against civilians; predictable humanitarian funding; justice and accountability; and stronger cooperation against trafficking, illegal arms, digital scams and the “narco-economy.”
Rahman noted that the humanitarian appeal had fallen from more than $934 million in 2025 to about $710 million this year, covering only minimum lifesaving needs.
“Bangladesh has carried its responsibility with humanity. Now the international community must carry its responsibility with conviction,” he added.

Ukraine's real gross domestic product (GDP) growth this year will be lower than the current forecast of 1.6%, due to intensified Russian shelling; a likely scenario in which it will amount to about 0.5% is being considered, Minister of Economy and Environment Oleksandr Kravchenko said.
"We are considering possible scenarios in which the additional decline will exceed 1 percentage point. In other words, we will grow by 0.5% – this is the figure we are currently reviewing within the Ministry of Economy. We are regularly reviewing the situation," he said at the Forbes Ukraine Economic Resilience Forum in Kyiv on Wednesday.

"While we saw 4% year-over-year growth in July, we're already seeing around 0% in August. All these problems, which we are well aware of – the blocking of exports and the disruption of logistics – are already putting significant pressure on businesses, and we expect that, unfortunately, this will only intensify in the second half of the year," he added.
As previously reported, due to the disruption in industry and trade and the deterioration of business expectations, the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) lowered its estimate for real GDP growth this year to 1.1-1.2%, down from the previous forecast of 1.8%.
In its Budget Resolution for 2027-2029, the government projected GDP growth of 1.6% this year and an acceleration to 4.5% and 5.3% in 2027 and 2028, respectively. However, the government's draft state budget for 2027 is based on a pessimistic scenario of 1.3% GDP growth with a deficit of 15% of GDP.

Is Israel committing genocide in Lebanon? (VIDEO)
Israel is facing accusations of genocide over its military campaign in Lebanon, where thousands have been killed and large areas devastated. RT correspondent Steve Sweeney reports from Nabatieh, a city in the south of the country that has been repeatedly hit by Israeli strikes.
More than 4,300 people, including over 250 children and 130 medical professionals, have been killed since the latest escalation began in March, according to Lebanon’s Health Ministry.
The Lemkin Institute for Genocide Prevention and Doctors Against Genocide have accused Israel of pursuing what they called a “genocidal policy of absolute destruction,” targeting the foundations of life of Lebanon’s Shia communities. The groups said attacks on medical personnel were part of a sustained pattern affecting “the very systems necessary for civilian survival.”
Around 56,000 hectares of agricultural land have been affected, with losses to the sector estimated at more than $1 billion, according to Lebanon’s Agriculture Ministry.
Israel denies that its campaign targets Lebanon’s Shia population, saying its operations are directed against Hezbollah, the Iran-backed Lebanese armed group. Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has warned, however, that Beirut’s predominantly Shia Dahiya district would “look like Khan Yunis,” referring to a war-devastated city in Gaza.
The latest Israeli campaign in Lebanon began in early March, after Hezbollah attacked Israel following the start of US-Israeli strikes on Iran. Israel responded with airstrikes and later expanded its military operations in Lebanon.
Israeli attacks have continued despite a US-brokered framework agreed upon in June aimed at ending the fighting. The deal calls for a progressive Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon alongside Lebanese Army deployments and the disarmament of armed groups, including Hezbollah, but implementation has stalled.
Under the 1948 Genocide Convention, genocide requires intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group. RT looks at whether the destruction and statements accompanying Israel’s campaign could meet that definition.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday criticized the current international system as "failing" and asserted that Washington will consistently prioritize its national interests over the international order.
Addressing journalists on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Rubio argued that multilateral bodies have lost their core purpose and failed to resolve major global flashpoints.
"The international system is not in good shape right now, and these international norms people talk about," Rubio said. In the absence of a functional system, nation-states must look out for their own security, Rubio said, emphasizing the administration's foreign policy approach.
"At the end of the day, the United States will always act. At least as long as President Trump is in office, we will always act in the national interest of our country, not in the interest of the international order," he stressed. "We will never put the international order above the interest of the United States."

Russian Mi-8 Helicopter Enters Polish Airspace Near Kaliningrad in 42-Second Violation
A Russian military helicopter briefly violated Polish airspace near the country’s border with Russia’s Kaliningrad region on September 23, prompting Poland to scramble fighter jets, the Polish Armed Forces Operational Command reported.
According to the Operational Command, the incident occurred at 11:08 a.m. north of the town of Braniewo, near the Polish-Russian border.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The aircraft was identified as a Russian Armed Forces Mi-8 helicopter flying from the Kaliningrad region. It entered Polish airspace to a maximum depth of approximately 300 meters and remained there for 42 seconds before leaving.
Polish military radar systems tracked the helicopter throughout the incident. In response, Poland scrambled fighter aircraft, while ground-based forces and assets were placed on standby, the command said.
“The nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defense,” the Operational Command said.
The airspace violation occurred on the same day that Poland activated military aviation, air defense systems, and reconnaissance assets in response to Russian aerial strikes on Ukraine. Operations at Rzeszów and Lublin airports were temporarily suspended to allow military aircraft greater freedom to operate, with both airports later resuming normal operations.
The incident also comes amid growing Polish concerns over potential Russian hybrid attacks. On September 17, Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that attacks involving drones and missiles against countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland, represent the most likely security scenario in the coming months.
“In short: there is a real risk that drones or other types of missiles could enter the territory of one or more countries on the eastern flank, even cause destruction, while the official version would be that it was an accident,” Tusk said.

McDonald's CEO expects high inflation, flat traffic are not going away for restaurant industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:08:30 UTC
01:08:30 KST

McDonald's is predicting that flat traffic and higher inflation will continue to weigh on the restaurant industry, CEO Chris Kempczinski said Wednesday.
"One of the things I've talked to our team about is we need to stop talking about that being a difficult environment, and just say that is the environment," Kempczinski said on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "Because I think, as we look out forward, we're not expecting things to change."
For years, Kempczinski has been warning investors and analysts about the "challenging environment" faced by McDonald's and the broader industry. The burger chain reported U.S. same-store sales growth of just 0.8% in its most recent quarter as traffic to its domestic restaurants fell.
Diners have been eating out less frequently, pushing back against higher menu prices as they face increased costs on everything from gas to groceries. From August 2025 to July 2026, industry operators surveyed by the National Restaurant Association reported a net decline in customer traffic in every month but one.
To attract customers, McDonald's and its rivals have leaned into discounts. But diners aren't the only ones facing higher costs.
Restaurant operators — like McDonald's and its franchisees — have seen beef prices soar. Kempczinski said that beef costs have nearly doubled over the last five years in the company's biggest markets. Other expenses, like labor and construction, have also ticked higher, putting more pressure on margins.
"Across the board, we're seeing that inflation is sticky," Kempczinski said. "It's sticky, not just in the U.S., but around the world."
Faced with tougher operating conditions, McDonald's is focusing on stealing diners from its rivals.
"The biggest thing that you need to do in an environment like this is you have to be able to earn share," Kempczinski said. "You have to be able to actually grab growth from your competitors."
While he said McDonald's will likely have to consider price increases, he added the chain will have to be careful not to drive diners away. He reiterated that the company believes it erred by raising prices too quickly in the years after the Covid pandemic.
Kempczinski and other McDonald's executives will share more details about the company's plans to gain market share during its investor day on Wednesday.

For a decade, Kyiv’s Language Lab has taught Ukrainian to foreigners, including online, and along the way become an informal support network for its students, helping with everything from everyday problems to calling an ambulance. Now, marking its tenth anniversary, the school is formalizing that role with Ukraine Connected, a curated community with coordinators, meetups and regular events that aims to become the biggest network for internationals in Ukraine.
For founder Ksenia Golubytska, reaching 10 years is about more than longevity.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“First and foremost, it’s about trust – the trust of my team, my clients, my close ones who supported me along the way, and myself,” she said.
She said the milestone also reflects a deeper shift in how people see the Ukrainian language: “More and more people are finding real importance and value in learning Ukrainian, and being part of that is something I cherish deeply.”
The road was not easy.
“We got through COVID, through the full-scale invasion and ongoing war, and everything that came with it – so reaching 10 years feels earned,” Golubytska said.
Finding its identity
Language Lab did not start out as a Ukrainian-language school. In its early years, Golubytska said, the team experimented with “different languages, different approaches, different formats.”
The school found its clear identity around the time of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, when it settled on Ukrainian and on a format that worked for its clients.
‘This Is My Personal Contribution to Ukraine's Victory’
“That gave us solid ground, a real foundation to build on,” she said.
Over the years, the school has had more than 1,500 clients and more than 200 organized events. Its client list includes major international humanitarian and aid organizations, as well as embassies and diplomatic staff, international and Ukrainian companies, and media outlets such as Kyiv Post, with which it has a partnership.
Golubytska said the school plans to widen its reach further. One goal is to serve Ukrainians in the diaspora who want to reconnect with the language, alongside new courses and formats for different kinds of learners.
More than a language school
Over the years, Language Lab’s role for many foreign students has gone well beyond grammar lessons.
“We’ve become something like an entry point for them into Ukraine,” Golubytska said. That has meant “supporting them, answering questions, helping with everyday problems, even things like calling an ambulance when needed.”
The school has also hosted cultural events and social meetups for its students. Ukraine Connected, Golubytska said, is designed to take that to the next level.
“It’s structured as a social initiative, and to us it feels like a natural, logical continuation of everything the school has been doing all along,” she said.
How Ukraine Connected will work
Members will be able to register and join organized chats around different topics. But Golubytska stressed that the chats are a means, not the goal.
“The main focus isn’t the chat itself – it’s real connection: people meeting in real life or online and doing things together,” she said.
Coordinators will curate who joins and help organize the community’s activities. Members will share recommendations, help each other with urgent questions, and suggest ideas for small meetups and activities. The whole community will gather for larger events at least once every six months.
The initiative is aimed at people who live or work in Ukraine, want to understand Ukrainian culture better, are looking for Ukrainian business partners, are interested in investment opportunities, or want to support and promote Ukraine abroad. Its stated mission is to help foreigners lead a comfortable and fulfilling life in the country.
The ambition is large.
“Our ambition is to build the biggest community for internationals in Ukraine,” Golubytska said.
A bet on Ukraine’s future
For Golubytska, the anniversary is ultimately about looking ahead.
“It’s about hope – hope that this will keep developing, that more people will visit, invest, and move to Ukraine, and that Ukraine will be in the spotlight in the way it deserves,” she said.
“More than anything,” she added, “we want Ukraine Connected to be an entry point – a place that helps people feel at home in Ukraine, genuinely welcomed and part of something, not just passing through.”

EU court strikes down sanctions extension against former Russian senator

EU court strikes down sanctions extension against former Russian senator
The EU has failed to provide sufficient evidence to keep a former Russian official on its sanctions blacklist, the bloc’s General Court ruled on Wednesday. The decision came a day after the EU removed two Russian businessmen from the list as part of a deal to extend restrictions on thousands of others.
The court annulled the September 2024 and September 2025 extensions of sanctions against former Russian Senator Oleg Tkach, who represented Kaliningrad Region in the Federation Council from 2004 to 2022. He was also involved in publishing, founding and chairing Olma Media Group.
The EU first sanctioned Tkach in March 2022 over his vote to ratify treaties with the Donetsk and Lugansk People’s Republics, which later became part of Russia following referendums rejected by Ukraine and most Western countries. The case centered on whether the EU Council had grounds to keep extending the restrictions after Tkach left office.
According to Wednesday’s ruling, the Council failed to demonstrate that Tkach retained close ties to Russian authorities. The court also found that his failure to publicly oppose Russia’s military operation in Ukraine did not, by itself, constitute continued support for the authorities.
Brussels had also cited Tkach’s publishing background, including his links to Olma Media Group and textbook publisher Prosveshcheniye. However, the court found the evidence insufficient to establish his current role or influence at the companies.
The ruling does not affect the EU’s most recent sanctions extension from March 2026, which Tkach is challenging separately. He argues that condemnation based on his former Senate position is outdated and that the Council’s evidence is unreliable and lacks a “sound factual basis.” He has also argued that the measures are disproportionate.
A day before Wednesday’s ruling, the EU agreed to remove Russian businessmen Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from its sanctions list. Both had previously mounted legal challenges related to EU restrictions, while Fridman has also filed a multibillion-dollar arbitration claim against Luxembourg.
Their removal came as part of a compromise to renew sanctions against around 3,000 other individuals and entities for three years, until September 2029, replacing the bloc’s usual six-month renewal cycle.

Race to evacuate war-damaged Gaza buildings after deadly apartment block collapse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:06:39 UTC
01:06:39 KST

Race to evacuate war-damaged Gaza buildings after deadly apartment block collapse
GAZA/CAIRO, Sept 23 - Officials in Gaza say plans to evacuate people from war-damaged buildings after the deadly collapse of an apartment block last week face major challenges, including a lack of demolition equipment and limited land to relocate residents.
Nearly a year since a ceasefire ended major fighting between Israel and Hamas, officials say tens of thousands of people, with few options for shelter, are living in buildings damaged during Israel's military campaign, despite repeated warnings that they should leave.
In the early hours of September 16, the danger became clear when the Al-Saada building in Gaza City's Al-Rimal neighbourhood collapsed, killing 21 people. At least 45 survivors were rescued from the rubble.
Gaza officials say more than 2,000 buildings have been classified as being at risk. Other war-damaged buildings have previously collapsed, causing casualties, including amid winter storms.
"These buildings now represent ticking time bombs for residents and displaced people in many places," said Husni Muhanna, spokesperson for the Gaza City municipality, adding that this presented a "real danger" with the weather set to deteriorate into the winter.
On Sunday, Gaza authorities announced an emergency plan to evacuate people from 255 buildings most at risk of collapse and demolish them.
An Egyptian-led relief body had offered to provide transport to move those evacuated to designated shelters, said Ismail Al-Thawabta, head of the Hamas-run Gaza government's media office.
But he said the plan faced major obstacles, "including some families refusing to evacuate unsafe buildings despite the warnings, severe funding shortages, a lack of heavy equipment needed for safe demolition, and limited safe land available to relocate displaced people."
SHORTAGE OF EQUIPMENT
Large-scale reconstruction in Gaza has yet to begin, with US-brokered efforts to get Hamas to disarm and Israeli forces to withdraw largely stalled. A population of more than 2 million lives confined to about a third of the enclave, mainly housed in makeshift tents or overcrowded rooms in damaged buildings. Deadly Israeli airstrikes, which Israel says target militants, have continued.
Most of Gaza's buildings were destroyed by airstrikes or bulldozed by Israeli forces, and almost all others have suffered damage.
Palestinian and UN officials blame Israel's restrictions on Gaza for the lack of heavy machinery to clear rubble and materials and equipment to rebuild homes.
In response to a request for comment, Israel's military said it was committed to minimising harm to civilians and that any activities, including against "terrorist infrastructure", were carried out based on operational necessity.
COGAT, the Israeli military agency that coordinates aid, said entry of heavy equipment and reconstruction materials would not be authorised until Hamas disarmed. It said Hamas exploited humanitarian aid, something the Palestinian militant group denies.
Alessandro Mrakic, head of the United Nations Development Programme office in Gaza, said a shortage of equipment meant people had to dig through the rubble with their hands when the Al-Saada building collapsed, and that oil and spare parts were needed to keep the machinery already in Gaza in service.
He estimated the number of buildings at risk of collapse at 400. "We know that these buildings will collapse, especially now with the upcoming winter," he said. "We are running against time."
RESIDENTS SAY THEY HAVE NOWHERE ELSE TO GO
The Al-Saada building was in an area that was hit by Israeli bombardment two days after a Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, triggered Israel's offensive in Gaza. Israel launched heavy airstrikes followed by a ground campaign which it said were aimed at destroying Hamas and its underground network of tunnels.
Mohammad Arafa, head of the Gaza Engineers Association, said that based on assessments by fellow engineers who inspected the Al-Saada building over the past year, its collapse resulted from structural weakness after bombardment damaged several concrete pillars supporting its foundations.
But people had sheltered there because they had nowhere else to go, said Feryal Abu Ghanem, whose daughter-in-law was staying with her family when the building collapsed and was among those killed.
Bassam Naseer, a displaced man living in another damaged building nearby, said he feared the same thing would happen there. "No one is looking after us. The conditions are very difficult," he said.
After the Al-Saada's collapse, the Israel Defense Forces said in a social media post that it had not struck the building during the war. It did not respond to questions about residents saying it had struck the building, or about whether the building had been damaged by strikes on the surrounding area.
Eyad Azzam, who lost his pregnant wife and a 3-year-old son in the Al-Saada building's collapse, showed a video on his mobile phone of another son, Abdel-Rahman, trapped in the wreckage of the building before he was pulled to safety.
Abdel-Rahman, 7, had reached towards his mother, hoping to protect her from fallen rock, his father said. "He put out his hand and it wasn't a rock that had fallen, it was the entire ceiling."
People continued to live under damaged ceilings or columns for lack of other options, Azzam said.
"Today people say, 'This is a dangerous place to live in.' But where shall I go?" he said. "Even in the street there's no place." REUTERS

President De La Espriella orders militarization of Colombian resort city amid gang retaliation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:05:43 UTC
01:05:43 KST

Laura Gamba Fadul
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
Colombian President Abelardo De La Espriella ordered the immediate militarization of Santa Marta on Tuesday night, deploying troops and launching low-altitude air patrols to regain control of the Caribbean port city following a violent offensive by a powerful narco-paramilitary cartel.
The security crisis erupted after the military killed a senior leader of the Autodefensas Conquistadoras de la Sierra Nevada (ACSN) along with six associates during an operation in the region. In retaliation, the armed group declared an "armed strike," threatening merchants and drivers to enforce a commercial lockout and transport shutdown across Santa Marta and neighboring Cienaga, local media reported.
The intimidation campaign paralyzed the coastal city of almost 600,000 residents, a major domestic and international tourism hub renowned for its beaches and proximity to Tayrona National Natural Park. Local business representatives estimated that around 95% of commercial establishments remained closed Wednesday morning, while public transit services suspended operations and schools closed.
Throughout Tuesday and into Wednesday, armed men on motorcycles set fire to trucks and buses, engaged in sporadic shootouts with security forces, and forced shopkeepers to pull down their shutters.
President De La Espriella traveled to Santa Marta late Tuesday night, posting video footage on social media showing him walking through heavily guarded streets to reassure residents.
"Those who do not submit will be taken down, and I will not allow them to continue bringing our people to their knees through terror," De La Espriella declared, confirming that three suspects had been arrested in connection with the arson attacks and threats.
In office since August, De La Espriella has pursued a militarized strategy against illegal armed groups, backed by enhanced security cooperation with the US. He emphasized that organizations such as the ACSN, Los Pachenca, and the Gulf Clan would face the full force of state power.
"We are going after all those bandits without mercy," the president said.
The ACSN traces its origins to legacy far-right paramilitary groups that originally formed to fight leftist guerrilla forces in the 1990s and 2000s. Today, the heavily armed criminal network finances its operations through international cocaine trafficking, illegal mining, and systematic extortion.

Ms Rachel doubles down on Palestine activism and being ‘political’ on SubwayTakes series
Renowned children's educator and YouTube star Ms Rachel has doubled down on her pro-Palestine stance, shedding light on the consequences of Israel’s brutal war on Gaza, following media furore calling on her to be ‘neutral’ and dubbing her ‘controversial’.
Ms Rachel, real name Rachel Accurso, appeared on a SubwayTakes episode on Wednesday with Egyptian-American host and producer Kareem Rahma.
In the episode, which has been viewed over 300,000 times at the time this article was published, she argued that late American chidren's TV personality Mr Rogers was political.
She describes how one of the episodes he aired showcased Black people swimming in a pool with white people during a period of widespread racism, which she said was a major turning point in how People of Colour were treated.
“In the media, they say that Ms Rachel should be like Mr Rogers and not be political, and actually he was political so much on the show. I think maybe they didn’t watch it or maybe they weren’t paying attention because he did so many things,” she said.
“He was against the nuclear arms race,” she said, adding that in one of his episodes there was a make-believe scenario where a king was building bombs, based on the belief that others around him also possessed them, and then said there was no more money left for music due to it being spent on bombs.
The children’s educator, who has been vocal on the war on Gaza since the offensive was launched in October 2023, hinted that the scenario was similar to how US taxpayers’ money was funding assaults in Gaza.
In the SubwayTakes episode, Ms Rachel also shed light on how Israeli restrictions on emergency aid in Gaza had left many children starving to death.
She also spoke about individual cases where Palestinian children had to have limbs amputated due to the offensive.
“They’re [Israel] blocking them from medical care, and the mums are like I’m watching my child die from something preventable and sometimes both siblings have the disease and die in front of the parents,” she said.
“…Why would we bomb kids and take their limbs and their schools, all of their schools and their hospitals and then say we can’t call this genocide? The UN said this is intentional targeting of children. Children were shot in the head and the chest,” she continued.
Ms Rachel went on to express her frustration at the continuing humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza, calling out the lack of action from international organisations and countries around the world.
Ms Rachel, who has amassed over 21 million followers on YouTube and signed a deal with Netflix in 2025, regularly uses her social media platforms to condemn the Israeli government over its actions in Gaza.
Earlier this month, she said she would match rapper Macklemore’s $1 million donation to a charity supporting Palestine, after the singer was booted as an opening act from Ed Sheeran’s tour for calling for a “free Palestine”.
In a social media post, she said every “wealthy white celebrity” should do the same.
Israel’s war on Gaza has killed over 73,000 Palestinians, displaced much of the population, and devastated entire neighbourhoods.
According to the UN, Gaza now hosts the largest group of child amputees in modern history.

A coalition of progressive Jewish leaders and Michigan Democrats sent a letter to former Vice President Kamala Harris on Sunday urging her to press Senate candidate Dr. Abdul El-Sayed on his positions regarding Jewish safety and Israel during their joint campaign appearance on Tuesday. However, the leaders expressed deep concern regarding El-Sayed's candidacy, stating that he "has had every opportunity to meet our request to support our basic needs" but "has declined even to respond." The coalition outlined five core principles candidates must address to guarantee Jewish safety, including for Zionists, protecting identity rights, upholding Jewish sovereignty in Israel, welcoming full political participation, and providing an affirmative vision for the Middle East.
El-Sayed has been criticized for blaming Israel for local issues in Michigan
The letter criticized past remarks by El-Sayed, pointing out that he has called Israelis "bloodthirsty," referred to American support for Israel as "purchased loyalty," blamed Israel for local issues in Michigan, and rejected Israel as a Jewish state. Emphasizing that support cannot be taken for granted, the coalition wrote in their open letter that "every constituency must occasionally remind its party that support is earned, not owed," describing the campaign as "a good faith effort to make our needs unmistakably clear, and to invite any candidate seeking public office — now or in the future — to engage, listen, learn, and grow."
Building on their message from the letter, coalition leaders expanded on these themes during a subsequent press conference. Rabbi Michael Moskowitz of Temple Shir Shalom captured the widespread unease felt by families, stating that “we have been greatly concerned in the midst of this campaign and the language that we hear being used,” expressing concern “when language comes out that is using antisemitic dog whistles, things that have concerned us greatly over the years it worries my community.” Moskowitz added that his congregants felt "homeless right now and not sure where they can turn,” and that his community is a Zionist congregation and said, therefore, “we want our candidates who are running for office that we want to support to understand that and appreciate our concerns and what matters to us as a Jewish community.”

Looking beyond the immediate election cycle, Joan Lowenstein, president of the Ann Arbor Jewish Federation, emphasized the deep ancestral connection to Israel, stating, “Both of these places are my home, and I have always been part of trying to convince people that the Jewish connection to Israel is not a political one. It's our ancestral home, and it's the center of 3,000 years of Jewish history.”
'You can’t untangle Judaism from Zionism'
David Kramer, a prominent Democratic fundraiser and community leader, underscored the political and moral imperative for leaders to act, stating that “You can’t untangle Judaism from Zionism,” and that “Jewish people and Zionism are one and the same, you can’t untangle them, and I think some of the efforts by particular candidates, the senate candidate being one of them, to imply that the Jews should be protected but Zionists are on their own is deeply troubling.”
Harris and El-Sayed held a roundtable discussion in Detroit on Tuesday, focused on maternal health, reproductive freedom, and black maternal mortality alongside healthcare experts and reproductive rights advocates. The recorded public roundtable focused entirely on healthcare and maternal mortality, with neither Harris nor other speakers addressing the letter or the controversies surrounding El-Sayed's past statements on Israel.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on X that another round of “message exchanges and clarifications” took place between Iran and the US through Qatari mediators on Tuesday.
Baghaei said Iran had clarified its conditions for resuming diplomacy during the two-hour exchange, including an understanding on ensuring safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz between the two coastal countries.
Iran’s stated conditions also include the lifting of US sanctions, including the naval blockade, an end to the war, and the release of frozen Iranian assets.

IRGC benefiting from false hopes of renewed negotiations, expert tells ‘Post’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:04:04 UTC
01:04:04 KST

The indirect talks between Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, which many have viewed as a sign of Tehran’s willingness to reengage in negotiations, are only “half” the “truth” of what is really taking place, INSS Iran expert Beni Sabti told The Jerusalem Post on Wednesday.
For the first time since the memorandum of understanding (MoU) failed in July, Araghchi and the US envoys communicated through mediators, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
Sabti said that the talks and promises to open Hormuz meant little when Iran was continuing to attack ships and attempting to assert control over the strait.
A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Tuesday that Tehran was willing to reopen Hormuz provided Washington openly committed to resolving the conflict diplomatically. However, only a day after the statement, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center reported that a cargo vessel was struck, resulting in two casualties.
Hassan Ghashghavi, spokesperson for the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, also confirmed on Tuesday that the Islamic Republic had no intention of abandoning its attempts to control the Strait of Hormuz. The parliament adopted provisions allowing the regime authorities to seize 20% of a vessel’s cargo, or its value, from ships violating Iran’s rules for passage through the strait.
'This is the Iranian way'
“They talk, and they attack, and this is the Iranian way, the terrorist organization way. It is exactly what Hamas did during the war,” Sabti said.
“There were negotiations, but there were also attacks and war. They want all their conditions to be met, and then there will be negotiations or an opening of the strait. They want all of the frozen money released, all the wars, especially by Israel against their proxies and against themselves, to stop, and other conditions,” he noted.
“These seven points cannot be fulfilled, and they know that. So they come for negotiations, but not with 100% desire and will, goodwill, or a true heart. It’s just kind of a theater, a lie that they bring,” Sabti added.
IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi admitted on Tuesday that he viewed negotiations as another strategy of the war, saying that “if the country’s interests require it, negotiations can be part of the battle while we remain prepared for combat… One war is fought with weapons; in negotiations, the war is fought with words, arguments, and diplomatic methods.”
In an interview with Agence France-Presse, Mohebbi also claimed that Iran had tightened its conditions to end the conflict and had refused Washington’s multiple attempts to return to the negotiating table.
The stark difference between Mohebbi’s narrative and what is being portrayed in New York is where the half-truth lies, Sabti explained. Those in New York were “not the relevant people to talk to” as the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps is firmly in control of Iran.
'This is the problem of the West'
“This is the problem of the West: They think the entire Iranian regime is one entity and that it is all the same: If you talk to the president or the foreign minister, it’s like talking to the whole regime because this is the way it is in the Western world,” he said, adding that those in the IRGC were profiting from Western naivety and using diplomats to “buy a little more time.”
With reports indicating that Saudi Arabia is restarting operations at its East-West Pipeline, potentially allowing 7 million barrels per day of oil to return to the global market amid growing frustration with the Houthis, Iran’s strategy of holding the strait hostage is slowly failing, he claimed.
With the Iranian economy suffering after years of sanctions that have intensified since August’s Operation Economic Outcast [US President Donald Trump’s “Economic D-Day”], IRGC officials running the country are hoping for some relief as a gesture of goodwill from the West – regardless of whether they have any real intention of following through, Sabti concluded.
