Poland accuses Russian military helicopter of violating its airspace
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:37:20 BST
00:37:20 KST

Poland accuses Russian military helicopter of violating its airspace
- Published
Poland has said a Russian military helicopter briefly violated its airspace, forcing the Nato member to scramble fighter jets while ground forces remained on alert.
Its military said the Mi-8 aircraft had crossed from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad on Wednesday morning, penetrating Polish airspace to a depth of about 300 metres (328 yards) and staying for 42 seconds north of Braniewo.
It said "the nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defence". Moscow did not comment immediately.
Poland and other European Nato members have recently said Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine - Moscow denies this.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Moscow does not plan to attack Nato states.
By contrast, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said this month that it was Europe that was constantly talking about preparing for war, and he warned: "If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war [from that in Ukraine], and it will be very short."
Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory, including the Crimea peninsula annexed in 2014.
In a statement, the Polish Army Operational Command said the brief incursion had happened at 11:08 (09:08 GMT), and the helicopter had been tracked by radar.
Poland's air defence units were operating around the clock ready to "ensure the safety of Polish airspace", it added.
A number of Russian drones and one unarmed Russian missile have landed in Poland since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which is not a member of Nato.
Last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggested Russia was planning drone and missile strikes against Poland and other countries on Nato's eastern flank.
"In recent weeks, the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans... has intensified," he said.
"The intent is to intimidate us and break our effort to support Ukraine. The result will be the exact opposite. We are not intimidated because we know that our security today and tomorrow is at stake in Ukraine."
French President Emmanuel Macron said shortly afterwards that his country had been targeted by Russian hybrid attacks in the past few weeks, vowing that this would not be left "without a response".
Macron said he had already ordered a plan to protect the country's critical infrastructure and defence industry sites.
Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary.
These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary.
There have recently been a number of suspicious fires and blasts at defence facilities in a number of European Nato members from Italy to Bulgaria to Estonia, with some of the affected countries blaming Russia.
Earlier this month, Germany said Russia was responsible for August's drone attack at Leipzig airport - an accusation denied by Moscow as "absurd".
And earlier this week, Lithuania's prime minister told the BBC that his country had already made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they would "not surrender" if attacked.
Ukraine said the drone's target "could have been the diplomatic train", while the Russian military said only that it had struck "railway infrastructure".

KUALA LUMPUR, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Malaysia's domestic tourism recorded 76.9 million visitors in the second quarter of 2026, up 4.3 percent from 73.8 million a year earlier and 3 percent from the previous quarter, official data showed on Wednesday.

The stronger growth in tourism expenditure compared with visitor numbers indicates an increase in domestic tourism spending during the quarter, the department said.
The second-quarter performance reflects continued growth in domestic travel, with both visitor and tourist numbers increasing from a year earlier, supporting tourism-related economic activity across the country. (1 ringgit equals 0.25 U.S. dollars) ■

Israel’s Central Elections Committee voted Wednesday to bar Arab-majority parties and two candidates from next month’s election, a move that could affect the balance of a closely contested vote but remains subject to Supreme Court review.
Israel’s Central Elections Committee voted Wednesday to disqualify the United Arab List, or Ra’am, from contesting the Oct. 27 election following a request from members of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s ruling coalition.
The decision is not final and must be reviewed by Israel’s Supreme Court, which has overturned most similar disqualifications in previous elections.
Ra’am made history in 2021 when it joined a governing coalition that ousted Netanyahu from power, becoming the first independent Arab party to participate in an Israeli government coalition.
The party recently took the unprecedented step of recruiting Jewish candidate Yoav Segalovitz, who served in the 2021-2022 government and was credited with efforts to improve security in Arab communities.
Palestinian citizens of Israel, largely descendants of Palestinians who remained following the establishment of Israel in 1948, account for about 20% of the population. Until 2021, Arab parties had remained outside governing coalitions.
The Central Elections Committee, whose composition reflects the balance of political parties in the Knesset, also voted to disqualify lawmaker Ofer Cassif and Sami Abu Shehadeh, leader of the Palestinian Balad party and a former Knesset member.
The committee said its decision against Abu Shehadeh was based on allegations that he denied Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state and supported armed struggle by an enemy state or terrorist organization against Israel.
The request to disqualify Abu Shehadeh was submitted by far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir, notoriously known for his radical views against Palestinians.
Abu Shehadeh rejected the decision and vowed to continue his political campaign.
“This development will not scare us,” he said. “Racists are afraid of equality, and Ben Gvir and Netanyahu are afraid of the Arab vote in this electoral battle.”
Adalah, a legal rights group representing Israel’s Arab minority as well as Cassif and Abu Shehadeh, said there was “no legal basis” for their disqualification.
Israel is scheduled to hold its general election Oct. 27, with Netanyahu seeking to remain in power amid a closely contested race.
The Supreme Court has overturned most previous attempts by the election committee to disqualify candidates. In 2019, however, it barred far-right candidate Michael Ben-Ari from running, overturning the committee’s decision to allow his candidacy.

Italian Parliament backs Meloni’s plan to restart nuclear power
Unknown

Italian Parliament backs Meloni’s plan to restart nuclear power
ROME, Sept 23 - Italy's upper house Senate on Wednesday gave final approval to a government plan to restart nuclear power generation, almost 40 years after a referendum led to the closure of Italy's reactors.
The government aims to deploy advanced modular reactors to help decarbonise industry and strengthen energy security, arguing that technological and safety advances have rendered the 1987 anti-nuclear vote obsolete.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's right-wing administration is seeking to shield the economy from a surge in energy prices triggered by the conflicts in the Middle East, reviving calls to reduce dependence on foreign energy supplies.
"Sustainable nuclear power, together with renewable energy sources, will make Italy a safe, independent and competitive country," Energy Minister Gilberto Pichetto Fratin said after the vote.
Italy relies heavily on energy imports, including electricity generated by nuclear plants in neighbouring countries such as France, but anti-nuclear campaigners argue that safety concerns and the lengthy time needed to build new reactors outweigh any benefits of restarting the sector.
Italians remain divided on the issue. A June poll by Demopolis found that 51% supported restarting nuclear power generation, but a majority opposed the construction of a plant near their homes.
When it unveiled the plan last year, the government estimated that nuclear energy accounting for at least 11% of Italy's energy mix could save €17 billion ($19 billion) in decarbonisation costs by 2050.
Italy's national energy and climate plan says the share could eventually rise to 22%.
The law gives the government 12 months to adopt the implementing decrees needed to relaunch nuclear power production. It also sets out provisions for decommissioning old facilities and establishing an independent regulator.
Centre-left opposition parties largely opposed the measure and urged the government not to allocate additional land for new reactors.
"Any new plants should be located primarily in areas that are already developed, degraded or affected by decommissioned industrial activities, without consuming additional land," said Five Star Movement senator Elena Sironi. REUTERS

Balad chairman barred from running in election following 31-4 Central Elections Committee vote

The Central Elections Committee voted 31-4 on Wednesday to bar Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh from running in the October 27 election. It accepted an Otzma Yehudit petition alleging that he supported armed struggle against Israel by a terrorist organization.
The decision is not final. Under Basic Law: The Knesset, the disqualification of an individual candidate requires Supreme Court approval before taking effect. The court is set to hear election disqualification cases next week.
Abu Shehadeh, who is No. 3 on the Joint List slate, said he would challenge the decision, which he said it an attempt to silence Arab society’s political voice and exclude it from the political arena.
In an exceptional move, Deputy Supreme Court President Noam Sohlberg, the committee’s chairman, joined the vote in favor of disqualification, departing from a two-decade practice under which committee chairmen have abstained to preserve their neutrality.
Sohlberg: Disqualification must remain a last resort
Sohlberg said Abu Shehadeh had failed to provide a satisfactory explanation for the statements at the center of the case.
“If there is a case in which the application is clear, this is the case,” he said.
The last committee chairman to participate in such a vote was Supreme Court justice Mishael Cheshin in 2003.
Sohlberg’s vote followed a warning at the beginning of the proceedings that disqualification must remain a last resort, since it denies an entire constituency the ability to support its chosen candidate.
Section 7A of Basic Law: The Knesset allows a candidate or list to be barred for rejecting Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, inciting racism, or supporting armed struggle against Israel by an enemy state or terrorist organization.
The Supreme Court has interpreted those grounds narrowly. Disqualification requires clear, convincing, and unequivocal evidence that the prohibited position lies at the heart of a candidate’s political activity, generally demonstrated through a sustained pattern rather than an isolated statement.
The Otzma Yehudit petition centered on an Arabic-language article Abu Shehadeh published on October 8, 2023, one day after the Hamas massacre.
In the article, he described the attack as an “important historic event” in military, political, and strategic terms.
If “small and besieged Gaza” could surprise Israel on that scale, others could do so more effectively, Abu Shehadeh wrote.
Otzma Yehudit said the article had praised Hamas’s massacre and encouraged others to learn from it. National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, Otzma Yehudit’s chairman, told the committee Abu Shehadeh’s subsequent explanations were implausible given what was already known about the killings and abductions.
Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara’s position was unusually severe compared with her responses to the other disqualification requests.
In their written submission, she and State Attorney Amit Aisman said the evidence, particularly the October 8 article, apparently indicated that Abu Shehadeh had expressed support for a terrorist organization’s armed struggle against Israel.
They initially stopped short of expressly recommending disqualification, noting that previous cases had involved extensive, long-term evidence of systematic conduct.
During Wednesday’s hearing, however, the Attorney-General’s Office said Abu Shehadeh’s explanations had remained unsatisfactory, and that there was a basis for the request. His failure to condemn the attack in the article was not a neutral omission; it had.
Abu Shehadeh: 'I oppose armed struggle'
Participating remotely, Abu Shehadeh said he had written the article on October 7 before he understood the full scale of the atrocities. He acknowledged that it should not have been published in that form.
“I have never called for violence or terrorism,” he told the committee. “I oppose armed struggle.”
Abu Shehadeh said his description of the attack as historically important meant that events after October 7 would not resemble those before it. The article had analyzed Israel’s intelligence failure and called for an end to the military path in favor of a diplomatic process led by the Palestinian Authority and Arab states, he said.
Abu Shehadeh also condemned the Hamas massacre and cited other writings in which he opposed armed struggle and harm to civilians.
Adalah, which represents Abu Shehadeh, said the decision depended on a false portrayal of his political record. His three decades of public activity, together with repeated condemnations of harm to Jewish and Palestinian civilians, had demonstrated a commitment to nonviolent political action, it said.
Adalah Director-General Hassan Jabareen said the article had contained no direct call for violence, and that its central conclusion favored a political solution.
He accused the attorney-general of applying an expansive interpretation to a single Arabic-language article while finding that broader records cited in petitions against Otzma Yehudit and the Religious Zionist Party did not reach the evidentiary threshold for disqualification on grounds of racist incitement.
The disqualification attracted support from coalition and opposition representatives.
The Democrats chairman Yair Golan said genuine democratic partnership required “redlines,” adding that his party opposed the blanket exclusion of Arab parties and would also support barring Ben-Gvir.
The plenum of the Central Elections Committee is primarily a political body composed of representatives of factions in the outgoing Knesset. Its decisions have frequently been overturned by the High Court of Justice, including previous decisions barring Balad and its candidates.
The combination of Sohlberg’s vote and the attorney-general’s position distinguishes Abu Shehadeh’s case from the other challenges heard this week.
The High Court will decide whether the exceptionally grave timing and language of the October 8 article can satisfy a legal test that has generally required a broader and more sustained body of evidence.
On Wednesday, the committee also voted to disqualify Hadash MK Ofer Cassif.
It also considered requests involving Ra’am, the Joint List, and Balad. Challenges against Otzma Yehudit, the Religious Zionist Party-Zehut list, and The Democrats are scheduled for Thursday.

More Range, More Payload: Ukraine’s Race to Build Better Drone Batteries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:31:00 UTC
00:31:00 KST

The next breakthrough in Ukraine’s drone war may not be a new aircraft or weapon, but the battery powering it.
One of the Ukrainian battery maker is betting on solid-state technology to make drones lighter, longer-range and capable of carrying heavier payloads, while seeking to scale production to as many as 10,000 battery units a day and reduce Ukraine’s reliance on foreign components.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Pavlo Yesyp, PAWELL’s co-founder, told Kyiv Post that the company is developing new battery technologies for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), electronic warfare systems and unmanned ground vehicles as Ukraine races to maintain its technological edge.
Yesyp spoke to Kyiv Post after the company took part in the world’s largest drone exhibition, where he said the scale of China’s technological development stood out most.
“What impressed me most was the level of technological advancement China has achieved,” he said.
He described seeing drone applications ranging from firefighting to systems designed to wash windows on high-rise buildings, saying there was “a distinct feeling that we were getting a glimpse into the future.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
Finland, Ukraine Seal Major Drone Deal as Stubb Exposes Russia’s Stalled Donbas Offensive
He added Ukraine remains highly competitive in military drone technology but said that Ukrainian companies did not have public exhibition booths, which he described as a security-driven decision given the presence of representatives from Russian military technology companies.
For the company, he said, the exhibition reinforced the need to develop domestic capabilities.
“To maintain and expand our advantage, we must localize the production of all components in Ukraine as quickly as possible,” Yesyp said. “Our goal is to achieve maximum technological independence.”
Moving beyond conventional drone batteries
According to Yesyp, one of the company’s main areas of development is solid-state battery technology.
According to him, the company is developing solid-state systems, which replace the liquid or gel electrolyte used in conventional batteries with a solid material. The company says its solid-state products can reduce battery weight by 30% compared with conventional lithium-ion alternatives of similar capacity.
Yesyp said the weight reduction is particularly important for unmanned platforms because every kilogram saved can be allocated to additional equipment.
“For UAVs, this is a critical advantage: the lower weight and stable operating temperature allow the drone to fly 30-50% farther while carrying a significantly heavier payload.”
He said the company is also working on sodium-ion battery packs, which he described as a lower-cost option for unmanned ground vehicles (UGV). Unlike lithium-based batteries, sodium-ion technology does not rely on scarce lithium resources, although Yesyp acknowledged that such batteries can be heavier.
Scaling production during wartime
PAWELL is targeting production capacity of up to 10,000 battery units per day, according to Yesyp, who said the goal is achievable despite the challenges created by Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Security is the biggest obstacle, he said, making decentralization central to the company’s expansion strategy.
Rather than relying on a single large facility, the company plans to develop a network of smaller production sites and protected locations. The company says its batteries are manufactured in Ukraine, with its own production and research-and-development capabilities.
Yesyp said the company is also applying LEAN management principles to standardize production, reduce waste and make facilities operate as a coordinated network. The broader objective, he said, is to build as much of the battery supply chain in Ukraine as possible.
“Our strategic goal is to achieve 100% localization of production within Ukraine itself,” Yesyp said.
He acknowledged that imported components remain part of the equation, particularly as Ukraine works with European partners and draws on technologies developed in Asia. But he argued that greater domestic production would reduce strategic dependence on foreign suppliers.
Bigger drones could transform battlefield logistics
Yesyp said drones capable of carrying payloads of up to 200 kilograms (440 pounds) over distances exceeding 250 kilometers (155 miles) could fundamentally change battlefield operations, moving beyond precision strikes toward what he called “scalable robotic warfare.”
He said such systems could target ammunition depots, command posts and fuel storage facilities deep behind the front line, while also delivering heavy cargo and evacuating wounded troops.
                                                                                                                                                                         
He linked these capabilities to the “Air-Land Economy” strategy championed by former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, which envisions unmanned and robotic systems taking on dangerous tasks on the ground and in the air, reducing the need to expose human personnel to risk.
But Yesyp said such capabilities depend heavily on battery technology.
“Lifting 200 kilograms and flying 250 kilometers requires energy of a completely different density,” he said, arguing that conventional batteries are too heavy for such applications.
Company’s solid-state technology, he added, is designed to provide the energy density needed for longer-range, heavier-payload drones.
“Our innovative solid-state solutions provide the technological ‘foundation’ that delivers the necessary energy density, enabling the Air-Land Economy concept to function not just on paper, but in actual combat,” he said.
Keeping production running under attack
Maintaining manufacturing capacity while Russian strikes continue against Ukrainian infrastructure presents another challenge.
Yesyp said PAWELL’s approach rests on three principles: decentralization, limiting sensitive information about production, and state support.
“We cannot afford to operate by the old rules,” he said, arguing that a distributed production network allows other facilities to continue operating if one location is affected.
He also stressed the importance of information security, saying companies must avoid publicly revealing details that could expose production facilities to attack.
“That is precisely why, as I mentioned earlier, we did not set up public Ukrainian stands at the international exhibition,” Yesyp said. “The enemy constantly monitors the information space, looking for targets.”
The next battery breakthrough
Looking ahead, Yesyp predicted rapid development in battery technology over the next two to three years.
He said the company expects advances in power systems to significantly increase the endurance of different UAV platforms, while new battery chemistries could eventually provide alternatives to lithium-based technologies.
“The lifecycle of any invention at the front is only three to six months – exactly the time the enemy needs to devise a countermeasure,” Yesyp said. “Consequently, we must win every subsequent cycle of innovation.”
Yesyp said improvements in power systems are essential for increasing a drone’s range and payload capacity.
“A drone’s ability to fly further and carry a heavier payload is made possible solely by improvements in power systems,” he said, adding that new battery chemistries are likely to emerge as lithium becomes increasingly scarce.
Scientists worldwide are already working to develop alternatives and maximize the amount of energy that can be stored in increasingly compact battery systems, Yesyp added.

Rubio says US will try to secure energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said Washington will try to secure an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, although he acknowledged that doing so would be difficult.
Source: Rubio's remarks at a press conference in New York, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Rubio said reaching an energy ceasefire will be difficult because both Russia and Ukraine have identified attacks on each other's energy sector as a strategic objective.
Quote: "The Ukrainians are inflicting pain on the Russians by hitting their energy sector, which is a revenue source. The Russian side is inflicting pain on the Ukrainian side by targeting their electric grid, especially as we head into winter. So, there is the challenge, it's that both sides have identified energy as a strategic objective of their war aims… So that's why it's not easy to overnight just say 'Let's reach an agreement'."
More details: Rubio said, however, that an energy ceasefire would benefit both Ukraine and Russia.
Quote: "I think if you asked President Zelenskyy, he would argue that the ability to protect his electric grid is at the core of their interests. And that's something that we can help achieve through a deal. And obviously, the Russian side is facing strikes it has not seen before, deep in Russian territory and against key industries."
More details: Rubio added that the United States regards a "deal on a limited base" between the sides as an important step and will continue its efforts.
Quote: "It's something that I think is worth investing in, trying to make that happen – because I think it will be beneficial to the world and beneficial to both countries… And I think we're prepared to play a positive role, if we can, in making that come about."
Background:
- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that Trump had not asked Ukraine to unilaterally stop strikes on Russia.
- At the start of his meeting with Zelenskyy in New York on 22 September, US President Donald Trump said he will be discussing Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries with the Ukrainian president.
- On 13 September, Trump urged Zelenskyy to stop strikes on Russian diesel fuel infrastructure, claiming that the attacks are causing a global shortage.
- Zelenskyy in fact said that Ukraine had proposed that its partners "secure an agreement with Russia that would stop the destruction of critical infrastructure".

United Kingdom Established a Unit to Protect Satellites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:22:50 UTC
00:22:50 KST

The Royal Air Force has established the No. III Space Effects Squadron, which is the country’s first unit dedicated to countering threats to British satellites.
Air Chief Marshal Harv Smith, Chief of the Air Staff, announced the unit’s creation at the UK Space Capabilities Conference, according to the country’s Ministry of Defense.
The new squadron will bring together specialists from various branches of the Armed Forces to counter hostile activities in orbit and protect satellite infrastructure.
Unlike the 1st and 2nd Squadrons, which handle surveillance and early warning, the 3rd Squadron will use electronic warfare capabilities to neutralize threats.
The newly formed unit will support both offensive and defensive space operations and will expand as new technologies become available.
In 2025, General Paul Tedman, head of Space Command, reported that Russia attempts to interfere with British military satellites on a weekly basis—both through ground-based jamming and by maneuvering its own spacecraft close to the United Kingdom’s orbital systems.
He emphasized that Russia and China have tested anti-satellite weapons and are also exploring the possibility of deploying nuclear weapons in space.

Iran 'victim' of terrorism, Israel kills, but Tehran gets sanctioned: Pezeshkian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:21:17 UTC
00:21:17 KST

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has rejected US President Donald Trump’s characterisation of Iran as a sponsor of terrorism, saying Tehran is itself a victim of terrorism.
“Yesterday, Trump said we are terrorists. We are not terrorists; we are victims of terrorism,” Pezeshkian told the 81st UN General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, referring to Trump’s address a day earlier in which the US president described Iran as the “number one sponsor of terror.”
Pezeshkian said Iran’s leader had been killed “without any justification", referring to the US-Israeli attacks against Iran that began earlier this year.
He also accused Israel of targeting neighbourhoods across Iranian cities and provinces and carrying out assassinations, describing such actions as “true terrorist” behaviour.
“The people of Iran have been defending their country for the past seven months,” Pezeshkian said.
"We have been the victims of terrorism. I come from an Iran in which our esteemed supreme leader was assassinated without any legal framework or reason. I come from an Iran where, in truth, they bombed a school," Pezeshkian said.
He said Iran had been attacked using the latest technology and weapons systems, but that the Iranian people had "stood steadfast" in the face of the assault.
Hormuz
Pezeshkian said Tehran would not allow the Strait of Hormuz to be used for aggression against his country.
"We cannot let some have free access and bolster their interests from the waterway while at the same time using that waterway to impose their aggression upon us," he said.
The Iranian president said that Iran has never started a war.
"Iran has never been an aggressor, has never started a war and has always shown her commitment to the negotiating table. They imposed the war on us, but we proved that we're not afraid of fighting," he said.
Iran's president struck a defiant tone, telling the US that Tehran would not "bend at the knee".
"US President Donald Trump must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, and increased bullying. We will never bow our head or bend at the knee," Pezeshkian said.
Israeli genocide
The Iranian president accused Israel of conducting assassinations “like a terrorist group” and committing genocide in Gaza, while arguing that Israel does not abide by international law.
“Israel kills, Tehran gets sanctioned,” he said, arguing that the international response to Israeli military actions and sanctions imposed on Iran demonstrated a double standard.
He said the world cannot speak of peace while ignoring Palestine.
“Gaza remains an example of failure of international mechanisms to prevent civilian suffering,” he said, adding that as long as occupation, aggression and injustice persist in the world, resistance will continue.
Nuclear technology
Pezekshian said Tehran’s defensive systems have been built so that no one can think that the bombing of Iranian cities will go unanswered.
“We do not accept nuclear technology being at the exclusive disposal of a handful; we need nuclear technology, not nuclear weapons,” he said.

Auchan’s Russian business gets a CEO from the Kremlin two days after transfer to “temporary management”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:21:04 UTC
00:21:04 KST

Ilya Berdnikov, who previously worked at Russia’s Federal Agency for State Property Management (Rosimushchestvo), has become CEO of Auchan Retail Russia. Berdnikov took up the post on Sept. 19 — two days after Vladimir Putin placed the French retailer’s Russian business under the temporary care of JSC L.E.V. Management.
As The Insider previously found, a week before the decree JSC L.E.V. was headed by former Ministry of Internal Affairs general Andrei Krayushkin, while the JSC itself was still listed among the ready-made shell companies available for purchase for 450,000 rubles ($5,340) — with the option to replace the CEO and complete the deal “same-day.”
The business outlet Kommersant reported Berdnikov’s appointment, citing Auchan’s press service. The previous CEO, Asya Balabai, will remain with the company as executive director.
Berdnikov held the post of executive director at Rosimushchestvo starting from December 2024, the paper writes, citing information from his social media accounts. Previously, he worked at the X5 retail group, the Georgian winemaker Askaneli, and the Canadian construction company Bothwell Accurate Co., and also developed the startup SolidRobots in Canada.
A Kommersant source in the retail market claims that previous CEO Balabai will in fact continue to run day-to-day operations, while Berdnikov will oversee the company. L.E.V. Management head Andrei Krayushkin, meanwhile, will manage the overall process without a formal job title at Auchan.
On Sept. 17, Putin placed the Russian assets of Auchan and Nestlé (along with those of several other companies) under the temporary authority of L.E.V. Management. The Insider found that L.E.V. Management was registered only in October 2024, with charter capital of 15,000 rubles ($178). In 2025 it had no revenue, posted a net loss of 15,000 rubles ($178), and had an average headcount of one employee.
On Sept. 10, one week before Putin’s decree, Andrei Krayushkin — the former first deputy head of Russia’s Main Directorate for Migration Affairs and a police major general — became CEO of L.E.V. Management.
After the assets were transferred, L.E.V. Management said it intended to keep Auchan operating as a single retail chain and to ensure that stores continued running without interruption. No leadership changes have yet been reported at the other companies placed under L.E.V.’s management. At Lemana PRO (formerly Leroy Merlin), the temporary administrator promised to preserve the existing management system and current senior leadership. Nestlé’s Russian division also continues to operate under executive director Denis Voityuk.
The mechanism for placing foreign assets under temporary management has been in effect in Russia since April 2023. Formally, the foreign owner retains ownership rights, but the structure appointed by Russian authorities receives broad powers to manage the assets. This scheme was previously applied to the Russian businesses of Danone and Carlsberg, which subsequently lost control of their companies in Russia.

Independent exit poll finds signs of over 10,000 stuffed ballots in Russian State Duma voting in Cyprus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:20:47 UTC
00:20:47 KST

Official turnout at Russian precinct election commission No. 8158 in Cyprus during the recent vote for the State Duma was about 10 times higher than the turnout recorded by the independent Vote Abroad exit poll, organizers told The Insider. According to their estimate, more than 10,000 ballots were stuffed in Cyprus. The additional votes appeared to benefit not only Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party, but also A Just Russia and the Liberal Democratic Party (LDPR).
Precinct commission No. 8158 covered voting locations in the coastal cities of Paphos and Limassol, as well as the Russian Embassy in the country’s capital, Nicosia. According to official data from the Russian Central Election Commission, 15,843 people voted at the precinct, where the ruling United Russia party received 10,897 votes — 68.78% overall. The LDPR came second with 1,095 votes (6.91%), the Communist Party was third with 954 (6.02%), New People was fourth with 785 (5.95%), and A Just Russia was fifth with 695 (4.39%).
Those results differ sharply from the independent Vote Abroad exit poll, which showed New People receiving 46.3% of the vote at the Cyprus polling locations, with United Russia taking just 12.8%. The exit poll’s organizers told The Insider that the discrepancy could only be explained by fraud. One of the organizers, Margarita Kuchusheva, said:
“At the three locations, we surveyed most of the people who came to vote and counted 945 people. We were there for almost 80% of the voting period. From 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Friday and Saturday in Paphos, from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Saturday in Limassol [voting in those cities took place only on Sept. 18 and 19], and on Friday, Saturday, and Sunday at the embassy in Nicosia from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., except during a heavy thunderstorm Friday morning and for two hours Saturday. During the storm, I was sitting in a car outside the embassy and recorded zero turnout.
All the polling places had one entrance and one exit. We counted turnout. How could the official turnout be about 10 times higher? The only major period we did not cover was Friday in Limassol. But that was a workday — it is impossible that 90% of voters came specifically during those hours, specifically in Limassol, on a working Friday. These are fantastical results. Even if you include embassy employees and their families, the numbers still do not add up. That means at least 10,000 ballots were stuffed. And they were added not only for United Russia, but also for A Just Russia and the LDPR.”
Voting in Cyprus also took place at precinct commission No. 8439 in Nicosia at the Russian Center for Science and Culture. That polling station was not covered by the independent exit poll, but it still remains statistically all but impossible that the official election results published for the country correspond to reality.
The Insider previously analyzed Central Election Commission data from overseas polling stations at Russian embassies worldwide, finding that New People’s share of the vote abroad was over three times higher than its official result inside Russia, while United Russia’s was about 18 percentage points lower. Russian voters abroad also produced results that differed significantly from the nationwide totals in the 2024 presidential election.
Cyprus, particularly Nicosia, stood out as one of the biggest anomalies in Russia’s 2024 presidential election abroad. Official results showed more than 53,000 votes cast in Cyprus (compared to just 5,276 in 2018), including about 42,000 at one Nicosia polling station, while independent monitors estimated actual turnout may have been closer to 13,000 and that roughly 40,000 official votes could have been fictitious or otherwise manipulated. Russian Election Monitor called the presidential vote in 2024 the “largest overseas electoral fraud in Russia's modern history.”

The Senate on Wednesday gave definitive approval to a law drafted by Environment and Energy Security Minister Gilberto Pichetto Fratin paving the way for Italy's return to nuclear power. 
    Italy abandoned nuclear power following a referendum in the wake of the Chernobyl disaster but Premier Giorgia Meloni's government wants to return to atomic energy with small latest-generation reactors to reduce reliance on imports and cut greenhouse gas emissions. 
    "Today, Parliament definitively approved the nuclear law," Meloni said on social media. 
    "After nearly 40 years, Italy once again has a regulatory framework to produce nuclear energy. A bold and sensible decision. 
    "Today we import electricity generated by nuclear power plants in neighbouring countries, but we cannot produce it ourselves. . 
    "This law is needed to change that. 
    "Now the government will draft the implementing regulations on safety, authorizations, waste management, and relations with local communities. 
    "It was a commitment we made to the Italian people. Another commitment we have kept". 
    The law gives the government the power to issue decrees regulating this issue and it also sets out the areas of intervention: the construction and operation of power plants, hydrogen production using nuclear energy, spent fuel management and safety, and the establishment of regulatory bodies. 
    Pichetto Fratin has said that he intends to issue the implementing decrees by the end of the year. 
    "A significant step is being taken to for the country's energy future with the final approval of the enabling bill on nuclear energy," said Stefania Craxi, the Senate whip of the centre-right Forza Italia (FI) party. 
    "Next-generation nuclear power offers a concrete solution to ensure Italy's energy independence, shielding it from price volatility. 
    "We must meet rising energy demand while achieving our decarbonization goals. 
    "To this end, we need to strengthen our system with next-generation nuclear power while continuing to drive the expansion of renewables. 
    "This challenge will enable us to create a balanced energy system capable of supporting the country's economic development". 
    There were also dissenting voices. 
    "The Right presents nuclear power as a sort of answer to the climate crisis, high energy costs, and the country's foreign (energy) dependency," said Green-Left Alliance (AVS) Senate whip Peppe De Cristofaro. 
    "It is a gigantic mass distraction—a smokescreen to avoid accountability for the government's failed energy policies. 
    "After four years of Meloni in power, the country still faces some of the highest energy prices in Europe. 
    "The question to ask is: what benefit could be gained from a return to nuclear power in the coming years? The answer is that nuclear power will yield no benefits. 
    "The (new-generation) power plants and technologies are not yet available; in the meantime, we will continue burning gas and relying on imports, while Italians keep paying exorbitant bills. 
    "All this propaganda regarding nuclear power is precisely the way to prolong our dependence on fossil fuels. 
    "The government wants to turn Italy into a gas hub without having gas, and into a nuclear power without having uranium. 
    "AVS says no to a return to nuclear power, and no to giving the government a blank cheque".

ICC refuses to withdraw arrest warrant against Netanyahu
The International Criminal Court (ICC) has taken no steps to withdraw arrest warrants or related applications concerning Israeli officials, despite mounting pressure and sanctions from the United States, Deputy Prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan has said.
“The case is still proceeding,” Khan told CNN in a weekend interview.
“We have taken no steps to try and withdraw any of those arrest warrant applications or the arrest warrants themselves, and the team continues to investigate in that situation.”
The ICC issued arrest warrants in November 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his then war minister, Yoav Gallant, over war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Gaza since October 2023.
Since then, the U.S. has imposed sanctions on most of the court's leadership, including the former chief prosecutor Karim Khan, the two deputy prosecutors, and nine judges including the court's president.
Israel has also taken steps to challenge the warrants at the ICC. Two appeals remain in progress, including one challenging the court's jurisdiction over Israeli nationals because Israel is not a member of the court.
Meanwhile, Middle East Eye has reported that the prosecutor’s office had pursued further cases against senior Israeli officials over the past two years.
In May, MEE reported that the prosecutor’s office had filed a confidential application seeking arrest for Israel’s Finance Minister Bezalal Smotrich over crimes committed against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
The charges included forced displacement as both a war crime and crime against humanity, transferring Israel’s civilian population into occupied territory as a war crime, and persecution and apartheid as crimes against humanity.
An evidence review had also been held to consider two further applications, including one targeting National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir.
Khan’s comments came amid an escalating campaign by the administration of President Donald Trump against the Hague-based court.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced in July that Washington would use every tool at its disposal to “dismantle the ICC – brick by brick, if necessary”, while urging member states to withdraw their support for the institution.
In other press statements, Rubio also described the court as a “stupid organization” run by “lunatics and crazies”, and warned that it would face consequences for attempting to exercise jurisdiction over American nationals.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot has said that the Israeli government's policies are jeopardising the country’s security, citing its failure to fulfil commitments under Trump’s Gaza peace plan and developments in the occupied West Bank
“The policy pursued by the current government of the State of Israel jeopardises Israel's security," Barrot said on Wednesday.
Barrot said this was reflected in what he described as Israeli authorities' "refusal" to fulfil their responsibilities under Trump's peace plan, as well as in the buffer-zone strategy being pursued in Lebanon and Syria.
He also pointed to the occupied West Bank, where he said there had been "an explosion of violence" by extremist occupiers against Palestinians and an "unprecedented acceleration" of illegal settlement activity.
"This weakens the prospect to which the international community is committed, which is the two-state solution," Barrot said.
"But it also poses a security risk to Israel and the Israeli population. This is something we cannot accept," he added.
France ready to deploy Strait of Hormuz mission
Barrot also said France had prepared an international mission for the Strait of Hormuz that was ready to deploy as soon as conditions allowed, with the aim of helping restore shipping through the strategic waterway as quickly as possible.
He said Paris wanted the resumption of traffic to translate into lower fuel prices for French consumers as soon as possible.
France was also working with European and regional partners to develop alternative trade routes that would be less vulnerable to similar conflicts in the future, Barrot said.
Turning to the Red Sea and Bab al Mandab Strait, he said France would remain involved through the EU's Aspides maritime security mission, which he said had protected hundreds of French vessels from Houthi attacks.
Barrot added that the escalation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia had also had a significant impact on fuel prices.

Azerbaijan Pardons French Citizen Martin Ryan After EU Lifts Sanctions on Russian Oligarch Usmanov
Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev pardoned French national Martin Ryan, previously accused of espionage, Reuters reported on September 23.
This came just one day after the European Union lifted sanctions on Russian billionaire Alisher Usmanov following an intense pressure campaign from France and Luxembourg.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ryan, the Chief Executive Officer of Baku-based food-import firm Mercorama, had been serving a 10-year prison sentence following an espionage conviction in March, according to Reuters.
Baku accused him of operating as an agent for France’s Directorate-General for External Security (DGSE), gathering sensitive information on Azerbaijan’s military cooperation with Türkiye and Pakistan, and secretly recruiting French-speaking Azerbaijanis—allegations Paris has consistently rejected.
Three European diplomats told Reuters that Ryan’s release appears to be the direct result of a highly controversial geopolitical trade that has fractured European unity.
The diplomats stated that Paris privately admitted Baku was using Usmanov’s sanctions designation to pressure France over its imprisoned citizens, leading France to successfully lobby Brussels to remove the metals and mining magnate from the EU sanctions list on September 22.
The pardon decree signed by Aliyev released Ryan alongside 19 others, including citizens from Türkiye, Pakistan, and a dual Russian-Israeli national, Reuters reported.
However, the deal did not secure the release of a second French national, Anass Derraz, an employee of French water management company Saur who was sentenced in 2025 to 12 years in prison on corruption charges.
A senior Azerbaijani diplomat rejected the allegations of a pressure campaign as “categorically unfounded,” telling Reuters that Baku openly supported Usmanov’s removal from Western sanctions lists but denied attempting to influence Western decision-making.
The delisting of Usmanov, alongside fellow Russian billionaire Mikhail Fridman, marks the first time the EU has removed sanctions against members of Russia’s billionaire elite who have not publicly condemned the war in Ukraine, Reuters noted.
The decision exposed deep divisions among EU governments, while Ukraine vehemently condemned the move as “shameful and unjustifiable,” according to the agency.
Relations between Paris and Baku have long been strained over France’s close ties to Armenia, Azerbaijan’s neighbor and rival, Reuters added. France maintains a large Armenian diaspora and actively supplies arms to Yerevan, compounding the diplomatic standoff surrounding the arrests.
In response to the EU’s decision to drop sanctions against Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, Latvia’s Cabinet of Ministers had recently ordered the drafting of national-level sanctions to prevent the billionaires' assets from circulating within its borders.
Riga had been the sole holdout against the EU delisting but ultimately chose to abstain to secure a 36-month extension for the broader European sanctions framework.

Russia’s Fast Geran-5 Drone “Exploded Like a Comet” After Ukrainian Intercept, Video
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:18:05 UTC
00:18:05 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Fast Geran-5 Drone “Exploded Like a Comet” After Ukrainian Intercept, Video
Ukrainian border guards shot down a Russian Geran-5 jet-powered strike drone on September 23, one of Moscow's newest and fastest attack UAVs.
Operators from the 105th Separate Border Detachment, named after Prince Volodymyr the Great, carried out the interception, ArmyInform added.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The State Border Guard Service of Ukraine released footage of the strike on its official Telegram channel the same day.
The drone "exploded like a comet," as described by ArmyInform. By what means the operators reached the Geran-5, the Border Guard Service did not specify, nor did it disclose the strike's location.
In the same Telegram post, the service listed a broader set of targets hit by the unit's operators on September 23:
- a jet-powered Geran-5 strike drone;
- 82mm automatic Vasylok mortars;
- fuel, lubricant, and ammunition depots;
- electronic warfare equipment and radar stations;
- military vehicles;
- fortified enemy shelters.
Jet-powered Gerans fly considerably faster than the propeller-driven Shaheds that Russia has used against Ukraine for years, a gap that demands different interception means, ArmyInform explained.
Russia first deployed the Geran-5 against Ukraine in early 2026, according to the Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine (HUR).
The jet-powered UAV closely resembles Iran's Karrar drone and reflects Moscow's shift toward faster, harder-to-intercept strike platforms.
According to HUR, the Geran-5 measures roughly 6 meters long, has a wingspan of up to 5.5 meters, and carries a warhead of about 90 kilograms.
Later assessments put its takeoff weight near 850 kilograms. The drone cruises at 450 to 600 kilometers per hour, with a range of up to 950 kilometers and a ceiling of up to 6 kilometers.
The drone runs on a Chinese TELEFLY TF-TJ2000A turbojet engine, and its airframe includes components sourced from China, the US, and Germany, HUR found.
The Geran-5 is estimated to cost around $100,000 per unit, similar to the newer Banderol cruise missile. That is far cheaper than a US-made Tomahawk, which runs more than $2 million.
The interception adds to a string of recent Geran-5 losses. Russian production of the jet-powered drone and its Banderol counterpart has expanded rapidly in recent months, moving from battlefield testing to large-scale manufacturing.
Ukrainian air defenses downed another Geran-5 over Kyiv's Holosiivskyi district in early September, when wreckage from the drone fell in the neighborhood.

Why is France's Gen Z turning to Catholicism?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:18:05 UTC
00:18:05 KST

Why is France's Gen Z turning to Catholicism?
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
As France prepares for Pope Leo XIV's visit, a surprising trend has emerged in recent years: the number of baptisms among teenagers and young adults has skyrocketed. More than 21,000 catechumens, those undergoing the period of preparation for baptism into the Christian Church, have been recorded so far in 2026. How can this renewed interest in the Catholic faith be explained? Florence Gaillard reports for France in Focus.
A pandemic, lockdowns, the return of war to Europe, climate change: all of these are proven sources of anxiety, even depression, among young people in France. With some feeling adrift, they're turning to religion and knocking on the door of the Catholic Church. In 2026, more than 21,000 adults and teenagers were baptised, a figure that has more than tripled in the past decade.
A search for meaning and community
For Johan, who had long prioritised athletic performance, his grandmother's death sparked a search for meaning and spirituality. For Morgane, who grew up in public housing with a single parent, the need for community became apparent. For Malick, who grew up in Senegal in a Muslim family, reading the Bible proved a turning point.
All three asked to be baptised as adults.
The growing role of friends
Charles Mercier, a historian of contemporary Catholicism, told FRANCE 24: "Religion is no longer an inheritance received at birth but has become an individual choice. Young people therefore no longer experience it as a constraint or an obligation."
In a secular, multicultural country, faith has become a topic of conversation and inspiration among friends. Johan, for instance, asked his friend Matthieu to take him to Mass for the first time, and later to be his godfather at his baptism.
The observance of Ramadan among young Muslims has also inspired young Catholics to rediscover their own traditions, particularly Lent in the lead-up to Easter.
The rise of influencers
A new era calls for new ways of communicating. According to a survey conducted by the French Bishops' Conference and La Croix, nearly 20 percent of catechumens say that influencers with thousands of followers on social media played an important role in their spiritual journey. Malick, for one, was guided to Trinity Parish in Paris, where a weekly Mass draws nearly a thousand young people, by influencer Brother Paul-Adrien.
For Mercier, the rise of catechumenates is not a return to tradition, as some believed when the phenomenon first began, but rather a new chapter in the history of the Catholic Church.

The Netherlands will join the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest after boycotting the event this year over Israel's participation, Dutch public broadcaster NPO said on Wednesday.
NPO took over from the original public broadcaster AVROTROS, which formally announced in August that they would not participate in the contest, stating that the event could "no longer be considered neutral" while a participating country, referring to Israel, remains involved in a large-scale military conflict, NL Time reported Wednesday.
In August, AVROTROS director-general Taco Zimmerman stated that the contest was meant to unite people and countries involved in international conflicts, undermining the contest's "neutrality" character, saying, "The Eurovision Song Contest was originally created to bring people and countries together." It is undeniable that international conflicts are increasingly affecting the contest, undermining its neutral character.”
The broadcaster noted that it had returned responsibility for Dutch participation in Eurovision to the NPO. This organization oversees the overall Dutch public broadcasting system.
The European Broadcasting Union (EBU) had initially set a September 15 deadline for countries to confirm their participation. NPO requested additional time to evaluate its options after taking over responsibility for the Netherlands’ Eurovision entry and was granted an extension until the end of September.
Countries weigh Eurovision return as Bulgaria prepares to host 2027 event
The Netherlands was among five countries, together with Ireland, Spain, Iceland, and Slovenia, that withdrew from the 2026 Eurovision contest in Vienna. Ireland’s broadcaster RTÉ has since said it will also skip and not broadcast the 2027 contest, while Spain and Iceland are still reviewing whether they will participate, according to Eurovoix.
The contest's final semi-final rounds ad grand final will be held in Burgas, Bulgaria May 11-15, 2027 hosted by Bulgarian National Television (BNT) alongside the European Broadcasting Union (EBU).
Reuters and Tzvi Jasper contributed to this report.

Poverty, child labor, and child marriage partially behind Iran’s unfilled classrooms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:13:38 UTC
00:13:38 KST

Thousands of Iranian children of elementary-school age have been unable to receive an education due to financial hardship, Iran’s Education Ministry reported on Tuesday.
Rezvan Hakimzadeh, deputy minister of primary education, said 140,562 students had been identified as not attending school last year, with the majority located in Sistan and Baluchestan, Tehran, Razavi Khorasan, and Khuzestan provinces. Of those children, 54,445 were in the first grade, he said.
Nearly 42,000 of the students had left Iran with their families, while 18,000 were not required to enroll due to disabilities, Hakimzadeh said. Thousands of others were out of school due to family financial hardship, child labor, a lack of adequate guardianship, or enrollment in unlicensed education centers, he added.
There were 86 cases in which a child of elementary-school age was not attending school because they had married, the report said.
Primary school in Iran is for children ages six to 12, while Iranian law generally requires girls to be 13 and boys to be 15 to marry. In some cases, however, a judge’s approval can allow for marriage at an earlier age.
The start of the school year in Iran has drawn greater attention to the country’s rapid demographic change.
According to the Razavi Foundation’s Astan Quds Razavi media site Quds Online, 1.154 million six-year-old children began primary school in Iran this year, about 76,000 fewer than last year.
Iran's challenged demography
Iran’s declining birth rates, delays in marriage and childbearing, economic pressures, and lifestyle changes have all impacted the country’s shifting demography, Quds Online reported.
Alireza Sajedi, head of Iran’s Population Monitoring Center of the National Organization for Civil Registration, told Quds Online the number of births had fallen from about 1.116 million in 2021 to fewer than 980,000 in 2024.
The downward demographic shift could eventually lead schools to reduce both classroom sizes and the actual number of classes in cities, Quds Online reported. In rural areas, however, it may no longer be viable to keep schools open, the report said.

Israel Navy moves toward semi-autonomous fleet with robotic ships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:13:26 UTC
00:13:26 KST

The Israeli navy is moving toward becoming a semi-autonomous force and may eventually become nearly fully autonomous, the IDF said.
It has been reported that the Israeli navy has operated autonomous sea vehicles in recent years, though it is unclear when swarms at sea will be ready to roll out.
Elbit Systems has already been among the Israeli companies developing such technologies, including its publicized 12-meter Seagull autonomous surface vessel, designed to patrol offshore infrastructure for up to four days. It also "incorporates mine countermeasures (MCM), anti-submarine warfare (ASW), maritime security (MS), electronic warfare (EW) and other advanced systems and technologies."
Other countries like France, Singapore, and the Netherlands are also shifting their navies toward more autonomous operations.
Despite those navies' progress, Israel's navy said it is even more advanced in using robots and autonomy.
The need for robots and autonomous operations is clear, given that ships can spend weeks or longer at sea.
Even the most resilient sailors have trouble with this amount of time at sea, and an overwhelming portion of the population is just incapable of doing it at all.
Israel faces growing naval threats from Turkey, Iran, Houthis
In addition, Israel faces growing naval threats from Turkey, and possibly from Iran, the Houthis in Yemen, and others.
The navy said this means it will need more ships in the future to secure Israel's maritime national security interests.
However, the navy does not believe the country or the military will grant it additional staffing power for more ships, so the only stable way to expand Israel's naval fleet sufficiently will involve fewer human soldiers per ship, and eventually zero or close to zero.
At one stage, Israeli soldiers can focus solely on maintenance and safety issues with robots and autonomous systems operating most other systems.
Robots are a double-edged sword
At a later stage, robots may be able to undertake all or much of the maintenance work.
But robots are a double-edged sword.
Enemy forces are also expected to use robots and autonomous systems against Israel.
This will create a number of challenges: land-to-sea and sea-to-sea.
In addition, the IDF is aware that China, Russia, and other countries have explored cutting underwater cables, which foreign reports have confirmed going back to at least 2023 in the Baltic Sea, near Britain, Norway, and at other locations.
Israel is working on and will need to expand its defense of these underwater cables going forward.

Gaza-based journalists who worked amid what photojournalist Motaz Azaiza has described as a “Hamas-controlled media environment” were given prominent platforms in Westminster, researcher Emma Schubart of the Henry Jackson Society (HJS) revealed to The Jerusalem Post exclusively on Tuesday.
Schubart’s discovery follows comments made by Gazan photojournalist Motaz Azaiza in a September 3 podcast interview with journalist Ahmed Biqui.
During this conversation, Azaiza mentioned the existence of a Hamas-administered WhatsApp group called Smart, which, he said, included “every journalist working in Gaza.” The group’s icon displayed a Hamas flag and was administered by “the director of media for the Rafah Border Crossing,” who has been identified as Wael Abu Mohsen.
According to Azaiza, the group coordinated media messaging and organized campaigns against journalists whose reporting departed from the sanctioned line.
“It was never a spontaneous thing,” he added.
Gazan photographers 'accustomed to lowering cameras' to criticism of Hamas
Azaiza added that photographers in Gaza had “become accustomed to lowering their cameras” when civilians criticized Hamas.
HJS reported that several journalists who operated within this Hamas-controlled media environment were subsequently welcomed into Westminster and presented to British parliamentarians as authoritative witnesses to the war. Other journalists from this environment have been involved more indirectly with the British government.
For example, Al Jazeera’s Gaza bureau chief Wael al-Dahdouh was hosted in Parliament in September last year.
MPs host Hamas-linked journalists
Hansard [the official report of all Parliamentary debates] records Labour MP Yuan Yang saying on September 10, 2025, that she had “co-hosted an event in Parliament for Wael al-Dahdouh” the previous evening.
During that visit, Dahdouh also met with Labour MP Afzal Khan for Manchester Rusholem (formerly Manchester Gorton), who posted publicly that he had met Dahdouh, calling the meeting “an honor.”
While neither the Post nor HJS has independently verified the membership of the group, Azaiza said it included every journalist working in Gaza at the time.
Then there is Azaiza himself, who on May 15, 2024, addressed a Nakba Day gathering at Westminster Central Hall, yards from Parliament, sharing the event with Sir Alan Duncan, the former Conservative Foreign Office minister.
Additionally, Scottish National Party (SNP) MP Brendan O’Hara co-organized a cross-party panel in a House of Commons committee room in mid-July 2025 with Oxfam GB and the Council for Arab-British Understanding.
Gaza journalist Abubaker Abed spoke alongside Oxfam’s then-CEO. Abed addressed MPs and journalists who were in attendance on conditions in Gaza and called for an end to UK arms support for Israel.
Finally, Al Jazeera and the International Centre of Justice for Palestinians (ICJP) held a sold-out Westminster screening of the documentary Gaza in October 2024, followed by a panel. Al Jazeera Gaza correspondent Youmna El Sayed appeared as a panellist, with MPs and peers attending.
“One of Gaza’s most famous ‘journalists’ has described, in his own words, how Hamas controlled the media environment,” Schubart said.
Schubart noted that this is of great importance to every international outlet that has relied on Gaza-based journalists yet still claims that their reporting is editorially independent of Hamas.
“The question is straightforward: Why were British politicians giving a parliamentary platform to journalism produced under Hamas control?”
Schubart has personally written to the Speaker of the House on these findings. The letter was viewed by the Post.

US targets Iranian airlines (VIDEO)
Iranian airlines are being cut off from international routes and airport services as Washington steps up pressure on the country’s aviation sector. Several regional connections have already been suspended or restricted, although some foreign flights continue, RT’s Saman Kojouri has reported from outside the Tehran headquarters of Mahan Air, one of Iran’s major carriers.
The US Treasury targeted 27 Iranian airlines earlier this month as part of a broader campaign against the country’s aviation sector. Foreign companies providing services to the carriers risk US secondary sanctions, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that the restrictions would effectively shut Iranian airlines out of international aviation from September 23.
”If they land, you cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets, or you will be knocked out of the dollar system,” Bessent said.
The impact is already spreading across the region, according to RT’s Kojouri. Azerbaijan has suspended flights operated by Iranian carriers, while Iraq has reportedly stopped accepting Iranian aircraft. Flights between Tehran and Muscat have also been suspended, while Georgia has said it will comply with sanctions affecting Iranian carriers.
Mahan Air is among the airlines facing the squeeze. Washington first sanctioned the carrier in 2011, accusing it of providing support to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Quds Force (IRGC-QF). The Treasury has since targeted companies abroad accused of providing commercial and logistical support to the airline.
The aviation crackdown comes as Washington ramps up pressure on Tehran while simultaneously pursuing diplomatic contacts on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. President Donald Trump threatened on Tuesday to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” if negotiations fail, saying he faced a “big decision” between reaching an agreement and further military escalation.
Most of the Iranian delegation walked out of the General Assembly hall during Trump’s speech, leaving only one representative seated. The US president defended the nearly seven-month US-Israeli war and accused Tehran of pursuing nuclear weapons and supporting terrorism.
Despite the hostile rhetoric, indirect contacts continued later in the day. US envoy Steve Witkoff said mediators had shuttled between the American and Iranian delegations during “lengthy talks,” while Tehran said it had used the channel to clearly convey its conditions to Washington, including lifting the US naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian assets.

MOSCOW, September 23. /TASS/. Nuclear weapons will not appear on Lithuanian territory in the near future, despite the decision by the Seimas (parliament) to lift the ban on their deployment, Ruslan Pankratov, a member of the Officers of Russia expert council, deputy chairman of the Union of Political Emigrants of Europe, and a former deputy of the Riga City Council has said.

Pankratov also emphasized that the practical value of deploying nuclear warheads in Lithuania for NATO is quite limited.
"The alliance is unlikely to rush the deployment of nuclear weapons right on the Russian and Belarusian borders, as this would sharply increase the risk of actual - rather than merely rhetorical - escalation for its domestic electorate," he explained.

Xi Jinping Is Coming to the US. Why Is He Skipping the UNGA?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:08:00 UTC
00:08:00 KST

If you read The Diplomat, you probably follow Asia-Pacific affairs – and thus you probably already know that Chinese President Xi Jinping is due to arrive in Washington, D.C. today for a much-anticipated summit with U.S. President Donald Trump.
According to the White House’s itinerary, Xi will land at Andrews Air Force Base on September 23, where he will be personally received by Trump himself. The next day, he’ll receive a formal welcome ceremony at the White House, followed by the actual summit and a state dinner. On September 25, Trump and First Lady Melania Trump will host Xi and his wife for tea; both couples will then visit the National Archives, “where they will view a variety of important records and documents significant to the American and Chinese relationship throughout history.” Then Xi and his delegation will fly home.
What’s most remarkable about this itinerary is what it doesn’t include: a stop in New York, where the United Nations’ General Assembly is currently holding its 81st session. Heads of state and government from around the world are making the trip to New York just for the UNGA, including top leaders from Bangladesh, Japan, Indonesia, Kyrgyzstan, Nepal, Mongolia, South Korea, and Vietnam, just to name a few from The Diplomat’s coverage region.
Meanwhile, Xi is making a trip across the Pacific Ocean and the entire continental U.S. and not bothering to take an extra jaunt up the coast to attend the United Nations’ most important annual event.
Instead, Vice President Han Zheng will be in New York from September 24 to 26 to represent China at the UNGA. According to China’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun, “On the sidelines of the general debate, Vice President Han will attend the High-Level Dialogue on the Fifth Anniversary of the Global Development Initiative hosted by China, and meet with [the] U.N. secretary-general, president of the 81st UNGA session, and leaders of relevant countries.”
Apparently, these are meetings Xi couldn’t be bothered to attend himself, despite being just an hour’s plane ride away.
Xi’s absence from the UNGA would seem to undermine China’s consistent rhetorical emphasis on the United Nations’ importance. China’s white paper on global governance, released in June 2026, repeatedly emphasized the U.N. as the “core” of the international order. “The United Nations is the primary platform for practicing multilateralism and advancing global governance,” the white paper declared. “Its leading position must be upheld and remain rock solid; its role can only be reinforced, not weakened.”
In the same press conference where Guo announced Han’s trip, the spokesperson repeated a similar line: “The United Nations is the core platform for global governance, and the general debate of UNGA is a vital opportunity for countries to build political consensus and coordinate multilateral actions.” But if the United Nations, and the UNGA, are so important, why can’t Xi be bothered to attend?
Xi has gone to the UNGA just once since becoming China’s top leader in late 2012. He went in 2015, to commemorate the United Nations’ 70th anniversary, and addressed the UNGA in person for the first and only time.
Notably, this coincided with Xi’s last state visit to the United States, when he included attendance at the UNGA within a broader itinerary that saw him also hold a summit with then-U.S. President Barack Obama. That makes the decision not to do the same thing in 2026 all the more notable.
In 2021, Xi gave a video address to the UNGA, in which he announced China’s Global Development Initiative. He has not delivered a speech before the UNGA since.
Perhaps most notably, Xi chose to skip last year’s UNGA – the 80th session. China puts much stock in these round-number anniversaries, pegging trips abroad and major upgrades in bilateral relations to special dates. Remember that Xi took the time to attend the United Nations’ 70th anniversary in person. That wasn’t an aberration – China’s top leader had attended every decennial anniversary of the U.N. since Jiang Zemin in 1995. That made Xi’s absence from the 80th anniversary in 2025 all the more conspicuous.
As I wrote at the time:
Instead [of attending the UNGA], Xi stayed in China, where he “extended festive greetings” for the farmers’ harvest celebration and visited Urumqi to mark the 70th anniversary of the founding of the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region.
Those events were duly splashed across the front-page headlines of People’s Daily, the official newspaper of the Chinese Communist Party. Premier Li Qiang’s presence at UNGA received just a one-line mention on the front page for September 24.
Xi has also stopped announcing China’s major global initiatives at the United Nations. He unveiled the Global Development Initiative at the UNGA back in 2021, albeit in a virtual speech. But in 2025, Xi chose to announce the new Global Governance Initiative – even more directly related to the United Nations’ mission – at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit held in China a month before the UNGA.
Similarly, China founded its own World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO) – “an independent intergovernmental international organization that… aims to promote international cooperation and global governance on artificial intelligence” – rather than working within the United Nations to legitimize its efforts toward the same ends. China announced WAICO at its own AI conference, rather than at the U.N. Global Dialogue on AI Governance held a month earlier.
Meanwhile, as Trump reduces U.S. funding for the United Nations, China hasn’t stepped up to fill the gap. Its own U.N.-assessed contributions have been chronically late and remain a mere fraction of what the United States was contributing prior to Trump taking office.
No matter the lip service China pays to the United Nations’ “core role” in global governance, Beijing clearly prefers to give attention, money, and prestige to settings where it exerts more control. That includes China-led groups like the SCO, but also purely bilateral meetings like the summit with Trump.
Nikkei Asia theorized that Xi’s decision to skip the UNGA was an attempt to position China as a true equal to the United States – a message that apparently would have been diluted by Xi rubbing elbows with leaders from smaller states in New York. That in itself is telling. For all China’s rhetoric about a multipolar world where all states have equal representation – and equal say – in global governance, when push comes to shove Beijing defaults to a different perspective.
As China’s top diplomat put it, fairly undiplomatically, in a heated ASEAN meeting back in 2010: “China is a big country and other countries are small countries, and that’s just a fact.” One of the perks of being a “big country,” as Trump has repeatedly shown, is the privilege of ignoring the United Nations to pursue national interests in other settings.
