South African central bank raises policy rate to 7.25 pct
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
22:44:10 CST
23:44:10 KST

JOHANNESBURG, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- The South African Reserve Bank (SARB) on Wednesday raised its policy rate by 25 basis points to 7.25 percent, citing heightened inflation risks amid renewed fuel price pressures and persistent global supply shocks.
The Monetary Policy Committee unanimously decided to raise the rate, with the decision effective on Sept. 25, according to the central bank.
SARB said escalating tensions in the Middle East and the Russia-Ukraine conflict were disrupting energy and food supplies, contributing to a large and persistent global supply shock.
The central bank raised its near-term inflation forecasts mainly due to higher fuel prices. Headline inflation is expected to rise above 5 percent later this year and early next year before easing as the fuel price shock recedes, and is projected to return to around the 3-percent target toward the end of 2027.
"A few months back, it seemed that the fuel-price shock might be unwinding, but now it has intensified," the statement said.
SARB also lowered its forecast for South Africa's economic growth this year to 1.2 percent from 1.4 percent, after the economy contracted by 0.2 percent in the second quarter. It expects growth to rebound in the second half of the year, while risks to the outlook remain tilted to the downside.
The rate hike came as South Africa's annual consumer inflation edged up to 4.4 percent in August from 4.3 percent in July. ■

KATHMANDU, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Nepal's foreign trade rose 35.64 percent in the first two months of the fiscal year 2026-27, according to a report released by the Department of Customs on Wednesday.
The country's total trade volume stood at 478.11 billion Nepali rupees (3.13 billion U.S. dollars) between mid-July and mid-September, compared with 352.47 billion rupees during the same period of the previous fiscal year, the department said.
Exports increased by 61.86 percent year-on-year to 76.59 billion rupees from 47.32 billion rupees, while imports rose by 31.58 percent to 401.52 billion rupees from 305.16 billion rupees during the corresponding period last year, according to the report.
Despite the substantial growth in exports, Nepal's trade deficit widened by 26.02 percent year-on-year to 324.93 billion rupees during the review period. (1 Nepali rupee equals about 0.0065 U.S. dollars) ■

‘A triumph of money, filth, and hypocrisy’: EU decision to lift sanctions on Russian billionaires Fridman and Usmanov draws backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:42:34 UTC
23:42:34 KST

‘A triumph of money, filth, and hypocrisy’: EU decision to lift sanctions on Russian billionaires Fridman and Usmanov draws backlash
The European Union maintains a large sanctions list drawn up in response to Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. It includes more than 3,000 people and companies. EU countries used to review the list every six months. On September 22, they agreed to extend it for a full three years, but with an important caveat: two billionaires with close ties to Russia, Mikhail Fridman and Alisher Usmanov, were removed from the list. Both men had long sought to have the sanctions lifted, both through European courts and other means. The final decision on their cases was political rather than judicial: Luxembourg intervened on behalf of Fridman, who has filed a lawsuit against the country for a huge sum, while France intervened for Usmanov and, in exchange, received a pardon for one of its citizens who had been convicted in Azerbaijan.
The lifting of European restrictions on Fridman and Usmanov has outraged figures in the Russian opposition in exile, Ukrainian officials, and some European politicians. Meduza has collected their reactions, presented here with minor cuts.
Russian opposition
Vladimir Kara-Murza
opposition politician
Shame on you [in the European Union].
Yulia Navalnaya
leader of the Navalny-founded Anti-Corruption Foundation
It turns out that for Europe, it doesn’t matter whether you support the war or not, or whether you’re friends with Putin or opposed to him. In the end, it seems, what matters far more is how much money is in your bank accounts.
If you’re rich, have a couple of yachts and the right connections, apparently your sanctions can be lifted without much trouble. But if you fled Russia with little more than a few belongings because of political persecution or the draft, because you don’t support the war, it’s a different story: you might be denied a visa, refused a bank account, faced with a mountain of obstacles, and effectively pushed back into the arms of Putin’s system. And accused of supporting the war on top of it.
Thanks to the European Commission for yet another reminder that in big politics, money still speaks louder than principles, and the fates of ordinary people often end up somewhere near the bottom of the list of priorities.
Leonid Volkov
head of political projects at the Anti-Corruption Foundation
On Fridman, this is simply a mistake. He hasn’t done anything, hasn’t changed anything, hasn’t even spoken up. Lifting his sanctions “just because” is foolish. Four years ago I proposed, and I still believe, that clear and transparent mechanisms should have been created for exiting sanctions for entrepreneurs like Fridman, in exchange for concrete steps to weaken Putin’s regime: everything from condemning the war to providing substantial help to Ukraine. That was entirely achievable, but it was never done.
On Usmanov, this isn’t just a mistake, it’s a moral catastrophe, and a double one at that. First, Usmanov is no “rank-and-file oligarch.” He is one of the key people in the system. And it’s not just that his personal kept man is former president and current drunken bully Medvedev, but also which assets Usmanov bought up on behalf of and at the direction of the Kremlin for censorship and lawlessness: from MegaFon to Kommersant. Remember: “I don’t use the internet, I develop it”? Well, Usmanov is one of the people who developed it into its current state.
Second, Usmanov achieved the lifting of sanctions through hostage-taking. Azerbaijani dictator Aliyev helped out as a friend, detained French citizens, and France came running to sort things out. Great! The path out of sanctions has been shown: expect new hostages!
In 2022, Leonid Volkov signed a letter to the European Commission asking that sanctions against Mikhail Fridman and other senior Alfa Group executives be lifted. The letter proposed that the EU adopt “a clear and simple set of criteria” for removing people from the sanctions list. “These criteria could be tied to a public condemnation of the war, compensation for damages, and severing ties with Putin and his regime,” the letter said.
The letter became public in 2023. Volkov called it his “major political mistake” and stepped down as head of the international Anti-Corruption Foundation, ACF International, though he remained one of its key figures.
Meduza wrote in detail about this story here.
Maria Pevchikh
former head of the investigations department at the Anti-Corruption Foundation
What a colossal, planetary-scale disgrace this lifting of sanctions on Fridman and Usmanov is. As I said a couple of years ago, when I proposed trading yachts for political prisoners (which for some reason caused quite a scandal), if that isn’t done, the sanctions will simply be lifted for nothing. There will be no yachts and no political prisoners released. That is exactly what is happening now.
A triumph of money, filth, and hypocrisy. Some people, to get a measly work visa in Europe, have to bend over backwards proving they’re sufficiently anti-war, that none of their relatives, down to a seventh cousin, work for Putin’s regime, and produce stacks of convictions handed down in absentia in Russia. But these two assholes, pardon my language, haven’t said a single word against the war, and yet, please, come on in, cruise around on your yacht, live in your villas, no problem at all.
Vyacheslav Gimadi
head of the legal department at the Anti-Corruption Foundation
Putin’s oligarchs Usmanov (against whom I won at the European Court of Human Rights over Navalny’s investigation into Medvedev’s corruption) and the no less notorious Fridman are being removed from EU sanctions. How could this happen? These decisions are made unanimously, meaning any of the 27 countries can block them regardless of the “interests of the majority.” That’s what the Hungarians, Austrians, and Slovaks did, and now apparently France too, from what I’ve read. This vulnerability and pliability, I believe, diminish the institution itself, since it encourages terrorists to pressure individual countries, or maybe even offer them [financial] incentives, though I have no proof of that, and to blackmail them. Other people on the list will surely want to follow the same successful path.
Ivan Zhdanov
former director of the Anti-Corruption Foundation
If the European Union adopts this decision (or has already adopted it), it will collapse the entire system of personal sanctions. Today I sent an urgent letter through whatever channels I had, describing Usmanov’s personal role in the persecution of Navalny and of me (my first criminal case was over Usmanov) and his funding of the warmonger Medvedev. A terrible injustice and an abandonment of its own values [on the part of the European Union].
Alexey Navalny had long been in conflict with Alisher Usmanov. Their dispute began in 2017, when the Anti-Corruption Foundation released an investigation titled On vam ne Dimon “He Is Not Dimon to You,” about Dmitry Medvedev’s alleged corruption. The film said that Usmanov had given a charitable foundation linked to Medvedev a mansion in the Rublyovka area. Navalny called this a bribe, and Usmanov sued him and won. The court ordered the film removed from all platforms, but Navalny and his associates never complied.
In 2022, after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Anti-Corruption Foundation published a “list of corrupt officials and warmongers” naming 6,000 people. The foundation proposed adding them to Western sanctions lists for strengthening Putin’s regime and supporting Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Usmanov, like Fridman, is on this list.
That history may explain why current and former Anti-Corruption Foundation representatives have been so vocal in criticizing the decision to lift sanctions on Fridman and Usmanov.
Ukrainian authorities
Volodymyr Zelensky
president of Ukraine
At a time when Russia is carrying out brutal attacks on our people – and even now, during the UN General Assembly, air raid alerts are ongoing in many regions because of drones and ballistic missiles – signals about lifting sanctions on individual Russian oligarchs are self-defeating and counterproductive. Wars end through resolve and strength, not concessions to the aggressor’s entourage. I’m grateful to [European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen] for her readiness to work on adding more Russian names to the EU sanctions lists. These are the kinds of steps that bring a just peace and guaranteed security closer.
Andrii Sybiha
foreign minister of Ukraine
The decision to remove Usmanov and Fridman from the sanctions list is shameful and entirely unjustified. Moscow is celebrating, having gotten exactly what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the European Union, and a split among Europeans. I call on all EU member states to declare now that they will impose their own national sanctions against these two individuals.
Vladyslav Vlasiuk
Ukrainian presidential commissioner for sanctions policy
We consider the EU’s decision not to extend sanctions against Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman very strange. […] Lifting restrictions on individual Russian businessmen should not become a new practice. That is why we will keep proposing new sanctions measures, in particular regarding Russian oligarchs connected to Russia’s military-industrial complex.
European politicians
Pina Picierno
vice president of the European Parliament
The decision to delist Usmanov and Fridman is disgraceful, cowardly and completely unacceptable. But let’s be crystal clear about where political responsibility lies: with the Member States in the Council, not the Commission.
Under the EU treaties (such rules that must change!), the High Representative proposes sanctions, working with the Commission on their economic aspects. But restrictive measures can only be adopted unanimously by the Council.
This unanimity rule makes the EU fragile and weak. We need a politically strong, sovereign Europe: one that is more than the sum of its Member States.
Andris Kulbergs
head of Latvia’s government
Latvia agreed to a compromise but is not changing its principled stance.
We opposed the removal of Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the European Union’s sanctions list until the very end. […] However, the government had to make a responsible decision. The choice was between changing the status of two individuals and risking the loss of the entire sanctions regime. That is why Latvia’s representative will abstain in the vote. […]
Latvia is not backing down. The Foreign Ministry has been instructed to prepare the legal grounds for imposing national sanctions against Usmanov and Fridman.
Mindaugas Sinkevičius
prime minister of Lithuania
Oligarchs are part of Russia’s war machine. The regime’s “wallets” must not be allowed to feel at ease in Europe while Ukrainians are being killed. I have instructed the relevant authorities to initiate the process for imposing national restrictive measures on Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman.
Margus Tsahkna
foreign minister of Estonia
The EU has just extended sanctions against nearly 3,000 individuals and entities linked to Russia’s aggression for another three years. This is a significant achievement, as it reduces the risk of future sanctions renewals becoming hostage to political bargaining.
However, to secure this agreement, sanctions against two prominent Russian businessmen, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, both known supporters of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, were lifted.
Estonia did not support this decision and abstained from the vote. We will now impose national sanctions on both individuals. Russia has not changed course. Neither should we.
Maciej Wąsik
member of the European Parliament from Poland
A compromising of the EU. Russian billionaires Usmanov and Fridman have been removed from the sanctions list. Only Latvia protested. Where was the Polish government? Where was the Polish protest?

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has called on U.S. President Donald Trump to organize a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin, saying the world leaders need to move "as quickly as possible" to bring an end to the war.
Zelenskyy spoke with Trump on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday.
The high-stakes meeting provided Ukraine's president with a rare sit-down opportunity to discuss ways to bring an end to Russia's full-scale invasion, further U.S. air defense support and security guarantees for Kyiv.
A winter package of Patriot missiles and licenses to produce the weapons domestically were two priorities for Ukraine over the coming months, Zelenskyy said.
"President Trump, our teams, and I spoke about how to end the war. This is the priority. We are ready. I'm not sure Russia is ready as of today, but anyhow, we spoke about an energy ceasefire," Zelenskyy said overnight via social media, providing a roundup of his comments to reporters at the General Assembly.
Ukraine's president confirmed Kyiv is ready to agree to an energy truce on the condition that Russia does not attack its energy, electricity and heating infrastructure as well as its water supplies.
Trump has previously called on Ukraine to stop targeting Russian oil refineries with drone strikes, which he says are "hurting the world" as fuel supply disruptions from the Ukraine and Iran wars propel U.S. diesel prices to a record high.
In a post Monday on Truth Social, the U.S. president said Russia had "unfortunately lost control" of its diesel oil industry due to the war.
"I think the most important move President Trump can make – he can organize a trilateral meeting where the leaders can raise all the sensitive issues and try to end the war," Zelenskyy said.
Asked whether his comments mean he's prepared to meet directly with Putin and Trump to bring an end to the war, Zelenskyy replied: "I'm ready. I said it, I'm ready anytime when all the sides will be ready. I think we all need to move as quickly as possible."
CNBC has contacted a White House spokesperson and Russia's embassy in London for comment and is awaiting a response.
A meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy before expert-level discussions have taken place would be a waste of time, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday, according to Russia's state-run news agency RIA Novosti.
"Regarding Putin's meeting with Zelensky, our position is well known. Putin said that Zelensky, if he wishes, can come to Moscow," Peskov said.
Zelenskyy: Xi has 'influence on Putin'
On his meeting with Zelenskyy, Trump told reporters that he had spoken with his Ukrainian counterpart about finding a solution to end Russia's war. He also referenced a diplomatic push to bring an end to the conflict during his speech to General Assembly delegates.
"We will get that one done," Trump said.
Diplomatic talks have stalled as the U.S. has shifted focus to its war against Iran, although negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff traveled to Ukraine for the first time for talks with Zelenskyy earlier in the month.
Ukraine, which has stepped up its strikes on Russian oil facilities and logistics infrastructure in recent months, also called on Trump to discuss ways to bring an end to the war with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday.
"I said to the President, very openly, that we think if he also engages President Xi – he has influence on Putin. If we want to end this war, not just in messages, we all have to work 24/7 for this, for the people," Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine has insisted that Russian energy sites are legitimate military targets as it continues to resist Russian forces that invaded the country in early 2022. Russia's Defense Ministry has said it is planning "massive strikes" on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, amplifying fears of another winter assault.

Pezeshkian accused Washington of “terrorism” for assassinating former supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei at the start of the conflict, insisting Tehran had never started a war.
On Sept 22, US President Donald Trump had told the UN he was weighing whether to “annihilate” Iran, but went on to hail renewed talks between Tehran and Washington’s negotiators.
In his steely speech, Pezeshkian made no reference to the talks to resolve the stalled war.
“(Trump) must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying. We will never bow our head or bend at the knee,” he said.
Pezeshkian insisted that Tehran would not allow the Strait of Hormuz, which it has choked off since the start of the war, causing global energy prices to spike, to be used as leverage against his country.
“We cannot let some have free access and bolster their interests from the waterway, while at the same time, using that waterway to impose their aggression upon us,” he said.
Pezeshkian’s attendance at the UN’s signature diplomatic event, in the heart of Manhattan, had been in doubt as it was unclear if the United States would issue a visa.
Ultimately, Washington granted the permit, but denied visas to several members of his entourage.
Soaring fuel prices threaten to cost Trump’s Republicans their control of Congress in November’s midterms, but the US President has sought to dismiss the domestic impact of the war.

Following weeks of worldwide headlines about the risks of uncontrollable artificial intelligence – and calls for a slowdown – industry leaders briefed the UN Security Council, calling for heightened vigilance.
“This moment calls for extreme care,” OpenAI chief executive officer Sam Altman said, while Anthropic’s Dario Amodei pledged to slow down where needed to ensure the safety of new AI releases.
In his speech on Sept 22, Trump rejected international regulation of AI, calling such proposals a “globalist scheme”.
Russia’s war against Ukraine also featured at the world body on Sept 23.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky accused his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin of using third-country fighters from 47 countries to continue Moscow’s war, which began with a 2022 invasion that has led to four years of bloody conflict.
Zelensky also warned that this winter, his forces could seek to target Russian heating and energy facilities to use the region’s bitter frost against Russia, as Moscow has done against Ukraine.
“Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us, but in response, we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia, too,” he told the UN.
‘Never had a woman leading’

“How can an organisation that claims to speak on behalf of the whole of humanity, never have had a woman leading” it, Sanchez said, adding that it was also overdue for the third-most populated continent to take the role.

Czech Republic expels Russians who were exposed filming for propaganda project Rybar, gives them three days to leave the country
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:35:51 UTC
23:35:51 KST

Czech police have detained and questioned Russians Vitaliy Chashchukhin and Igor Dolmatov, whom local journalists from the publication Seznam Zprávy had lured to a meeting in Prague that they secretly recorded. Chashchukhin and Dolmatov, who were working on behalf of the sanctioned Russian propaganda project Rybar, have now both been ordered to leave the Czech Republic within three days as undesirable persons, Seznam Zprávy reported on Sept. 22.
Czech police confirmed that procedural steps had been taken involving Chashchukhin but declined to disclose the outcome.
“We performed procedural acts with the mentioned person. Unfortunately, it is not possible to inform third parties about their result,” Ondřej Moravčík, spokesman for the Police Presidium, told Seznam Zprávy.
According to Seznam Zprávy’s sources, cameraman Igor Dolmatov received the same order to leave the country. The expulsion orders came after both of the Russians said during questioning that they worked for the Russian outlet Izvestia, a media organization that is also under European Union sanctions.
Filming organizer Boris Dvorkin, who was not physically present in Prague, told journalists that Chashchukhin was questioned for about nine hours.
“Vitaliy was interrogated by the Czech police for approximately nine hours. Subsequently, he was issued a document ordering him to leave the Czech Republic, after which he returned to Germany, where he legally resides. He obeyed this order,” Dvorkin said.
According to his own words during the hidden camera conversation he had with Czech journalists after his arrival in Prague, Chashchukhin has held permanent residency in Germany for about a decade and has performed work there for sanctioned Russian media outlets Izvestia, Channel Five, and REN TV. In his reports, he portrays Germany as a country in economic decline and argues that an end to arms supplies to Ukraine and a restoration of relations with Russia would remedy the situation. According to Seznam Zprávy’s sources, Czech security agencies are continuing to review Chashchukhin’s activities and have already informed their German counterparts.
Meanwhile, André Lenz, a spokesperson for Germany’s General Customs Directorate, told journalists that it is impossible to determine in advance whether working as a journalist for a sanctioned Russian media outlet constitutes a crime.
“Specific facts indicating a possible violation of sanctions are carefully reviewed in all individual cases. The competent public prosecutor's office decides on the initiation of investigative proceedings,” Lenz explained.
Seznam Zprávy’s operation to lure in the propagandists to Prague
Seznam Zprávy published an investigation on Sept. 22 describing how its journalists set a trap for participants in Rybar’s European influence operation. Representatives of the sanctioned Russian project had approached Czech media literacy and disinformation expert Bohumil Kartous and asked him to give an interview for a documentary series about the political and economic situation in Europe. Kartous agreed, and the Czech journalists then arranged a hidden-camera recording.
Chashchukhin and Dolmatov traveled from Berlin to Prague for the meeting. During the conversation, Chashchukhin acknowledged on hidden camera that: “It’s the Rybar project. You might know it. It’s Rybar.” Then, when Seznam Zprávy journalists approached, identified themselves, and began asking questions, both of the Russians ran off in different directions.
Journalists established that the filming was organized by Moscow-based documentary filmmaker Boris Dvorkin, who had not previously been publicly linked to Rybar. One of Dvorkin’s past projects was funded by the History of the Fatherland Foundation — an organization created by the decree of Vladimir Putin and chaired by Sergei Naryshkin, the head of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR).
After the first investigation, Dvorkin claimed that Chashchukhin had only helped him with one interview in his spare time and had not been paid. However, journalists found that Rybar representatives had organized filming in other European countries and had tried to recruit politicians, experts, and public figures to take part as subjects.
Rybar founder Mikhail Zvinchuk is under European Union sanctions, and official documents state that he is a member of a working group created by Vladimir Putin to coordinate Russia’s mobilization efforts in support of the war against Ukraine. Rybar’s main Telegram channel has more than 1.5 million subscribers. In 2024, the United States offered a reward of up to $10 million for information about the project’s employees as part of an effort to combat Kremlin-backed influence operations.

Israeli government's policies jeopardizing country's security: French foreign minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:34:22 UTC

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said Wednesday that policies pursued by the Israeli government were jeopardizing the country's security, citing what he described as Israel's refusal to fulfill its responsibilities under US President Donald Trump's Gaza peace plan and developments in the occupied West Bank.
"Our position is known. Our commitment to Israel's existence and security is unwavering," Barrot said.
"But the policy pursued by the current government of the State of Israel jeopardizes Israel's security," he added.
Barrot said this was reflected in what he described as Israeli authorities' "refusal" to fulfill their responsibilities under Trump's peace plan, as well as in the buffer-zone strategy being pursued in Lebanon and Syria.
He also pointed to the occupied West Bank, where he said there had been "an explosion of violence" by extremist occupiers against Palestinians and an "unprecedented acceleration" of illegal settlement activity.
"This weakens the prospect to which the international community is committed, which is the two-state solution," Barrot said.
"But it also poses a security risk to Israel and the Israeli population. This is something we cannot accept," he added. 
France ready to deploy Strait of Hormuz mission
Barrot also said France had prepared an international mission for the Strait of Hormuz that was ready to deploy as soon as conditions allowed, with the aim of helping restore shipping through the strategic waterway as quickly as possible.
He said Paris wanted the resumption of traffic to translate into lower fuel prices for French consumers as soon as possible.
France was also working with European and regional partners to develop alternative trade routes that would be less vulnerable to similar conflicts in the future, Barrot said.
Turning to the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb Strait, he said France would remain involved through the EU's Aspides maritime security mission, which he said had protected hundreds of French vessels from Houthi attacks.
Barrot added that the escalation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia had also had a significant impact on fuel prices.

Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:32:57 EEST
23:32:57 KST

The National Energy and Utilities Regulatory Commission (NEURC) was forced to postpone its meeting scheduled for Wednesday due to the security situation in Kyiv and technical problems with communications.
“Because there are constant air raid alerts in Kyiv, two of our colleagues are on business trips and, unfortunately, we cannot currently ensure normal communications quality, we will consider one issue and postpone the others until tomorrow, when our colleagues return,” commission member Kostiantyn Ushchapovsky, who chaired the meeting, said during an online broadcast, according to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.
Only three of the seven NEURC members were present at the meeting, while some of the others joined online.
The only issue considered by the regulator was imposing a fine on VolynElectrozbut LLC, in particular over its debt to household solar power plants.
Among the 44 items on the agenda was the issue of setting price caps on the electricity spot markets from October 31. According to the explanatory note to the draft resolution on price caps for the next six months, they were planned to remain at the current levels set from April 30.
The current 24-hour maximum price caps on the day-ahead market (DAM) and intraday market (IDM) are UAH 15,000/MWh, and UAH 17,000/MWh on the balancing market (BM). The minimum price caps on the DAM and IDM are UAH 10/MWh, and UAH 0.01/MWh on the BM.
As reported, Russia launched a massive attack on Kyiv on Wednesday, hitting filling stations, commercial facilities, nonresidential buildings and transport infrastructure, while internet problems were also reported. Head of JSC Market Operator Oleksandr Havva reported damage to the company's infrastructure, leaving its website and support service unavailable and affecting the organization of trading on the spot markets operated by the company.

Azerbaijan pardons Frenchman after EU lifts sanctions on Russian billionaire
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:32:42 BST
23:32:42 KST

Azerbaijan pardons Frenchman after EU lifts sanctions on Russian billionaire
- Published
French national Martin Ryan has been pardoned and his release from prison ordered by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev after he was jailed on charges of spying.
His release came hours after the EU agreed to lift sanctions on two Russian billionaires, prompting anger from Ukraine. Diplomats had indicated that France had pushed for an end to restrictions on one of the businessmen, Alisher Usmanov.
Ryan, who denied espionage, is one of 20 people pardoned by Aliyev.
However, a second Frenchman, Anass Derraz, remains in jail in Azerbaijan accused of accepting a Russian bribe.
It was not clear what had led to pressure for sanctions on Russian-Uzbek billionaire Usmanov to be lifted - the EU also agreed to take Russian-Israeli oligarch Mikhail Fridman off its sanctions list.
Slovakia is understood to have pressed for Usmanov's name to removed initially, and France then backed the move, highlighting national security concerns.
Both men have been under EU embargo since the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and until now EU sanctions on more than 3,000 "individuals and entities" have had to be renewed every six months. The latest agreement extends the sanctions on the others for three years.
Usmanov was cited by the EU in its 2022 listing, external as having "particularly close ties" to Russia's President Vladimir Putin, and of having "supported materially or financially and benefited from Russian decision-makers responsible for the annexation of Crimea and the destabilisation of Ukraine".
The metals and mining billionaire denied this characterisation of him. He has also been sanctioned by the UK and US governments.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha bitterly criticised the EU decision to lift sanctions on the two men, complaining that Moscow was "celebrating, because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans".
Latvia had initially opposed the move, but decided to abstain, announcing instead that it would impose its own measures on the two men.
Foreign Minister Baiba Braže said it was "dangerous and sends completely the wrong signal at a time when Russia's behaviour is becoming more aggressive". Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said later that France's President Emmanuel Macron had agreed to start talks on Latvia's "accession to the French nuclear deterrence initiative".
French relations with Azerbaijan have been poor in recent years, largely because of France's close relations with neighbouring Armenia. However, in May, Macron discussed developing ties with Aliyev, who later spoke of a "new era" in their relations.
Under Aliyev's decree on Wednesday, Ryan is one of 20 people including Azerbaijanis and Turks given a pardon.
Detained in December 2023, he was handed a 10-year jail term last March for espionage, charges denied by the French government.
Prosecutors alleged he had co-operated with employees of France's security services in Baku and gathered information about Azerbaijan's relations with Turkey, Iran and Pakistan, as well as companies linked to Russia and China.
"I did not spy. I am not a spy, and during the court case I tried to prove this," Ryan had told the court.
Another man he went on trial with, Azad Mamedli, was given 12 years in jail. Mamedli was not among the 20 prisoners pardoned by Aliyev.

MOSCOW, September 23. /TASS/. All shipments of military supplies, destined for Ukraine, are becoming a legitimate target for the Russian military, the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Spokeswoman, Maria Zakharova, said, commenting on the signing of the 100-year partnership declaration by Canada and Ukraine.
The diplomat said that Canada announced the transfer of interceptor missiles worth 350 million Canadian dollars (about $248 million) to Ukraine.
"We would like to offer the signatories a word of advice: such agreements lead to no good. Flooding Ukraine with weapons only delays peace and draws Western countries directly into the conflict, making them accomplices in the crimes, committed by Ukrainian neo-Nazis," she said. "Furthermore, any shipments of military supplies destined for Kiev become legitimate targets for the armed forces of the Russian Federation. We have issued warnings about this more than once."
Zakharova went on to say that Vladimir Zelensky is "touring the world in search of support," including military assistance that he needs "to continue the bloodshed that he unleashed against his own people."
"Unbiased commentators are already asking on social media: will Canadian taxpayers really have to financially support Ukraine over the next hundred of years? Will there be any tax write-offs in connection with Zelensky and his entourage, like there are for dependents? It’s hard to disagree with this framing: the Kiev junta has long been an international dependent, which the West has been carrying on its back," the diplomat said.
"A hundred of years is a serious timeframe. One can only wish Canadian citizens patience. The logic of Ottawa, as well as Washington, should be clear to them: the longer the conflict burns, the more orders the defense industry receives. However, as it is well known, any patience has its limits. Sooner or later, Canadians will start to question why their money is directed to financing a conflict on the other end of the world rather than on healthcare and roads," Zakharova added.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Vladimir Zelensky signed declarations on 100-year partnership and on cooperation in defense and security in Calgary, Alberta, on September 100. The 100-year partnership declaration implies that a corresponding treaty will be signed in the future. The other document envisages, among other things, joint projects and the localization of defense production on the territory of Ukraine and Canada.

Military low flying: RAF operational low flying training timetable
Royal Air Force (RAF) operational low flying training timetables in 3 areas of the UK.
Documents
Details
Timetables for operational low flying (OLF) training by RAF fast jets and Hercules aircraft. These timetables cover 3 tactical training areas (TTA) only. These are:
- LFA 7(T): central Wales
- LFA 14(T): northern Scotland
- LFA 20(T): the borders of southern Scotland and northern England
When the TTA is not in use, there may be other flying activity in the area. The MOD is unable to provide a timetable for all low flying activity as the information can very quickly become outdated due to weather conditions and training requirements.

YouTube’s Custom Feeds Give You More Control Over the Algorithm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:30:00 UTC
23:30:00 KST

My YouTube algorithm is sacred, with years of data about my preferences and viewing history fermenting into whatever videos it picks for my home screen. YouTube’s algorithm, while not perfect, sure knows what I want to see. The current top three videos on my front page are an Apple Watch analysis, a Big Brother season 28 update, and something called “I Lost to the Muppets” from comedian Chris Fleming. Click. Click. Click.
As part of its Made on YouTube event Wednesday, Google released several new features, including a Custom Feeds button for adjusting what videos pop up on your front page. It’s a rare chance for users to directly tweak their algorithmic feed on YouTube, in ways that go beyond just pressing thumbs up on a video or blocking a creator.
To try it out, users can click the Your custom feeds button below the search bar and type a request for the feed they’d like to see. YouTube uses large language models to process your request and whip up a freshly personalized homepage. “I want a rainy Shanghai vibe: café jazz, street food, and vlogs,” read one of my suggested prompts.
YouTube tested Custom Feeds as an experimental feature earlier this year, before deciding that it was a good fit. The company plans to roll it out soon as an option for all US users, whether viewing on mobile, desktop, or TV.
“Users are always telling us that they want more control,” says Emily Moxley, YouTube’s vice president of product management. “They want more ability to steer their algorithm. With custom feeds, we're giving them a natural-language way that they can do that. They can tell us exactly what they want.”
So, I told YouTube exactly what I wanted to see: “Gooey macaroni and cheese recipe videos, Caleb Hearon clip compilations, and crystal singing bowl videos under 15 minutes.” And the feed it generated was exactly that. My perfect zen blend for rotting on the couch after a long day. YouTube suggested potential additions to expand my prompt, like “uploaded this month” and “without talking or commentary.” Not bad.
The Custom Feeds button sits next to other topic tabs below the search bar, like “Music” and “Podcasts.” Experimenting with this tool doesn’t replace your standard homepage, which you can access anytime by clicking the “All” button. Users can save multiple custom feeds.
This feature feels most helpful when blending multiple preferences. It’s better than a standard YouTube search at responding dynamically to complex video requests, whether that’s showing videos on multiple topics under a certain length or attempting to capture a specific vibe for your current mood.
YouTube's event for 2026 focused heavily on generative AI features, including expanding the Ask YouTube tool. Launched earlier this year at Google I/O, Ask YouTube is a chatbot-style addition to its search capabilities that lets users ask more specific questions about videos. The tool is now better equipped to answer questions when shopping for specific products.
The product team at YouTube also tested a feature that let users directly steer their overall recommendation algorithm, but ultimately decided against shipping it. “We found users were nervous and afraid to do that,” Moxley says. “They were worried about messing it up.” The Custom Feeds button is designed to give users a low-stakes place to experiment.
YouTube’s Custom Feeds feature is part of a larger trend of software companies letting users slightly adjust their algorithms using requests sent through generative AI tools. Late last year, Meta launched the Your Algorithm feature on Instagram, letting users adjust the kinds of posts they see. Spotify similarly dropped a Prompted Playlists tool to customize your music-listening habits.

Iran’s president said Wednesday that his people have been "victims of terrorism" by the United States, delivering a rare wartime speech at the UN General Assembly a day after U.S. President Donald Trump said he could “annihilate” the Islamic Republic.
President Masoud Pezeshkian held up photos of the late Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and the more than 150 schoolchildren killed on the first days of the war.
“We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists,” Pezeshkian said at the General Assembly. “Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country. And we defended ourselves with utmost strength. America and Israel attacked us.”
He added of the United States: “Yes, they did hit us, but we did not bend the knee.”
Arriving in New York under heavy security and scrutiny, Pezeshkian — who, within Iran’s political landscape, is considered a moderate politician — will address world leaders a day after U.S. President Donald Trump used the same stage to suggest he may “annihilate” the Islamic Republic if a deal isn’t reached soon to end the nearly seven-month war.
Hours later, Trump told reporters that his chief envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, met for about three hours with the Iranian officials on the sidelines of the annual gathering. But he offered few details about how the discussions transpired or the substance of the exchange.
“It was a very good meeting,” Trump said. The president later added that the Iranian officials were “not the highest level, but it’s something.” Also on Tuesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump is open to meeting with Pezeshkian while he’s in New York.
But Tehran downplayed Tuesday's unscheduled exchange, which were the first indirect talks between U.S. and Iranian officials since a June ceasefire unraveled. Esmail Baghaei, an Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson, maintained the country's negotiating position in talks with U.S. officials, demanding that Washington end its blockade of Iranian ports and release frozen Iranian assets,
Baghaei said the talks — conducted indirectly through Qatari mediators — were “not anything new.”
Pezeshkian will have the chance to elaborate on where Tehran stands as more than a year of start-stop negotiations between the two longtime adversaries have failed to produce a sustainable solution. His speech comes as intermittent attacks continued in the Strait of Hormuz off Iran’s coast, where commercial shipping remained below prewar levels.
His address last year came months after the 12-day Israel-Iran war that saw the assassination of many of the Islamic Republic’s highest military and political leaders and once again broke down weeks of negotiations with the United States.
“Ladies and gentlemen, you all bore witness that this past June, my country was subjected to a savage aggression and flagrant contravention of the most elementary principles of international law,” Pezeshkian said at the time.

German chemicals giant reveals details of downsizing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:28:40 UTC
23:28:40 KST

German chemicals giant reveals details of downsizing
German chemicals giant Evonik is overhauling its domestic operations amid what it has described as a “structural and economic crisis” in the industry.
The German and wider European chemical sector has been hit by plant closures, job losses and high energy costs following the loss of cheap Russian supplies; the US-Israeli war with Iran has added new pressure.
The measures, announced on Tuesday, include site closures, job cuts and a reshaping of Evonik’s six main German plants, even as the company considers increasing investment in Asia and the Americas, where it sees “good opportunities for growth.”
Evonik’s plans to eliminate 2,150 jobs in Germany through 2029 have drawn criticism from industrial policy spokesman for the opposition Left Party (Die Linke) Mirze Edis, who called the cuts “a damning indictment” of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Economy Minister Katharina Reiche.
“Their inaction regarding chemical industry sites has now become a nationwide economic risk,” Edis said.
Evonik produces chemicals and additives used in everything from car tires and plastics to cosmetics and medicines, making it a key supplier across the economy.
Germany’s chemical sector has been among the hardest hit by the country’s energy problems. Berlin moved to end its dependence on Russian energy following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022 and turned to alternative suppliers, leaving energy-intensive manufacturers facing substantially higher costs.
Evonik said at the time that it consumed around 15 terawatt-hours of natural gas annually, more than a third of it in Germany, and warned that losing Russian supplies could “seriously jeopardize chemical production” in the country.
The war with Iran and disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have added to the pressure this year. While Germany gets most of its LNG from the US rather than the Persian Gulf, the de facto closure of the strait disrupted flows accounting for almost 20% of the global LNG supply, tightening the market and driving up European prices.
The crisis extends beyond Germany. Permanent chemical plant closures across Europe have surged sixfold from pre-2022 levels amid high energy costs, weak demand and cheaper overseas competition, according to the European Chemical Industry Council (Cefic).
British chemicals giant INEOS said this week it would close its three acetyl plants in Hull, the last major facilities of their kind in Europe, blaming soaring energy costs and carbon taxes. It said natural gas in Europe now costs 12 times as much as it does in the US, making even highly efficient plants uncompetitive.

Magnitude 1.4 quake shakes northwestern Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:28:00 UTC
23:28:00 KST

Magnitude 1.4 quake shakes northwestern Estonia
A 1.4 magnitude earth tremor was recorded on Sunday, Maaleht reported, the second to be recorded in the region this year.
The Estonian Geological Survey (Eesti geoloogiateenistus) said the quake was recorded at 7:42 p.m. on Sunday, September 20, near the villages of Änglema and Alliklepa in Harju County, around 70 kilometers from Tallinn.
The quake's epicenter was located at a depth of about eight kilometers.
In early August, a magnitude 0.5 earthquake occurred near the island of Naissaar, in Tallinn Bay; usually only about one earthquake is detected in Estonia every two years on average.
Northwestern Estonia, together with the surrounding sea area, is broadly considered the country's most seismically active region.
In June 2022, two earthquakes with magnitudes of 2.3 and 1.4 were recorded about five kilometers from the epicenter of the latest incident.
Estonia's strongest known earthquake occurred near Osmussaar, an island of the northwest coast, in 1976, with a magnitude of 4.5 on the Richter scale.
Despite being a long way from any of the world's major geological fault lines, earth tremors occur in Estonia due to the crystalline basement being crossed by numerous ancient faults.
When stresses accumulated underground exceed the strength of the rocks, these zones of weakness can shift slightly and trigger an earthquake.
On the whole however earthquakes are generally modest in Estonia compared with those seen in more tectonically active places; the magnitude 1.4 Änglema quake is fairly typical by Estonian standards, Maaleht reported.

Israel squeezing UN Palestinian refugee agency ahead of polls, says its chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:28:00 UTC
23:28:00 KST

Israel squeezing UN Palestinian refugee agency ahead of polls, says its chief
NEW YORK – Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing government is squeezing the UN’s agency for Palestinian refugees ahead of elections in Israel in an effort to boost its appeal to voters, the agency’s leader said.
UNRWA’s acting commissioner-general Christian Saunders said Israel was being “extremely difficult” about letting in vital supplies like engine oil to Gaza for relief operations while permitting luxury commercial products.
“About 30 per cent of what’s coming in is humanitarian aid – the rest is commercial... I would consider some of the stuff coming in to be luxury goods. I mean, you do not need Nutella to survive,” he told AFP late on Sept 22.
Speaking at the UN’s signature New York diplomatic gathering, Saunders also warned he would be forced to cut long-term services to refugees if his agency could not begin to bridge a US$100 million (S$128 million) shortfall in the next two months.
“We implemented a number of austerity measures, including putting the staff on an 80 per cent work week with a 20 per cent reduction in salary... although you cannot keep people on an 80 per cent work week and a 20 per cent reduction in salary forever,” he said.
Saunders said he believes Israel’s Oct 27 elections are contributing to UNRWA’s challenges because “the current government is pushing to implement as much of their programme before the elections as they can”.
Netanyahu, who heads the most right-wing government in Israeli history, is locked in a tight election race and is focusing his campaign on security concerns ahead of October’s vote.
UNRWA has long attracted Netanyahu’s ire.
“I think they’re trying to show the Israeli public why they should re-elect them,” Saunders added.
In September, Israeli forces took control of a vocational training centre run by the UN agency for Palestinian refugees in an East Jerusalem suburb.
The raid drew condemnation from UN chief Antonio Guterres, and followed warnings by UNRWA that the Israeli authorities were threatening its Qalandia training centre, located between the East Jerusalem neighbourhood of Kafr Aqab and the Qalandia refugee camp.
The centre was established in 1952 and offers vocational training to around 340 Palestinians from the occupied West Bank every year, according to UNRWA.
“We’ve been doing this for 76 years. We will find alternative ways in which to provide those young people with the necessary training,” Saunders said.
In January, Israel began demolitions at UNRWA’s headquarters in East Jerusalem, in what the organisation called an “unprecedented attack”.
Netanyahu’s government has repeatedly accused UNRWA of providing cover for Hamas militants, claiming that some of its employees took part in the group’s Oct 7, 2023, attack on Israel that sparked the war in Gaza.
Legislation severing ties with the agency and banning it from operating on Israeli territory took effect in January 2025.
A series of investigations, including one led by France’s former foreign minister Catherine Colonna, found some “neutrality-related issues” at UNRWA but stressed Israel had not provided conclusive evidence for its headline allegation. AFP

The moment Antonelli knew he had been transformed as an F1 driver
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:26:47 BST
23:26:47 KST

The moment Antonelli knew he had been transformed as an F1 driver
- Published
Kimi Antonelli says he knew from the first moment he drove this year's Mercedes that he would be transformed as a Formula 1 driver in 2026.
The 20-year-old Italian, who is running away with the world championship in only his second season in F1, is reflecting on his breakthrough year in the sport in an exclusive interview with BBC Sport.
A difficult debut season last year had left external expectations of Antonelli low at the start of 2026. But on a typically damp and cold January day at Silverstone, he already sensed that something special might be on the cards.
"It was just a few laps in the wet," Antonelli says, "but I just felt better in the car, much better than I felt last year. Also the car felt well, but I just felt better mentally in the car. Less tense, more relaxed and more mature."
Last year, he says, was "not great". "I was driving very tense most of the time, I wasn't able to extract the potential out of me," he says.
"This year, it's a lot different. The mindset has been the biggest change."
Fast forward eight months and the effects of that new headspace are plain to see.
After 14 grands prix, and with either eight or nine remaining depending on the war in the Middle East, Antonelli is a massive 81 points clear of team-mate George Russell.
Not only that, but he looks so in control. Always fast, always composed, a factor in every grand prix. Everyone knows the championship is basically over, barring some kind of dramatic misfortune.
Even then, Antonelli says he is "still finding my way" in F1.
The journey Antonelli has been on in the past two years is remarkable, and he says even he is "surprised" by the extent of his progress this year.
He was comprehensively outperformed by Russell in 2025. So when it was obvious that Mercedes would start the new regulatory era with an advantage, it was the Briton who started the season as championship favourite.
Russell duly won the opening race in Australia, but Antonelli was less than three seconds behind him at the flag. This, he says, was the second moment of realisation of what might be possible.
"I had a big, big crash in FP3," Antonelli recalls. "But then thanks to the mechanics - who all throughout the season have done an incredible job, but on that specific occasion, it is a miracle - I was able to go back in the car and push again in the high speed and getting close to the limit.
"The crash, definitely it compromised a little bit qualifying and the race because we couldn't set up properly the car. I mean, the car was still very quick. But it was not easy.
"Still being able to stay close despite that, I was like, 'OK, you know, it's not going to be a walk in the park. It's going to be very tough', but I knew already that it was a different story compared to last year.
"If it would have happened last year, I wouldn't have been able to overcome that."
Monza 2024 memory made Antonelli 'afraid to do a mistake'
Antonelli's first season in F1 was haunted by an incident that happened the first time he drove on a grand prix weekend.
At the 2024 Italian Grand Prix, the day before they formally announced Antonelli was the replacement for Ferrari-bound Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes gave him an outing in first practice at Monza.
He was blindingly fast on his first flying lap - but then crashed heavily on his second.
Team principal Toto Wolff played it down at the time, saying he was well aware there would be mistakes from Antonelli as he found his feet in F1. But behind the scenes the incident had had a big impact on the young man.
"Monza stayed in my head for a very long time," Antonelli says. "I think all throughout last season, at least. Definitely that was a big thing that was kind of slowing me down.
"This memory of being afraid to do a mistake, also because going through the difficult period (in the middle of 2025), this memory was even stronger in my head, if you know what I mean.
"Because it was already a difficult period and I was like, 'If I even do a mistake or I crash, it's even worse.'
"So yeah, it's been a thing that has been bothering me a lot last year. This year I was able to just put it behind."
Doing so has involved a lot of work behind the scenes, analysing what happened in 2025, understanding what had gone well, what had not, and why, and what he could do to improve.
"The mindset going into this season, it was mainly trying to be able to extract more out of my potential," Antonelli says. "Trying to, first of all, do a better job than previous year. But as well trying to put things more together.
"The preparation that I did in pre-season was very, very intense. But it helped me a lot to arrive ready for this season.
"Plus, I did a lot of work with my mental coach. Trying to get my head right, my thoughts right on understanding the goal, and understanding that the most important thing is to be ready and to stay present in the moment.
"Not trying to think about final results or what would happen if I wouldn't achieve that. But just trying to be present and trying to do the best with what you can do in the moment."
'First win, first pole, took a lot of weight off my shoulder'
Still, though, he admits to be "definitely surprised" at how much progress he has made.
"I knew that I was going to be better than my first year," he says. "Obviously, because I think last year, towards the end of the season, I started to put things more together, starting to extract more performance. But still, it was still not great.
"Whereas this year, it's a lot different. Also as well, with the first win, the first pole, it took a lot of weight off my shoulder."
Antonelli has blossomed. Everything seems to be coming so easily to him. If he drops back in a race, he recovers seamlessly and quickly. Overtaking moves are done quickly and decisively. There's not been a circuit on which he has lacked pace.
Russell, by contrast, has admitted to struggling and - while not trying to take anything away from Antonelli, who he is always quick to praise - has expressed his opinion that his his driving style does not suit this year's new cars.
All of which raises a key question - how much of what is happening this year is Antonelli stepping it up, and how much Russell falling back?
"That's a very difficult question," Antonelli says. "I've definitely stepped up.
"This year definitely everything is new. So it requires also a little bit of a different approach. And trying to adapt to a different car, which hasn't been easy."
His consistency this year, he says, has come from the fact he has found "a nice rhythm in the season".
"I always try to follow my routines," Antonelli says, "the way I approach the weekend. I try to approach it all the time the same.
"I'm still finding my way, but I've found a way that helps me to be consistent and also helps me to be consistently ready when I go in the car."
There are still moments when he misjudges things, though. He cites the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix, just days after his outstanding win in Monaco, one of the most dominant at that storied track for years.
"Monaco was a very high moment for me in the season, and then I went to Barcelona and I was probably a bit too excited, especially over a single lap," he says.
"So I was overdriving, I was chasing the lap time and the result didn't come in qualifying. I was actually a bit far back and didn't do a good lap.
"But that's because I was trying to do a bit too much after a very high moment in my career. And then I understood that that is not the way."
The lesson was applied after his spellbinding win from 19th on the grid at Monza, his home race, a result that Wolff said "closed a cycle" from his 2024 crash.
Antonelli says: "After Monza, I reminded myself, 'Don't make the same mistake as you did after Monaco.'"
He won the Spanish Grand Prix seven days later, an eighth victory from 14 races so far this season.
Success has inevitably led to fame, and with it attention.
"Life has changed a lot," Antonelli says. "I'm not going to lie. It's been a big change, but it's nice to see so much support. Definitely, one side is very nice, but on the other side, you have to be careful. You've got to protect yourself a bit more because obviously you're more exposed."
All year, Antonelli has talked about focusing on process, about doing the best he can on every single day, not thinking about the big picture.
Now, though, for the first time, he acknowledges the title - an achievement that would make him the youngest world champion in F1 history - is on his mind.
"Yes, I thought about it," he says. "But again, thinking about it, I came always to the same conclusion that the earlier I finish all this, the better it is.
"So I've got to just keep pushing. I keep doing the best I can every race. Because, yeah, that's the way. Just not finish. And until it's done, it's not over."

India to begin mass production of new laser anti-drone system — newspaper
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:23:35 UTC
23:23:35 KST

NEW DELHI, September 23. /TASS/. India’s Defense Research and Development Organization (DRDO) plans to begin mass production of a new mobile laser system designed to destroy drones, The Times of India reported.
The 30-kW laser system is capable of intercepting unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) at a distance of up to 5 km. In August 2025, the platform underwent successful testing and will be ready for mass production in a few months at one of the DRDO’s partner companies.
This new development will allow the Indian Armed Forces to reduce their reliance on more expensive air defense systems to counter the threat posed by UAVs.
Previously, the DRDO developed a 2-kW laser weapon for destroying drones, which is already being manufactured by defense companies Adani, Astra, and Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL). India has also developed a 10-kW laser weapon for engaging aerial targets, with production contracts awarded to Larsen & Toubro and BEL.
As part of India’s ongoing Sudarshan Chakra program to develop a multi-layered air defense system, the DRDO is working on the development of 50-kW and 100-kW laser systems.

IDF reservist Neria Leiter, an American citizen and son of Ambassador to the US Yechiel Leiter, was seriously wounded in a car-ramming terrorist attack at Maccabim (Bell) checkpoint on Route 443 near Modi’in-Maccabim-Re’ut on Wednesday.
In 2023, one of Leiter’s other sons, Maj. (res.) Moshe Yedidya, was killed in Gaza. He was a company commander in the 551st Brigade’s 697th Battalion.
Neria Leiter is currently in serious condition and is being treated at Shaare Zedek Medical Center in Jerusalem. In a Wednesday night statement, the hospital announced that Neria had undergone a multi-hour brain surgery, alongside other treatments, and that "his condition remains very serious, and his life is in danger."
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited Neria Leiter’s family at the hospital before leaving for the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA). At the same time, Yechiel Leiter is returning to Israel from the United States. He will not join Netanyahu at the UNGA on Thursday.
“I am grateful to the IDF, to the medical team at Shaare Zedek who are now fighting to save the life of Neria Dov ben Chana, and for the prayers of the people of Israel,” Leiter wrote on X/Twitter on Wednesday. “I believe in the power of prayer, and I believe that when the people of Israel unite, miracles happen. Neria needs a miracle."
“Neria continued to serve in the reserves after losing his older brother, Moshe Yedidya Leiter, of blessed memory. Since October 7, he has served hundreds of days in the reserves on multiple fronts.
“Palestinian terrorism seeks to uproot the people of Israel from their land. They choose death – we choose life,” Leiter said.
In a post on X, Netanyahu said he and his wife, Sara, “together with all the people of Israel, are praying for a miracle. Yechiel, my dear, we are all with you.”
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee said that he is standing with Leiter and his family.
"Pray for Yechiel Leiter & entire family. They lost a son in Gaza, killed by Hamas. Now a Palestinian terrorist attempts to murder IDF soldiers at a checkpoint. Standing w/ Yechiel Leiter," Huckabee wrote on X.
Yechiel, my dear friend, my heart is with you, Chana, and your entire family," Israel's Ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, shared on X. "All of Israel is praying for your son, Neria Dov ben Chana, who was critically wounded in today’s heinous terrorist attack. May God heal him and give your family strength."
Defense Minister Israel Katz sent his support to Leiter’s family and prayers for Neria’s speedy recovery.
“Yechiel, I stand with you and your family, and I pray alongside the entire nation of Israel for your son’s recovery,” Katz said. “I commend the heroic fighters who eliminated the terrorist. To the soldiers of the IDF and the security forces: I believe in you and trust you; we will not allow terror to rear its head.”
"Yechiel, you are a warrior, and your sons are warriors," wrote Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar on X. "My heart and prayers are with you."
President Isaac Herzog also offered a "prayer for the complete and speedy recovery of Neria Leiter, a reservist soldier who was run over today in a heinous terror attack at the Maccabim checkpoint."
“Neria Leiter is the brother of Major Moshe Leiter, of blessed memory, a hero of Israel who fell at the beginning of the Swords of Iron War in Gaza," Herzog wrote in an evening statement. “We send our wishes for a complete recovery to Neria, and strength to his wife and to his parents, Hannah and Yechiel Leiter, Israel's Ambassador to the United States."
"Neria is fighting for his life at this very hour, and we will pray for his recovery. We all stand with this dear family and send them our strength.”
Police Commissioner Daniel Levi, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, Economy and Industry Minister Nir Barkat, and Ofir Akunis, Israel's consul general in New York, also offered Leiter their support.
“We join all the residents of Samaria in praying for the victim’s recovery and offer our support to his family during this difficult time,” Samaria Regional Council head Yossi Dagan said. “The Council will assist the victim’s family, and together with the community, we will embrace and support them in every way possible. The entire nation of Israel is united in prayer for his recovery.”
“We must respond to murderous terrorism with a firm hand and restore deterrence. We send our support to the security forces on the front lines who are protecting the citizens of Israel.”
IDF troops kill 29-year-old terrorist
The terrorist was killed by IDF troops who were at the scene as he attempted to flee. He has been identified as Muhammad Mahmoud Suleiman, 29, a resident of Beit Ur al-Tahta.
According to KAN News, Suleiman was very familiar with the area and carried out the attack on his own using a stolen Israeli license plate taken from a car that had been taken off the road several months ago.
He is not known for prior security-related offenses, had not applied for a work permit within Israel, and was not supposed to be inside the Green Line, KAN reported, citing security officials.
IDF and Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) have reportedly questioned Suleiman's family members as part of the ongoing investigation into the attack.
Israel Police stated that the terrorist had hit a police patrol vehicle belonging to the Judea and Samaria District. An officer and a soldier were inside the vehicle as part of a joint operation.
“United Hatzalah’s dispatch center sent us to the scene of a vehicular ramming attack near Bell checkpoint,” United Hatzalah paramedics Itzik Kara and Netanel Cohen said. “Assisted by IDF medical teams, we provided initial medical treatment at the scene, including respiratory support, the administration of life-saving medication, bandaging, and splinting to a man who was subsequently transported to the hospital in serious condition.”
Palestinian shot after reported car-ramming attack attempt near Hebron
Earlier on Wednesday, two Palestinians reportedly attempted to run over the owner of a farm in the Hebron Hills.
The farm owner began shooting at them in accordance with the “suspect arrest procedure,” wounding one of the individuals in the leg, according to reports.
IDF troops were deployed to the area, N12 News reported, adding that the incident is under review.

IDF: Drakon submarine has stronger weapons, longer underwater capabilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:22:08 UTC
23:22:08 KST

The German-made INS Drakon submarine, which will be officially accepted in Israel at a ceremony on Thursday, has stronger weapons and longer underwater capabilities than prior Israeli submarines, according to the IDF.
The Drakon submarine is the sixth submarine to join the Israeli Navy’s fleet in recent years and the third of the Dolphin class – specifically, the Dolphin II variant equipped with an Air-Independent Propulsion system.
This AIP system allows the submarine to generate energy and recharge its batteries while submerged for extended periods, with no need to surface or access external air.
Earlier submarines could only remain submerged for a couple of days, eventually a couple of weeks, but the Dolphin-II class Drakon can do so for much longer.
Part of the Drakon’s system utilizes hydrogen and oxygen to generate energy, which enables the submarine to extend the duration of its covert underwater operations and maintain operational capability over time.
The submarine measures over 70 meters in length, making it approximately 30% larger than the original Dolphin-class submarines. The section visible above the water accounts for less than one-fifth of its total size.
While neither Israel nor the German company ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems (TKMS) has revealed why the Drakon has an expanded design or confirmed what new systems it has installed, experts have speculated that the expanded design could include new capabilities – such as possible vertical launching systems (VLS).
These systems, if present, could substantially increase the submarine’s potential uses by enabling it to deploy additional weapons, cruise missiles, unmanned underwater systems (UUVs), intelligence equipment, or special operations capabilities.
Some experts have speculated that the expansion could also relate to launch cells, but the precise internal configuration remains unknown.
What has been published is that the Drakon has 10 torpedo tubes located in the bow: six standard 533 mm tubes and four oversized 650 mm tubes. The wider tubes can launch heavier weapons, specialized equipment, and even UUVs.
According to reports, the submarines are able to deliver nuclear weapons. Multiple foreign publications have noted that Israeli submarines are part of a triad of nuclear deterrence that Israel possesses, along with land-based and air-based weapons.
During Defense Ministry Director-General Amir Baram and other senior defense officials’ stay in Germany in December 2025, they made new progress regarding the ongoing submarine deals, which have unique offensive and defensive capabilities, The Jerusalem Post reported at the time.
Though Israel has never publicly admitted to possessing nuclear weapons, former prime ministers and others, notably Ehud Olmert, have at times slipped up and alluded to such a weapons program.
The arrival of the Drakon completes the second generation of Israeli Navy submarines built in Germany, which Israel has said symbolizes the long-standing defense partnership between the two countries.
The voyage from Germany to Israel covers a distance of approximately 4,000 nautical miles (8,000 kilometers) and took the Drakon just over three weeks, but it can also take up to a month.
Possible delays due to various diplomatic maritime issues Israel has encountered
There may have been delays due to various diplomatic maritime problems that Israel has encountered, which have been publicly reported since the beginning of the Israel-Hamas War.
Departing from the TKMS shipyard in Kiel, Germany, the Drakon transited across part of the Atlantic Ocean near Western Europe and passed through the Strait of Gibraltar to the Mediterranean Sea.
The vessel’s arrival in Israel was the culmination of over 12 years of development, including months of trials and preparations.
Close cooperation was maintained throughout the project among the Israeli Navy, the German Navy, and the German Defense Ministry, as well as the German professionals involved in the submarine’s construction.
Israeli direct involvement in joint naval projects with Germany continues
Israeli involvement in the project has spanned approximately 20 years, managed by an Israeli project directorate operating in Germany that oversaw the design, construction, and testing phases.
Officers and engineers from the Israeli Navy served in the project directorate, relocating to Germany with their families for periods of several years. Submarine squadron crews joined the project at a later stage, participating in drills at sea, testing, and the process of judging the ship’s readiness and delivering it to the Israeli Navy.
Israeli direct involvement in joint naval projects with Germany continues, looking ahead to the next generation of submarines – the Dakar-class – which are currently under construction and have an expected delivery start date in 2031.
The Drakon incorporates advanced technological capabilities that expand the Israeli Navy’s operational toolkit, enabling it to operate across a diverse range of arenas and missions.
Beyond the technology, the submarine squadron relies on its human capital – young crews demonstrating high levels of professionalism, responsibility, composure, and operational sharpness.
Submariners operate complex combat systems over extended periods in distant maritime theaters, working in challenging conditions of secrecy and isolation from the outside world.

As many as 17 people killed by bear attacks in Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:21:30 UTC
23:21:30 KST

KRASNOYARSK, September 23. /TASS/. The number of people killed by bear attacks in Russia in recent months has risen to 17. Such attacks have occurred in the Siberian and Far Eastern federal districts, according to TASS estimates.
The highest death toll was recorded in the Krasnoyarsk Region in Siberia, where six people have died in bear attacks. Three people have been killed in each of the Tomsk and Irkutsk Regions, while two deaths have been reported in Buryatia. Fatal bear attacks on people have also been recorded in Altai, Kamchatka and the Khabarovsk Region.
Forest fires in the Krasnoyarsk Region and a poor pine nut harvest were among the reasons for the large number of bears coming into contact with people. The latest case was reported on September 23, when a bear attacked a guard at a truck parking lot in northern Krasnoyarsk Region.
Overall, TASS estimates that bears have approached populated areas in 41 Russian regions in 2026. The situation has been particularly difficult in Eastern Siberia. Bears have approached schools and military units and tried to enter private homes in the north of the region. Bears have also been spotted in popular tourist recreation areas in Krasnoyarsk, including the Gremyachaya Griva eco-park, near the Krasnoyarsk Pillars National Park and in an upscale cottage community in the Udachny neighborhood.
A heightened-alert regime has been introduced throughout the Irkutsk Region, while a curfew is in effect in Baikalsk. A heightened-alert regime has also been introduced in the city of Abaza in southern Khakassia, where, according to local authorities, bears have placed the city under "de facto siege." Regional authorities plan to extend the regime to the entire republic.

US sanctions could make ICC operations impossible, lawyer says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:20:49 UTC
23:20:49 KST

MOSCOW, September 23. /TASS/. US sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC) could make its day-to-day operations and investigations impossible due to restrictions related to the US financial system and technology, Artur Gulasaryan, an associate professor at the Kutafin Moscow State Law University (MSAL), told TASS.
Reuters earlier reported, citing two sources, that US President Donald Trump’s administration had prepared a full package of sanctions against the ICC as an organization and planned to announce their introduction soon.
"Cutting the ICC off from US technology and the financial system makes it impossible to conduct its day-to-day operations and investigations," Gulasaryan said.
The lawyer explained that due to the sanctions, the ICC could lose access to US financial and technology services without special authorization from the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). "The financial aspect of the restrictions involves the inevitable blocking of dollar correspondent accounts and transactions, which, under strict banking compliance rules, effectively isolates the ICC from the international settlement system and makes standard cross-border payments impossible," he said. "The court’s operations are further paralyzed by the severe deterioration of its IT infrastructure: due to OFAC restrictions, the institution loses legal access to US-licensed software, cloud data storage services and secure communications systems."
