The leaders of Denmark, Greenland and the United States are expected to sign a security and defense agreement concerning Greenland on Tuesday.
The ceremony is scheduled for 10:30 a.m. local time, or 4:30 p.m. Danish time, at the United Nations headquarters in New York.
The Danish Prime Minister’s Office described it as “a joint agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic region.”
The agreement will be signed by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, US President Donald Trump and Jens-Frederik Nielsen, head of Naalakkersuisut, Greenland’s government.
Few details about the agreement have been released since it was announced Friday.
Trump said on Truth Social that the agreement gives the United States “permanent control over security and all other necessities in Greenland.”
Frederiksen has said the agreement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, as well as Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
“We are not ceding sovereignty, and I can give a guarantee that I never will as Danish prime minister,” Frederiksen told Danish broadcasters DR and TV 2 on Monday.
She said sovereignty could be maintained alongside closer defense cooperation with other countries.
The USA plans to reopen a former military base in Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland and establish a military presence on Greenland’s east coast, Reuters reported Monday.
The eastern site is currently used by the Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, a Danish military unit operating in Greenland.
Reuters attributed the information to three unnamed sources familiar with a defense agreement involving Greenland, Denmark and the USA. Danish public broadcaster DR also reported that the USA plans two new bases.
The agreement’s text has not been published, and its details may change before it is signed, Reuters reported.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, US President Donald Trump and Greenlandic head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen are expected to sign the agreement Tuesday at the United Nations headquarters in New York.
The Danish Prime Minister’s Office said the agreement would strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.
Trump has said it gives the USA “permanent control over security and all other necessities in Greenland.”
Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said the agreement recognizes the Kingdom of Denmark’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
“We do not surrender sovereignty, and I can give a guarantee that I will never do that as Danish prime minister,” Frederiksen told DR and Danish broadcaster TV 2.
More than 20 percent of Nordic teenagers drink energy drinks at least once a day, according to a survey of 4,916 people ages 15 to 19.
The study covered Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden. Six in 10 respondents drank energy drinks at least weekly.
Almost half said they could not get through the day without an energy drink or sometimes felt that way.
The report found that 46 percent began drinking energy drinks at age 14 or younger. One in 10 started before age 12.
Among those who consumed the drinks, 30 percent reported feeling unwell or experiencing other negative health effects. Heart palpitations and sleep problems were among the most common complaints.
“When a habit begins to affect sleep, well-being, or everyday life, there is reason to act,” said Sabina Litens Karlsson, a toxicologist at Livsmedelsverket, Sweden’s national food authority, which conducted the study.
Taste was cited by 73 percent of consumers, while 51 percent wanted more energy and 34 percent wanted to stay awake.
Weekly consumption was highest in Sweden at 75 percent and lowest in Denmark at 43 percent.
Norway has banned sales to people under 16. Denmark has no legal age limit, but its food authority advises children under 15 not to consume energy drinks.
Denmark now expects to complete the final compensation cases for the mink industry in the third quarter of 2028, at least six months later than previously planned.
The Danish Civil Aviation and Railway Authority disclosed the delay in a briefing shared with the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“The decisions on compensation have unfortunately proven to be more time-consuming than assumed,” said Transport and Rural Affairs Minister Signe Munk of the Socialist People’s Party.
The authority previously expected the final cases to be completed during 2027.
The delay is linked to European Commission approval for state aid, which expires on April 1 and cannot be extended.
Officials must prioritize partial decisions determining whether applicants qualify for compensation before that deadline. Two teams have been reassigned to the Mink Secretariat unit preparing those decisions, leaving fewer employees to complete final compensation awards.
The delay could add about 40 million DKK in costs, the authority estimated.
At the beginning of 2026, the total expected cost of compensation, farm demolitions and administration was 29.1 billion DKK.
Denmark ordered all 15 million farmed mink killed in November 2020 over concerns about a mutated coronavirus.
When lawmakers agreed on compensation in 2021, the total bill was expected to be between 15.6 billion DKK and 18.8 billion DKK.

Seven emergency medical vehicles in Denmark’s Central Denmark Region will begin using direct blood pressure monitoring during cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or CPR.
The regional prehospital emergency service said the method could help staff adjust chest compressions and improve survival after cardiac arrests outside hospitals.
“With blood pressure measurements, we get a better idea of whether the cardiopulmonary resuscitation sufficiently drives the blood around the body, or whether we need to adjust and adapt the chest compressions,” emergency doctor Jesper Fjølner said.
Fjølner, who developed the project, said the method had already contributed to successful resuscitation in several cases.
The procedure, called invasive blood pressure measurement, involves placing a catheter with a monitor into an artery. Hospitals already use it to monitor patients in operating rooms and intensive care units.
Using the method outside a hospital is more complex and requires training, equipment and experience.
Chief physician Allan Bach said the service expects the procedure to help resuscitate more people without reducing patient safety or the quality of CPR.
The European Resuscitation Council, which prepares European guidelines for cardiac arrest treatment, recently recommended the method. The Central Denmark service said it is among the first in the world to introduce it.
About 5,000 people experience cardiac arrest outside hospitals in Denmark each year. Around 15 percent survive.
Diabetes patients taking a low dose of Novo’s experimental drug Cagrisema lost more weight than those taking a low dose of Eli Lilly’s tirzepatide in a new study.
Patients receiving 1 milligram of Cagrisema lost an average of 12.4 percent of their weight over 60 weeks, Danish pharmaceutical company Novo said.
Those receiving 5 milligrams of tirzepatide lost 9.1 percent during the same period. Tirzepatide is the active ingredient in Eli Lilly’s approved weight-loss drug Zepbound.
Cagrisema has not been approved. Novo expects the US Food and Drug Administration to decide on its application near the end of 2026.
The treatment combines semaglutide, the active ingredient in Novo’s Wegovy, with a newer substance called cagrilintide. Novo hopes the combination can produce greater weight loss than semaglutide alone.
Results from another study released in February favored tirzepatide. Participants taking tirzepatide lost 25.5 percent of their weight over 84 weeks, compared with 23 percent for those receiving Cagrisema.
Novo shares fell more than 16 percent after those earlier results.
The company released the new findings during its capital markets day. Novo shares were down more than five percent around 1:15 p.m. Monday, and the announcement did not significantly change the share price.
Drivers using Denmark’s Vejlefjord Bridge should expect daily queues and longer travel times while two expansion joints are replaced, the Danish Road Directorate said.
Preparation work will take place during the final two weeks of September. The main repairs will run from early October until early November, with work continuing seven days a week.
Two of the bridge’s five expansion joints in the southbound lanes will be replaced.
Expansion joints are movable sections that allow a bridge to expand and contract as temperatures change. The joints have repeatedly caused problems in recent years, leading to emergency repairs, delays and traffic queues.
The Road Directorate, the Danish government agency responsible for national roads, expects the work to reduce the need for emergency repairs in the near future.
Almost 100,000 vehicles cross the nearly 50-year-old bridge each day.
“When we take lanes for a work area, and road users only have one lane in each direction, queues will occur,” project manager Allan Højgaard Madsen said.
Queues are expected in both directions from about 7 p.m. and for several hours afterward throughout the repair period.
Morning and afternoon rush-hour traffic is expected to face delays only in the southbound direction.

Most Danes want the government to temporarily cut taxes on gasoline and diesel as fuel prices reach unusually high levels, a Voxmeter poll for the Danish news agency Ritzau shows.
In September, diesel reached a record 19.19 DKK per liter at gas stations.
The poll found that 53.8 percent supported temporary tax cuts, while 33.3 percent opposed them. Another 12.9 percent did not know.
Torben Kudsk, policy chief at FDM, Denmark’s main car owners’ organization, said rising prices were creating serious problems for motorists.
“Fuel is historically expensive. As far as we can see, prices have not been higher in recent times,” Kudsk said.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats said the government was monitoring the situation.
“If energy prices continue to rise, and the situation develops further, we are of course ready to do more,” he wrote on Facebook. He did not describe possible measures.
The poll also asked what should guide decisions on fuel taxes. A total of 39.2 percent said reducing motorists’ costs should come first.
Another 27.2 percent said taxes should remain because of climate and environmental concerns, while 25.9 percent gave both issues equal weight. The remaining 7.7 percent did not know.
The price increases have been linked to wars and conflicts causing a global fuel shortage.

Denmark registered 502 suicides in 2025, the lowest annual number recorded from 2015 through 2025, according to the Centre for Suicide Research.
The total included 370 men and 132 women older than 15. It was 91 lower than in 2024.
Denmark’s suicide rate fell to 9.9 deaths per 100,000 people, an 18 percent decline from 2015. The rate dropped 30 percent among women and 12 percent among men.
Erik Christiansen, research head at the center, linked the decline partly to a national action plan introduced in 2024 and greater willingness to discuss suicide.
“At one time it was believed that it was dangerous to talk about suicide because it could inspire doing it. Today we know that this assumption is incorrect,” Christiansen said.
Doctors asking people directly about suicide risk can help them receive support earlier, he added.
Merete Nordentoft, a professor, chief physician and member of Denmark’s Council for Suicide Prevention, said help had become more accessible.
Suicide prevention clinics in Denmark’s five regions received additional funding to offer consultations to more people with suicidal thoughts or previous suicide attempts.
Livslinien, Denmark’s national suicide prevention helpline, received about 28,000 inquiries in 2025, up from fewer than 16,000 in 2019. Current funding allows it to answer about half of them.

Paella is a traditional Spanish rice dish originating from Albufera, south of Valencia. Farmers originally cooked it over an open fire using local rice and available vegetables.
The dish takes its name from the large, flat pan used to prepare it. The pan allows the rice to form a thin, crisp layer.

Denmark’s plan to send foreign prisoners sentenced to deportation to a prison in Kosovo has been delayed again.
The 300 prison places are now expected to become available at the end of 2027 at the earliest and possibly not until the beginning of 2028, Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen informed the parties behind the agreement Friday.
“I have been informed by the Danish Prison Agency that the construction of the prison in Kosovo is delayed, so the prison places can at the earliest be put into use at the end of 2027 and possibly not until the beginning of 2028,” Wammen said in a written statement to Ritzau.
Denmark reached a political agreement in 2021 to lease 300 prison places in Kosovo to reduce pressure on Danish prisons.
When the agreement with Kosovo was finalized, the first foreign nationals sentenced to deportation were expected to begin serving their sentences there in early 2023.
The latest delay means the prison could open about five years later than originally planned.
Wammen said the project remains an important priority for the government so “we can relieve pressure on the Danish prisons and get criminal foreign nationals sentenced to deportation out of the country.”
“It must happen as quickly as possible, and I naturally would have very much liked for us to have long since begun sending inmates there. Therefore, I am of course far from satisfied that the project is further delayed,” he said.
According to the Ministry of Justice, authorities in Kosovo have now emptied the prison of inmates.
An agreement with a contractor was signed in July, and the renovation work is expected to take about a year.
The project has previously been delayed by the approval process in Kosovo’s parliament, where opposition parties did not support international agreements.
Danish prisons have faced overcrowding for years, adding pressure to make the Kosovo prison places available.
The number of people injured in traffic accidents in Denmark increased in 2025, while the number of deaths fell slightly, according to new figures from Statistics Denmark.
Police recorded 2,832 people as injured or killed in traffic accidents during the year, an increase of 313 compared with 2024.
The number of traffic deaths fell from 145 in 2024 to 143 in 2025.
Denmark has now recorded fewer than 200 traffic deaths a year for 10 consecutive years. This is well below levels seen between 1965 and 1973, when more than 1,000 people were killed in traffic each year.
Of those recorded in 2025, 1,732 were seriously injured and 957 suffered minor injuries.
The number of injured road users increased across almost all forms of transport, with mopeds the exception.
Injuries among people riding electric bicycles increased from 173 in 2024 to 211 in 2025. Nearly three-quarters of those injured in this group were aged 45 or older.
The police figures do not show the full number of people injured on Danish roads because they only cover accidents reported to police.
Hospital emergency departments keep separate records of traffic injuries. In 2024, they registered 29,589 injured people, more than 1,000 above the previous year’s figure.
Denmark will bring forward and increase a military aid package for Ukraine to DKK 1.8 billion, days after a Russian frigate fired two flares toward a Danish military helicopter.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates and Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats announced the decision Friday after a meeting of the Danish Parliament’s Foreign Policy Committee.
Most of the money will go toward air defense systems produced in Ukraine. The support had been requested by Ukraine.
Løkke described the incident involving the Danish helicopter as a “severe Russian provocation.”
“If they think they can provoke us into being restrained with our support for Ukraine, then they are mistaken,” he said.
Ukraine has faced difficulties defending itself against Russian ballistic missile attacks because of shortages of suitable air defense missiles, including Patriot missiles produced by the United States.
The decision follows an incident Monday involving a Danish Air Force Fennec helicopter and a Russian frigate in international waters off Gedser in southern Denmark.
The Danish Defence said the helicopter was carrying out routine photographic surveillance of the Russian vessel when the frigate fired two flares toward it. One passed close to the helicopter.
According to Bruus, the Russian ship did not establish radio contact with the helicopter before firing the flares.
NATO has described the incident as an “irresponsible Russian act.”
“This fits into a pattern we are seeing around Europe, where Russia is escalating and constantly testing boundaries. It serves the purpose of shaking our unity and our support for Ukraine, and that must not work,” Løkke said.
Denmark summoned the Russian ambassador following the incident. Russia has said the Danish helicopter acted “provocatively.”
“If the Russians think that they can rattle us by doing this kind of thing, then our counter-response is that we will step up our support for Ukraine faster than we had intended,” Bruus said.
The captain of the Russian frigate has since received an award from Russia for his actions, according to the Danish report.
Denmark has been a major supporter of Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. However, since December, Denmark has announced only one other major aid package in addition to Friday’s package.
The Danish Ukraine Fund, which has financed much of the country’s support, has almost run out of available money. Further support would therefore require politicians to find funding elsewhere.
So far, much of Denmark’s support has been financed through the government’s projected future fiscal surplus.

Half of young Australian adults now living with parents, up from 39 per cent in 2001, survey shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:01:05 UTC
23:01:05 KST

Half of young Australian adults now living with parents, HILDA survey shows
In short:
Half of young Australian adults aged 18 to 29 are now living at home with their parents, up from 39 per cent in 2001.
Australians are more stressed about housing and money, and half of workers feel over-educated for their job, but their long-term relationships are relatively strong.
What's next?
The latest Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) survey has shown how people's lives have changed between 2001 and 2024.
Australia, we have good news, bad news and confirmation about life's hardships, which is no news to anyone.
The bad news, according to a quarter century of data on social and economic trends that shape the nation, is that we're more stressed about housing and money, tired, worried about our cognitive health, living much longer at home as young adults, and half of us have jobs we're over-qualified for.
The good news is employment is high, many more women hold university degrees, and our long-term relationships are in pretty good health.
That's the snapshot of the nation from this year's Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) annual survey, which "shows both the joys and the challenges of life", says lead author Inga Lass.
Drawing on data collected from 2001 to 2024, the annual HILDA report is Australia's largest longitudinal study of its kind in Australia, following the same 17,000 people each year to understand how our lives are changing.
It tracks issues including housing affordability and housing stress, labour market mismatches, relationship quality, cognitive health, and financial stress, among many other things.
Noticeable rise in young adults living at home for longer
This year's survey found half of young adults aged 18 to 29 were living with their parents in 2024, up from 39 per cent in 2001.
Two-thirds of young adults who had left the parental home were renting privately, but young renters also reported higher rates of housing inadequacy and lower satisfaction than those who remained with parents or who entered home ownership.
Housing stress among young mortgage holders has remained relatively stable over the last two decades, ranging from 8.6 per cent in 2001 to 9.9 per cent in 2024, despite substantial increases in housing costs.
The report's authors say that suggests that mortgage entry has become increasingly restricted to young adults with higher earnings, substantial savings or access to family wealth.
"For the majority of young adults who rent privately, the picture is more concerning," it says.
"In mainland capital cities, 25.3 per cent of young private renters are now in housing stress, up from 17.6 per cent for the equivalent cohort in 2001," it says.
Workers are better educated, but half feel over-qualified for their jobs
The report says half of Australian workers feel over-qualified for their job, and a quarter feel over-skilled.
Both types of mismatches are more prevalent among younger workers under 25 years of age, in certain occupations (e.g. sales workers, labourers), and in certain industries (e.g. accommodation and food services).
"With 50 per cent of Australian workers reporting they believe they are over-educated for their role, we're exactly where we were in 2012,"
"This suggests that the labour market has broadly kept up with increasing educational levels, with the number of jobs that require bachelor's or master's degrees growing the fastest, and jobs that require a maximum of Year 11 of schooling or less education declining."
Being born in a non-English-speaking country and having a casual work contract are associated with higher probabilities of both over-education and over-skilling.
Job mismatches are associated with lower job and life satisfaction, and a higher probability of job quitting, with over-skilling generally having stronger negative effects than over-education.
The trend of rising educational attainment among women has continued over the last quarter-century: well over half of women aged 25 to 44 now hold a university degree (compared to 40 per cent of men in that age group).
Men's educational attainment has also grown, but much more slowly. As a result, in all age groups below 65, women now have considerably higher educational attainment than men.
The report highlights that a particular demographic is being left behind:
"Men aged 25 to 44 who did not complete Year 12 have become less likely to be in full-time work and more likely to be outside the labour force," report co-author Dr Kyle Peyton said.
"Their full-time employment rate fell from 70 per cent in 2001 to 63 per cent in 2024, while the share outside the labour force rose from 12 per cent to 22 per cent."
Life partnerships are very strong
But the survey also found that most Australians in long-term relationships (married or otherwise) feel their relationship is very strong, although men consistently report higher relationship satisfaction than women.
When asked to rate the quality of their relationship across six dimensions, on a scale of 1 to 5, most respondents gave high scores dominated across all six dimensions.
Questions about love received the highest ratings overall, but questions about how well partners meet their needs and how well relationships meet original expectations received the lowest ratings.
An equal division of housework, child care, and earnings was a significant predictor of stronger relationship quality.
Couples caring for children, living with disability, or experiencing financial stress tended to report lower relationship scores.
Relationship quality is highest among childless couples with relatively even earnings (who also tend to share paid and unpaid work relatively equally) and lowest in couples with dependent children where the woman is the primary earner (and who typically undertakes most paid and unpaid work).
Relationship quality is also highest among recent unions and very long-term unions, but notably lower for relationships of intermediate duration, reaching its lowest point about 24 years after partners move in together.
"When you think about the trajectory of a relationship, there's a good chance that potentially stressful factors like work, bills and raising children start to ease around the 25-year mark, allowing couples to prioritise their relationship," Dr Lass said.
Employment high, but more people suffering financial and housing stress
The survey notes that most of the interviews in the survey were conducted between July and October 2024.
Around that time, the consumer price index (CPI) increased by roughly 19.5 per cent between the December quarter of 2019 and the September quarter of 2024.
Over that same period, the rent price index increased by around 16.8 per cent, and the Reserve Bank had hiked interest rates rapidly a couple of years earlier.
The survey found that stagnant wages and the rising cost of living had cancelled out any sense of the vast improvement in employment in 2024.
"Employment rates have jumped dramatically, particularly for women, since the survey started in 2001," report co-author Professor Roger Wilkins said.
"However, our earnings are not rising enough to keep up with the big increases in housing costs and other non-discretionary spending, so the average person is likely to be under more financial pressure."
The survey found that the hourly gender wage gap reached 10.2 per cent in 2024, which was the second-lowest since 2001.
But some large gender disparities remain, with 43 per cent of women working full-time, compared to 70 per cent of men.

Orexin neurons act as an effort-tracking system in the brain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:00:47 UTC
23:00:47 KST

A new study found that specialized brain cells called orexin neurons act as an effort-tracking system that spikes in activity when an animal expects a reward. The research suggests that turning these cells on or off can directly adjust how hard an animal is willing to work for a goal. The findings were published in PNAS.
Orexin neurons are a small but highly influential group of cells located deep in the hypothalamus. This region at the base of the brain manages basic survival functions like body temperature, thirst, and fatigue. Originally discovered for their role in regulating sleep, wakefulness, and appetite, these neurons also play a massive role in motivated behavior.
Motivation is the internal psychological drive that initiates and sustains our actions toward a goal. To successfully reach a goal, an animal must evaluate a situation, predict the outcome, and apply the right amount of effort.
A 2014 review established the foundational idea that orexin does not just regulate sleep and hunger, but acts as a central engine for motivating animals to pursue goals. Building on this concept, a 2024 study in mice indicated that orexin neurons are essential for choosing to expend physical effort instead of settling for easy temptations.
“Orexin has traditionally been studied for its role in wakefulness, with much of the evidence coming from studies,” study author Hiroyuki Mizoguchi, an associate professor in the Department of Neuropsychopharmacology and Hospital Pharmacy at Nagoya University Graduate School of Medicine, told PsyPost. “Although previous work has also implicated orexin neurons in motivated behavior in mice, exactly how their activity relates to reward prediction and effort has remained unclear.”
To bridge this gap, the research team, which also included Yutao Dong, developed a genetically modified rat model that allowed them to monitor and manipulate orexin neurons as the animals worked for food. Rats are particularly useful for this type of research because their advanced learning abilities make them well-suited for complex behavioral tests.
First, the researchers used a chemical technique called chemogenetics to selectively activate orexin neurons. They trained hungry rats to interact with a touchscreen to receive a small food pellet. To measure motivation, they used a progressive ratio test, where the amount of effort required to get a single food pellet steadily increased. For example, a rat might need to touch the screen five times for the first reward, but eventually have to touch it dozens of times for the next.
This escalating test continued until the rats gave up, providing a “breakpoint” that reflects their maximum willingness to work. When the researchers artificially activated the orexin neurons, the rats’ motivation increased. They displayed a higher breakpoint, meaning they were willing to tap the screen many more times to secure a single reward compared to their baseline performance.
Next, the team used a technique called fiber photometry to observe the natural activity of these cells in real time. When a neuron fires, calcium floods into the cell. By tracking these calcium signals, the scientists could monitor exactly when the orexin neurons were active while the rats performed tasks requiring varying levels of effort.
The researchers noticed a distinct pattern. As the rats tapped the screen and expected a food pellet, orexin neuron activity sharply increased. Once the rats received and ate the food, the cell activity dropped back down to normal levels.
The intensity of this brain signal also scaled with the amount of effort required. The neurons fired more strongly during the difficult progressive ratio test than during an easy task that required only one or two screen taps.
Additionally, the researchers tested what would happen if they tricked the rats by withholding the expected food pellet after a completed task. In these frustrating scenarios, the orexin activity stayed high. This suggests the cells maintain a state of prolonged expectation or stress when a predicted goal is not met.
“We were surprised that orexin neuronal activity changed across several distinct situations,” Mizoguchi said, noting that the neurons became active during reward prediction “rather than only when the reward was received.”
To test whether this burst of activity is directly tied to goal-directed action, the scientists used optogenetics. This method uses targeted flashes of light to turn specific brain cells on or off. The researchers trained the rats to tap the screen five times for a reward.
Right after the rats made their final tap, the researchers flashed a blue light into the brain to temporarily silence the orexin neurons during the brief window of reward anticipation. Suppressing the cells at this exact moment caused the rats to perform poorly. They took noticeably longer to complete the trials compared to when their brain activity was left alone, indicating that their drive to seek the reward had been interrupted.
“Our findings suggest that orexin neurons are part of a broader brain system that helps translate reward expectations into motivated action,” Mizoguchi explained. “Motivation does not depend on orexin alone, but these neurons may help the brain determine whether a reward is worth the effort.”
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2016, which found that blocking orexin signaling reduced compulsive drug-seeking behavior. A study covered by PsyPost in 2017 similarly observed that turning down these receptors lowered drug intake. It is worth noting that those earlier experiments examined extreme cocaine addiction models rather than general reward prediction, but they still point to orexin’s fundamental role in driving animals toward a desired outcome.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind regarding the current study. The researchers only used food as a reward, so it is still unknown if orexin neurons act the same way for other types of goals. Future research will need to explore whether similar brain activity occurs during social interactions, mating behaviors, or avoiding danger.
Additionally, the light manipulation targeted the entire population of orexin neurons at once. The hypothalamus contains different sub-groups of these cells, and future studies might need to separate them to see if they handle motivation differently. The team also noted that while turning the neurons off reduced effort, artificially stimulating them with light did not reliably increase motivation. This might be because the hungry rats were already operating at near-maximum motivation, making it hard to push their effort levels even higher through artificial means.
“A key caveat is that the relationship between orexin neuronal activity and motivated behavior is not straightforward; its effects may vary with the experimental conditions and with how neuronal activity is manipulated,” Mizoguchi pointed out. “Moreover, because this was a basic study in rats, not all of the findings can necessarily be applied to humans.”
Moving forward, the research team aims to map the broader neural circuits involved in these processes. “Our long-term goal is to understand how orexin neuronal activity is regulated and how these neurons influence motivated behavior,” Mizoguchi said. “We aim to identify the signals that orexin neurons transmit to downstream targets and the factors that stabilize or destabilize their activity.”
“Difficulty maintaining motivation can have substantial social and medical consequences,” he added. “Although the present study did not examine specific disorders or treatments, we hope that our findings will ultimately contribute to a better understanding of conditions involving reduced motivation and provide a foundation for future therapeutic research.”
The study, “Reward prediction is encoded by orexin neuron activity during motivated behavior,” was authored by Yutao Dong, Sheikh Mizanur Rahaman, Wenjun Zhu, Ayumu Inutsuka, Daisuke Ono, Rinako Tanaka, Tetsuo Matsuzaki, Eiji Shibata, Madoka Isobe, Shuntaro Izawa, Akihiro Yamanaka, Kiyofumi Yamada, and Hiroyuki Mizoguchi.

Federico Stefanovich revamps studio in 1920s Mexico City building to showcase his lighting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:00:24 UTC
23:00:24 KST

Federico Stefanovich revamps studio in 1920s Mexico City building to showcase his lighting
Mexican lighting designer Federico Stefanovich has worked with local interiors firm Nama Studio to renovate his studio in a hotel-turned-arts building in Mexico City's Centro neighbourhood.
Known for his expressive metal lighting, Federico Stefanovich renovated the interior of the balcony-clad Edificio Humboldt, a historic building designed by Canadian architect Thomas Sinclair Gore and completed in 1922.
Today it holds dozens of art and design studios and workshops.
Stefanovich and Nama Studio carefully preserved the historic details while adding rich colours and textures to showcase Stefanovich's designs and provide working space. It serves as a studio, showroom and production workshop.
"The balconies were one of the elements I immediately fell in love with when I first saw the space," Stefanovich told Dezeen.
"The large original windows, which open completely onto the balconies, had already been carefully restored before our intervention, preserving details from the 1920s, including their handles and iron latches."
Visitors enter the studio area via a seating area with showcase shelving that leads out into the long, main space with a lounge area at one end and a long table for displaying goods on the other.
In this primary showroom area, Edificio Humboldt's windows bring in plenty of natural light – which can present a problem for showcasing lighting designs.
To get around this and take full advantage of the light-filled rooms, panels were added to create backdrops for the lights, including a custom-designed modular panel system with metal poles interspersed with wooden blocks supporting them on the edges.
The panel's blue colour was created by layering tones almost like a limewash.
"I would describe it as a muted mineral blue, with a slightly weathered quality," said Stefanovich. "We wanted the colour to have depth and variation rather than read as a completely flat or uniform surface."
"The perimeter panel system is interrupted by the windows, creating a rhythm between the new architectural elements and the historic structure."
In the main space, this "muted mineral blue" is complemented by chocolate-toned plaster and brown-stained wood in the furniture, pedestals and wainscotting.
Aged flooring hints at the age of the building.
The lounge area, completely lined by the blue panel system, features a semi-circular sofa custom-made by Stefanovich's team.
Running along the elongated showroom is another panelling system. Instead of blue, the team opted for fibreglass that is yellowy and opaque but translucent enough to let light through, reminiscent of Japanese washi paper.
These fibreglass panels are part of a sliding door system that reveals the workshop area with utilitarian elements such as plywood furniture, MDF panels and steel storage racks.
Overall, Stefanovich said that the space was meant to reference his design style directly, which he described as ornate but not overly so.
"There is a subtle mid-century quality to the space, combined with handmade processes and certain more expressive, almost baroque gestures," he said.
"The intention was to bring these references together in a contemporary way, creating an environment that feels sophisticated but not overly formal, and that allows the architecture and my pieces to exist as part of the same language."
For the opening of the studio, Stefanovich collaborated with gallery Ago Projects to display his Salina Collection. The designer said the fibreglass in the studio space references the fibreglass of the collection.
Other self-designed studios include Jasmine Fisher's atmospheric studio in London and Victoria Yakusha's studio with a "living island" in Miami.
The photography is by Alejandro Ramirez Orozco.

The US Air Force is shutting down a major research centre dedicated to open-source analysis of the Chinese military’s air, space, cyber and missile capabilities.

Swedish prisoners complaining of conditions in Tartu prison

Unknown Publisher

22:58:00 KST

Swedish prisoners complaining of conditions in Tartu prison
Swedish offenders transferred to Tartu Prison have complained to Swedish media through their relatives about living conditions, including the soup served for dinner and having to eat from metal bowls, Postimees writes.
Swedish prisoners transferred to Estonia's Tartu Prison based on a prison rental agreement between the two countries are complaining about unfamiliar food and stricter security, according to relatives interviewed by Expressen. They describe eating from metal bowls resembling dog bowls, repetitive meals dominated by soups and stews and alleged weight loss. Armed escorts, transport cages and nighttime checks have also unsettled them. Journalists have not been allowed to interview the prisoners directly.
Swedish prison official Niklas Bellström said differences in food were anticipated: Estonian staff visited Swedish prison kitchens and received menus. Sweden also negotiated exemptions from some Estonian security practices, including hourly nighttime switching-on of cell lights.
Some prisoners feel good behavior has effectively been punished with transfer to Estonia. Estonia rejected many initially proposed inmates on security grounds, prompting Sweden to change its selection criteria.
The first prisoners arrived on August 18. The agreement envisages up to 200 Swedish inmates by the end of 2026 and 600 during 2027. Sweden covers all costs, paying €61.2 million annually at full capacity.

How much is UK supporting Saudi Arabia in its war with Iran-backed Houthis?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:57:50 UTC
22:57:50 KST

How much is UK supporting Saudi Arabia in its war with Iran-backed Houthis?
UK to refuel Saudi fighter jets and France to secure energy infrastructure amid fighting with Yemen’s Houthi group.
The United Kingdom will provide Saudi Arabia with military support in its escalating war against Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi group, the British government said this week.
The UK agreed to provide air-to-air refuelling of Saudi fighter jets that are conducting missions after the kingdom requested air-defence support, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3A simple guide to the Yemen conflict
- list 2 of 3UK to refuel Saudi jets to help counter Houthi attacks
- list 3 of 3Houthis battle for strategic heights in Yemen as thousands more flee homes
However, it will not directly join Riyadh’s renewed conflict with the Houthis, which began in 2014 after the Houthis seized Yemen’s capital Sanaa along with large areas of northwest Yemen, driving the internationally recognised government to Aden. The two sides had reached a United Nations-mediated ceasefire in 2022, before fighting broke out again this year amid the US-Israel war on Iran.
Particularly heavy fighting erupted again two weeks ago as the Houthis advanced against Yemeni forces to the Red Sea coast, taking the strategic port city of Mocha and Mayyun Island in the middle of the Bab al-Mandeb, the entry point for shipping entering the Red Sea from the south.
Since then, the group has targeted Riyadh as well as Saudi oil infrastructure, including taking out a section of the vital East-West Pipeline that had allowed Saudi to make oil exports despite disruption in the Strait of Hormuz triggered by the Iran war.
Before the latest bout of fighting broke out, the Houthis had also declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and Red Sea, through which about 12 percent of global trade passes.
Here is what you need to know about what support the UK will provide:
What has the UK announced?
British PM Burnham said London had accepted a Saudi request for what he called “defensive air-to-air refuelling”. Britain will deploy one Royal Air Force Voyager tanker aircraft to assist with this in the coming days.
“We have received a request from the kingdom of Saudi Arabia for military support,” Burnham told reporters on his way to the UN General Assembly in New York this week, adding that he had agreed to the request on the advice of his defence and foreign secretaries.
Burnham said the arrangement would be “time-limited” and would be kept under review. However, the UK’s Ministry of Defence (MoD) has not specified a timetable.
Burnham said the UK was “acting to secure the interests of Britain and the wider region”, linking the need to keep oil export routes open.
In a statement, the MoD told Al Jazeera that the decision to provide support “builds on the UK’s existing military contribution to Saudi Arabia’s air defence”, including the deployment of “air defence equipment and UK personnel helping to protect against missile and drone attacks”.
“Saudi Arabia and Yemen are long-standing partners of the United Kingdom, and play a vital role in regional stability. It is in the UK’s interest to protect regional stability, protecting vital trade and energy supplies and encouraging a diplomatic resolution to the conflict in Yemen,” the MoD said.
What is air-to-air refuelling?
Air-to-air refuelling is the transfer of aviation fuel from one aircraft to another in mid-air.
Refuelling in mid-air will allow Saudi fighter jets to remain airborne past their fuel limits, in order to spend more time patrolling Saudi airspace or responding to incoming threats.
Saudi Arabia faces potential threats to cities, military installations and energy infrastructure spread across a very large area.
While the Houthis have largely targeted Saudi cities in the south of the country, close to the Yemeni border, they have hit targets in the capital city, Riyadh, in the country’s centre.
During Israel’s war on Gaza, the Houthis also launched missiles towards Israel.
What’s the UK-Saudi Arabia military relationship?
Britain has particularly deep military ties with Saudi Arabia, one of the biggest buyers of British military equipment, stretching back for decades.
Under the Conservative Party government of John Major in the 1990s, and the later Labour governments of Tony Blair and Gordon Brown from the late 1990s to 2010, the UK supplied Tornado and Hawk aircraft and other equipment to the kingdom, involving the UK defence company BAE Systems.
The relationship was expanded to include Eurofighter Typhoon combat aircraft. In 2006, Saudi Arabia agreed to buy 72 Typhoons in a deal worth $40bn that also included technology transfer and training.
London has also provided defensive assistance during the ongoing regional conflict. Earlier this year, the UK deployed its Sky Sabre air-defence system to Saudi Arabia to help defend the kingdom from Iranian missile attacks on United States military assets and other infrastructure on Saudi territory.
Will this make a difference?
The air refuelling assistance from London could improve Saudi Arabia’s ability to defend itself to some degree, but what the UK has announced so far is limited, experts say.
The UK’s support carries more political weight than military significance, according to Chris Doyle, director of the Council for Arab-British Understanding.
“In military terms this is not a major change-up,” Doyle said, arguing that what matters more for Saudi Arabia right now is having visible international backing as it confronts the Houthis.
Riyadh will be keen to avoid appearing “isolated” in the conflict, particularly as other countries remain reluctant to become directly involved, he said. Most significantly, the administration of US President Donald Trump has already indicated it will not involve itself in the Saudi-Houthi fighting or against Houthi blockades on Saudi-linked shipping in the Red Sea.
Trump said the Houthis had assured US officials that they had no intention of attacking US shipping in the Red Sea.
As for other states, “Many are reluctant to get involved. They see this as being part of the wider US-Iran conflict, and they just are hesitant,” Doyle said.

Water, housing and tax: Inside UK Greens' new economic plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:57:31 UTC
22:57:31 KST

Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Inside UK Greens' plan to overhaul Britain's economy
The New Arab has obtained a copy of the Green Party's economic plan for Britain, which proposes sweeping changes to the country's fiscal rules, banking system and approach to public spending.
The report, titled Fiscal Referees: A New Economic Framework for People and Planet, is due to be voted on as a motion at the party's upcoming conference. If approved, its proposals would be adopted as official party policy.
The Green Party of England and Wales will hold its autumn conference in Brighton from 2 to 4 October, where members can vote on party policy.
Here are some of the key proposals in the report.
A focus on 'responsible' economics
The Green Party has previously said it wants to build a more equitable and environmentally responsible economy. The report sets out in greater detail how it believes this could be achieved.
Under the proposals, a Green government would distinguish between economic activity it considers socially beneficial and activity deemed environmentally or socially damaging, while prioritising investment in sustainable and ethical production.
One example given is the renationalisation of the country's water companies. The report estimates this would cost around £50 billion.
Private water companies have faced growing public criticism over sewage discharges, rising bills and the payment of dividends to shareholders.
A YouGov poll found that 82% of Britons supported bringing water companies into public ownership, while water companies discharged sewage into rivers and seas for a combined 1.8 million hours in 2025.
In August, regulator Ofwat provisionally approved up to £3.4 billion in additional expenditure by water companies for infrastructure and other projects, with a final decision expected later this year.
England and Wales have a fully privatised water and sewerage system.
Under the economic framework proposed in the report, the Greens argue that the cost of nationalisation should be considered alongside its social and environmental outcomes rather than judged solely on its upfront price.
Renationalisation would involve acquiring existing infrastructure, including reservoirs and pipes. The report says such a move would also require an assessment of its wider economic effects, including its potential impact on exchange rates and demand for water.
The report is primarily focused on domestic finances and does not go into detail about international trade.
However, the Green Party has previously said it would scrutinise the ethical impact of international trade, including by banning arms sales to Israel.
A new banking system
The report also proposes an overhaul of the banking system, including the establishment of a publicly owned bank.
Under the plan, the public bank could absorb private banks if they fail rather than the government bailing them out, as happened during the 2008 financial crisis.
The bank would offer current accounts and payment services to all UK residents, while a Green government would also establish a network of local community banks to provide funding to small and medium-sized businesses.
The report describes cryptocurrencies as "volatile" and "speculative" and proposes stronger regulation of cryptoassets such as Bitcoin and Ethereum.
The approach contrasts with Reform UK, which has proposed cutting capital gains tax on cryptocurrency gains.
Reform's policies towards the sector have come under particular scrutiny after the party received two £36 million donations from cryptocurrency billionaires Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, totalling £72 million.
Changes to fiscal accountability
Since 2010, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) has provided independent analysis of the UK's public finances.
The Green Party report proposes replacing it with an Office for Fiscal Transparency (OFT), which would work alongside an advisory Fiscal Policy Committee (FPC).
While the OBR produces forecasts of the economy and public finances and assesses the government's performance against its fiscal targets, the proposed OFT would be given a broader remit.
It would assess government budgets using economic indicators such as unemployment and productivity alongside their ecological impact.
Under the proposals, major spending plans would also include assessments detailing the workers, land and energy required for a project and how those resources could be managed without creating excessive inflation or environmental harm.
Strategic taxation
The report also proposes a system of "strategic taxation", under which taxes would be used not only to raise revenue but also to influence demand, prices and the allocation of resources. One example given in the report is the taxation of private rental properties.
The aim would be to encourage private landlords to sell properties, which could then potentially be bought by councils and converted into social housing.
Higher taxes on landlords can be passed on to tenants through higher rents, although the extent to which this happens is disputed.
The report argues that moving more properties into the social housing sector could lower housing costs. Social housing is, on average, £828 a month cheaper than private renting in England.
However, the report does not address in detail the potential impact of higher landlord taxation on private rents for people unable to access social housing.
Preventing underspending
The Greens' economic plan also seeks to address what the party views as chronic underspending and underinvestment.
The report argues that decades of underinvestment have contributed to deteriorating infrastructure, housing shortages and Britain falling behind in the development of green industries.
It argues that underspending can be damaging in the same way as excessive spending and proposes requiring the Chancellor to justify significant underspending to Parliament, as well as overspending.
The change would represent a shift from the traditional emphasis on controlling government expenditure, with the Greens arguing that failing to invest enough can carry its own long-term economic, social and environmental costs.

What to cook with pumpkin: the top 7 best recipes
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:57:31 EEST
22:57:31 KST

What to cook with pumpkin: the top 7 best recipes
Kyiv • UNN
A selection of seven simple pumpkin dishes and drinks: soup, carbonara, casserole, stew, latte, waffles, and burrata.
It is in autumn that pumpkin traditionally comes into season. It can be used to prepare a multitude of dishes, desserts, and even beverages, so UNN has compiled a top 7 of delicious and simple recipes using the main vegetable of autumn.
How to choose the right pumpkin
Before cooking, it is worth paying attention to the size and appearance of the fruit. Pumpkins weighing from 3 to 5 kg are considered the tastiest, as they have moderate sweetness. A large, slightly flattened pumpkin with a segmented shape and orange, light, or gray skin has dense flesh and a not-too-sweet taste. It is well suited for side dishes, vegetable caviar, soups, jam, and baking. Round or oval pumpkins with very hard skin are usually orange or greenish in color and are less sweet, so they are recommended for meat dishes and side dishes. Particular attention should be paid to the butternut squash. It has an elongated pear shape, thin skin, and sweet, tender flesh. This type of pumpkin is suitable for porridges, salads, desserts, and fillings for baked goods. A pumpkin’s ripeness can be determined by its stem: it should be dark and dry. If there is no stem, such a pumpkin should not be stored for long.
Pumpkin cream soup
Ingredients:
-  pumpkin - 1 kg; 
-  potatoes - 2; 
-  onion - 100 g; 
-  butter - 20 g; 
-  vegetable or meat broth - 1 l; 
-  garlic - 1 clove; 
-  cream - 150 ml; 
-  cumin - 0.5 tsp.; 
-  salt - to taste; 
-  black pepper - to taste; 
-  parsley - to taste; 
-  pumpkin seeds - 2 tbsp. 
Preparation:
1. Cut the pumpkin into cubes approximately 3–5 cm in size. Cut the onion into pieces half as small.
2. Sauté the onion together with the pumpkin over medium heat for about 5 minutes, stirring occasionally.
2. Transfer the vegetables into the broth, add the chopped potatoes, and cook over low heat for 20–30 minutes, until the vegetables become soft.
3. Add salt, pepper, chopped garlic, and ground cumin.
4. Blend the contents of the pot with an immersion blender until smooth.
5. Return the soup to the heat, add the cream, and bring to a boil.
6. Before serving, sprinkle the soup with chopped parsley and roasted pumpkin seeds.
The soup can also be served with croutons, cracklings, grated cheese, or shrimp sautéed in garlic sauce.
Pumpkin carbonara
Ingredients:
-  pumpkin - 300 g; 
-  onion - 1; 
-  garlic - 1 head; 
-  olive oil - 3 tbsp.; 
-  smoked pork belly - 250–300 g; 
-  20% cream - 250–300 g; 
-  Parmesan - 300 g; 
-  spaghetti - 500 g; 
-  salt - 1 level tsp.; 
-  egg yolk - 1. 
Preparation:
1. Peel the pumpkin, cut it into medium-sized cubes, and transfer it to a baking dish.
2. Peel half of the head of garlic, crush it, and add it to the pumpkin.
3. Peel the onion, cut it into strips, and place it with the pumpkin.
4. Add 2 tablespoons of olive oil and salt. Bake at 200°C for about 2 hours, stirring occasionally.
5. Finely chop the smoked pork belly.
6. Chop the remaining garlic as well. Sauté it in a frying pan, then add the pork belly and cook for about 7 minutes over medium heat.
7. Boil the spaghetti and rinse it with water.
8. Blend the roasted pumpkin, onion, and garlic. Cool the resulting sauce to room temperature.
9. In a separate bowl, combine the cream, egg yolk, and Parmesan.
10. Add the pumpkin sauce to the cream mixture and mix well.
11. Transfer the spaghetti to the frying pan with the pork belly and sauté for 5 minutes.
12. Pour the sauce over the pasta and simmer for another 5 minutes.
13. Before serving, place on a plate and garnish with herbs.
Cottage cheese and pumpkin casserole
Ingredients:
-  for the pumpkin batter: roasted pumpkin - 600 g, eggs - 2, flour - 3 tbsp., sugar - 60 g; 
Delicious and nutritious rice dishes: top interesting recipes22.08.25, 18:31 • 54330 views
-  for the cottage cheese batter: cottage cheese - 400 g, eggs - 2, sugar - 80 g, vanilla sugar - to taste, flour - 4 tbsp. 
Preparation:
1. Roast the pumpkin. It can first be cut into small cubes and cooked in the microwave for 7–10 minutes, depending on the variety.
2. Separately, blend all the ingredients for the pumpkin batter and the cottage cheese batter.
3. Place both mixtures into the baking dish alternately.
4. Using a toothpick, create a flower-shaped pattern by drawing from the edge of the dish upward through the batter.
5. Bake at 170°C for approximately 40 minutes.
Pumpkin Stew
Ingredients:
-  pumpkin - 0.5 kg; 
-  smoked chicken fillet - 200 g; 
-  Adyghe cheese - 200 g; 
-  red onion - 1; 
-  parsley - to taste; 
-  salt - to taste; 
-  pepper - to taste; 
-  spices - to taste. 
Preparation:
1. Cut the pumpkin, chicken, cheese, and onion into cubes of approximately the same size.
2. Add salt, pepper, and spices, then mix.
3. Add a little olive oil and place in the oven for approximately 40 minutes.
4. Cook until the pumpkin becomes soft.
5. Sprinkle the finished dish with chopped parsley.
Italian cuisine at home: five pasta recipes for every taste06.08.25, 15:01 • 60904 views
Pumpkin Latte
Ingredients:
-  pumpkin purée - 200 g; 
-  or pumpkin syrup - 100 ml; 
-  freshly brewed coffee - 300 ml; 
-  milk - 100 ml; 
-  sugar - to taste; 
-  cinnamon - to taste; 
-  nutmeg - to taste; 
-  vanilla sugar - to taste; 
-  cocoa - for decoration. 
Preparation:
1. To make the purée, bake the pumpkin and blend it. If desired, pass it through a sieve.
2. Add sugar and spices to the pumpkin purée. Place over heat, bring to a boil, and cook for 5-7 minutes over low heat, stirring constantly.
4. Brew the coffee.
5. Pour the hot coffee into cups and add the pumpkin purée or syrup with spices.
6. Heat the milk and add it to the coffee. If desired, froth the milk until thick foam forms.
7. Garnish the drink with cocoa, cinnamon, or grated chocolate.
Pumpkin Waffles
Ingredients:
-  baked or stewed pumpkin - 300 g; 
-  eggs - 3; 
-  quark - 150 g; 
-  vanilla sugar - 1 packet; 
-  salt - a pinch; 
-  baking powder - 1 tsp.; 
-  stevia or honey - 2 tbsp.; 
-  flour - 7-8 tbsp.; 
-  refined oil - 50 g; 
-  yogurt - 180 g. 
Preparation:
1. Mash the stewed pumpkin with a fork.
2. Add the eggs, stevia or honey, salt, baking powder, yogurt, and vanilla sugar.
3. Add the quark and flour, then mix the batter with a spoon.
4. Bake the waffles until golden brown.
Burrata with Pumpkin-Tomato Cream
Ingredients:
small pumpkin - 1;
tomatoes - 200 g;
garlic - 2 cloves;
olive oil - 1-2 tbsp.;
nutmeg - a pinch;
salt - to taste;
burrata - 1 (125 g);
pumpkin seeds - 2 tbsp.;
balsamic cream - for serving;
herbs - for serving.
Preparation:
1. Cut off the top of the pumpkin and remove the seeds.
2. Place the chopped tomatoes and peeled garlic inside. Add a little salt and olive oil.
3. Bake the pumpkin at 180-190°C for 40-45 minutes, until the flesh becomes soft.
4. Remove the baked flesh together with the tomatoes and garlic, and blend until creamy.
5. Add olive oil, a pinch of nutmeg, and a little more salt if needed.
6. Place the pumpkin purée on a plate and put the burrata in the center.
7. Sprinkle with toasted pumpkin seeds, garnish with herbs, and drizzle with balsamic cream.

Feature: 15 years On, Chinese-built Kribi port powers Cameroon's growth, improves livelihoods
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:57:00 CST
22:57:00 KST

by Arison Tamfu
YAOUNDE, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Fifteen years ago, Mboro was a remote fishing hamlet on the edge of Kribi in southern Cameroon, with a handful of homes connected by narrow, winding dirt tracks.
Today, the same stretch of coastline is home to one of Central Africa's most modern deep-water ports, with the surrounding area being reshaped by a growing industrial and logistics economy.
Since the 1970s, Cameroon has envisioned a deep-water port to complement the Port of Douala, the country's only major port, which sits in a shallow estuary unable to accommodate large vessels. That decades-old ambition has been realized with the completion of the first and second phases of the Kribi Deep Seaport.
CITY OF FUTURE
Gu Gaobai was among the first Chinese workers to arrive in 2011 with China Harbor Engineering Company (CHEC), the builder of the Kribi Deep Seaport.
"When we headed to the project site, we bumped along narrow dirt trails. At the selected location, all we saw was a small sandy beach and a few reefs. At the time, those reefs were the only reference points for the port's location," recalled Gu, now general manager of CHEC's Cameroon Project Clusters.
The transformation is visible along the roads leading to the port. A narrow track is now a dual carriageway with a pedestrian crossing in the middle. New buildings, businesses and public facilities have emerged as economic activity has expanded.
For 50-year-old lifelong resident Jean-Kalvin Assembe, the changes have reached into everyday life. "For one thing, I'm happy and fulfilled in this city," he said.
The influx of workers and businesses has created more opportunities for local residents and supported household incomes. "Even the little neighborhood shop gets customers. It's really bringing positive changes," Assembe said.
Multi-story buildings, hospitals, universities and shopping malls now dot Kribi. Streetlights illuminate roads that were once dark, while the port area remains brightly lit after nightfall.
Truck drivers are among those who have benefited from the port's development. Long queues of trucks now fill the port area daily.
"The port has given us the opportunity to discover the region," said 68-year-old veteran driver Aboubakar Yaya, who has driven across four Central African countries. "Kribi has made things easier. The service is fast, too."
"Many clients and experts who know China often say Kribi is Cameroon's Shenzhen, a 'City of the Future,'" Gu said.
HUB FOR INDUSTRIALIZATION, REGIONAL INTEGRATION
As the port has grown, so too has its industrial complex.
Patrick Mpila Ayissi, chief infrastructure officer of Kribi Port Industrial Zone, said investment in the zone has accelerated since operations began in 2018.
"Since 2018, industrial operators have invested nearly 400 billion CFA francs (about 700 million U.S. dollars), and 93 occupancy permits have been issued, with 18 companies already operating," Ayissi said. "The ambition has grown from an initial 455-hectare logistics zone to today's 4,000-hectare integrated industrial zone."
The zone is expected to attract close to 900 million dollars in investment and create 50,000 direct jobs, with up to 150,000 direct and indirect jobs combined, over the next 15 years, he said.
The seaport has also become a strategic hub for Central Africa, serving neighboring markets.
"Container traffic has quadrupled since 2018, surpassing 555,000 TEU in 2025, while overall cargo volumes exceeded 12.7 million tonnes in 2024. Trade already flows from Kribi to Gabon, the Central African Republic, Chad, Congo, and Equatorial Guinea," Ayissi said, adding that the port's regional connections have been reinforced by shipping lines such as MSC.
To support the growing logistics network, CHEC also built the Kribi-Lolabe highway.
"This highway connects the Kribi Deep Seaport with major cities nationwide, facilitating personnel travel and goods transportation, thus promoting Cameroon's industrialization," said Emmanuel Nganou Djoumessi, Cameroon's minister of public works.
LIFE-CHANGING SKILLS
The changes brought by the port are also reflected in the careers of local workers.
In 2013, Ngatugirius Ndenya left his welding job in Yaounde to join CHEC in Kribi. "When I arrived here in 2013, the beginning was very difficult for me," said the 53-year-old.
CHEC adopted the approach of pairing Cameroonian workers with experienced Chinese colleagues, which allowed them to gain hands-on experience before taking on tasks independently.
"Before coming here, I was just a platform welder. But now, I can do everything concerning welding," Ndenya said. "The young people that came here were not technicians, but today they are technicians."
For some workers, the port has also brought changes to their livelihoods.
"When I arrived here, I had absolutely nothing. I left a job where I was earning maybe 100,000 CFA francs a month," said Armand Guehoada, now a business specialist with CHEC. "After a while, I was able to buy a vehicle. Today, I'm on my third. I can easily take care of my family."
"Over the past 15 years, we have trained a large cohort of local professionals in port construction and mega-project engineering. Many of those who worked on the port now contribute to the adjacent industrial zone," Gu said.
This year marks the 55th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic ties between China and Cameroon, while the Kribi Deep Seaport marks 15 years since construction began.
"Kribi remains a visible symbol of Cameroon-China cooperation. Its development has been structured from the outset around concessional financing from Chinese institutions, reflecting a genuinely long-term partnership." Ayissi said.
For Patrice Melom, general manager of the Port Authority of Kribi, the port's development has opened up new possibilities for the city and the country.
"The future of the port of Kribi looks promising, bringing concrete results and extremely positive prospects," Melom said. "It is now up to us to mobilize all our energies and make this infrastructure a true driver of sustainable growth, serving national prosperity and sub-regional integration." ■

Chinese premier meets Kyrgyz cabinet chief

HANGZHOU, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Wednesday met with Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers of Kyrgyzstan, Adylbek Aleshovich Kasymaliev, who is attending the fifth Global Digital Trade Expo, in Hangzhou, the provincial capital of Zhejiang in east China.

TOKYO, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Teenage swimmers Yu Zidi and Zhang Zhanshuo led China's charge at the 2026 Asian Games on Wednesday, with Yu completing a hat-trick of individual titles and Zhang claiming his fourth gold as China won six swimming events.
Yu, 13, completed a sweep of her three individual events by winning the women's 400-meter individual medley in 4 minutes, 28.56 seconds, setting an Asian Games record. She led from the opening leg and finished 3.95 seconds ahead of teammate Ke Wenxi.
Yu had already won the 200-meter butterfly and 200-meter individual medley, setting an Asian record of 2:06.10 in the latter. Despite her success, the teenager admitted that her demanding schedule had taken its toll.
"There wasn't really a feeling that it was easy. I'm quite tired," Yu said.
"I was just a little short of the Asian record today, but I also improved my time, so I think that's okay," she added.
Zhang, 19, claimed his fourth gold of the Games by winning the men's 200-meter freestyle in an Asian record of 1:43.49. South Korea's Hwang Sun-woo took silver in 1:44.62, while Japan's Tatsuya Murasa finished third in 1:44.81.
Zhang had previously won the 1,500-meter freestyle and helped China secure gold in the 4x200-meter free and 4x100-meter medley relays. He anchored the former in 1:42.92 as China set an Asian record of 7:00.17.
"It was quite unexpected. Before the race, I didn't think I could swim such a time," Zhang said. "Form is built up race by race, and it will keep getting better and better."
Elsewhere, China's Yu Yiting edged teammate and defending champion Zhang Yufei by just 0.03 seconds to win the women's 100-meter butterfly in 56.41 seconds.
Neither swimmer was entirely satisfied with her performance, with Yu acknowledging that the narrow victory highlighted the importance of finishing strongly.
"Sometimes it comes down to the final 15 meters. For both of us, it was valuable experience," she said.
China's Peng Xuwei won the women's 100-meter backstroke in 59.30s, ahead of Japan's Rio Shirai in 59.89 and South Korea's Kim Seungwon in 1:00.10.
Peng said she had struggled with her pacing despite securing gold and described the Games as an important test ahead of the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
"The Asian Games is like a 'midterm exam' for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. It's an opportunity to test and show the results of my training," she said.
Tang Qianting added another gold for China in the women's 100-meter breaststroke, setting a Games record of 1:04.98.
In the men's 100-meter butterfly, China's Xu Fang took silver behind Japan's Shoon Mitsunaga, who set a Games record of 50.56 seconds.
China rounded off the evening by successfully defending its mixed 4x100-meter medley relay title, completing its six-gold haul.
For Zhang Yufei, the relay victory provided a positive end to a frustrating evening after her narrow defeat in the individual butterfly event.
Competing alongside longtime teammate Xu Jiayu in a reshuffled relay lineup, Zhang said his continued improvement had given her renewed confidence in her own prospects.
"Seeing him come back from the bottom makes me feel that I can do it too," she said.
"Even though I made some mistakes this time and didn't swim the result I wanted, I still believe in my training and look forward to finding what I can do in the next race." ■

BRUSSELS, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- The European Commission on Wednesday proposed unlocking 4.2 billion euros (about 4.8 billion U.S. dollars) in cohesion funding for Hungary, which has been suspended over rule-of-law concerns under the country's previous government.
The Commission said it had proposed that the Council of the European Union (EU) should lift protective measures imposed on Hungary in 2022 under the bloc's Conditionality Regulation, concluding that the country had addressed the rule-of-law breaches.
If approved by the Council, the decision would not only reinstate the suspended cohesion policy commitments, but also restore full access to the Erasmus+ student exchange program and the Horizon Europe research program for students and researchers at universities maintained by Hungarian Public Interest Trusts.
"Hungary has taken important steps to strengthen the rule of law and protect the Union's financial interests," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said, adding that the decision showed that "reforms deliver results."
According to the Commission, Hungary has addressed shortcomings in public procurement, the country's anti-corruption framework, conflicts of interest, and the effectiveness of prosecutorial action.
These shortcomings were identified by the EU in 2022, leading to the freezing of 55 percent of budgetary commitments for three Hungarian cohesion policy programs. Restrictions were also imposed on EU funding for Hungarian Public Interest Trusts, affecting participation in Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe.
Prime Minister Peter Magyar, who took office after defeating Orban in the April 2026 parliamentary election, has made restoring Hungary's access to the suspended EU funds a key government priority.
The Council of the EU now has one month to decide whether to approve the Commission's proposal.
Hungarian Minister of Transport and Investment David Vitezy has welcomed the announcement, saying the European Commission had officially initiated the closure of the rule-of-law procedures against Hungary. ■

Mohammad Sio
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa said Wednesday that the Golan Heights, occupied by Israel, will remain Syrian territory and that all annexation measures are null and void under UN Security Council resolutions.  
Addressing the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York, Sharaa said attempts to impose facts on the ground cannot undermine Syria’s sovereignty, the rule of law or the applicability of international law. 
“The Golan will remain Syrian land,” he said, adding that all annexation measures are invalid under UN Security Council Resolution 497. 
Sharaa also referred to a UN General Assembly vote in December 2025 in which 123 countries backed a resolution concerning the occupied Syrian Golan, thanking countries that supported it and urging those that abstained to reconsider Resolution 497. 
He accused Israel of carrying out nearly 500 air and artillery strikes, more than 1,200 incursions and around 300 arrests and detentions of Syrians, saying the actions threaten Syria’s stability, defy the global consensus, and revive painful memories of an era Syrians had barely managed to leave behind. 
Sharaa said Damascus remains committed to the 1974 Disengagement Agreement and continues to call for Israeli forces to withdraw to the lines held before Dec. 8, 2024. 
He rejected Israel’s attempts to impose “new facts on the ground” and said Israeli actions across the region undermine security and stability. 
The address marked Sharaa’s second consecutive appearance before the UN General Assembly. He attended the 80th session in September 2025, becoming the first Syrian president to participate in the gathering since 1967.
