Golan Heights will 'remain Syrian', President Ahmed al-Sharaa vows at UN
Syria's President Ahmed al-Sharaa told the UN Wednesday that the contested Golan Heights region would "remain Syrian" despite ongoing military occupation by Israel. The Syrian leader also used his second turn at the UN rostrum to denounce repeated Israeli strikes on his country.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa insisted at the UN Wednesday that the Golan Heights region will remain Syrian after Colombia last month recognised Israeli sovereignty over the strategically important territory.
Read moreUN General Assembly live: Iran’s Pezeshkian tells UN his country is ‘victim’ of US ‘terrorism’
"Any attempts that violate our sovereignty, violate international law, will be stopped. Golan will remain Syrian territories," al-Sharaa said at the UN meeting of world leaders in New York.
Colombia's new hard-right government in August recognised Israel's claim over the Golan Heights, which it captured from Syria in 1967.
The United States had until then been the only country to recognise Israel's annexation of the territory in 1981.
The United Nations maintains that the plateau is Syrian territory under Israeli military occupation.
In July UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres reiterated that the Golan Heights were part of Syria, describing Israeli occupation as "totally unacceptable".
Israel's Defence Minister Israel Katz responded by saying that the Golan Heights would remain under Israeli sovereignty "forever".
"My clear response to the Syrian president, who made bombastic declarations from the UN podium: The Golan under Israeli sovereignty is an inseparable part of the State of Israel forever," Katz said in a video statement.
Al-Sharaa also used his second turn at the UN rostrum to denounce repeated Israeli strikes on his country since the fall of former dictator Bashar al-Assad.
"Israel is launching attacks against Syria. There have been 500 air strikes, more than 1,200 incursions, and 300 detentions. This is at odds with the orientation we're seeing at global level," he said.
"It is reminiscent of a era that we thought was long gone."
But he held out hope that despite repeated "aggressions" by Israel, "the opportunity for peace and security is available to those who wish to live in peace – a just peace that maintains the rights of all."
During a discussion at the Atlantic Council on Tuesday, al-Sharaa said Syria wanted a peaceful solution with Israel and that negotiations between the two countries had resolved nearly 90 percent of the outstanding issues needed for a security agreement.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Military police investigate death of Dutch woman in Aruba crash
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Military police are investigating the death of a 23-year-old Dutch woman after an all-terrain vehicle overturned on the Caribbean island of Aruba.
Local police initially said Kimberly van Ardenne, from Rotterdam, was driving the vehicle when the accident happened on Sunday, September 13, but her family said they had heard conflicting accounts.
Relatives have posted an appeal on Facebook appealing for witnesses to the crash, which happened at 3pm.
Two male naval officers were with Kimberly in the car at the time, one of whom was a friend she was staying with on the island.
The Dutch military police force (Koninklijke Marechaussee) said it was investigating the crash because it involved armed forces personnel. The force has pledged to “get to the bottom” of the incident.
Several tour guides are said to have witnessed the incident, according to local news website Aruba.nu, some of whom said they had seen the vehicle make a “manoeuvre” just before it overturned.
“Not a daredevil”
One family member told NOS Kimberly was not a keen driver. “You’d describe her as more of a cautious person than a daredevil. We can’t understand how this could have happened if she was behind the wheel.”
The family’s lawyer, Peter Schouten, told RTL Nieuws he was making his own enquiries on behalf of the family.
“We are investigating whether there is any question of liability, whether this is a case of reckless driving and whether anyone has made false statements,” he said.
“We already have a lot of information from social media, but we are still looking for witnesses.”
The family has asked anyone with information to contact them through the Facebook post or via Whatsapp on +31 6 40580456.

After Trump and Zelensky meet in New York, Ukrainian president says he hopes war will end ‘before winter’
Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelensky met on September 22 on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York, holding talks that lasted about 40 minutes. The two leaders discussed, among other things, prospects for negotiations with Russia, military aid to Ukraine, and a possible energy truce between Kyiv and Moscow.
Even before the meeting, Trump said from the U.N. podium that he expects the war to end soon: “We are working very closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine, and we will see this through to the end. It will happen, I think, sooner than people realize.”
After the talks, Zelensky also spoke about when the war might end:
I hope we will end this war, I hope that President Trump will help us end it. I think we need to do this as soon as possible — before winter, preferably before winter.
Zelensky’s hopes are shared elsewhere in Europe. “People are looking for a partial ceasefire come winter,” Finnish President Alexander Stubb said in an interview with Bloomberg.
Just two weeks earlier, speaking to Trump’s special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Kyiv, Zelensky had said he expected the war to continue into winter.
In an interview with The Wall Street Journal after the meeting, Zelensky suggested that Trump would now try to reach an agreement with Moscow on an energy truce. Putin, he said, is unlikely to go along without additional pressure from Washington, such as increased sanctions. He added that Ukraine is willing to accept any format of truce and that he is ready for a three-way meeting with Putin and Trump.
The talks also covered a “winter package” of military aid. Zelensky asked Trump to give Ukraine Patriot missiles from American stockpiles, offering in exchange to later hand over to the United States part of the missiles Kyiv expects from a future delivery under an agreement with Germany. Trump did not agree, but Zelensky called the fact that he did not immediately reject the idea a “good step.”
The Kremlin said there are currently no preconditions for peace talks, though Putin is ready to meet with Trump. Presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov called a meeting with Zelensky without prior expert-level preparation a waste of time and reiterated that it could only take place in Moscow.
Putin said that Zelensky, if he wants, can come to Moscow. All necessary security guarantees will be provided to him. He knows very well what decisions need to be made.
Discussions about the energy truce are expected to continue on September 23, when U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is set to meet with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in New York, where he arrived for the U.N. General Assembly session. The U.S. State Department announced the meeting after the Trump–Zelensky talks.

Mahan Sirjan: Upstream Link in the Steel Chain
Operating as the contractor for Golgohar Ore Body No. 5, Mahan Sirjan Processing Development functions as the vital upstream supplier feeding Mahan Holding's vertically integrated steel operations.
Mahan Sirjan extracts approximately 3 million tons of raw iron ore annually from reserves totaling 35.9 million tons with an average iron grade of 50.68%. Employing roughly 900 operational personnel, the company acts as an operational contractor rather than an independent mine owner. The mined ore directly supplies direct reduced iron (sponge iron) production at Baft Steel, which feeds Sanat Bonab Steel's rolling mills. To improve integration, an expansion pipeline adding 2.5 million tons each of concentrate and pelletizing capacity is underway.

How the British Crown profited directly from human trafficking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:23:50 UTC
22:23:50 KST

How the British Crown profited directly from human trafficking
The question of slavery and reparations has recently returned to the center of international debate, particularly in Africa and the Caribbean. The conference held in Ghana on reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and slavery, as well as the petition filed by a Jamaican delegation to the British king, engaged in the struggle for historical recognition. The debate has also been brought into sharper focus by an investigation published by The Guardian, which examined the involvement of the British monarchy in the system of slavery and the historical links between the Crown and the trafficking of Africans.
Taken together, the developments raise a fundamental question: How can the British monarchy and the British state genuinely address a past in which the Crown was directly connected to the economic and political structures of slavery?
There are symbols that, on their own, encapsulate centuries of history. A crown branded with a red-hot iron onto the skin of an enslaved human being is one of them. It was a real, documented practice carried out by the South Sea Company, directly supported by the British monarchy during the reign of Queen Anne.
In 1713, this partnership secured for Britain the exclusive right to deliver nearly 4,800 enslaved Africans every year to the Spanish colonies in the Americas. This chilling figure was only the beginning of a broader system in which the British monarchy was a central actor.
The monarchy as a shareholder
History often portrays the transatlantic slave trade as an impersonal economic phenomenon, driven by commercial companies, far removed from political power. The reality is very different though. The Royal African Company, one of the most important slave-trading companies in British history, was directly led by James, Duke of York, who would later become King James II. Under his leadership, the company forcibly transported at least 150,000 Africans across the Atlantic.
Around 13,000 investors in the British slave trade have been identified, more than 10,500 of whom now have detailed biographical information. They include members of parliament, merchants, more than a thousand women from the aristocracy and bourgeoisie, as well as members of the royal family itself.
In total, the British slave trade forcibly removed more than 3 million Africans from their homeland and sent them to plantations in the Americas and the Caribbean, a figure that conveys the true human cost of the prosperity created by British colonialism.
Words, but no action
In the face of these facts, the official response of the contemporary monarchy remains, at best, cautious. King Charles III has described slavery as an “atrocious tragedy” and expressed support for historical research into the links between the monarchy and the slave trade. This is a symbolic gesture, and it marks a departure from decades of near-total silence on the subject.
However, a cold fact remains: To date, no official apology has been issued by the British government, and no serious discussion of possible reparations has been initiated at the state level.
The calculated caution is not unique to the United Kingdom, but it takes on particular significance there because it is precisely the monarchy, an institution supposedly embodying the continuity and unity of the nation, that is directly implicated by the historical evidence. Acknowledging “links” with slavery, as current royal communications do, is one thing. Acknowledging direct responsibility, with all the political, moral, and financial consequences that this entails, is another. Between the two lies the space in which the struggle over Britain’s colonial memory has been unfolding for years.
From the Koh-i-Noor to the Benin Bronzes
This unease can also be seen in the objects that the monarchy continues to possess. The Koh-i-Noor, the colossal diamond taken from the Indian subcontinent during the colonial era, is the most emblematic example. At her coronation in 2023, Queen Camilla chose not to wear the Queen Mother’s crown in which the stone is set, a choice apparently dictated by diplomatic caution rather than by any fundamental reconsideration, since the diamond remains preserved, as if nothing had happened, among the royal jewels.
The same pattern can be seen with the Benin Bronzes, looted during the 1897 British military expedition and still largely displayed at the British Museum, far from the African soil from which they were taken.
In both cases, the British position remains the same: Discuss, study, postpone – but do not return. These objects are material evidence of an organized system of looting, which official diplomacy continues to treat as a secondary issue.
This British debate is part of a much broader movement, driven for years by countries and peoples that directly experienced the slave trade and colonialism. Jamaica’s recent demand for reparations from the British government is one example among many, as are similar claims advanced by several African and Caribbean nations through international institutions and Pan-African forums.
These demands raise a very concrete question of the moral and material debt created by centuries of exploitation, a debt that the direct heirs of this system continue largely to evade.
The origins of the current wealth
One obvious fact, too often minimized, must be recalled here: The wealth accumulated by the British monarchy and by a large part of its aristocracy was not created in a vacuum. To a significant extent, it rests on forced labor, deportation, and the suffering of millions of human beings torn from the African continent. To celebrate royal heritage – its crowns, diamonds, and palaces – without clearly naming this origin is to erase an essential part of history.
Acknowledging “links” with slavery without drawing any concrete consequences turns a crime against humanity into a page of history accessible in archives. Words of compassion, however sincere, do not replace official apologies, reparations, or the restitution of looted cultural property.
For African peoples and their descendants in the diaspora, this question concerns the full recognition of a historical crime, the restitution of what was stolen – wealth, objects, and dignity – and the construction of an honest relationship at last between the former colonial power and the nations it plundered. As long as this recognition remains cautious and without concrete consequences, the debate will continue to impose itself with increasing force in British and international public life.

Drones are approaching gas stations: Kyiv is preparing a targeted alert system for filling stations
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:22:05 EEST
22:22:05 KST

Drones are approaching gas stations: Kyiv is preparing a targeted alert system for filling stations
Kyiv • UNN
Gas stations in the capital will be able to operate during some alerts and suspend service only when a drone approaches. The protection is funded by network owners.
The capital's gas stations are planning to connect to an additional alert system for approaching enemy drones, which will allow gas stations to operate during part of an air raid alert and stop serving visitors only if an aerial target is directly approaching. This was stated by Kateryna Pop, a spokesperson for the Kyiv City Military Administration, on the air of Den.LIVE, reports UNN.
Details
According to Pop, gas stations in the capital are already subject to security protocols established by decisions of the Kyiv Defense Council. However, a separate alert system for the movement of enemy aerial targets is also being developed for them.
"Gas stations are subject to the protocols developed through the Defense Council's decisions on security levels, and an additional alert system for the approach of enemy targets to gas stations will be developed so that they can operate until an enemy target begins moving in their direction, and during that period finish accepting visitors and shut down the gas station," the KCSA spokesperson said.
The spokesperson clarified that this concerns a more targeted response system under which gas stations would not necessarily have to cease operations for the entire period of a prolonged drone threat. If an aerial target is detected moving directly toward a specific facility, staff will be able to finish serving customers in advance and switch to a safe operating mode.
However, funding for the engineering protection of the gas station complexes themselves will be the responsibility of the private owners of the networks. This includes, in particular, installing protective structures and shelters intended to reduce risks to employees and visitors in the event of a strike.
What preceded this
The new system is part of broader measures to protect fuel infrastructure following a series of Russian attacks on gas stations in Kyiv.
At the beginning of September, the capital introduced a differentiated alert system for aerial threats. It provides for different modes depending on the type of danger. The yellow level is used, in particular, during a drone threat, while the red level applies in the event of a missile, combined, or larger-scale attack. Such protocols are intended to allow businesses to continue operating during a less critical level of danger, provided they comply with the established safety requirements and have access to shelters.
Separately, on September 12, the government held an urgent meeting with fuel market operators following an increase in the number of Russian strikes on gas station complexes in the capital and along international highways. At the time, officials reported that they were testing a software solution intended to show the direction of enemy drones' movement and automatically warn gas stations of their approach. After testing at gas station complexes, a similar mechanism may also be applied to other types of businesses.
In addition, strengthening the physical protection of gas stations was discussed, including the installation of additional protective structures for above-ground infrastructure and the construction of shelters.
Similar measures began to be implemented earlier in the Kyiv region. On September 15, the Kyiv Regional Defense Council decided to provide gas station complexes with access to a special digital aerial-awareness system. It allows responsible gas station employees to receive real-time information about the movement of aerial targets and make decisions regarding the temporary suspension of operations.
Series of attacks on gas stations
The strengthening of security measures is taking place against the backdrop of a series of Russian attacks on the capital's gas station infrastructure.
On September 10, a Russian drone struck a gas station in Kyiv's Holosiivskyi district. People were injured in the attack. The Ukrnafta company reported at the time that the station was not operating when it was struck, and that staff and visitors had left the premises after the alert was announced.
On September 11, strikes on gas stations were recorded in the capital's Dniprovskyi and Obolonskyi districts, and on September 15, drones again attacked gas stations in the Darnytskyi and Holosiivskyi districts.
On September 23, strikes on two gas stations were recorded again in Kyiv. One of the UAVs hit a gas station in the Holosiivskyi district, while a fire broke out on the roof of another gas station in the Darnytskyi district.
Ukrnafta said that the strike on September 23 was already the sixth attack on the company's infrastructure in Kyiv over the past few weeks. According to the company, the personnel were in a shelter during the attack, so no one was injured at the affected facility.
Against the backdrop of regular attacks, fuel market operators have also begun installing mobile concrete shelters and gabions at gas stations. Previously, this practice was more common in frontline regions, but now protective structures are increasingly appearing in the capital as well.
According to Kateryna Pop, around 300 gas stations operate in Kyiv, with another approximately 600 in the Kyiv region. The Kyiv City Military Administration emphasizes that Russia has already used the tactic of striking fuel and transport infrastructure in frontline regions.
At the same time, the exact timeline for the full launch of an additional alert system for the capital's gas stations, the list of networks that will be connected to it, and the technical mechanism for transmitting warnings have not yet been publicly specified.

Why California Just Declared a State of Emergency Due to El Niño
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:21:35 UTC
22:21:35 KST

California’s governor Gavin Newsom has declared a state of emergency ahead of a potentially historic El Niño. In a statement released Sept. 22, Newsom said the declaration is meant to ensure communities have the resources they need to handle the impacts expected this winter.
“California is strongest when we look out for one another. That is what this action is about,” Newsom said. “Giving communities the support they need, giving first responders the tools to do their jobs, and giving families the confidence that their state is ready.”
Read more: How Should You Prepare For A Super El Niño?
The state of emergency allows the government to mobilize state resources: readying flood-fighting supplies such as sandbags and pumps, preparing the National Guard to assist with flood response and search and rescue efforts, and fortifying roads and infrastructure. State environmental and natural resources agencies will also fast-track permitting and engage in other efforts to better prepare for flooding and landslides.
How will El Niño impact California?
El Niño typically brings wetter, more intense winters to California—which could leave the state more vulnerable to severe winter storms, heavy rainfall, landslides, and flooding. An El Niño year does not guarantee that these conditions will occur, but it does increase the likelihood.
Climate change is also supercharging weather events, and El Niño is no exception. One study published in August found that El Niño events are now nearly 40% stronger than before the Industrial era. This year’s El Niño is predicted to be the strongest in recorded history.
What impacts has California already felt from this year's El Niño?
The governor’s office noted that the state has already experienced coastal flooding attributable to El Niño. The state can expect to see Kelvin waves, slow moving pulses of water that can stretch thousands of miles and raise sea levels along the coastline—increasing the risk for coastal flooding and erosion, and offshore Pacific hurricanes. Climate scientists also warn that the Pacific can expect to see a temporary 6-inch to 2-ft. rise in sea levels this winter.
A number of southern California towns, including Malibu, Laguna Beach, and Long Beach, have already seen significant coastal erosion due to El Niño and Pacific hurricanes this year.
How can Californians prepare for El Niño?
The state has urged residents to take action to prepare for El Niño by signing up for emergency alerts and learning their flood risk, and having an evacuation plan and emergency kit at the ready.
It’s all part of an effort to ensure that the state is not caught off guard by El Niño. “We are not waiting for this season’s storms to be on our doorstep,” Cal OES director Caroline Thomas Jacobs said in a statement. “By planning early and coordinating resources ahead of El Niño, we are working to ensure communities and first responders have the personnel, equipment, and support they need to prepare for severe weather, respond quickly when conditions change, and protect lives and property across California.”

Norwegian broadcaster voices concerns over Israel's participation in Eurovision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:18:54 UTC
22:18:54 KST

Norway's public broadcaster NRK has sent a letter to the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) following this year's Eurovision Song Contest, citing concerns about Israel's participation and how the competition rules were applied.
NRK's entertainment editor Jostein Olseng confirmed the letter on Wednesday, which was first reported by Norwegian newspaper VG.
“We send letters after each final to provide feedback on how the competition can be improved,” Olseng said, according to NRK, adding that the editorial team had raised “clear concerns” related to Israel's participation.
Olseng said NRK was particularly concerned about whether the contest's voting system reflects musical preferences or could instead be influenced by national or geopolitical considerations.
"We have come to suspect that the voting does not reflect which songs are the best, but rather which nation we support," he said.
Olseng stressed that NRK's position is that the rules should be applied equally to all participating countries.
"For us, it is important that the rules the EBU has are followed. If not, we are worried that the competition will be something other than what is intended," he said.
Asked whether NRK believes Israel should be allowed to participate, Olseng said countries that comply with the rules and are EBU members should be eligible to take part.
The Eurovision Song Contest has faced increased scrutiny over Israel's participation amid the genocidal war in Gaza and wider political tensions surrounding the contest.
Several countries, including Spain, the Netherlands and Ireland, boycotted this year's Eurovision Song Contest in protest over Israel's participation.

Swiss move house five times on average
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

An advocate for the laws of war in a world that no longer believes in them     
    
        
            Read more: An advocate for the laws of war in a world that no longer believes in them         
    
Swiss move house five times on average
Swiss residents move home five times on average during their lives, and despite a housing shortage, only about half spend more than three months searching for a new place.
These are the two main findings of a survey conducted by the property portal Newhome, which interviewed 1,273 Swiss residents aged between 18 and 79.
On average, people moved house 4.9 times in their lifetime. One-third moved a maximum of twice, 41% between three and five times, and 32% over five times. Unsurprisingly, the proportion of those who have never moved house or have done so only once is particularly high amongst those under 29.
More
                
        Housing    
        
        Buy or rent? Find out where you can afford to live in Switzerland
This content was published on Where do you stand the best chance of finding affordable housing? Where is renting cheaper than buying? Find out using the housing calculator.
Read more: Buy or rent? Find out where you can afford to live in Switzerland
Buying a property was the main reason for moving for one in three people. Twenty-four per cent cited a change in their relationship status and 27% a change in family circumstances as the reason for their most recent move. It is less common to look for new accommodation due to a new job or education (19%).
The survey also reveals some regional differences. For example, it is easier to find a home in canton Ticino in southern Switzerland than elsewhere – 35% took less than a month. Nationally, however, one in ten had to search for over a year, a figure that rises to 18% among 45–59-year-olds.

Confirmed Russian War Dead Top a Quarter Million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:17:24 UTC
22:17:24 KST

More than 250,000 Russian soldiers are confirmed to have died in Ukraine, and the actual figure is probably twice that, a report published jointly by the BBC and Russian outlet Mediazona on Tuesday says.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine started in 2022, a total of 258,980 individuals serving in the Russian military, identified by name, died either in combat or as a result of it, the report says.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The figure came from years of research into publicly available, verifiable sources such as social media posts by relatives, death notices and obituaries, reports in local media and statements from regional authorities.
The updated report marked the fourth anniversary of the Kremlin’s emergency mobilization of reservists following the September 2022 collapse of Russian defenses on the northwestern Kharkiv front to a Ukrainian counteroffensive.
The last time the Kremlin made public numbers of war dead and wounded was on Sept. 21, 2022, when then-Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu said that 5,937 Russian service members had been killed in combat.
Practically all sources, including pro-Moscow milbloggers at the time, said the figure was minuscule and not credible.
According to current estimates published by Kyiv’s top headquarters, the General Staff, Russian military personnel losses in the war through Sept. 22, 2026, sit at 1,520,880 men killed or seriously wounded. The General Staff said its figures are backed by hard evidence, predominantly overhead drone video of the Russian soldier or soldiers hit.
Russian Mi-8 Helicopter Briefly Violates Polish Airspace, Poland Scrambles Fighters
International observer estimates are generally on par with Ukrainian estimates on Russian losses: The head of Britain’s armed forces, Air Chief Marshal Sir Rich Knighton, said British intelligence assessed about 1.5 million Russian military casualties since February 2022, including wounded, of whom about 500,000 had been killed, in his Sept. 11 comments to the media.
Per the Mediazona research, geographically, the death toll for Russian soldiers in Ukraine has been highest in peripheral territories with weak economies, particularly the interior Kuban region between the Black and Caspian Seas, and in the depressed regions in and around Chelyabinsk and Yekaterinburg.
The report says territories with majority non-ethnic Russian populations have been particularly hard-hit relative to their populations, including the predominantly Muslim Tatarstan and Bashkortostan along the upper Volga, and Buryatia and Zabaikalsky Krai near Mongolia.
Death rates in major cities with relatively well-off and educated populations, like the capital Moscow, along with the Russian heartland cities such as St. Petersburg, Tver, Yaroslavl, Vladimir and Smolensk, have been three or four times lower than in less-developed territories, data and graphics published in the report show.
Russian President Vladimir Putin and other Kremlin officials have, since the invasion, insisted Russia will eventually defeat Ukraine because Russia’s manpower reserves can support a continuous offensive that relentlessly gains ground and conquers parts of Ukraine the Kremlin wants to become part of the Russian Federation.
But increasing and sometimes rocketing soldier losses, especially since Ukrainian drone dominance made Russian armored operations obsolete and Russian troops shifted tactics to launching attacks on unarmored motorcycles or all-terrain vehicles (ATVs), have forced Kremlin recruiters to offer potential new recruits massive signing bonuses and to drum up volunteers in state prisons.
According to a report on current Russian recruiting practices published by the Conflict Intelligence Group (CIG) on Tuesday, the Russian state is working to replenish its ranks with a variety of tactics, but has not made the politically dangerous decision to conscript men into the army for combat operations.
Under current Russian law, a man drafted into army service may serve only on Russian Federation territory, though pressure on conscripts to “volunteer” for service in Ukraine is widely reported.
According to most reports, only a small percentage of potential recruits, despite those efforts, choose to go to war over Russian civilian life.
“In [the remote northeastern Siberian city of] Bratsk, the 2025 recruitment plan was increased from 548 to 645, but by Nov. 1, only 369 had been recruited,” the CIG report states.
“To fulfill the plan, city authorities visited over 14,000 addresses, conducted nearly 3,000 interviews, and targeted, among others, debtors, conscripts, foreigners, people with criminal records, and orphans. Of the 261 orphans and orphanage graduates ‘treated,’ only one signed a contract,” it adds.
Recruitment tactics used to fill the gap include offering the equivalent of a year’s factory worker’s salary as a signing bonus in the depressed central Russian region of the Republic of Mordovia, sending funding to and setting recruitment quotas for local governments and convincing them to sign up as soldiers in Yarsolavl, and even imposing fines and, in some cases, criminal liability on local officials failing to meet quotas, as seen in Stavropol, the CIG article says.
Cases of Russian unit commanders denying invalid soldiers, among them cripples and epilepsy sufferers, medical separation from the service, so that there might be more men available for the next attack are “multiplying,” as are incidents of men arrested on minor violations being forced by police to sign an army contract, a Tuesday Mediazona report says.
The article cited husbands of confirmed cases in the cities of Kirov, Penza, Petrozavodsk and greater St. Petersburg who were picked up by police for “questioning” and released only after signing an army contract.
Ukrainian news platforms and combat unit information feeds, citing Russian prisoners of war, have long reported limited training for new Russian recruits, usually 10 days to two weeks. Captured Chinese soldiers offered a broadly similar account of their training in their April 2025 press conference.
In a video published by Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps from the eastern Lyman sector, Ukrainian troops encountered and took prisoner frontline Russian soldiers claiming not to have received food for days.
The images showed a poorly equipped Russian soldier, at one point unarmed except for a stick, surrendering to a 3rd Army Corps assault team. Four other Russian soldiers died in that single small battle, the same unconfirmed Ukrainian army report says.

Russian Mi-8 Helicopter Briefly Violates Polish Airspace, Poland Scrambles Fighters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:11:17 UTC
22:11:17 KST

A Russian Mi-8 military helicopter briefly violated Polish airspace on Wednesday, flying up to 300 meters (984 feet) into Polish territory near the town of Braniewo, Poland’s Operational Command said.
The helicopter entered Polish airspace from Russia’s Kaliningrad Oblast at 11:08 a.m. local time and remained there for 42 seconds, according to the statement.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Polish military radar systems detected the aircraft, prompting the scrambling of fighter jets. Ground-based air defense forces and other military assets were also placed on standby.
“The nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defense,” the Operational Command said.
Polish air defense crews remain on round-the-clock watch, the command added.
Earlier incidents
The incident is the latest in a series of Russian military aircraft and drone incursions into Polish airspace since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
On Feb. 11, 2025, a Russian Su-24MR military aircraft entered Polish airspace over the Gulf of Gdańsk, penetrating about 6.5 kilometers (4 miles) and remaining there for roughly 72 seconds. Russia later acknowledged the incident and attributed it to a navigation-system malfunction.
On April 25, 2025, a Russian military helicopter also entered Polish airspace over the Baltic Sea’s territorial waters. Poland said the incident appeared to be an attempt to test its air-defense readiness.
NATO Keeps Article 5 Trigger ‘Deliberately Ambiguous’
The most serious incident came on Sept. 9-10, 2025, when 19 Russian drones violated Polish airspace during a large-scale Russian attack on Ukraine. Poland scrambled fighter jets and subsequently requested NATO consultations under Article 4.
Most recently, Poland has repeatedly scrambled aircraft in response to Russian attacks on Ukraine and increased military activity near its borders, although not every such incident has involved a violation of Polish airspace.

Russia Seeks to Destroy and Depopulate Odesa. Can It Withstand the Pressure?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:10:00 UTC
22:10:00 KST

Odesa is Ukraine’s key Black Sea port, a city of one million people, and a major industrial and resort center. Every year, tons of grain and metallurgical products are exported from here.
This is Ukraine’s maritime gateway. Three major ports in and around the city provide key routes for Ukrainian exports, which create jobs across the country and generate an inflow of foreign currency.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
From the very first day of the full-scale invasion, Odesa became one of Russia’s priority targets. Russian forces tried to reach Odesa by land but were defeated near Mykolaiv, a major city 150 kilometers (93 miles) to the northeast. They then turned to a naval blockade of the city. However, after the sinking of the cruiser Moskva and the liberation of Snake Island – a key position in the Black Sea – maritime trade resumed.
Nevertheless, as part of its attempts to destroy Ukraine’s entire trading sector, Russia resumed attacks on the city and port in 2026.
Firefighter Vladyslav Prykhodko is one of those who regularly deal with the aftermath of Russian strikes on Odesa’s civilian infrastructure. He says what is happening now is very different from his work during “peacetime.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
Confirmed Russian War Dead Top a Quarter Million
“The difference is that at any moment a missile or a Shahed could appear, posing a threat to our lives and the lives of civilians. The difference is that in normal times, we simply have an established procedure for dealing with a fire. But during shelling, we have to react very quickly and everything is always different. There was a strike near the radio market, there were several strikes there, there was a dormitory, it was hit, we went up in the ‘basket’ to put out the fire in the building, and we received an air-raid alert that there had been further missile launches, so we moved away from the building as quickly as possible,” Prykhodko says.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Everything is being used – loitering munitions, KAB guided aerial bombs, drones, and missiles. Strikes occur every day. Sometimes there are days when the number of hours under air-raid alerts exceeds the number of hours without them, with dozens of targets heading toward Odesa.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Russian forces often attack chaotically, hitting everything in their path. Shopping centers and residential buildings come under attack, including this high-rise not far from the coast. Like this one on the coast, being stroked directly in apartment during the night of Sept. 12th.
                                                                                                                                                                         
“The hardest thing is the moral… the psychological situation. When you are at a fire or clearing rubble, you don’t think about whether you have any strength left or anything else – you just work. The hardest thing is that people are waiting for you to reach their relatives. People are waiting and hoping that everything will be all right with their loved ones,” Prykhodko says.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Vladyslav’s supervisor, Denys Voronin, says people work around the clock. Some become exhausted, but no one wants to stop or give up.
“Why is the enemy doing this? It is difficult to understand. There are repeated strikes. A strike hits a residential area or infrastructure, we go there, and then there is another strike in the same place – to harm the rescuers – firefighters, medics, those who come to help. The guys take 24-hour shifts. My schedule is somewhat different because I am the deputy head of the unit. I go with them to all major fires and strikes. It is difficult for us, but we work as one mechanism,” Voronin says.
                                                                                                                                                                         
The Russians’ main target is the port. As a result of the attacks, shipping has been disrupted, more than 300 vessels have been damaged or destroyed, and hundreds of sailors have been wounded, with some killed, says Dmytro Barinov, president of the Ukrainian Ports Association.
“During this time, more than 300 vessels have been damaged or completely or partially destroyed. And, as we have already said, they have intensified this kind of hunting. I can use that word: they are hunting civilian vessels flying foreign flags with international crews, citizens of different countries,” Barinov says.
                                                                                                                                                                         
He says this is not only a Ukrainian problem, but a global one.
“It is not only about agricultural products, but also iron ore. We are a major producer and exporter of such commodities. You know, when there was a complete blockade in 2022, the price of wheat on the New York Stock Exchange immediately jumped by 25%. Now Ukraine is not present on the agricultural market. And neither is Russia, because at that time, in 2022, Russia was still trading. But now – no. That is why one-third of global wheat production and consumption is blocked. It was intended for certain regions, such as Turkey, North Africa, Tunisia, Algeria, Morocco, Egypt, and the Middle East. That is why I think this will also have a negative impact on the global economy,” Barinov says.
The question is whether exports can be redirected to other ports until effective protection of Odesa is ensured. Options for exporting through Danube ports or transporting grain out of Ukraine by rail or truck have been discussed. However, Barinov is skeptical, saying the capacity of the ports is so large that it is unlikely to be replaced by other means.
“I will give you a very simple example. One vessel, even not a very large one, is 100,000 tons. That is Cape-size. Or somewhere between Panamax and Cape-size. So, we can load it within three days. Then the vessel goes to its destination. If you calculate it in terms of trucks, that means 5,000 trucks. Can you imagine? That is 5,000 drivers, 5,000 sets of documents, and 5,000 border-crossing procedures. If we calculate it in terms of smaller vessels that can reach the Danube region through the Sulina Canal, where the draft is limited to 7.2 meters [23 feet], it costs money. Again, that means 20 or 30 vessels, 20 or 30 pilotage procedures. Romania has become a member of the Schengen Area, so their procedures have become more complicated and take more time,” Barinov says.
The situation is frightening for some residents, and they are trying to leave, says local historian and activist Vladyslav Balynskyi. He believes the strikes are part of a strategy aimed not only at the economy but also at the Ukrainian population of Odesa more broadly.
“I travel a lot, and I can say this not only about Odesa, but also about Maiac, on the border with Moldova. I see that after large-scale shelling, the flow of cars leaving Odesa increases. People are still frightened by this. As for the strikes on the port, it is clearly an attempt by Russia to stop grain exports. But as for the shelling on the historic center of the city, I don’t understand it. But if we proceed from the logic we have seen over the past 12 years, then this is simply genocide, an attempt to destroy Ukraine within its borders, to intimidate and drive people out so that there would be a desert here. Ukrainians as such are not needed by it, and it seems that people in Odesa have understood this,” Balynskyi says.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Nevertheless, most residents remain. Odesa’s entire social sphere continues to operate, as do public transport, restaurants, bars, and most of its industry, like Odesa opera.
                                                                                                                                                                         
People continue to go to the theater and take tourists to the beach even in September.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Russian strikes are causing casualties and damage, but Odesa is not prepared to give up, while Ukraine is looking for ways to unblock shipping. What could they be? Our sources identify two options – either a ceasefire on terms that include a halt to strikes on the ports or strong US and European sanctions against Russia that would force it to end the endless war.

Chinese vice premier calls for advancing rural revitalization
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:09:42 CST
22:09:42 KST

WUHAN, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Vice Premier Liu Guozhong has called for mobilizing efforts across society to build a beautiful and harmonious countryside for people to live and work in and steadily advance rural revitalization.
Liu, who is also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, visited central China's Hubei Province from Monday to Wednesday, and attended a national event in celebration of the ninth Chinese farmers' harvest festival.
In Xiangyang's Xiangzhou and Zaoyang, Liu inspected autumn grain production, agricultural machinery services and rural environmental improvement, and joined farmers in celebrating the harvest festival.
This year, China has overcome adverse factors, including natural disasters, to achieve a record summer grain harvest, maintain stable early rice output, and put the autumn grain harvest on track for a bumper crop, he noted.
Liu called for strengthening late-season management of autumn grain crops and disaster prevention and reduction, and ensuring well-organized harvesting and grain purchases. He also urged efforts to develop high-standard farmland, develop distinctive rural industries, and expand channels for farmers to increase their incomes.
In Shiyan's Danjiangkou, Liu inspected water source protection and water diversion projects. He called for stronger water source protection, safe project operation and reliable water quality, along with strict controls on construction quality and production safety, stronger oversight of funds, and faster development of a modern water network.
The Chinese farmers' harvest festival is the first national festival created specifically for the country's farmers. Launched in 2018, the festival coincides with the Autumnal Equinox each year, which is one of the 24 solar terms of the Chinese lunisolar calendar and usually falls between Sept. 22 and 24, during the country's agricultural harvest season. ■

Chinese Mid-Autumn Festival celebrated in Benin
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:09:42 CST
22:09:42 KST

COTONOU, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese Cultural Center in Benin's Cotonou and the Confucius Institute of the University of Abomey-Calavi celebrated the traditional Chinese Mid-Autumn Festival Tuesday evening in Cotonou.
Held under the theme "Under the Same Moon: A Mid-Autumn Poetry Gathering," the event brought together more than 100 people, including Chinese nationals residing in Cotonou, staff members of the Chinese Embassy in Benin and the Chinese Cultural Center, students from the Confucius Institute, diplomats accredited to Benin, and Beninese people interested in Chinese culture.
Through a poetry performance accompanied by music and presented in Fon and Mandarin, students from the Confucius Institute showcased the richness of Chinese culture, including traditions, symbols, stories, and ancestral practices passed down from generation to generation.
"The Mid-Autumn Festival is one of the major traditional Chinese festivals. Every year, on the 15th day of the eighth month of the lunar calendar, families gather to admire the moon, enjoy mooncakes and express their feelings through poetry," said Shen Si, charge d'affaires a.i. and minister counselor at the Chinese Embassy in Benin.
Carole Borna, representative of Benin's Minister of Culture, Arts and Heritage, said the celebration demonstrated that despite the distances separating families and peoples, shared values brought them closer together.
"Cooperation between Benin and China is not limited to the economic and institutional fields. It is also built through cultural, artistic and heritage exchanges, which enable our two peoples to better understand each other and strengthen their friendship," she said, adding that the Mid-Autumn Festival embodies universal values of transmission, heritage, sharing and dialogue among peoples. ■

Folk cultural activities held at ancient town of Zouma in SW China's Chongqing ahead of holidays
China

Portugal's face-covering ban enters into force
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:09:40 CST
22:09:40 KST

LISBON, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Portugal's law banning the concealment of the face in public spaces entered into force on Wednesday, introducing fines of up to 3,000 euros (3,420 U.S. dollars) for those who cover their faces in public without an accepted justification.
The law also establishes that anyone who coerces another person into covering face is subject to a prison sentence of up to two years, with penalties increased by one third if the victim is a minor.
Under the legislation, public spaces are defined as public roads, locations open to the public, areas assigned to public service and places providing services generally accessible to citizens.
Exemptions apply in aircraft, diplomatic and consular premises, places of worship and other sacred sites, as well as in cases involving health, professional, artistic, advertising, security or climate-related justifications, or where another legal provision permits face covering.
According to local media reports, the law originated as a proposal of the far-right Chega party explicitly targeting the wearing of the burqa by women in Portugal. After being approved in parliament, it was promulgated by President Antonio Jose Seguro in August. ■

====================================================================================================

Economic Watch: Chinese motorcycles pick up pace on new-energy track
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:09:33 CST
22:09:33 KST

CHONGQING, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- In an exhibition hall in southwest China's Chongqing Municipality, an electric off-road motorcycle drew a crowd of onlookers. Nearby, retro-styled e-motorcycles, urban commuters and high-performance electric bikes stood in rows, waiting for their turn in the spotlight.
But the motorcycles were not the only things attracting attention. Buyers moved from booth to booth, stopping to examine batteries, motors and intelligent control units -- the components powering a new generation of electric two-wheelers.
The scene at the 24th China International Motorcycle Trade Exhibition offers a glimpse into a broader shift in the country's motorcycle industry: new-energy models are no longer a niche attraction. They are drawing increasing attention from manufacturers and buyers.
Held in Chongqing from Saturday to Tuesday, the exhibition brought together 1,120 exhibitors and more than 100 global motorcycle and electric vehicle brands, showcasing over 3,000 vehicles. Thousands of international buyers and dealers from more than 80 countries and regions came to explore new Chinese products.
For manufacturers, the change is reflected in the products on display. Electric motorcycles are being developed for an increasingly diverse range of uses, from intercity long-distance travel and performance-oriented commuting to competitive racing and off-road riding.
And their push is extending beyond China's borders. Some brands have already gained a foothold in European and American markets, with their electric motorcycles now sold across dozens of countries and regions.
"Electric motorcycles represent the future trend," said Hernan Holguin, a Colombian buyer, as he weaved between different booths, taking a close look at Chinese electric motorcycles.
For buyers like Holguin, the appeal goes beyond the exhibition floor. Rising fuel prices, growing urban transportation needs and a booming express delivery sector are driving South American markets to turn to Chinese e-motorcycles, he said. He hopes to reach cooperation agreements during his trip and bring more Chinese e-motorcycles to Latin American markets.
The growing interest is also drawing attention from industry insiders.
New-energy motorcycles will become an important part of urban transportation in many countries and regions, said Zhang Hongbo, secretary-general of the China Chamber of Commerce for Motorcycle (CCCM). As technology advances, the industry is moving toward greener and smarter development, he said, adding that Chinese new-energy motorcycles are expected to see further growth in global markets.
Analysts say the country's vast and well-established motorcycle industry is expected to provide a solid foundation for the growth of the electric motorcycle sector.
China is the world's largest motorcycle producer, with an industrial chain valued at nearly 500 billion yuan (74.6 billion U.S. dollars). According to the CCCM, the country produced more than 22.1 million motorcycles and sold nearly 21.97 million in 2025.
Chongqing, a major production hub where roughly one in every three motorcycles made in China rolls off the production line, offers a close-up view of the industry's evolution.
Here, fuel-powered and electric motorcycles are developing side by side. Major manufacturers such as Zonsen and Shineray are accelerating their new-energy plans, while battery makers are also rolling out new technologies and products, gradually broadening the industry's electric offerings.
In the first half of this year, Chongqing exported 117,000 electric motorcycles and mopeds worth 515 million yuan. Export volume jumped 130.5 percent year on year, while export value increased 66.6 percent, statistics from the municipal commission of economy and informatization show.
For many manufacturers, the next step is clear: bringing electric models into their product lines.
Founded in 2024, ZXMOTO rapidly built a presence in the market with large-displacement fuel-powered motorcycles. Now, it is turning its attention to electric models.
The company has already secured the necessary qualifications and related R&D is well underway, its founder Zhang Xue said at the event.
As more manufacturers embrace electrification, industry experts see potential for electric motorcycles to follow the growth trajectory of China's electric auto industry.
The motorcycle sector can follow, replicate and even surpass the electrification path of China's automotive industry, said Chen Qingquan, an academician of the Chinese Academy of Engineering, noting that both vehicle and battery technologies have now reached a mature stage.
"The era of rapid development for the electric motorcycle industry has arrived," Chen said. ■

South Sudan president dissolves transitional gov't ahead of December elections
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:09:17 CST
22:09:17 KST

JUBA, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- South Sudan President Salva Kiir dissolved the transitional government on Tuesday evening, ahead of the country's first elections scheduled for December.
The presidential decree dissolved South Sudan's national legislature and state governments, removed the first vice president and four other vice presidents from their posts, and named a caretaker government to manage the transition to the Dec. 22 elections.
Riek Machar, who holds the post of first vice president, has been suspended since September 2025 and is on trial on charges including treason.
The presidential decree, which was broadcast on the state-run South Sudan Broadcasting Corporation, stated that Kiir will remain president throughout the election period until a newly elected leader is sworn in.
Parliament passed amendments to the National Elections Act on Monday, and Kiir signed them into law on Tuesday. The amendments allow the president to stay in office during the election period and remove all vice presidents appointed under the 2018 peace deal.
According to the decree, the judiciary and security institutions will remain intact, while presidential advisers and envoys will continue serving directly under Kiir's authority.
Government ministries and state institutions were instructed to transition immediately to caretaker status to ensure operational continuity.
Kiir appointed caretaker ministers to oversee key ministries, including presidential affairs, cabinet affairs, foreign affairs, defense, interior, justice, national security, finance, petroleum, trade, information and communications technology, East African Community affairs and peacebuilding.
South Sudan gained independence in 2011 but was soon plunged into a devastating five-year civil war.
General elections are scheduled for Dec. 22, having already been postponed twice. ■

Feature: At 55, Pakistani table tennis player makes Asian Games debut
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:09:01 CST
22:09:01 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- On a table tennis court filled with young athletes, Nosheen Aslam stood out.
At 55, she was the oldest player in the women's team competition at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, competing alongside athletes decades younger.
Then she picked up her paddle.
Nosheen represented Pakistan in two team matches on the opening day of the women's competition on Sunday. She did not play in Pakistan's final group match the following day, but her presence in Nagoya had already marked a personal milestone.
It was her first Asian Games. It was also her first time traveling abroad for an international competition.
"The Asian Games is my dream," Nosheen said. "It's a great event, very well organized. All the people are very nice, and it's a great experience for me. I'm enjoying it."
The experience was a dream come true for Nosheen, but it also came with plenty of nerves. "I was very nervous, and I didn't perform very well," she said.
The results did not go her way, but after their matches ended, Nosheen and her teammates gathered courtside for photographs, smiling and enjoying a moment that meant far more than the score.
Nosheen is from Lahore, the capital of Punjab and Pakistan's second-largest city. She took up table tennis 12 years ago, when she was already a mother of three boys, and quickly fell in love with the sport.
"It makes me active. It makes me fit, and I enjoy playing table tennis," she said.
Her three sons all play cricket. Many of Nosheen's table tennis partners and opponents, meanwhile, are around the same age as her children. One of her teammates in Nagoya, Aleena Khan, is just 15.
But once Nosheen steps onto the court, the age gap disappears.
"Every time I play, I feel happy and forget the worries of my life," she said. "Age is just a number. I think table tennis is a sport of skill. If your skills are good, then nothing else matters."
Finding time to train has never been easy. As a mother and a working woman, Nosheen has had to juggle table tennis with caring for her children, cooking and work.
She often trains at night, squeezing practice into whatever time she can find after finishing her daily responsibilities, and has kept at it for years.
Nosheen's experience also reflects how table tennis is developing in Pakistan. In Lahore, there are many clubs with good facilities, and both boys and girls regularly play the sport. Nosheen also enjoys helping younger players learn basic techniques.
The sport is also reaching younger players through schools.
A pilot of the International Table Tennis Federation's School Program began in late 2025 and has since expanded to six countries across four continents. In Pakistan, the program introduced table tennis as a regular school sports activity at four schools, involving 80 students.
The initiative aims to make table tennis part of school life and promote skills such as confidence, teamwork and discipline.
For Nosheen, the growth of the sport means more young players are coming through, making competition increasingly challenging.
She spent two to three months preparing for the Asian Games, with her husband and children encouraging her throughout. But in Nagoya, facing younger players competing at a high level, she could see the gap.
Despite the losses, Nosheen left Nagoya with another target in mind. Retirement is not yet on her mind. Her next goal is the South Asian Games, scheduled to be held in Pakistan next April.
"I think my physical condition is still good," she said. "Maybe I can play for another two or three years."
Then she smiled and added: "Maybe next time my performance will be better." ■

WHO warns DR Congo Ebola outbreak still uncontrolled as cases surge in North Kivu
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:08:57 CST
22:08:57 KST

KINSHASA, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) remains uncontrolled despite signs of improvement in some affected areas, as cases have risen sharply in the eastern province of North Kivu, a senior World Health Organization (WHO) official said Wednesday.
Marie Roseline Belizaire, director of the WHO emergencies program in the African region, said during an online press briefing. The country had recorded 7,773 confirmed cases, including 3,759 deaths as of Monday, according to the DRC health authorities.
"We are beginning to see the first encouraging signs of progress," Belizaire said.
Between Aug. 31 and Sept. 20, cases declined by about 26 percent in Ituri Province, the long-time epicenter of the outbreak, and by around 15 percent in Haut-Uele Province. North Kivu, however, recorded a 73-percent increase over the same period, she said.
"This clearly shows that the outbreak continues to evolve differently across the affected areas," Belizaire said, noting that each of the seven affected provinces has its own transmission pattern.
"The outbreak is still not under control," she said. "This outbreak continues to pose a significant risk to regional and global health security."
Children under five remain particularly vulnerable, with a case fatality rate of more than 60 percent, compared with around 40 percent among adults, according to the WHO official.
While contact follow-up has improved to nearly 88 percent, too many new infections are still being detected without a known epidemiological link, highlighting persistent gaps in surveillance, she said.
Belizaire stressed that the response must now focus resources on areas where transmission and risks are highest while maintaining essential health services.
"We must consolidate the progress made in Ituri, strengthen the response in North Kivu and other emerging hotspots, detect cases earlier, reduce community deaths, and maintain strong cross-border preparedness," she said.
The outbreak, declared in May, has become the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the DRC and the second-largest Ebola outbreak globally, after the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic. ■

BRATISLAVA, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Slovakia will cap the retail margin on petrol and diesel at 10 euro cents (11 U.S. cents) per liter from Oct. 1, the country's Prime Minister Robert Fico announced Wednesday.

Brazil has record number of Indigenous candidates for general election
RIO DE JANEIRO, Sept 23 - Almost 200 Indigenous candidates, a record, are running for public office in Brazil's general election next month, official data showed, campaigning on environmental protection in an increasingly conservative political landscape where agribusiness interests wield significant influence.
"We Indigenous women need to have a voice, and we need to occupy decision-making spaces. We have to be in those decision-making spaces as part of our struggle for our territories, for Mother Earth, and for the environment," said Tereza Arapium, who is running for a seat in the state congress in Rio de Janeiro, using actual leaves as campaign leaflets.
The record comes as Indigenous groups push the government for faster official recognition of their territories, a status that grants these lands legal protection against invasions, while seeking to shield their interests in legislative houses from agribusiness, as well as energy and infrastructure projects.
Brazil's electoral authorities have registered 191 Indigenous candidates, the highest number since ethnicity data on candidates started being published in 2014, data gathered by Indigenous umbrella group APIB showed, but still a tiny fraction of the almost 21,000 candidates registered with electoral authorities.
APIB has publicly supported the re-election of leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who opinion polls show is neck and neck with the main opposition candidate Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of far-right firebrand and former President Jair Bolsonaro.
The group welcomed Lula's creation of a Ministry of Indigenous Affairs and the resumption of official recognitions of Indigenous lands, but criticized the pace of such recognitions and the government's push for oil drilling near the mouth of the Amazon River.
Lula has claimed the drilling would be done in the safest way possible. REUTERS

Swiss archaeologists uncover rare medieval heating system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:06:35 UTC
22:06:35 KST

Swiss archaeologists uncover rare medieval heating system
Archaeologists in Basel have uncovered an almost intact medieval hot-air heating system during renovation work at the site of the former Gnadental monastery, a find described as unique in Switzerland.
The heating system was uncovered in the courtyard of the former vocational school at Petersgraben 52, it was announced on Wednesday. It was located beneath the walls and mortar floors of the former medieval convent of Gnadental and is thought to have heated the community’s dining hall.
+ Why Switzerland is an archaeological treasure trove
Based on architectural and historical considerations, the experts dated the system to the 13th to 14th centuries. According to a statement, the structure consisted of an underground chamber lined with stones for heat storage and a firebox channel beneath it. Warm air flowed into the room above through eight closable openings.
A unique find in Switzerland
Such stone-chamber air-heating systems are extremely rare in Switzerland. The Basel find is said to be unique due to its almost complete state of preservation and is also considered one of the most significant examples in Europe. The find is to be incorporated into the renovation project at Petersgraben 52.
More
Structures of 11th-century castle discovered in Switzerland
Gnadental Convent was built around 1231 outside the city walls of the time for the Franciscans. But they moved to the newly founded Barfüsser Convent just 20 years later. The buildings then housed Cistercian nuns and Poor Clares. The monastery took its name in 1279 from lay sisters from Gnadenthal near Niederwil, Aargau. These were incorporated into the Order of the Poor Clares and remained there until the monastery was dissolved in the wake of the Reformation.
More
Unearthing a cemetery from the Middle Ages
After the Reformation, some of the convent buildings continued to be used. In 1573, for example, a granary was built using building materials from the convent, particularly from the church. At the end of the 19th century, the granary was demolished to make way for the vocational school. This marked the disappearance of the last visible remains of the monastery. It was only the recent excavations that brought these remains back to light.

Samar Yazbek's Your Presence is a Danger to Your Life on Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:05:49 UTC
22:05:49 KST

Breadcrumb
'It seemed as though we had entered hell': Samar Yazbek's chilling Gaza testimonies in Your Presence is a Danger to Your Life
There are sentences in this remarkable, painful book that imply an entire universe of horror. Like this: "We brought my daughter’s leg and buried it next to her brother and sister." Or this: "A boy was blowing air into a dismembered woman’s corpse, trying to bring her back to life – she was his mother."
Your Presence is a Danger to Your Life – the title is taken from the flyers dropped by the Israelis minutes before they bombed civilian targets – documents the Gaza genocide, or at least the genocide as experienced by 26 men, women and children interviewed at length throughout 2024 while they were receiving medical treatment in Qatar.
The interviewer, editor and shaper of these narratives is the Syrian novelist and non-fiction writer Samar Yazbek.
Yazbek has already produced three documentary texts from the Syrian Revolution and war – Woman in the Crossfire and others.
In the introduction, she explains how the destruction of Gaza reenacted for her the destruction of Syria. She hints at the continuum of experience between the two disasters, and describes her work as "testament to a dream of justice for those living beneath the grindstone of this violent era."
But there are key differences, terrifying "novel details" involving the technological sophistication of the Israeli genocidaires and their "algorithms of murder."
Many of the witnesses are householders hit at home in the midst of family life. A child asks for a sandwich, and then, in a flash, life is irretrievably broken.
"My brain couldn’t interpret what had happened" is a phrase repeated by several. "It seemed as though we had entered hell" is another.
Some witnesses are doctors, nurses, or volunteers who helped in hospitals. They recount Israeli soldiers bombing maternity wards, storming the intensive care department, methodically destroying the medical equipment.
One doctor is forced into the role of human shield. Several witnesses remember Israeli soldiers torturing the maimed and dying in their beds.
There are descriptions of dismemberment, of heads split open, of cats red-faced from human meals. Someone recalls "a grandmother as gentle as the breeze … innocent children, splendid as roses, evaporated in an instant;" others talk of children who bleed to death alone, or children who lose their entire families: parents, grandparents, siblings, cousins, aunts and uncles.
For the survivors, or semi-survivors, there is endless pain, vomiting after drinking poisoned water, the stink of sewage, of infected, maggot-filled wounds, of corpses rotting under the rubble.
There is the shame of being unable to stop screaming in a room full of strangers.
'Things that cannot be spoken'
Yazbek preserves the creative uses of Palestinian war idiom in the witness accounts. For instance, the popular word for a vacuum bomb is ‘shafat’ — meaning ‘suction’ — an idea which is then animated: "It took no more than two seconds to suck up twenty-five souls."
One of the accounts ends with the words, "And then there are all the things that cannot be spoken." This silence contains both general and specific meanings.
In general, as Yazbek writes in her introduction, "humans are capable of brutalizing each other in ways that challenge language’s very capacity of expression." More specifically, women witnesses would describe to Yazbek rapes and sexual abuse perpetrated on other women, but never on themselves.
None of this can be described as easy reading. The accounts provoke a visceral response, and sometimes the reader feels a near compulsion to put the book aside, go for a walk, and observe the emotional tumult it has unleashed.
Horror, grief and rage are natural responses to the reality expressed here. And yet there is a contrary compulsion to keep reading, to know the worst of it, to bear witness alongside Yazbek. Each distinct Palestinian voice, full of character, leads us through the maelstrom.
Yazbek understands genocide as an erasure: "The erasure of dismembered bodies; the erasure of our ability to see clearly; the erasure of the profound act of bearing witness to the agony of others; the erasure of language."
This book, then, no less than the writing of Primo Levi and other survivors of the Holocaust, seeks to transform erasure into narrative.
The effort to do so is particularly valuable given the welter of Zionist propaganda erasing the past and present existence of Palestinians.
To render them invisible and inaudible, Israel has prevented international journalists from entering Gaza and has assassinated at least 267 Palestinian journalists since 7 October 2023, according to the International Federation of Journalists.
A history of erasure
The attempted erasure of Palestinians and their rights reaches back through the repeated military assaults and the quarter-century-long siege of Gaza, back through the decades of massacre and dispossession, all the way to the erasure of hundreds of villages and towns that marked the birth of the Zionist state.
In this book, unlike in her documentations of Syrian suffering, Yazbek largely erases her own presence in favour of the Palestinians she so carefully listens to.
She notices the most pertinent details of their narratives and closely reproduces the idiomatic style and substance of their voices. What emerges is the eloquence of ordinary people under extraordinary pressure, a testament to Palestinian resilience, and a record of one of the greatest crimes of the age.
Unlike the crimes in Ukraine, Syria or Sudan, this one has been funded and armed by the United States and rhetorically supported by most Western governments and media outlets. In other words, the states that until recently claimed to promote universal human rights and international law have abandoned that pretence in order to stand with Zionist barbarism.
This has obvious implications for us all, not just Palestinians.
The genocide is still underway today, though more slowly, and will continue until we finally move to stop it.
"For over seventy years," says Abu Yahya, father of two murdered and two maimed children, "everyone has abandoned us."
Robin Yassin-Kassab co-wrote Burning Country: Syrians in Revolution and War and is the English editor at the ISIS Prisons Museum. His latest book is The Blood Between Us: Syria After the Fall of Assad

First series of adult T. rex footprints hints at its walking speed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

First series of adult T. rex footprints hints at its walking speed
An estimated speed of 1.6 meters per second roughly matches a person’s brisk walking pace
Four ancient footprints are helping scientists step into a T. rex’s shoes.
The prints form the first set of tracks probably left behind by an adult Tyrannosaurus rex, researchers report September 8 in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology. Measurements of the 7-meter-long trackway suggest the ancient predator was ambling along at about 1.6 meters per second, roughly equivalent to a person’s quick walking pace.
A few single adult T. rex footprints exist in the fossil record, as do trackways possibly from T. rex juveniles or other dinosaur species, says Peter Falkingham, a paleontologist at Liverpool John Moores University in England. “But an individual track doesn’t tell you a lot. A trackway tells you more about foot placement as the animal’s moving along.” And younger and older dinosaurs probably walked differently, just as human toddlers and adults do.
“Finding an adult trackway is cool,” Falkingham says. “It’s unique. It brings something new.”
High school teacher and paleontologist Kent Hups stumbled on the footprints in 2025, while fossil hunting along a steep incline in the Hell Creek Formation in North Dakota. The tracks stick up out of the ground because sediment filled in the originally muddy footprints, which then eroded away more slowly than the surrounding rock.
When Hups saw the first track, he noted that it was three-toed and enormous, measuring 80 centimeters across. “I’m going, ‘this has to be a T. rex,’” says Hups, of Northglenn High School in Colo. and the Denver Museum of Nature and Science.
Slender toe impressions and fossils unearthed in the area signal a T. rex left behind the footprints roughly 66.5 million years ago. “There’s always the possibility that we haven’t found the skeletons of some species that we don’t know about,” Falkingham says. “But as far as our knowledge goes, T. rex is about the only track maker that could have made these.”
The team used stride length and body size to calculate the dinosaur’s speed. Unfortunately, the footprints aren’t well-preserved and estimating speed from tracks is tricky, so the T. rex may have been walking slightly faster or slower than calculated. Better tracks could have revealed whether the foot landed flat or toe-to-heel, or how foot pads supported the predator’s weight.
More tracks are sure to follow. In fact, a fifth step may be concealed in the hill. But the team is waiting for Mother Nature to wear away the surrounding rock, Hups says. “I can’t wait to get back out there and keep looking for more.”
