America loves free speech, except when it comes to Palestine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Ed Sheeran thought he was taking the safe route. Prioritizing personal gain over principle, he thought he had more to fear from the corrupt, pro-genocide billionaire Robert Kraft than he did from the general public.
It turned out he was wrong.
Sheeran’s decision to bow to the billionaire and kick Macklemore off his tour was met with a resounding howl of condemnation. And that response has been so strong that it is swiftly turning into a major, and very important victory for the struggle for Palestinian rights.
While the importance of the response must not be understated, the decision by Kraft to shut down speech about the genocide in Palestine does not stand alone.
Palestine is both a major issue for right wing forces and the vanguard issue for their assault on free speech and dissent more broadly. Robert Kraft’s ability to control speech in the public sphere is a problem we must address more broadly.
A billionaire can call a few of his friends and slam the door on an artist who wants to use his stage to express solidarity with people suffering genocide and apartheid. In other areas, politicians try to use state power to silence critics of Israel’s actions and the United States’ support for it.
They do all of this because Palestine is an exception to the principles of free speech and the right to dissent. But if it is not successfully challenged, the assault on free speech will not end with Palestine, it will only begin there.
What Macklemore said
It all began in New Jersey, where Macklemore was opening for Sheeran at MetLife Stadium. Introducing his song, “Hind’s Hall,” the rapper explained to the crowd what the song was communicating. It’s worth examining what he said in full.
I’ve been trying to figure out a way to say this all day. One of the reasons why I wanted to come on this tour was because I wanted to stand up here on stages and stadiums across America and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: Free Palestine.
I said, Free Palestine.
I want those words to be loud and clear, so the people from Gaza, all the way to the occupied West Bank, know that we have not forgotten them.
And this next song was inspired by the bravery of Columbia University students who led an encampment movement that mobilized the entire world; open up hearts, myself included, so thank you to those students that risked their diplomas, that risked their tuition, that risked their scholarships, that stood up and said, no. CUAD students, Students for Justice in Palestine, and Jewish Voices for Peace. Thank you, guys.
To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters: criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you. My message is for peace; love for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect, and equality.
So I say Free Palestine, I say Free Lebanon, I say Free Cuba, I say Free Congo, Free Sudan, I say Free all people in America living in fear of this terrorist organization, ICE. None of us will be free until we are all free.”
It was a genuine call for freedom, for equality, for justice and respect for the rights of all at the expense of, and with the exception of no one.
Somehow, Bob Kraft twisted that into what he called “hate speech.”
Kraft himself is a leading sponsor of propaganda trips to Israel, and for anti-Palestinian advocacy in the United States. He has been a leader in conflating criticism of Israel with antisemitism, while supporting initiatives that strengthen the apartheid economy, sometimes under the guise of creating “opportunity for Palestinians”.
He is, unsurprisingly, a major donor to AIPAC, an actual hate group with the power to act on their agenda, unlike Macklemore.
When Columbia University students protested their university’s involvement in Israel’s genocide, Kraft withdrew support from Columbia because it was too slow, in his view, in stifling the dissent from students. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu once said that “Israel has no greater friend than Robert Kraft.”
What is perhaps most distressing is that we have a system where someone like Kraft can own the public sphere, and thus can dictate what is permitted in that sphere.
Control of the public sphere
While Massachusetts case law says that Kraft cannot cancel an existing contract over constitutionally protected speech, federal law does not. But this is also one reason that Kraft went out of his way to claim that Macklemore was engaging in “hate speech.”
Macklemore might have grounds to sue Kraft in Massachusetts, and we can hope that he would. The idea that “Free Palestine” is hate speech must be challenged in court, and this would be the perfect opportunity to do so.
Yet as egregious as Kraft’s action is, it is far from an isolated incident.
In Texas, the University of Texas, Austin is facing controversy over hosting pro-Palestine Twitch streamer Hasan Piker.
That appearance, scheduled for the end of this month, was condemned by Texas officials and members of Congress from both parties, including Governor Greg Abbott, Senator Ted Cruz, Senate candidate Ken Paxton (all Republicans) and Democratic Congressman Henry Cuellar.
Their condemnation came with calls for the university to cancel Piker’s appearance.
While the university has not, thus far, agreed to force the cancellation of the event, the students who organized it report that the school has refused to give them a space for it that can accommodate the much larger than anticipated number of people that signed up to attend Piker’s September 30 talk. This could put the event at risk based on safety concerns.
While Piker’s public persona has generated a lot of attention and overhyped controversy, it cannot go without notice that the University of Texas is a public institution. It is not owned by a billionaire like Robert Kraft, but rather by the state. As such, First Amendment protections are unequivocal.
Despite this, a bipartisan group of legislators have called for the university to cancel the Piker event. While I can’t claim to be a constitutional lawyer, I can certainly state that this violates the spirit of the First Amendment, if not the letter.
This is hardly new. Free speech is treasured in the United States like nowhere else in the world, one of the few truly positive claims the U.S. can still cling to. But, like any expression of popular will, it is inconvenient for those with power.
That’s where the Palestine Exception serves such a useful purpose.
Palestine stands above and beyond other controversial issues in its ability to stifle free speech because it can so readily be manipulated to be presented as antisemitism. Where the focus of pro-Israel advocacy has long been to equate criticism of Israel with antisemitism, now any expression that affirms Palestinian rights has been twisted into an attack on Jews.
Across the country, in local, state, and federal courts and legislatures, the battle is being waged. Even the online world has become a battlefield.
But in the face of the supremely cynical effort to portray “Free Palestine” as antisemitic, it’s impossible not to recall the chant, made into a song in the 1980s to “Free Nelson Mandela.” An Afrikaner of the day might have argued that this was hate speech because it called for the freeing of a convicted terrorist, thus making them feel “unsafe.”
The idea seems absurd. But if so, is not calling “Free Palestine” hate speech even more insane? That is an explicit call for restoring the human, civil, and national rights of an entire people, the overwhelming majority of whom cannot, even in the harshest, most prejudiced view, be accused of being guilty of anything except the “crime” of being Palestinian.
By labeling Palestine solidarity as hate speech, pro-Israel forces open a door to quash political speech they disagree with. The same could have been done with South African apartheid if Afrikaners were perceived as a group targeted for hate. That was impossible; so much so that when, more than three decades after apartheid, Afrikaners still weren’t treated like minorities in western (and other) states so often are, white supremacists like Donald Trump and Elon Musk had to make up stories of their persecution.
Jews, of course, have a horrific history of persecution, and there is real and growing antipathy and bigotry against us today. That circumstance is cynically used to quash not just the rightful accusations of genocide and other crimes against humanity that Israel commits as a matter of course—and has done since long before October 7, 2023—it is used to silence even the claim that Palestinians deserve the same rights as every other human being on Earth. Indeed, it is meant to send the message that Palestinians are less than human.
The idea that “Free Palestine” is threatening to supporters of Israel is probably true, and not limited only to Jewish supporters. But why is it threatening?
For the same reason that “Free Nelson Mandela” was threatening—oppressors fear that if the oppressed escape from under their boot, they will seek retribution. Not just accountability, but vengeance.
It is the same racist fear that always reinforces supremacist thinking.
But the response to Ed Sheeran dropping Macklemore from his tour shows that the force needed to stand against that weaponized fear is here. Even when that weapon is used by powerful billionaires or politicians, more and more people are resisting.
There has been a realization among people everywhere that Palestinians are suffering unspeakable cruelty and that this must be confronted. First they will try to eliminate the Palestinian people, but it will not stop there. As more people realize that fact, the numbers in support of Palestinian rights will grow even more quickly.
Whether it’s Macklemore, Hasan Piker, Palestinian-American human rights lawyer Prof. Noura Erakat (who was just arrested for insisting on public debate about Florida’s intention to invest in Israel bonds), or your neighborhood activist, this is a fight to make sure billionaires and politicians cannot stop free speech and will have to hear the calls to “Free Palestine” whether they like it or not.

ICC convicts ex-CAR militia leader of crimes against humanity
Mahamat Said Abdel Kani oversaw brutal detention tactics, including torture, at Bangui facility, ICC judges rule.
The International Criminal Court (ICC) has convicted a Central African Republic militia commander of crimes against humanity, including torture.
Judges in The Hague on Wednesday found Mahamat Said Abdel Kani guilty over his role of running a Seleka detention facility in Bangui, where supporters of then-President Francois Bozize were rounded up and tortured during the country’s 2013 civil war.
Recommended Stories

- list 2 of 4Mladic died a happy man
- list 3 of 4Convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic gets hero’s burial in Serbia

Said, 56, was acquitted of three war crimes charges as the judges ruled that the armed conflict had already ended when some of the alleged crimes happened.
A separate hearing will determine his sentence.
Judge Miatta Maria Samba said Said oversaw the torture at the Central Office for the Repression of Banditry, where detainees were whipped, waterboarded and bound using a method called “Arbatacher”, in which detainees’ hands, elbows and feet are tied together behind their backs.
Some prisoners were held in underground cells with no bathrooms or showers.
“The floor was covered in waste, and it smelled of faeces and urine,” Samba said.
She said a victim described how his life had been destroyed by the mistreatment.
Said, who denied the charges, appeared in court in jeans and a blue sweatshirt, looking unbothered as he shook his head when the verdict was read.
He was a senior figure in the Seleka coalition, which ousted Bozize in 2013, plunging the country into a conflict that killed thousands of people.
Bozize’s response, arming the “anti-Balaka” militia, fuelled more bloodshed before French troops helped secure the country in 2014 under a United Nations mandate.
The ICC has investigated violence in the Central African Republic since 2014 and has already convicted two anti-Balaka leaders, including former Sports Minister Patrice-Edouard Ngaissona, who was sentenced to 12 years, and former MP Alfred Yekatom who was sentenced to 15 years.
Said is the first Seleka member to be convicted.
The country has experienced relative stability since a 2019 peace agreement.

South Africa sends black rhinos to Botswana
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:57:30 UTC
21:57:30 KST

South Africa sends black rhinos to Botswana
The World Wildlife Fund (WWF) South Africa’s Black Rhino Range Expansion Program (BRREP) has successfully translocated 20 black rhinos from KwaZulu-Natal to Botswana.
The rhinos were moved in early September in a cross-border conservation operation involving two 36-hour road trips to a remote and secure location where the animals can breed and establish a new population.
The translocation effectively doubles Botswana’s black rhino population. The International Rhino Foundation estimates that about 25 black rhinos remained in the country following years of poaching pressure, particularly in the Okavango Delta region.
The 20 rhinos were captured in KwaZulu-Natal in early June and held in a boma during a quarantine period before being transported to their new home. According to BRREP leader Jeff Cooke, all 20 animals have arrived safely and are settling in well.
The Botswana operation is only the second cross-border translocation undertaken by BRREP. The first took place in 2019, when rhinos were moved to Liwonde National Park in Malawi. Since 2003, the programme has moved groups of up to 20 rhinos to suitable areas to help re-establish populations. It targets areas of about 20 000 hectares or more to provide sufficient space for populations to grow.
Cooke said finding areas large enough with suitable habitat for black rhinos is becoming increasingly difficult, prompting the programme to expand its operations across national borders.
”These newly translocated populations serve as incubators for the broader continental species recovery programme,” he said, adding that they could support further local range expansion in other black rhino range states.
WWF South Africa CEO Dr Morné du Plessis thanked the South African and Botswanan governments, Ezemvelo KZN Wildlife, funding and donor partners, and the recipient site owners for their role in the operation.
The organisation said the initiative demonstrates the value of collaboration and coordinated conservation efforts in supporting black rhino population recovery.

SIR row explodes into political confrontation as Opposition demands action against CEC
NEW DELHI: The reported objections raised by two Election Commissioners to decisions linked to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls triggered a major political confrontation on Wednesday, with opposition parties demanding action against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, an immediate halt to the SIR exercise and fresh elections in states where polls have already been held.The ruling BJP, however, defended the Election Commission, saying differences expressed by Election Commissioners during internal deliberations showed that the poll panel was functioning democratically rather than under a “dictatorial” system.
The political row followed a media report which said Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised objections at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders related to the SIR process and electoral rolls.The Election Commission has rejected the suggestion that the reported objections indicated a breakdown in its functioning.It said differing views and observations were a normal part of institutional deliberations and maintained that its decisions, including those concerning SIR, had been taken unanimously.

He also sought a fair probe “into everything that transpired within the EC and those responsible should be held accountable”, according to news agency PTI.Stalin alleged that the report had raised doubts about the results of Assembly elections held after the SIR exercise and said his party had consistently opposed the deletion of voters from electoral rolls in the name of SIR.

The Commission operates as a multi-member constitutional body. Written notes, observations, technical suggestions and internal checks-and-balances are standard, ongoing practices designed to ensure complete transparency, legal compliance and operational rigour,” it said.The commission said all official orders, decisions and administrative directions carried full legal sanction and followed established statutory procedures. It added that operational queries or inputs raised by members during the drafting stage were part of standard administrative practice aimed at safeguarding voter rights and improving electoral processes.The EC further said differing views and observations were a normal part of deliberation before a final decision was taken.
“Not only the three Commissioners, but every officer of the Commission is fully authorised to give his suggestions to the Commission for improving the electoral system,” it said.The commission said focusing on specific internal notes and observations over 10 months while overlooking its wider body of approvals, decisions, instructions and initiatives presented only one part of the picture.It said it had taken numerous decisions, issued instructions and introduced around 40 new initiatives and electoral reforms, including electoral-roll revision and SIR across the country.
“All these decisions are an outcome of the unanimous decisions of the full Commission in the past one year,” the EC said.The commission also pointed to the conduct of elections in Bihar, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, Assam and West Bengal during the period and said it remained committed to carrying out its constitutional duties.

Estonia's government sector deficit comes to €696 million in Q2
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:56:00 UTC
21:56:00 KST

Estonia's government sector deficit comes to €696 million in Q2
The budget deficit stood at 1.6 percent of GDP over the past four quarters, while public debt stood at 26.1 percent, Statistics Estonia said.
According to Pauline Kommer, head of government finance services at Statistics Estonia, the central government had the largest deficit at the end of the second quarter of 2026, with spending exceeding revenue by €703.9 million.
Social security funds also ended the second quarter with a deficit of €64.2 million. Local governments were the only part of the public sector to record a surplus by the end of the first half of the year, at €72.4 million, Kommer added.
In the second quarter, general government revenue rose 2.7 percent and spending rose 4.4 percent compared with the same period in 2025. By the end of the first half of the year, general government spending exceeded revenue by €695.8 million.
Investment costs growing the fastest
Investment spending rose the most compared with the second quarter of 2025, increasing 23.6 percent to €851.1 million in the second quarter of 2026. Kommer said the increase reflected investments in both national defense and infrastructure.
Personnel costs also rose, increasing 8.4 percent from the same period last year. "The increase was mainly driven by salary costs in national defense and internal security, in line with what was agreed in the state budget," Kommer explained.
Value-added tax revenue helped slow the growth of the deficit. Compared with the second quarter of last year, receipts rose because of both the VAT rate increase in July 2025 and an overall expansion of the tax base as the economy recovered. VAT receipts in the second quarter were €73.9 million, or 6.9 percent, higher than a year earlier. Social tax revenue also slowed the growth of the deficit, rising by €71.7 million, or 5.4 percent, from the second quarter of last year as wages increased overall.
Consolidated general government debt, also known as Maastricht debt, stood at €11.3 billion at the end of the second quarter of 2026, up €1.2 billion, or 12.1 percent, from the end of 2025.
Central government debt rose 12.5 percent from the end of last year to €10.8 billion at the end of the second quarter.
The combined debt of local governments stood at €1.6 billion at the end of the second quarter of 2026, down 3 percent from the end of 2025.
The social security funds — the Estonian Health Insurance Fund and the Estonian Unemployment Insurance Fund — did not contribute to general government debt.
In Estonia, general government is divided into three parts: central government, local governments and social security funds. Central government comprises state budget institutions, foundations and public-law legal entities. Local governments include city and rural municipality institutions and their foundations, while the social security funds comprise the Estonian Health Insurance Fund and the Estonian Unemployment Insurance Fund.

Source: Statistics Estonia

Ethiopia civil war fears escalate after rebel forces ‘seize airport’
Forces in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region have reportedly taken control of the airport in its capital, Mekelle, prompting state-owned Ethiopian Airlines to suspend services to three local destinations. The takeover marks a sharp escalation nearly four years after a peace deal ended a brutal two-year civil war in the East African country.
The carrier announced in a social media post on Wednesday that services to Mekelle, Shire, and Axum have been halted “due to the current situation in Tigray region,” without elaborating. “We sincerely apologize to our valued customers for any inconvenience caused by this suspension. We will inform you when flight operations resume,” the state-owned airline stated.
Two local sources told Reuters that Tigrayan forces have taken control of Mekelle airport from federal police in an overnight operation.
In a statement on Wednesday, Tigray’s regional government said its forces have entered a defensive war against federal troops. It accused the federal government of launching a ground offensive after air and artillery strikes across parts of Tigray on Tuesday.
The federal government has yet to publicly comment on the alleged takeover and the airstrikes.
The development came days after seven armed groups, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), the political party that runs Tigray, announced an alliance seeking to overthrow Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and establish a transitional administration. In a statement on Sunday, the coalition, known as the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, accused the ruling Prosperity Party of imposing “dictatorial” rule and pushing the East African country toward disintegration.
On Monday, Abiy’s spokesperson, Billene Seyoum, accused the alliance of collaborating with financial backing from neighboring Eritrea. The authorities in Eritrea have repeatedly denied backing the groups.
Ethiopia has struggled to secure lasting stability in Tigray since a 2022 peace agreement ended the two-year war between federal forces and the TPLF. The conflict killed hundreds of thousands of people. Recent clashes and reported drone strikes have threatened the fragile peace. World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus warned last month that Ethiopia was on the brink of renewed war.
The latest disruption to Ethiopian Airlines schedule follows an earlier suspension of flights to Tigray in January amid reports of renewed military activity. At the time, passengers received cancellation messages citing unplanned circumstances, while a security official linked the interruption to fighting between federal and regional forces.

====================================================================================================

Meta’s Muse AI Assistant Rolled Out With a Serious Security Flaw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:54:58 UTC
21:54:58 KST

Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg has gone to great lengths to hype the security of its new AI assistant, Muse, claiming it is “built from the ground up for privacy and security.” A zero-day vulnerability that gives locally run apps and terminal commands complete control of the agent raises serious doubts. Further raising questions, Amazon on Sunday began blocking Muse from its site.
Meta introduced Muse a few weeks ago. The assistant “books appointments, fills out forms, and handles customer service,” “proactively takes tasks off your plate,” and can “make purchases, generate images, create documents, and connect with your favorite apps and services.” The macOS app (curiously, there’s no Windows version) also works with a user’s WhatsApp, email, calendar, and social media accounts. When a task requires a tool that doesn’t exist, Muse creates one on the fly.
Meta Doth Hype Muse Security Too Much
Of course, for Muse to do any of these things, users must first give it access to their accounts. This includes authenticating the assistant to each service and, because the app runs on macOS, giving it permissions to a broad range of operating system-restricted device resources, like writing files to disk, accessing the mic and camera, and monitoring location and calendars. Apple has spent years developing these defenses to prevent installed apps or commands entered into the terminal from accessing these resources, clearly because the company considers them a security threat. Muse completely undoes these default measures.
The zero-day allowed any app or terminal command to gain access to the token that authenticates users to their Muse account. Meta developers designed the assistant so that any locally installed app or executed code, regardless of the macOS permissions it has, can change a long list of undocumented settings. Most of them are fairly innocuous, such as controlling dark mode. One setting, however, was anything but innocuous. It allowed processes to change the end point where transcription occurs. Normally, it’s a server address operated by Meta. Attackers could have exploited this flaw by changing the location to their own end point. If that happened, the attackers would have had the token that gives complete control over the Muse account.
“We can manipulate the agent and leverage its privileges to do whatever we want,” Patrick Wardle, the macOS security expert who discovered the zero-day, told Ars ahead of the hotfix. “So instead of us having to write a very comprehensive Mac malware stealer, we can just leverage the AI assistant itself.” Wardle said he has developed several proof-of-concept attacks that do things like writing malicious files to disk and snapping pictures, in many cases with no indication to even an alert user.
More than 12 hours after this post went live, Meta said it released a hotfix that patched the 0-day.
Meta has published two posts in as many weeks documenting the design decisions that went into ensuring an assistant with such extraordinary access to user data and resources is secure and private. The posts come amid revelations that internal testing of models from Anthropic and Google has resulted in security breaches of external, third-party networks that the engineers involved never intended to target. In traditional human-only hacking, these actions could likely result in the filing of criminal charges. The Meta posts are likely mindful of the resulting blowback and the calls to slow down AI development in response.
Wardle said that Meta developers made several design decisions that made his exploit possible. One is the choice for Muse dictation to occur in the cloud, where Meta can log it. macOS has long provided a simple means for apps to handle dictation and transcription in processes that stay securely on the device. Had the developers chosen this safer alternative, the attack wouldn’t have been possible.
Another flawed decision is for any app to control all of the undocumented settings. It’s likely Meta intended for apps working with Muse to control UI settings, and for understandable reasons. The ability for any app or command to control an end point where sensitive user speech is processed is an entirely different matter. Together, the design decisions raise questions about just how much effort developers put into designing and testing the security and privacy of the new assistant.
“To me, the bar is infinitely higher in terms of the security of these apps. They don’t have to be perfect, but when you take a look at Muse, it’s like they didn’t, in my opinion, think about security, which is really worrisome,” Wardle said. “At the very least, they should be thinking about security from the very start, and they are just not.”
Roughly 12 hours before Wardle disclosed the zero-day, Amazon started blocking people from using Muse to shop on the site. Users who tried received a message saying Muse was an “unauthorized AI agent [that] violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use.”
“We think it’s fairly straightforward that third-party applications that offer to make purchases on behalf of customers from other businesses should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate,” Amazon said in an emailed statement. “This helps ensure a safe, secure, and reliable customer experience, and it is how others operate including food delivery apps and the restaurants they take orders for, delivery services apps and the stores they shop from, and online travel agencies and the airlines they book tickets with for customers. Agentic third-party applications such as Muse have the same obligations, and we’ve requested that Meta remove Amazon from the experience.”
A Single ClickFix Is All It Takes
There are several ways for attacks to work. One is for an attacker’s server to act as a proxy that’s placed between the Muse user and Meta end point. Once the user enters the voice prompt, the attacker’s server adds a prompt invoking a malicious command, such as sending an archive of all WhatsApp messages to the attacker. Once that happens, the attacker gains permanent control over the Muse account because the token is automatically sent to the malicious server as well.
Wardle is the creator of the Objective-See Foundation, a nonprofit focused on macOS security. He is also the author of the The Art of Mac Malware book series and a former employee of NASA and the National Security Agency. Wardle said he plans to discuss the vulnerability in more detail and other AI assistant threats at the Objective by the Sea security conference in November.
One of the counterarguments raised by developers of apps that can be exploited once a device is compromised is that once that happens, all security bets are off. This standard doesn’t fit well in this case. Wardle found that a simple variation of ClickFix attack—a technique that has become remarkably effective in tricking people into infecting their devices—is all that’s required for an attacker to take control of a Muse account.
Wardle demonstrated using a simple terminal command to surreptitiously send a prompt to the Meta end point, which triggered a response. To prevent attackers from cutting and pasting the prompt in live attacks, Wardle’s prompt asks only how it’s possible it’s coming from an unprivileged attacker. Muse incorrectly responded that such an action isn’t possible.
Meta’s 12-hour-late statement conveniently ignored the ease ClickFix attacks provide in triggering exploits, a scenario I specifically asked the company to address. The Meta statement said the 0-day was “not a remote exploit” even though an increasingly effective social engineering scam has the same effect. Meta also makes no acknowledgement that the flaw dismantled a security architecture Apple has spent years building. Meta has yet to explain why it used cloud-based transcription rather than the on-device option built into macOS.
As already noted, the extraordinary access Muse requires to work as intended places an additional burden on its designers. Like most such AI agents—and contrary to Meta’s claims—Muse can’t be trusted. It’s not clear when or if it ever can.
This story originally appeared on Ars Technica.

The Board of Peace will unveil a six-month, $2.45 billion plan for Gaza’s post-war recovery during a meeting on Wednesday, Axios reported.
The 66-project proposal reflects a year of input from dozens of people representing the 28-member Board of Peace and the Palestinian technocratic government.
It includes projected funding for temporary housing, rubble removal, hospital repairs, economic recovery and the deployment of a multinational security force.
“The plan shows how to stand up a government from nothing, an economy from shambles and a territory from disaster,” a Board of Peace official said.
The Board of Peace was established in January as part of US President Donald Trump’s broader peace plan for Gaza, with Trump serving as its chairman.
The initiative, backed by UN Security Council Resolution 2803, is tasked with overseeing Gaza’s transition, including governance, security and reconstruction.
Since October 8 2023, Israel has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and wounded more than 174,000 others in its genocidal war on Gaza, while around 90 percent of the enclave’s infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed.

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:51:40 EEST
21:51:40 KST

Education Ombudsman Nadiia Leshchyk has called for no reduction in 2027 state budget spending on the construction of shelters at educational institutions.
"We are seeing a deterioration in the security situation due to frequent air raid alerts both in Kyiv and in Kyiv, Chernihiv, Zhytomyr and other regions. Children are forced to spend most of their school time in shelters, where it is often impossible to fully organize the educational process. As a result, educational institutions have to switch to remote or blended learning, which reduces the quality of education and affects children's psychological state and socialization," the ombudsman's statement said.
She said the 2027 state budget draft provides for only UAH 3.7 billion, compared with UAH 6 billion in 2026, including UAH 5 billion for general secondary education institutions and UAH 1 billion for preschool education institutions.
Leshchyk therefore called for shelter funding to be maintained at last year's level and, if possible, increased in 2027 compared with 2026.
She also called for consideration of extending such shelter subsidies beyond general secondary education institutions to vocational education institutions, as training for a skilled profession is difficult to provide remotely.
"Funding for shelters at preschool education institutions should also continue, as this ensures children's access to preschool education and enables parents to work, supporting our country's economy," the statement said.
In addition, she proposed that communities exchange experience on the procedures for obtaining and allocating subsidies among educational institutions and using the funds, including through training, so that communities ultimately take up the available shelter funding and build the facilities.
"Creating a safe educational environment and protecting the lives and health of participants in the educational process should be one of the priorities of state policy when implementing the right to education under martial law," the ombudsman said.
As reported, the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Education, Science and Innovation opposes reducing the subsidy for the construction of shelters at educational institutions from UAH 6 billion in 2026 to UAH 3.7 billion in 2027.

Kremlin accuses UK of trying to stoke anti-Russian sentiment in UN address
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:42:22 UTC
21:42:22 KST

Burç Eruygur
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
The Kremlin on Wednesday accused the UK of trying to stoke anti-Russian sentiment in Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s address to the UN General Assembly.
Responding to a question about Burnham's announcement of a new center to combat Russian “disinformation,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told a press briefing that the UK premier said nothing new in his UN speech and that London is “stoking Russophobic sentiment and maintaining an atmosphere of total Russophobia.”
“And now, the Germans, the French, and a number of other European states are likely doing the same, in lockstep with Britain,” Peskov said.
He described the approach as an “utterly shortsighted policy” from Moscow's perspective.
“It in no way brings us closer to steps that could eventually lead to a reduction of tensions and de-escalation on the European continent,” he added.
On Tuesday, Burnham told the General Assembly in New York that the UK would be “relentless” in building up its hard power and deterrence but would “not play Russia's game of trading escalatory rhetoric.”
“Unlike Russia, we do not seek confrontation. Instead, we will be prepared but not panicked,” Burnham said.
He accused “Russian agencies” of amplifying far-right narratives and said the UK has evidence that they tried to interfere with the country's 2019 general election.
“The Kremlin spends around £1.3 billion ($1.7 billion) each year on manipulating information,” Burnham said, adding that the UK would begin work on a new National Centre for Information Defence to “detect, attribute and disrupt these kinds of hostile state information attacks.”  
Ukraine, Syria
Peskov also said Ukrainian strikes on Russia continue and that there are no indications yet of a shift toward peace negotiations to end the ongoing war.
“As the Russian side, we remain open to peace negotiations,” Peskov said, noting that Moscow’s stance on an in-person meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not changed.
“The leader of the Kiev regime can come to Moscow if he wishes to contact us, and all security guarantees will be offered to him,” he said.
Peskov also argued that an international summit on a Ukrainian settlement would be “inappropriate” and a “waste of time” until “work is completed at the expert level.”
Turning to the fate of Russian military bases in Syria, Peskov said Moscow remains in contact with Damascus.
“We are satisfied with how the discussions are proceeding. And we look forward to continuing to reach an understanding with our Syrian counterparts on the most complex issues,” he added.
Russia maintains two key military facilities in Syria: a naval logistics base in Tartus and the Hmeimim air base in the northwestern province of Latakia.
Last month, Damascus and Moscow announced a memorandum of understanding to reorganize Russia's presence at the Hmeimim and Tartus bases following about 18 months of negotiations.
The Syrian Foreign Ministry said on Aug. 9 that under the memorandum, Syria would assume control of civilian facilities, while Russian military facilities would be redefined as joint training and rehabilitation centers under new arrangements.
The memorandum gave the two sides up to three months to complete the transition.

MV-8 Komodo Heavy UGV Equipped with Cobra Bridge-Laying System
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:40:48 UTC
21:40:48 KST

The Croatian-German company Rheinmetall Unmanned Vehicles (formerly DOK-ING) is testing the MV-8 Komodo heavy tracked UGV in a bridge-laying configuration.
Local publication Hrvatski Vojnik reported on this, citing company representatives.
The drone is equipped with the Cobra MLC 90 bridge-laying system from the European division of the American company General Dynamics European Land Systems.
The installed system weighs approximately 5.3 metric tons. It can withstand the passage of tracked vehicles weighing up to 81.7 metric tons or wheeled vehicles weighing up to 93.9 metric tons. When deployed, the bridge is 15 meters long and 3.75 meters wide.
This length allows it to cross not only anti-tank trenches but also natural obstacles, including rivers, swamps, and heavily rugged terrain.
Rheinmetall UV has named the system the Unmanned Gap Crossing System (UGCS). When folded, the Cobra MLC 90 approximately doubles the height of the vehicle’s base silhouette at its highest point, and its overall length also roughly doubles. Meanwhile, the Komodo’s width increases by approximately 60 centimeters.
At the same time, the company’s engineers claim the increased dimensions do not affect the vehicle’s stated maximum speed, mobility, range, or other key tactical and technical characteristics.
The Komodo has become a platform for various weapon systems. Reports indicate that the Skorpion 2 remote-controlled mining system and the MANGART anti-drone system with a 25-mm cannon have been integrated onto it.
The MVC8 Komodo is a heavy tracked robotic system designed to perform tasks in conditions that are hazardous to humans.
The vehicle has a hybrid power plant that allows it to operate, in particular, in areas with low oxygen levels and high temperatures.
It can be equipped with a variety of sensors and detectors, including devices for detecting chemical and radiological substances, temperature, oxygen, and explosive gases, as well as a lidar and a weather station.
The Komodo has a modular design and can be equipped with various interchangeable equipment, including combat gear.
In its base configuration, the vehicle weighs approximately 17 metric tons. It is 7.2 meters long, 2.3 meters wide, 2.9 meters tall, and has 34 centimeters of ground clearance. Its maximum speed is limited to 30 km/h.
The Komodo is controlled remotely. The claimed range of the communication system under line-of-sight conditions is up to 1.5 km.

Current El Nino could cause 451,000 heat-related deaths, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:39:48 UTC
21:39:48 KST

Gizem Nisa Demir
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
This year's El Nino could cause an estimated 451,000 additional deaths from extreme heat worldwide in the first half of the climate pattern, according to a University of Chicago report released Wednesday.
The mortality projections cover the period from June 2026, when the current El Nino began, through February 2027.
The Climate Impact Lab estimates the number of extremely hot days could rise by 44% compared with normal years, with the heaviest toll expected in countries with fewer resources to adapt.
The Sahel region is projected to record 66,800 additional heat deaths from September through February. Southeast Asia could see nearly 39,000 additional deaths, while India and Brazil are projected to record 15,800 and 13,300, respectively.
“This is such a large number that it can be numbing, but it is made up of parents and children, grandparents and neighbors, people going to work, caring for families, and living their lives,” says Michael Greenstone, a co-founder of the Climate Impact Lab
Researchers said tens of thousands of deaths could be prevented through targeted emergency response and resilience measures, including early-warning systems, cooling centers and protections for outdoor workers.
They said reducing deaths from extreme temperatures should be central to preparations for El Nino, alongside efforts to address food security risks.
The report described the current El Nino as a “postcard from our future,” saying it is bringing temperatures similar to what could become normal in about 20 years without greater adaptation.
“Increasing emergency response and better targeting our efforts can save many lives this year. But 20 years from now, once today's extreme temperatures become the new normal, we don't want to be in a constant state of emergency,” said Tamma Carleton, the Climate Impact Lab's faculty head of research, urging preparation and resources to prepare for the future.
Researchers said they will update the death projections as El Nino develops.
The World Meteorological Organization has also warned that the current El Nino could become the strongest on record.

Tallinn, Riga and Vilnius expect a positive response from von der Leyen in a matter of weeks, with the money arriving by the end of the year, according to the sources.

NEW DELHI: India on Wednesday hit back at the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) over references to Jammu and Kashmir in a joint communique of its Contact Group, calling them “unwarranted and factually incorrect” and asserting that the grouping has no locus standi to comment on matters that are strictly internal to India.The ministry of external affairs said the entire Union territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh are an “integral and inalienable part of India”, adding that “no amount of repetition of politically motivated propaganda can change this reality”.The response came after Pakistan’s foreign ministry said on X that deputy prime minister and foreign minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar had addressed a ministerial meeting of the OIC Contact Group on Jammu and Kashmir on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York.According to Pakistan, Dar urged OIC member states to maintain a “unified position” on Jammu and Kashmir at the United Nations and other international fora. He also reiterated Pakistan’s commitment to a “just and peaceful settlement of the dispute in accordance with the relevant UN Security Council resolutions and the wishes of the Kashmiri people”.The references to Jammu and Kashmir drew a strong response from New Delhi.
“India categorically rejects the unwarranted and factually incorrect references to India in the Joint Communique of the so-called OIC Contact Group on Jammu & Kashmir. The OIC has no locus standi to pronounce on matters that are strictly internal to India,” the MEA said in a statement.
MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal shared the statement on X, reiterating India’s position on the OIC communique.The ministry also questioned the credibility of the grouping over its repeated backing of what it described as politically motivated narratives.“Repeated endorsement of such motivated narratives only raises serious questions on the credibility of OIC,” the MEA said.India further turned its focus on Pakistan, saying the OIC should address terrorism emanating from Pakistani territory instead of providing Islamabad a platform for what New Delhi called “fabricated and motivated propaganda”.
“Instead of offering a platform to Pakistan to peddle its fabricated and motivated propaganda, OIC will be better advised to counsel Pakistan, which has a well-documented record of supporting and sponsoring terrorism, to look inwards and address the continuing threat of terrorism emanating from territories under its control,” the MEA said.

“Shouldn't a school always be a safe place?”: Minab student asks US schoolchildren

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23

“Shouldn't a school always be a safe place?”: Minab student asks US schoolchildren
TEHRAN – A student from Minab has addressed American students, calling for schools to remain safe spaces for children and remembering classmates who were killed when Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School was struck in a US military attack.
The student read a message in English to US schoolchildren on Wednesday at a ceremony marking the start of the new school year at the site of Shajareh Tayyebeh School in Minab County.
“We don't know your names, and you don't know ours. But as you begin another school year, we wanted to write to you, student to student, before anything else gets in the way.
All of us know the feeling of the first day of school: a new notebook, the smell of unused pages, seeing friends again. We imagine your first days feel much the same — a little nervous, a little excited. These are small things. But they are what make a childhood feel safe.
On February 28, one of our schools did not get to have that ordinary day. Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in Minab was full of children just like you, sitting at their desks, when it was struck in a military attack. More than 120 children never went home. In total, across the recent wars our country has endured, 277 students never got to finish their education. Their notebooks are still on their desks in some homes,” the message reads.
Addressing students in the United States, the message drew parallels between the experiences of children starting a new school year, from opening new notebooks to reuniting with friends, saying that such ordinary moments are what make childhood feel safe.
It recalled February 28, when Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School was struck while children were in their classrooms. More than 120 children were killed in the attack, while 277 students in total lost their lives during the recent wars involving the country and never had the opportunity to complete their education.
The student emphasized that the message was not intended to make American students feel guilty, but to help them understand what happened to children their own age. The letter posed a simple question: “Shouldn't a school always be a safe place?”
“We are not writing to make you feel guilty. You did not choose this, just as we did not. We are writing because we believe you deserve to know what happened to children your own age, in a place you may have only heard about on the news — if at all.
We have one simple question: shouldn't a school always be a safe place? In every country, a classroom is supposed to be one of the safest places in the world for a child. That is not political. It is something all of us, as students, should agree on without argument: children in war must never be targets. Striking a school is not a strategy — it is a crime. The United Nations itself has said there are reasonable grounds to believe war crimes were committed in the attacks on our schools.
We ask you to sit with that question for a moment — not to feel sad for us, but to ask whether it could ever be justified. We believe the answer is no.”
The message also referred to United Nations findings that there were reasonable grounds to believe war crimes had been committed in attacks on schools in the country.
The message further urged American students to learn about Iran beyond news headlines, pointing to the country's ancient civilization, literature, history and cultural heritage. It mentioned figures such as Hafez and Rumi and sites such as Persepolis, while emphasizing that Iranian children, like their peers elsewhere, share hopes for education and a better future.
The letter concluded by noting that school bells were ringing again in Minab as students returned to rebuilt classrooms and took seats that some of their classmates should have occupied.
Despite the pain of returning to school without their friends, the students said they had chosen to continue their education, expressing hope for a future in which no school anywhere becomes a target.
“We also want to ask something else, gently: get to know us — not through headlines, but through history. Iran is one of the oldest civilizations on Earth, home to poets like Hafez and Rumi, to ancient cities that were centers of learning, to a culture of hospitality and family that has endured for thousands of years. We are not only a headline about war. If you ever get the chance to study a country beyond your own, we hope you'll learn about ours — not the Iran distorted by American media and politicians, but the Iran of Persepolis and poetry, of children who, just like you, love their school and their future.
Today, our school bells are ringing again. We are returning to rebuilt classrooms, to seats some of our classmates should have filled. It isn't easy. But we choose to return, because that is what our friends would have wanted for us.
Wherever you are, whenever your bell rings this year, we hope you'll think — just for a moment — of children far away who deserved, as much as you do, the safety to simply be students.
 
 With hope for a world where no school is ever a target again,” the message concluded.

Dramatic eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:31:31 BST
21:31:31 KST

Dramatic eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage
- Published
The dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman from the home in Madrid where she lived for seven decades has drawn attention to the depth of Spain's housing crisis.
The tenant of the flat in the Retiro area of central Madrid, Maricarmen, was unable to pay the rent set by the investment firm that owns it.
Maricarmen's father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent.
However, the company that bought the property in 2018, Urbagestión, cited a legal glitch allowing it to raise her rent from €500 (£428; $572) to €2,650.
It subsequently lowered the new rent to €1,650 but Maricarmen was still unable to pay it with her monthly pension of €1,350.
Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts and the case has received increasing media attention.
Supporters of Maricarmen camped outside the building on Tuesday night, joined by celebrities including Javier Bardem's brother, Carlos, and the singer Ana Belén, who read out the poem Desahucio (Eviction) by Rafael Alberti.
Several hundred people, mostly youngsters, had gathered by the morning in a bid to prevent the eviction from taking place, chanting "Maricarmen stays". Some activists blocked the stairs inside the building.
In a video posted on social media, a tearful Maricarmen thanked those who had come out to support her against "this cruel struggle by someone who wants to earn money".
- The hard men removing squatters in Spain 
  - Published26 August 2021
- Taking back Barcelona's apartments 
  - Published12 December 2015
- 'Sometimes I want to cry': Eviction in a pandemic 
  - Published14 December 2020
Police cordoned off a section of the street and removed people from the entrance to the building, including members of the media, striking some protesters with batons.
A representative of tenants' organisation Sindicato de Inquilinas shouted at the police through a megaphone: "Think for 10 seconds about Maricarmen, who could be your own grandmother."
"There is a police deployment as if this were a military operation," said Beatriz Duro, Maricarmen's lawyer. "This is the fourth time [they've tried to evict her] but the first time they've come right to the door of the property. It's completely disproportionate."
In June, the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights called for the pensioner's eviction to be halted and for her to be offered affordable alternative accommodation. The local government said she had declined its offer of a place in an elderly care home.
The central government said Urbagestión had refused its repeated attempts to negotiate Maricarmen's situation. The BBC has attempted to contact the company.
The possibility of a last-minute reprieve for Maricarmen appeared when an anonymous donor offered to pay most of her rent. However, Urbagestión reportedly rejected the offer and the eviction went ahead.
"Today is a very sad day, a very dramatic day, when it's plain to see the effects of unbridled speculation, of not wanting to control the market, of putting out the red carpet for the vultures and the speculators," said Housing Minister Teresa Rodríguez.
A shortage of available housing has been blamed for soaring rental costs in recent years, which have left millions of Spaniards struggling to find affordable homes.
In Madrid, rentals have increased by more than 100% over the last decade, according to property site Idealista, with a 10% rise over the last year.
The Socialist-led government of Pedro Sánchez has frequently targeted companies whose investment pushes up housing costs. In January, the prime minister said he aimed to "protect those who are most exposed to that speculation and that greed".
However, some critics of the government say it needs to work harder to build new homes, and others warn that its rhetoric discourages many owners from placing their properties on the rental market.

Foreign-language population in Uusimaa projected to double by 2045
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:31:28 EEST
21:31:28 KST

The number of foreign-language speakers living in Finland’s Uusimaa region is projected to reach about 674,000 by 2045, close to twice the current level, according to a new regional population projection. Helsinki, Espoo and Vantaa are expected to account for most of the increase over the next two decades.
At the end of 2024, Uusimaa had about 339,500 residents whose registered language was neither Finnish, Swedish nor Sámi.
They represented around 19 per cent of the region’s population and 56 per cent of all foreign-language speakers in Finland.
The share in Uusimaa is projected to reach about 25 per cent by 2035.
Population experts from Helsinki, Espoo and Vantaa prepared the 2025–2045 projection with the Helsinki-Uusimaa Regional Council. Their estimates point to annual growth of about 15,000 foreign-language speakers between 2025 and 2029, followed by annual increases of about 16,000.
The Helsinki metropolitan area will account for most of that growth. About 86 per cent of Uusimaa’s foreign-language-speaking residents already lived in its largest cities in 2024.
Helsinki is projected to have about 191,000 foreign-language speakers in 2035, rising to 238,000 in 2045. Espoo is expected to reach 131,000 in 2035 and 181,000 in 2045. Vantaa’s corresponding figures stand at 116,000 and 158,000.
Espoo and Vantaa are projected to record faster growth than Helsinki. In 2020, Helsinki still had more foreign-language speakers than Espoo and Vantaa combined. By 2035, the combined total in Espoo and Vantaa is projected to exceed Helsinki’s figure by close to one third.
Growth is expected across every age group. The number of working-age foreign-language speakers is projected to almost double by 2045, while the number of pension-age residents in the group is projected to rise almost fivefold.
Despite that change, foreign-language speakers are expected to retain a younger age profile than Uusimaa’s population overall. People aged 65 and over are projected to make up just over 10 per cent of foreign-language speakers in 2045. Statistics Finland’s population projection puts the corresponding share for Uusimaa’s total population at more than twice that level.
Languages originating in Asia outside the Middle East, the Middle East and North Africa, along with Russian and other languages of the former Soviet Union, are projected to form the largest groups across Uusimaa in 2045.
The projection identifies migration levels as its main source of uncertainty. Changes in immigration policy, security conditions, labour demand and economic developments in Finland and abroad would alter the population path.
The study covers Helsinki, Espoo, Vantaa, Kauniainen, municipalities surrounding the Helsinki region and the rest of Uusimaa. Researchers based the figures on assumptions concerning migration, births and deaths and divided the population into eight language groups.

Chocolate industry past worst of cocoa crisis, say Swiss experts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:30:36 UTC
21:30:36 KST

Chocolate industry past worst of cocoa crisis, say Swiss experts
After two difficult years, there are growing signs of a recovery in the chocolate industry, say experts. Cocoa prices have fallen significantly from their record highs and there are signs of increased demand.
Analysts at the Swiss bank Vontobel say the sector is close to a possible turning point. “We believe that the low point in sales volumes is now behind us,” they wrote in a report on the Swiss chocolate industry published on Wednesday. But they add that the recovery is still at an early stage.
The latest data nonetheless suggests that the long-awaited improvement in demand for chocolate may be on the horizon.
The crisis was triggered by a historic surge in the price of cocoa. In 2024, the price of cocoa rose at times to more than £10,000 (CHF10,900) per tonne. Poor harvests in West Africa, plant diseases and ageing trees led to supply shortages. Speculation on the commodities markets further exacerbated the situation.
Prices up to 50% higher
Manufacturers such as Lindt & Sprüngli responded with massive price hikes. According to Vontobel, leading suppliers have raised the prices of their products by a cumulative 25-50% since 2024. This increasingly took its toll on demand, with consumers turning more frequently to cheaper own-brand products.
Figures from Chocosuisse illustrate just how hard the shock has hit the Swiss industry. In 2025, the volume of Swiss chocolate sold fell by 7.9%, and exports by as much as 9.3%. At the same time, turnover rose by 11.8% due to the higher prices. Per capita chocolate consumption also fell by 2.7%.
More
Villars CEO: ‘The key is to boost our visibility while keeping costs under control’
Signs of a recovery are now emerging. Although the price of cocoa, roughly £4,500, is still roughly twice the historical average, it is 60% below its peak. At the same time, global cocoa grindings rose in the second quarter of 2026 for the first time after six consecutive declines. This is regarded as an important leading indicator of demand for chocolate.
Barry is growing again
Swiss chocolate maker Barry Callebaut also recently given signs of recovery. In the third quarter of the 2025/26 financial year, its sales volume rose by 5.7% – the first growth in volume in two years.
Luxury chocolate manufacturer Lindt & Sprüngli is also hopeful of a return to growth in 2027. In the first half of 2026, organic revenue grew by 4.3%, though this increase was still driven primarily by price rises of 11.8%. Sales volumes consequently remained under pressure.
More
With West Africa cocoa under strain, can Brazil supply more to Switzerland?
El Niño remains a risk
But Vontobel experts say the crisis is not over yet. The El Niño weather phenomenon, which is expected to be particularly strong this year and next, could significantly impact the cocoa harvest in West Africa. It may bring higher temperatures and less rain to the region, thereby increasing the risk of droughts.
Ivory Coast, Ghana, Nigeria and Cameroon together account for around three-quarters of global cocoa production. Unlike with other agricultural commodities, shortfalls there can hardly be offset by other regions. Consequently, harvest problems can have a significant impact on prices. Vontobel therefore expects volatility to remain high.
More
Lindt pulls plug on Dubai chocolate store over Iran war concern
Barry Callebaut recently said a repeat of the cocoa crisis of 2023 and 2024 is unlikely, despite El Niño. In July, Chief Financial Officer Peter Vanneste pointed to higher cocoa stocks and noted that the market was entering the new harvest season with a surplus, rather than following several years of shortages as had been the case previously.

Al-Qudwa, Hamas, Islamic Jihad and Dahlan join together for Palestinian elections
Multiple sources told The New Arab that a political alliance to contest the Palestinian legislative elections has been formed in Cairo, bringing together the Palestinian Democratic National Gathering, the Reformist Current of the Fatah movement, Hamas and Islamic Jihad. It is expected to be officially announced within two days.
Nasser al-Qudwa, head of the Palestinian Democratic National Gathering, told TNA that currently underway in Cairo is a push for the formation of a non-factional national list to participate in the Palestinian Legislative Council elections scheduled for November.
"Bilateral and multilateral meetings and contacts have taken place over the past two days between the Palestinian Democratic National Gathering, the Reformist Current in the Fatah movement, Hamas and Islamic Jihad. An agreement was reached to form a non-factional national list that includes a broad spectrum of Palestinian national figures and anyone who wishes to be part of this expanded national list," Al-Qudwa added.
He further said efforts will continue in the coming days to draft the political statement and determine the names of participants for the electoral list.
The meetings were attended by Nasser al-Qudwa, head of the National Current; Mohammed Dahlan; Hamas Political Bureau members Hussam Badran and Zahar Jabarin; and Islamic Jihad Secretary-General Ziad al-Nakhalah.
These political groups, along with the Democratic Front and Popular Front, took part in a meeting in Cairo on 20 August, where they discussed the idea of an expanded, non-factional national list to contest the legislative elections.
Reportedly, the Popular Front requested more time at the time to consider the matter and present it to its organisational bodies. It later announced a political initiative, the main feature of which was the establishment of a transitional national council.
However, the initiative received no response from President Mahmoud Abbas and the Fatah movement.

Asked whether Barghouti's rejection would lead to the alliance not being formed, the source said, "We know that Barghouti does not want to head a list in the Legislative Council elections because he has decided to run in the presidential elections, and we are waiting to hear what he will say over the next two days."
The source stressed that "the alliance will continue".
It appears that the Popular Front has not only been absent from this alliance but has also yet to decide whether to participate in the Legislative Council elections.
Informed sources also told TNA that contacts between the Popular Front and the "Alliance for Change and National Liberation" list have ceased, indicating that the Popular Front will not be part of this electoral alliance.
The Alliance for Change and National Liberation brings together a group of national and independent elites and figures and grassroots groups, the National Initiative Movement, and the "Palestinian Popular Conference 14 Million".
The Central Elections Commission set the nomination period from the morning of Saturday, 26 September, until the evening of Wednesday, 7 October, and outlined several conditions; these include that nominations must be submitted only through electoral lists, with individual nominations not accepted; and an electoral list must be formed by a party, a coalition of parties or a group of voters for the purpose of participating in elections for membership of the Legislative Council.
The commission also stipulated that the list of candidates must be closed in terms of the order of names, with the seats won by each list distributed among its candidates according to the order of their names on the list, with the first candidate followed by the next, and so on.
The electoral list's nomination application must be submitted through the list coordinator and authorised representative, who represents it in all matters before the commission, including submitting all applications and documents on its behalf to the commission.

A discrepancy of UAH 73.5 million: how much did the NHSU actually pay the Odrex clinic?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:30:16 EEST
21:30:16 KST

A discrepancy of UAH 73.5 million: how much did the NHSU actually pay the Odrex clinic?
Kyiv • UNN
The NHSU reported that the Odrex clinic received more than UAH 37.5 million in 2025 under the Medical Guarantees Program. At the same time, according to other data, the clinic received UAH 111 million—almost three times as much.
In April, the National Health Service of Ukraine (NHSU) told UNN that in 2025 it had paid the Odrex clinic slightly more than UAH 37.5 million under the Medical Guarantees Programme. Several months later, an entirely different figure appeared in the Forbes ranking — UAH 111 million, which, according to the publication, was provided by the company itself. The difference between the figures is about UAH 73.5 million, UNN writes.
Details
Thus, the National Health Service of Ukraine and the private Odesa clinic Odrex effectively named two different amounts that the medical facility allegedly received for the same period. This raises a simple question: how much budgetary funding did Odrex actually receive in 2025 — UAH 37.5 million or UAH 111 million?
In response to a journalist’s inquiry, the NHSU not only named the total amount but also detailed which specific medical services Odrex received funding for in 2025.
The clinic received the largest payment for primary healthcare — about UAH 15.4 million. Odrex received another UAH 11.38 million for treating acute stroke, and more than UAH 5.2 million for inpatient rehabilitation. The NHSU transferred about UAH 2.35 million to the clinic for treating acute myocardial infarction, more than UAH 1.56 million for palliative care, and more than UAH 1.52 million for outpatient rehabilitation.
That is, a significant portion of the payments went toward assisting patients with acute and severe conditions: strokes and heart attacks, as well as subsequent rehabilitation.
Against this background, the figure of UAH 111 million cited in the Forbes ranking requires a separate explanation. According to the publication itself, this figure was provided directly by the Odrex clinic.
Thus, the difference between the NHSU’s official response and the data that Odrex itself provided to Forbes amounts to about UAH 73.5 million. This is no longer an error or rounding discrepancy, but an almost threefold difference in the figures for the same year.
To recall
The company "House of Medicine," which operates under the Odrex brand, reduced its revenue by 24% in 2025, to UAH 839 million, while its profit fell by 44%, to UAH 73 million. This occurred despite overall growth in the private healthcare market, where most major players were instead increasing their turnover.
The high-profile scandals surrounding the clinic may have been the cause of the "financial hole." According to the Prosecutor General’s Office, Odrex appears in 10 criminal proceedings, while former patients and the families of deceased patients publicly describe negative treatment experiences that those affected themselves call "draining money." In addition, people dissatisfied with treatment at the clinic created the StopOdrex public movement, which collects and publishes reviews of the medical facility.

GENEVA, September 23. /TASS/. With the connivance of Western countries, Ukraine has become one of the largest hubs for the global black market in weapons, said head of the Russian delegation at the Vienna talks on military security and arms control Yulia Zhdanova.
"Obviously, because the West and Kiev ignored the basic principles of the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) on conventional weapons transfer in order to achieve their political and defense industry goals, Ukraine in fact became one of the major hubs of the international black market in weapons," she said. "This is a threat not only to the OSCE member states, but also to countries on other continents."
"However, the West is not even thinking about how to prevent a destabilizing accumulation of conventional weapons in Ukraine. On the contrary, it is facilitating it," she told the plenary meeting of the Forum for Security Cooperation at the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
The diplomat went on to say that illegal trade in Western weapons and military equipment in Ukraine has become widespread and is now largely controlled by Ukrainian and international organized crime groups, operating under the protection of state officials, Ukrainian military commanders and intelligence services.
In Zhdanova’s words, the illegal trade is being supplied primarily with weapons delivered to the Kiev regime by OSCE members from the West.
"In the context of today’s discussion, it is extremely important to note that these supplies are being carried out in violation of the OSCE Principles Governing Conventional Arms Transfers (1993) and the OSCE Document on Small Arms and Light Weapons (2000)," the Russian diplomat added.

Lithuanian minister decides to close visa centres in Central Asia over ‘terrorism risks’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:30:00 UTC
21:30:00 KST

Lithuania will close external service centres in several Muslim countries in Central Asia and Europe, citing potential national security and terrorism risks, Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said Wednesday.
“I have made the decision to close the branches of the external service provider in Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan and Bosnia and Herzegovina,” Katelynas said in a Facebook post.
The centres process applications for residence permits and initiate migration procedures for foreigners seeking to come to Lithuania. Katelynas said an assessment of security risks and the threat of terrorism found no justification for continuing their operations.
“When the State Security Department warns of potential terrorism risks and has already identified individuals from Central Asia with radical views or links to terrorism, the state cannot wait for a risk to become an incident,” Katelynas said.
He said Lithuania did not plan to open new external service centres in other countries following the closures.
The decision comes as Lithuania has tightened controls on labour migration from Central Asia. Migration Department Director Indrė Gasperė said Tuesday that the number of workers arriving from the region had increased in recent years, but applications from Central Asian citizens seeking to enter Lithuania for employment are currently no longer being accepted. The department said the external service centres had been suspended after receiving very large numbers of employment-related applications.
Lithuania’s 2026 quota for foreign workers is 24,706. Once the quota is exhausted, temporary residence permits for employment can generally be issued only when additional statutory conditions are met, including higher salary thresholds or employment in certain high-value, shortage occupations.
The closures will also affect Bosnia and Herzegovina, where Lithuania opened an external service provider centre in October 2025 as part of a broader restructuring of the countries in which foreigners could apply for Lithuanian residence permits and national visas.
As of September 1, nearly 227,000 foreign nationals held valid residence permits in Lithuania, according to Migration Department data. Ukrainians accounted for about 80,000, followed by nearly 48,000 Belarusians and about 13,000 Russian citizens. Uzbekistan had about 12,600 citizens with valid permits, while India and Tajikistan accounted for about 9,400 and 7,500, respectively.
The number of Central Asian nationals living in Lithuania has grown significantly in recent years. Official data show that the number of Uzbek citizens holding valid residence permits rose from about 10,500 at the beginning of 2026 to more than 12,600 by September 1, while the number of Tajik citizens increased to about 7,500.
