Can Baghdad ever bring Iraq's militias under state control?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:55:03 UTC
20:55:03 KST

Breadcrumb
Can Baghdad ever bring Iraq's militias under state control?
A relative pause in fighting between the United States and Iran that ended in early September has brought the region back into a state of geopolitical tension.
As the exchange of strikes, retaliations, and signalling between Washington and Tehran continues, there is a heightened expectation from Washington that the US pullout from Iraq should coincide with Iranian-backed militias in the country being disarmed.
A looming US withdrawal
At a meeting at the White House in July, Iraq’s new prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi, met with President Donald Trump and indicated that Baghdad would work to disarm the pro-Iranian Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF).
“The fact that both Trump and Zaidi are following through means this is a bipartisan vision in the United States and a continued commitment from Zaidi, who took over the premiership from Sudani as the Coordination Framework’s candidate,” Hamzeh Hadad, an Adjunct Fellow with the Center for New American Security, told The New Arab.
The withdrawal of US forces now places a greater burden on the government in Baghdad to determine the future of the PMF.
“The US pullout removes a key lever for Baghdad and forces tougher bargaining at home,” Dr Inna Rudolf, Senior Research Fellow in the War Studies Department at King’s College London, told The New Arab.
“Coalition forces had been both an excuse some factions used for pursuing greater autonomy but also a tool Washington could use to push for change.”
The US continues to pressure Baghdad for the disarmament of the PMF through diplomatic channels, but the threat of further sanctions and tariffs has been floated by the Trump administration.
On 21 September, Zaidi requested more time beyond the 30 September deadline agreed with the United States, and the next day it was announced that it would be pushed back to 30 June 2027.
Baghdad will now have nine months to continue negotiations with the factions while avoiding potential US financial or economic sanctions.
“The Iraqi government needs to have a more honest dialogue with Washington about its situation and vision,” Haddad told The New Arab.
“But this needs to take place without wishful statements from the Iraqi side that they backtrack on, as they already have to deal with strong foreign pressure on the issue.”
The plan to dismantle and reorganise the PMF fighters into existing brigades and retire older commanders who have served since 2014 will reportedly start implementation in January 2027.
The government also intends to establish a new directorate to monitor the integration.
Zaidi's disarmament push
Iraq’s new prime minister has sought to strengthen Baghdad’s image as a government that can rein in corruption, ensure security, and pursue economic development with the international community.
“Zaidi, entering politics, a new face, with no prior experience in public office, wanted to build on the US backing that saw him come to power, and so he boldly stated that he would enforce a deadline for armed groups outside of the state apparatus to disarm,” said Hadad.
The Iraqi government is currently waging a campaign to curtail the PMF’s power in the country. In mid-August, Iraqi security forces detained a senior commander from the Nujaba Movement, one of the primary Iranian-backed militias that make up the PMF coalition.
“There is a different understanding between what constitutes armed groups outside of the state apparatus in Iraq than in Washington,” Hadad noted.
Hiba Abdulwahhab, an Iraqi researcher and analyst, told The New Arab, “The relationship between the Iraqi government and these factions resembles a Catholic marriage, a union with no easy divorce. They are deeply intertwined politically, institutionally, and economically”.
An uncertain security situation
The US military will also be removing the air defence systems, including Patriot and C-RAM systems, from the Kurdistan Region. The depletion of US air defence system interceptors during the conflict with Iran has contributed to the declining security situation.
In March 2026, Kataib Hezbollah, one of the key factions of the PMF, released a two-minute video that went viral showing an FPV drone flying over the Camp Victory complex near Baghdad International Airport, a site that continued to host US and NATO-linked facilities.
A drone attack that Saudi officials reported originated from Iraq struck the East-West pipeline in Saudi Arabia on 11 September. Baghdad later confirmed the pipeline attack came from Iraqi territory and dismissed security officials responsible for Maysan Province near the Iranian border and closed the area’s border crossing.
Still, some PMF groups have sought out a political advantage by appearing to adhere to the government’s calls. One militia, Asaib Ahl al-Haq, announced over the summer that it formally withdrew from the PMF coalition and handed over its weapons to the government.
Other groups, such as the Sayyid al-Shuhada Brigades and the Nujaba Movement, have stated they will not turn over their weapons, saying that certain conditions had to be met before they did so.
“[Zaidi’s] reasoning is that there will be no more American forces present in Iraq and therefore no more excuse for armed groups to exist after that,” Hadad told The New Arab.
Dr Rudolf agrees. “Losing that pretext gives negotiators cleaner rhetorical space to press for stricter control as it strips the factions of their usual talking point that foreign troops justify armed resistance outside the formal chain of command.”
Finding a path to disarmament
Iraqi leaders have advocated for the PMF to function as a state security institution and slowly reduce their political nature.
In May, the militia of prominent Shia cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, Saraya al-Salam, announced it would begin disarmament and integrate into the state. While this group is not technically part of the PMF and Shia Coordination Framework, it could be interpreted as a sign of the direction the wind is blowing in Iraq.
However, it is likely that the groups will utilise this approach to reposition themselves without totally surrendering their arms.
“The most likely outcome is therefore adaptation and repositioning rather than genuine disarmament,” Abdulwahhab told The New Arab.
“Weapons could remain in faction-controlled depots, be transferred to affiliated units, or be placed nominally within the PMF’s official structure without being brought under effective government command.”
Observers of Iraq are right to be sceptical that the PMF will do little else other than rebrand and retain their loyalty to informal chains of command and external ties with Tehran.
Regarding the extension of the disarmament deadline, Abdulwahhab said, “The progression raises serious doubts about the government’s ability to act against factions deeply embedded in Iraq’s political and security institutions”.
She added, “The extension is more likely to give Iran-aligned factions time to reorganise and protect their networks than to give the government the power to disarm and dismantle them,” further noting that Baghdad had to take concrete steps now, otherwise June 2027 may bring another postponement rather than a resolution.
Some positive steps have been taken, but it is still early in the process to understand how far Baghdad can go.
“Without tangible incentives and accountability mechanisms, ‘integration’ will feel like administrative rebranding,” Rudolf said. “The public will see it as window dressing.”
The long-term outlook will depend on the future of the financial and military support from Iran as well as Baghdad’s own ability to assert control over the militias.
For now, the government in Baghdad will have to navigate the post-US withdrawal environment on its own.
Christopher Solomon is a Middle East analyst, researcher, editor, and writer based in the Washington, DC area. He is the author of the book In Search of Greater Syria (Bloomsbury)

However, the secondary legislation needed to bring the measures into force could take six to nine months to pass through Parliament.

Financing, insurance and guarantees are required before construction can begin.
The project has been delayed for years because of concerns over its impact on prospects for a two-state solution, which is backed by many Western and Gulf states.
Israel has occupied the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since 1967. The international community considers Israeli settlements built on occupied land illegal under international law, a position rejected by Tel Aviv.
Around 750,000 Israeli occupiers live in 156 illegal settlements and 360 settlement outposts across the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem.
Palestinians have faced repeated attacks by occupiers aimed at forcing them from their land.

WHO pledges to support health ministry to turn global patient safety commitments into action
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:53:46 UTC
20:53:46 KST

WHO pledges to support health ministry to turn global patient safety commitments into action
TEHRAN – Commemorating World Patient Safety Day 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) Country Office in Iran reaffirmed its commitment to turn global patient safety commitments into practical action across hospitals, primary health care and communities as the Ministry of Health and Medical Education advances its patient safety agenda.
Hosted by the Health Ministry, the hybrid event brought together senior officials, including Deputy Ministers and Vice-Chancellors for Curative Affairs and Public Health from universities of medical sciences, as well as hospital and primary health care managers, university focal points, and WHO colleagues. Participants reaffirmed the importance of patient safety as a core component of quality health services and resilient health systems, the WHO website announced in a press release on September 21.
WHO provided technical and advocacy support for the commemoration, sharing the global messages and priorities of World Patient Safety Day and highlighting the need to integrate patient safety across all levels and settings of care. In his remarks, Dr Jean Jabbour, WHO Representative and Head of Mission in the Islamic Republic of Iran, reaffirmed WHO’s commitment to making safety an integral part of every health care interaction. He underscored that safer care contributes to improved health outcomes, prevents avoidable harm, and strengthens trust in health systems.
The event also highlighted the need for safe and continuous care for people living with non-communicable diseases (NCDs) during crises and emergencies, when disruptions to essential health services can put patients and communities at greater risk.
A message from the WHO Regional Director for the Eastern Mediterranean, delivered by Dr Adham Ismail, Officer-in-Charge, was presented during the ceremony, with subtitles in Farsi, reinforcing the regional and global commitment to advancing patient safety.
The ceremony highlighted several priorities aligned with the global patient safety agenda, including: strengthening reporting and learning systems for patient safety incidents; building a culture of safety among health care providers; engaging patients, families and communities; improving health literacy; addressing medication-related risks such as polypharmacy; and extending patient safety efforts beyond hospitals to primary health care and other levels of care.
The commemoration also provided an opportunity for WHO and the Ministry of Health and Medical Education to identify areas for continued technical collaboration, including: knowledge exchange; strengthening patient safety assessment; and follow-up on capacity-building under the Hospital Patient Safety Assessment Manual and the Patient Safety Assessment Manual for Primary Care.
These discussions reflect WHO’s role in bringing global evidence, standards and tools to the national context, facilitating knowledge exchange, supporting capacity-building and convening partners around practical actions to strengthen patient safety.
World Patient Safety Day is observed on September 17 every year and serves as an opportunity to raise public awareness, enhance collaborations among healthcare stakeholders, and expedite measures to reduce preventable harm associated with the delivery of health services.
Each year, the day is observed under a specific slogan. In 2026, it focuses on safe care for NCDs, under the theme ‘Safe care for life!’.
NCDs such as cardiovascular diseases, cancers, diabetes, and chronic respiratory diseases are among the most significant global health challenges, accounting for 74 percent of deaths worldwide; they affect people of all ages and require constant, lifelong care. Patients’ frequent interactions with the healthcare system can put their safety at risk. These risks are also influenced by health system challenges and the broader determinants of health.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), 1 in 10 patients is harmed during health care, with around half of this harm being considered preventable. People living with NCDs are particularly vulnerable to harm due to the long-term nature of their conditions, ongoing treatment needs, and frequent interactions with health systems.
With some conditions, such as cancer, up to 1 in 3 patients experience adverse events during care. Many people also live with multiple chronic conditions, further increasing the risk of harm.
Addressing NCDs is a global priority, reflected in the United Nations political declaration on NCDs and mental health, which calls for strengthened prevention and long-term management of NCDs. Achieving these commitments requires access to safe and quality care.
Improving safety in NCD care requires addressing risks related to the complexity of care, strengthening health systems through a primary health care approach and tackling wider determinants that can increase the risk of harm. The day also highlights the importance of engaging people with lived experience in the design and delivery of NCD services and in their own care.

Netflix's Best of the Best faces backlash over Kabul punchline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:48:30 UTC
20:48:30 KST

Breadcrumb
'Our trauma isn't your punchline': Netflix's Best of the Best faces backlash over Kabul evacuation joke
Netflix's new Bollywood-influenced film Best of the Best has sparked backlash over a joke about the chaotic 2021 evacuation from Afghanistan, with viewers accusing its makers of turning one of the country's most traumatic recent episodes into a punchline.
The comedy dance movie, which began streaming on Netflix on 18 September, includes a scene in which lead character Maya, played by Maitreyi Ramakrishnan, tells a friend: "Guys throw themselves at you like you're the last plane out of Kabul."
The line has prompted anger among social media users, who said it trivialised the desperation and deaths witnessed at Kabul airport as hundreds of Afghans tried to flee the Taliban takeover in August 2021.
One social media user directly addressed co-writer Hasan Minhaj on X, writing: "You should be embarrassed, Hasan Minhaj. Explain the joke."
"Is the funny part the Afghans falling from planes? The terrified families at the airport? The people desperately trying to escape the Taliban?" the post continued. "Our trauma isn't your cheap punchline."
Others called on Netflix and the filmmakers to acknowledge the backlash and apologise.
The anger centres on the scenes that unfolded at Hamid Karzai International Airport in August 2021, when thousands of Afghans rushed to escape the country as Taliban forces entered Kabul.
Footage from the airport showed hundreds of people running alongside a US Air Force C-17 transport aircraft as it taxied along the runway, with some clinging to the outside of the plane.
At least two people were reported to have fallen from the aircraft after it took off, including Zaki Anwari, a member of Afghanistan's national youth football team.
The evacuation continued amid deadly scenes at and around the airport. Images of people clinging to departing aircraft and the aftermath of an Islamic State suicide bombing outside the airport became defining images of the crisis.
The final US military flight left Kabul shortly before midnight on 30 August, bringing America's two-decade military presence in Afghanistan to an end. More than 100,000 people were evacuated during the operation, while many Afghans seeking to leave were left behind.
Best of the Best follows childhood friends Maya and Anjali as they join UCLA's competitive Bollywood-fusion dance team.
The film was directed by Lena Khan and written by Minhaj and Prashanth Venkataramanujam.
The New Arab has contacted Netflix, Khan, Minhaj and Venkataramanujam for comment on the backlash but did not receive any response at the time of publication.

Bulgarian cabinet to criminalise customs violations, tighten control on gambling

News
Bulgarian cabinet to criminalise customs violations, tighten control on gambling
Wednesday 23 September 2026 13:39
Wednesday, 23 September 2026, 13:39
Prime Minister Rumen Radev
PHOTO BTA
Font size
The Bulgarian cabinet will introduce amendments to the Criminal Code to criminalise customs violations. "We are tightening customs controls, while smuggling will become a serious criminal offence,” Prime Minister Rumen Radev said at the beginning of the government meeting on September 23.
According to the prime minister, customs violations have so far been treated as administrative offences, while there has been no political will to change this over the years.
“The provisions we are proposing strike at one of the most lucrative areas of organised crime: the movement of goods across the EU’s external borders to the detriment of European and national finances,” Radev said.
“The law will apply not only to smugglers and rank-and-file customs officers, but also to so-called ‘on-call officials’ within the customs administration who deliberately turn a blind eye to such violations,” the prime minister explained.
Radev also announced that the government would introduce an effective blanket ban on gambling advertising, with the sole exception of advertising supporting sport through branding on sportswear and sports facilities.
He said a new, much stricter model for regulating and monitoring the gambling sector would be introduced, aimed at greater transparency, fairer taxation and curbing gambling addiction.
The prime minister also said that a substantial increase in the tax on online gambling was planned, alongside mechanisms to channel part of the resulting revenue towards sport and education.
All foreign operators licensed to operate in Bulgaria will be required to register as financial entities in the country, Radev explained.

In the mountains, predominantly sunny weather is expected. On Friday, the cloud cover will increase from west to east, with rain in places in western Bulgaria. Winds will be light, temporarily shifting to the southeast before turning north again. Temperatures will be one to two degrees higher.

Ukraine National Bank to require investor guarantee letters in insurer recovery plans
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:45:59 EEST
20:45:59 KST

An insurer shall submit to the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) a letter of intent from an investor as an integral part of the insurer's business recovery plan or financing plan if the measures envisaged by them are to be implemented using investors' funds.
This is stipulated in a draft resolution approving amendments to the Regulation on the procedure for preparing and updating an insurer's business continuity plan, business recovery plan and financing plan, which the NBU has proposed for public discussion, the regulator said on its website.
A letter of guarantee will be required if the plan provides for: an increase in the insurer's authorized capital; the purchase of assets that are not included in eligible assets for calculating regulatory capital; or the raising of funds in the form of subordinated debt.
In the letter of guarantee, the investor will confirm its intention to ensure the implementation of the respective measures in the amount and within the time frames specified in the plan, as well as indicate the sources of funds and undertake to provide the documents necessary for approving the plan and implementing measures to restore the insurer's financial condition, the statement said.
The National Bank is accepting comments and proposals on the draft until October 5, 2026.

UNITED NATIONS, September 23. /TASS/. David Adeang, the president of the Pacific island nation of Naoero, formerly known as Nauru, announced the country’s withdrawal from the International Criminal Court (ICC) while addressing the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York.
According to the president, the ICC has lost its relevance to Naoero, which is why the country will cease participating in the court’s activities and withdraw its membership.
Adeang added that, before departing New York, he would submit the documents on the termination of Naoero’s participation in the organization’s activities to the depositary of the Rome Statute.
The day before, US President Donald Trump, speaking from the podium of the UN General Assembly, called on all countries to withdraw from the ICC, which he called a "rogue institution."
To date, five countries have announced their withdrawal from the ICC: Venezuela, Chad, Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger.
The International Criminal Court was established under the 1998 Rome Statute. It is not part of the UN and is accountable to the countries that have ratified the statute. Among the states that are not parties to the statute are Russia (which signed but did not ratify), the United States (which signed but later withdrew its signature), and China (which has not signed the Statute). In 2016, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree stating that Moscow would not become a party to the ICC. According to the Russian Foreign Ministry, the court "has not lived up to the hopes placed in it and has not become a truly independent body of international justice."

Gold dust and egg yolks behind Tallinn theater's luxurious interior decor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:45:00 UTC
20:45:00 KST

Gold dust and egg yolks behind Tallinn theater's luxurious interior decor
Gloria Palace opened in Tallinn in 1926 as a luxury movie theater promising an unprecedented experience. It survived the March 1944 bombing and remains largely intact.
In 2026, the building that houses Downtown Theater (Südalinna teater) marks its centennial. A hundred years ago, Estonia's first and only luxury movie theater, Gloria Palace, opened beside Tallinn's Freedom Square. Before that, people watched films in single-story wooden buildings that did not even have heating.
That changed when Leon Falštein, a movie enthusiast from a wealthy family, decided in the early 1920s that his hometown of Tallinn deserved better. He built his first theater in Riga, however. According to guide Oksana Talisainen, it was the first luxury movie theater in the Baltic states.
"It has survived in its original form. It has an ivory-colored auditorium seating a thousand people, with full-size golden palm sculptures. Latvians had never seen anything like it," she said.
Within three years, Falštein had earned enough money in Riga to build a theater in his hometown as well. He brought along the architects he had hired from Europe.
"For the Tallinn theater, he told the architects that absolutely no expense was to be spared. It had to be a breathtakingly luxurious movie palace."
Estonian architects were less impressed when the building opened in 1926. Newspapers criticized it as a return to Byzantium that did not fit Estonian culture. They did, however, admire its exterior facade, created by the Estonian artist Jaan Koort.
"So the facade was beautiful, but the moment you crossed the threshold, it was the height of bad taste. It was criticized for its eclecticism and its excessive, overdone luxury, especially the amount of gold used in the building," Talisainen said.
But not all that glitters is gold. By the final stage of construction, the money had nearly run out and Falštein had to decide whether to delay the opening or find a way to finish the work. The solution was egg yolks.
"Apparently, someone on Leon Falštein's artistic team was a highly educated man because he remembered how religious images, or icons, came to be painted in Byzantium. The gold on Byzantine icons is not solid gold. It is a little gold mixed with egg yolk. Falštein's construction workers went to Tallinn's markets, bought up every egg they could find, separated the yolks, mixed them with gold powder and coated the Gloria Palace luxury theater like a holiday pastry," Talisainen said.
While architects criticized the interior, ordinary people liked it, according to the guide. Tickets were expensive, but they bought a memorable experience.
"You got two films in one visit. You came here dressed in your finest, just as you would to the theater. You watched one feature-length film accompanied by an orchestra, then went to stroll through the grand foyers: to be seen, talk and socialize with others. Then you watched the second film," Talisainen said.
A dance club opened in the theater's basement in 1930. Along with a dance floor, it had its own restaurant and cigar room. "That business began bringing in more money than the luxury movie theater," the guide said.
The fact that the building can celebrate its centennial this year is something of a miracle. Thousands of bombs fell on central Tallinn during the March 1944 bombing, but none struck Gloria Palace. As a result, almost everything audiences see in the theater today is original. Only the seats in the main auditorium are a different color.
--

Lukashenko will use potash to get most out of U.S. — ambassador-at-large of MFA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:45:00 UTC
20:45:00 KST

Lukashenko will use potash to get most out of U.S. — ambassador-at-large of MFA
Yaroslav Chornohor, Ambassador-at-Large of the Ukrainian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, expressed this view in a comment to Ukrinform.
“The statement Lukashenko made about potash is, in essence, an attempt not to publicly reject Trump, but also not to make any specific commitments regarding volumes or timelines. This confirms that these issues may be the subject of further discussions,” the diplomat noted.
According to him, it is important for the Belarusian leader to retain the ability to use the potash issue not only as an economic tool but also as a political one.
“For Lukashenko, this is actually a wonderful opportunity, as it gives him a reason, so to speak, to talk—even remotely—with Trump. If Lukashenko had made the deliveries right away, it wouldn’t have created any added value for him,” Chornohor explained.
He emphasized that potash can serve as a tool of Belarus’s foreign policy.
“Potash can be sold to various countries, and the money will be more or less the same. But if he sells it to Russia, that’s one option; to China, another; and to the United States, that’s a completely different option,” the diplomat noted.
In his view, Lukashenko has no interest in rushing into specific agreements, as he can use the issue of supplies to impose additional conditions.
“Potash itself is a bargaining chip that helps negotiate other issues. And this isn’t just about political prisoners; it’s about lifting sanctions, unfreezing funds, possibly securing other preferences, and the ability to exert pressure on neighbors or allies—even on Russia itself. In other words, Lukashenko gains more room to maneuver, and that’s what matters most to him,” Chornohor noted.
In this context, the diplomat predicted that the self-proclaimed president of Belarus will make maximum use of this leverage to resolve his own problems.
“If, hypothetically, Trump becomes increasingly embroiled in a trade war with Canada, potash will be an important factor in U.S. domestic politics, and Lukashenko will try to get the most out of it. Simply selling potash to the U.S. is a very rudimentary option. The fact that Trump needs this resource makes it more valuable—it provides him with a certain political added value. Lukashenko will continue to try to exploit this, especially since the United States is making concessions in many areas,” stated the Foreign Ministry’s ambassador-at-large.
At the same time, the diplomat noted that the so-called major deal between the U.S. and Belarus regarding the purchase of potash fertilizers at a price lower than that of Canada has been under discussion for more than a month, and the idea for it emerged at the end of last year. He recalled that initially the focus was on the humanitarian aspect—Belarus’s release of more than a thousand political prisoners—but the specific terms of this agreement remain unclear.
“In fact, we don’t know what the United States and Lukashenko agreed upon. We don’t know any details—neither major nor minor—of the agreement… In reality, we see the recent release of 25 people and the lifting of sanctions against two Belarusian companies,” the diplomat noted.
According to him, further developments may reveal exactly what Washington and Minsk agreed upon. Specifically, whether there will be requirements regarding the transit of potash to Ukraine, the Baltic states, or Poland, and what further political or humanitarian steps Lukashenko will take.
Chornohor added that the continued release of political prisoners could be one possible indicator of progress on the agreements.
“If we now see, for example, that a large number of people are released, then we will understand that, apparently, something has been agreed upon and the deal will move forward. Lukashenko now sees that he is important and is trying to use this to his maximum advantage,” the diplomat concluded.
As reported by Ukrinform, President Donald Trump announced on September 21 that the U.S. is working with Belarus to secure additional potash supplies amid a trade dispute with Canada, a major supplier of this raw material for fertilizer production.
Belarus’s self-proclaimed president, Alexander Lukashenko, stated on September 22 that the country has no surplus potash fertilizer.
On September 16, Lukashenko pardoned and released 25 political prisoners following talks with U.S. Special Envoy for Belarus John Cole in exchange for the lifting of U.S. sanctions against the Belarusian companies “Lakokraska” and “Bellesbumprom.”

Nearly 10% of borrowers opted for riskier mortgages last week, as rates soared over 7%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:44:32 UTC
20:44:32 KST

Mortgage rates soared to the highest level since 2024 last week, causing loan demand to fall back again and more borrowers to opt for riskier loans. Total application volume decreased 1.5% from the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index.
The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, increased to 7.12% from 6.97%, with points rising to 0.73 from 0.72, including the origination fee, for loans with a 20% down payment.
Applications to refinance a home loan dropped 3% for the week and were 62% lower than the same week one year ago. That was the lowest level since February 2025. The 30-year fixed loan was 78 basis points, or more than three-quarters of a percentage point lower, at the same time last year.
Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home fell 1% for the week and were 11% lower year over year. The fall housing market, usually the second busiest compared with spring, is now underway, but real estate agents are already noting a sharp pullback due to higher rates. Buyers and current homeowners are also searching for savings anywhere they can find them, even in riskier, adjustable-rate loans.
"With fixed rates much higher, more borrowers opted for ARMs, with the ARM share reaching 9.8%, as rates for 5/1 ARMs were more than a percentage point lower than those for fixed rate loans," said Mike Fratantoni, senior vice president and chief economist at the MBA.
The ARM share of applications the week before last was just 8.4%. During the first years of the pandemic, when rates were hitting multiple record lows, the ARM share was barely 3%. ARMs can carry a fixed rate for up to 10 years but will adjust either higher or lower depending on where the market is when that term is up.
Mortgage rates moved slightly lower to start this week, according to a separate survey from Mortgage News Daily, as the price of oil fell and bond yields moved lower as a result.

We, the Foreign Ministers and high-level representatives of the European and Indo-Pacific Partners (EIPP) - Australia, France, Germany, Japan, New Zealand, Poland, Republic of Korea, and the United Kingdom - meet today for the second time in the margins of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. We reaffirm our belief that by standing together, we can effectively promote peace, stability, sustainability, and prosperity across the Indo-Pacific and European regions, and that UN member states can and should contribute to these goals.

We will work in partnership to drive forward UN reforms to strengthen the organisation and improve its efficiency and resilience.

We reaffirm our support for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all states. Regarding Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, we stress the importance of a full ceasefire and reaffirm the need for a just and lasting peace, in line with the principles of the UN Charter and international law, including independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity.
We emphasize the importance of maintaining peace and stability in the Indo-Pacific. We encourage dialogue and oppose any unilateral attempts to change the status quo across the Taiwan Strait. 
We stand together in our commitment to upholding UNCLOS. Disruption of sea lanes, including the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab-el-Mandab Strait, whether by force, threat or the introduction of unlawful tolls or conditions for transit, threatens security and prosperity of all, especially the world’s most vulnerable, and are unacceptable. We call on all countries to speak out wherever it occurs.

What the historic agreement could do
Over the past year, the US Department of Defense and its Ukrainian counterpart have reportedly developed a framework that would expand the testing and production of Ukrainian defense technology in the US.
The agreement would go beyond individual contracts with Ukrainian manufacturers. It is expected to establish a broader system allowing leading Ukrainian defense companies to cooperate directly with American firms and the US military.
The two countries had already drafted an initial memorandum in May. Ukraine’s Ambassador to the US, Olha Stefanishyna, said at the time that the document was being reviewed by institutions on both sides.
The proposed arrangement could allow Ukraine to export selected military technologies and establish joint ventures with American companies. Kyiv has also insisted that Ukrainian intellectual property must be protected and that exports must not deprive its own military of urgently needed equipment.
Germany Probes Drone and Suspected Explosives Near Air Base
Ukraine’s advantage lies not only in producing inexpensive drones but also in continuously adapting them against Russian electronic warfare, air defenses, and changing battlefield tactics.
“It’s not just about having the tech. It’s about how the tech is used,” Deborah Fairlamb, founding partner at Green Flag Ventures, told CBS News.
Ukrainian drones helped defend US bases
The negotiations have gained urgency after Ukrainian equipment and specialists reportedly helped protect US military installations in the Middle East from Iranian Shahed-type attack drones.
When Iran retaliated against US and Israeli strikes in March, then-US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll reportedly contacted former Google chief executive Eric Schmidt, whose company Perennial Autonomy works with Ukrainian defense technology.
Driscoll sought 13,000 Merops interceptor drones and 10,000 Bumblebee reconnaissance and strike drones for deployment in the region, according to CBS News.
The aircraft were shipped within days, but making them operational took several weeks due to essential Ukrainian components arriving later. The Merops interceptors reportedly use artificial intelligence beacons produced by Ukraine’s Sine Engineering, as well as Ukrainian-made warheads.
Ukrainian specialists were also needed to integrate the drones with American air-defense radars and teach personnel how to operate them as part of a coordinated interception system.
Kyiv additionally sent interceptor drones and Ukrainian pilots to the region as Iran targeted American military facilities with one-way attack drones.
US seeks Ukraine’s battlefield experience
The agreement comes as the Pentagon attempts to rapidly expand the US military’s comparatively small drone fleet.
Under its Drone Dominance Program, the Pentagon has invited American and selected foreign manufacturers, primarily Ukrainian companies, to compete for large procurement orders. Washington reportedly hopes to acquire more than 200,000 drones by 2027.
Ukrainian manufacturer SkyFall won the program’s first competition, while Perennial Autonomy and Neros Technologies succeeded in the second.
Zelensky has said Ukraine aims to manufacture as many as 10 million drones this year. By comparison, the US Army acquired approximately 50,000 drones in 2025, according to Driscoll.
American interest in Ukrainian technology is already producing individual contracts. Previously the US Army awarded a $10.64 million contract for Ukrainian-developed Raybird reconnaissance drones produced by Skyeton.
The proposed agreement would transform such individual purchases into a wider and more permanent defense partnership.
If finalized, it would give American manufacturers access to technology tested during years of high-intensity warfare. Ukraine, in turn, could receive US financing, production capacity, and access to a significantly larger defense market.
The deal has not yet been signed, and its final provisions have not been made public. But its reported scope suggests that Washington increasingly views Ukraine not only as a recipient of military assistance, but as a source of technology and combat expertise capable of strengthening US defenses.

Mourners claim diabetic man who died under arrest was “murdered”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:37:04 UTC
20:37:04 KST

Mourners claim diabetic man who died under arrest was “murdered”
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Around 150 people joined a funeral procession on Wednesday for a man who died while being detained by police who stopped him while searching for a stolen fatbike.
The body of 51-year-old Alfredo Goeloe was carried in a white coffin in a carriage drawn by two white horses to the Zuiderbegraafplaats in Rotterdam, 10 days after he collapsed while being pinned to the ground and handcuffed.
Friends and relatives who followed the coffin carried banners with slogans including “samen tegen onrecht omdat we om elkaar geven” (united against injustice because we care for each other).
One of the mourners, Yenci Vargas, told Nieuwsuur: “He was murdered. I’m not talking about racism, but he was murdered by the negligence and stupidity of the police.”
Another, Marsha Mabosa, said: “Last month we were out in a café and he asked me to dance the bachata. He was a very good dancer. And now we have to miss him in a way that is very unjust.”
Stolen fatbike
Goeloe was stopped by police while riding a fatbike through Rotterdam on the evening of Saturday, September 12.
Police initially said he was suspected of stealing the bike, but later changed their story to say he had been stopped because he was riding too fast. Just before Goeloe’s arrest a fatbike had been reported stolen by a couple aged around 40.
Goeloe tried to run from police when they tried to arrest him for not carrying ID. His family said he had borrowed his sister’s bike to go out to get medication for his diabetes.
He was chased down and passed out while he was being restrained on his belly. Video footage showed he cried out that he had diabetes and was in pain as he lay on the ground.
Official complaint
Goeloe’s family have filed a criminal complaint against four police officers. Lawyer Gerard Roethof said they viewed it as “a case of manslaughter, or in any event severe assault with fatal consequences.”
Jan Schalkwijk, a lawyer with Control Alt Delete, an organisation that monitors racial profiling in the Netherlands, said the use of force by police was excessive.
“The officers were far superior in number, according to reports he was unarmed, and he could have been approached with less force,” Schalkwijk argued.
Restraint guidelines
But Jaap Timmer, a political scientist at the VU university in Amsterdam who specialises in police use of force, said there was no indication from the film footage that the police had failed to follow protocol.
He said police guidelines said people should be pressed against the ground for as short a time as possible when under arrest, but it was unsafe to let them stand up before they had been handcuffed.
“I understand the police were looking for a fatbike and this man was riding too fast. That could be a reason to ask his identity,” he said.
“He then ran away fast and resisted his arrest. That has nothing to do with ethnic profiling, but with the man’s behaviour.”

Births fall by more than half in 6 Greek regions over 15 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:34:21 UTC
20:34:21 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
Births fell by more than half in six mainland Greek regions between 2009 and 2024, according to a demographic study reported by Greek newspaper To Vima on Wednesday.
Nationwide, births fell by about 42%, from around 117,440 in 2009 to 68,310 in 2024.
The six regions where births more than halved were Thesprotia, Grevena, Phthiotis, Kozani, Evrytania and Florina.
The study, by demographer Byron Kotzamanis at the Institute for Demographic Research and Studies, also traced a decline in births spanning more than four decades.
Annual births fell from an average of about 148,000 in 1979-80 to roughly 67,000 in 2024-25, while the average age of women giving birth rose from 26.2 to 32.2.
Births have been declining since the late 1970s, apart from a modest increase between 2003 and 2009. The study linked that rise largely to immigration after 1990.
It also found that women were having fewer children across successive generations.
Those born in the late 1950s had an average of two children, compared with fewer than 1.5 among those born around 1985.
The total fertility rate fell from 2.2 children per woman in 1979-80 to 1.24 in 2024-25.
The decline in births was less pronounced on some islands. Six island regional units recorded decreases of less than 30% between 2009 and 2024, with declines below 15% in the Cyclades and Zakynthos.
The study also highlighted wide differences in the balance between births and deaths.
Only five of Greece’s 74 regional units recorded more births than deaths in 2024: Thira, Mykonos, Kos, Naxos and Rethymno.
By contrast, Serres, Evrytania and Grevena recorded at least 3.5 deaths for every birth.

"Not like any role before": Tom Cruise opens up about his new film from the Oscar-winning director

Tom Cruise said that his character in "Digger" is unlike any previous role. The film will be released worldwide on September 30.
Hollywood actor Tom Cruise called his character in the film "Digger" "absolutely incredible" and unlike any role he had encountered before. The movie star made the statement at the film’s world premiere in London on Tuesday, September 22, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
"He’s the kind of character who says things that some people think about, and some people can’t even imagine," the Hollywood star told Reuters.
"I have never read about a character like this. I have never read about a film like this," Cruise added.
The release of "Digger" was marked by a royal premiere attended by Britain’s Prince William and Princess Kate, following what actress Sandra Hüller described as nearly 10 years of work by Oscar-winning director Alejandro G. Iñárritu.
The film generated considerable anticipation after the trailer showed Cruise transforming into eccentric oil magnate Digger Rockwell, with gray hair, facial prosthetics and a soft jumpsuit.
Cruise said that this transformation was far from the most demanding aspect of the role, pointing instead to a 10-minute monologue filmed in a single take.
Hüller, the star of "Anatomy of a Fall," said it was "wonderful" to watch Cruise perform. "It feels as though everything he has learned during 46 years of acting has come together in this character," she added.
In the film, Rockwell inadvertently triggers an environmental catastrophe that pushes the world to the brink of nuclear war before he sets out to save the planet. But the filmmakers have revealed little about the story, fueling speculation about the plot and rumors that it could be a musical, which Cruise denied.
"If you watch the film without knowing anything about it, it’s much better than if you (knew) beforehand," Hüller said, adding that the secrecy was not intended to create intrigue for its own sake.
Although Cruise described the story as an exploration of "power and greed... responsibility and irresponsibility," Australian actress Sophie Wilde said it also contains a message that art is a "vessel for catharsis."
Iñárritu, whose previous works include "Birdman" and "The Revenant," compared the process of making "Digger" to painting, saying that every shot was carefully created to immerse viewers in the film’s world.
For Emma D’Arcy, this attention to detail made working with the Mexican director feel like being part of an orchestra led by a conductor. "In "Digger," musicality was really, really important... it’s a comedy, so rhythm is kind of key," they noted.
Michael Stuhlbarg, the star of "Call Me by Your Name," recalled scenes that kept evolving during filming, with new dialogue, alternative versions and unexpected additions emerging day by day.
The actor joked that so much unusual material had been filmed that he hoped a DVD with additional production footage would be released one day.
"It was a lot of fun," he said.
"Digger" will begin its worldwide theatrical release on September 30 and will be released in cinemas in the United States and the United Kingdom on October 2.

 Britain is set to take another look at its agreement to transfer sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, after US President Donald Trump made clear that he does not support the deal in its current form.
UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting told the BBC on Wednesday that Washington’s position became clear following Trump’s description of the agreement as a “terrible deal” during talks with Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the UN General Assembly in New York.
Under the agreement negotiated by former Premier Keir Starmer’s government, Mauritius would take sovereignty over the Chagos archipelago, while Britain would pay about £101 million ($136 million) a year on average to retain access to the joint UK-US military facility on Diego Garcia.
The arrangement was put on hold indefinitely in April after Trump withdrew his backing. Streeting said the government would now work with the US to alter the agreement sufficiently to secure its support.
“We have to do more work with our American allies, with President Trump and his administration, to get the deal to a place where he can support it,” he said.
The future of Diego Garcia is at the center of the dispute. Britain has maintained that uncertainty over the island’s sovereignty could threaten the long-term security of the base.
Mauritius disputes the existing territorial settlement, arguing that it was compelled to surrender the islands in 1965 as part of the process leading to independence.
Starmer said he had “inherited the situation” and that a resolution was needed, stressing the importance of protecting the base.
The government is not expected to launch a formal review with a fixed timetable. According to the BBC, officials have indicated that the fundamental position remains unchanged: any final agreement would need the backing of the United States.

BEIJING, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese mainland welcomes more discussion in Taiwan on national reunification and is willing to conduct broad and in-depth democratic consultations with people from various sectors on the island on relations across the Taiwan Strait and the future of the Chinese nation, a mainland spokesperson said on Wednesday.
Zhu Fenglian, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, made the remarks at a regular press conference when commenting on a recent article by a Taiwan scholar suggesting that the mainland should explore ways to end hostility and build mutual trust across the Taiwan Strait before reunification.
The Taiwan question stems from China's civil war fought between the forces led by the Communist Party of China (CPC) and the Chinese Kuomintang (KMT) about eight decades ago. In 1949, the defeated KMT retreated to Taiwan, and the People's Republic of China (PRC) was founded under the leadership of the CPC.
The unresolved civil war, combined with foreign interference, has kept the two sides of the Taiwan Strait in a prolonged state of political confrontation. However, the fact that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory has never changed.
Zhu said that peaceful reunification and "one country, two systems" remain the basic policy for resolving the Taiwan question and the best way to achieve national reunification.
She said the Taiwan plan under a proposed "one country, two systems" framework would fully take into account Taiwan's realities, absorb opinions and suggestions from people on both sides of the Strait, and consider the interests and feelings of Taiwan compatriots.
"On the common political basis of adhering to the 1992 Consensus and opposing 'Taiwan independence,' we are willing to carry out broad and in-depth democratic consultations with political parties, groups and people from all sectors in Taiwan on cross-Strait relations and the future of the Chinese nation," Zhu said.
She added that the mainland welcomes suggestions from Taiwan compatriots on advancing national reunification, saying that earlier and broader discussions on reunification could create more opportunities for Taiwan's economic and social development and bring more tangible benefits to Taiwan compatriots.
Her remarks came as a recent annual survey on cross-Strait relations in Taiwan showed that more than 60 percent of respondents supported continuing cross-Strait exchange platforms, expanding tourist exchanges and increasing exchanges in areas such as film, arts and sports.
Zhu said the findings demonstrated that peace, development, exchanges and cooperation remain the mainstream public opinion in Taiwan and a broad consensus among different sectors in Taiwan.
She said the mainland will continue to uphold the principle that people on both sides of the Strait are one family, roll out more policies and measures benefiting Taiwan compatriots, strengthen institutional support for cross-Strait integrated development, and promote personnel exchanges and cooperation in various fields.
Separately, Zhu said the mainland would continue to promote cross-Strait economic exchanges and cooperation so that people on both sides of the Strait can share the benefits of peaceful and integrated development of cross-Strait relations.
She noted that relevant parties on both sides have been working to implement 10 policy measures announced by the mainland in April to promote cross-Strait exchanges and cooperation, helping more Taiwan farmers and fishermen expand into the mainland market.
According to Zhu, multiple Taiwan packaging plants, orchards and food enterprises have been registered on the mainland, while customs clearance efficiency has improved and logistics have become more convenient.
On transportation links, Zhu said direct cross-Strait passenger air services have yet to fully return to normal due to obstruction and interference by the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities.
From January to August this year, 4.22 million passenger trips were made on direct cross-Strait flights, up 12.9 percent year on year, reflecting strong market demand and a strong desire for exchanges among people on both sides of the Strait, Zhu said.
She called on the Taiwan side to remove unreasonable restrictions on cross-Strait air transportation and allow airlines on both sides to arrange flights based on market demand.
Commenting on the annual Shanghai-Taipei City Forum, Zhu described it as an important platform for city-to-city exchanges across the Strait and said both cities had remained in communication over arrangements for this year's event.
The forum, which has been held for 16 consecutive years, has developed well-established practices and is expected to proceed as scheduled this year, she said.
In response to recent remarks by Taiwan leader Lai Ching-te on increasing Taiwan's "defense spending" to "safeguard peace through strength," Zhu reiterated the mainland's position that there is only one China in the world and Taiwan is part of China.
She said the DPP authorities' stubborn pursuit of "Taiwan independence," deliberate escalation of confrontation across the Taiwan Strait, and attempts to seek "Taiwan independence" through military means and external support make them the chief culprit in undermining peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait.
No matter how much is spent on military budgets or weapons purchases, Zhu said, it cannot change the historical trend toward national reunification. ■

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Six-time Dakar Rally champion Nasser Al-Attiyah added another title to his remarkable sporting career on Wednesday, helping Qatar win the men's skeet team gold medal at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games.
The 55-year-old, who claimed his sixth Dakar Rally title in January, secured his third Asian Games gold medal and sixth shooting medal overall, 32 years after making his debut at the 1994 Hiroshima Games.
"To start from the Hiroshima Asian Games and to come back here again, and today for our team to win two gold medals, is really amazing," Al-Attiyah said.
Despite having just two months to prepare for the Games because of his rallying commitments, Al-Attiyah hit 120 of 125 targets in qualification, posting one of the day's three highest scores. He qualified third for the individual final but finished fifth.
"My performance was really very good and strong," he said. "I made a very high score, one of the highest scores in the field."
"Motorsport is very important to me, but when it comes to the Asian Games or the Olympic Games, I put everything into it and try to achieve the best result."
Al-Attiyah made his Asian Games debut in Hiroshima in 1994, finishing 17th in men's skeet. He subsequently won team gold medals at Busan 2002 and Guangzhou 2010 before claiming team silver and individual bronze at Hangzhou 2023.
His international shooting career stretches back even further. Having taken up the sport in 1993, he qualified for his first Olympics at Atlanta 1996 and went on to compete at six consecutive Games.
He finished sixth at Sydney 2000 and fourth at Athens 2004 before finally reaching the Olympic podium at London 2012, where he won bronze in men's skeet at the age of 41.
Alongside his shooting career, Al-Attiyah has established himself as one of rallying's leading competitors.
He made his Dakar Rally debut in 2004 and narrowly missed out on the title in 2010 before securing his first victory in the car category the following year.
In January, he claimed his sixth Dakar crown after holding the overall lead throughout the final four days of the 13-day event.
While shooting and rallying demand different skills, Al-Attiyah believes his involvement in both sports has helped him maintain his competitive edge.
"They work together," he told Xinhua.
"Shooting helps me a lot in rallying, and rallying also helps me a lot in shooting, especially in making me mentally stronger, so I love both sports."
Despite competing against athletes considerably younger than himself, Al-Attiyah believes experience remains one of his greatest assets.
"I'm still strong," he said. "My advantage is experience."
Having last competed at the Olympics in Rio de Janeiro in 2016, Al-Attiyah is now targeting a seventh appearance at Los Angeles 2028.
"The World Championship will be in Qatar, and there will also be quota places for the next Olympic Games," he said.
Should he qualify, his Olympic career would span 32 years, from Atlanta 1996 to Los Angeles 2028, another milestone in a sporting career that has taken him from Olympic shooting ranges to the deserts of the Dakar Rally. ■

A voter casts a ballot at a polling station in Rabat, Morocco, Sept. 23, 2026. Polling stations opened on Wednesday morning across Morocco for legislative elections to renew the 395 members of the House of Representatives, parliament's lower house. (Photo by Aissa/Xinhua)
RABAT, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Polling stations opened on Wednesday morning across Morocco for legislative elections to renew the 395 members of the House of Representatives, parliament's lower house.
Voting is scheduled to run until 7:00 p.m. local time (1900 GMT), and approximately 15.8 million voters are expected to cast ballots.
Of the 395-seat House of Representatives, 305 are contested through local electoral constituencies, while the remaining 90 are allocated exclusively to women through regional lists.
According to the Interior Ministry, a total of 7,288 candidates registered nationwide, representing 28 political groups in the election.
Women account for 2,658 of the candidates registered for the election, representing 36.47 percent of the total, it added.
Morocco has a bicameral parliament consisting of the House of Representatives and the House of Councilors. The 2026 election will determine the members of Morocco's House of Representatives across the country's 12 regions. The election of the House of Councilors is scheduled for 2027.
The major parties in the election are the National Rally of Independents, the Authenticity and Modernity Party, and the Istiqlal Party, which formed the outgoing government.
They will compete alongside the Justice and Development Party, which led coalition governments following the 2011 and 2016 general elections, the Socialist Union of Popular Forces, the Popular Movement, and the Party of Progress and Socialism.
Under the constitution, Morocco's king appoints the prime minister from the party that wins the most seats, which then forms a government. ■

Global economic growth projected at 2.9 pct in 2026: OECD
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:28:33 CST
20:28:33 KST

PARIS, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Global economic growth is projected to be 2.9 percent in 2026 and 3.0 percent in 2027, according to the Economic Outlook Interim Report released by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) on Wednesday.
Growth in the advanced G20 economies, as well as in the G20 emerging-market economies, is projected to remain broadly stable, the report said.
G20 headline inflation is expected to rise from 3.4 percent in 2025 to 4.1 percent in 2026, before easing to 3.6 percent in 2027, according to the report.
In the advanced G20 economies, headline inflation is projected to rise from 2.5 percent in 2025 to 3.2 percent in 2026, before falling to 2.6 percent in 2027, while in emerging-market G20 economies it is expected to increase from 4.1 percent to 4.8 percent before easing to 4.3 percent.
The OECD noted that the projections are based on a technical assumption that Brent crude prices and TTF gas prices will peak in the fourth quarter of 2026 and then decline steadily through the end of 2027.
The assumed Brent crude price path is broadly consistent with the "short disruption" scenario in the OECD's June 2026 Economic Outlook, while the assumed gas price path is about 60 percent higher.
Persistent uncertainty over the evolution of the conflict in the Middle East remains a key risk to the baseline projections, the OECD warned, adding that constraints on exports through the Strait of Hormuz, additional disruptions to alternative export routes such as the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, or further significant damage to energy production facilities in the region could prompt a further sustained rise in energy prices and potentially lead to shortages of key commodities, particularly in net importing countries.
Low European gas reserves and uncertain scope for sustained further reductions in oil inventories in some countries could exacerbate supply disruption risks.
"Further monetary policy rate adjustments may be needed," the OECD said, noting that faced with renewed energy price shocks, stronger-than-expected demand pressures, and above-target inflation in many economies, central banks need to ensure that underlying inflation pressures are durably contained.
The OECD also called for further structural policy reforms to help economies cope with future supply shocks, including diversifying energy supply, improving energy efficiency, enhancing product and labor market adjustment, and ensuring workers have adaptable skills. ■

ISTANBUL, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Türkiye is taking a series of measures to contain the fallout from a major investment fund crisis that has triggered a sharp stock market sell-off, fund liquidations and a widening investigation.
The developments have raised concerns among nearly half a million investors and prompted high-profile arrests.
The full scale of the investor base affected by the liquidation became clearer on Wednesday. The country's Capital Markets Board (SPK) said 455,758 unique investors were registered in the 131 funds involved in the crisis.
The funds, managed by seven portfolio management companies, were ordered to be liquidated on Sept. 17.
The SPK urged investors to rely solely on official statements amid conflicting reports, stressing its commitment to protecting investor rights and maintaining confidence in the capital markets.
The crisis stems from alleged stock market manipulation that created the appearance of rapid and substantial gains, attracting retail investors.
Resat Yilmaz, a gold trader and financial expert at Istanbul's Grand Bazaar, highlighted the devastating consequences for retail investors.
"The number of victims is truly very high. We witnessed shares intrinsically worth 5 liras (about 0.1 U.S. dollars) suddenly pumped to 500 liras through aggressive manipulation," Yilmaz told Xinhua.
Investors were trapped when the scheme eventually collapsed, he said. "The financial cost to these small retail investors has been devastating."
Yilmaz warned of broader macroeconomic consequences, particularly the flight of foreign investment.
"Developing countries like ours rely heavily on foreign capital. The panic and manipulation we witnessed create significant hurdles for foreign investors. This is a very painful period for our national market," he said.
However, Yilmaz expressed confidence that the Turkish authorities would implement strict regulatory measures to restore market trust.
Regulators extended the liquidation period for the affected funds from three to six months, citing the funds' portfolio structures and market conditions and allowing their assets to be sold under more favorable conditions.
Clarifying this process, capital markets lawyer Yalcin Ozge Okat explained that fund liquidation differs from a standard corporate bankruptcy.
Speaking to a local broadcaster, Okat noted that the process involves selling off the funds' assets, calculating debts and receivables, and distributing the remaining balance to investors.
He said investors' legal rights remain intact, though exact payment timelines depend on forthcoming SPK regulations.
The liquidation process comes as a criminal investigation widens following a sharp sell-off on Borsa Istanbul last week. The benchmark BIST 100 index plunged more than 7.5 percent at one point, sparking concerns over market stability.
In recent days, Turkish authorities have detained or arrested dozens of suspects, including high-ranking fund management executives.
Authorities have also frozen assets, imposed travel restrictions and blocked social media accounts as part of the investigation into suspected illicit gains. ■

First stellar stream beyond the Milky Way could reveal dark matter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:23:11 UTC
20:23:11 KST

First stellar stream beyond the Milky Way could reveal dark matter
- Date:
- September 23, 2026
- Source:
- University of Copenhagen
- Summary:
- Astronomers have discovered the first globular cluster stellar stream beyond the Milky Way, opening a new way to study dark matter in distant galaxies. These faint trails of stars trace a galaxy’s gravitational structure and could eventually help scientists map invisible matter across the universe.
- Share:
A faint ribbon of stars can be seen stretching across the galaxy in the image above. Known as a globular cluster stellar stream, this type of structure preserves clues about its past motion and evolution. By studying these streams, astronomers can learn more about how galaxies developed and how dark matter is distributed within them.
Because these stellar streams respond to gravity, they can act as tracers of dark matter that cannot be seen directly. Until recently, their extreme faintness made them very difficult to detect and analyze. Improvements in massive astronomical datasets and advanced analysis methods are now turning stellar streams into one of the most promising tools for studying galaxies.
First Stellar Stream Found Beyond the Milky Way
An international team led by PhD student Julie Kiel Holm of the Niels Bohr Institute and Associate Professor Sarah Pearson of DTU Space has now reported a first-of-its-kind discovery. The results were published in Nature, one of the world's most prestigious scientific journals.
"We have discovered a globular cluster stellar stream in another galaxy. This is the first time such a stream has been observed outside our own galaxy, the Milky Way, which makes the discovery particularly exciting," says Julie Kiel Holm.
Finding this kind of structure beyond the Milky Way is especially difficult because the stellar stream itself produces such a weak signal. The newly detected stream is also located inside an ultra-diffuse galaxy, a type of galaxy that gives off very little light.
That combination makes the detection particularly striking.
"This opens entirely new possibilities. Not only can we now search for globular cluster stellar streams in other galaxies, but in the long term, we may also be able to measure the dark matter content of more ultra-diffuse galaxies," says co-author Sarah Pearson, who contributed to the discovery during her employment at the Niels Bohr Institute.
What is a globular cluster stellar stream?
A globular cluster stellar stream is a long, narrow trail of stars that originated in a globular cluster, a dense collection of stars held together by gravity.
These streams develop when the gravity of the surrounding host galaxy gradually pulls stars away from the globular cluster through a process called tidal stripping.
Because gravity determines the shape and motion of stellar streams, astronomers can study them to learn how mass is distributed throughout a galaxy. That makes the streams useful for investigating dark matter, which represents approximately 80-85 percent of all matter in the universe even though its fundamental nature remains unknown.
A New Way to Map Dark Matter
The importance of the finding goes beyond simply identifying a stellar stream in another galaxy. The researchers also show for the first time that globular cluster stellar streams can be used to measure dark matter in galaxies outside the Milky Way.
That ability could be valuable because dark matter accounts for most of the Universe's mass, yet scientists still do not know what it is made of.
"We show that a well-established tool from studies of the Milky Way can be used to understand other galaxies, where measuring the distribution of dark matter has traditionally been very challenging," says Julie Kiel Holm.
The team focused on the ultra-diffuse galaxy UGC9050-Dw1 and produced new estimates of both its total mass and how that mass is distributed. Their analysis suggests that the galaxy contains a large amount of dark matter, consistent with expectations for ultra-diffuse galaxies.
"Our results are consistent with previous studies and what they have shown about dark matter in this ultra-diffuse galaxy. We are measuring it with a completely new tool, demonstrating that this method also works beyond our own galaxy," says Julie Kiel Holm.
Extending Dark Matter Studies to Other Galaxies
Although the research centers on just one galaxy, the method could eventually have much wider applications. Demonstrating that globular cluster stellar streams can be studied beyond the Milky Way could allow astronomers to investigate dark matter in many different types of galaxies.
"The insights into dark matter that we have previously been able to gain from globular cluster stellar streams have been limited to a single galaxy - our own. Being able to observe these streams in entirely different kinds of galaxies opens the door to using them to build a much broader understanding of how dark matter behaves," says Julie Kiel Holm.
Researchers expect the number of detectable globular cluster stellar streams to rise dramatically as observatories such as the Euclid Space Telescope and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope provide new views of faint galaxies and stellar structures.
About the study
- The study reports the first detection of a globular cluster stellar stream outside the Milky Way.
- The researchers also show that these streams can be used to constrain both the dark matter halo mass and the dark matter density profile of galaxies beyond our own.
- The study has been published in Nature.
- The following authors contributed to the study: Julie Kiel Holm, Sarah Pearson, Jacob Nibauer, David J. Sand, Adrian M. Price-Whelan, Tjitske Starkenburg, David Hendel and Catherine Fielder.
- The study is funded by the Villum Foundation and the European Research Council.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Copenhagen. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Julie Kiel Holm, Sarah Pearson, Jacob Nibauer, David J. Sand, Adrian M. Price-Whelan, Tjitske Starkenburg, David Hendel, Catherine Fielder. Evidence for the first globular cluster stellar stream beyond the Milky Way. Nature, 2026; 656 (8129): 843 DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10878-w

Tomchyshak was among 103 battle-hardened squad commanders pulled from the front line by Ukraine’s military and put through an intensive three-month course this summer aimed at increasing their effectiveness as leaders.
As Russia wages its war in Ukraine, the Ukrainian army is trying to transform itself – not just in terms of technological innovation, but also in its culture and leadership.
That means dismantling a Soviet-era culture of rigid, top-down command and encouraging more initiative from battle-tested troops.
Despite innovating its way through more than four years of war to hold back a bigger, better-armed enemy, Ukraine’s military has faced criticism for heavy losses in some units and poor treatment of some troops – factors blamed by some for discouraging men from joining the military.
Expectations are high that the new commander-in-chief, 43-year-old General Mykhailo Drapatyi, will deliver on his pledge to promote better command practices and prioritise soldiers’ lives.
Many of the men and women on the course are in their twenties and early thirties.
It aims to train a younger generation of leaders – already expert in infantry tactics, drone warfare, artillery and logistics – to make autonomous decisions on the battlefield.
Crowded around a map covered in tokens denoting military units, a dozen commanders are war-gaming how to repel a Russian assault on a village.
A roll of a dice decides whether operations succeed or fail, forcing them to improvise and communicate with colleagues.
Run by the Military Institute of Kyiv National University and partly financed by charity Come Back Alive, the Captain’s Course has trained more than 1,200 officers since it was launched during the first year of the war.
With Ukraine struggling to draft frontline troops, the emphasis is on preserving manpower, said Artem Chukharev, a 23-year-old sergeant in the Territorial Defence Forces.
This is in stark contrast to Russian infantry assaults that have come at a high human cost.
“We simply cannot afford to treat them the way our age-old enemy does,” Chukharev said, praising the course for encouraging commanders to take informed decisions.
“I finally realised what an officer is, and what he should be like.”
The programme is not easy.
Although 88 commanders graduated on July 18, 15 students did not – two for health reasons and the remainder for academic shortcomings.
Old habits
Battlefield flexibility is not a traditional feature of Ukraine’s military.
Despite efforts to modernise after Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014, Soviet-style attitudes have persisted among some senior officers trained at traditional top-brass institutes, said battalion commander “Houston”, asking to be identified only by his military call sign.
“Officers there are immediately instilled with a certain hatred toward sergeants and soldiers,” said Houston, a career soldier who signed up long before the war, unlike much of Ukraine’s 800,000-strong military.
Drapatyi took over as commander-in-chief in July from 61-year-old Oleksandr Syrskyi, whose critics said he tolerated heavy losses and imposed a heavy-handed style, micromanaging the 1,200km front line.
In September, Drapatyi held a high-level meeting with senior sergeants to discuss ways to empower the NCO corps.
“A sergeant was a soldier himself yesterday. Today, he is the commander who is closest to the soldier,” he said. “They are the ones who care about the interests and needs of the ordinary soldier first and foremost.”
Ukraine’s armed forces, in response to questions for this article, said Drapatyi had published a list of problems to be addressed after the meeting – including an expansion of powers for non-commissioned officers, a clearer command structure and better pay.
Work on solving the problems was underway, it said.
Drapatyi has promoted several senior commanders known for embracing NATO-style command culture – including Andriy Biletsky, who commands the Third Army Corps - to oversee critical parts of Ukraine’s eastern defences.
‘Never stand still’
With new technology rapidly changing the nature of warfare, the course pushes commanders “to constantly seek out and find new solutions, adapt old solutions, modify them, modernise them,” Chukharev said. “But never stand still.”
Tomchyshak, who did not comment on the reforms at the highest level of the military, said that showing initiative was still often punished, particularly among sergeants.
Letting local commanders take more of the initiative would hand Ukraine an advantage on the battlefield, he said, especially over an enemy known for treating its troops poorly.
“We would begin to see radical change,” he said. REUTERS
