Ukrainian Drone Forces Target 38 Energy Sites in Mid-September, Bringing Total to 412
Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces (SBS) have targeted 412 energy infrastructure sites in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories and inside Russia since launching the “Crimean Switch Off” operation in July, SBS Commander Robert “Madyar” Brovdi reported on September 22.
According to Brovdi, Ukrainian drone units carried out the strikes between July 6 and September 22, targeting energy infrastructure supporting Russian operations across temporarily occupied territories and Russia. The campaign comes in response to continued Russian strikes on Ukraine, including attacks on the country’s energy infrastructure.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
During the second ten-day period of September alone, USF units successfully targeted another 38 energy facilities. These included 10 sites in temporarily occupied Crimea, nine in the occupied part of Donetsk region, 13 in the occupied part of Luhansk region, four inside Russia, and one each in the Kharkiv and Zaporizhzhia regions.
Among the facilities targeted were several major electrical substations, including the 220-kV Krasnodonska substation near Prokhladne in the Luhansk region and the 220-kV Amvrosiivka substation in the Donetsk region. Other reported targets included 110-kV substations near Kypuche, Selidove, and Bilovodsk.
Inside Russia, Ukrainian drone units targeted the 110-kV Bolshaya Chern and Znamenskaya substations in the Oryol region, as well as other energy infrastructure.
The operation has also focused on gas infrastructure in occupied Crimea. Brovdi reported strikes against gas distribution stations at Orlivka, Bakhchysarai, Bilohirsk, Kyr-Bailar, Kholmivka, Hornostaivka, Klepynine, and Islam-Terek, with the Kholmivka facility targeted more than once.
Other reported targets included the Kreidyanka gas distribution station in Russia, the Rodakove gas distribution station in the occupied Luhansk region, and the Tasunove compressor station in Crimea.
Multiple SBS formations are involved in the operation, including the 414th “Madyar’s Birds,” 412th “Nemesis,” 9th, 20th “K-2,” and 429th “Achilles” Separate Unmanned Systems Brigades, as well as the 413th “Raid” Brigade, 427th “Rarog” Brigade, the USF’s 1st Separate Center, and the Phoenix unit of Ukraine’s State Border Guard Service.
The campaign is part of broader SBS operations targeting Russian infrastructure. On September 22, Brovdi also reported that Ukrainian forces had disabled 300 vessels belonging to Russia’s so-called shadow fleet in the Azov and Black seas over an 11-week period.
The reported strikes were carried out as part of Operation “MoLoChKa,” another SBS campaign that has been underway since July 6.

US Democrats to introduce bill sanctioning individuals involved in Israel's E1 settlement project
Unknown

2026-09-23
10:51:05 UTC
19:51:05 KST

A group of US Senate Democrats will introduce legislation on Wednesday to sanction individuals or groups that facilitate Israel's "E1 project," a widely condemned West Bank settlement plan cutting across land the Palestinians seek for a state, according to a copy of the legislation seen by Reuters.
The introduction of the bill is the latest sign of growing friction between Democrats in Congress and the Israeli government over its handling of the West Bank, with many in the party - and a few Republicans - calling for curbs on US military aid to Israel over its conduct of the war in Gaza.
US Democratic lawmakers have also recently urged Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to rein in violence by West Bank settlers and mass arrests of Palestinians by Israeli security forces in the area.
The measure's lead sponsors are Chris Coons of Delaware, Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, Ron Wyden of Oregon, and Ruben Gallego of Arizona.
"As Palestinian civilians face a campaign of devastation and fear from violent extremist settlers, the United States must send a strong message that this behavior is unacceptable and that it remains committed to freedom, security, prosperity and self-determination for all Israelis and Palestinians," Coons said in a statement.
Democrats control minority of Senate, could win majority in midterms
The bill has at least 10 co-sponsors, all Democrats.
Democrats currently control only 47 seats in the 100-member Senate, but polls show they could win majorities in November 3 midterm elections from US President Donald Trump's Republicans, who have aligned themselves closely with Netanyahu.
The bill would impose sanctions on foreign companies, individuals, or other entities that the Treasury Department determines to have been responsible for or complicit in the construction of any Israeli settlements or related structures in the E1 area of the West Bank, including by submitting a bid for E1 tenders.
It also would sanction those who attempt to organize, direct, finance, or facilitate the transfer of Israeli civilians into settlements in the E1 area.
Approval of the E1 project, which would bisect the West Bank and cut it off from east Jerusalem, was announced in August 2025 by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.
Two-state solution could be undermined by E1 project
The two-state solution to the decades-old Israeli-Palestinian conflict envisages a Palestinian state in east Jerusalem, the West Bank, and Gaza, existing side by side with Israel.
Western capitals and campaign groups have opposed the E1 settlement project due to concerns that it could undermine a future peace deal with the Palestinians and diminish the chance for the two-state solution.
Most of the international community considers Israeli settlements in the West Bank illegal under international law.
Israel disputes this, citing historical and biblical ties to the area and saying the settlements provide strategic depth and security.
Congress's lower chamber, the US House of Representatives, is currently not in session, so even in the unlikely chance of the bill's passage in the Senate, the House would not be expected to take it up before the midterms.

jenny holzer’s truisms and the power of the public screen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:50:42 UTC
19:50:42 KST

When Jenny Holzer put Truisms on a Times Square billboard
In 1982, sentences appeared between advertisements on a giant electronic billboard in Times Square. PRIVATE PROPERTY CREATED CRIME. TORTURE IS BARBARIC. ABUSE OF POWER COMES AS NO SUPRISE. They were not selling anything, offering directions, or announcing a new product. Jenny Holzer had placed her Truisms inside the Spectacolor board, turning one of New York’s most conspicuous commercial surfaces into a vehicle for ambiguous, confrontational statements.
The gesture was sharp because Holzer used the visual language used for advertising — the scale, movement and glow of the billboard remaining the same, but instead of selling a product, it delivered short, unsettling statements. For a few seconds, a space designed for advertising became a place to encounter language.
More than forty years later, Holzer’s Wrong Answers at the Serralves Museum of Contemporary Art in Porto revisits some of the same ideas in a very different media landscape. Screens are no longer unusual or concentrated in a few places. They are part of buildings, streets, public transport, and the phones we carry every day. In 1982, Holzer was finding a way to put critical language on the commercial screen. Today, the challenge is making people stop and read it. Holzer has spent her career testing what happens when words are taken out of books and put into the world around us. They appear on walls, buildings, stone, lightboxes, and screens, changing the way we encounter and read them.
Holzer’s move toward the electronic screen was preceded by years of experimentation with how language could inhabit the city. Beginning in 1977, she pasted Truisms across New York on sheets of paper. The statements were anonymous, direct and deliberately difficult to classify. Some sounded like political slogans, others like conventional wisdom, threats, advertisements or fragments of philosophical argument. On a city wall, the words did not arrive with the institutional framing of a museum. They were encountered while walking, waiting, shopping or just passing through.
Holzer soon began testing what happened when the material changed. Her Living series transferred language onto bronze plaques, giving subjective observations the visual authority of civic markers. The text remained, but its status shifted. Paper suggested the temporary and unofficial; bronze suggested permanence, history and institutional weight.
The Spectacolor board took that experiment into the architecture of mass communication. The system Holzer used consisted of thousands of incandescent bulbs arranged as a large matrix, capable of displaying simple animated images and text. Through the public art project Messages to the Public (1982-1990), artists were given access to a surface otherwise dedicated to advertising. Holzer’s intervention lasted only seconds within a much longer commercial sequence. The work appeared where an advertisement was expected to appear. Passersby looking up at Times Square encountered something that initially behaved like an advertisement but refused to resolve into one. The billboard became a space for reading.
The conditions that made the Spectacolor intervention so effective have changed. In 1982, a giant electronic billboard was unusual enough to command attention. Today, Times Square is surrounded by screens, while the individual viewer carries another one in their pocket. Advertising has moved from broadcast messages addressed to everyone toward systems that target individuals through data, algorithms and personalized feeds. The commercial screen is part of the atmosphere. That changes the possibilities for artistic intervention.
Holzer’s Wrong Answers in Porto, installed across Serralves, brings together paper works, stone inscriptions, LED installations and newer pieces responding to contemporary political communication. The works create different conditions for reading, moving between the permanence of stone and the instability of electronic text.
In READY FOR YOU (2023–25), contemporary political language becomes particularly difficult to separate from the media systems that circulate it. The work incorporates material connected to Donald Trump alongside AI-generated transformations, reflecting an information environment in which political statements are endlessly reproduced, altered and accelerated. Here, the problem is no longer that critical language cannot access the screen, but that the screen is already full.
The Truisms appeared on the Spectacolor billboard for only a few seconds before the next commercial message took over. That brevity was part of their character. You could catch a sentence, think about it, and then it was gone. The situation is very different now. Screens no longer need to fight for attention because they are already woven into almost every part of daily life. There is always another image, headline, notification or message waiting behind the one in front of us. This is also why Holzer’s use of different materials remains important.
At Serralves, the words move between paper, stone, paint and LED. A text printed on a sheet of paper has a different presence from one carved into stone; an LED message can appear and disappear before you have had time to take it in. The exhibition makes these differences tangible. You walk closer to some works and pass others at a distance. Some stay with you; others are gone almost as soon as you have read them.
Holzer has been doing this for decades, changing not only the words but the places and materials through which they reach us. The setting is never quite neutral. A poster on a city wall, a sentence on a bronze plaque, or a message glowing across a screen each carries a different kind of weight. In 1982, the unexpected thing was finding Holzer’s words on a billboard. Today, the unexpected thing may be finding enough quiet to read them.

Estonia, Canada convene first Canada-NB8 ministerial meeting
Estonia and Canada convened the first Canada-Nordic-Baltic Eight (NB8) ministerial meeting in New York Tuesday, bringing together foreign ministers from eight countries.
The ministers, in New York for the UN General Assembly, reaffirmed support for Ukraine, opposition to changing borders by force, and coordination on Baltic Sea, North Atlantic and Arctic security.
Estonia's Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) and his Canadian counterpart Anita Anand convened the meeting with the foreign ministers of Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, Norway and Sweden on Tuesday .
During the meeting, the Nordic-Baltic countries and Canada reaffirmed their commitment to the rules-based international order, international law and the UN Charter.
They said they stand united against any attempt to change borders by force and will continue close coordination in the context of the UN, OSCE and NATO and with the EU, to uphold these principles and ensure accountability.
The ministers reaffirmed that EU-Canada relations support shared goals on trade diversification, supply chains and strategic partnerships, and highlighted Canada's role in European security, including through its agreement with the EU to participate in the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) instrument.
Together, Canada and the NB8 reaffirmed their common interests in the Euro-Atlantic region. Ministers stressed that the Baltic Sea, the North Atlantic and the Arctic are interconnected elements of allied security, noting the importance of responding to Russian threats to critical infrastructure, including energy, and hybrid activities across these regions.
The ministers reaffirmed their unwavering support for Ukraine for as long as it takes and steadfast support for Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity. They committed to continued coordination to ensure their efforts remain effective, complementary and responsive to Ukraine's evolving needs, and emphasized the importance of restoring a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in Ukraine. They reiterated Ukraine's call for Russia to agree to a full and immediate ceasefire.
Ministers also underscored the need to sustain international pressure on Russia to cease its aggression, with particular attention to repeated strikes on civilians and civilian infrastructure. Canada welcomed the participation of senior NB8 delegations at the September 28–29 Pathways to Peace conference in Toronto on returning Ukrainian children, detained civilians and prisoners of war.

They identified concrete opportunities to deepen practical cooperation on defense industrial cooperation, maritime security, critical infrastructure protection and economic security, and discussed strengthening collective security and readiness, including efforts to counter hybrid threats and foreign information manipulation.
The leaders agreed to remain in close contact, regularly convene in the Canada-NB8 format, and continue advancing shared security, defense and resilience priorities under Norway's forthcoming NB8 chairmanship.

The reality behind Trump’s misleading UN address
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:49:15 UTC
19:49:15 KST

The reality behind Trump’s misleading UN address
TEHRAN — Donald Trump’s address to the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly was a cascade of verifiable falsehoods, internal logical collapses, and explicit threats of destruction.
Speaking from the podium of an institution founded to prevent aggressive war, the American president presented world leaders with a binary ultimatum regarding Iran: accept unilateral submission or face total physical erasure.
Ten minutes into the speech, the Iranian diplomatic delegation stood up and walked out of the hall. They left behind a single junior representative sitting stone-faced in an empty row.
The Cuban delegation exited shortly after when Trump branded their government a failed state.
The walkout was a deliberate refusal to validate an argument grounded in coercion rather than international law.
Outside the UN complex near Dag Hammarskjöld Plaza, protesters clashed with New York police while chanting against U.S. military aggression, carrying placards denouncing Trump, including one that read, “TRUMP is a WAR CRIMINAL.”
The nuclear 'obliteration' lie and the asymmetric reality
Trump’s primary justification for the nearly seven-month-old war against Iran relies on a claim he has repeated since June 2025.
"Operation Midnight Hammer," he insisted, "obliterated" Iran's nuclear program "beneath mountains of rubble."
That statement collapses under the weight of Washington’s own timeline.
Leaked Defense Intelligence Agency assessments and International Atomic Energy Agency claims following the June 2025 strikes confirmed that hardened facilities such as Fordow suffered structural damage, not total destruction.
By February 2026, Trump himself cited resumed Iranian uranium enrichment as his explicit justification to launch the current campaign of aggression.
A program permanently erased in 2025 cannot serve as the rationale for launching a massive military campaign in 2026.
His assertions regarding conventional military damage follow the same pattern.
Trump claimed that the war launched on February 20206 sank "all 159 ships" of "Iran's navy" while "erasing" its air force, radar networks, air defenses, and missile production.
CENTCOM claimed destroying roughly 17 surface ships in the war's initial weeks. But conventional surface warships have never formed the core of Iranian maritime strategy.
For 30 years, Tehran designed its defense around asymmetric survival.
The doctrine relies on the Islamic Revolution Guard Corps Navy, operating mobile shore-based anti-ship missile batteries, fast attack craft, and extensive naval mining capabilities embedded along mountainous terrain, now combined with the effective strength of the IRGC Aerospace Force equipped with various types of state-of-the-art missiles and drones.
Degrading conventional surface ships does not mean the Iranian navy was destroyed.
As for Iran’s missile prowess, months of missile attacks on U.S. bases across the region have demonstrated that its missile forces remain an effective and operational component of its military power.
Hormuz escorts and the munitions shortage contradiction
If Iran's naval capabilities were truly resting on the seabed, Washington would not be forced to deploy naval escorts to protect commercial energy shipments.
Trump boasted that the U.S. Navy has escorted over one billion barrels of oil through the Strait of Hormuz, moving groups of "up to 37 ships" every day and night.
The claim refutes his own argument. A state whose maritime defenses have been erased does not have the ability to move global energy markets and does not require daily naval convoys to pass through a strategic choke point.
Trump’s claims regarding military logistics proved equally contradictory.
He attacked critics who highlighted U.S. ammunition shortages, calling them "cowards and traitors" and claiming America possesses "more munitions than we could ever possibly even think of using."
He then announced that 18 massive new munition plants are currently under construction across the United States.
Both statements cannot be true. A nation possessing inexhaustible stockpiles does not undertake an emergency industrial expansion in the middle of a war.
Reports from the Pentagon’s Inspector General and defense analysts outside the Pentagon confirm that seven months of intense missile strikes against Iranian targets, alongside ongoing arms transfers to Israel and Ukraine, have severely depleted critical stocks of precision-guided munitions and air-defense interceptors, including Tomahawk cruise missiles and PAC-3 air-defense interceptors.
The U.S. military has been forced to expend multi-million-dollar interceptors against low-cost drones and conventional missiles.
The construction of 18 new facilities is an admission of industrial exhaustion under a sustained war of attrition.
'Strategic desperation' of 'a deranged sociopath'
The central foreign policy statement of the address supposedly offered Iran a choice between capitulation and destruction.
"Do I annihilate the Islamic Republic," Trump asked, promising to drive the nation "into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations."
Delivered before the United Nations, this language directly violates Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, which strictly prohibits threats or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state.
Legal analysts have noted that explicitly threatening the total destruction of nation meets the threshold of genocidal intent defined under the Rome Statute and the UN Genocide Convention.
Trump added a bizarre domestic calculation to this threat, predicting that Tehran would sign a deal "right after the election" because Iranian leaders were "waiting to see how I do in the midterm election."
He then corrected himself mid-sentence, noting that he is not running in the midterms.
The slip revealed a profound misreading of Iranian defense strategy. Iranian national security policy is not calibrated around American congressional election cycles.
Iran and the Resistance Front operate on a long-term structural defense against the hegemony of the U.S. and Israel and their proxies, regardless of which American political party holds majorities in Washington.
Reactions to the speech were swift and scathing.
In Tehran, Iran’s General Staff and Central Khatam al-Anbiya Headquarters dismissed Trump’s remarks as “a tool for domestic propaganda,” arguing that repeated threats reflected U.S. “strategic deadlock” and military exhaustion rather than strength.
They said the rhetoric showed “strategic desperation” and warned that Iran’s armed forces were prepared to respond with “even harsher, more devastating, and unpredictable blows.”
Media commentator Brett Erickson called Trump "a global embarrassment to the United States," adding that "taking 30 minutes at the UN General Assembly to spew hatred, nonsense, and propaganda" was "single-handedly dismantling American credibility."
Independent American journalist Glenn Greenwald highlighted the shifting pretexts of American interventionism, pointing out how administration narratives shifted from liberation to open aggression once initial arguments dissolved.
Political analyst Andy Ostroy responded bluntly: "Only a deranged sociopath would make a comment like this."
Imperial plunder in Caracas, Greenland, and Gaza
Trump abandoned diplomatic euphemism when describing U.S. military interventions elsewhere in the world.
Discussing the U.S. military operation in Caracas that led to the capture of President Nicolás Maduro and the deaths of more than 100 Venezuelans and Cubans, Trump cited the deal covering 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil, summarizing his doctrine in five shameless words: “To the victor belong the spoils.”
That statement constitutes an explicit admission of state piracy. Pillage and the expropriation of sovereign economic assets from subjugated nations are explicit war crimes under the Geneva Conventions.
Combined with his announcement of an agreement granting the U.S. permanent security control and two major military bases in Greenland, the Venezuela declaration exposes American strategy as an unvarnished effort to seize global energy and territorial assets.
Trump applied the same transactional framing to Palestine, claiming he had "ended the war in Gaza" through a 20-point plan and an international "Board of Peace" chaired by himself.
The claim ignores the reality on the ground. Since the so-called ceasefire and implementation of Trump’s plan began in October 2025, more than 1,394 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, while the Strip continues to face widespread destruction, severe shortages and acute humanitarian needs.
Trump’s "Board of Peace" includes no Palestinian representation, functioning instead as a colonial management mechanism designed to bypass Palestinian self-determination and replace statehood with foreign administration funded by Arab states in the Persian Gulf.
Collapsing domestic consensus and global rejection
Trump’s attempt to project absolute global dominance comes at a moment when domestic support for his foreign policy is rapidly eroding.
A CNN poll released on the day of his speech revealed that 71 percent of Americans disapprove of his handling of foreign affairs, a record high across both of his terms. Only 26 percent of Americans approve of his handling of the war against Iran.
78 percent believe he is not doing enough to end the conflict, while 76 percent conclude that the human and financial costs of the war, which has already exceeded $45 billion in direct Pentagon spending and over $132 billion in broader economic damage, are not worth it.
Republican approval for his Iran policy dropped from 73 percent in March to sixty percent in September.
Trump arrived at the United Nations demanding complete global isolation for Iran and asserting total victory across multiple war zones.
The facts on the ground tell a different story. The war in the Persian Gulf remains active, U.S. military stockpiles are straining under attrition, global energy markets are disrupted, and domestic public opinion has turned decisively against Trump’s war on Iran.

Chief of the Air Staff, Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth's speech at the UK Space Power Conference
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:47:54 BST
19:47:54 KST

Chief of the Air Staff, Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth's speech at the UK Space Power Conference
Chief of the Air Staff, Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth delivered the opening keynote of the UK Space Power Conference, setting out how the UK will defend its interests in space.
Well, good morning, everyone. I think I am in control of the PowerPoint. There we go. The Minister has just said to me it’s boiling up there so I’m glad I wore my woollen Spitfire suit.
It’s really good to see so many distinguished guests, colleagues, allies and friends here and welcome to the UK Space Power Conference here in what is a relatively unexpected sunny London, which is great. It’s so good to see lots of familiar faces in the audience – I’m slightly worried that there’s a sea of light blue at the back there to hold me to account on what I’m about to say.
But I’m particularly glad to see so many new faces and to meet so many new characters from across the space enterprise, scientists, academics, industry experts. We’ve got some leaders in finance and of course, there is a good group here from across government. So thank you all for supporting the conference. I really do from a personal perspective, I appreciate that.
I stood here just a few months ago alongside many of my fellow international air and space chiefs at what was the Global Air and Space Chiefs Conference. And then I outlined how the RAF is now formally on a journey to becoming Europe’s first sixth generation air force with the Global Combat Air Programme and now our new Collaborative Combat Air programme, the Storm Fighter, operating alongside F-35, Typhoons and a range of many other autonomous systems. But these capabilities will never fulfil their potential without space. And that’s why these conferences and this discussion over the next two days are so very important.
From my perspective, I don’t think I can get to a sixth-generation air force if I still have a fourth-generation space force. And that is a topic that I’m hoping we can cover over discussions in the coming two days. Space is obviously a prerequisite for modern air power. Every element of a sixth-generation air force depends intimately on space, the networks, the targeting, the navigation, the command and control.
Space is no longer just simply supporting air power from the sidelines. It is completely embedded within it. It is essential. It’s actually part of the DNA and you don’t have to scratch too far to see that. And space is no less relevant to the other domains. The effective use of space is critical to the ability of our new integrated force to understand, to communicate, to move and to fight. And as we learn critical lessons from ongoing conflicts in places like Ukraine and the Middle East, it is clear that a pivot to uncrewed systems is required at pace.
And of course, if we’re going to do this, an uncrewed force is broadly a space-dependent force, once again reinforcing the importance of this vital domain to defence. We often refer to space as the ultimate high ground, through which the integrated force gains a decisive operational edge, enabling it to act with greater speed, better precision, and overall better effectiveness. It is an advantage we must maintain, and if possible, deny to our adversaries.
Space services are not just the invisible thread between our ships at sea, our soldiers on the land and our aircraft in the skies. They now completely underpin our whole approach to strategic deterrence, command and control, and decision advantage. And more broadly, across the fabric of our society, space underpins our modern way of life.
Just coming here, being linked to space told me, if I don’t hurry up, I’m going to be late. And the Air and Space Commander was panicking, thinking he was going to have to do this keynote. It’s been six years since I was appointed as the first director of space for the MOD, as Anu mentioned. Space was an important topic then, but I would argue now it is a critical matter which must be better understood and better championed across the whole of government, specifically if we are serious about our approach to modern deterrence. It is our responsibility to make sure that everyone in defence knows that the integrated force will not succeed without space. Space must become embedded in how defence generates and operates force.
To reflect this, the Royal Air Force’s headquarters at RAF High Wycombe transitioned to become Air and Space Command just a few weeks ago. I’m sure some of you saw that announcement. This is more than just a simple name change. We are demonstrating that space is no longer just a supporting function. Space is now seen as a warfighting domain in its own right and with equal importance to the other domains.
It is a contested, congested and competitive environment where our operational edge and strategic advantage can be won but can also be very quickly and easily lost. Space can no longer be delayed, no longer deferred, or delegated. It must now be delivered and that has been my big message into our own department on this topic.
But importantly it cannot be delivered via national means only and we know in UK we cannot do this alone and I’m delighted that we are joined today by so many international colleagues from around the globe. Our greatest strength is our coalition of space partners spanning the world, an alliance that is envied and feared in equal measure by our potential adversaries, with all members bringing different capabilities from unique geography to unique on-orbit assets, making our collective security greater than the sum of the space parts.
In the UK, NATO is of course our most critical alliance. And whilst we are building sovereign space capabilities, these will always be part of a NATO force, always part of our strategic deterrence approach. NATO led the way by recognising space as a domain in 2019. And two years later, NATO expanded the scope of our collective defence policy, making it clear that attacks to, from, or within space present a clear threat to the alliance and could possibly trigger an Article 5. This was a major statement of intent. In short, an attack on one of us in space is an attack on all of us, just as it is in the other, more traditional domains.
And whilst UK strategy is NATO first, we are not only NATO. Earlier this April, I went to Colorado to meet with my counterparts from 10 other nations, from the USA in the West to New Zealand in the East for the Principals Board of the Combined Space Operations Initiative, or CSpO. There we agreed to redouble our efforts to deliver capabilities in support of combined space operations, creating a web of global space power, generating and delivering mutually supportive capabilities that no adversary can match. Again, a fundamental approach to our collective deterrence posture.
And central to this is Multinational Force Operation Olympic Defender. This is now our primary international operational framework within which we deliver responsible, combined space operations, and these are happening on a very routine basis at this very moment.
Last September, we delivered the first ever UK-US space operation under the banner of OOD. We completed a Rendezvous Proximity Operation in geostationary orbit, moving one of our SKYNET satellites close to a satellite operated by US Space Command. 35,776 kilometres from Earth’s surface, to be precise. These satellites were traveling at 11,000 kilometres per hour. That’s 3 kilometres per second. So, a collision would most definitely be catastrophic, creating substantial, long-standing debris in an orbit that is congested, full of critical assets.
That is why operations like this must only ever be delivered with the utmost of care, with the utmost of precision, communication, expertise and most importantly, collaboration and agreement. When another nation manoeuvres their satellite close to ours without collaboration, that is unacceptable. It is dangerous and it is unprofessional. It is no different than flying an aircraft to within 50 feet of my aircraft without coordination.
Unfortunately, we are now seeing more and more irresponsible and provocative actions from our adversaries in flagrant disregard of the norms for responsible behaviour by space-faring nations. In May of this year, we tracked a series of unusual and significant manoeuvres by 5 Russian military satellites, moving to within rapid reach of two finished commercial satellites. These manoeuvres were uncommon and dangerous, raising serious questions about Russia’s intent in space. And the next month, in June, it was confirmed that a Russian satellite constellation had caused disruptions to GPS signals across the breadth of Europe, Greenland and Canada over at least 75 days since 2019.
We all know and we all rely on GPS. It’s an excellent system operated by our colleagues in the US Space Force. It is used by billions of people and industries around the world and of course it’s used by many global military forces. Major disruption to GPS would cost the UK economy to the tune of £1.4 billion of impact every day. Sat-Nav systems would fail, congestion on the roads would create havoc. Our emergency services would take much, much longer to reach those in need.
So make no mistake, the satellite services you may have taken for granted now face unprecedented threats. And losing these services, be it the Sat-Nav that keeps ups moving, the timing signals for financial transactions, the Earth observation that allows us to monitor the weather or the effects of climate change. All of this would make every sector sitting in this room less efficient, less prosperous and less secure.
Our adversaries know this. They are developing sophisticated space systems and they have both the capability and the intent to use them. Last year, and most of you will know this handsome chap, last year, the commander of UK Space Command, Tedders (ret. Major General Paul Tedman) here today. He’s not. He knew I was putting this picture up. So our previous commander of UK Space Command denied that Russia is attempting to jam UK military satellites with ground-based systems every week. At the same time, Germany’s defence minister said that Russia had been shadowing their military satellites. Alongside grey zone activity across all domains, space is a region of growing strategic competition. Space has become a warfighting domain, whether we like that or not. And the UK, as well as its partners and allies, must be prepared for this.
Fortunately, this is now recognised across government here in the UK. And in June of last year, we had the Strategic Defence Review, it outlined that space remains a critical national infrastructure sector. Space underpins 20% of the UK’s GDP. In real money, that’s almost £500 billion. But it is also a site of growing competition. The SDR set out the MOD’s requirement to invest in space control decision advantage, reconnaissance, navigation, and timing signals. And if the SDR set out what we in defence would call the ends, this year’s defence investment plan set out our means.
And I just heard the Minister for Space talk about the DIP. £9 billion of new space capability already earmarked for 2030 to 2035. And from this year to 2030, £2.3 billion for satellite communications, £880 million for space-based ISR and space control, and a further £440 million for novel space technology. And now we have a new UK Space Strategy issued just this month. A strategy that outlines how the UK government will act as one regards space, making our nation a competitive space power, assertive in protecting our interests and driving our own economic growth. To protect the nation and also to help it prosper is MOD’s aim.
Space has never been more important for our nation’s defence and security, for our prosperity and our daily lives. And our adversaries are not waiting until we’re ready for them. We must now get on with delivery of space capability and operational effect at pace. At the heart of the UK space arsenal and a major offer to our global alliance is Skynet and many of you in this room will know of our Skynet programme and the capability that offers. It’s the backbone of UK’s sovereign global comms capability and provides command and control for our entire integrated force.
And I’m grateful that the Defence Investment Plan allocated an additional £50 million to extend the life of our in-service SKYNET 5 satellites. And these will be joined next year with the launch of our new SKYNET 6 series, SKYNET 6A. While our demand for SATCOM only increases, and as threats in space grow more serious, SKYNET will be supplemented with allied and commercial SATCOM services. These will provide additional capacity, coverage, and resilience, with resilience being the keyword. Using both SKYNET and commercial SATCOM, UK armed forces will be able to make and communicate decisions quickly around the world. And this is an incredibly important keystone of our quest for decision superiority in today’s modern warfare.
And the decision-making of our integrated force will be further improved by space-based intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance. Through our ISTARI programme, we’re delivering a constellation of satellites to provide a multi-sensor, multi-spectral capability to observe activity on the Earth, day or night, heat wave or snowstorm. One of these satellites, the Tyche, is now in space. Over the next two years, three more will be launched: Titania with in-space missions, Juno with SSTL, and Oberon with Airbus Defence Space.
ISTARI will feed our nascent digital targeting web, which in itself has been allocated £1.8 billion under the DIP, an initiative which will truly make our armed forces a single integrated force, connecting sensors, deciders, and effectors driving speed and how we decide to degrade or destroy an identified target in any domain underpinned by world leading AI and software. Our integrated force also relies on these services, so we must monitor them.
We deliver this through world leading sensors, both military and commercial, on the ground and in space. and many of you will recognise these pictures, including RAF Fylingdales, the UK’s primary military space sensor, and the only three-faced and foreign-operated radar in the US space surveillance network. Alongside Fylingdales, we will have our new deep space advanced radar capability, the DARC, a trilateral programme with sites in Australia, the UK, and the USA, enabling us to detect, identify, and trap objects in the deepest of orbits.
But Fylingdales and DARC aren’t simply radars. They too are part of the integrated battle management architecture, forming part of defence’s pervasive multi-domain sensor network. NOCTIS 2, the first sovereign UK sensor for our National Space Ops Centre, or the NSPOC, declared fully operational capability this year. This high-precision optical sensor system, developed in partnership with Spaceflux, is now observing the vital satellites we rely on for military ops around the world. NOCTIS 1 will be soon followed by NOCTIS 2, another advanced sensor which will achieve even higher rates of precision and fidelity.
And we are building the infrastructure for these sensors to be modular, changeable and transportable. So we can swap out and move them as strategic demand evolves. This way, our space domain awareness capabilities would be agile, integrated and ready to support the integrated force anywhere in the world. And unsurprisingly, we will establish more advanced sensors to enhance our SDA using cutting edge technology.
This includes neuromorphic sensors which will help search for unexpected activity around our own satellites. Neuromorphic technology will allow us to monitor large volumes of space with drastically reduced power consumption, latency and data bandwidth, allowing us to detect events in orbit whilst increasing both our global sensor footprint and our observation capability.
However, it isn’t all about the sovereign sensors and what we’re building within the military. Commercial data procured from our industry partners will always be part of the hybrid, flexible and resilient SDA effort. This year, many of us will have avidly and I’m sure excitedly kept on top of the groundbreaking Artemis II mission. The first crewed Artemis flight and the first lunar flyby since 1972. Our team in the NSPOC using data from Spaceflux tracked this historic mission, demonstrating easily just how we can monitor significant events in orbit using the sensors and the data from our space industry partners.
The value of commercial data for our space domain awareness is shown day in and day out by the Joint Commercial Ops Initiative, the JCO. The JCO programme now encompasses over 20 nations with the JCO UK team and UK Space Command leading the Meridian region between the Americas to our west and the Pacific to our east. JCO teams worldwide are providing unclassified information on activity in orbit, strengthening integration with the commercial sector and integrating public information into military operations. But this SDA will be of limited value unless we can convert it into effective decision making. And so this year, our BOREALIS command, control and data processing system developed by CJI as part of a five-year, £65 million contract reached initial operating capability six months ahead of schedule. I don’t often get to say that.
This system used by No.1 Space Ops Squadron in the NSPOC is providing timely, quality information to government and military commanders, allowing us to make effective decisions and provide operational understanding of the space domain to the whole of the integrated force. Through all of these capabilities, space is now the connective tissue of that integrated force and we must protect these vital capabilities from the threats we see growing every day. This month’s new UK Space Strategy outlined the UK’s Control of Space requirement.
Through a whole of government approach, the UK will safeguard allied space interests, we will gain and maintain our freedom to operate in space, and we will deny our adversaries that same freedom.
But we are not doing this for its own sake. We’re doing this to enable our own freedom of action and for that of NATO and for our overall security. We’re protecting the command and control of our integrated force by defending global strategic communications and the systems that generate our decision advantage and combat edge. To help our nation fulfill the control of space requirement, UK defence is now developing capabilities for orbital warfare.
This can be described as actions and effects conducted within space to achieve military objectives, electronic warfare and capabilities to counter anti-satellite weapons. Alongside other supporting operations, these capabilities will help us to deter threats, defend our critical space infrastructure and reduce an adversary’s freedom to operate against the UK and against our allies.
To deliver these capabilities, I am incredibly proud today to announce that we are forming No. 3 Space Effects Squadron, UK defence’s first dedicated squadron to deliver operations in support of the UK’s Control of Space mission. No. 3 SES will disrupt, degrade and deny hostile activity to defend UK space interests and gain operational advantage for the integrated force.
The squadron will be staffed by specialist personnel from across defence and will support offensive and defensive space operations, safeguarding the critical space services which are so incredibly precious to us.
But with all of this said, let’s be very clear, and this is particularly important for this audience. No one wants a war in space. We are positioning to deter this. The UK will always operate responsibly in ways that promote stability and avoid escalation.
Alongside our colleagues across government, we aim to promote norms, rules and responsible behaviours in space so that space is preserved as a safe, secure and sustainable domain for prosperity, research and exploration. Our approach to control of space will always be transparent and rooted in international collaboration and norms.
We will never escalate military activity in space, but we must respond responsibly to a rapidly changing environment in which threats to our critical space systems are growing every single day.
UK Space Command and its associated Space Squadrons operating under the newly established HQ Air and Space Command will deliver space power to protect this nation. We already have No. 1 Space Ops Squadron working as part of the NSPOC and No. 2 Space Warning Squadron delivering the operational activity that we all know so well from our RAF Fylingdales. Our new No. 3 Space Effects Squadron will deliver precise, integrated effects to safeguard our national interests in space. And we are planning more. Numbers 4, 5 and 6 Squadrons, including a Space Tactics and Training Squadron, and squadrons which will deliver the deep space advanced radar capability. And a Space Defence function working as part of the newly established Integrated Air, Space and Missile Defence Operations Centre.
The Strategic Defence Review gave us the ends. We’ve discussed that here. The Defence Investment Plan gave us the means, and I’ve talked to some of those numbers. Together though, I think we are all the ways.
And it is time for us to harness our resources. It is time to get moving. It’s time to act. and it’s time to deliver more meaningfully with our space capabilities.
To work with all of you to turn our approved budget lines into real, tangible capability so that we can monitor space, make effective decisions, deter our adversaries, and if necessary, prevail in this vital yet increasingly contested domain.
Thank you very much indeed and thanks again for supporting us.

Risks of creating biological weapons with AI help are real — Brazilian BWC official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:47:27 UTC
19:47:27 KST

MOSCOW, September 23. /TASS/. Risks of creating biological weapons using artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are real, Frederico Meyer, chairman of the Working Group on Strengthening the Convention on the Prohibition of Biological and Toxin Weapons (BWC), said on Wednesday.
According to Meyer, who also serves as permanent representative of Brazil to the Conference on Disarmament (CD), US technology company Anthropic recently announced that it had "detected and prevented several attempts by artificial intelligence to create biological weapons."
"This case illustrates how the combination of artificial intelligence and biotechnology can lower barriers to accessing and applying biological knowledge. At the same time, it boldly demonstrates the dual nature of these technologies," Meyer noted in his opening speech at a seminar on the national implementation of the Convention on the Prohibition of Biological and Toxin Weapons.
According to him, "this is exactly why the BWC must address these tasks in order to maintain and support the achievements of scientific and technical institutions, while ensuring the preservation of capabilities that would not facilitate actions prohibited by the Convention."
"This also highlights the urgency of our work and the importance of achieving positive results at the Working Group’s final session in December," Meyer concluded.

Denmark says Russian invasion of NATO country 'highly unlikely' but cannot be ruled out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
10:48:34 UTC
19:48:34 KST

European countries have been on high alert for any Russian interference, with fears that Moscow could target Kyiv's Western backers as the Kremlin's invasion of Ukraine drags on into its fifth year.
The Danish Defence Intelligence Service (DDIS) said on Thursday that the risk of Russian military action against NATO countries was growing and an outright invasion was "highly unlikely" but possible.
"There is a low but growing risk that Russia will launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries bordering Russia," Thomas Ahrenkiel, the head of the DDIS, told a press conference at which he presented an updated assessment of the threat from Russia.
He said that the agency still considered it "highly unlikely that Russia would see any interest in invading a NATO country, but we cannot rule it out".
In the DDIS assessment, the agency said that Russia would likely carry out more so-called "hybrid attacks" against targets in the West.
It noted that in the past such attacks had "mainly been aimed at creating fear and weakening public support for aid to Ukraine".
But they had now started to include actions meant to stop support from reaching Ukraine, such as sabotage against defence companies or railway transports carrying military equipment, the agency said.
The DDIS said it thought Russia would intensify such attacks, which could also include "destructive cyber attacks that cripple critical societal functions."
The agency also said there was a low risk of a limited military attack even if the war in Ukraine continued, as an attempt to redirect European resources away from Ukraine.
"A limited military attack would be a desperate move on Russia's part and, like the intensified hybrid attacks, could potentially take place in the coming months," the agency said.
However, the DDIS also noted that "a build-up of forces would require several months of preparation and will be difficult to conceal."
Ahrenkiel also stressed that although "Russia's increased willingness to take risks has consequences for the security situation in Denmark," notably through hybrid attacks, this does not mean that Russia is going to attack the Scandinavian country.
"We do not expect a conventional Russian military attack against Denmark," he stressed.
European countries have been on high alert for any Russian interference, with fears that Moscow could target Kyiv's Western backers as the Kremlin's invasion of Ukraine drags on into its fifth year.
Earlier this month, Danish intelligence agency PET sais that Russia was “actively” preparing sabotage operations against the country.
"The Russian intelligence services are actively preparing acts of sabotage targeting the defence industry in Denmark," Danish Security and Intelligence Service (PET) said in a statement to AFP.
They are recruiting "ordinary Danes" on social media to take photos that can be used in planning acts of sabotage, it said.
Warning from the UK
Meanwhile, in June, former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer said Russia could attack a NATO country within four years according to western intelligence assessments.
"It is our intelligence assessment and the assessment of other countries in NATO that there could be an attack by Russia on NATO as soon as 2030," Starmer said.
"So you can see the urgency and the priority that we're putting behind this now," he added during a visit to a drone manufacturer in southwest England.
Just two months later in August, US President Donald Trump said that Vladimir Putin was "not going to attack" NATO territory, pushing back against media reports that Washington was concerned about a possible Russian move on Europe.
Trump's comments came just days after the CIA Director John Ratcliffe flew to Moscow for surprise talks that the Wall Street Journal and CBS News said was an attempt to dissuade Russia from attacking NATO members, amid US intelligence assessments that Moscow could seek to test the alliance.
"I've had good talks with him. He's not going to be attacking a NATO territory," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office when asked if the Russian president had agreed not to do so.

Geopolitics, Bulgarians abroad in focus as presidential campaign begins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
10:52:01 UTC
19:52:01 KST

News
Geopolitics, Bulgarians abroad in focus as presidential campaign begins
Thursday 24 September 2026 13:14
Thursday, 24 September 2026, 13:14
PHOTO president.bg
Font size
Bulgaria’s presidential election campaign is just hours away from officially getting under way, with the vote exactly one month away, on October 25.
Although this is a regular presidential election, it follows an event without precedent in Bulgaria’s political history. At the beginning of the year, the country’s fifth president, Rumen Radev, announced in an address to the nation that he was stepping down a year before the end of his term. At the early parliamentary election on April 19, Progressive Bulgaria, the coalition whose political architect is Radev, won an outright majority. This allowed him to form a single-party government and become the first Bulgarian president to go on to serve as prime minister.
Under the Constitution, the vice president can complete the president’s term if the head of state is removed from office, resigns or dies while in office. Radev’s resignation therefore brought Iliana Iotova to the presidency, making her the first woman to serve as President of the Republic of Bulgaria.
Rumen Radev and Iliana Iotova
PHOTO BGNES
She is now among the candidates seeking a full term at Dondukov 2, with journalist and Bulgarian News Agency Director General Kiril Valchev as her candidate for vice president.
Another 26 presidential and vice-presidential pairs are in the race, with six women standing for president. For the first time since it was founded in 2009, GERB has not nominated a presidential ticket. The Movement for Rights and Freedoms, led by Delyan Peevski, registered for the election with the Central Election Commission but did not nominate a candidate. Vazrazhdane is the only party represented in parliament to put forward its own leader for president.
Parvan Simeonov of the Myara polling agency told Radio Bulgaria that several different kinds of campaign were likely – some more institutional, others sharper or more radical, with another potentially fierce campaign coming from the sidelines. Voter turnout, he said, would also be worth watching.
Parvan Simeonov
PHOTO BTA
Presidential elections in Bulgaria traditionally go to a second round rather than producing a winner in the first. Simeonov says voters tend to see the runoff as something of a “football final”, usually pitting the two strongest political currents of the moment against each other.
The issues each candidate chooses to emphasise will therefore matter:
“We will certainly hear a great deal about geopolitical issues and about quality of life. Another very important theme will be what the different campaign teams have already prepared. As we have seen, they have cards up their sleeves for a negative campaign as well,” Simeonov says.
He was referring to remarks by MP Assen Vassilev, who recently said that while serving as vice president, Iliana Iotova had pardoned 28 people, five of whom had been convicted of drug-related offences or drug trafficking. One of them, Ognyan Atanasov, was pardoned in 2022 and caught with drugs again in 2025. The case prompted MPs from We Continue the Change and Democratic Bulgaria to call on the current president to withdraw from the race.
PHOTO Alamy / Reuters
One geopolitical issue that will be impossible to avoid is the war in Ukraine, where Simeonov expects two competing narratives:
“In one case, we will probably hear criticism framed around ‘West versus East’. In the other, the emphasis will be on the need for peace and following the national interest. Both narratives have their audiences, and we will probably see their strength measured at the polls. I would not rush to make predictions, especially as there is no data yet. In political analysis, we are entitled to make assumptions. Mine is that the two camps are not particularly evenly matched in terms of support, and that will probably become apparent in the first round.”
The political instability of recent years has repeatedly given Bulgarians a chance to see how candidates seek their trust and how they choose to communicate with voters. Many have preferred live broadcasts on social media to direct meetings with people around the country. Will this campaign bring more of the same?
“We will see. What I can say is that some candidates are strong on social media, while others are stronger in the more traditional, institutional approach of meeting people on different occasions around the country. Both approaches have their potential advantages and we will probably see both, but I have no prediction as to which will work better.”
PHOTO Archive
Simeonov is also convinced that Bulgarians living abroad will feature prominently during the month-long campaign. Relations with Bulgarian communities around the world have traditionally been among the vice president’s areas of responsibility.
“One of the specific features of this campaign is that one of the tickets has a very substantial record of work on this issue over the years. That is because it includes a recent vice president and a person whose work has been aimed at building networks among Bulgarians abroad. So we will probably hear a great deal about it. On the other side are people whose electorate includes voters abroad and who will be directing their message towards them, since more liberal communities have a substantial number of supporters outside Bulgaria. Bulgarians abroad will also be an issue for some of the more radical candidates with a more nationalist profile.”
Simeonov noted that the presidential institution has relatively limited powers and responsibilities. Its role is more closely connected with Bulgaria’s position internationally and its relationship with Bulgarian communities abroad. This suggests, he said, that Bulgarians overseas will feature in the campaign less in terms of policies governing their ties with Bulgaria and more in terms of questions of identity.
The campaign to elect Bulgaria’s seventh president officially begins at midnight on September 25 and ends 24 hours before voting starts on October 25, 2026.
Editor: Elena Karkalanova

Health mediators – bridging the gap between people in need and institutions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
10:51:45 UTC
19:51:45 KST

Article
Health mediators – bridging the gap between people in need and institutions
Thursday 24 September 2026 13:21
Thursday, 24 September 2026, 13:21
PHOTO Facebook/ Ivailo Tournev
Font size
In areas where poverty persists and information regarding health fails to reach the population, there live people whose survival depends on qualities embodied in the word "humanness." Thus, the profession of the health mediator emerged in 2001 to connect people in need with the institutions in Bulgaria capable of caring for them.
Prof. Ivailo Tournev began working with the Roma community over 30 years ago. The head of the Neurology Clinic at Alexandrovska Hospital in Sofia spent months travelling through these neighbourhoods and today he says there is hardly a place he has not visited at least once.
Prof. Ivailo Tournev
PHOTO Alexandrovska Hospital
"I encountered poverty, lack of access to healthcare, and severe social issues that I initially tried to address by acting as a mediator between health and social institutions and the affected families," Ivailo Tournev told the BNR. "The scale of the need turned out to be immense and at one point I realized it was an overwhelming task for one person. Yet, I was firmly resolved to try to help the people from these communities. I then looked into the European experience and discovered that similar mediation programs had existed in Western Europe for over 40 years, targeting not just the Roma community but all kinds of vulnerable ethnic minorities. Together with Dr. Pim de Graaf from the Dutch Ministry of Health, we began developing a Bulgarian model for health mediation. We visited several neighbourhoods to demonstrate how this model works."
PHOTO Facebook/ Ivailo Tournev
The first neighbourhood where five mediators began working is "Iztok" in Kyustendil. They familiarized themselves with the health and social issues of each family in order to identify their needs and provide assistance. Today, there are 370 health mediators across more than 160 municipalities. Their primary task is to facilitate access to health and social services for disadvantaged groups, improve relationships between doctors and patients from vulnerable communities, and raise health awareness among ethnic minorities. "One of the requirements for them is to be members of the community - to live locally, understand the issues, and speak the same language," the professor says.
PHOTO Facebook/ Ivailo Tournev
Health mediators undergo specialized training conducted jointly by the Faculty of Public Health at the Medical University of Sofia and the National Network of Health Mediators Association, and receive a certificate upon completion.
PHOTO National Network of Health Mediators
"The initiative expanded to include the training of medical professionals - not only nurses but also doctors, dentists, and pharmacists," Ivailo Tournev adds. "Our team has trained over 50 Roma who have either become doctors or are currently medical students. Our goal is to bring together health mediators, Roma doctors, and nurses into teams that will work in Roma neighbourhoods."
PHOTO Facebook/ Ivailo Tournev
"When
we were starting the program, I thought it would be temporary and
that the deficit would be overcome in about 20 years and the program
would become unnecessary," Ivailo Tournev adds. "Unfortunately,
I believe it is even more relevant now, as the situation in many Roma
neighbourhoods is appalling and many children live in great poverty
that precludes access to adequate health and social care. The
mediators are truly working miracles; to a large extent, they are
like missionaries - working for minimum wage, they are sought out by
various institutions around the clock, and it is difficult to sustain
such a pace of life."
Although he inspires awe, Prof. Tournev wins the trust of the
people he works with because he encourages them to move forward with
a fatherly approach. "I love them, but at the same time I am
very strict with them", he admits and defines as his main
mission to preserve the motivation and high spirit reigning in a
profession "significant and infinitely useful" for society.
Text: Diana Tsankova (based on an interview by Mihailina Pavlova and Valeri Lekov from the "Hristo Botev" program of BNR)

The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) expects Bulgaria’s economy to grow by 2.7% in 2026 and 2.5% in 2027, leaving its forecasts unchanged from June. Real GDP grew by 2.8% year on year in the first half of 2026, after growth of 3.4% in 2024 and 3.1% in 2025.
In its September Regional Economic Prospects report, the EBRD said Bulgaria’s economy remained resilient in the first half of 2026, helped by strong domestic demand, investment and improving exports, despite higher inflation and weaker public finances.

Indian oil and gas heir made professor of sustainability at Newcastle University
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
10:26:44 UTC
19:26:44 KST

Newcastle University is facing a backlash from conservationists over the appointment of the heir to an Indian oil and gas fortune who runs a controversial mega-zoo as a professor of sustainability.
The university announced that Anant Ambani had been given a professorship of practice for “his work in conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship” and “significant contributions to advancing a more sustainable future”.
Ambani is the son of India’s richest person, Mukesh Ambani, who made his fortune primarily in oil and gas, owns the world’s largest oil refinery and has close ties with the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Mukesh Ambani has enthusiastically praised BJP policies, and firms linked to his Reliance conglomerate have recently made significant donations to the party. The prime minister, Narendra Modi, attended Anant Ambani’s lavish 2024 wedding in Mumbai.
Anant Amabani, 31, who is leads on renewable energy on the Reliance Group’s executive board and is worth an estimated £90bn, has set up Vantara, a 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo near the family’s oil refining facilities in Gujarat, which reportedly has more than 150,000 animals including 200 lions, 250 leopards and 900 crocodiles, and where he hosted his opulent pre-wedding celebrations attended by celebrity guests and politicians.
Conservation groups have previously raised questions about how some of the animals were sourced, given many were endangered species. Vantara has never been found guilty of any wrongdoing.
The university’s announcement was met with incredulity and derision from academic staff and Indian and international conservationists and environmentalists.
Ramachandra Guha, a leading Indian public intellectual and the author of the book Speaking With Nature: The Origins of Indian Environmentalism, said: “I must say that it is a rather mystifying choice. As a scholar of Indian and global environmentalism, I can name at least 50 – perhaps 100 – individuals who are far better qualified to be thus honoured. They include soil scientists, energy scientists, water conservation experts, community forest workers, ecologists, pollution abatement experts etc who have made real and tangible contributions to a more sustainable future for India and Indians.
“I wonder on whose advice Newcastle University has acted, and whether it did due diligence on what has and has not been done in these fields. Its appointment of Mr Ambani is puzzling in the extreme, and is likely to adversely affect the university’s institutional credibility and intellectual standing.”
Bhuvan Mangalore, an Indian investigator into illegal wildlife trade who is completing a dissertation on Vantara at Anglia Ruskin University, asked: “Is this a joke?”
Prof Matt Perry, the chair of the University and College Union branch at Newcastle University, said staff members had objected to the appointment citing environmental concerns.
Prof Lyla Mehta, the head of the climate, environment and sustainability department at the University of Sussex’s Institute of Development Studies, shared concerns that “as public funding for universities falls, there is a real danger that billionaire and corporate money begins to shape academia”.
She said: “Universities are supposed to be places that question power and hold corporations to account, not give them academic legitimacy.”
In April, Anant Ambani launched Vantara University, billed as the world’s first global university dedicated to wildlife conservation and veterinary science.
Lorne Stockman, a research co-director at Oil Change International, said: “At a time when the climate crisis demands an urgent phaseout of oil and gas, we must demand our publicly funded institutions do better.”
In 2025, an investigation by the German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung found that many animals delivered to Vantara arrived through countries with opaque wildlife trading networks such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the United Arab Emirates, raising concerns that endangered species may have been illegally trafficked.
In August last year, an investigation by India’s supreme court, which lasted less than three weeks, cleared the zoo’s operators of any wrongdoing. A subsequent fact-finding mission into the zoo by Cites, the UN body that regulates the trade of endangered species, found that some of the permits used to bring animals to Vantara were probably forged.
Its report said: “There is a need for caution to ensure that imports of large numbers of animals by these facilities are not inadvertently creating a demand for illegally sourced animals.”
Cites recommended restrictions on India’s imports of endangered wild animals. However, it subsequently reversed its decision after objections from India, the US and Japan at a Cites meeting after they argued there was not enough proof of illegal imports.
In August, the zoo launched a “reset” in its operations by appointing a former Cites head to oversee its operations and said it would voluntarily pause all wildlife imports until June next year.
Vantara has declined to comment. The Ambani family and Vantara have previously denied the allegations of wildlife trafficking. They have said: “Our mission and focus continues to be the rescue, rehabilitation and care of animals.”
A Newcastle University spokesperson said: “The award of a professorship of practice recognises Mr Ambani’s contributions to conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship through his work with Vantara, a wildlife rescue and conservation initiative, and as the executive lead for the Reliance Group’s transition toward a green energy future.”

US returns 36 ancient antiquities to Syria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
10:38:32 UTC
19:38:32 KST

Thirty-six antiquities worth more than $5 million have been returned to Syria in what the Manhattan District Attorney’s Office described as a historic repatriation of cultural heritage.
Manhattan District Attorney Alvin L. Bragg Jr. announced the return at a ceremony on Wednesday, saying the artefacts had been recovered through a complex, international investigation involving law enforcement, museums and officials across multiple countries.
“Repatriation ceremonies are a powerful reminder that preserving cultural heritage transcends any border or nationality,” Bragg said, thanking the partners involved in the investigation.
Mohamad Naser Kanatri, chargé d’affaires of the Syrian Arab Republic’s embassy in Washington, called the return a demonstration of Syrian-American cooperation and a shared commitment to protecting cultural heritage.
Ancient treasures recovered from trafficking investigations
Among the objects returned are a monumental stone relief from the ancient Syrian city of Palmyra and 14 mosaics from a Roman-era villa in Syria.
The Manhattan DA’s Antiquities Trafficking Unit said the artefacts were among 31 Middle Eastern and North African antiquities allegedly trafficked into New York by Lebanese antiquities dealer Georges Lotfi.
The Palmyran relief, weighing more than 1,000 pounds, dates to the late second century CE. The limestone funerary sculpture depicts a reclining man surrounded by a woman and three children and was originally part of a Palmyrene tomb.
Investigators said the relief was removed from Palmyra and smuggled to Dubai before the ancient city suffered extensive destruction by Daesh terror group between 2015 and 2017.
Another highlight is the Telete and Eros Mosaic, a monumental third-century B.C.E. floor mosaic depicting the mythological wedding of Telete and Eros alongside Aphrodite and the Three Graces.
Artefacts linked to major New York investigations
Thirteen of the returned antiquities were seized from the Metropolitan Museum of Art. The Manhattan DA’s Office said it has seized 402 antiquities valued at $98.7 million from the museum since 2017.
Four other objects came from the collection of billionaire investor and ancient-art collector Michael Steinhardt. The office previously seized 180 antiquities valued at $70 million from Steinhardt following a multiyear international investigation.
Steinhardt entered a 2021 deferred prosecution agreement that included a lifetime ban on acquiring additional antiquities.
The latest repatriation also includes three Syro-Hittite female idols dating to the second millennium CE and originating in northwest Syria.
According to the DA’s Office, the idols appeared on the art market in New York in the late 1980s and early 1990s and were later acquired by Steinhardt.

Eesti Energia CEO: Data centers benefit the power system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
10:41:00 UTC
19:41:00 KST

Eesti Energia CEO: Data centers benefit the power system
Eesti Energia CEO Andrus Durejko told ERR that data centers help balance the energy system. In his assessment, Estonia will not introduce nuclear energy before 2040.
Durejko noted that the energy consumption of Google and Microsoft data centers planned in Finland is almost as high as Estonia's total peak demand.
"The 200-megawatt Microsoft data center will feed waste heat from its processors into Espoo's district heating network. An additional €200 million investment has been made to put that heat to use. Solutions like these can generate economic benefits while also benefiting society. This is definitely a direction we should follow and, where possible, emulate," Durejko said.
"On the positive side, we are also seeing the first signs of data centers in Estonia, which I am pleased about. I wish Estonian investors strength and perseverance — this needs to be done," he added.
According to Durejko, Estonia has enough electricity to serve the planned data centers. He noted that the Greenergy data center will add 20 megawatts of demand, making it Estonia's second-largest electricity consumer after Estonian Cell.
"When that 20 megawatts of demand comes online in December, there will be greater demand on the market in winter and one more energy consumer. This development will help us address the summer energy surplus, but it will make things more difficult in winter, meaning the energy deficit will deepen. Overall, however, it is beneficial for the energy system because the price signal enables new investments," he said.
"The winter problem will inevitably remain and we also have oil shale-fired power plants to deal with it. When prices are high, they can cover that peak in demand," Durejko added.
Eesti Energia expects electricity consumption in Estonia to increase over the next 10 to 15 years.
"The fact is that electricity use is growing and replacing all other forms of energy. The question, of course, is how that electricity is generated," Durejko said.
"At the same time, parallel processes are underway: Better and more efficient equipment is being introduced, but all in all, electricity consumption in society is still growing. This has left its mark on our strategy. Since we all want a clean environment, increasing the share of clean electricity is certainly a priority," he said.
According to Durejko, in the long term, nuclear power is one of the few viable options for Estonia.
"Technological solutions that reduce the negative aspects of nuclear energy will certainly improve, but we do not see nuclear energy being introduced in Estonia before 2040. The alternatives available today, however, are relatively inadequate," he said.
